parts.label: a
parts.text:
An electron micrograph of a cell from the pancreas shows four structures, described below.
P: a stack of flattened, curved membrane-bound sacs with small vesicles budding from the edges
Q: an organelle with a double membrane; the inner membrane is folded into shelves
R: a network of flattened membrane-bound sacs with many small dark granules attached to the outer surface
S: a large structure bounded by two membranes with gaps (pores) in them
Name structures P, Q, R and S.
parts.answer: P Golgi body (Golgi apparatus); Q mitochondrion; R rough endoplasmic reticulum; S nucleus (nuclear envelope)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept Golgi complex for P. Do not accept 'ER' alone for R.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two functions of structure P.
parts.answer: Any two: modifies proteins (e.g. adds carbohydrate to make glycoproteins); packages proteins into (secretory) vesicles; makes lysosomes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: modifies/processes proteins (or lipids); adds carbohydrate / forms glycoproteins; packages/sorts into vesicles for secretion (exocytosis); forms lysosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in both plant and animal cells but is never found in prokaryotic cells?
A 70S ribosome
B Golgi body
C cell wall
D circular DNA
parts.answer: B Golgi body
parts.working: The Golgi body is a membrane-bound organelle, found only in eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes, circular DNA and a cell wall (peptidoglycan), so A, C and D are found in prokaryotes; a cell wall is also absent from animal cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A palisade mesophyll cell from a mango leaf is compared with a liver cell (hepatocyte). Name three structures found in the palisade mesophyll cell that are not found in the liver cell.
parts.answer: Cell wall; chloroplasts; large permanent vacuole (with tonoplast) — also accept plasmodesmata
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: cellulose cell wall; chloroplast; large (permanent) vacuole / tonoplast; plasmodesmata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one structure found in the liver cell that is not found in the palisade mesophyll cell.
parts.answer: Centrioles (centrosome)
parts.working: Centriole(s). Also accept microvilli. Do not accept lysosome or mitochondrion (both types of cell have these).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Liver cells contain a large amount of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER). State two functions of SER.
parts.answer: Synthesis of lipids (including steroids/phospholipids); detoxification of drugs/toxins (e.g. alcohol)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lipid synthesis; steroid synthesis; detoxification; storage of calcium ions (in muscle).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organelle in which most ATP is produced in a cell respiring aerobically.
parts.answer: Mitochondrion
parts.working: Mitochondrion / mitochondria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion as seen in an electron micrograph.
parts.answer: Surrounded by an envelope of two membranes; the inner membrane is folded into cristae; the inside is a fluid matrix; the matrix contains 70S ribosomes and circular DNA
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: double membrane / envelope; inner membrane folded into cristae; matrix; 70S (small) ribosomes in matrix; circular DNA (loop) in matrix; intermembrane space.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The middle section of a human sperm cell is packed with mitochondria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The tail (flagellum) needs a lot of ATP for movement; mitochondria release energy/produce ATP by aerobic respiration close to where it is used
parts.working: 1 mark: (aerobic) respiration produces large amounts of ATP. 1 mark: ATP needed for beating of the tail / swimming to the egg.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of the nucleolus?
A makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits
B makes proteins that are secreted from the cell
C controls the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus
D stores the chromosomes during interphase
parts.answer: A makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits
parts.working: The nucleolus is where rRNA is transcribed and combined with proteins to form ribosome subunits. Secreted proteins are made on the rough ER (B); the nuclear envelope and its pores control movement in and out (C).

stem:
Researchers in a laboratory in Karachi supplied pancreatic cells with radioactive amino acids for a short time and then followed where the radioactivity was found. The time after supply at which radioactivity was highest in each place is shown.
rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): 3 min
Golgi body: 20 min
secretory vesicles: 40 min
outside the cell: 90 min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the order in which the radioactivity peaks in the structures listed above.
parts.answer: Amino acids are joined into protein on ribosomes of the RER first; the protein is moved in vesicles to the Golgi body where it is modified and packaged; secretory vesicles carry it to the cell surface membrane; it is then released from the cell
parts.working: 1 mark each: (1) protein synthesised by ribosomes on RER (first peak at 3 min); (2) transported in (transport) vesicles to Golgi body; (3) modified/packaged in Golgi, e.g. glycosylated, (peak 20 min); (4) secretory vesicles (40 min) move to and fuse with cell surface membrane, so protein appears outside (90 min).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which the protein leaves the cell.
parts.answer: Exocytosis
parts.working: Exocytosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Vesicles move through the cytoplasm towards the cell surface membrane. Explain the role of microtubules in this movement.
parts.answer: Microtubules form tracks along which vesicles are carried; motor proteins (using ATP) move the vesicles along the microtubules
parts.working: 1 mark: microtubules act as tracks/part of the cytoskeleton. 1 mark: vesicles moved along them by motor proteins / using ATP.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cells lining the bronchi of people living in a city with heavy winter smog have both cilia and microvilli. Describe two differences between cilia and microvilli in structure and function.
parts.answer: Cilia contain microtubules (9 + 2 arrangement) and are longer; microvilli are small finger-like folds of the cell surface membrane with no microtubules. Cilia beat to move mucus; microvilli increase the surface area for absorption
parts.working: Max 3: cilia contain microtubules, microvilli do not; cilia are larger/longer; cilia move/beat (to waft mucus), microvilli do not move; microvilli increase surface area (for absorption/exchange); both covered by cell surface membrane (no credit alone).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Particles in smog can stop the cilia in the bronchi from beating. Suggest and explain one effect this has on the person.
parts.answer: Mucus (with trapped dust and bacteria) is no longer moved up and out of the airways; it builds up in the bronchi, so the risk of infection increases / the person coughs to remove it
parts.working: 1 mark: mucus not moved towards the throat / accumulates in airways. 1 mark: trapped bacteria/particles remain, so more infections (e.g. bronchitis) / coughing / narrowed airways.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a lysosome.
parts.answer: A small vesicle surrounded by a single membrane, containing hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes
parts.working: Membrane-bound sac/vesicle containing hydrolytic enzymes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A neutrophil engulfs a bacterium. Explain how lysosomes are involved in destroying the bacterium.
parts.answer: The bacterium is enclosed in a phagocytic vacuole; lysosomes fuse with the vacuole; hydrolytic enzymes are released into it and digest (hydrolyse) the bacterium
parts.working: 1 mark each: bacterium in phagocytic vacuole/phagosome; lysosome fuses with vacuole; enzymes (e.g. proteases, lysozyme) hydrolyse/digest the bacterium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lysosomal enzymes work best at about pH 5, but the cytoplasm is at about pH 7.2. Suggest how this protects the cell if a lysosome bursts.
parts.answer: At pH 7.2 the enzymes have much lower activity (are partly denatured / active site shape is changed), so they do little damage to the cell's own molecules
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes are less active at cytoplasm pH. 1 mark: so cell components are not digested / cell protected from self-digestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which organelles are surrounded by a double membrane?
1 nucleus
2 mitochondrion
3 Golgi body
4 chloroplast
A 1, 2 and 4
B 2 and 4 only
C 1, 2 and 3
D 2, 3 and 4
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: The nuclear envelope, mitochondrial envelope and chloroplast envelope each have two membranes. The Golgi body is made of single-membrane sacs, so any option containing 3 is wrong. B forgets that the nuclear envelope is a double membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure and function of plasmodesmata.
parts.answer: Narrow channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, lined with cell surface membrane and containing cytoplasm; allow movement of substances (water, ions, sugars) / communication between cells
parts.working: 1 mark structure: pores/channels through cell walls connecting cytoplasm of neighbouring cells. 1 mark function: transport of substances/communication between cells (symplast pathway).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the large permanent vacuole helps to support a non-woody plant such as a spinach seedling.
parts.answer: The vacuole (cell sap) has a low water potential so water enters by osmosis; the vacuole swells and pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall, making the cell turgid
parts.working: 1 mark: water enters vacuole by osmosis (across tonoplast). 1 mark: cell becomes turgid, pressing on the cell wall, so tissues are firm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Root hair cells do not contain chloroplasts. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They are underground / receive no light, so cannot photosynthesise
parts.working: Roots are in the dark so photosynthesis is not possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fish living in the sea lose water to the sea water and gain salts. 'Chloride cells' in their gills pump chloride ions out of the blood into the sea water, against a concentration gradient. Electron micrographs show that these cells contain very many mitochondria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Pumping ions against a concentration gradient is active transport, which needs ATP; mitochondria supply ATP by aerobic respiration
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport (against gradient). 1 mark: requires ATP from (aerobic) respiration in mitochondria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cell surface membrane of a chloride cell is highly folded. Suggest the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Increases the surface area of membrane; more carrier proteins/pumps can be present so more ions transported per unit time
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area. 1 mark: more transport (carrier) proteins / faster rate of ion transport.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of a respiratory poison such as cyanide on the movement of chloride ions by these cells.
parts.answer: Movement of chloride ions out would (almost) stop, because no/little ATP is made, so the pumps cannot work
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport stops/decreases. 1 mark: aerobic respiration inhibited so ATP not produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plasma cells develop from B-lymphocytes and secrete large quantities of antibody. Explain why plasma cells have an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum.
parts.answer: Antibodies are proteins; RER has ribosomes that synthesise proteins (and transports them / folds them) for secretion
parts.working: 1 mark: antibodies are proteins (glycoproteins). 1 mark: ribosomes on RER synthesise proteins; RER transports/folds them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plasma cells also have a large Golgi body.
parts.answer: The Golgi body modifies the antibody (adds carbohydrate to form glycoprotein) and packages it into secretory vesicles for exocytosis
parts.working: 1 mark: modification/glycosylation. 1 mark: packaging into (secretory) vesicles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In one study, RER made up 5 % of the cytoplasm volume in a resting B-lymphocyte and 35 % in a plasma cell. Calculate how many times greater the proportion of RER is in the plasma cell.
parts.answer: 7 times

parts.label: a
parts.text: Leydig cells in the testis secrete the steroid hormone testosterone. Beta cells in the pancreas secrete the protein hormone insulin. Suggest and explain which organelle is likely to be more abundant in each cell type.
parts.answer: Leydig cells: much smooth ER, because steroids are lipids made by SER. Beta cells: much rough ER (and Golgi), because insulin is a protein made by ribosomes on RER
parts.working: 1 mark: Leydig – SER. 1 mark: Beta – RER (and Golgi). 1 mark: correct reason linking SER to lipid/steroid synthesis and RER to protein synthesis (both needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both cell types contain many secretory vesicles. Testosterone, however, can pass straight through membranes. Suggest why testosterone does not need to be released by exocytosis.
parts.answer: Steroids are lipid-soluble/non-polar, so they can diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer of the cell surface membrane
parts.working: 1 mark: lipid-soluble/non-polar. 1 mark: diffuses through phospholipid bilayer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Colchicine is a drug that stops tubulin molecules joining together to form microtubules. Predict and explain the effect of colchicine on a dividing cell in a root tip.
parts.answer: Spindle cannot form (spindle fibres are microtubules), so chromosomes / chromatids cannot be separated and mitosis stops (at metaphase)
parts.working: 1 mark: no spindle formed. 1 mark: chromatids not pulled apart / mitosis cannot be completed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the effect of colchicine on a pancreatic cell that is secreting enzymes.
parts.answer: Secretion reduced, because vesicles from the Golgi are moved along microtubules to the cell surface membrane; without microtubules they are not transported
parts.working: 1 mark: less exocytosis/secretion. 1 mark: vesicle transport depends on microtubules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Centrioles are made of microtubules. State where centrioles are found in an animal cell.
parts.answer: In the centrosome, near the nucleus
parts.working: Near the nucleus / in the centrosome (a pair at right angles).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chloroplasts contain two structures that are also found in prokaryotic cells. Name these two structures.
parts.answer: 70S ribosomes; circular DNA
parts.working: 1 mark each: 70S/small ribosomes; circular DNA (loop of DNA).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the stacks of membranes inside a chloroplast and state their function.
parts.answer: Grana (stacks of thylakoids); site of the light-dependent stage / contain chlorophyll that absorbs light
parts.working: Grana/thylakoids AND absorb light / light-dependent reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the fluid surrounding these stacks.
parts.answer: Stroma
parts.working: Stroma.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron micrograph shows a mitochondrion with an image length of 24 mm. The magnification is ×12 000. Calculate the actual length of the mitochondrion in µm.
parts.answer: 2 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A transmission electron microscope can show ribosomes but a light microscope cannot. What is the reason?
A Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so resolution is higher.
B Electron microscopes have higher magnification, so small objects appear larger.
C Ribosomes are stained only by heavy metals.
D Light passes straight through ribosomes.
parts.answer: A Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so resolution is higher.
parts.working: Resolution depends on wavelength: the shorter wavelength of electrons lets two points closer together than about 200 nm be distinguished. Magnifying more (B) without better resolution only gives a larger, blurred image.

stem: A student in Faisalabad looks at a leaf epidermis with a light microscope fitted with an eyepiece graticule. Using the ×40 objective lens, 40 eyepiece graticule units line up exactly with 25 divisions of a stage micrometer. Each stage micrometer division is 0.01 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule unit in µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The lengths of five guard cells measured in eyepiece units were 11, 12, 10, 13 and 12. Calculate the mean actual length of the guard cells in µm.
parts.working: M1: mean = 58 ÷ 5 = 11.6 eyepiece units. A1: 11.6 × 6.25 = 72.5 µm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be calibrated again if the student changes to the ×10 objective lens.
parts.answer: The eyepiece graticule stays the same size in the eyepiece, but the specimen's image size changes with magnification, so each eyepiece unit represents a different actual length
parts.working: 1 mark: graticule scale does not change when objective changes. 1 mark: magnification of specimen changes so value of each unit changes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A micrograph of a leaf cell has a scale bar labelled 5 µm. The scale bar is 18 mm long on the micrograph. A chloroplast in the same micrograph is 27 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the chloroplast in µm.
parts.answer: 7.5 µm
parts.working: M1: 27 mm = 27 000 µm. A1: 27 000 ÷ 3600 = 7.5 µm (allow ecf from a).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A nucleus has a diameter of 8 µm. A student draws it at a magnification of ×2500. What is the diameter of the drawing?
A 2.0 × 10¹ mm
B 2.0 × 10⁰ mm
C 3.2 × 10⁻³ mm
D 2.0 × 10² mm
parts.answer: A 2.0 × 10¹ mm
parts.working: 8 µm × 2500 = 20 000 µm = 20 mm = 2.0 × 10¹ mm. B comes from dividing by 10 000 instead of 1000 when converting µm to mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ribosome has a diameter of 25 nm. Calculate the diameter of its image in mm if it is viewed at a magnification of ×1500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The resolution of a light microscope is about 200 nm. Explain why ribosomes cannot be seen as separate structures with a light microscope, even though their image could be made larger by greater magnification.
parts.answer: Ribosomes (25 nm) are much smaller than the resolution limit, and are closer together than 200 nm; the wavelength of light is too long, so they cannot be distinguished as separate points – increasing magnification only enlarges a blurred image
parts.working: 1 mark: ribosomes smaller than/closer together than 200 nm limit (wavelength of light too long). 1 mark: magnifying beyond the resolution limit gives no more detail / image is blurred.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using a light microscope rather than an electron microscope to study malaria parasites inside red blood cells.
parts.answer: Living cells can be observed (e.g. to watch movement); or colour can be seen with stains; or cheaper/portable for field clinics
parts.working: Any one: living specimens can be viewed; natural/stained colour seen; quicker/simpler preparation; cheaper/portable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On an electron micrograph a bacterium that is 2 µm long has an image length of 50 mm. Calculate the magnification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bacteriophage virus attached to the same bacterium has an image length of 2.5 mm. Calculate the actual length of the virus in nm.
parts.answer: 100 nm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature that would be visible in a transmission electron micrograph of the bacterium but would not be seen in a scanning electron micrograph.
parts.answer: Internal structures, e.g. ribosomes / DNA (nucleoid) / cell wall in section
parts.working: SEM shows only the surface; TEM shows internal detail, e.g. ribosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between magnification and resolution.
parts.answer: Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the actual object; resolution is the ability to distinguish two points close together as separate (the smallest distance between two points that can be seen as separate)
parts.working: 1 mark each correct definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. In a textbook drawing its diameter is 30 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vibrio cholerae is the bacterium that causes cholera. State four ways in which the structure of Vibrio cholerae differs from the structure of a cell lining the inside of the human cheek.
parts.answer: Vibrio: no nucleus (DNA free in cytoplasm); circular DNA (not linear chromosomes with histones); 70S ribosomes (not 80S); peptidoglycan cell wall (cheek cell has no wall); no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria/ER/Golgi; may have plasmids and a flagellum; much smaller
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four comparative points: no nucleus/nuclear envelope; circular DNA not linear; DNA not associated with histones; 70S v 80S ribosomes; cell wall of peptidoglycan present; no membrane-bound organelles (named); plasmids present; smaller size (1–5 µm v about 50 µm).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is present in all viruses?
A a protein capsid
B a phospholipid envelope
C ribosomes
D DNA
parts.answer: A a protein capsid
parts.working: Every virus has nucleic acid surrounded by a protein coat (capsid). Only some viruses, such as HIV and influenza, have an envelope (B); some viruses contain RNA instead of DNA (D), and no virus has ribosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why viruses are not considered to be cells.
parts.answer: They have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or cell surface membrane of their own / no metabolism; they can only reproduce inside a host cell using the host's machinery
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: no cytoplasm; no ribosomes/organelles; no cell surface membrane (envelope comes from host); cannot carry out metabolism/respire; only replicate inside host cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the structure of an enveloped virus such as influenza.
parts.answer: Nucleic acid (RNA in influenza) core; surrounded by a protein capsid; outer envelope of phospholipid (from host cell membrane) with (glyco)protein spikes / attachment proteins
parts.working: 1 mark each: nucleic acid core (RNA or DNA); capsid made of protein (capsomeres); phospholipid envelope with surface glycoproteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cells of a Streptococcus bacterium have a diameter of 0.8 µm. Calculate how many of these cells could fit side by side in a line 1 mm long.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some antibiotics bind to 70S ribosomes. Explain why these antibiotics stop bacteria growing but have little effect on the cells of the person taking them.
parts.answer: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes, so their protein synthesis is stopped; human cells make proteins in the cytoplasm on 80S ribosomes, which have a different shape and are not affected
parts.working: 1 mark: bacterial protein synthesis inhibited at 70S ribosomes. 1 mark: human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S / different shape so antibiotic does not bind.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the main polymer in the cell wall of a bacterium.
parts.answer: Peptidoglycan (murein)
parts.working: Peptidoglycan. Do not accept cellulose or chitin.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about prokaryotic cells is correct?
A The DNA is linear and enclosed by a nuclear envelope.
B The ribosomes are 70S and are free in the cytoplasm.
C The cell wall is made of cellulose.
D Aerobic respiration takes place in mitochondria.
parts.answer: B The ribosomes are 70S and are free in the cytoplasm.
parts.working: Prokaryotes have only 70S ribosomes, which are not attached to any membranes. Their DNA is circular and not enclosed (A), the wall is peptidoglycan (C) and they have no mitochondria (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Giardia is a single-celled organism that lives in the human gut and causes diarrhoea, often after drinking contaminated water. Studies of Giardia show:
• it has two nuclei, each surrounded by a nuclear envelope
• its DNA is linear and associated with proteins
• it has 80S ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum
• it has no mitochondria
• it has several flagella
A student says Giardia is a prokaryote because it is unicellular and has no mitochondria. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Giardia is a eukaryote: it has a nucleus with a nuclear envelope, linear DNA with proteins, 80S ribosomes and ER; prokaryotes never have these. Being unicellular and lacking mitochondria does not make it a prokaryote (many eukaryotes are unicellular)
parts.working: 1 mark: has nuclei/nuclear envelope (prokaryotes have none). 1 mark: 80S ribosomes / ER / linear DNA with histones are eukaryotic features. 1 mark: eukaryotes can be unicellular / absence of mitochondria is not enough to classify it as prokaryotic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A Giardia cell is about 12 µm long. A typical gut bacterium is 1.5 µm long. Calculate how many times longer the Giardia cell is.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: a
parts.text: A coronavirus particle has a diameter of 120 nm. In an electron micrograph its image diameter is 6 mm. Calculate the magnification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why viruses can be seen only with an electron microscope.
parts.answer: They are smaller than the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 200 nm); electron microscopes have much higher resolution
parts.working: Virus (120 nm) is below the 200 nm resolution of the light microscope.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Patients with a viral infection sometimes ask doctors for antibiotics. Explain why antibiotics are not effective against viruses.
parts.answer: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures/processes such as peptidoglycan cell walls or 70S ribosomes; viruses do not have these (they use the host cell's machinery)
parts.working: 1 mark: antibiotics target bacterial cell walls/70S ribosomes/bacterial enzymes. 1 mark: viruses have no cell wall/ribosomes/metabolism of their own.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three components of a DNA nucleotide.
parts.answer: Deoxyribose (a pentose sugar); a phosphate group; a nitrogenous (organic) base
parts.working: All three for 2 marks; any two for 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the bond that joins adjacent nucleotides in one strand of DNA.
parts.answer: Phosphodiester bond
parts.working: Phosphodiester. Do not accept 'hydrogen bond' or 'peptide bond'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the two purine bases found in DNA.
parts.answer: Adenine and guanine
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two differences between the structure of a DNA molecule and the structure of an mRNA molecule.
parts.answer: DNA has deoxyribose, mRNA has ribose; DNA has thymine, mRNA has uracil; DNA is double-stranded, mRNA is single-stranded; DNA is much longer
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two comparative differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sample of double-stranded DNA from a goat contains 18 % adenine. What percentage of the bases are cytosine?
A 18 %
B 32 %
C 36 %
D 64 %
parts.working: A = T = 18 %, so A + T = 36 % and G + C = 64 %. Since G = C, cytosine = 64 ÷ 2 = 32 %. D gives G + C together, not cytosine alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a molecule of ATP.
parts.answer: Adenine (base) joined to ribose (pentose sugar), with a chain of three phosphate groups attached to the ribose
parts.working: 1 mark each: adenine; ribose; three phosphate groups. (Accept 'a nucleotide with adenine, ribose and three phosphates' as 3 marks.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP is well suited to be the immediate energy source in cells.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases energy in one step / quickly; releases a small, usable amount of energy; it is small and soluble so moves easily in the cell; it is quickly regenerated from ADP + Pi
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: energy released by a single hydrolysis reaction; small manageable quantities of energy (less wasted as heat); water soluble/easily transported; rapidly resynthesised; can phosphorylate other molecules making them more reactive.

stem: Strand 1 of a short DNA molecule from a rice gene has the base composition: adenine 22 %, thymine 30 %, guanine 28 %, cytosine 20 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the percentages of each base in strand 2 (the complementary strand).
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct. Base pairing A–T and G–C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Strand 1 is used as the template for transcription. Give the percentages of each base in the mRNA.
parts.working: 1 mark: uracil replaces thymine (U 22 %). 1 mark: other three correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of guanine in the whole double-stranded molecule.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which describes the structure of ATP?
A adenine, deoxyribose and three phosphate groups
B adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
C adenosine, ribose and two phosphate groups
D adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups joined by hydrogen bonds
parts.answer: B adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
parts.working: ATP is adenine + ribose (together adenosine) + three phosphate groups, joined by covalent bonds. A has the DNA sugar; C describes ADP; D is wrong because the phosphates are linked covalently, not by hydrogen bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by saying that the two strands of DNA are antiparallel.
parts.answer: The strands run in opposite directions: one runs 5′ to 3′ and the other 3′ to 5′ (the deoxyribose sugars point in opposite directions)
parts.working: 1 mark: opposite directions. 1 mark: reference to 5′/3′ ends or orientation of the sugar–phosphate backbone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why adenine pairs with thymine but not with cytosine.
parts.answer: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine so the molecule has a constant width; adenine and thymine form two hydrogen bonds with each other, but adenine and cytosine cannot form matching hydrogen bonds
parts.working: 1 mark: purine–pyrimidine pairing (both A and C fit the width rule, so this alone is not enough). 1 mark: A and T form 2 hydrogen bonds / hydrogen-bonding positions match only for A–T (G–C forms 3).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A DNA fragment is 120 base pairs long, and 35 % of its bases are guanine or cytosine. Calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds holding the two strands together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a tRNA molecule.
parts.answer: Single polynucleotide strand of RNA folded into a clover-leaf shape, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; has an anticodon (three bases) at one end/loop; an amino acid attachment site at the 3′ end
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: single strand of RNA nucleotides; folded (clover-leaf) with some base pairing/hydrogen bonds; anticodon of three bases; amino acid binding site (3′ end, CCA).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A polynucleotide contains 250 nucleotides. State how many molecules of water are needed to hydrolyse it completely into separate nucleotides.
parts.working: One water molecule per phosphodiester bond; 250 − 1 = 249 bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between the structure of a tRNA molecule and an mRNA molecule.
parts.answer: tRNA is folded (clover-leaf) with hydrogen-bonded regions, mRNA is a straight/unfolded strand; tRNA has an anticodon and amino acid binding site, mRNA has codons; tRNA is much shorter (about 80 nucleotides); all tRNA molecules have the same length/shape
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid comparisons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a molecule of DNA is replicated by semi-conservative replication.
parts.answer: DNA helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between bases and the strands separate; both strands act as templates; free DNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G); DNA polymerase joins nucleotides by phosphodiester bonds (in the 5′ to 3′ direction); each new molecule contains one original strand and one new strand
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: helicase; breaks hydrogen bonds/unwinds; both strands are templates; free (activated) nucleotides; complementary base pairing; DNA polymerase; phosphodiester bonds formed; DNA ligase joins fragments (lagging strand); each daughter molecule has one old and one new strand.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bacteria grown for many generations with only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) were moved to a medium containing only light nitrogen (¹⁴N). DNA was extracted after two generations in ¹⁴N. Which result supports semi-conservative replication?
A all DNA hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N)
B 50 % hybrid DNA and 50 % light DNA
C 25 % hybrid DNA and 75 % light DNA
D 50 % heavy DNA and 50 % light DNA
parts.answer: B 50 % hybrid DNA and 50 % light DNA
parts.working: After one generation every molecule is hybrid. In the second generation each hybrid molecule gives one hybrid and one light molecule, so half are hybrid and half light. A is the result after one generation; D is what conservative replication would give.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the role of each of these enzymes in DNA replication: (i) DNA helicase, (ii) DNA polymerase, (iii) DNA ligase.
parts.answer: (i) unwinds DNA and breaks hydrogen bonds between bases; (ii) joins new nucleotides to form a new strand (forms phosphodiester bonds); (iii) joins short fragments (Okazaki fragments) of the lagging strand
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one new strand (the leading strand) is made continuously while the other (the lagging strand) is made in short sections.
parts.answer: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in one direction (to the 3′ end, building 5′ to 3′); the two template strands are antiparallel; so on one template the polymerase follows the replication fork, but on the other it must work away from the fork in short fragments that are later joined
parts.working: 1 mark: polymerase works only 5′ → 3′ / adds to 3′ end. 1 mark: strands are antiparallel. 1 mark: on lagging strand synthesis is away from the fork, so fragments are made and joined by ligase.

stem: A student repeats a classic experiment using E. coli grown first in ¹⁵N medium, then transferred to ¹⁴N medium. DNA is separated by density after each generation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of DNA molecules that would be hybrid (one ¹⁵N strand and one ¹⁴N strand) after three generations in ¹⁴N.
parts.working: M1: after 3 generations there are 2³ = 8 molecules from each original; only 2 contain an original ¹⁵N strand. A1: 2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 25 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the results after one generation ruled out the conservative model of replication.
parts.answer: After one generation all DNA was of intermediate (hybrid) density; conservative replication would have given one band of heavy DNA and one band of light DNA
parts.working: 1 mark: all intermediate/single hybrid band. 1 mark: conservative model predicts heavy + light bands (no hybrid).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The circular chromosome of a bacterium contains 4.6 million base pairs. Replication starts at a single origin and proceeds in both directions around the circle. Each replication fork adds 1000 nucleotides per second to each new strand. Calculate the time to replicate the whole chromosome, in minutes, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 38.3 min

parts.label: b
parts.text: A human chromosome contains about 50 times as much DNA, but replication forks in human cells move more slowly. Suggest how human cells can still replicate each chromosome within a few hours.
parts.answer: Replication starts at many origins along each chromosome at the same time, so many forks work simultaneously
parts.working: 1 mark: many origins of replication. 1 mark: replication happens simultaneously in many places/replication bubbles join.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A mutant bacterium makes a non-functional DNA ligase. What is the most likely result when it replicates its DNA?
A The lagging strand stays as many separate short fragments.
B Hydrogen bonds between the template strands are not broken.
C Free nucleotides cannot pair with the template strands.
D The leading strand is made as many short fragments.
parts.answer: A The lagging strand stays as many separate short fragments.
parts.working: DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand with phosphodiester bonds. Breaking hydrogen bonds (B) is done by helicase; the leading strand is made continuously (D), so it does not need ligase in this way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the process of transcription in a eukaryotic cell.
parts.answer: The DNA double helix unwinds and hydrogen bonds break at the gene; one strand acts as the template; free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (U with A); RNA polymerase joins the nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds; this forms a primary transcript, which is spliced (introns removed) to form mRNA
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: occurs in nucleus; DNA unwinds/H bonds broken; only template strand used; free (activated) RNA nucleotides; complementary base pairing, uracil pairs with adenine; RNA polymerase; phosphodiester bonds; primary transcript; introns removed/exons joined to form mRNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The base sequence of a triplet on the template strand of DNA is GCA. What is the anticodon on the tRNA molecule that brings the matching amino acid?
A CGT
B CGU
C GCA
D GCU
parts.answer: C GCA
parts.working: Template GCA is transcribed into the mRNA codon CGU. The tRNA anticodon is complementary to the codon: GCA. B is the codon, not the anticodon; A contains thymine, which is not found in RNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the roles of mRNA, tRNA and ribosomes in translation.
parts.answer: mRNA carries the code (sequence of codons) from the nucleus to the ribosome; tRNA carries a specific amino acid and its anticodon pairs with the complementary codon; the ribosome holds the mRNA and tRNA in place and moves along the mRNA; peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids on the ribosome
parts.working: 1 mark each: mRNA – sequence of codons / template; tRNA – brings specific amino acid; anticodon–codon complementary base pairing; ribosome – binding site for mRNA and two tRNAs / catalyses peptide bond formation / moves one codon at a time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by saying that the genetic code is degenerate.
parts.answer: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet/codon
parts.working: More than one codon for (most) amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The coding sequence of the mature mRNA for a polypeptide has 1203 nucleotides, including one stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
parts.working: M1: 1203 ÷ 3 = 401 codons. A1: 401 − 1 stop codon = 400 amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The primary transcript of this gene is much longer than 1203 nucleotides. Explain why.
parts.answer: The primary transcript contains introns (non-coding sequences); these are removed by splicing, and the exons are joined to form the mature mRNA
parts.working: 1 mark: introns present in primary transcript. 1 mark: introns removed / exons joined (splicing).

stem: The primary transcript of a gene in a cow contains 8400 nucleotides. Its introns contain 5250 nucleotides in total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the primary transcript that is made of introns.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume that the whole mature mRNA codes for the polypeptide and ends in one stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
parts.working: M1: mature mRNA = 8400 − 5250 = 3150 nucleotides; 3150 ÷ 3 = 1050 codons. A1: 1050 − 1 = 1049 amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The same gene can produce two different polypeptides in muscle cells and in liver cells. Explain how this is possible.
parts.answer: Alternative splicing: different combinations of exons are kept in the mRNA in different cell types, so the mRNAs have different base sequences and code for different amino acid sequences
parts.working: 1 mark: different exons included/removed (alternative splicing). 1 mark: different mRNA sequence → different primary structure.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Part of an mRNA molecule has this sequence of codons:
AUG GCU UUU GAU CCA UGG AAA UAA
Codons: AUG = Met (start); GCU = Ala; UUU = Phe; GAU = Asp; CCA = Pro; UGG = Trp; AAA = Lys; UAA = stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the sequence of amino acids coded for by this mRNA.
parts.answer: Met – Ala – Phe – Asp – Pro – Trp – Lys (then stop)
parts.working: 2 marks all correct in order; 1 mark if one error. Stop codon UAA adds no amino acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the base sequence of the DNA template strand for the first two codons.
parts.answer: TAC CGA
parts.working: Complementary to AUG GCU, with T instead of U: TAC CGA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A mutation changes the codon UGG to UGA, which is a stop codon. Explain the effect on the polypeptide.
parts.answer: Translation stops at this codon, so the polypeptide is shorter (only Met–Ala–Phe–Asp–Pro); it will have a different structure and probably not function
parts.working: 1 mark: translation ends early / shorter polypeptide (five amino acids). 1 mark: missing amino acids alter folding/tertiary structure, so protein likely non-functional.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Some events in making a secreted protein are listed.
1 tRNA anticodon pairs with an mRNA codon
2 RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides
3 mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore
4 a peptide bond forms between two amino acids
5 introns are removed
What is the correct order?
A 2, 5, 3, 1, 4
B 2, 3, 5, 1, 4
C 5, 2, 3, 4, 1
D 2, 5, 3, 4, 1
parts.working: Transcription (2) and splicing (5) occur in the nucleus before the mRNA leaves (3); on the ribosome, tRNA must pair with the codon (1) before a peptide bond can form (4). B splices outside the nucleus, which is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ribosome adds 15 amino acids per second to a growing polypeptide. Calculate how long it takes one ribosome to make a polypeptide of 450 amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a cell making large amounts of this protein, many ribosomes are attached to each mRNA molecule at the same time. Explain the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Many polypeptides are made from one mRNA at the same time, so a large amount of protein is made quickly without extra transcription
parts.working: 1 mark: several polypeptides translated simultaneously (polysome). 1 mark: faster/greater production of protein from one mRNA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a tRNA molecule carries the correct amino acid to the ribosome.
parts.answer: Each tRNA has a specific anticodon; a specific amino acid is attached to the tRNA (by an enzyme, using ATP) according to that anticodon, at the amino acid binding site
parts.working: 1 mark: specific amino acid attached to tRNA at binding site (3′ end), using ATP/enzyme. 1 mark: anticodon is specific to that amino acid and pairs with the codon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rifampicin, an antibiotic used to treat tuberculosis, inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase. Explain why this stops the bacteria making proteins.
parts.answer: No transcription, so no new mRNA is made; without mRNA no translation can take place
parts.working: 1 mark: transcription prevented / no mRNA. 1 mark: no template for translation at ribosomes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Death cap mushrooms contain α-amanitin, which inhibits the RNA polymerase that makes mRNA in human cells. Symptoms of liver failure often appear only two to three days after eating the mushroom. Suggest why.
parts.answer: mRNA and proteins already present in the liver cells continue to work; as these are broken down over time they are not replaced; when key enzymes/proteins run out the cells die
parts.working: 1 mark: existing mRNA still translated for a time. 1 mark: existing proteins/enzymes still function. 1 mark: they are gradually broken down and not replaced, so cell function fails later.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why rifampicin does not stop transcription in the nuclei of human cells.
parts.answer: Human nuclear RNA polymerase has a different structure/shape so rifampicin does not bind to it
parts.working: Different shape of human RNA polymerase (no binding site for rifampicin).

stem:
The coding (non-template) strand of a short gene section is:
5′ ATG GTC ACC TGA 3′
Codons: AUG = Met; GUC = Val; ACC = Thr; UGA = stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the base sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this gene section, showing the 5′ and 3′ ends.
parts.answer: 5′ AUG GUC ACC UGA 3′
parts.working: Same as coding strand with U in place of T, same direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the base sequence of the template strand, showing the 5′ and 3′ ends.
parts.answer: 3′ TAC CAG TGG ACT 5′
parts.working: Complementary to the coding strand and antiparallel (accept 5′ TCA GGT GAC CAT 3′).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the information given, state the number of amino acids coded for by this section, and name them in order.
parts.answer: 3 amino acids: Met – Val – Thr
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 (UGA is a stop codon and codes for no amino acid). 1 mark: Met, Val, Thr in order.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why only one strand of a gene is transcribed.
parts.answer: Only the template strand has the base sequence complementary to the required mRNA; transcribing the other strand would give a different (complementary) sequence of codons and the wrong amino acid sequence
parts.working: 1 mark: mRNA must be complementary to the template strand only. 1 mark: the other strand would give a different codon sequence/different polypeptide (or a non-functional one).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gene has six exons. In different tissues, exon 1 and exon 6 are always kept, but each of exons 2, 3, 4 and 5 can either be kept or removed during splicing. Calculate the maximum number of different mature mRNAs that this gene could produce.
parts.working: M1: each of 4 exons has 2 possibilities (kept or removed). A1: 2⁴ = 16.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the existence of alternative splicing means that the human genome, with only about 20 000 protein-coding genes, can produce many more different proteins.
parts.answer: One gene can give several mRNAs with different exon combinations; each codes for a polypeptide with a different primary structure, so the number of proteins exceeds the number of genes
parts.working: 1 mark: one gene → several mRNAs. 1 mark: different amino acid sequences / different proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where in a eukaryotic cell (i) transcription and (ii) translation take place.
parts.answer: (i) nucleus; (ii) ribosomes in the cytoplasm / on rough ER
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme that catalyses transcription.
parts.answer: RNA polymerase
parts.working: RNA polymerase. Not DNA polymerase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of bond formed between amino acids during translation.
parts.answer: Peptide bond
parts.working: Peptide bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term gene mutation.
parts.answer: A change in the base (nucleotide) sequence of DNA of a gene
parts.working: Change in base sequence of DNA (in a gene).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three types of gene mutation.
parts.answer: Substitution, insertion (addition), deletion
parts.working: All three for 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the deletion of a single base near the start of a gene usually has a greater effect than the substitution of a single base.
parts.answer: Deletion causes a frameshift: every codon after the deletion is changed, so many amino acids change (and a stop codon may appear early); a substitution changes only one codon, which may code for the same amino acid (degenerate code) or only one different amino acid
parts.working: 1 mark: deletion causes frameshift. 1 mark: all following triplets/amino acids altered (or premature stop). 1 mark: substitution affects only one codon / may be silent because the code is degenerate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutation in the gene for the β-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin. Which row describes this mutation?
A substitution; glutamic acid replaced by valine
B deletion; valine replaced by glutamic acid
C substitution; valine replaced by glutamic acid
D insertion; glutamic acid replaced by valine
parts.answer: A substitution; glutamic acid replaced by valine
parts.working: A single base substitution (GAG → GTG on the coding strand, GAG → GUG in the mRNA) changes one codon, so glutamic acid is replaced by valine. C has the amino acids the wrong way round; an insertion would cause a frameshift.

stem:
Part of an mRNA for an enzyme reads: AUG CUU GAA GGA …
Codons: AUG = Met; CUU = Leu; GAA = Glu; GAG = Glu; AAA = Lys; GGA = Gly; UAA = stop.
Three different mutations each change the third codon (GAA):
Mutation 1: GAA → GAG
Mutation 2: GAA → AAA
Mutation 3: GAA → UAA

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each mutation, state the change, if any, in the amino acid sequence.
parts.answer: Mutation 1: no change (GAG still codes for Glu); Mutation 2: Glu replaced by Lys; Mutation 3: translation stops – polypeptide ends after Leu (Met–Leu only)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which mutation is most likely to produce a non-functional protein.
parts.answer: Mutation 3: a stop codon is formed, so the polypeptide is very short / most amino acids are missing, so it cannot fold into the correct tertiary structure
parts.working: 1 mark: mutation 3 (nonsense/stop codon). 1 mark: truncated polypeptide, wrong tertiary structure/shape.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why mutation 2 may have little effect on the function of the protein in some cases.
parts.answer: If the amino acid is not in the active site/an important region, or Lys has similar properties, the tertiary structure may hardly change
parts.working: Change outside active site / does not change folding much.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The mRNA for a short peptide is:
AUG GCU AAA GGC UUU GAU UGG UAA
Codons: AUG = Met; GCU = Ala; AAA = Lys; GGC = Gly; UUU = Phe; GAU = Asp; UGG = Trp; UAA = stop; UUG = Leu; AUU = Ile; GGU = Gly.
A mutation in the gene deletes the first G of the fourth codon (GGC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the amino acid sequence coded for by the mutated mRNA, as far as the codons given allow.
parts.answer: Met – Ala – Lys – Ala – Leu – Ile – Gly (then incomplete codon AA…)
parts.working: Mutated sequence: AUG GCU AAA GCU UUG AUU GGU AA… 2 marks all correct; 1 mark first three correct and frame shifted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name for this kind of effect and explain why the stop codon is lost.
parts.answer: Frameshift; the reading frame moves one base, so the triplets are read differently and UAA is no longer read as a codon in frame
parts.working: 1 mark: frameshift. 1 mark: codons regrouped so original stop codon no longer in reading frame.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the deletion of three adjacent bases is often less harmful than the deletion of one base.
parts.answer: Removes one codon/one amino acid only; reading frame is kept for the rest of the gene
parts.working: One amino acid lost, no frameshift.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The most common mutation causing cystic fibrosis deletes three nucleotides from the CFTR gene, so phenylalanine at position 508 is missing. Explain why the rest of the amino acid sequence is unchanged.
parts.answer: Three bases = one whole codon is removed, so the reading frame is not shifted; all codons after the deletion are read as normal
parts.working: 1 mark: three nucleotides correspond to one codon/triplet. 1 mark: no frameshift so downstream codons unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The normal CFTR protein contains 1480 amino acids. Calculate the number of nucleotides in the coding sequence of the normal mRNA, including the stop codon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: CFTR is a channel protein in the cell surface membrane. Suggest why the loss of one amino acid can stop the protein from working.
parts.answer: Changes the primary structure, so the polypeptide folds into a different tertiary structure; misfolded protein does not form a working channel / is broken down and does not reach the cell surface membrane
parts.working: 1 mark: altered folding/tertiary (3D) shape. 1 mark: channel not formed or protein not inserted in the membrane / destroyed by the cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of an antibody molecule.
parts.answer: Four polypeptide chains: two heavy and two light; held together by disulfide bonds; variable regions at the tips form two antigen-binding sites; constant region (same in all antibodies of that class); hinge region gives flexibility
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: four polypeptides; two heavy and two light chains; disulfide bonds; variable region(s); antigen-binding sites (two); constant region; hinge region; Y-shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how antibodies cause bacteria to clump together (agglutination) and why this helps to protect the body.
parts.answer: Each antibody has two antigen-binding sites so it can bind to antigens on two different bacteria, linking many together; clumps cannot spread easily and are easier for phagocytes to engulf
parts.working: 1 mark: two binding sites link several bacteria. 1 mark: clumped bacteria easily engulfed by phagocytes / cannot spread/enter cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cells secrete antibodies?
A plasma cells
B T-helper cells
C memory T-cells
D macrophages
parts.answer: A plasma cells
parts.working: Plasma cells are differentiated B-lymphocytes that make and secrete antibodies. T-helper cells (B) release cytokines that stimulate B-lymphocytes, but do not make antibodies themselves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the comparison of B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes by stating, for each type: (i) where it matures, (ii) one way in which it helps to destroy pathogens.
parts.answer: B-lymphocytes: mature in bone marrow; become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral response). T-lymphocytes: mature in the thymus; T-helper cells release cytokines / T-killer (cytotoxic) cells destroy infected cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: B – bone marrow; B – antibodies via plasma cells; T – thymus; T – cytokines from T-helper cells or killing infected cells by T-killer cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how B-lymphocytes respond during the primary immune response to a bacterium that the body has never met before.
parts.answer: Only a B-lymphocyte with receptors (antibody) complementary to the antigen binds to it (clonal selection); stimulated by cytokines from T-helper cells; divides by mitosis to form a clone (clonal expansion); some cells differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies; others become memory cells
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: specific B-cell receptor binds antigen; clonal selection; activation by T-helper cells/cytokines; mitosis/clonal expansion; plasma cells; secrete antibodies specific to antigen; memory cells formed; response is slow (several days).

stem:
A volunteer received an injection of a harmless antigen on day 0 and the same antigen again on day 28. Antibody concentration in the blood (arbitrary units, a.u.):
day 0: 0 | day 7: 10 | day 14: 40 | day 21: 15 | day 28: 12 | day 35: 350 | day 42: 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the antibody response to the first exposure with the response to the second exposure. Use the data in your answer.
parts.answer: Second response is faster (high levels within 7 days of the second exposure v about 14 days); much larger (peak 400 v 40 a.u.); lasts longer / antibody stays high
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three, at least one with data: faster; greater; longer-lasting; quoted values (e.g. 400 v 40, peak at day 42 v day 14).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the peak antibody concentration was after the second exposure.
parts.answer: 10 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two responses.
parts.answer: Memory cells were made during the first response; on second exposure memory B-cells recognise the antigen quickly; they divide rapidly to produce many plasma cells, so more antibody is made sooner
parts.working: 1 mark each: memory cells formed in primary response; memory cells remain in blood/long-lived; rapid clonal expansion/differentiation into plasma cells on second exposure.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the roles of T-helper cells and T-killer (cytotoxic) cells in the immune response.
parts.answer: T-helper cells: bind to antigen presented by macrophages; release cytokines; stimulate B-cells to divide/become plasma cells and stimulate macrophages/T-killer cells. T-killer cells: recognise antigens on the surface of infected cells; attach and release substances (e.g. perforin/toxins) that kill the infected cell
parts.working: Max 2 for T-helper: recognise antigen-presenting cells; secrete cytokines; activate B-cells/T-killer cells/phagocytes. Max 2 for T-killer: bind infected/cancer cells with matching antigen; secrete toxins/perforin making holes; destroy infected cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: HIV infects and destroys T-helper cells. Explain why people with untreated HIV infection become ill with other infections such as tuberculosis.
parts.answer: Fewer T-helper cells so B-cells are not stimulated to make antibodies and T-killer cells are not activated; the immune system cannot respond effectively to other pathogens (opportunistic infections)
parts.working: 1 mark: less activation of B-cells/T-killer cells/phagocytes. 1 mark: weakened immune response so other pathogens not destroyed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an autoimmune disease.
parts.answer: The immune system fails to distinguish self from non-self; it makes antibodies/T-cells against the body's own antigens and attacks its own cells
parts.working: 1 mark: immune system attacks body's own cells/tissues. 1 mark: self antigens treated as non-self / lymphocytes not removed during maturation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies bind to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle cell membranes at neuromuscular junctions. Suggest how this causes muscle weakness.
parts.answer: Antibodies block receptor binding sites so acetylcholine cannot bind; receptors may also be destroyed/removed; fewer sodium ion channels open so less depolarisation of the muscle membrane; fewer action potentials so muscle contracts weakly
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: antibodies block/compete with acetylcholine; receptors destroyed/fewer receptors; less depolarisation (fewer Na⁺ channels open); threshold not reached / fewer impulses in muscle fibre; weaker contraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an antibody that binds to an antigen on the surface of the measles virus cannot bind to an antigen on the mumps virus.
parts.answer: The antigen-binding site (variable region) has a specific shape determined by its amino acid sequence; it is complementary only to the shape of the measles antigen; the mumps antigen has a different shape so it cannot fit/bind
parts.working: 1 mark each: variable region/antigen-binding site; specific amino acid sequence gives specific tertiary structure/shape; complementary to one antigen only (mumps antigen different shape). Do not credit 'active site' or 'receptor'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some antibodies neutralise bacterial toxins. Suggest how binding of an antibody to a toxin molecule prevents it harming cells.
parts.answer: The antibody covers the part of the toxin that binds to cell receptors / changes its shape, so it cannot attach to or enter body cells; antibody–toxin complexes are removed by phagocytes
parts.working: 1 mark: blocks toxin's binding site/prevents entry into cells. 1 mark: complex engulfed by phagocytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During their development, some lymphocytes are found to have receptors that bind to the body's own (self) antigens. What happens to these lymphocytes?
A They are destroyed or made inactive.
B They develop into memory cells.
C They divide to form a clone of plasma cells.
D They become T-helper cells.
parts.answer: A They are destroyed or made inactive.
parts.working: Lymphocytes that react with self antigens are removed (by programmed cell death) so that the immune system does not attack the body. If they became memory or plasma cells (B, C), an autoimmune response would result.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each example as natural active, natural passive, artificial active or artificial passive immunity:
(i) a baby receives antibodies in its mother's breast milk
(ii) a child is given oral polio vaccine drops
(iii) a man recovers from measles and does not catch it again
(iv) a farmer in Sindh bitten by a snake is given an injection of antivenom
parts.answer: (i) natural passive; (ii) artificial active; (iii) natural active; (iv) artificial passive
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which would give long-term immunity to measles?
A an injection of an attenuated (weakened) measles virus vaccine
B an injection of antibodies against measles
C antibodies crossing the placenta from an immune mother
D a course of antibiotics
parts.answer: A an injection of an attenuated (weakened) measles virus vaccine
parts.working: A vaccine stimulates an active immune response, producing memory cells that last for years. Injected or placental antibodies (B, C) give passive immunity, which lasts only weeks because no memory cells are made; antibiotics do not affect viruses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how vaccination provides protection against a disease.
parts.answer: The vaccine contains antigens (dead/weakened pathogen, toxoid or parts of the pathogen); it stimulates a primary immune response; B- and T-lymphocytes specific to the antigen form clones and memory cells; on infection memory cells give a fast secondary response, destroying the pathogen before symptoms appear
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: vaccine contains antigens; specific lymphocytes activated/clonal selection; antibodies produced; memory cells formed; secondary response faster and greater on infection; pathogen destroyed before causing disease.

stem: A district health office ran a measles vaccination campaign. Before the campaign there were 840 cases per year. Two years later, with 95 % of children vaccinated, there were 63 cases per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in measles cases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some children in the district were too young or too ill to be vaccinated, but their risk of catching measles still fell. Explain why.
parts.answer: Herd immunity: so many people are immune that the virus has few susceptible hosts; chains of transmission are broken; so unvaccinated individuals are less likely to meet an infected person
parts.working: 1 mark each: herd immunity (named or described); fewer infected people/carriers to pass on the virus; transmission chain broken so contact with infected people unlikely.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why a few vaccinated children still caught measles.
parts.answer: Some people do not respond fully to the vaccine (e.g. poor immune response, malnutrition); vaccine may have been stored incorrectly (cold chain broken); only one dose received; vaccinated too young while maternal antibodies were present
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible reasons.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Smallpox was eradicated worldwide by 1980. Explain the features of smallpox and its vaccine that made eradication possible.
parts.answer: The virus had stable antigens (did not mutate much), so one vaccine worked everywhere; the vaccine was live, effective and gave long-lasting immunity; infected people were easy to identify (clear symptoms) so cases could be isolated and contacts vaccinated (ring vaccination); no animal reservoir / only infected humans; vaccine was heat-stable/freeze-dried and easy to give
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: little antigenic variation; effective live vaccine; long-lasting immunity; easy to identify cases; ring vaccination/isolation; no animal reservoir; heat-stable vaccine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it has been much more difficult to develop a highly effective vaccine against malaria.
parts.answer: Plasmodium is a eukaryote with many antigens and several stages in its life cycle; it hides inside liver cells and red blood cells, and shows antigenic variation, so antibodies cannot reach it easily
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: different antigens at different life-cycle stages; intracellular (liver/red blood cells) so hidden from antibodies; antigenic variation; many strains.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A newborn baby has antibodies against tetanus that came from its mother across the placenta. Why does this protection last for only a few weeks?
A The baby makes no memory cells and the antibodies are gradually broken down.
B The baby's memory cells die soon after birth.
C The antibodies are destroyed by the baby's plasma cells.
D The antibodies are digested in the baby's stomach.
parts.answer: A The baby makes no memory cells and the antibodies are gradually broken down.
parts.working: This is natural passive immunity: the antibodies were made by the mother, so the baby has no memory cells for tetanus and the antibodies are broken down. B is wrong because no memory cells were formed in the first place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new influenza vaccine is produced every year. Explain why.
parts.answer: The influenza virus mutates frequently, changing its surface antigens (antigenic variation/drift); memory cells and antibodies from earlier vaccines are not complementary to the new antigens; so a new vaccine matching the current strains is needed
parts.working: 1 mark each: mutation/antigenic variation; new antigen shapes not recognised by existing memory cells/antibodies; vaccine updated to match strains expected that season.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some vaccines contain mRNA coding for a viral surface protein, enclosed in lipid droplets. Explain how such a vaccine leads to immunity.
parts.answer: Lipid droplets fuse with/enter body cells; the mRNA is translated by the cell's ribosomes to make the viral protein (antigen); this protein is displayed on the cell surface/released, triggering a primary immune response with production of antibodies and memory cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: mRNA enters cells; translated to produce viral antigen; antigen presented/displayed and activates lymphocytes, forming memory cells (and antibodies).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A boy in Multan is bitten by a dog that may have rabies. Doctors inject both rabies antibodies and rabies vaccine. Explain the reason for giving both.
parts.answer: The antibodies give immediate (artificial passive) protection by binding to/neutralising the virus straight away; but they are broken down within weeks and no memory cells form; the vaccine stimulates artificial active immunity, but antibodies take a week or more to appear; the vaccine gives long-term protection through memory cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: antibodies act immediately (passive); antibodies short-lived/no memory cells; vaccine stimulates own immune response (active) but slower; vaccine gives memory cells/long-term protection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rabies virus travels slowly along nerves from the bite to the brain, which can take weeks. Suggest why this makes vaccination after the bite effective.
parts.answer: There is time for the primary immune response to produce antibodies and T-cells before the virus reaches the brain; so the virus is destroyed before it causes disease
parts.working: 1 mark: long incubation period gives time for primary response/antibody production. 1 mark: virus neutralised before reaching the central nervous system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced using the hybridoma method.
parts.answer: Inject a mouse with the antigen; mouse makes B-lymphocytes/plasma cells specific to the antigen; remove B-cells from the spleen; fuse them with myeloma (cancer) cells to form hybridoma cells; select hybridomas making the required antibody; clone these cells and culture them; collect and purify antibody
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: antigen injected into mouse; B-lymphocytes/plasma cells taken from spleen; fused with myeloma cells; using polyethylene glycol/electric shock; hybridoma cells; screened for correct antibody; cloned/cultured (divide indefinitely); antibody harvested.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why are B-lymphocytes fused with myeloma cells when producing monoclonal antibodies?
A Myeloma cells can divide indefinitely.
B Myeloma cells make large quantities of antibody of their own.
C Myeloma cells provide the specificity of the antibody.
D Myeloma cells prevent the mouse rejecting the antibody.
parts.answer: A Myeloma cells can divide indefinitely.
parts.working: B-lymphocytes do not divide in culture; fusing them with cancerous myeloma cells gives hybridomas that both divide continuously and secrete the specific antibody. The specificity comes from the B-lymphocyte, not the myeloma cell (C).

stem: A home pregnancy test strip detects the hormone hCG in urine. Near the bottom of the strip are mobile monoclonal antibodies against hCG, each attached to a coloured bead. Further up are a test line of immobilised antibodies against hCG and, above it, a control line of immobilised antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a positive result appears at the test line.
parts.answer: hCG in the urine binds to the mobile antibodies, which carry coloured beads/dye; the hCG–antibody complex moves up the strip with the urine; at the test line, immobilised antibodies that are also specific to hCG bind the complex; coloured beads build up so a coloured line appears
parts.working: 1 mark each: hCG binds to mobile (labelled) antibody; complex moves up strip; immobilised antibody at test line binds hCG (at a different site); colour accumulates at test line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a coloured line should always appear at the control line, whether or not the woman is pregnant.
parts.answer: Immobilised antibodies at the control line bind to the mobile antibody itself (not to hCG); so mobile antibodies with coloured beads always collect there, showing the urine has moved up the strip and the test has worked
parts.working: 1 mark: control antibodies bind the mobile antibodies (with or without hCG). 1 mark: shows test is working / liquid has flowed past test line.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody used to treat some breast cancers. It binds to a receptor protein (HER2) found in very large numbers on the surface of these cancer cells. Explain why trastuzumab binds to the cancer cells but rarely to other cells.
parts.answer: Its antigen-binding sites are complementary to HER2 only; normal cells have few HER2 receptors, so little binding occurs
parts.working: 1 mark: specific/complementary binding site to HER2. 1 mark: HER2 present in large numbers only on these cancer cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Monoclonal antibodies for treatment are usually 'humanised'. Explain why antibodies made entirely by mouse cells are not suitable for repeated treatment.
parts.answer: Mouse antibodies have mouse-specific (constant region) amino acid sequences that act as foreign antigens; the patient's immune system makes antibodies against them, destroying them / causing an allergic reaction, so later doses work less well
parts.working: 1 mark: mouse antibodies are non-self/antigenic. 1 mark: patient produces an immune response (antibodies) that removes them or causes side-effects.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why patients need repeated doses of trastuzumab over several months.
parts.answer: Antibodies are proteins that are broken down in the body over time; cancer cells continue to be present and divide, so the antibody concentration must be kept high
parts.working: 1 mark: antibodies broken down/removed (no memory cells, passive). 1 mark: need to keep binding to cancer cells as they continue to divide.

stem:
A rapid test for dengue fever uses a monoclonal antibody against a dengue virus protein (NS1). In a hospital in Lahore it was tested on 400 patients. A laboratory method showed that 150 patients were infected and 250 were not.
Of the 150 infected patients, 138 tested positive.
Of the 250 uninfected patients, 10 tested positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate (i) the percentage of infected patients correctly identified by the test (its sensitivity), (ii) the percentage of uninfected patients correctly identified as negative (its specificity).
parts.working: (i) 138 ÷ 150 × 100 = 92 % (2 marks; M1 correct division). (ii) uninfected testing negative = 250 − 10 = 240; 240 ÷ 250 × 100 = 96 % (1 mark).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why some uninfected patients tested positive.
parts.answer: The monoclonal antibody may bind to a similar antigen from another related virus (cross-reaction), e.g. a protein of shape similar to NS1; or contamination/misreading of a faint line
parts.working: 1 mark: antibody binds a different antigen of similar shape (cross-reactivity). 1 mark: e.g. related virus such as Zika / or a technical error.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about a sample of one type of monoclonal antibody is correct?
A All the molecules have identical antigen-binding sites.
B The molecules are made by many different clones of B-lymphocytes.
C The molecules bind to several different antigens.
D The molecules have different constant regions.
parts.answer: A All the molecules have identical antigen-binding sites.
parts.working: Monoclonal antibodies come from a single clone of hybridoma cells, so every molecule is identical and binds the same antigen. B describes polyclonal antibodies produced in a normal immune response.

stem: A sandwich ELISA test detects a virus antigen in blood serum. A monoclonal antibody against the antigen is fixed to the bottom of a plastic well. The serum is added, then the well is washed. A second monoclonal antibody, which binds to a different part of the antigen and is linked to an enzyme, is added; the well is washed again. Finally a colourless substrate is added that the enzyme converts to a coloured product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the wells must be washed after the sample is added, and again after the second antibody is added.
parts.answer: Washing removes any unbound antigen/proteins, and then any unbound enzyme-linked antibody; otherwise unbound enzyme would cause a colour change even when no antigen is present (false positive)
parts.working: 1 mark: removes unbound molecules (sample proteins/second antibody). 1 mark: prevents colour change not caused by antigen / false positive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the intensity of colour indicates the amount of antigen in the sample.
parts.answer: The second antibody can only stay in the well if it is bound to antigen held by the first antibody; more antigen means more enzyme bound, so more substrate is converted to coloured product
parts.working: 1 mark: second (enzyme-linked) antibody binds only where antigen is captured. 1 mark: more enzyme → more coloured product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the two antibodies used must bind to different parts (epitopes) of the antigen.
parts.answer: If both bound the same site, the first (fixed) antibody would block it so the second antibody could not bind
parts.working: Second antibody must bind while the antigen is held by the first.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a suitable control well for this test.
parts.answer: A well with a sample known to contain no antigen (e.g. buffer or serum from an uninfected person), treated in the same way
parts.working: Negative control with no antigen (or a positive control with known antigen).

author: HomiLabs

stem: After a single dose, the concentration of a humanised therapeutic antibody in a patient's blood was 160 µg cm⁻³. Its concentration halves every 21 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration remaining 63 days after the dose.
parts.answer: 20 µg cm⁻³
parts.working: M1: 63 ÷ 21 = 3 half-lives. A1: 160 × (½)³ = 20 µg cm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same antibody made entirely by mouse cells had a much shorter half-life in patients after the first few doses. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Patient's immune system recognised the mouse antibody as foreign/non-self; antibodies against it were produced and the complexes were removed by phagocytes, so it disappeared faster
parts.working: 1 mark: mouse protein is antigenic / triggers immune response. 1 mark: anti-mouse antibodies bind and remove it (phagocytosis) more quickly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline how scientists 'humanise' a mouse monoclonal antibody.
parts.answer: Genetic engineering: keep the mouse variable regions (antigen-binding sites) but replace the constant regions (and most other parts) with human antibody sequences
parts.working: 1 mark: variable/antigen-binding region from mouse retained. 1 mark: rest/constant region changed to human sequence (by altering the genes).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a neutrophil destroys a bacterium by phagocytosis.
parts.answer: Neutrophil is attracted to the bacterium (by chemicals/chemotaxis); receptors on its membrane bind to the bacterium (or to antibodies on it); it engulfs the bacterium by endocytosis, forming a phagocytic vacuole; lysosomes fuse with the vacuole and hydrolytic enzymes digest the bacterium
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: chemotaxis/moves towards bacterium; attachment/recognition; engulfing by cell surface membrane/pseudopodia (endocytosis); phagocytic vacuole (phagosome); lysosomes fuse; hydrolytic enzymes digest/hydrolyse bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly compares neutrophils and macrophages?
A neutrophils are short-lived and arrive first; macrophages are long-lived and act as antigen-presenting cells
B neutrophils are long-lived and present antigens; macrophages are short-lived and arrive first
C neutrophils secrete antibodies; macrophages engulf bacteria
D neutrophils have a round nucleus; macrophages have a lobed nucleus
parts.answer: A neutrophils are short-lived and arrive first; macrophages are long-lived and act as antigen-presenting cells
parts.working: Neutrophils are the first, short-lived phagocytes to reach an infection; macrophages live longer and present antigens to lymphocytes. Neither secretes antibodies (C), and it is the neutrophil that has a lobed nucleus (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where phagocytes are produced.
parts.answer: Bone marrow
