parts.working: 1 mark: differ in solubility in solvent. 1 mark: differ in affinity for/adsorption to paper, so travel different distances.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an absorption spectrum and an action spectrum.
parts.answer: An absorption spectrum shows how much light of each wavelength is absorbed by a pigment (or pigments); an action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light.
parts.working: 1 mark: absorption = amount of light absorbed at each wavelength. 1 mark: action = rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorophyll a absorbs very little light between 450 nm and 550 nm, yet the rate of photosynthesis at 480 nm is still quite high. Explain why.
parts.answer: Accessory pigments such as carotene and xanthophylls (and chlorophyll b) absorb light at these wavelengths (blue-green); they pass the energy to chlorophyll a in the reaction centre of the photosystem; so light at these wavelengths is still used for photosynthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark: accessory pigments named (carotenoids/chlorophyll b). 1 mark: absorb blue/blue-green light around 450–500 nm. 1 mark: transfer energy to primary pigment / reaction centre chlorophyll a.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why most leaves appear green.
parts.answer: Green light (about 500–560 nm) is absorbed least by the pigments, so it is reflected or transmitted to the eye.
parts.working: 1 mark: green wavelengths reflected/not absorbed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a photosystem and explain how it captures light energy.
parts.answer: A photosystem is a cluster of pigment molecules held by proteins in the thylakoid membrane; a light-harvesting system (antenna complex) of accessory pigments and chlorophyll molecules surrounds a reaction centre; pigments absorb photons and pass energy from molecule to molecule towards the reaction centre; the reaction centre contains a pair of chlorophyll a molecules (P680 in PSII, P700 in PSI) which, when excited, emit an electron to an electron acceptor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: in thylakoid membrane, pigments + proteins; light-harvesting/antenna complex of many pigments; energy transferred to reaction centre; reaction centre = chlorophyll a (P680/P700); excited electron emitted / passed to electron acceptor (photoactivation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some red seaweeds live in coastal seas at depths where most red and blue light has been absorbed by the water and mainly green light remains. These seaweeds contain a red accessory pigment called phycoerythrin. Suggest how phycoerythrin helps them to grow at these depths.
parts.answer: Phycoerythrin absorbs green light (it looks red because it reflects red); the absorbed energy is passed to chlorophyll a in the reaction centres, so the seaweed can still photosynthesise using the light available at depth.
parts.working: 1 mark: absorbs green light / wavelengths that reach that depth. 1 mark: energy passed to reaction centre chlorophyll so photosynthesis continues.

stem:
Chloroplasts were broken open and separated into a thylakoid fraction and a stroma fraction. Each was incubated under different conditions.
Tube 1: thylakoids, light, water — oxygen released
Tube 2: stroma, light, water — no oxygen released
Tube 3: stroma, dark, CO₂ + ATP + reduced NADP — CO₂ fixed into sugars
Tube 4: stroma, dark, CO₂ only — almost no CO₂ fixed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for tubes 1 and 2.
parts.answer: Thylakoids contain the photosystems and electron transport chains; in light, photolysis of water releases oxygen (tube 1); the stroma has no photosystems, so no oxygen is produced (tube 2); without light, no photoactivation and no oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: thylakoids are site of light-dependent stage / photosystems. 1 mark: photolysis of water in light releases O₂. 1 mark: stroma lacks photosystems/chlorophyll so no O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for tubes 3 and 4.
parts.answer: The stroma contains the Calvin cycle enzymes (rubisco); ATP and reduced NADP, normally supplied by the light-dependent stage, were added, so CO₂ could be fixed even in the dark (tube 3); without ATP and reduced NADP, GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate and RuBP cannot be regenerated, so fixation stops quickly (tube 4).
parts.working: 1 mark: stroma contains Calvin cycle enzymes/rubisco. 1 mark: ATP and reduced NADP are the products of the light-dependent stage needed, so light not directly required. 1 mark: without them GP not reduced / RuBP not regenerated so fixation stops.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a cucumber plant was measured at two CO₂ concentrations. Temperature was kept at 25 °C.
Light intensity / arbitrary units: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Rate at 0.04 % CO₂ / arbitrary units: 0, 3.2, 5.4, 5.9, 6.0, 6.0
Rate at 0.10 % CO₂ / arbitrary units: 0, 3.2, 6.1, 8.8, 10.4, 10.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a limiting factor.
parts.answer: The factor that is in shortest supply (furthest from its optimum) and so restricts the rate of a process; increasing it increases the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis at 2 arbitrary units of light intensity at both CO₂ concentrations. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Light intensity; at low light intensity the rate is the same at both CO₂ concentrations and rises as light intensity increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: light intensity. 1 mark: rate same for both CO₂ levels / rate increases with light intensity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the factor limiting the rate at 10 arbitrary units of light intensity in 0.04 % CO₂. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration; the rate has levelled off so increasing light has no effect, but the rate is higher at 0.10 % CO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ concentration. 1 mark: plateau with light, but higher rate at higher CO₂ (data quote: 6.0 vs 10.8).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A tomato grower compared yields in two greenhouses. One had normal air (0.04 % CO₂) and the other was enriched to 0.10 % CO₂. Light and temperature were the same.
Normal air: 9.6 kg of tomatoes per m²
Enriched: 14.2 kg of tomatoes per m²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield in the enriched greenhouse. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why increasing the CO₂ concentration increases the yield.
parts.answer: CO₂ is often the limiting factor in bright light; more CO₂ means rubisco fixes more CO₂ with RuBP; more GP and triose phosphate are made, so more sugars/biomass are produced (faster growth, more fruit).
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ was limiting. 1 mark: more CO₂ combines with RuBP (via rubisco) / faster Calvin cycle. 1 mark: more triose phosphate → more sugars, starch, growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the grower also keeps the greenhouse warm in winter, and why there is no benefit in raising the CO₂ concentration further on dull, cloudy days.
parts.answer: Warmth increases the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions (Calvin cycle), so temperature does not limit the rate; on dull days light intensity is the limiting factor, so extra CO₂ cannot increase the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: warmth so temperature is not limiting / enzymes faster. 1 mark: on dull days light is limiting.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rates of photosynthesis of a cotton leaf were measured at different temperatures in high light and high CO₂.
Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40
Rate / arbitrary units: 2.1, 3.4, 5.0, 6.6, 7.8, 5.2, 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis shown by these results.
parts.answer: The rate increases from 10 °C to a maximum (optimum) at 30 °C (from 2.1 to 7.8 units), then decreases sharply at 35 °C and 40 °C (to 1.5 units at 40 °C).
parts.working: 1 mark: increases to optimum at 30 °C. 1 mark: then decreases above 30 °C; data quote with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis between 10 °C and 30 °C and above 30 °C.
parts.answer: Below the optimum, rising temperature gives enzymes (e.g. rubisco) and substrates more kinetic energy; more frequent collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes form, so the Calvin cycle is faster. Above the optimum, enzymes begin to denature: hydrogen bonds break and the active site changes shape, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form; stomata may close at high temperature, reducing CO₂ uptake.
parts.working: 1 mark: Calvin cycle/light-independent stage is enzyme-controlled. 1 mark: more kinetic energy, more collisions / E–S complexes. 1 mark: above optimum enzymes denature, active site shape changes. 1 mark: stomatal closure reduces CO₂ entry (or increased photorespiration not required).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A piece of pondweed was placed in hydrogencarbonate solution and a lamp was placed at different distances. The number of bubbles released per minute was counted.
Distance / cm: 10, 15, 20, 30, 40
Bubbles per minute: 17, 16, 15, 8, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Light intensity is proportional to 1/d², where d is the distance from the lamp. Calculate the relative light intensity (10 000/d²) for each distance.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for three or four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between relative light intensity and the rate of oxygen production.
parts.answer: Rate increases as light intensity increases from 6.25 to 25 (from 4 to 15 bubbles per minute) but levels off at higher intensities (16–17 bubbles per minute at 44.4 and 100).
parts.working: 1 mark: increases at low intensity. 1 mark: levels off/plateaus at high intensity with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two factors that may be limiting the rate when the lamp is 10 cm away and explain why the lamp's heat might be a source of error.
parts.answer: CO₂ (hydrogencarbonate) concentration; temperature; (number of chloroplasts/amount of chlorophyll or enzyme). A lamp close to the plant warms the water, so temperature changes as well as light intensity, which also affects the rate (the independent variable is no longer the only factor changing).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two limiting factors (CO₂ concentration, temperature, amount of chlorophyll/rubisco). 1 mark: heat raises water temperature, which changes rate – use a heat shield/LED/water bath.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by photolysis of water and give the equation for it.
parts.answer: The splitting of water using light energy (at photosystem II): 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂
parts.working: 1 mark: splitting of water by light (energy). 1 mark: correct balanced equation (accept H₂O → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ + ½O₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to each product of photolysis.
parts.answer: Electrons replace those lost from the chlorophyll in photosystem II; protons (H⁺) build up in the thylakoid space and are then used (with electrons) to reduce NADP; oxygen diffuses out of the leaf (or is used in respiration).
parts.working: 1 mark each: e⁻ replace electrons lost by PSII; H⁺ reduce NADP (after contributing to gradient for ATP synthesis); O₂ by-product released / used in respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation by giving four differences.
parts.answer: Cyclic involves PSI only; non-cyclic involves PSI and PSII. Cyclic produces ATP only; non-cyclic produces ATP and reduced NADP. Cyclic involves no photolysis of water / no O₂ released; non-cyclic involves photolysis and releases O₂. In cyclic, electrons return to PSI; in non-cyclic, electrons end up on NADP (electrons from water replace those lost from PSII).
parts.working: 1 mark for each difference, max 4: photosystems involved; products (ATP only vs ATP + reduced NADP); photolysis/oxygen; fate of electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one similarity between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.answer: Both make ATP by chemiosmosis using ATP synthase / both use an electron transport chain in the thylakoid membrane / both involve PSI and photoactivation of chlorophyll.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of non-cyclic photophosphorylation in the thylakoid membrane.
parts.answer: Light absorbed by photosystem II; chlorophyll a in the reaction centre is photoactivated and emits excited electrons to an electron acceptor; electrons are passed along an electron transport chain of carriers to photosystem I, losing energy; this energy is used to pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space; light excites PSI, whose electrons pass to a second carrier and then reduce NADP (with H⁺) to form reduced NADP; electrons from PSII replace those lost by PSI; photolysis of water supplies electrons to PSII, releasing H⁺ and O₂; H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), producing ATP from ADP and Pi.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: light absorbed by PSII; photoactivation – electrons excited and emitted; electron acceptor; ETC, electrons lose energy; H⁺ pumped into thylakoid space / proton gradient; PSI excited; electrons reduce NADP (NADP reductase) to reduced NADP; PSII electrons replace those lost from PSI; photolysis replaces electrons in PSII, O₂ released; chemiosmosis through ATP synthase; ATP formed from ADP + Pi.

stem: Isolated thylakoids were kept in the dark in an acidic buffer at pH 4.5 until the thylakoid space reached pH 4.5 (step 1). They were then transferred, still in the dark, to a buffer at pH 8.0 containing ADP and phosphate (step 2). ATP was produced for a short time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the concentration of H⁺ is in a solution at pH 4.5 than at pH 8.0. (pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]). Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: About 3200 times (3.2 × 10³)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP was made in step 2 even though the thylakoids were in the dark.
parts.answer: The thylakoid space had a high H⁺ concentration (pH 4.5) compared with the outside (pH 8.0), so there was a proton gradient across the membrane; H⁺ diffused out through ATP synthase; the flow of protons drove the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (chemiosmosis); light is normally needed only to generate the gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: proton/H⁺ gradient across thylakoid membrane. 1 mark: H⁺ diffuse through ATP synthase (channel). 1 mark: energy from proton flow used to make ATP from ADP + Pi – chemiosmosis, light not directly needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A chemical that makes the thylakoid membrane permeable to H⁺ was added to illuminated chloroplasts. Predict and explain the effect on ATP production and on the reduction of NADP.
parts.answer: ATP production falls (stops) because H⁺ leak back across the membrane, so no proton gradient forms to drive ATP synthase; reduction of NADP continues because electron flow along the chain still occurs.
parts.working: 1 mark: ATP production decreases, no proton gradient. 1 mark: NADP still reduced / electron transport continues.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzyme that catalyses the fixation of carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle.
parts.answer: Rubisco (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table to show the number of carbon atoms in each molecule.
RuBP | GP | triose phosphate
parts.answer: RuBP 5; GP 3; triose phosphate 3
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline how GP is converted to triose phosphate, naming the products of the light-dependent stage that are needed.
parts.answer: GP is reduced to triose phosphate using hydrogen from reduced NADP and energy from ATP.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduction (by reduced NADP). 1 mark: ATP provides energy / phosphate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two uses of triose phosphate in the plant.
parts.answer: Any two: regenerating RuBP; making glucose/sucrose/starch/cellulose; making lipids (glycerol and fatty acids); making amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Cells of a single-celled green alga were kept in bright light with plenty of CO₂, and the concentrations of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) and ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) were measured. The light was then switched off. During the next minute the GP concentration increased and the RuBP concentration decreased.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the changes in the concentrations of GP and RuBP after the light was switched off.
parts.answer: No light means no ATP or reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage; GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate, so GP accumulates; RuBP is still used up as it combines with CO₂ (to form GP); RuBP cannot be regenerated from triose phosphate because there is no ATP (and no TP being made), so RuBP falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: no ATP/reduced NADP. 1 mark: GP not converted to TP so GP rises. 1 mark: RuBP still used in fixation of CO₂. 1 mark: RuBP not regenerated (needs ATP/TP) so falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a second experiment the light was kept on, but the CO₂ concentration was suddenly reduced. Predict the changes in GP and RuBP concentrations and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: RuBP rises and GP falls; less CO₂ is available to combine with RuBP, so RuBP is not used but is still regenerated from TP; GP is still converted to TP but less is formed.
parts.working: 1 mark: RuBP increases and GP decreases (both needed). 1 mark: less CO₂ fixed with RuBP while regeneration / GP reduction continue.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the Calvin cycle, fixing one molecule of CO₂ and regenerating RuBP uses 3 molecules of ATP and 2 molecules of reduced NADP. Calculate the number of molecules of ATP and of reduced NADP needed to make one molecule of sucrose (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁).
parts.answer: 36 ATP and 24 reduced NADP
parts.working: M1: sucrose has 12 carbon atoms, so 12 CO₂ must be fixed. A1: 12 × 3 = 36 ATP and 12 × 2 = 24 reduced NADP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the Calvin cycle, including the regeneration of RuBP.
parts.answer: In the stroma, CO₂ combines with RuBP (5C); catalysed by rubisco; forming an unstable 6C compound that splits into two molecules of GP (3C); GP is reduced to triose phosphate using reduced NADP; and ATP; five out of every six triose phosphates are used to regenerate RuBP; using ATP; one in six is used to make glucose and other organic compounds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: CO₂ + RuBP; rubisco; two GP formed (via unstable 6C intermediate); GP reduced to TP; reduced NADP and ATP used; most TP (5/6) regenerates RuBP; ATP used in regeneration; some TP leaves to make sugars, amino acids, lipids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of an aquatic plant such as Elodea. Your plan should include how you would measure the rate and how you would control other variables.
parts.answer: Cut a piece of Elodea of fixed length (e.g. 8 cm) and place it upside down in a boiling tube of 1 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution (excess CO₂); stand the tube in a beaker of water at 25 °C as a heat shield/water bath; place a lamp (LED) at distances 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 cm (or measure light intensity with a light meter); leave 5 minutes at each distance to acclimatise; collect the gas in a photosynthometer/capillary tube for a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) and measure the volume/length of bubble; repeat three times at each distance and calculate means; carry out in a darkened room so the lamp is the only light source.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: IV light intensity varied by lamp distance (≥5 values) or light meter; same plant piece/length, same species; NaHCO₃ in excess for CO₂; temperature controlled with water bath/heat shield/LED; acclimatisation time at each new intensity; DV measured as volume of gas (photosynthometer/syringe) in fixed time (not just bubble count); darkened room / no other light; at least 3 repeats and mean; rate = volume ÷ time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the leaves are blended in a buffer solution that is ice-cold and has the same water potential as the leaf cells.
parts.answer: Ice-cold: slows enzyme activity (e.g. enzymes that damage chloroplasts) / reduces damage. Same water potential: prevents water entering or leaving chloroplasts by osmosis, so they do not burst or shrink. Buffer keeps pH constant so proteins are not denatured.
parts.working: 1 mark for ice-cold reason. 1 mark for same water potential or buffer reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of temperature on the rate of the Hill reaction, using a chloroplast suspension and DCPIP.
parts.answer: Prepare chloroplast suspension by blending spinach leaves in ice-cold buffer, filtering and centrifuging, then resuspending the pellet; set up tubes with the same volume of chloroplast suspension and the same volume and concentration of DCPIP; equilibrate tubes in water baths at five temperatures, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C; place each tube at the same distance from the same lamp; measure the time for the blue DCPIP to become colourless, or measure absorbance with a colorimeter (red filter) every 30 s; rate = 1/time; controls: tube kept in the dark and tube with boiled chloroplasts; three repeats at each temperature and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: method for extracting chloroplasts (blend, filter, centrifuge); same volumes/concentrations of DCPIP and suspension; ≥5 temperatures with thermostatic water bath; equilibrate before mixing; constant light intensity (same lamp, same distance); DV time to decolourise or colorimeter reading against colour standard; rate = 1/t; control in dark or with boiled chloroplasts; repeats and means.

author: HomiLabs
stem: To study the Hill reaction, a chloroplast suspension is prepared by blending spinach leaves in an ice-cold buffer solution that has the same water potential as the leaf cells. DCPIP is a blue dye that becomes colourless when it is reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline a method using leaf discs to investigate the effect of the colour (wavelength) of light on the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Cut discs from the same leaf with a cork borer, avoiding large veins; infiltrate the discs with 0.2 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution by drawing them into a syringe and pulling the plunger to remove air, so they sink; place ten discs in the same volume of hydrogencarbonate solution in each of several beakers; illuminate each with a different colour of LED (red, blue, green, white), each at the same light intensity measured with a light meter and the same distance; keep temperature constant with a water bath; record the time for five of the ten discs to float; repeat three times and use 1/time as a measure of rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: discs same size and from same plant/leaf; infiltration with NaHCO₃ using syringe so discs sink; same number of discs and volume of solution; different colours via filters/LEDs; same light intensity (light meter) or same distance and lamp; constant temperature; DV time for (e.g.) half of the discs to float; rate = 1/t; repeats and mean; control in dark.

stem: An aquatic plant with a fresh mass of 2.5 g was placed in a photosynthometer. In 5 minutes, the gas collected formed a bubble 18 mm long in a capillary tube with an internal radius of 0.4 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of gas collected, using volume = π r² l. Give your answer in mm³ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 9.05 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of gas production per gram of plant in mm³ min⁻¹ g⁻¹. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.72 mm³ min⁻¹ g⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate of gas production underestimates the true rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Some oxygen produced is used in respiration by the plant (or dissolves in the water), so not all is collected.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen used in respiration / dissolves in water.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A Hill-reaction experiment measured the time for DCPIP to be decolourised by a chloroplast suspension at two temperatures.
20 °C: 240 s, 252 s, 246 s
30 °C: 150 s, 156 s, 300 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and explain why it should not be included in the mean.
parts.answer: 300 s at 30 °C; it is far from the other two readings (150 and 156 s), so it is probably due to an error (e.g. wrong volume or tube shaded) and would distort the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: 300 s at 30 °C identified with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean time at each temperature, leaving out the anomalous result, and then the rate of reaction as 1000/mean time. Give rates to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 20 °C: mean 246 s, rate 4.07; 30 °C: mean 153 s, rate 6.54 (rates as 1000/s)
parts.working: 1 mark: mean 246 s. 1 mark: mean 153 s (anomaly excluded). 1 mark: rates 4.07 and 6.54.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate from 20 °C to 30 °C. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student uses a photosynthometer to measure the volume of gas given off by a piece of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution when a lamp is placed at different distances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: light intensity (distance of lamp). Dependent: volume of gas (oxygen) produced per minute.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and explain how each could be kept constant.
parts.answer: Temperature – water bath / heat shield / LED lamp; CO₂ concentration – same concentration and volume of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, in excess; plant – same piece/length of the same species; time of collection – stopwatch; background light – darkened room.
parts.working: 1 mark for each variable with a valid method (max 3).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sodium hydrogencarbonate solution should be in excess.
parts.answer: So that CO₂ concentration is not a limiting factor and does not fall during the experiment; only light intensity limits the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigates the effect of sodium hydrogencarbonate concentration (0.0 %, 0.1 %, 0.2 %, 0.4 %, 0.8 %) on the time taken for infiltrated leaf discs to float in bright light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why all the leaf discs should be cut from the same plant and should avoid large veins.
parts.answer: Same plant: discs have similar chlorophyll content / genotype / age, so differences are due to CO₂ concentration. Avoid veins: veins have fewer chloroplasts and different density/air spaces, which would affect floating time.
parts.working: 1 mark: same plant – reduces variation in chlorophyll/genetics. 1 mark: veins differ in chloroplasts/buoyancy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and explain what it shows.
parts.answer: Discs in distilled water with no sodium hydrogencarbonate (no added CO₂) under the same light; shows that floating depends on CO₂ for photosynthesis (discs should not float or float very slowly). Or discs in hydrogencarbonate kept in the dark – shows light is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid control (no NaHCO₃ or dark). 1 mark: what it shows.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a change in temperature during the experiment would make the results less valid.
parts.answer: Temperature affects the rate of the enzyme-controlled reactions of photosynthesis (Calvin cycle), so the floating time would no longer depend only on CO₂ concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes/rubisco affected by temperature. 1 mark: rate would change for a reason other than the independent variable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will add DCPIP to chloroplast suspensions kept at 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 °C in light and record how quickly the blue colour disappears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As temperature increases from 10 °C to 35 °C, the rate of DCPIP reduction by chloroplasts increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: testable, directional statement linking temperature and rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no relationship between temperature and the rate of DCPIP reduction.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict and explain the results you would expect if the range were extended to 60 °C.
parts.answer: Rate increases up to an optimum (around 35–40 °C) because molecules have more kinetic energy and electron carrier/enzyme proteins work faster; above the optimum the rate decreases sharply because proteins in the photosystems/electron carriers are denatured and thylakoid membranes are damaged.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase then decrease (optimum). 1 mark: more kinetic energy / faster reactions below optimum. 1 mark: denaturation of proteins (photosystems, carriers) / membrane damage above optimum.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate of photosynthesis (arbitrary units) of a tomato leaf at 25 °C was measured at different CO₂ concentrations in low and in high light.
CO₂ / %: 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12
Low light: 2.9, 3.6, 3.6, 3.6
High light: 4.1, 7.9, 12.6, 12.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded: 'Increasing CO₂ concentration always increases the rate of photosynthesis.' Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Supported at high light: the rate rises from 4.1 to 12.6 as CO₂ increases from 0.02 to 0.08 %. Not supported at low light: the rate rises only from 2.9 to 3.6 and stays at 3.6 above 0.04 %, because light is limiting. Also at high light the rise slows (12.6 to 12.8 from 0.08 to 0.12 %), so another factor becomes limiting – 'always' is not justified; no replicates or variability shown.
parts.working: 1 mark: support at high light with data. 1 mark: at low light rate levels off at 3.6 – light limiting. 1 mark: plateau at high CO₂ in bright light / no repeats, so 'always' not valid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which factor is limiting the rate at 0.12 % CO₂ in high light.
parts.answer: Temperature (or the amount of rubisco/chlorophyll; possibly light intensity).
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature (accept enzyme/chlorophyll amount).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four tubes each contained 1 cm³ of blue DCPIP solution.
A: chloroplast suspension, in light – colourless after 6 minutes
B: chloroplast suspension, in the dark – still blue after 30 minutes
C: boiled chloroplast suspension, in light – still blue after 30 minutes
D: buffer only (no chloroplasts), in light – still blue after 30 minutes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result for tube A.
parts.answer: In light, the chloroplasts carry out the light-dependent stage; electrons from photolysis/photoactivated chlorophyll pass along the electron transport chain; DCPIP acts as an electron acceptor (instead of NADP) and is reduced, so it turns from blue to colourless.
parts.working: 1 mark: light-dependent stage / photoactivation. 1 mark: electrons released. 1 mark: DCPIP accepts electrons and is reduced (blue → colourless).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for tubes B and C.
parts.answer: B: no light, so no photoactivation of chlorophyll and no electrons released – DCPIP stays blue. C: boiling denatured the proteins of the photosystems/electron carriers (and damaged membranes), so no electron flow.
parts.working: 1 mark for B. 1 mark for C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the purpose of tube D.
parts.answer: To show that the colour change is due to the chloroplasts and not to light acting on DCPIP alone.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student counted the bubbles released from a cut stem of pondweed in a beaker of tap water for one minute at each of five lamp distances. A filament bulb was used and the lab blinds were open. He moved the lamp and started counting immediately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three sources of error in this method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Bubbles differ in size, so counting is inaccurate – collect gas in a photosynthometer/gas syringe and measure volume. Lamp heats the water – use an LED or a water bath/heat shield and check temperature. No time for the plant to adjust to each new light intensity – leave 5 minutes before counting. Other light in the room – use a darkened room. Only one count – repeat three times and calculate the mean. CO₂ in the tap water may run out – use sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in excess.
parts.working: 1 mark per error and 1 mark per matching improvement, for three pairs (max 6).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The rate of oxygen production (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹) was measured for five leaves from plants of the same species grown in full sunlight and five grown in shade, all measured under identical conditions.
Full sunlight: 12.4, 13.1, 11.8, 12.9, 12.6
Shade: 8.2, 9.0, 7.6, 8.8, 8.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation for the plants grown in full sunlight. Give the standard deviation to 2 decimal places. (s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)])
parts.answer: Mean 12.56; standard deviation 0.50
parts.working: 1 mark: mean 12.56. 1 mark: SD 0.50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The standard deviation for the shaded plants is 0.55 and the mean is 8.40. Calculate the standard error (SE = s ÷ √n) and the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) for both groups. Give values to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: SE sun = 0.503 ÷ √5 = 0.22. 1 mark: SE shade = 0.55 ÷ √5 = 0.246 → 0.25. 1 mark: both intervals correct: 12.56 ± 0.45 and 8.40 ± 0.49 (allow 7.90–8.90 from rounded SE).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the confidence intervals show.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference in mean rate between sun and shade plants is significant (not due to chance).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean rates of photosynthesis of a pondweed (arbitrary units) at different temperatures, with standard deviations:
Temperature / °C: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40
Mean rate: 2.0, 3.3, 4.8, 6.4, 6.9, 4.1
Standard deviation: 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.4, 0.6, 0.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should present these data as a graph, including how to show the variability of the results.
parts.answer: Line graph with temperature / °C on the x-axis and mean rate / arbitrary units on the y-axis, both with linear scales using most of the grid; plot the mean values as crosses and join with ruled straight lines point to point; draw error bars of ± standard deviation (or 95 % CI) through each point.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature on x-axis, rate on y-axis, labelled with units. 1 mark: points plotted and joined by ruled lines (not extrapolated). 1 mark: error bars showing SD/range for each mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the rate at 27 °C by linear interpolation.
parts.answer: 5.4 arbitrary units (5.44)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student cannot state the exact optimum temperature from these results.
parts.answer: Readings are 5 °C apart; the true optimum could lie anywhere between 30 °C and 40 °C – more readings at intervals of 1–2 °C are needed around 35 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Spinach leaves will be blended in ice-cold buffer with a kitchen blender, filtered and centrifuged. The chloroplast suspension will be mixed with DCPIP solution in test-tubes placed in a water bath next to a bench lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this procedure and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Blender blades are sharp – switch off and unplug before handling, do not put fingers inside; centrifuge spinning at high speed – balance tubes and keep the lid closed until it stops; lamp gets hot and is electrical near water – keep water away from the lamp and plug, do not touch the bulb; DCPIP may irritate eyes/skin – wear eye protection and gloves; glassware may break – handle carefully.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Low (to medium) – the chemicals are of low hazard in small volumes and all hazards can be controlled with simple precautions.
parts.working: 1 mark: level with justification.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why it is important to maintain biodiversity.
parts.answer: Any three: moral/ethical duty to other species and future generations; economic value – food, timber, crops, ecotourism; source of medicines and new genes for crop breeding; ecosystem services – pollination, nutrient recycling, flood control, oxygen; stability of food webs/ecosystems; aesthetic/cultural value.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three different reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Indus river dolphin lives only in the Indus river system and is endangered. Its range is split into sections by barrages built for irrigation. Suggest three threats to this species, other than barrages.
parts.answer: Any three: low water flow in the dry season because water is taken for irrigation; pollution from industry, sewage and agricultural chemicals; accidental capture in fishing nets (bycatch); dolphins stranded in irrigation canals; reduced fish prey from overfishing; noise/boat traffic; small, isolated populations losing genetic diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three suitable threats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the roles of zoos in the conservation of endangered species such as the snow leopard.
parts.answer: Captive breeding to increase numbers; maintaining genetic diversity using studbooks and exchanging animals between zoos (avoiding inbreeding); reintroduction of animals into the wild; research into behaviour, nutrition and reproduction; education of the public and fund-raising for conservation in the wild; keeping a safe population if wild populations are lost.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: captive breeding; studbooks/exchange to keep genetic diversity; reintroduction; research; education/raising awareness; fund-raising; safe 'reserve' population; assisted reproduction (IVF, AI).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a captive population started from only a few founder animals may have problems after several generations.
parts.answer: Small gene pool / low genetic diversity; inbreeding increases the chance of offspring being homozygous for harmful recessive alleles; this reduces fertility and survival (inbreeding depression) and the population is less able to adapt to change or disease.
parts.working: 1 mark: low genetic diversity / small gene pool. 1 mark: inbreeding → more homozygous recessive harmful alleles expressed. 1 mark: reduced fitness/fertility or less able to adapt (e.g. to disease).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and embryo transfer could be used to produce offspring of a rare antelope, using a female of a common, closely related species as a surrogate mother.
parts.answer: Give the rare female hormones to stimulate many eggs to mature (superovulation); collect eggs (from ovaries); collect sperm from a rare male (or use frozen sperm); mix eggs and sperm in a dish (in vitro) for fertilisation; grow embryos for a few days in culture; implant embryo into the uterus of the surrogate female of the common species, whose cycle has been synchronised with hormones.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: hormones to stimulate egg production; eggs collected; sperm collected / thawed from frozen store; fertilisation in a dish/outside the body; embryos cultured; embryos implanted into surrogate; surrogate's cycle synchronised / prepared with hormones.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the advantages of using a surrogate of a common species and of keeping frozen embryos and sperm in a 'frozen zoo'.
parts.answer: Rare females are not put at risk by pregnancy and can produce more eggs/offspring; more offspring per year from each rare female; frozen material can be stored for many years and transported between countries instead of animals; genetic diversity is preserved and can be reintroduced into future populations, even from animals that have died.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: protects rare female / more offspring; many embryos per rare female; long-term storage; easy transport between zoos/countries; preserves genetic diversity for the future; use material from dead animals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how seeds are prepared and stored in a seed bank.
parts.answer: Seeds are cleaned and checked; dried to a low water content (about 5 %); sealed in airtight containers; stored at low temperature (about −20 °C); samples are germinated regularly to check viability, and new seed is grown when viability falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: dried to low water content; airtight containers; low temperature (e.g. −20 °C); germination tests at intervals; regrow to collect fresh seed; records kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many farmers in northern Pakistan have replaced old local wheat varieties with modern high-yielding varieties. Explain why seeds of the old local varieties are being collected and stored.
parts.answer: Old varieties contain alleles not found in modern varieties (genetic diversity); some may give resistance to diseases, drought, cold or salinity; these alleles could be bred into future crop varieties as the climate or pathogens change; once the varieties are no longer grown they may be lost for ever.
parts.working: 1 mark: preserves genetic diversity / alleles. 1 mark: useful traits (e.g. drought or disease resistance). 1 mark: for future breeding / prevent loss (extinction of variety).

stem: Prosopis juliflora, a shrub from Central and South America, was introduced to Pakistan to provide fuel wood and to stabilise sand. It has since spread over large areas of grazing land and river banks in Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why Prosopis juliflora has been able to spread so rapidly in Sindh.
parts.answer: No natural predators, herbivores or diseases that control it in its new range; it tolerates drought and salty soils better than native plants; it produces many seeds that are spread by livestock eating the pods; it outcompetes native plants for water and light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: lack of natural predators/pathogens; tolerance of drought/salinity; large seed production; seeds dispersed by animals; outcompetes native species (deep roots for water, shading).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the spread of an invasive species such as P. juliflora can reduce biodiversity.
parts.answer: It outcompetes native plants, which decline or disappear locally; animals that depend on those plants for food or habitat also decline, so species diversity (and the variety of habitats) falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: native plants outcompeted / lost. 1 mark: knock-on loss of animals that depend on them / habitat becomes uniform.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two methods that could be used to control P. juliflora and give one disadvantage of one of them.
parts.answer: Mechanical removal (uprooting/cutting); herbicides; using the wood for fuel/charcoal to encourage harvesting; introducing a biological control agent (seed-eating insect) after testing; replanting native species. Disadvantage: e.g. herbicides may kill native plants or pollute water; cutting is labour-intensive and stumps resprout; a biological control agent might attack native species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two methods. 1 mark for a valid disadvantage of one of them.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the elephant population in a fenced reserve may need to be controlled.
parts.answer: With no natural predators and no way to migrate out of the reserve, the population grows beyond the carrying capacity; elephants destroy trees and vegetation, reducing habitat and food for other species (and for themselves), lowering biodiversity.
parts.working: 1 mark: population exceeds carrying capacity / no predators or migration. 1 mark: overgrazing / habitat damage reduces biodiversity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of culling and of contraception as methods of controlling the population.
parts.answer: Culling: reduces numbers quickly; meat/ivory/hide may provide income; but it is unpopular/ethically controversial, disturbs social groups and causes stress to remaining animals. Contraception (e.g. immunocontraceptive vaccine darted into females): humane and reversible, keeps social groups intact; but slow to reduce numbers (elephants are long-lived), must be repeated, expensive and needs each female to be identified and treated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four, with at least one advantage and one disadvantage for each method: culling fast / income vs ethical objection / social disruption; contraception humane / reversible / groups intact vs slow effect / repeated treatment / cost / labour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the role of CITES in conservation.
parts.answer: CITES is an international agreement that regulates or bans international trade in endangered species and products made from them; species are listed in appendices according to how threatened they are (e.g. Appendix I – commercial trade banned; others need permits).
parts.working: 1 mark: international agreement controlling trade in endangered species / their products. 1 mark: species listed in appendices with different levels of restriction / permits needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one mountain area of Pakistan, a small number of permits to hunt old male markhor are sold each year to foreign hunters. Most of the money goes to the local community, which employs game guards. Suggest how this scheme can help the markhor population to increase.
parts.answer: Local people gain income from markhor, so they value live animals and stop poaching; game guards protect markhor from illegal hunting; only a few old males past their prime breeding age are taken, so the breeding population is hardly affected; money can also be used for habitat protection and community projects.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: income gives incentive to conserve; reduced poaching / guards employed; only few old males removed so breeding not affected; funds habitat protection; community support for conservation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The markhor's IUCN Red List category improved from Endangered to Near Threatened. State what the IUCN Red List is.
parts.answer: A list that assesses and classifies species according to their risk of extinction (e.g. Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how national parks such as Khunjerab National Park help to conserve endangered species.
parts.answer: Habitat is protected from development, farming and logging; hunting is banned or controlled; whole ecosystems are protected, so food chains and interactions are kept; species can be monitored and studied.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: habitat protected; hunting/poaching controlled; whole ecosystem/all species protected; monitoring/research; controlled tourism raises money.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Astola Island became Pakistan's first marine protected area. Suggest two activities that might be restricted in a marine protected area and explain how one of them benefits marine species.
parts.answer: Fishing (especially trawling or net fishing); collecting corals/shells; anchoring boats; dumping waste/pollution; development of the coastline. E.g. banning fishing lets fish populations recover and breed; this provides food for other species and fish spread to surrounding areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two restricted activities. 1 mark for a valid explanation of benefit.

stem:
Forty captive-bred gazelles were released into a protected desert reserve in 2014. The population was counted every two years.
Year: 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024
Number: 40, 52, 71, 66, 94, 118

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in population from release (2014) to 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest reasons for the fall in numbers between 2018 and 2020.
parts.answer: Drought/reduced food or water; disease; predation; poaching; animals moving out of the reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: All 40 animals released came from one captive population. Discuss whether this reintroduction can be considered a long-term success.
parts.answer: Success: population has nearly tripled and is breeding in the wild. Concerns: all descended from 40 related animals, so genetic diversity is low – risk of inbreeding and less ability to adapt to disease or climate change; numbers fluctuate and the population is still small; long-term success needs continued monitoring, protection and perhaps introduction of unrelated animals.
parts.working: 1 mark: evidence of success (increase, breeding). 1 mark: low genetic diversity / founder effect / inbreeding risk. 1 mark: still small/fluctuating, needs further protection or new genetic stock.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the taxonomic ranks in order from domain to species.
parts.answer: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
parts.working: 2 marks all in correct order; 1 mark with one error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tiger is Panthera tigris and the lion is Panthera leo. State the lowest taxonomic rank that both share and explain how you know.
parts.answer: Genus; both have the same first part of the binomial name (Panthera), which is the genus.
parts.working: 1 mark: genus. 1 mark: first name in binomial = genus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the domain and kingdom to which the tiger belongs.
parts.answer: Eukarya; Animalia.
parts.working: 1 mark (both needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table to compare the three domains.
Feature | Bacteria | Archaea | Eukarya
nucleus surrounded by envelope | ? | ? | ?
size of ribosomes in cytoplasm | ? | ? | ?
peptidoglycan in cell wall | ? | ? | ?
membrane lipids | ? | ? | ?
parts.answer:
nucleus: absent, absent, present
ribosomes: 70S, 70S, 80S
peptidoglycan: present, absent, absent
membrane lipids: unbranched fatty acids with ester bonds; branched chains with ether bonds; unbranched fatty acids with ester bonds
parts.working: 1 mark per correct row.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why organisms in the domain Archaea were once classified with bacteria.
parts.answer: They are prokaryotic: single cells with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, similar in size and shape to bacteria.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature in which Archaea are more similar to Eukarya than to Bacteria.
parts.answer: Their RNA polymerase is more complex (similar to that of eukaryotes) / some have histone proteins associated with DNA / similar initiation of protein synthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem:
Descriptions of four eukaryotic organisms:
W: multicellular body made of thread-like hyphae; cell walls of chitin; feeds by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products; stores glycogen
X: single cell with chloroplasts and one flagellum; no cell wall; can also take in food when kept in the dark
Y: multicellular; cellulose cell walls; chloroplasts; stores starch
Z: multicellular; no cell walls; heterotrophic, ingests food; nervous coordination

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the kingdom to which each organism belongs.
parts.answer: W Fungi; X Protoctista; Y Plantae; Z Animalia.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why organism X is not placed in the plant kingdom, even though it has chloroplasts.
parts.answer: It is unicellular and has no cellulose cell wall; plants are multicellular with cellulose cell walls (and it can move by a flagellum and feed heterotrophically).
parts.working: 1 mark: unicellular (plants are multicellular). 1 mark: no cellulose cell wall / has flagellum.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Information about the genetic material of four viruses:
Influenza virus: RNA, one strand, in eight segments
Smallpox (variola) virus: DNA, two complementary strands
T4 bacteriophage: DNA, two complementary strands
HIV: RNA, one strand (two identical copies per particle)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why viruses are not classified in any of the three domains.
parts.answer: Viruses are not cells (acellular: no cytoplasm, ribosomes or cell membrane); they cannot metabolise or reproduce outside a host cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: not made of cells / no ribosomes or cytoplasm. 1 mark: only replicate inside host cells / no metabolism.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the two features of the nucleic acid that are used to classify viruses.
parts.answer: Whether it is DNA or RNA; whether it is single-stranded or double-stranded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use these features to classify each virus.
parts.answer: Influenza virus: single-stranded RNA; smallpox virus: double-stranded DNA; T4 bacteriophage: double-stranded DNA; HIV: single-stranded RNA.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A segment of the gene for ribosomal RNA was sequenced in four organisms. The table shows the number of base differences between each pair of organisms in a 100-base region.
J–K: 31; J–L: 33; J–M: 6; K–L: 35; K–M: 30; L–M: 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, state which organism is most closely related to organism J and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Organism M; it has the fewest differences in its rRNA gene sequence from J (6), so they shared a common ancestor most recently.
parts.working: 1 mark: M. 1 mark: fewest base differences → most recent common ancestor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Organisms J and M are prokaryotes that live in hot, acidic springs. Organism K is a bacterium found in soil. Organism L is a yeast. Suggest which domain J and M belong to, giving a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Archaea; J and M differ from K (a bacterium) by about as many bases as from L (a eukaryote), so they are not closely related to bacteria even though they are prokaryotes.
parts.working: 1 mark: Archaea. 1 mark: as different from bacterium K as from eukaryote L (data quote: 31 and 33 differences).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why comparing sequences of genes such as ribosomal RNA genes led to the three-domain classification system.
parts.answer: rRNA genes are found in all organisms and change slowly by mutation; the number of differences reflects time since organisms shared a common ancestor; sequencing showed archaea were as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes, so three groups were needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: all organisms have the gene / differences accumulate over time (molecular clock). 1 mark: archaea shown to be distinct from bacteria, giving three domains.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Biodiversity can be considered at three levels. Name and describe each level.
parts.answer: Ecosystem (habitat) diversity – the range of different ecosystems/habitats in an area; species diversity – the number of different species and the evenness of their abundance (species richness and relative abundance); genetic diversity – the variety of alleles within a species/population.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ecosystem/habitat diversity; species diversity (number and relative abundance of species); genetic diversity (variation of alleles within species).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a student could place quadrats randomly in a grassland, and explain why random sampling is used.
parts.answer: Lay two tapes at right angles along two sides of the area to form axes; use a random number generator to select pairs of coordinates; place the quadrat at each coordinate. Random sampling avoids bias in choosing where to sample, so the samples are representative of the whole area.
parts.working: 1 mark: grid / tapes as axes. 1 mark: random number generator / table for coordinates. 1 mark: avoids bias, representative samples (allows statistical testing).

stem:
A student counted the plants of each species in quadrats in two areas of the Margalla Hills: site A, natural forest edge, and site B, a pine plantation.
Site A (species 1–6): 18, 12, 9, 7, 3, 1
Site B (species 1–4): 38, 6, 4, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Simpson's index of diversity (D = 1 − Σ(n/N)²) for each site. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Site A: D = 0.76; site B: D = 0.40

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the biodiversity of the two sites and suggest a reason for the difference.
parts.answer: Site A (natural forest) has higher diversity: more species and more even numbers; site B is dominated by one species. The plantation has one tree species, so fewer niches/habitats and food sources; management (clearing undergrowth) removes other plants.
parts.working: 1 mark: A higher diversity – more species and more even abundance (B dominated by species 1). 1 mark: plantation = single tree species / fewer niches / management.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pitfall traps were set in a cotton field near Multan. 60 ground beetles were caught, marked with a dot of non-toxic paint on the underside and released. Two days later 75 beetles were caught, of which 12 were marked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the estimated population size of ground beetles using the Lincoln index.
parts.answer: 375 beetles

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three assumptions that must be true for this estimate to be valid.
parts.answer: Marked beetles mix randomly with the rest of the population; marks do not rub off; marking does not affect survival or behaviour (e.g. make beetles more visible to predators); no significant births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples; all beetles equally likely to be caught.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An ecologist recorded the percentage tree cover and the number of bird species at eight sites around Islamabad.
Site: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Tree cover / %: 12, 25, 38, 47, 55, 63, 71, 84
Bird species: 9, 14, 12, 19, 17, 24, 28, 26

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between percentage tree cover and the number of bird species.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Show your working. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1: ranks – tree cover 1–8 in order; bird species ranks 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7. M1: Σd² = 6. A1: 1 − 36 ÷ 504 = 0.93.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.738. Explain what your result shows.
parts.answer: 0.93 is greater than 0.738, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant positive correlation between tree cover and the number of bird species (more tree cover, more bird species).
parts.working: 1 mark: rs > critical value, reject null. 1 mark: significant positive correlation (not chance at p < 0.05).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a high tree cover is associated with more bird species.
parts.answer: More trees provide more niches – nesting sites, shelter and food sources (insects, fruit) for different species.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student placed 10 quadrats, each 0.5 m × 0.5 m (0.25 m²), at random on a school playing field of area 1200 m² and counted the dandelion plants in each.
Numbers: 3, 5, 2, 0, 4, 6, 1, 3, 2, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of dandelion plants per quadrat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean density of dandelions per m².
parts.answer: 12 per m²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the total number of dandelions on the field.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why this estimate may not be accurate.
parts.answer: Only 10 quadrats sampled (small sample); dandelions may be clumped/unevenly distributed; counting errors at quadrat edges.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one valid reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A survey estimated the number of mature individuals of a vulture species in a region at 3400 in 2014 and 1450 in 2024.
One criterion used by the IUCN states that a population reduction over 10 years of at least 80 % qualifies a species as Critically Endangered, at least 50 % as Endangered and at least 30 % as Vulnerable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the population between 2014 and 2024. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the criterion given to state the category the species qualifies for, and explain your choice.
parts.answer: Endangered, because the decline (57.4 %) is at least 50 % but less than 80 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: Endangered with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean decrease in number of individuals per year.
parts.answer: 195 individuals per year

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a survey of mature individuals, rather than all individuals, is used to judge extinction risk.
parts.answer: Only mature individuals can breed and produce the next generation, so their number determines whether the population can recover.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students compared seaweed cover on two rocky shores near Karachi. On each shore they chose five places that looked typical, placed a 1 m² quadrat at each and estimated by eye the percentage cover of each seaweed species. One shore was sampled at low tide on a morning, the other in the afternoon a week later when the tide was coming in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three limitations of this method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Percentage cover estimated by eye is subjective – use a quadrat divided into 100 small squares/point quadrat, and the same person to estimate. Quadrats placed where the student chose – use random coordinates (or regular intervals along a belt transect). Only 5 quadrats – sample more (e.g. 20) until the running mean levels off. Some species may be misidentified – use an identification key/photograph. Samples taken at different states of the tide or on different days – sample at the same time on the same day.
parts.working: 1 mark per limitation and 1 mark per matching improvement, for three pairs (max 6).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Students used mark–release–recapture to estimate the number of land snails in a garden. They noted three problems:
1: water-based paint used to mark the shells washed off in rain
2: bright paint was put on the top of the shell, where birds could see it
3: the second sample was taken 20 minutes after release, close to the release point

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each problem, explain how it would affect the population estimate (too high or too low).
parts.answer: 1: marked snails in the second sample are fewer than they should be, so the estimate is too high. 2: if marked snails are eaten more, fewer marked are recaptured, so the estimate is too high. 3: marked snails have not mixed, so recapturing near the release point gives too many marked snails (estimate too low) – or too few if sampling elsewhere (too high).
parts.working: 1 mark each: (1) too high; (2) too high; (3) explained either way – not randomly mixed, so ratio not representative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement for each problem.
parts.answer: 1: use waterproof, non-toxic paint/permanent marker and check it does not rub off in a trial. 2: mark on the underside or in an inconspicuous place / use a dull colour. 3: leave a longer time (e.g. 24 h) for mixing and sample from the whole area.
parts.working: 1 mark per improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Belt transects were used to sample butterflies at six urban and six rural sites near Lahore. Simpson's index of diversity was calculated for each site.
Urban: mean D = 0.62, 95 % confidence interval ± 0.07
Rural: mean D = 0.81, 95 % confidence interval ± 0.05

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that butterfly diversity is higher in rural sites than in urban sites. Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Mean D is higher in rural sites (0.81 vs 0.62). The 95 % confidence intervals (rural 0.76–0.86, urban 0.55–0.69) do not overlap, so the difference is significant and the conclusion is supported for these sites. But only 6 sites of each type, sampled in one season/year, in one city, so it may not apply generally.
parts.working: 1 mark: rural higher with data. 1 mark: CIs do not overlap so significant. 1 mark: limitation – few sites / one season / one region.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why butterfly diversity is lower in urban areas.
parts.answer: Fewer flowering plants/nectar sources and larval food plants; habitat loss and fragmentation by buildings and roads; pollution/pesticide use; higher temperature/light at night.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lichen diversity on tree trunks was recorded at seven distances (5 m to 200 m) from a busy road. Spearman's rank correlation between distance from the road and lichen diversity gave rs = 0.86. The critical value for n = 7 at p = 0.05 is 0.79.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that pollution from vehicles on the road causes the decrease in lichen diversity. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The significant positive correlation shows lichen diversity increases with distance from the road (rs = 0.86 > 0.79), which is consistent with pollution from traffic. However, correlation does not prove causation; other variables also change with distance, e.g. dust, light, humidity, trampling, tree species or bark pH; pollution was not measured; only one road and 7 points, so the conclusion is tentative.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation significant and positive, supports link. 1 mark: correlation ≠ causation. 1 mark: named confounding variable(s) changing with distance. 1 mark: pollution not measured / small sample / one road.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one further measurement that would test whether vehicle pollution is the cause.
parts.answer: Measure the concentration of nitrogen dioxide/sulfur dioxide (or particulates) in the air at each distance and correlate with lichen diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the species richness of plants in a grazed area and an ungrazed (fenced) area of hillside.
parts.answer: Choose two areas of similar slope, aspect and soil; mark out each with tapes as axes; use random number coordinates to place 1 m² (or 0.25 m²) quadrats; use at least 20 quadrats in each area (or until a running mean levels off); count the number of different plant species in each quadrat, using an identification key; also record abundance/percentage cover if Simpson's index is to be calculated; sample both areas at the same time of year; calculate mean species per quadrat and compare with a t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: areas matched for other variables (slope, aspect, soil); random sampling method with coordinates; quadrat size stated; sufficient number of quadrats (≥10, ideally 20+); DV species per quadrat identified with key; same time/season; abundance recorded for Simpson's index; means calculated; t-test to compare.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field investigation into how the abundance of a fern changes with light intensity from the inside of a woodland into an open field.
parts.answer: Lay a tape from inside the wood, across the edge and into the field; place quadrats at regular intervals (e.g. every 2 m) along the tape – a belt or interrupted belt transect; in each quadrat record the abundance of the fern as percentage cover or number of fronds; measure light intensity at ground level in each quadrat with a light meter, at the same height and at the same time of day (or several readings averaged); repeat with two or three more transects at random positions along the wood edge; also record soil moisture/temperature as other variables; plot abundance against light intensity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: transect line across the edge; quadrats at regular intervals (belt/interrupted belt); abundance measure (% cover, count); light meter readings at each quadrat; same time of day / weather / height of meter; repeat transects; record other variables (soil moisture, pH, temperature); at least 10 sampling points; plot scatter graph of abundance against light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test that should be used to analyse the results and explain your choice.
parts.answer: Spearman's rank correlation – to test for a correlation between two variables (light intensity and abundance) whose data may not be normally distributed.
parts.working: 1 mark: Spearman's rank with reason (testing correlation between two variables).

stem: A student wants to find out whether the number of mayfly larvae in streams flowing into Rawal Lake is related to the concentration of dissolved oxygen in the water. She will use a kick-sampling net for 1 minute at each site and measure dissolved oxygen with a meter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: dissolved oxygen concentration (site). Dependent: number (abundance) of mayfly larvae.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a field study the other variables cannot be controlled. Name three variables that might affect the number of mayfly larvae and describe how the student could take account of them.
parts.answer: Any three: water temperature; flow rate; type of stream bed (stones vs mud); depth; pH; shading. Choose sites that are similar in these variables (e.g. same depth and stone size), and measure them at each site (thermometer, flow meter, pH probe) so that their effects can be considered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three variables (max 3). 1 mark for: choose similar sites or measure and record them to take into account.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
A wetland plant was counted in four zones of equal area around a pond. The total was 120 plants.
Zone 1: 28; zone 2: 41; zone 3: 19; zone 4: 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: The plants are distributed evenly (randomly) across the four zones; any difference from the expected numbers is due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of χ², using χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom is 7.82. Explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: 8.33 > 7.82, so reject the null hypothesis; the difference between observed and expected numbers is significant – the plants are not evenly distributed (more in zone 2, fewer in zone 3).
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² greater than critical value, reject null. 1 mark: distribution significantly different from even / not due to chance.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students will collect invertebrates by kick-sampling in a shallow, fast-flowing stream in the hills and measure the water temperature and flow rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Slipping or falling into the stream/drowning – work in pairs, wear boots with grip, stay in shallow water, check water level and weather. Infection from contaminated water (e.g. bacteria from animal urine or sewage) – wear gloves, cover cuts, wash hands. Sunburn/heat stroke – hat, sunscreen, drinking water. Insect or snake bites – long sleeves, look before placing hands. Getting lost – tell someone the route and return time.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium – working in or near flowing water has a risk of serious harm, although it can be reduced by the precautions.
parts.working: 1 mark: level with justification (accept low with good justification of shallow water and supervision).

author: HomiLabs

stem: An ecologist plans to measure Simpson's index of diversity of plants in quadrats at 100 m intervals from 100 m to 1000 m from a cement factory, where dust from the factory settles on the vegetation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Species diversity of plants increases as distance from the cement factory increases.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between distance from the factory and plant species diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the results and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Diversity will be lowest near the factory and increase with distance, because dust settling on leaves near the factory blocks light and stomata (and changes soil pH), so only a few tolerant species survive there.
parts.working: 1 mark: prediction (diversity increases with distance). 1 mark: explanation (dust reduces photosynthesis / alters soil pH; only tolerant species survive).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During which stage of mitosis do the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids move to opposite poles of the cell?
A prophase
B metaphase
C anaphase
D telophase
parts.answer: C anaphase
parts.working: In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle microtubules shorten, pulling the chromatids (now chromosomes) to opposite poles. B is wrong: at metaphase the chromosomes are lined up on the equator but the chromatids are still joined.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Tomato cells have a diploid number of 24 chromosomes. How many chromatids are present in one tomato cell at metaphase of mitosis?
A 12
B 24
C 48
D 96
parts.working: DNA was replicated in S phase, so each of the 24 chromosomes consists of two sister chromatids: 24 × 2 = 48. B is the number of chromosomes, not chromatids.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cell in G1 of interphase contains 16 arbitrary units of DNA. How much DNA is in the cell at the end of G2, and in each daughter cell immediately after cytokinesis?
A end of G2 16; each daughter cell 8
B end of G2 32; each daughter cell 16
C end of G2 32; each daughter cell 32
D end of G2 16; each daughter cell 16
parts.answer: B end of G2 32; each daughter cell 16
parts.working: DNA is replicated in S phase so G2 has 2 × 16 = 32 units; mitosis shares this equally, so each daughter has 16 units, the same as the parent in G1. A halves the DNA as if this were meiosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about mitosis is correct?
A Homologous chromosomes pair up during prophase.
B The daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell.
C The chromosome number is halved in each daughter cell.
D Crossing over between chromatids produces new combinations of alleles.
parts.answer: B The daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell.
parts.working: Mitosis produces two genetically identical nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent. A, C and D all describe meiosis.

stem:
A student made a squash of a stained garlic root tip and counted the cells in each stage of the cell cycle.
Interphase 412; prophase 46; metaphase 18; anaphase 9; telophase 15.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mitotic index of this root tip. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 cells in mitosis = 46 + 18 + 9 + 15 = 88; total = 500. A1 mitotic index = 88/500 = 0.176.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cell cycle in this root tip lasts 24 hours. Assuming the number of cells seen in a stage is proportional to the time spent in that stage, calculate how long the cells spend in metaphase. Give your answer in minutes to the nearest minute.
parts.answer: 52 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a root tip, rather than a region 2 cm behind the tip, was used to find the mitotic index.
parts.answer: The root tip contains a meristem where cells are actively dividing, so many cells are in mitosis.
parts.working: B1 meristem / zone of cell division at the tip; cells further back are elongating or differentiating and no longer divide.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A farmer in Punjab cuts his hand on a sickle. Over the next ten days the skin heals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three roles of mitosis in multicellular organisms.
parts.answer: Any three of: growth; repair of damaged tissue; replacement of worn-out cells; asexual reproduction; clonal expansion of lymphocytes in an immune response.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: growth (increase in cell number); repair / wound healing; replacement of cells such as skin or gut lining or red blood cell precursors; asexual reproduction (e.g. potato tubers, Hydra budding); clonal expansion of B and T lymphocytes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that the daughter cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical to the parent cell when skin is repaired after a cut.
parts.answer: The new cells must have the same genes so they can produce the same proteins and function as skin cells; genetic stability keeps the tissue working and avoids harmful mutations.
parts.working: B1 same genetic information / same alleles as the parent cells; B1 so new cells can carry out the same function / make the same proteins as the cells they replace.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the behaviour of the chromosomes during prophase and metaphase of mitosis.
parts.answer: Prophase: chromosomes condense / shorten and thicken and become visible as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere; nuclear envelope breaks down. Metaphase: chromosomes attach to spindle microtubules at their centromeres/kinetochores and line up on the equator.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: chromosomes condense / coil / become visible (prophase); each seen as two chromatids joined at the centromere; nuclear envelope / nucleolus disappears so chromosomes lie in the cytoplasm; spindle fibres attach at centromere / kinetochore; chromosomes lined up on the equator / metaphase plate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens during telophase.
parts.answer: Chromosomes arrive at the poles and uncoil / decondense; a nuclear envelope reforms around each group, giving two nuclei; spindle breaks down.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: chromatids reach poles; chromosomes uncoil / become less visible; nuclear envelope and nucleolus reform; spindle disappears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Colchicine prevents tubulin molecules joining together to form microtubules. Explain why cells treated with colchicine do not complete mitosis.
parts.answer: No spindle forms, so chromosomes cannot attach to spindle fibres, cannot line up at the equator, and chromatids cannot be pulled apart to the poles in anaphase.
