parts.answer: Lipid gives more energy per unit mass, so the bird carries less weight for the same energy store (and produces metabolic water).
parts.working: B1 more energy per gram so lighter load (accept metabolic water).

author: HomiLabs

stem: An adult body contains about 250 g of ATP at any one time, yet hydrolyses about 70 kg of ATP per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of times each ATP molecule is resynthesised from ADP and Pi per day.
parts.answer: 280 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relative molecular mass of ATP is 507. Hydrolysis of one mole releases 30.5 kJ. Calculate the energy released per day by hydrolysis of ATP, in kJ, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why cells do not store large amounts of ATP.
parts.answer: ATP is unstable / readily hydrolysed so cannot be stored for long; it is quickly regenerated from ADP and Pi when needed, so a small pool recycled rapidly is enough; energy is stored instead in glycogen or lipid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: ATP unstable / hydrolyses easily; rapid turnover from ADP + Pi makes storage unnecessary; would affect water potential / takes up space; energy stored as glycogen / starch / lipid instead.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methylene blue is a redox indicator that turns colourless when it is reduced by the hydrogen released by dehydrogenase enzymes in respiring yeast. Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration of yeast using methylene blue.
parts.answer: Prepare yeast suspension (e.g. 10 g dried yeast in 100 cm³ of 5 % glucose solution) and leave to activate; place 10 cm³ yeast suspension in tubes in thermostatically controlled water baths at 5 temperatures (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C) for 10 min to equilibrate; add 1 cm³ of 0.05 % methylene blue, mix by inverting once, start timer; record time for blue colour to disappear (compare with a colour standard of yeast suspension without indicator); do not shake (oxygen would reoxidise the dye); control: boiled yeast; rate = 1/time; 3 repeats at each temperature and mean; standardise yeast concentration, glucose concentration and volume, dye volume and concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: at least 5 temperatures with suitable range; method of controlling temperature (water bath, thermometer check); equilibration of yeast and dye separately before mixing; same volume and concentration of yeast suspension; same concentration of glucose; same volume of methylene blue; measure time taken to decolourise; end point standardised (colour standard); avoid shaking / cover with liquid paraffin to keep oxygen out; control with boiled yeast; rate = 1/t; 3 repeats and mean; safety (e.g. methylene blue stains, hot water).

stem: A student wants to find out whether yeast respires glucose, sucrose, maltose and lactose at different rates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would make 50 cm³ of a 2 % sugar solution of each sugar, from solid sugar and distilled water.
parts.answer: Weigh 1.0 g of sugar, dissolve in some distilled water and make up to 50 cm³ in a volumetric flask (or measuring cylinder).
parts.working: M1 2 g per 100 cm³ → 1.0 g per 50 cm³; A1 dissolve and make up to total volume 50 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could compare the rate of respiration of yeast with each sugar by measuring carbon dioxide production.
parts.answer: Mix the same volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of each sugar solution with the same mass of yeast (e.g. 1 g) in a flask connected to a gas syringe; keep at 30 °C in a water bath; allow 5 min to equilibrate; measure volume of gas collected every minute for 10 min (or total volume in a fixed time); rate = volume ÷ time; control with water and no sugar; repeat 3 times.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: same yeast mass / suspension volume; same volume and concentration of each sugar; collect CO₂ in gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder over water; constant temperature water bath; equilibration time; measure volume over a fixed time / calculate rate; control with no sugar; repeats and mean.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The time taken for methylene blue to decolourise in tubes of yeast suspension at different temperatures:
20 °C: 480 s
30 °C: 300 s
40 °C: 190 s
50 °C: 120 s
60 °C: 260 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of respiration at each temperature as 1000/t, where t is time in seconds. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 1000/t for each; A1 all five correct to 1 d.p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate between 20 °C and 50 °C, using unrounded rates. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A respirometer containing 2.0 g of woodlice and soda lime was set up at 20 °C. The distance moved by the liquid in the capillary (radius 0.4 mm) from the start was recorded.
1 min: 8 mm
2 min: 17 mm
3 min: 25 mm
4 min: 33 mm
5 min: 42 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed between the readings at 1 minute and 5 minutes. Use V = πr²l and give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 17.1 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per gram per hour. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 128 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured the oxygen uptake of germinating seeds using a simple respirometer on the laboratory bench next to a sunny window. She sealed the tube with a rubber bung, started timing immediately and took one reading of the position of the liquid after 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three sources of error in this investigation and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: e.g. room temperature changed during the experiment → place respirometer in a thermostatically controlled water bath; no thermobarometer, so pressure changes not allowed for → set up a control tube with glass beads of the same volume; leaks at joints → seal with petroleum jelly and test for leaks; difficult to read meniscus position → use a scale with mm divisions and read at eye level / mark with fine pen; seeds not given time to equilibrate → leave for 10 min with tap open before starting; only one reading → repeat three times.
parts.working: For each of three: B1 error relevant to this method; B1 matching improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student used respirometers to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration of fly maggots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two standardised variables.
parts.answer: IV: temperature. DV: rate of oxygen uptake (distance moved by liquid per minute). Standardised (any two): mass of maggots; number / age / species of maggots; volume and mass of soda lime; diameter of capillary; time allowed to equilibrate; time of measurement.
parts.working: B1 IV temperature; B1 DV rate of oxygen uptake / distance per unit time; B1 any two standardised variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a control for this experiment and explain why it is needed.
parts.answer: A respirometer with an equal volume of glass beads (or dead maggots) instead of living maggots, to show that movement of the liquid is due to respiration and to correct for temperature and pressure changes.
parts.working: B1 tube with glass beads / no living organisms; B1 shows changes are due to respiration / allows correction.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Yeast was added to a sealed flask containing 5 % glucose solution at 30 °C. The total volume of CO₂ released (cm³) was recorded every 10 hours.
0 h: 0
10 h: 4
20 h: 11
30 h: 19
40 h: 24
50 h: 26
60 h: 26

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the total volume of CO₂ produced over the 60 hours.
parts.answer: CO₂ production rose slowly at first (0–10 h), then rapidly between 10 and 30 h, then slowed and stopped at 26 cm³ after 50 h.
parts.working: B1 initial slow increase then rapid increase; B1 levels off / no further increase at 26 cm³ from 50 h.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain these results using your knowledge of respiration in yeast.
parts.answer: At first the yeast population is small / adjusting, so little CO₂; yeast then multiplies and respires glucose rapidly, aerobically while oxygen lasts then anaerobically, releasing CO₂ in the link reaction and Krebs cycle and by decarboxylation of pyruvate to ethanal; CO₂ production stops because glucose is used up and/or ethanol accumulates to a toxic concentration, killing yeast / inhibiting enzymes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: lag – few yeast cells / enzymes being synthesised; population increases so more respiration; oxygen used up so anaerobic respiration (fermentation); CO₂ from decarboxylation (pyruvate → ethanal, or Krebs cycle while aerobic); glucose substrate runs out; ethanol accumulates and is toxic / denatures enzymes; pH falls as CO₂ dissolves.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The volume of oxygen absorbed by 20 g of germinating pea seeds was measured.
0 min: 0.0 cm³
2 min: 1.8 cm³
4 min: 3.6 cm³
6 min: 5.5 cm³
8 min: 7.3 cm³
10 min: 9.0 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would plot these results on a graph.
parts.answer: Time (min) on the x-axis and volume of oxygen absorbed (cm³) on the y-axis; both axes labelled with units; scale using more than half the grid with even intervals; points plotted as small crosses; line of best fit drawn (points lie close to a straight line).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: correct axes orientation; labels with units; suitable linear scale using > half the grid; accurate plotting; ruled line of best fit (or point to point if justified).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake between 2 and 8 minutes, in cm³ per minute, to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.92 cm³ min⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to measure the rate of CO₂ production by yeast in glucose solutions of 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: The rate of respiration of yeast increases as glucose concentration increases (until a maximum is reached).
parts.working: B1 testable hypothesis linking glucose concentration and rate, with direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the shape of the graph of rate of CO₂ production against glucose concentration and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Rate increases steeply at low glucose concentrations, then levels off at high concentrations; at low concentration glucose is the limiting factor; at high concentration enzymes / glucose transport proteins are saturated (or yeast concentration limits), so rate cannot rise further; very high concentrations may decrease the rate by causing water loss by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 rises then levels off (plateau); B1 glucose limiting at low concentration / more collisions with enzymes; B1 enzymes / carrier proteins saturated or another factor limiting at high concentration (allow fall due to osmotic water loss).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rate of oxygen uptake by germinating wheat grains (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) at different temperatures:
10 °C: 4.2
20 °C: 8.1
30 °C: 15.6
40 °C: 18.0
50 °C: 6.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on the rate of oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Rate increases from 4.2 at 10 °C to a maximum of 18.0 at 40 °C, then falls sharply to 6.3 at 50 °C.
parts.working: B1 increase up to 40 °C, then decrease; B1 data quoted with units, e.g. maximum 18.0 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 40 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results between 40 °C and 50 °C.
parts.answer: Respiratory enzymes (dehydrogenases, ATP synthase) are denatured: hydrogen bonds break, the active site changes shape so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured / bonds in tertiary structure broken; B1 active site shape changed, substrate no longer fits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student concluded that the optimum temperature for respiration in these seeds is 40 °C. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The highest rate recorded was at 40 °C, but the true optimum could be anywhere between 30 and 50 °C because readings were taken only every 10 °C; more readings between 35 and 45 °C would be needed; no repeats shown.
parts.working: B1 highest rate at 40 °C so supports; B1 large intervals — optimum could be between 30 and 50 °C / need smaller intervals / repeats.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
One student in Islamabad skipped for different lengths of time and measured her pulse rate immediately afterwards, resting for 15 minutes between trials.
0 min: 72 beats per minute
1 min: 98 beats per minute
2 min: 118 beats per minute
3 min: 131 beats per minute
4 min: 134 beats per minute

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the duration of skipping and the pulse rate.
parts.answer: Pulse rate increases as duration increases, from 72 beats per minute at rest to 134 after 4 minutes; the increase gets smaller each minute and the rate levels off between 3 and 4 minutes.
parts.working: B1 positive relationship / increases; B1 levels off (increase of only 3 between 3 and 4 min) with data quote.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in pulse rate after 2 minutes compared with resting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why these results cannot be used to draw a conclusion about all students.
parts.answer: Only one student was tested (no repeats, no range of ages, fitness or sex).
parts.working: B1 single individual / small sample.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
100 wheat grains were placed on filter paper soaked in sodium chloride solutions of different concentration. The percentage that germinated after 7 days was recorded.
0 mmol dm⁻³: 96 %
50 mmol dm⁻³: 90 %
100 mmol dm⁻³: 71 %
150 mmol dm⁻³: 38 %
200 mmol dm⁻³: 9 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion that can be drawn from the data.
parts.answer: Increasing salt concentration decreases the percentage germination of wheat seeds (most sharply above 50 mmol dm⁻³).
parts.working: B1 higher salt concentration → lower germination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your knowledge of water potential to explain the results.
parts.answer: Salt lowers the water potential of the solution; the water potential gradient between the solution and the seed is reduced (or reversed), so less water enters the seed by osmosis; water is needed to activate enzymes / mobilise food stores (e.g. amylase hydrolysing starch) so fewer seeds germinate.
parts.working: B1 solution has lower (more negative) water potential; B1 less water absorbed by osmosis / imbibition; B1 water needed for enzyme activity / hydrolysis of stores / cell expansion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers in parts of Punjab have soils that are becoming more saline. Suggest one further investigation that would help them choose which wheat variety to plant.
parts.answer: Compare germination (or growth) of several varieties at the same salt concentrations found in their soil.
parts.working: B1 compare different varieties at a range of salt concentrations / test using their own soil samples.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured the light intensity and the height of 12 plants of one species growing along a path from under trees into open ground. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs, was calculated as 0.81.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the value of rs shows about the relationship between the two variables.
parts.answer: A strong positive correlation: plants receiving more light grew taller.
parts.working: B1 strong positive correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of rs at p = 0.05 for 12 pairs of readings is 0.587. State what the student can conclude.
parts.answer: 0.81 > 0.587 so the null hypothesis (no correlation) is rejected; the positive correlation is significant – the probability it is due to chance is less than 5 %.
parts.working: B1 compares rs with critical value correctly; B1 reject null / significant correlation (not due to chance).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student then concluded that light intensity causes plants to grow taller. Explain why this conclusion is not fully justified by the data.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show cause; other factors that vary with light in the field (e.g. soil moisture, temperature, nutrient levels, trampling) were not controlled and may affect height.
parts.working: B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 named uncontrolled variable that could vary with position.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Potato cylinders were left in sucrose solutions for 24 hours. The mean percentage change in mass was:
0 mol dm⁻³: +12.4 %
0.2 mol dm⁻³: +5.8 %
0.4 mol dm⁻³: −1.6 %
0.6 mol dm⁻³: −7.9 %
0.8 mol dm⁻³: −12.1 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the sucrose concentration at which there would be no change in mass, assuming a straight line between the two readings either side of zero. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.36 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this concentration tells you about the potato tissue.
parts.answer: At this concentration the water potential of the sucrose solution equals the water potential of the potato cells, so there is no net movement of water by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 water potential of tissue = water potential of solution; B1 no net osmosis / no net water movement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the results are given as percentage change in mass rather than change in mass.
parts.answer: The cylinders had different starting masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison.
parts.working: B1 different initial masses.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student counted the stomata in ten fields of view on each surface of bean (Phaseolus) leaves.
upper surface: mean 36 stomata per mm², standard deviation 9
lower surface: mean 248 stomata per mm², standard deviation 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the stomatal density on the two surfaces.
parts.answer: The lower surface has many more stomata (mean 248 per mm²) than the upper surface (mean 36 per mm²), about seven times as many; the lower surface also shows more variation (SD 22 compared with 9).
parts.working: B1 lower surface has more stomata, with figures; B1 comparison of spread (SD) or ratio ≈ 7 times.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an advantage to the plant of having most stomata on the lower surface.
parts.answer: Less water loss by transpiration, because the lower surface is shaded and cooler / not in direct sunlight.
parts.working: B1 reduces water loss (cooler, shaded, less air movement).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Students measured their reaction time using a ruler-drop test after drinking either an energy drink or water.
energy drink: mean 0.250 s, standard error 0.007 s
water: mean 0.270 s, standard error 0.0085 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) for each group.
parts.answer: Energy drink: 0.236 to 0.264 s; water: 0.253 to 0.287 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company that makes the drink claims that it 'significantly improves reaction time'. Use the data to evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: Mean reaction time is shorter after the drink (0.250 s compared with 0.270 s), but the confidence intervals overlap (0.253–0.264 s), so the difference is not shown to be significant; also the sample size, whether the trial was blind, and other variables (sleep, time of day, practice effect) are not stated.
parts.working: B1 mean is lower with drink; B1 confidence intervals overlap so difference not significant; B1 further limitation (sample size / no placebo or blinding / practice effect / variables not controlled).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of pH on the activity of catalase in potato tissue. Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
parts.answer: Use buffer solutions at pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; cut potato into discs of equal size (cork borer, same diameter and thickness) or use same mass of blended potato; place discs with 5 cm³ of buffer in a boiling tube connected to a gas syringe / upturned measuring cylinder in water; add 5 cm³ of 3 % hydrogen peroxide (same volume and concentration); keep at 25 °C in a water bath; measure volume of oxygen collected in 2 minutes; repeat 3 times at each pH and calculate mean; calculate rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: at least 5 pH values using buffers; same mass / surface area of potato; same volume and concentration of H₂O₂; constant temperature with water bath; collect O₂ in gas syringe or by displacement of water (or count bubbles / measure foam height); measure volume in fixed time / calculate rate; control (boiled potato or no potato); equilibrate tubes before mixing; 3 repeats and mean; safety: goggles as H₂O₂ is an irritant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution and distilled water, describe how to make 10 cm³ of each of 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4 and 0.2 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solutions. Present the volumes in a table.
parts.answer: 1.0 mol dm⁻³: 10.0 cm³ sucrose + 0.0 cm³ water; 0.8 mol dm⁻³: 8.0 cm³ sucrose + 2.0 cm³ water; 0.6 mol dm⁻³: 6.0 cm³ sucrose + 4.0 cm³ water; 0.4 mol dm⁻³: 4.0 cm³ sucrose + 6.0 cm³ water; 0.2 mol dm⁻³: 2.0 cm³ sucrose + 8.0 cm³ water
parts.working: B1 correct volumes of stock (concentration ÷ 1.0 × 10 cm³); B1 correct water volumes making 10 cm³ each, table with headings and units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a simple dilution was used here rather than a serial dilution.
parts.answer: The concentrations form an even (linear) series; a serial dilution gives concentrations that fall by the same factor each time (e.g. halving).
parts.working: B1 equal intervals needed / serial dilution gives proportional (e.g. 1.0, 0.5, 0.25) concentrations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Hydrilla. Include how variables will be controlled and how the results will be processed.
parts.answer: Place a 5 cm piece of Hydrilla (cut end up) in a boiling tube of 0.2 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at 25 °C in a water bath; place a lamp at distances 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cm (light intensity ∝ 1/d²); use a heat filter / glass of water between lamp and plant; darken the room; allow 5 min to adjust at each distance; count bubbles per minute or collect gas in a photosynthometer / measure length of gas bubble in capillary for 5 min; repeat 3 times and calculate mean rate; plot rate against 1/d².
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: light intensity varied by lamp distance (≥ 5 distances) and relationship 1/d²; same length / mass of pondweed, same species; constant temperature (water bath / heat shield); excess CO₂ / same concentration of NaHCO₃; other light excluded (dark room); acclimatisation time at each intensity; measure O₂ volume (photosynthometer) or bubble count in fixed time; calculate rate; repeats ≥ 3 and mean; graph of rate against light intensity; safety (lamp hot, electricity near water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method the ecologist could use to compare the abundance of a grass species in a grazed and an ungrazed area of a hillside in the Margalla Hills.
parts.answer: Mark out a 20 m × 20 m area in each site; use random number tables to generate coordinates; place a 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrat at each coordinate; estimate percentage cover of the grass (or count plants / use a 100-point frame) in each quadrat; at least 20 quadrats per area; sites matched for slope, aspect, altitude and soil type; calculate mean percentage cover for each area; use a t-test to see whether the difference is significant.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: two areas of equal size marked out; random sampling method (random numbers / coordinates on grid); quadrat size stated; abundance measure (percentage cover / frequency / density) described; at least 10 quadrats per area; areas matched for slope / aspect / soil / altitude; same time of year; calculate mean (and SD); t-test to compare means.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the permeability of beetroot cell membranes, using a colorimeter to measure the amount of red pigment that leaks out.
parts.answer: Cut beetroot cylinders with a cork borer and cut to equal lengths (e.g. 1 cm); rinse in distilled water until no more pigment leaks; place one cylinder in 10 cm³ of distilled water in tubes in water baths at 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 °C for 30 min; remove cylinders, shake tubes; zero colorimeter with distilled water using a blue-green filter; measure absorbance of each solution; 3 repeats at each temperature; calculate mean absorbance.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: cylinders of same size / surface area (cork borer and ruler); rinsed to remove pigment from cut cells; same volume of water; at least 5 temperatures (range up to ~70 °C) in water baths; water equilibrated before adding cylinders; same time in water; colorimeter zeroed with distilled water / blank; appropriate filter (blue-green); absorbance (or transmission) recorded; repeats and mean.

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
A student measured the mean length of leaf hairs (µm) on plants of one species growing at different heights above the valley floor (m) along a hillside in the Swat valley.
height 120 m: hair length 14.0 µm
height 250 m: hair length 13.1 µm
height 380 m: hair length 16.2 µm
height 510 m: hair length 18.5 µm
height 640 m: hair length 17.9 µm
height 770 m: hair length 21.4 µm
height 900 m: hair length 24.0 µm
height 1030 m: hair length 22.8 µm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs, using rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n³ − n). Show your working. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 ranks for height 1–8; ranks for leaf length 2, 1, 3, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7; M1 Σd² = 6; A1 rs = 1 − 6 × 6/(512 − 8) = 0.93.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 8 pairs of readings is 0.738. State and explain the conclusion.
parts.answer: rs = 0.93 > 0.738, so reject the null hypothesis: there is a significant positive correlation between height above the valley floor and leaf hair length.
parts.working: B1 compares with critical value; B1 significant positive correlation / reject null hypothesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rank was a suitable test for these data.
parts.answer: The investigation looks for a correlation between two variables measured on the same plants / data may not be normally distributed; at least 5 (here 8) pairs.
parts.working: B1 testing for correlation between two variables (non-normally distributed data / paired readings).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: A student counted the number of seeds in six pea pods from one plant: 23, 27, 25, 31, 22, 28.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of seeds per pod.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation using s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation shows about the data.
parts.answer: It shows the spread of the values around the mean (about 68 % of values lie within one SD of the mean).
parts.working: B1 spread / variation of data about the mean.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each investigation, name the most suitable statistical test and give a reason.
(i) comparing the mean body length of two populations of snails
(ii) testing whether the number of hours of sunshine is correlated with the number of butterflies seen
(iii) testing whether the observed numbers of red-flowered and white-flowered plants fit an expected 3 : 1 ratio
parts.answer: (i) t-test – compares two means of continuous, normally distributed data; (ii) Spearman's rank correlation – tests for a correlation between two variables; (iii) chi-squared test – compares observed and expected frequencies of categories.
parts.working: B1 each test with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis for investigation (i).
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean body lengths of the two snail populations.
parts.working: B1 no significant difference between the means of the two named populations.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Wing lengths (in arbitrary units) of fruit flies reared at two temperatures.
28 °C: n = 7, mean 68.4, standard deviation 4.1
18 °C: n = 9, mean 74.9, standard deviation 5.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of degrees of freedom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for this number of degrees of freedom is 2.145. State and explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: t = 2.77 > 2.145, so the null hypothesis is rejected: the mean wing length of flies reared at 18 °C is significantly greater than at 28 °C (less than 5 % probability that the difference is due to chance).
parts.working: B1 t greater than critical value; B1 significant difference / reject null hypothesis, with direction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigates the effect of hydrogen peroxide concentration on the rate of oxygen production by catalase in pieces of liver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of hydrogen peroxide. Dependent: volume of oxygen produced in 1 minute (rate of reaction).
parts.working: B1 IV H₂O₂ concentration; B1 DV volume of O₂ per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that must be standardised.
parts.answer: Any three of: temperature; pH; mass / surface area of liver or potato (concentration of catalase); volume of hydrogen peroxide; time of measurement; source of enzyme.
parts.working: Three correct = 2 marks; two correct = 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why temperature must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Temperature affects the kinetic energy of molecules and hence the rate of enzyme activity, so a change would affect the volume of oxygen produced.
parts.working: B1 temperature changes rate of collisions / enzyme activity, altering the DV.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the percentage germination of okra seeds using Petri dishes placed in incubators at 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the following variables, describe how the student could keep it constant.
(i) the volume of water available to the seeds
(ii) light
(iii) the type of seed
parts.answer: (i) add the same volume (e.g. 10 cm³) of water to each dish using a syringe / measuring cylinder, and cover dishes to prevent evaporation; (ii) keep all dishes in the dark (or same light) inside incubators; (iii) use seeds of the same variety from the same packet, of similar size.
parts.working: B1 each variable with a practical method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why at least 20 seeds should be used in each dish.
parts.answer: Germination varies between individual seeds; a larger sample reduces the effect of a few non-viable seeds, making the percentage more reliable.
parts.working: B1 reduces effect of individual variation / non-viable seeds, results more representative.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher compares the resting heart rate of adults in Lahore who walk for at least 30 minutes a day with those who do not exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two variables, other than exercise, that could affect resting heart rate in this study, and explain why each should be taken into account.
parts.answer: e.g. age – heart rate changes with age; sex – mean resting rates differ; caffeine / smoking – stimulates heart rate; body mass / fitness level; time of day; stress; medication. Each must be matched or recorded because it would change heart rate independently of exercise.
parts.working: For each of two: B1 variable; B1 explanation of its effect on heart rate / why it must be matched.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to standardise all variables in investigations using humans.
parts.answer: People differ genetically and in lifestyle, and it is unethical or impractical to control their diet and activity completely.
parts.working: B1 natural variation / ethical or practical limits on controlling lifestyle.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student tested the hydrolysis of starch by amylase.
Tube A: starch + amylase
Tube B: starch + amylase that had been boiled and cooled
Tube C: starch + distilled water
Samples were tested with iodine solution every minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of tube B and of tube C.
parts.answer: Tube B (boiled amylase) shows that the disappearance of starch is due to active enzyme and not to the heat treatment / other substances in the solution; tube C (no enzyme, water) shows that starch does not break down on its own (and that the iodine test works).
parts.working: B1 B: confirms the effect is due to active (non-denatured) enzyme; B1 C: shows starch is stable without enzyme / acts as a colour standard.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student found that starch disappeared slowly in tube B as well as tube A. Suggest an explanation and how the method could be improved.
parts.answer: The amylase in tube B was not fully denatured (not boiled long enough, or allowed to cool and some enzyme remained active); boil for at least 10 minutes in a water bath / check the boiled solution reached 100 °C.
parts.working: B1 enzyme not completely denatured; B1 improvement: boil for longer / at 100 °C for a set time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student cut one potato cylinder for each sucrose concentration, weighed it on a balance reading to 0.1 g, left it in an open beaker of solution for 2 hours, then dried it with a paper towel and weighed it again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this procedure and suggest how each could be reduced.
parts.answer: e.g. cylinders blotted differently, so different amounts of surface water → blot each cylinder in the same way (roll once on paper towel); cylinders cut to slightly different lengths / some with skin → use a ruler and scalpel, remove skin; balance reading only to 0.1 g → use a balance reading to 0.01 g; solutions evaporated → cover tubes; only one cylinder per concentration → use three cylinders per concentration.
parts.working: For each of two: B1 error; B1 improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student mixed starch and amylase and every 30 seconds placed a drop of the mixture into iodine solution on a white tile. She recorded the time when the drop no longer turned blue-black.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the timing of the end point is a source of error.
parts.answer: Deciding when the blue-black colour has disappeared is subjective, as the colour changes gradually; samples are only taken every 30 s, so the true end point could be up to 30 s earlier.
parts.working: B1 judging colour change is subjective / gradual; B1 sampling interval means end point time is imprecise (±30 s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements that would make the measurement of the end point more accurate.
parts.answer: Use a colorimeter to measure absorbance of samples; take samples more frequently (e.g. every 10 s); compare with a colour standard (iodine in water); have the same person judge the end point against a white tile.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The time taken for a piece of milk agar to clear after protease was added was measured five times at 35 °C: 42 s, 45 s, 44 s, 61 s, 43 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean of the remaining results.
parts.answer: 61 s is anomalous; mean = 43.5 s
parts.working: B1 61 s identified (much higher than others); B1 (42 + 45 + 44 + 43)/4 = 43.5 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage error in the mean if it had been calculated including the anomalous result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one possible cause of the anomalous result in this experiment.
parts.answer: e.g. timer started late / end point misjudged; temperature of the water bath dropped; less enzyme added in that repeat; tube not mixed.
parts.working: B1 any plausible cause linked to the procedure.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
stem:
A student heated test tubes of glucose solution with Benedict's solution and recorded the time taken for the mixture to turn brick-red.
0.5 % glucose: 150, 142, 149 seconds
1.0 % glucose: 97, 94, 98 seconds
2.0 % glucose: 60, 63, 59 seconds
4.0 % glucose: 38, 36, 40 seconds

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table to record these results, including the mean time for each concentration (to the nearest second).
parts.answer: Columns: concentration of glucose / % | time to turn brick-red / s: trial 1, trial 2, trial 3 | mean time / s. Means: 0.5 % 147 s; 1.0 % 96 s; 2.0 % 61 s; 4.0 % 38 s.
parts.working: B1 independent variable in first column with units in heading only; B1 dependent variable heading with unit (s), three trial columns; B1 all raw data entered correctly; B1 means correct to the nearest second, consistent decimal places.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
stem:
A student recorded the mean length of bean shoots grown at different light intensities in this table (columns separated by | ):
Results | Light
4 cm | low
5.5 cm | medium
6.25 cm | high

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three faults in the way the table has been drawn and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: 1 Units written in the body of the table (cm) – units should be in the column heading only; 2 inconsistent number of decimal places (4, 5.5, 6.25) – record all to the same precision (e.g. 1 d.p.); 3 the independent variable is not in the first column – put light intensity first; 4 the heading 'Results' is not a variable name – use 'mean length of shoot / cm'.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three faults with correction.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Percentage change in mass of onion tissue in salt solutions:
0 mol dm⁻³: +8.2 %
0.1 mol dm⁻³: +4.9 %
0.2 mol dm⁻³: +2.1 %
0.3 mol dm⁻³: −1.0 %
0.4 mol dm⁻³: −3.8 %
0.5 mol dm⁻³: −6.9 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would draw a graph of these results.
parts.answer: Concentration (mol dm⁻³) on the x-axis, percentage change in mass on the y-axis, with the x-axis crossing at 0 % and the y-axis extending to negative values; axes labelled with units; scales even and using more than half the grid; points plotted as small crosses; ruled line of best fit (or smooth curve) through the points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: correct axes with labels and units; negative values shown / x-axis at y = 0; suitable linear scales; accurate plotting; line of best fit (not extended beyond data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how you would use your graph to find the concentration of salt solution at which there is no change in mass, and explain why the line of best fit should be used rather than the two plotted points nearest to zero.
parts.answer: Find where the line of best fit crosses the line of 0 % change in mass (the x-axis) and read the concentration vertically down from that point; the line of best fit uses all six readings, so it reduces the effect of an error in any single reading.
parts.working: B1 read the x-value where the line crosses 0 % change (draw a vertical guide line to the x-axis); B1 line of best fit is based on all the data / averages out random errors in individual points (answer about 0.27 mol dm⁻³).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student in Faisalabad grew tomato plants with three different fertilisers, A, B and C, and calculated the mean yield per plant and the standard error for each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of chart that should be drawn and describe how the error bars should be added.
parts.answer: A bar chart (fertiliser type is categoric); bars of equal width, not touching; each bar height = mean yield; error bars drawn as a vertical line from mean − 2SE to mean + 2SE (95 % CI) with short horizontal caps.
parts.working: B1 bar chart because categoric independent variable; B1 bars separated, labelled axes with units; B1 error bars extend 2 × SE (or 1 SD as stated) above and below the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The error bars for fertilisers A and B overlap but those for B and C do not. State what this suggests.
parts.answer: The difference between A and B may not be significant (could be due to chance); the difference between B and C is likely to be significant.
parts.working: B1 A and B not significantly different; B1 B and C probably significantly different.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A piece of carrot tissue had a mass of 2.45 g. After 4 hours in distilled water its mass was 2.71 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mass. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of mass change in g per hour over the 4 hours.
parts.answer: 0.065 g per hour

author: HomiLabs

stem: Numbers of five species of invertebrate found in leaf litter samples from a garden in Multan: 34, 21, 12, 8, 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second plot near a busy road had D = 0.42. Compare the diversity of the two plots.
parts.answer: The first plot (0.71) is more diverse than the plot near the road (0.42), because D closer to 1 means higher diversity.
parts.working: B1 first plot more diverse; higher D = greater diversity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students cut samples of potato, apple and onion with scalpels, crushed them with water, and tested the extracts with iodine solution and with Benedict's solution in a boiling water bath.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this practical and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: e.g. scalpel – sharp, cut on a tile away from the body; hot water bath / boiling water – scalds, use tongs and a test-tube holder; Benedict's solution (copper sulfate) – irritant, wear goggles and wash skin; iodine solution – stains / irritant, wear gloves and goggles; glassware breaking – handle with care, sweep up with brush.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hazards with matching precautions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A photomicrograph of a leaf epidermis has a scale bar labelled 100 µm that is 25 mm long. One epidermal cell measures 38 mm long on the photomicrograph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the cell, in µm.
parts.answer: 152 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why measuring several cells and finding the mean gives a better estimate of cell length.
parts.answer: Cells vary in size and may be cut at different angles; a mean reduces the effect of this variation.
parts.working: B1 variation between cells / sectioning angle.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Asiatic cheetah once lived across south-west Asia, including parts of Pakistan and India. Today only a very small population survives, in Iran.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four reasons why populations and species may become extinct.
parts.answer: Climate change; competition (e.g. from introduced/invasive species or livestock); hunting/poaching by humans; degradation and loss of habitat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: climate change; competition (for food, space – e.g. from other predators, invasive species or livestock); hunting/overexploitation by humans; habitat loss/destruction; habitat degradation/fragmentation; (accept disease, pollution).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cheetahs feed mainly on gazelles. Suggest how the hunting of gazelles by people could contribute to the decline of the cheetah.
parts.answer: Less prey for cheetahs, so they starve or breed less successfully; cheetahs may then kill livestock and be killed by herders.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: reduced food supply/prey; fewer cubs survive/lower reproduction; cheetahs travel further, more contact with people/roads; attack livestock so are persecuted.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coral reefs, such as those in the Red Sea and around Astola Island, contain a very high biodiversity. Reef-building corals contain single-celled photosynthetic algae inside their cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a rise in sea temperature caused by climate change can lead to the death of corals.
parts.answer: High temperature causes corals to expel their algae (bleaching); the coral loses the sugars made by algal photosynthesis; if the high temperature lasts, the coral starves and dies.
parts.working: B1 corals expel/lose algae (bleaching); B1 algae supply most of the coral's food/organic compounds from photosynthesis; B1 coral starves/is weakened and more likely to die from disease if high temperatures persist.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the death of reef-building corals reduces the number of fish species on the reef.
parts.answer: Corals provide the physical habitat – shelter, breeding sites and food – for many fish; without them niches are lost, so many species leave or die out.
parts.working: 1 mark each: loss of habitat/shelter/breeding sites; loss of food (coral polyps or organisms that live on coral) / fewer niches.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why making a reef into a marine protected area cannot fully protect it from climate change.
parts.answer: Sea temperature rise is caused by global greenhouse gas emissions, which cannot be controlled within the boundary of the protected area.
parts.working: B1 the cause (warming/acidification) is global and not affected by local rules on fishing or development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Arabian oryx, a desert antelope, became extinct in the wild in 1972. Animals bred in captivity were later released back into the wild in Oman and other countries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the steps that should be taken before captive-bred animals are released into the wild.
parts.answer: Make sure the original cause of decline (e.g. hunting) has been removed; check the habitat is suitable with enough food and water; screen animals for disease; choose animals with as much genetic diversity as possible; acclimatise them in a fenced area (soft release); plan monitoring.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: remove/control the threat that caused extinction (poaching); assess/restore habitat – food, water, space; health checks/quarantine so disease is not introduced; select genetically diverse, unrelated animals (studbook); acclimatise in an enclosure/soft release so they learn to find food; educate/involve local people; fit radio collars/plan monitoring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of returning captive-bred oryx to the wild rather than keeping the species only in zoos and captive breeding centres.
parts.answer: In the wild the oryx again fills its niche in the desert ecosystem (grazing, food for predators, seed dispersal); natural selection acts on the wild population so it stays adapted to wild conditions and keeps natural behaviours; a wild population can grow much larger than captive space allows, giving more genetic diversity and less risk from a single disease outbreak or disaster in one zoo.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: restores the species' role/niche in the ecosystem; natural selection continues so adaptations (and wild behaviour) are kept, not lost by adaptation to captivity; larger population/more genetic diversity than captive space allows; cheaper long-term than captivity; not all eggs in one basket – reduced risk from disease/disaster in one centre.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cane toads were introduced to north-eastern Australia in 1935 to control beetles that damaged sugar cane. They did not control the beetles but spread across a large part of the country. Their skin contains a poison that kills many native predators that try to eat them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an invasive alien species.
parts.answer: A species introduced by humans to an area outside its natural range that spreads and harms native species, ecosystems or the economy.
parts.working: B1 non-native/introduced by humans and spreads causing harm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cane toads have reduced the populations of some native predators and of some native frogs.
parts.answer: Predators that eat toads are poisoned and die; toads compete with native frogs for food and breeding sites; toads have no natural predators or diseases in Australia, so their numbers are very large.
parts.working: 1 mark each: native predators not adapted to the toxin die after eating toads; competition with native frogs for food/space/breeding ponds; no natural predators/parasites to control toad numbers so they reach very high densities (and eat native invertebrates).

parts.label: c
parts.text: It has been suggested that a disease organism that kills toads should be introduced. Suggest one risk of this method.
parts.answer: The disease organism might also infect and kill native frogs or other species.
parts.working: B1 non-target species harmed / the control organism itself becomes invasive / cannot be removed once released.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A seed bank stores seeds of a wild relative of wheat collected in Balochistan. Seeds are dried and kept at −20 °C. Every 5 years a sample of 200 seeds is removed and germinated.
Years in storage: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20
Seeds germinated (out of 200): 188, 183, 176, 161, 142

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination after 0 years and after 20 years.
parts.working: M1 germinated ÷ 200 × 100; A1 94.0 % and 71.0 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The seed bank regrows a fresh batch of seeds when the percentage germination falls below 85 % of its value at the start. Use the data to state the first test at which this happens. Show your working.
parts.answer: 20 years: 85 % of 94.0 % = 79.9 %; at 15 years germination is 80.5 % (above), at 20 years it is 71.0 % (below).
parts.working: M1 0.85 × 94.0 = 79.9 %; A1 year 20 (80.5 % at year 15 is still above the limit).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the seeds are dried and kept at −20 °C.
parts.answer: Low water content and low temperature slow metabolism/enzyme activity, so stored food is used up very slowly and seeds stay viable for longer; drying also prevents ice crystals damaging cells and stops fungal growth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: reduces respiration/metabolic rate/enzyme activity; reserves last longer so seeds remain viable; dry seeds do not form ice crystals that damage cells when frozen; prevents growth of fungi/bacteria/germination in store.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Seeds of mango cannot be stored in this way. Suggest why, and suggest how the genetic diversity of mango varieties could be conserved instead.
parts.answer: Mango seeds are killed by drying (they need a high water content); conserve as living trees in field gene banks/orchards, or freeze embryos or tissue in liquid nitrogen (cryopreservation).
parts.working: B1 seeds die/lose viability when dried (recalcitrant); B1 field gene bank of living trees / tissue culture / cryopreservation of embryos in liquid nitrogen.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A large forest in South Asia has been cleared for farms and roads, leaving four separate forest fragments. Leopards live in all four fragments but cannot cross the farmland safely. Geneticists measured genetic diversity (mean heterozygosity) in the leopards: 0.62 in a large, unbroken forest elsewhere and 0.41 in the fragments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much lower, as a percentage, genetic diversity is in the fragments than in the unbroken forest. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why small, isolated populations such as these have a high risk of extinction.
parts.answer: Inbreeding increases homozygosity for harmful recessive alleles, lowering survival and fertility; genetic drift removes alleles, so less variation to adapt to change or disease; chance events (fire, disease, few births of one sex) can wipe out a small population; no immigration to replace losses or bring new alleles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: inbreeding / mating between relatives; more homozygous recessive harmful alleles expressed (inbreeding depression); genetic drift/loss of alleles; reduced variation so less able to adapt to environmental change/new disease; random events (disease, fire, drought, unequal sex ratio) have a bigger effect; no gene flow/immigration from other populations; each fragment may be below carrying capacity needed for a viable population.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how planting forest corridors between the fragments would help to conserve the leopards.
parts.answer: Leopards could move between fragments, so the fragments act as one larger population; this allows gene flow, reducing inbreeding, and lets animals recolonise a fragment if its population dies out.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: allows movement/migration between fragments; gene flow/interbreeding between populations increases genetic diversity; larger effective population; recolonisation after local extinction; access to more prey/territory.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The mango tree has the scientific name Mangifera indica. Two pine trees that grow in the hills of northern Pakistan are the chir pine, Pinus roxburghii, and the blue pine, Pinus wallichiana.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two rules that are followed when writing a scientific (binomial) name.
parts.answer: The genus name comes first and starts with a capital letter; the species name comes second and starts with a small letter; the name is printed in italics (or underlined when handwritten).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: genus first, then species; genus has a capital letter; species (specific epithet) all lower case; italics in print / underlined in handwriting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the names tell you about how the chir pine and the blue pine are related.
parts.answer: They are in the same genus (Pinus) but are different species; so they share many features and a fairly recent common ancestor.
parts.working: B1 same genus, different species; B1 closely related / recent common ancestor / also share family, order, class etc.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why biologists use scientific names rather than local names such as 'chir'.
parts.answer: Local names differ between languages and regions, and one local name may be used for several species; a scientific name is unique and understood by scientists worldwide.
parts.working: 1 mark each: one species may have many local/common names (in Urdu, Pashto, English…); the same common name may refer to different species; binomial name is unique/international, avoiding confusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The names of the taxonomic groups to which the house sparrow belongs are listed below in random order:
Passeridae, Aves, Eukarya, domesticus, Animalia, Passer, Chordata, Passeriformes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Arrange these names in order from domain to species and name the rank of each.
parts.answer: Eukarya (domain), Animalia (kingdom), Chordata (phylum), Aves (class), Passeriformes (order), Passeridae (family), Passer (genus), domesticus (species).
parts.working: 3 marks all eight correct in order with ranks; 2 marks 6–7 correct; 1 mark 4–5 correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the scientific name of the house sparrow correctly.
parts.answer: Passer domesticus (genus with capital, species lower case, italics/underlined).
parts.working: B1 Passer domesticus with correct capitalisation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a hierarchical classification.
parts.answer: Organisms are placed in groups, which are placed in larger groups at the next rank, and so on; groups do not overlap – each group at one rank belongs to only one group at the rank above.
parts.working: B1 small groups within larger groups / ranks from domain to species; B1 no overlap between groups.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student made a table comparing three eukaryotic kingdoms.
Feature | Plantae | Fungi | Animalia
1 material of cell wall | ? | ? | ?
2 type of nutrition | ? | ? | ?
3 main storage carbohydrate | ? | ? | ?
4 chloroplasts present | ? | ? | ?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the table by giving the entry for each feature in each kingdom.
parts.answer: 1: cellulose; chitin; no cell wall. 2: autotrophic (photosynthesis); heterotrophic by external digestion and absorption (saprotrophic or parasitic); heterotrophic by ingestion (holozoic). 3: starch; glycogen; glycogen. 4: yes (in some cells); no; no.
parts.working: 1 mark per complete correct row (all three entries).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features shared by organisms in all three kingdoms.
parts.answer: Cells have a nucleus with a nuclear envelope; membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria; 80S ribosomes; linear DNA with histones.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two eukaryotic features: nucleus; mitochondria/ER/Golgi; 80S ribosomes in cytoplasm; linear chromosomes with histones.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Methane-producing microorganisms (methanogens) live in the stomachs of buffalo and in the biogas digesters used on farms in Punjab. They are placed in the domain Archaea. Other archaea live in hot springs, salt lakes and deep-sea vents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features that archaea share with bacteria.
parts.answer: No nucleus (prokaryotic); no membrane-bound organelles; 70S ribosomes; circular DNA; mostly single-celled and small.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no nucleus/nuclear envelope; no membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, chloroplasts); 70S ribosomes; circular DNA (not in chromosomes with a nucleus); unicellular, similar size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why archaea were classified with bacteria until the 1970s and why they are now placed in a separate domain.
parts.answer: Under the microscope they look like bacteria (prokaryotic, similar size and shape); comparison of rRNA gene/base sequences and biochemistry showed that they are as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes; e.g. no peptidoglycan in cell walls and different membrane lipids, so they form a separate domain.
parts.working: B1 similar appearance/structure to bacteria; B1 molecular evidence (rRNA sequences) became available; B1 any biochemical difference: no peptidoglycan / membrane lipids with branched chains (ether links) / some have histones / RNA polymerase like eukaryotes.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Five eukaryotic organisms:
1 yeast: single cell; cell wall of chitin; absorbs sugars from fruit juice; reproduces by budding
2 giant kelp: large seaweed up to 30 m long; photosynthetic; no roots, xylem or phloem
3 moss: small multicellular green plant; cellulose cell walls; embryo develops inside the parent plant
4 Paramecium: single cell; no cell wall; moves using cilia; ingests bacteria
5 Penicillium: thread-like hyphae; chitin cell walls; feeds saprotrophically

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the kingdom to which each organism belongs.
parts.answer: 1 Fungi; 2 Protoctista; 3 Plantae; 4 Protoctista; 5 Fungi.
parts.working: 3 marks all five correct; 2 marks four correct; 1 mark three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why yeast is placed in the kingdom Fungi even though it is unicellular.
parts.answer: It has the defining features of fungi: chitin cell wall, heterotrophic nutrition by absorption, no chloroplasts, stores glycogen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: chitin cell wall; heterotrophic/absorbs food (saprotrophic); no chloroplasts/cannot photosynthesise; stores glycogen; reproduces by spores (as well as budding).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why giant kelp is not placed in the plant kingdom, even though it is multicellular and photosynthetic.
parts.answer: It lacks the tissues and organs of plants (no roots, stems, leaves or vascular tissue) and does not develop from an embryo protected by the parent; it has different photosynthetic pigments/food stores and evolved separately from plants.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: no vascular tissue/true roots, stems, leaves; no embryo protected inside parent tissue; different pigments/food store (not starch); not closely related to plants – shares ancestry with other algae/protoctists.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three microorganisms, P, Q and R, were isolated from a salt mine and the soil around it.
P: no nucleus; cell wall contains peptidoglycan; growth stopped by the antibiotic streptomycin, which binds to the type of ribosome found in this cell
Q: no nucleus; cell wall without peptidoglycan; membrane lipids with branched hydrocarbon chains; grows only in very salty water; growth not affected by streptomycin
R: nucleus present; 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm; cell wall containing chitin

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the domain to which each organism belongs.
parts.answer: P Bacteria; Q Archaea; R Eukarya.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one piece of evidence from the descriptions for your answer for Q.
parts.answer: No nucleus (prokaryote) but no peptidoglycan in its wall / branched membrane lipids, which bacteria do not have.
parts.working: B1 prokaryote + any archaeal feature (no peptidoglycan / branched lipids / unaffected by streptomycin).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why streptomycin does not affect the growth of R.
parts.answer: R is a eukaryote with 80S ribosomes in its cytoplasm; streptomycin binds to bacterial 70S ribosomes, so protein synthesis in R is not inhibited.
parts.working: B1 R has 80S ribosomes (different shape/proteins); B1 streptomycin binds only bacterial 70S ribosomes so translation in R continues.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The percentage of each base in the nucleic acid of four viruses was measured.
Virus | A | C | G | T | U
E | 24 | 19 | 31 | 0 | 26
F | 22 | 28 | 28 | 0 | 22
G | 30 | 20 | 20 | 30 | 0
H | 25 | 24 | 18 | 33 | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to classify each virus by the type of nucleic acid it contains and whether it is single-stranded or double-stranded. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: E: single-stranded RNA – contains U not T, and A ≠ U, G ≠ C. F: double-stranded RNA – U present, A = U and G = C. G: double-stranded DNA – T present, A = T and G = C. H: single-stranded DNA – T present but A ≠ T and G ≠ C.
parts.working: B1 U (no T) means RNA, T means DNA; B1 equal amounts of complementary bases (A = T or A = U, and G = C) indicate double-stranded (base pairing); 3 marks for the four classifications: all four correct 3, three correct 2, two correct 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another virus, J, contains double-stranded DNA. 18 % of its bases are guanine. Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases.
parts.working: M1 C = G = 18 % (base pairing), so A + T = 100 − 36 = 64 %; A1 A = T = 32 %.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The amino acid sequence of the same 150-amino-acid protein was compared in five species of mammal, V to Z. The number of amino acid differences between each pair is shown.
V–W 4; V–X 21; V–Y 22; V–Z 38
W–X 20; W–Y 21; W–Z 37
X–Y 6; X–Z 36
Y–Z 37

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage similarity between the protein in species V and in species W. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to describe the relationships between the five species.
parts.answer: V and W are very closely related (4 differences) and X and Y are closely related (6); the V/W pair and X/Y pair are more distantly related to each other (20–22 differences); Z is the most distantly related to all the others (36–38 differences), so it diverged earliest.
parts.working: B1 V and W closest pair; B1 X and Y close pair, the two pairs share a more distant common ancestor; B1 Z most distantly related/earliest divergence, with data quoted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why comparing the DNA base sequences of the gene would give more information than comparing the amino acid sequences.
parts.answer: The genetic code is degenerate, so some base substitutions do not change the amino acid (silent mutations) and are not seen in the protein; DNA also includes non-coding regions (introns) that change faster, so more differences can be detected between closely related species.
parts.working: B1 degenerate code/silent (synonymous) mutations not detected in protein; B1 introns/non-coding DNA also compared / more differences detected so finer distinctions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The vultures of Asia and Africa (Old World vultures) and those of the Americas (New World vultures) look very similar. Both have large broad wings for soaring, a bare head and a hooked beak, and both feed on dead animals. They were once placed in the same family. Studies of their DNA show that they are not closely related.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the two groups of vultures look so similar although they are not closely related.
parts.answer: They live in a similar way (soaring and eating carrion), so similar selection pressures have led to similar adaptations evolving independently (convergent evolution).
parts.working: B1 same niche/way of life/selection pressures; B1 features evolved independently/convergent evolution, not inherited from a recent shared ancestor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why classification based on DNA sequences is thought to show evolutionary relationships more accurately than classification based on physical features.
parts.answer: DNA differences arise by mutation and build up over time, so the number of differences reflects how long ago two groups shared a common ancestor; similar physical features can arise by convergence or be lost; DNA comparisons are objective and quantitative and can compare many genes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: number of base differences proportional to time since divergence; mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate; physical similarities may be due to convergent evolution/similar environments; DNA gives large amount of data/quantitative/less subjective; not affected by the environment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other type of molecular evidence that could be used to check the relationship between the two groups.
parts.answer: Amino acid sequences of a protein such as cytochrome c (or haemoglobin) / mitochondrial DNA sequences.
parts.working: B1 any valid example.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three organisms placed in the kingdom Protoctista:
Chlamydomonas: single cell; one chloroplast; cellulose cell wall; two flagella
Amoeba: single cell; no cell wall; engulfs food particles by phagocytosis
Plasmodium: single cell; parasite that lives inside red blood cells and liver cells of humans

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one feature that all three organisms share that places them in the domain Eukarya.
parts.answer: A nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope (or membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, or 80S ribosomes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Chlamydomonas is not placed in the kingdom Plantae and Amoeba is not placed in the kingdom Animalia.
parts.answer: Both are single-celled; plants and animals are multicellular with specialised tissues and develop from embryos.
parts.working: B1 unicellular; B1 plants and animals are multicellular with differentiated tissues/organs (develop from an embryo).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why some biologists say that the Protoctista is a 'group of convenience' rather than a natural group.
parts.answer: It contains all the eukaryotes that do not fit into the other kingdoms, so its members are very varied (plant-like, animal-like and fungus-like); some protoctists are more closely related to plants, animals or fungi than to each other, so they do not share one common ancestor that excludes other kingdoms.
parts.working: B1 defined by not fitting other kingdoms / very diverse; B1 members not all descended from one common ancestor/some more closely related to other kingdoms than to each other.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The markhor is a wild goat that lives on steep, rocky mountain slopes in northern Pakistan, where it feeds on grasses, herbs and the leaves of shrubs such as oak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms species and habitat.
parts.answer: Species: a group of organisms with similar features that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Habitat: the place where an organism or population lives.
parts.working: B1 species – interbreed to give fertile offspring (similar morphology/physiology); B1 habitat – the place/area where an organism lives (e.g. rocky slopes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term niche and use the information to describe part of the niche of the markhor.
parts.answer: Niche: the role of a species in its ecosystem, including how it gets food, its interactions with other species and the conditions it needs. The markhor is a herbivore that grazes grasses and browses oak leaves on steep slopes and is prey for snow leopards.
parts.working: B1 definition – role in ecosystem / all biotic and abiotic interactions; B1 a correct aspect for markhor (herbivore/primary consumer feeding on grasses and shrub leaves, prey for predators).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define the term ecosystem.
parts.answer: A community of interacting organisms of different species together with the non-living (abiotic) environment with which they interact.
parts.working: B1 community/all populations + abiotic factors, interacting.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students want to sample the animals in a wildlife reserve that has woodland, grassland and a stream.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable sampling method for each of these groups of animals:
(i) beetles that run over the ground at night
(ii) insects that live on the tops of long grass
(iii) larvae of insects living among stones in the stream
(iv) moths that fly at night
parts.answer: (i) pitfall traps; (ii) sweep net; (iii) kick sampling with a net held downstream; (iv) light trap.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a pitfall trap is set up and suggest one way to stop trapped animals from eating each other.
parts.answer: Dig a hole and sink a jar or plastic cup so its rim is level with the soil surface; place a cover (e.g. a raised stone or tile) above it to keep out rain and larger animals; empty it regularly (e.g. every 12 hours) / add leaf litter as shelter so predators and prey can hide.
parts.working: B1 container sunk with rim level with the ground; B1 cover/roof raised above to keep out rain and predators; B1 check frequently / add leaf litter or small stones / separate compartments.

author: HomiLabs

stem: On a hillside the abundance of grasses was recorded using a 1 m² quadrat divided into 100 small squares. The abundance of a woodland herb with large separate plants was recorded by counting the plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the abundance of grasses is recorded as percentage cover and not by counting individual plants.
parts.answer: Grasses spread by runners/tillers and grow in dense mats, so it is impossible to tell where one plant ends and another begins; percentage cover is quicker and avoids this problem.
parts.working: B1 individual plants cannot be distinguished/grow in clumps or mats; B1 counting would be too slow/inaccurate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the 100-square quadrat is used to estimate percentage cover of one species of grass.
parts.answer: Count the number of small squares that are more than half covered by the species; each square counts as 1 %.
parts.working: B1 count squares in which the species covers at least half; B1 each square = 1 % so the number of squares = percentage cover.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some ecologists use an abundance scale, ACFOR (abundant, common, frequent, occasional, rare), instead. State one advantage and one disadvantage of this scale.
parts.answer: Advantage: very quick and needs no counting, so many quadrats or sites can be recorded. Disadvantage: subjective – different people may give different categories, so results are hard to compare and cannot be used in calculations such as Simpson's index.
parts.working: B1 quick/easy; B1 subjective/qualitative/not easily compared or analysed statistically.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student placed 50 quadrats, each 0.5 m × 0.5 m, at random on a lawn. White clover was present in 32 of the quadrats.
In a second survey, a point frame with 10 pins was lowered at 20 random positions in the same lawn (200 pins in total). Clover leaves were touched by 46 of the pins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage frequency of white clover.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage cover of white clover from the point frame data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why percentage frequency can give a misleading impression of how abundant a species is.
parts.answer: Frequency only records presence or absence, so one small plant in a quadrat counts the same as a quadrat full of the species; the result also depends on quadrat size.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: presence/absence only, not number or cover; one individual scores the same as many; value depends on quadrat size; a widely scattered sparse species may have high frequency.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Students used a pond net to sample a village pond near Faisalabad. The animals were sorted and counted.
mayfly nymphs 14; caddis fly larvae 9; water boatmen 21; pond snails 6; leeches 3; damselfly nymphs 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², for this sample. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second pond, which receives water from a fish farm, has D = 0.31. Suggest what this tells you about the second pond compared with the first.
parts.answer: The second pond has a lower diversity: fewer species and/or one or two species dominate; it is probably polluted (e.g. low oxygen from organic waste), so only tolerant species survive.
parts.working: B1 lower diversity – fewer species or less even numbers/dominated by few species; B1 suggestion of pollution/eutrophication/low oxygen favouring tolerant species.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a value of D close to 1 indicates a high diversity.
parts.answer: A value near 1 means that two individuals picked at random are very likely to belong to different species.
parts.working: B1 probability that two randomly chosen individuals are different species is high / many species with even numbers.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A belt transect was laid from the edge of a tidal creek inland through a mangrove area at Sandspit, near Karachi. A 1 m² quadrat was placed every 10 m along the transect and the percentage cover of two plant species recorded.
Distance from creek / m: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Mangrove (Avicennia marina) cover / %: 5, 30, 55, 60, 35, 10
Salt-tolerant grass cover / %: 0, 0, 5, 15, 40, 65

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a belt transect was used rather than quadrats placed at random over the whole area.
parts.answer: The aim is to show how the plants change with distance along an environmental gradient (from the creek inland); random quadrats would not sample systematically along the gradient, so the change might be missed.
parts.working: B1 there is a gradient/change in conditions with distance from the creek; B1 systematic sampling along the line shows the zonation/pattern of change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the distribution of the two species along the transect.
parts.answer: Mangrove cover rises from 5 % at the creek to a peak of 60 % at 30 m and then falls to 10 % at 50 m; grass is absent up to 10 m and then increases steadily to 65 % at 50 m; grass replaces mangrove further inland.
parts.working: B1 mangrove peaks at 30 m (60 %); B1 grass absent at 0–10 m and increases to 65 % at 50 m; B1 overlap/where one decreases the other increases, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two abiotic factors that could explain these distributions and how they could be measured.
parts.answer: Time covered by the tide each day (measured by recording water level at each quadrat over a tidal cycle); soil/water salinity (measured with a conductivity meter on soil water samples).
parts.working: 1 mark each for factor + method, any two of: tidal flooding/submergence time; salinity (conductivity meter/refractometer); soil water content (mass loss on drying); soil oxygen/waterlogging.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ecologists estimated the number of grasshoppers in a field of fodder crop. They caught 84 grasshoppers with sweep nets, marked each one with a small dot of non-toxic paint and released them. The next day they caught 96 grasshoppers, of which 14 were marked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the Lincoln index to estimate the population size.
parts.answer: 576 grasshoppers

parts.label: b
parts.text: Later, the ecologists found that one quarter of the marks had rubbed off before the second sample was taken. Calculate a corrected estimate, assuming the marked grasshoppers were otherwise caught at random.
parts.answer: 432 grasshoppers
parts.working: M1 the 14 marked animals seen are 3/4 of the marked animals actually recaptured, so true number = 14 ÷ 0.75 = 18.7; A1 84 × 96 ÷ 18.67 = 432.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why loss of marks makes the original estimate too high.
parts.answer: Fewer marked animals are recognised in the second sample, so the denominator is too small and the calculated population too large.
parts.working: B1 fewer recaptures recorded → smaller divisor → larger estimate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Genetic diversity was compared in a wild population of rice and in a modern high-yielding rice variety. The number of different alleles at five gene loci was counted.
Locus: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Wild population: 8, 6, 9, 7, 5
Modern variety: 3, 2, 4, 2, 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of alleles per locus for each type of rice.
parts.answer: Wild 7.0; modern 2.8
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the modern variety has a lower genetic diversity.
parts.answer: It was produced by selective breeding/inbreeding from a few parent plants chosen for high yield, so many alleles were lost; plants of a variety are bred to be uniform.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: selective breeding from few parents/founder effect; inbreeding/self-pollination increases homozygosity; selection for uniformity eliminates alleles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is important to conserve the genetic diversity of wild relatives of crop plants.
parts.answer: Wild relatives may carry alleles for resistance to disease, pests, drought or salinity; these can be bred into crops to cope with new diseases or climate change.
parts.working: B1 source of useful alleles (named example); B1 future breeding/adaptation to new conditions or food security.
