parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variable + method.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one ethical consideration for this investigation.
parts.answer: Use temperatures within the natural range so that hatching success and the sex ratio of released turtles are not harmed; release all hatchlings to the sea.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Some populations of a grass grow on spoil heaps from an old copper mine, where the soil contains a high copper concentration. A researcher wants to compare copper tolerance of the mine population with a population from a nearby pasture. She collects seeds from both populations, grows the seedlings for 4 weeks in ordinary compost, then places cuttings in solutions with and without copper and measures root growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plants are first grown from seed in the same compost, rather than being dug up from the two sites and tested directly.
parts.answer: Plants dug up from the mine may already have been affected by their environment (acclimatised or damaged), so any difference could be environmental rather than genetic; growing both in the same conditions means differences in tolerance must be inherited.
parts.working: B1 removes environmental effects/acclimatisation; B1 so differences are genetic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the dependent variable should be expressed to allow fair comparison between plants of different sizes.
parts.answer: As a tolerance index: root growth in copper solution ÷ root growth of a similar cutting in solution without copper (× 100), so each plant is compared with its own growth without copper.
parts.working: B1 ratio/percentage of growth in copper to growth without copper; B1 accounts for differences in vigour/size between plants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other variables that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Concentration of other mineral ions in the solutions; temperature and light; size/age of cuttings; time in solution; aeration of solutions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a field trial, cotton plants were enclosed in mesh cages. Some cages had parasitic wasps added to control whiteflies; others had no wasps. A scientist noticed that the whiteflies in all the caged plants grew more slowly than on uncaged plants in the same field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the cages might affect whitefly numbers even without wasps.
parts.answer: Cages change the microclimate – shade, temperature, humidity and wind – and keep out (or keep in) other predators; so whitefly growth differs from uncaged plants.
parts.working: B1 altered microclimate (named factor); B1 exclusion of other predators/immigration of whiteflies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the treatment without wasps must also be caged, and why uncaged plants are useful as an additional comparison.
parts.answer: Caged plants without wasps control for the effect of the cage itself, so the only difference between treatments is the presence of wasps; uncaged plants show how whiteflies behave in natural field conditions, so it can be judged whether the caged results represent the field.
parts.working: B1 cage control so only one variable (wasps) differs; B1 any difference then due to wasps; B1 uncaged plants show natural conditions/effect of cage on population.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A microbiologist isolated two single-celled prokaryotes, J and K, from a hot spring at 70 °C. To help decide whether each belongs to the Bacteria or the Archaea, she tested the effect of the antibiotic penicillin, which prevents the formation of peptidoglycan cell walls, by spreading each organism on agar plates with paper discs containing penicillin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the result expected for an archaean and explain your answer.
parts.answer: No clear zone (growth right up to the disc), because archaea have no peptidoglycan in their cell walls, so penicillin has no target.
parts.working: B1 no inhibition zone; B1 no peptidoglycan.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the controls and standardised variables needed for this test to be valid.
parts.answer: Discs soaked in sterile water (no penicillin) as a negative control; a known bacterium sensitive to penicillin tested at the same time as a positive control; same concentration and volume of penicillin on each disc; same volume of culture spread; incubate at the organisms' growth temperature (e.g. 70 °C) for the same time; aseptic technique to avoid contamination.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: negative control disc (water/solvent only); positive control organism; same antibiotic concentration/volume/disc size; same culture density/volume; same incubation temperature and time; aseptic technique.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this test alone is not enough to place an organism in a domain.
parts.answer: Some bacteria are naturally resistant to penicillin (e.g. those lacking a cell wall or with resistance genes), so rRNA sequencing or membrane lipid analysis is also needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Researchers are investigating the effect of salinity on the growth of seedlings of the mangrove Avicennia marina, for a restoration project in the Indus delta. They consider measuring growth as (1) increase in stem height, (2) increase in fresh mass, or (3) final dry mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate each of the three measures of growth.
parts.answer: Height: quick and non-destructive, so the same plant can be measured repeatedly, but ignores growth in leaves and roots and thickness. Fresh mass: includes the whole plant but water content varies with salinity and time of day, so it is unreliable. Dry mass: the best measure of organic material/biomass, but plants must be killed, so separate plants are needed for each time point.
parts.working: B1 height – non-destructive but only one dimension; B1 fresh mass – variable water content (especially relevant with salinity); B1 dry mass – most valid measure of biomass; B1 dry mass destructive/needs more plants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the dry mass would be determined accurately.
parts.answer: Wash off sediment, heat in an oven at about 80–90 °C, and weigh repeatedly until the mass is constant.
parts.working: B1 oven at suitable temperature (not so hot that tissue burns); B1 dry to constant mass.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The shell lengths of eight dog-whelks (sea snails) on a rocky shore were measured.
Shell length / mm: 32, 35, 29, 38, 31, 34, 36, 33

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean shell length.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation, s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 deviations from 33.5 squared, Σ(x − x̄)² = 58; M1 58 ÷ 7 = 8.286; A1 √8.286 = 2.88 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation shows about the data.
parts.answer: It measures the spread of the lengths around the mean – most shells are within about 2.9 mm of 33.5 mm.
parts.working: B1 spread/variation about the mean.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Four ecological investigations are described.
1 Is the number of moth species caught in a light trap correlated with night-time temperature? The data are not normally distributed.
2 Is the mean leaf length of a shrub different in a sunny and a shaded habitat? The data are normally distributed.
3 Do woodlice in a choice chamber show a preference for damp or dry conditions?
4 Is the wing length of a bird species linearly correlated with its body mass? Both are normally distributed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the most suitable statistical test for each investigation.
parts.answer: 1 Spearman's rank correlation; 2 t-test; 3 chi-squared test; 4 Pearson's correlation coefficient.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: The lengths of 16 pine needles from a tree were measured. Mean = 18.4 mm; standard deviation = 3.2 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean, SE = s ÷ √n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval of the mean, using mean ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the 95 % confidence interval tells you.
parts.answer: There is a 95 % probability that the true mean needle length for the tree lies within this range.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: A student wants to know whether the mean number of lichen species per tree differs between two villages, and plans to use a t-test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean number of lichen species per tree in the two villages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a probability of 0.05 when deciding whether a result is significant.
parts.answer: If the probability of getting a difference this large by chance alone is 5 % or less, the null hypothesis is rejected; so there is a 5 % (1 in 20) chance of wrongly concluding there is a real difference.
parts.working: B1 5 %/1 in 20 probability the difference is due to chance; B1 below this, reject the null hypothesis/the difference is significant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two conditions that the data should meet for a t-test to be used.
parts.answer: Data are continuous/measured (interval) and approximately normally distributed; samples are independent and similar in size/variance; sample sizes are less than about 30 per group (for the t-test as used here).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: normal distribution; continuous/interval data; independent samples; similar variances; small samples (< 30).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The lengths of ten leaflets from the sunny side and ten from the shaded side of a neem tree were measured.
Sun / mm: 52, 48, 55, 50, 47, 53, 49, 51, 46, 54
Shade / mm: 61, 58, 64, 57, 62, 59, 66, 60, 63, 58

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate t, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). The standard deviations are s(sun) = 3.03 mm and s(shade) = 2.94 mm. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 both means; M1 √(3.03²/10 + 2.94²/10) = 1.335; A1 7.71 (accept 7.72 from unrounded standard deviations).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 with 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 7.71 > 2.10, so reject the null hypothesis: shade leaflets are significantly longer than sun leaflets (probability the difference is due to chance < 5 %).
parts.working: B1 comparison and rejection of null hypothesis; B1 conclusion in context.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
60 woodlice were placed in the centre of a choice chamber with four equal sections. After 15 minutes their positions were recorded.
Dark and damp: 27; dark and dry: 14; light and damp: 12; light and dry: 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: E = 15 in each section; χ² = 14.53
parts.working: M1 expected 15 each; M1 (O − E)²/E values 9.6, 0.067, 0.6, 4.267; A1 14.53.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom and use the critical value 7.82 (p = 0.05) to state a conclusion.
parts.answer: 3 degrees of freedom; 14.53 > 7.82 so reject the null hypothesis – the woodlice are not distributed randomly and prefer dark, damp conditions.
parts.working: B1 df = 3; B1 conclusion, significant preference (dark and damp).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The nitrate concentration and the number of frog species breeding in nine village ponds were recorded.
Nitrate / mg dm⁻³: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 18, 22, 27, 35
Frog species: 7, 6, 7, 5, 4, 4, 2, 3, 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks with ties averaged (7, 7 → 8.5; 4, 4 → 4.5, ranking from lowest); M1 d² values; M1 Σd² = 232; A1 −0.93.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value for n = 9 at p = 0.05 is 0.700. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.700 (ignoring the sign), so there is a significant negative correlation – ponds with more nitrate have fewer frog species.
parts.working: B1 comparison and reject null; B1 significant negative correlation in context.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The mass of single seeds was measured for a wild and a cultivated population of a grain crop.
Wild: mean 42.0 mg, standard deviation 6.0 mg, n = 36
Cultivated: mean 47.5 mg, standard deviation 7.5 mg, n = 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error and the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) for each population.
parts.answer: Wild: SE = 1.0 mg, 95 % CI 40.0–44.0 mg. Cultivated: SE = 1.5 mg, 95 % CI 44.5–50.5 mg.
parts.working: M1 SE = s ÷ √n; A1 1.0 and 1.5; M1 ± 2 SE; A1 both intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the confidence intervals suggest about the difference between the populations.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap (44.0 < 44.5), so the difference in mean seed mass is likely to be significant – cultivated seeds are heavier; a t-test would confirm this.
parts.working: B1 no overlap; B1 difference likely significant/not due to chance.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The wing length and body mass of eight house sparrows were measured. Both variables are normally distributed.
Wing length / mm: 74, 76, 73, 78, 75, 77, 79, 76
Body mass / g: 27.1, 28.0, 26.5, 29.2, 27.8, 28.3, 30.1, 28.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient, r = (Σxy − n x̄ ȳ) ÷ ((n − 1) sₓ s_y). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 means; M1 standard deviations; M1 Σxy and substitution; A1 0.96.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value for 8 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.707. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.96 > 0.707, so there is a significant positive linear correlation between wing length and body mass.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Simpson's index of diversity was calculated for five transects at each of two sites on a hillside: site 1 is a protected forest reserve and site 2 is a forest where firewood is cut.
Site 1: 0.72, 0.68, 0.75, 0.70, 0.66
Site 2: 0.58, 0.63, 0.55, 0.61, 0.60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation for each site. Give the standard deviations to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 both means; B1 s(site 1) = 0.035; B1 s(site 2) = 0.030.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: t = 5.24 (5.21 if unrounded standard deviations are used)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 is 2.31. State the degrees of freedom and a conclusion, and suggest a reason for the difference.
parts.answer: df = 8; 5.24 > 2.31 so reject the null hypothesis – diversity is significantly higher in the protected reserve; firewood cutting removes trees and shrubs, destroying habitats/niches and favouring a few disturbance-tolerant species.
parts.working: B1 df = 8; B1 significant difference, reserve higher; B1 valid reason.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: In 100 quadrats, plant species A was present in 60 and plant species B in 40. Both were present together in only 16 quadrats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of quadrats for each combination (both present, A only, B only, neither) if the two species were distributed independently.
parts.answer: Both 24; A only 36; B only 16; neither 24
parts.working: M1 expected both = 60 × 40 ÷ 100 = 24; A1 all four expected values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The observed numbers were: both 16; A only 44; B only 24; neither 16. Calculate χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With 1 degree of freedom the critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State the conclusion and the type of association, and suggest a biological reason.
parts.answer: 11.11 > 3.84 so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant negative association – the species occur together less often than expected; e.g. they compete for the same resources, one releases inhibitory chemicals, or they need different soil conditions.
parts.working: B1 significant association; B1 negative because observed 'both' (16) < expected (24); B1 biological reason.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
A student counted a rare beetle in 12 quadrats in each of two meadows, and planned to compare the means with a t-test.
Meadow 1 counts: 0, 0, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 8, 0, 2, 0, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the meadow 1 counts. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a t-test is not suitable for these data.
parts.answer: The standard deviation is about twice the mean, and most counts are zero with a few large values, so the data are strongly skewed, not normally distributed; a t-test assumes normal distribution; counts are discrete and the samples small.
parts.working: B1 SD > mean indicates skew (values cannot be negative); B1 many zeros/not normally distributed; B1 t-test requires normally distributed data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be changed to compare the beetle's occurrence in the two meadows.
parts.answer: Record presence or absence in many more quadrats and use a chi-squared test on the numbers of quadrats with and without the beetle in each meadow (or use larger quadrats).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Hatchling turtles were weighed at two hatcheries: hatchery P, where eggs are buried in natural beach sand, and hatchery Q, where eggs are kept in polystyrene boxes.
P (n = 12) / g: 23.1, 24.5, 22.8, 25.0, 23.9, 24.2, 22.5, 23.6, 24.8, 23.3, 24.0, 23.7
Q (n = 10) / g: 21.9, 22.6, 23.0, 21.5, 22.8, 22.1, 23.4, 21.8, 22.4, 22.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of each sample. Give the means to 2 decimal places and the standard deviations to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 both means; B1 s(P); B1 s(Q).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), and state the number of degrees of freedom.
parts.working: M1 substitution; A1 4.56; B1 df = 12 + 10 − 2 = 20.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 with 20 degrees of freedom is 2.09. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 4.56 > 2.09, so hatchlings from the beach-sand hatchery are significantly heavier.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The abundance of a fern was recorded at 5 m intervals from the edge of a forest into a field, using a scale: 5 = abundant, 4 = common, 3 = frequent, 2 = occasional, 1 = rare.
Distance / m: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45
Abundance score: 5, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rank correlation, not Pearson's correlation coefficient, must be used for these data.
parts.answer: The abundance scores are ordinal (ranked categories), not measurements on an interval scale, and cannot be normally distributed; Spearman's uses ranks so is suitable.
parts.working: B1 ordinal/categorical scale; B1 Pearson's requires normally distributed interval data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 10 at p = 0.05 is 0.648. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.92 > 0.648 (ignoring sign) so there is a significant negative correlation: fern abundance decreases with distance from the forest edge.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A class will sample seaweeds and animals on a rocky shore near Karachi, using quadrats along a transect from the low-water mark up the shore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Rising tide cutting off the group – check tide tables, start as the tide goes out and finish well before low water ends; slippery, seaweed-covered rocks causing falls – wear shoes with good grip, walk carefully, no running; large waves sweeping people off rocks – check the weather/sea forecast, stay away from exposed edges; sunburn/heat stroke – hats, sunscreen, drinking water; cuts from barnacles or shells – wear gloves and shoes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for a matching precaution, any three pairs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students used Tullgren funnels with 60 W lamps to extract small animals from soil samples into beakers of 70 % ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this practical and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hot lamp – burns: allow to cool before touching, keep away from paper; ethanol is flammable – keep away from the hot lamp and naked flames, use a small volume; soil may contain bacteria such as Clostridium tetani (tetanus) – wear gloves, cover cuts, wash hands; glassware breaking – handle with care, sweep up with a brush; electrical equipment near liquids – keep cables and liquids apart.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any three pairs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students will go pond dipping in a village pond that is also used by buffalo and has rats living on its banks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two biological hazards and one physical hazard, and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease) from water contaminated with rat urine – cover cuts with waterproof plasters, wear gloves, wash hands; faecal bacteria from buffalo dung – do not touch face/eat, wash hands with soap; drowning/falling in – stay on a firm bank, kneel, work in pairs, nets with long handles, teacher supervision.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each precaution; two biological and one physical.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a laboratory germination test, students place seeds on filter paper moistened with sodium chloride solutions (up to 0.2 mol dm⁻³) in Petri dishes, and later measure roots with a ruler. The seeds have been treated by the seed company with a fungicide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two hazards in this investigation and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Fungicide on seeds may be toxic/irritant – wear gloves and wash hands, do not eat; dilute salt solution – low hazard but can irritate eyes, wear eye protection; glass Petri dishes breaking – use plastic dishes or handle carefully.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any two pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Low – the chemicals are dilute and the only significant hazard (fungicide) is easily controlled with gloves.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A team will survey reptiles and plants in the Thar desert in May, walking along transects during the day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Heat stroke and dehydration – work early in the morning, carry plenty of water, wear hats; venomous snakes and scorpions – wear boots and long trousers, do not put hands under rocks, carry a first-aid kit and know the nearest hospital; getting lost – use GPS/map, work in groups, tell someone the route and return time; sunburn – sunscreen, long sleeves.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any three pairs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To compare bacteria from two soils, students will spread diluted soil suspensions on nutrient agar plates and count the colonies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain why each of these precautions is used:
(i) the plates are incubated at 25 °C, not 37 °C
(ii) the lids are held on with two short pieces of tape, not sealed all round
(iii) the plates are not opened after incubation
(iv) all plates are autoclaved before disposal
parts.answer: (i) 37 °C is human body temperature, which favours growth of human pathogens; (ii) allows oxygen in so anaerobic bacteria (which include many dangerous pathogens) are not encouraged, while preventing accidental opening; (iii) colonies may include pathogens, and opening could release spores/bacteria; (iv) high temperature and pressure kill all microorganisms and spores so waste is safe.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other precaution needed when spreading the suspensions.
parts.answer: Aseptic technique: flame the spreader after dipping in ethanol and keep the ethanol away from the flame / disinfect benches / wash hands.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school club traps moths overnight in a garden using a light trap with a mercury vapour lamp connected to the mains electricity supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet light from the lamp can damage eyes – do not look at the lamp, use a shielded lamp or UV-blocking glasses; electric shock if rain wets the lamp or cable – use a residual current device (RCD) and rain guard, outdoor cables; hot lamp can burn skin or crack if rain falls on it – allow to cool, use rain guard; tripping over cables in the dark – use torches, mark/tape down cables.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any three pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce harm to the moths.
parts.answer: Place egg-box shelters in the trap, empty it early the next morning, identify moths quickly and release them in cover away from birds.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a mark–release–recapture study, wild mice are caught in baited live traps, marked by clipping a small patch of fur, and released.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two risks to the people handling the mice and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Bites – wear thick gloves/handle with a bag; diseases carried by rodents (e.g. hantavirus, leptospirosis) – gloves, wash hands, avoid stirring up dust from nests.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a risk with precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three ways the study should be designed to protect the welfare of the mice.
parts.answer: Check traps often (e.g. every few hours) so mice do not suffer from heat, cold or hunger; put bedding and food in the trap; handle quickly and gently; use a marking method that causes no pain and does not make them more visible to predators; release at the point of capture; avoid trapping when females are feeding young.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to compare the leaves of a rare orchid growing in two valleys by collecting 20 whole plants from each valley.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this plan is a risk to the organisms being studied and suggest how the investigation should be changed.
parts.answer: Removing 40 plants could reduce a small population and remove reproductive individuals, increasing the risk of local extinction; measure leaves on living plants in place (non-destructive), photograph them with a scale, or take one small leaf from each plant only if allowed.
parts.working: B1 removal of plants threatens rare population/reduces reproduction; B1 non-destructive measurement in the field; B1 permission/permit from the authorities or use photographs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other permission or ethical point the student should consider.
parts.answer: Permission from the landowner or park authority/wildlife department; avoid trampling and disturbing the habitat.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A risk assessment lists these activities:
1 measuring the girth of trees with a tape in a park
2 collecting water samples from a fast-flowing river in flood
3 counting snails on a garden wall
4 using a sweep net in long grass where ticks are common

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assign a level of risk (low, medium or high) to each activity and justify each choice.
parts.answer: 1 low – little chance of injury; 2 high – risk of drowning/being swept away, severe harm likely; should not be done; 3 low – minimal hazard, wash hands; 4 medium – tick bites can transmit diseases, so long trousers tucked into socks, check skin afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for level with valid justification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a safer way to collect a water sample from the river in activity 2.
parts.answer: Wait until the flood has passed, or take the sample from a bridge or bank using a bottle on a long pole/rope, with a partner and no one entering the water.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A class will survey crabs and mangrove seedlings on the mudflats of a mangrove creek near Karachi at low tide, in June. A student's risk assessment says: 'Hazard: getting muddy. Precaution: wear old clothes. Risk: low.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this risk assessment.
parts.answer: It is incomplete and the risk is underestimated: it misses the incoming tide cutting off the group or flooding the creek channels; sinking and getting stuck in soft mud; cuts from oyster shells, barnacles and sharp mangrove roots (pneumatophores), which can become infected in dirty water; heat stroke and sunburn in June; bites from crabs. 'Old clothes' do not control any real hazard – suitable footwear, gloves and checking tide tables are needed; the risk should be medium, and there is no plan for supervision, first aid or emergencies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: tide hazard missing (check tide tables/times); soft mud/getting stuck missing; cuts from shells/roots and infection missing; heat/sun hazard missing (June); precaution given does not reduce any harm – boots/gloves needed; risk rating underestimated with reason; no emergency plan (supervision, phone, first aid, working in pairs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two changes to the plan of the fieldwork itself to reduce the risk.
parts.answer: Time the survey to start just after high tide as the water falls and finish well before the tide returns; work only on firm mud near the edge, using boards to stand on and a fixed route; work in pairs with a supervisor; survey early in the morning to avoid the hottest part of the day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: timing linked to tide tables; stay on firm ground/boards/marked route; work in pairs/supervision/head count; early-morning timing to avoid heat; first-aid kit and clean water to wash cuts.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An entomology club traditionally killed collected insects in 'killing jars' containing ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate) on cotton wool, then pinned them for a reference collection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazards of using ethyl ethanoate and suggest precautions.
parts.answer: Highly flammable – no naked flames; vapour harmful/irritant if inhaled – use in a well-ventilated place/outdoors, keep lids on, small volumes; irritant to eyes – eye protection; keep the jar labelled and stored securely.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: flammability + precaution; harmful vapour/inhalation + ventilation; eye/skin irritant + goggles/gloves; storage/labelling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether killing insects is justified for a school survey of insect diversity, and suggest an alternative.
parts.answer: Killing reduces local populations, may include rare species, and raises ethical concerns; it may be justified when species cannot be identified alive and a reference collection is needed for accuracy; alternative – identify alive in the field with keys, photograph with a scale, use pooters and release; only a few specimens of common species collected.
parts.working: B1 harm to populations/ethics; B1 justification for scientific accuracy/identification; B1 alternative (photograph, identify and release, minimal collection).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student suggests collecting water from a canal just below a sewage outfall, culturing it on agar at 37 °C in the school laboratory to count faecal bacteria, and comparing the count with water from upstream.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this plan is unsafe for a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Sewage contains human pathogens (e.g. Salmonella, E. coli O157, cholera bacteria); incubating at 37 °C encourages these pathogens to multiply to very high numbers; handling and disposing of large numbers of pathogens needs a specialist laboratory with higher containment.
parts.working: B1 sewage contains pathogens; B1 37 °C selects for/grows human pathogens; B1 school labs do not have suitable containment/disposal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a safer way for the student to compare the pollution of the water above and below the outfall.
parts.answer: Use a biotic index of invertebrates collected by kick sampling, or measure dissolved oxygen with a meter, or use commercially prepared test kits (e.g. nitrate/ammonia strips); wear gloves and wash hands after handling the water.
parts.working: B1 safer method (biotic index/oxygen/chemical test kits); B1 suitable precaution when collecting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the level of risk of sample collection from the bank and justify it.
parts.answer: Medium – risk of infection from contaminated water and falling in, but it can be reduced with gloves, waterproof plasters and working from a firm bank.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two methods are proposed to survey birds in a wetland reserve: (1) mist-netting, in which fine nets catch birds that are then identified, weighed and released by trained bird ringers; (2) point counts, in which observers record birds seen or heard from fixed points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the risks of the two methods to the birds and to the investigators.
parts.answer: Mist-netting: birds can be injured, stressed or die if nets are not checked often or in bad weather; requires licensed trained handlers; investigators risk pecks/scratches and diseases (e.g. avian influenza) – gloves, hand washing. Point counts: no handling, so almost no risk to birds; investigators face only general fieldwork risks (wet ground, insects, sun).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mist-netting injury/stress to birds; need for trained/licensed ringers and frequent net checks; zoonotic disease/handling injury to people; point counts no contact so minimal risk to birds; point counts low risk to observers (general field hazards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest when the extra risk of mist-netting could be justified.
parts.answer: When data can only be obtained by handling birds, e.g. body mass, age, moult or ringing to follow survival and migration, or to identify similar-looking species; and the benefit to conservation outweighs the small risk.
parts.working: B1 data not obtainable otherwise (mass, ringing, close identification); B1 conservation benefit outweighs risk when done by trained people.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will germinate seeds of a wild rice in sodium chloride solutions of 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200 mmol dm⁻³ and record percentage germination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As salt concentration increases, the percentage germination of wild rice seeds decreases.
parts.working: B1 directional relationship between IV and DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no relationship (correlation) between salt concentration and percentage germination.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the biological reason for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Higher salt concentration lowers the water potential of the solution, so less water enters the seed by osmosis; the seed cannot take up enough water to activate enzymes and germinate (salt ions may also be toxic).
parts.working: B1 lower water potential outside, less water uptake by osmosis; B1 water needed to activate enzymes/hydrolyse food stores for germination.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A park manager stopped mowing one half of a large lawn. Two years later, students will compare plant species diversity in the mown and unmown halves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis and a null hypothesis for this comparison.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: plant species diversity is higher in the unmown half than in the mown half. Null hypothesis: there is no difference in mean plant species diversity between the mown and unmown halves.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test that would be used to test the null hypothesis, if the diversity values are normally distributed.
parts.answer: t-test

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mayfly nymphs absorb oxygen through gills on their abdomen. A student will measure dissolved oxygen and count mayfly nymphs at ten stream sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the relationship between dissolved oxygen and the number of mayfly nymphs, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Positive correlation – more mayfly nymphs where dissolved oxygen is higher; the nymphs need a high oxygen concentration for aerobic respiration, and with low oxygen they cannot absorb enough through their gills, so they die or move away.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 need oxygen for aerobic respiration; B1 low oxygen → death/migration/fewer survive.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Statements from a student's plan:
1 'Lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide.'
2 'Lichen cover will be lower on walls 100 m from the factory than on walls 2 km away.'
3 'There is no correlation between distance from the factory and lichen cover.'
4 'Lichen cover increases as distance from the factory increases.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which statement is: (i) the null hypothesis, (ii) a testable hypothesis, (iii) a specific prediction, (iv) background information.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Brine shrimps are placed in a long tube; one half is lit and the other half is dark. After 10 minutes the number of shrimps in each half will be counted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis that would be tested with a chi-squared test.
parts.answer: There is no difference between the numbers of brine shrimps in the light and dark halves (any difference from equal numbers is due to chance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: If 50 brine shrimps are used, state the expected number in each half under the null hypothesis.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A researcher is investigating whether nitrate from farmland affects aquatic plant diversity. She considers two designs:
Design 1: measure nitrate and Simpson's index in 12 ponds across a district.
Design 2: compare Simpson's index in 10 ponds next to fertilised fields with 10 ponds in an unfarmed reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis suitable for each design.
parts.answer: Design 1: there is no correlation between nitrate concentration and Simpson's index of plant diversity. Design 2: there is no difference between the mean Simpson's index of ponds next to fertilised fields and ponds in the reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark each – correlation for design 1, difference in means for design 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test for each design, assuming design 1 data are not normally distributed and design 2 data are normally distributed.
parts.answer: Design 1: Spearman's rank correlation; design 2: t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: On many trees in a forest in Murree, a student notices that more moss grows on the north side of the trunks than on the south side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a hypothesis to explain this observation.
parts.answer: The north side of the trunk receives less direct sunlight, so it stays damper/has higher humidity, which mosses need.
parts.working: B1 linked to light/moisture/temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Make a prediction from your hypothesis that could be tested by measurement.
parts.answer: Bark moisture content (or air humidity next to the bark) will be higher on the north side than on the south side, and moss cover will be greater where bark moisture is higher.
parts.working: B1 measurable variable predicted to differ; B1 linked to moss cover.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how you would test the prediction.
parts.answer: On several (e.g. 15) trees of the same species, measure bark moisture with a moisture meter (or humidity with a probe) and moss percentage cover in a 10 cm × 10 cm grid quadrat at the same height on the north and south sides; compare with a paired t-test or correlate moisture and cover with Spearman's rank.
parts.working: B1 measurements on both sides of many trees at same height; B1 suitable analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Limpets cling to rocks on the shore. A student thinks that on exposed shores, where waves are strong, limpets have flatter shells (a lower height ÷ base length ratio) than on sheltered shores.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis and a null hypothesis for the investigation.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: the mean shell height ÷ base ratio is lower on exposed shores than on sheltered shores. Null: there is no difference in mean shell ratio between exposed and sheltered shores.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological reasoning behind the hypothesis.
parts.answer: A flatter shell has a smaller surface facing the waves, so less drag; limpets with flatter shells are less likely to be dislodged and survive to reproduce, so natural selection favours them on exposed shores (or they grow flatter in response to waves).
parts.working: B1 reduced drag/less likely to be washed off; B1 better survival/selection on exposed shores.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Parthenium hysterophorus has invaded grazing land in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. An ecologist will compare native plant species in paired 1 m² quadrats: one inside a Parthenium patch and one 5 m outside it, at 20 patches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis and predict the results if your hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: Parthenium reduces native plant species richness. Prediction: in most pairs the number of native species will be lower in the quadrat inside the patch than in the quadrat outside it.
parts.working: B1 hypothesis; B1 prediction linked to the paired design.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the quadrats are placed in pairs close to each other.
parts.answer: Each pair shares similar soil, slope, grazing and rainfall, so the main difference between them is the presence of Parthenium; this controls for differences between sites.
parts.working: B1 other variables similar within pairs; B1 so difference can be attributed to Parthenium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a lower native richness inside patches would not, on its own, show that Parthenium caused it.
parts.answer: Parthenium may simply invade places that already had few native species (e.g. disturbed or overgrazed ground) – the cause and effect could be the other way round.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A fence has been built to keep goats out of an area of hillside grassland that was previously heavily grazed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how plant species diversity inside the fence will change over the next 10 years and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Diversity will first increase as grazing-sensitive species recover and flower; later it may decrease as tall, fast-growing grasses and shrubs become dominant and shade out smaller species (succession/competition).
parts.working: B1 initial increase; B1 reason – grazing-sensitive species recover/seed; B1 later decrease due to competitive dominant species/succession without disturbance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a control that should be used when testing this prediction.
parts.answer: Similar unfenced areas nearby, still grazed, surveyed at the same times.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Many mangrove seedlings planted in the Indus delta die in their first year. Two hypotheses are proposed:
H1: seedlings die because the soil water is too salty.
H2: seedlings die because crabs eat them.
Survival after one year: open plots at low salinity 34 %; open plots at high salinity 30 %; plots with crab-proof mesh at low salinity 81 %; plots with crab-proof mesh at high salinity 76 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to evaluate the two hypotheses.
parts.answer: H2 is strongly supported: excluding crabs more than doubles survival (34 → 81 % at low salinity, 30 → 76 % at high salinity, an increase of about 46–47 percentage points); H1 is only weakly supported: high salinity lowers survival by only 4–5 percentage points, with or without crabs; crabs are the main cause of death, though salinity may have a small effect that needs a statistical test.
parts.working: B1 crab exclusion large increase, with figures; B1 H2 supported; B1 salinity small effect, with figures; B1 H1 weakly supported/may not be significant – need replicates/statistics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the mesh itself could have affected the results, and how this could be tested.
parts.answer: Mesh may shade seedlings or reduce wave damage/trap sediment; test with a 'partial cage' control – mesh with gaps large enough for crabs to enter, so the only difference is crab access.
parts.working: B1 mesh alters other conditions (shading, water flow, sediment); B1 control of mesh with openings/roof-only cage.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Frogs from two neighbouring valleys look identical but their mating calls are different. A biologist proposes the hypothesis that they are two separate species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Make three predictions that would be expected to be true if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: Females will respond (move towards) only to calls of males from their own valley; in mixed captive groups they will not interbreed, or hybrids will be infertile/inviable; DNA sequences (e.g. mitochondrial genes) will differ more between the valleys than within each valley, by an amount similar to that between other recognised frog species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three testable predictions: call preference/behavioural isolation; no interbreeding or infertile hybrids; greater genetic difference between than within populations; no gene flow where ranges meet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a result that agrees with a prediction does not prove the hypothesis.
parts.answer: The result could have another explanation (e.g. call differences due to local learning or temperature, or populations recently separated but still able to interbreed); further evidence could still contradict the hypothesis, so it is supported, not proved.
parts.working: B1 alternative explanations possible; B1 hypotheses can only be supported/falsified, not proved.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A botanist has records of the altitudes at which an alpine flower was found on a mountain in Gilgit-Baltistan in 1975. She will survey the mountain again this year to test the hypothesis that climate warming has caused the species to move to higher altitudes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis and two predictions that follow from the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Null: there is no difference between the altitudes at which the flower is found in 1975 and now. Predictions: the lowest altitude at which the species grows is higher now than in 1975; the mean (or upper limit) altitude of the population is higher now.
parts.working: B1 null; 1 mark each for two predictions about lower limit, mean or upper limit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons, other than climate warming, why the survey might find the flower at higher altitudes.
parts.answer: Grazing or land use change has removed it from lower slopes; the new survey may search higher areas more thoroughly (different sampling effort/methods); trampling or collecting at lower, more accessible sites.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one additional piece of evidence that would strengthen the link with climate warming.
parts.answer: Temperature records showing warming over the same period, or similar upward shifts in many other species on the same and other mountains.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In green turtles, eggs incubated at higher sand temperatures produce more female hatchlings. A conservation team is concerned that shade from new beach buildings will cool some nesting sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis about the effect of shading on the sex ratio of hatchlings and a prediction that could be tested at the hatchery.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: shaded nests have a lower sand temperature, so they produce a lower proportion of female hatchlings. Prediction: if half of a set of clutches is incubated under shade cloth, those nests will have a lower mean temperature and fewer female hatchlings than unshaded nests.
parts.working: B1 hypothesis linking shade, temperature and sex ratio; B1 testable prediction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the team should record sand temperature in every nest, not just whether it is shaded.
parts.answer: Temperature is the actual factor that determines sex; shade may affect other factors (moisture), and temperature varies between nests for other reasons, so recording it allows the relationship between temperature and sex ratio to be analysed directly.
parts.working: B1 temperature is the causal variable; B1 shade is only an indirect/variable proxy – allows correlation analysis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why, for conservation, a population producing almost only female hatchlings could be a problem.
parts.answer: Too few males for mating in future, reducing reproductive success and genetic diversity.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student in Peshawar mixed 2 cm³ of yeast suspension with 2 cm³ of glucose solution and 1 cm³ of dilute methylene blue in a test tube at 35 °C. Methylene blue becomes colourless when it is reduced by hydrogen released in respiration. The time for the blue colour to disappear was recorded.
glucose 0 %: no colour change after 600 s
glucose 1 %: 312 s
glucose 2 %: 205 s
glucose 3 %: 158 s
glucose 4 %: 151 s
glucose 5 %: 149 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of glucose concentration on the time taken for the methylene blue to decolourise.
parts.answer: As glucose concentration increases from 1 % to 3 % the time falls steeply (312 s to 158 s); above 3 % the time falls only slightly / levels off (151 s, 149 s); no decolourisation without glucose.
parts.working: B1 time decreases as concentration increases; B1 levels off above 3 % with data quoted (or no change in 600 s at 0 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rate of decolourisation can be found as 1000 ÷ time. Calculate the rate for 2 % glucose. Give your answer to 3 significant figures and state the unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student concluded: 'The rate of respiration of yeast is directly proportional to the glucose concentration.' Use the data to explain whether this conclusion is supported.
parts.answer: Not supported: doubling glucose from 2 % to 4 % does not double the rate (205 s → 151 s, rate 4.88 → 6.62 s⁻¹); rate levels off at high concentration.
parts.working: B1 not supported; B1 calculated or quoted comparison showing rate not doubling / plateau.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Strips of red onion epidermis were placed in sodium chloride solutions for 20 minutes. For each strip, 100 cells were observed with a light microscope and the number of plasmolysed cells was counted.
0.00 mol dm⁻³: 0 %
0.10 mol dm⁻³: 4 %
0.20 mol dm⁻³: 18 %
0.30 mol dm⁻³: 42 %
0.40 mol dm⁻³: 76 %
0.50 mol dm⁻³: 95 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between sodium chloride concentration and the percentage of plasmolysed cells.
parts.answer: Percentage plasmolysed increases as concentration increases; few cells plasmolysed up to 0.10 mol dm⁻³, steepest increase between 0.20 and 0.40 mol dm⁻³, almost all (95 %) at 0.50 mol dm⁻³.
parts.working: B1 positive trend; B1 detail with data (e.g. steepest rise 0.30–0.40, 95 % at 0.50).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming a straight line between the two readings either side of 50 %, estimate the sodium chloride concentration at which 50 % of the cells are plasmolysed. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.32 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what can be concluded about the epidermal cells at the concentration found in (b).
parts.answer: This is incipient plasmolysis: the water potential of the solution is about equal to the (mean) water potential of the cell contents / cell sap; cells vary, so half have lower and half higher water potential.
parts.working: B1 water potential of solution ≈ water potential of cells; B1 idea of an average / cells differ in water potential.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student placed single Daphnia (water fleas) in caffeine solutions for 5 minutes and counted heartbeats using a microscope. Each value is the mean for 5 Daphnia.
0 mg dm⁻³: 212 beats per minute
10 mg dm⁻³: 228 beats per minute
20 mg dm⁻³: 241 beats per minute
40 mg dm⁻³: 262 beats per minute
80 mg dm⁻³: 270 beats per minute

parts.label: a
parts.text: The hypothesis was: 'The heart rate of Daphnia increases as caffeine concentration increases.' State whether the results support the hypothesis and give a reason using the data.
parts.answer: Supported (partly): heart rate rises from 212 to 270 beats per minute between 0 and 80 mg dm⁻³; but the increase is much smaller between 40 and 80 mg dm⁻³ (262 to 270).
parts.working: B1 supports with data; B1 note that increase slows / levels off at higher concentrations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate between 0 and 80 mg dm⁻³ caffeine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the result cannot be used to predict the effect of caffeine on human heart rate.
parts.answer: Daphnia is a different organism (invertebrate, ectotherm, different heart/regulation and metabolism of caffeine); concentrations reaching the human heart are unknown.
parts.working: B1 any one valid reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A microbiologist in Lahore spread a lawn of bacteria on agar plates and placed four discs, each soaked in a different antibiotic, P, Q, R and S, on each plate. After 24 hours the diameter of the clear zone around each disc was measured on 6 plates.
P: mean 18.2 mm, standard deviation 1.1 mm
Q: mean 24.6 mm, standard deviation 3.8 mm
R: mean 22.9 mm, standard deviation 1.2 mm
S: mean 9.5 mm, standard deviation 0.6 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: The paper discs had a diameter of 6 mm. Calculate the mean area of the clear zone for antibiotic R, not including the area of the disc. Use π = 3.14 or the π key. Give your answer to the nearest mm².
parts.answer: 384 mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: The microbiologist concluded that antibiotic Q was the most effective. Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Q has the largest mean diameter, so supports; but Q has a very large standard deviation (3.8 mm) so results are variable; mean ± SD for Q (20.8–28.4 mm) overlaps R (21.7–24.1 mm), so the difference between Q and R may not be significant; a t-test would be needed.
parts.working: B1 Q largest mean; B1 Q large SD / less reliable; B1 overlap of ranges with R so difference may not be significant / need statistical test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons, other than how effective each antibiotic is at killing bacteria, why the clear zones might differ in size.
parts.answer: Antibiotics diffuse through agar at different rates (molecule size/solubility); different concentration or amount of antibiotic on each disc; different time for diffusion before bacterial growth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A leafy shoot of a guava plant was set up in a potometer. A fan was placed at different distances from the shoot to give different air speeds, and the rate of water uptake was measured.
0 m s⁻¹: 4.2 mm³ min⁻¹
1 m s⁻¹: 7.9 mm³ min⁻¹
2 m s⁻¹: 10.8 mm³ min⁻¹
3 m s⁻¹: 12.0 mm³ min⁻¹
4 m s⁻¹: 12.3 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of air speed on the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: Rate increases as air speed increases from 0 to 3 m s⁻¹ (4.2 to 12.0 mm³ min⁻¹); the increase is smaller at higher speeds and rate almost levels off between 3 and 4 m s⁻¹ (12.0 to 12.3).
parts.working: B1 increase; B1 levels off with data quoted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your knowledge of transpiration to explain the results.
parts.answer: Moving air removes the layer of humid air / water vapour near the stomata; this keeps the water potential gradient between air spaces in the leaf and the outside air steep; so more water vapour diffuses out of the stomata; at high air speed another factor limits, e.g. stomatal aperture / rate of evaporation from mesophyll cell walls / stomata may partly close.
parts.working: B1 humid layer removed; B1 steeper water potential / water vapour gradient, faster diffusion through stomata; B1 levelling explained by another limiting factor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the potometer measures the rate of water uptake rather than the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Some of the water taken up is used by the shoot (photosynthesis, kept in cells for turgor), so uptake is not exactly equal to water lost.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Lipase was added to full-cream milk containing sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator, which is pink in alkaline conditions. As fatty acids are released the pH falls and the pink colour disappears. The time taken for the colour to disappear was recorded at five temperatures.
15 °C: 540 s
25 °C: 290 s
35 °C: 170 s
45 °C: 205 s
55 °C: 610 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate (1000 ÷ time, in s⁻¹) at each temperature. Give each value to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 1000 ÷ time; A1 all five correct to 2 d.p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concluded that the optimum temperature of lipase is 35 °C. Explain why this conclusion is not fully justified and describe how the experiment could be changed to find the optimum more precisely.
parts.answer: Readings are 10 °C apart, so the optimum could be anywhere between 25 °C and 45 °C (rate at 45 °C is quite high, so likely between 35 and 45 °C); repeat with smaller intervals, e.g. every 2 °C from 30 °C to 44 °C; repeat each temperature at least three times and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 interval too large / optimum between 25 and 45 °C; B1 extra temperatures at smaller intervals around 35–45 °C; B1 replicates and means.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The chlorophyll content of mango leaves was measured in an orchard near Multan. Two leaves from the sunny outer canopy and two leaves from the shaded inner canopy were taken from each of 8 trees (n = 16 in each group).
sun leaves: mean 1.42 mg chlorophyll per g fresh mass, standard deviation 0.24
shade leaves: mean 1.86 mg chlorophyll per g fresh mass, standard deviation 0.32

parts.label: a
parts.text: The 95 % confidence interval is mean ± 2 × standard error, where standard error = SD ÷ √n. Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for each group. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: sun leaves: 1.30 to 1.54 mg g⁻¹; shade leaves: 1.70 to 2.02 mg g⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the confidence intervals show about the difference in chlorophyll content between sun and shade leaves.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference is (very likely) significant / not due to chance; shade leaves have a higher chlorophyll content per gram.
parts.working: B1 no overlap → significant; B1 shade higher.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a higher chlorophyll content is an advantage to leaves in the shade.
parts.answer: Light intensity is low in the shade, so light is the limiting factor; more chlorophyll (more photosystems) absorbs a greater proportion of the available light, so more light-dependent reaction / ATP and reduced NADP for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 low light intensity limiting; B1 absorbs more of available light → more photosynthesis.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the leaves in both groups were taken from the same 8 trees.
parts.answer: To control genetic differences / age / health of trees between groups, so only light (position) differs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students measured the nitrate concentration and the number of algal cells per cm³ of water in 10 farm ponds near Sheikhupura. They calculated Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 0.89.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between nitrate concentration and the density of algal cells in the ponds.
parts.working: B1 must refer to correlation and both variables (not 'no difference').

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of rs for 10 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.648. State what can be concluded from rs = 0.89.
parts.answer: 0.89 is greater than 0.648, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant positive correlation between nitrate concentration and algal density (probability of this being due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 compare with critical value, reject null hypothesis; B1 significant positive correlation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The students also calculated rs = −0.55 between nitrate concentration and the number of invertebrate species found in each pond. Using the same critical value, state and explain what this result shows.
parts.answer: There is a negative correlation, but 0.55 (ignoring the sign) is less than 0.648, so it is not significant at p = 0.05; accept the null hypothesis – the apparent trend could be due to chance (more ponds would need to be sampled).
parts.working: B1 compares magnitude 0.55 with 0.648 (sign ignored), not significant / accept null hypothesis; B1 trend may be due to chance / no significant correlation shown.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A farmers' group said: 'The data prove that nitrate fertiliser running off fields causes the growth of algae.' Discuss whether this statement is justified.
parts.answer: Not justified: correlation does not show cause; other variables may vary with nitrate, e.g. phosphate, temperature, light / pond depth; the source of the nitrate was not identified (could be animal waste or sewage); only 10 ponds sampled once, so "prove" is too strong; but a causal link is plausible because algae need nitrogen to make amino acids and nucleotides; an experiment adding nitrate to identical tanks would test cause.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: correlation ≠ causation; named other variable; source of nitrate not shown; small sample / single sampling; biological reason it is plausible; suggested controlled experiment.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Cabomba was measured by counting bubbles per minute at different light intensities (arbitrary units) in two sodium hydrogencarbonate concentrations, at 25 °C.
light intensity: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
low hydrogencarbonate (0.01 mol dm⁻³): 6, 11, 19, 23, 24, 24
high hydrogencarbonate (0.05 mol dm⁻³): 6, 12, 23, 34, 41, 42

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis at the low hydrogencarbonate concentration
(i) at light intensities 1 and 2
(ii) at light intensities 8 and 10.
Give a reason for each answer.
parts.answer: (i) light intensity – rate is the same at both hydrogencarbonate concentrations / rate rises as light rises; (ii) carbon dioxide (hydrogencarbonate) concentration – rate no longer rises with light but is higher with more hydrogencarbonate.
parts.working: B1 each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate at light intensity 10 when the hydrogencarbonate concentration is increased. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The rate at the high hydrogencarbonate concentration levels off at about 42 bubbles per minute. Suggest two factors that could be limiting the rate at this point.
parts.answer: Temperature; amount / activity of rubisco (enzymes of the Calvin cycle); amount of chlorophyll / number of chloroplasts; carbon dioxide still limiting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student in Rawalpindi is preparing solutions for an investigation into the hydrolysis of starch by amylase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a 2.0 % starch solution and distilled water, describe how to make 20 cm³ of each of these starch concentrations: 0.25 %, 0.50 %, 1.00 %, 1.50 % and 2.00 %. Show the volumes in a table.
parts.working: B1 table with headings and units (concentration / %, volume of 2.0 % starch / cm³, volume of water / cm³); B1 starch volumes correct; B1 water volumes correct (each pair totals 20 cm³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second student needed glucose solutions of 1.0, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 mol dm⁻³. Describe how she could make these by serial dilution from a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ glucose solution.
parts.answer: Put 10 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ in a beaker (keep as first solution); take 1 cm³ of it and add 9 cm³ distilled water and mix → 0.1 mol dm⁻³; take 1 cm³ of this and add 9 cm³ water → 0.01; repeat → 0.001 mol dm⁻³; use a clean pipette / syringe each time and mix thoroughly.
parts.working: B1 1 cm³ + 9 cm³ water (×10 dilution, or equivalent volumes); B1 each new solution made from the previous one; B1 mixing / clean syringe or graduated pipette.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rennin is an enzyme that clots milk by acting on the protein casein. A student has milk, a 1 % rennin solution, test tubes, syringes, water baths and a stopwatch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the time taken for rennin to clot milk. Your method should be detailed enough for another person to follow.
parts.answer: Use at least five temperatures, e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C in thermostatically controlled water baths; place 5 cm³ milk and 1 cm³ rennin in separate tubes in the bath for 5 minutes to reach the temperature; mix and start the timer; tilt the tube every 30 s / check until the milk forms a solid clot that does not flow; record time; keep volume and concentration of milk and rennin, and pH (buffer) the same; repeat three times at each temperature and calculate the mean; calculate rate as 1 ÷ time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: range of at least 5 temperatures with values; water bath / thermostat method; equilibration before mixing; clear end point (milk no longer flows when tilted) and timing; two named standardised variables with how (volumes, concentrations, pH buffer, type of milk); replicates and mean / rate = 1 ÷ time. Max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a control for this investigation and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: Milk + boiled (denatured) and cooled rennin (or water instead of rennin) at each temperature; shows that clotting is caused by the active enzyme and not by temperature alone.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 purpose.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has dried yeast, sucrose, distilled water, boiling tubes fitted with bungs and delivery tubes, a beaker of water, a water bath and a stopwatch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could use this apparatus to investigate the effect of sucrose concentration on the rate of respiration of yeast.
parts.answer: Make sucrose solutions (e.g. 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 %) by diluting a stock with water; add the same volume (e.g. 10 cm³) of the same yeast suspension to the same volume of each sucrose solution; place tube in a water bath at a fixed temperature (e.g. 35 °C); leave 5 minutes to equilibrate; count the bubbles of carbon dioxide leaving the delivery tube into the water / limewater in a fixed time (e.g. 3 minutes); repeat 3 times and calculate the mean; rate = bubbles per minute.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: range of concentrations; dilution from stock; same volume/concentration of yeast; temperature controlled (water bath); acclimatisation time; dependent variable measured (bubbles counted in fixed time or gas syringe); replicates and means. Max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why counting bubbles may give inaccurate results and how a gas syringe would improve this.
parts.answer: Bubbles are different sizes / some carbon dioxide dissolves; a gas syringe measures the volume of gas directly.
parts.working: B1 reason; B1 improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Urease is an enzyme that catalyses the hydrolysis of urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to prepare 15 cm³ of each of five urea solutions, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0 mol dm⁻³, using a 2.0 mol dm⁻³ stock solution and distilled water.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = concentration ÷ 2.0 × 15 (3, 6, 9, 12, 15 cm³); A1 water volumes 12, 9, 6, 3, 0 cm³ so each totals 15 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of urea concentration on the rate of activity of urease. Ammonia produced by urease raises the pH, and phenol red indicator changes from yellow to red-pink when the pH rises above 8.
parts.answer: Add equal volumes of urea solution and phenol red (e.g. 5 cm³ + 3 drops) to tubes; add a buffer at a starting pH below 8; equilibrate tubes and urease solution in water bath at e.g. 30 °C; add a fixed volume (1 cm³) of the same urease solution and start timer; record time for indicator to reach a set colour, judged against a colour standard / white background, or use a colorimeter; repeat three times and calculate mean; rate = 1 ÷ time; plot rate against urea concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: same volumes of urea and indicator; temperature control with method; same volume and concentration of urease; starting pH / buffer control; clear end point using colour standard or colorimeter; replicates, mean and rate = 1 ÷ time. Max 6.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Copper ions are non-competitive inhibitors of many enzymes. A student has amylase solution, 1 % starch, iodine solution, copper sulfate solution, a pH 7 buffer and a colorimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of copper sulfate concentration on the activity of amylase, using a colorimeter to measure the starch remaining.
parts.answer: Use copper sulfate concentrations e.g. 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10 mol dm⁻³ made by dilution; mix same volume of amylase with same volume of each copper sulfate solution; equilibrate at 30 °C in a water bath with the starch solution; add a fixed volume of 1 % starch and start timing; after a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) remove a sample and add to iodine solution; place in a cuvette and measure absorbance with a red / orange filter, after zeroing with distilled water / iodine blank; higher absorbance = more starch left = less amylase activity; convert to starch concentration using a calibration curve of known starch concentrations; buffer pH; repeat three times and calculate mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: range of at least 5 copper concentrations; same volume/concentration of amylase and starch; temperature controlled with method; fixed time then sample into iodine (or stop reaction); colorimeter zeroed with blank and suitable filter; calibration curve or interpretation of absorbance; pH buffered; replicates and mean. Max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a calibration curve is needed to convert absorbance readings into starch concentrations.
parts.answer: Absorbance is not necessarily directly proportional to concentration (and depends on the colorimeter/iodine used); reading absorbance of known starch concentrations allows unknown concentrations to be read off.
parts.working: B1 known concentrations measured; B1 used to read unknowns / relationship may not be linear.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has fresh spinach leaves, a cork borer, a syringe, 0.2 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, beakers, a lamp, coloured filters and a stopwatch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could investigate the effect of light colour (wavelength) on the rate of photosynthesis using the floating leaf disc method.
parts.answer: Cut equal-sized discs with a cork borer, avoiding veins, from the same spinach leaf / same plant; remove air from discs with a syringe so they sink in 0.2 % sodium hydrogencarbonate; place 10 discs in each beaker of the same volume of the same solution; cover lamp or beaker with coloured filters (e.g. red, blue, green, yellow) or use LEDs of known wavelength; same light intensity (same distance, lux meter) and same temperature (heat shield/water bath); record time for 5 of 10 discs to float, or number floating after 10 minutes; repeat and calculate mean; rate = 1 ÷ time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: identical discs from same leaf; air removal so discs sink; same volume/concentration of hydrogencarbonate; at least 3 colours by filters/LEDs; light intensity controlled with method (lux meter); temperature controlled; measurement of floating (time for half to float); replicates / rate. Max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the discs float as photosynthesis takes place.
parts.answer: Oxygen produced by photolysis collects in the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll; this lowers the density of the disc so it rises.
parts.working: B1 oxygen produced fills air spaces; B1 density decreased / buoyancy.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans a step test with classmates in a school in Karachi. She has a set of steps of different heights, a metronome and a stopwatch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method the student could use to investigate the effect of step height on the time taken for breathing rate to return to the resting rate.
parts.answer: Use volunteers of the same sex/age range and similar fitness, who are healthy (none with asthma/heart conditions); measure resting breathing rate by counting breaths for 1 minute after sitting for 5 minutes; step on and off a step at a fixed rate (metronome, e.g. 30 steps per minute) for 3 minutes; use steps of 5 heights, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cm; count breaths in each 30 s period after stopping until the rate returns to the resting value; record recovery time; full rest between trials / different days; repeat for several volunteers and calculate mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: range of step heights; same stepping rate and duration; resting rate measured after sitting; method of counting breaths after exercise to find recovery time; volunteers matched for at least one named variable; rest between trials / random order; replicates/mean. Max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two ethical or safety points the student should consider.
parts.answer: Informed consent / volunteers can withdraw at any time; screen for medical conditions (asthma, heart problems); stop if dizzy or short of breath; anonymise data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students working in a mangrove forest near Karachi noticed that crab burrows seemed more common close to a creek. They have tape measures, quadrats and a tide table.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the students could find whether there is a correlation between the distance from the creek edge and the density of crab burrows.
parts.answer: Lay a tape measure (transect) from the creek edge at right angles across the mud to the highest point reached by the tide; place a 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrat at regular intervals, e.g. every 2 m (interrupted belt transect); count all burrow openings in each quadrat and convert to burrows per m²; repeat with at least 4 more transects at randomly chosen positions along the creek; sample at the same time of day/state of tide on the same day; also record a variable such as mud water content; calculate Spearman's rank correlation between distance and burrow density.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: transect from water's edge; quadrat with size; regular sampling interval stated; count converted to density; repeated transects at random positions; same tide/time; Spearman's rank (or Pearson if normal) used. Max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for the statistical test.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between distance from the creek edge and the density of crab burrows.
parts.working: B1 must be about correlation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one hazard of this fieldwork and how the risk could be reduced.
parts.answer: Incoming tide / soft mud — check tide tables and work only on a falling tide / stay on firm ground / work in pairs; sharp shells or mangrove roots — wear boots.
parts.working: B1 hazard with matching precaution.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gibberellin from the embryo of a germinating barley seed stimulates the aleurone layer to make amylase, which breaks down starch in the endosperm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to make a range of five gibberellin concentrations from 100 mg dm⁻³ down to 0.01 mg dm⁻³ by serial dilution.
parts.answer: Each step: 1 cm³ of the previous solution + 9 cm³ distilled water, mixed: 100 → 10 → 1 → 0.1 → 0.01 mg dm⁻³.
parts.working: B1 ×10 dilution volumes; B1 each made from the previous solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of gibberellin concentration on amylase production by barley seeds. You should use half seeds without the embryo, placed cut-side down on starch agar.
parts.answer: Cut barley seeds in half and keep the endosperm halves (no embryo, so no natural gibberellin); sterilise the surface (dilute bleach then rinse); soak sets of 10 half-seeds in each gibberellin concentration and in distilled water (control) for the same time; place cut-side down on starch agar plates, same number per plate; incubate at the same temperature (e.g. 25 °C) for the same time (48 h); flood plates with iodine solution; measure the diameter of the clear (yellow-brown) zone around each half-seed; calculate the mean area of the cleared zone; repeat with several plates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: surface sterilisation or aseptic technique; equal soaking time in each concentration; control soaked in distilled water; same number of half-seeds, incubation temperature and time; iodine added and diameter/area of clear zone measured; replicate seeds/plates and mean. Max 5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the half-seeds without embryos are used.
parts.answer: The embryo produces its own gibberellin, which would cause amylase production regardless of the gibberellin added.

author: HomiLabs

stem: DCPIP is a blue dye that is decolourised by ascorbic acid. A student in Larkana wants to know whether boiling guava juice reduces its vitamin C content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to compare the vitamin C (ascorbic acid) content of fresh guava juice and guava juice that has been boiled for 10 minutes, using DCPIP solution.
