parts.answer: Iodine solution is dilute and used in small amounts; it is only a mild irritant / stains skin and clothes; precaution: wear gloves / eye protection and wash skin if splashed.
parts.working: B1 reason; B1 precaution.

stem: Students carry out a quadrat survey on a steep hillside along a walking trail in the Margalla Hills in June.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and suggest how the risk from each can be reduced.
parts.answer: Steep or slippery slopes – stay on paths, wear boots with grip; sun / heat stroke – hats, sunscreen, carry water; stings or bites from insects and snakes – long trousers, look before putting hands in vegetation; getting lost / separated – work in groups with a teacher, carry a phone, tell someone the route; uncertain weather – check the forecast.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hazard + precaution pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a risk assessment should be written before the trip rather than on the day.
parts.answer: So precautions (equipment, clothing, first aid, supervision) can be planned and prepared in advance.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The biuret test uses sodium hydroxide solution and dilute copper sulfate solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the hazard associated with each solution and explain whether this makes the risk of the biuret test medium rather than low.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive at 0.5 mol dm⁻³ and above (irritant when more dilute) and can cause serious eye damage; dilute copper sulfate solution is of low hazard / harmful if swallowed or irritant; with small volumes and eye protection the risk is low, but if sodium hydroxide of 0.5 mol dm⁻³ or more is used, or eye protection is not worn, the risk becomes medium.
parts.working: B1 sodium hydroxide corrosive / damages eyes (irritant only when very dilute); B1 copper sulfate low hazard / harmful / irritant; B1 risk depends on concentration and precautions, with a conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what a student should do if sodium hydroxide splashes into the eye.
parts.answer: Wash the eye immediately with plenty of running water (eye wash) for at least 10 minutes and tell the teacher / seek medical help.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student heats a test tube containing glucose solution and Benedict's solution by holding it directly in a Bunsen burner flame.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this method and suggest a safer method for each.
parts.answer: Heating directly over a Bunsen flame can make the mixture boil and spit out (scalding) – use a beaker of boiling water / water bath instead; tube held by hand / pointing at people – use a test-tube holder or rack, point the tube away from people; hot water bath – handle with tongs, place on heat-proof mat.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 for a matching safer method, two pairs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students scrape cells from the inside of their own cheeks with a cotton bud, smear them onto a slide and stain them with methylene blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and the precautions needed.
parts.answer: Body cells / fluids can carry pathogens – use only your own cheek cells; methylene blue stains and is harmful if swallowed – wear gloves, do not eat or drink in the lab; glass slides and cover slips can break – handle carefully.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two with precautions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how used cotton buds and slides should be disposed of.
parts.answer: Placed in disinfectant (e.g. 1 % sodium chlorate(I)) / a bag for autoclaving before disposal.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students separate photosynthetic pigments from spinach leaves by grinding them with propanone and running a thin-layer chromatogram in a solvent containing ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard and state two precautions.
parts.answer: Propanone / ethanol is highly flammable; no naked flames in the room (warm with a water bath heated electrically, if needed); use small volumes, keep containers closed; work in a well-ventilated area / fume cupboard because vapour is harmful.
parts.working: B1 flammable solvent; 1 mark each for two precautions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the solvent should not be left in an open beaker.
parts.answer: Vapour escapes – can be inhaled / increases fire risk; also the solution becomes more concentrated.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans an investigation of the effect of temperature (20–60 °C) on the hydrolysis of milk protein by trypsin. The pH is followed with phenolphthalein (dissolved in ethanol) and sodium carbonate solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a risk assessment for this practical in a table with columns for hazard, risk and precaution. Include at least three different hazards.
parts.answer: trypsin powder / solution – can cause allergic reaction / sensitiser if inhaled or on skin – make solution in a fume cupboard or have it made by technician, wear gloves and goggles; sodium carbonate solution – irritant – goggles; phenolphthalein in ethanol – flammable / irritant – no flames nearby; hot water bath (up to 60 °C) – scalding – handle with care, use tongs, place on stable surface; broken glass – sweep up with brush, do not use bare hands.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct table layout; 1 mark each for up to three hazards with risk and matching precaution; 1 mark for identifying the enzyme as a sensitiser / allergen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Low (to medium) – dilute solutions in small volumes and temperatures below 60 °C, with goggles and gloves; enzyme sensitisation is reduced by using solutions not powder.
parts.working: B1 level with justification.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student uses a respirometer containing soda lime to measure the oxygen uptake of woodlice at temperatures from 10 °C to 40 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards to the student in this investigation and suggest precautions.
parts.answer: Soda lime is corrosive / irritant – handle with a spatula and gloves, keep it in a gauze-covered compartment; glass capillary tubes may break – handle gently; coloured liquid / ethanol may be flammable or toxic.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two hazard + precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the ethical issues of using live woodlice and describe how harm to them can be minimised.
parts.answer: Animals should not suffer unnecessarily; soda lime must not touch them (use a gauze platform); keep the experiment short and at temperatures they would meet in nature (not above about 30 °C); ensure enough oxygen and a damp environment; use the smallest number needed; return them to their habitat afterwards; consider using germinating seeds instead.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wrote this risk assessment for an investigation into the effect of antibiotic concentration on the growth of bacteria: 'Hazards: chemicals and equipment. Precautions: be careful, wear a lab coat. Risk: none.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this risk assessment, identifying three weaknesses.
parts.answer: It lists no specific hazards (e.g. the ethanol used to sterilise is flammable, hot water bath) – too general; 'be careful' and 'wear a lab coat' are not specific precautions matched to hazards; does not mention bacteria / need for aseptic technique and disposal by autoclaving; gives no risk level; nothing about what to do in an emergency (spills, burns).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three weaknesses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite one entry so that it is a good risk assessment entry.
parts.answer: Hazard: ethanol used to flame-sterilise spreaders is highly flammable; risk: fire if the beaker of ethanol is near the Bunsen flame (medium); precaution: keep ethanol beaker covered and well away from the flame, dip only the end of the spreader and let it burn off away from the beaker.
parts.working: B1 specific hazard with harm; B1 matching specific precaution.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of the time of exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light on the survival of yeast cells spread on agar plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard of the UV lamp and describe how the risk can be reduced.
parts.answer: UV radiation damages the eyes (and skin) – may cause burns / is a mutagen; use the lamp inside a closed box / cabinet, switch on only when covered, wear UV-protective goggles and gloves, limit exposure time.
parts.working: B1 hazard; B1 precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other hazards in this investigation and precautions for each.
parts.answer: Yeast cultures could be contaminated with other microorganisms – aseptic technique, dispose of cultures by autoclaving; mutated yeast cells – do not release into environment; hot agar / Bunsen burner – heat-resistant gloves; glass Petri dishes breaking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two with precautions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the overall risk of this investigation is higher than that of a typical enzyme practical.
parts.answer: It involves a mutagenic radiation source and culturing microorganisms, so harm could be serious unless strict precautions are followed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: With a ×10 objective, 40 eyepiece graticule divisions lined up exactly with 25 divisions of a stage micrometer. Each stage micrometer division is 10 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule division.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A xylem vessel measured 18 eyepiece divisions across. Calculate its actual width.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A chloroplast has an actual length of 5 µm. In an electron micrograph its image is 30 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the electron micrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula linking image size, actual size and magnification.
parts.answer: magnification = image size ÷ actual size

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Convert:
(i) 0.25 mm to µm
(ii) 4500 nm to µm
(iii) 7.2 µm to nm
(iv) 1.8 mm to µm
parts.working: B1 each.

stem: A student's drawing of a stoma from a maize leaf has a magnification of × 800. The length of the stoma on the drawing is 46 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the stoma (pair of guard cells) in µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should write the magnification of the drawing, not the magnification of the microscope, under the drawing.
parts.answer: The drawing may be larger or smaller than the image seen in the microscope, so its magnification is different.

author: HomiLabs

stem: With the ×10 objective, one eyepiece graticule division was 10 µm. With the ×40 objective it was 2.5 µm. A xylem vessel in a sunflower stem was 12 divisions wide with the ×40 objective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual width of the vessel.
parts.answer: 30 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be calibrated again when the objective lens is changed.
parts.answer: The eyepiece graticule stays the same size in the eyepiece, but the specimen is magnified more/less; so each division represents a different actual length at each objective.
parts.working: B1 graticule not magnified by objective; B1 value of a division changes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: With a ×10 objective the diameter of the field of view is 1.6 mm. A student counted 20 onion epidermal cells end to end across the diameter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length of one cell in µm.
parts.answer: 80 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the diameter of the field of view when the ×40 objective is used instead of the ×10.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in this method.
parts.answer: Cells are not all the same length; partial cells at the edges must be estimated; cells may not lie exactly along the diameter.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A photomicrograph of cells in a root tip has a scale bar labelled 20 µm. The scale bar is 16 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The nucleus of one cell measures 9.3 mm on the photomicrograph. Calculate its actual diameter. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: One eyepiece graticule division = 2.5 µm. The lengths of ten guard cells from a lily leaf, in eyepiece divisions, were: 16, 18, 17, 15, 19, 18, 17, 16, 18, 16.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length of the guard cells in µm.
parts.working: M1 mean 17 divisions; A1 × 2.5 = 42.5 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of guard cell lengths in µm.
parts.answer: 37.5 µm to 47.5 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is better to measure ten guard cells than one.
parts.answer: Guard cells vary in length; a mean of several is more representative / reduces the effect of an unusual cell.

author: HomiLabs

stem: With a ×40 objective, 100 eyepiece graticule divisions matched 0.25 mm on a stage micrometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece division in µm.
parts.answer: 2.5 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A root hair measured 5 divisions wide and 240 divisions long. Calculate its width and its length in µm.
parts.answer: width 12.5 µm; length 600 µm
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the root hair's large length compared with its width is an advantage to the plant.
parts.answer: Large surface area for absorption of water (osmosis) and mineral ions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student draws a hibiscus pollen grain with an actual diameter of 40 µm. The drawing is 60 mm across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the student's drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student wants to show the pollen grain at × 2000 instead. Calculate the diameter the drawing should have, in mm.
parts.answer: 80 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two features of a good biological drawing.
parts.answer: Clear, continuous thin pencil lines; no shading; correct proportions; drawn large (fills the space); labels with ruled label lines that do not cross.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student viewed a filament of the alga Spirogyra with a ×40 objective. One eyepiece graticule division = 2.5 µm. Student X measured one cell as 32 divisions long. Student Y lined the graticule up along a row of 5 cells end to end and found the row was 156 divisions long. Each reading has an uncertainty of ± 0.5 division.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cell length in µm found by each student.
parts.answer: X: 80.0 µm; Y: mean 78.0 µm per cell

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in each student's reading. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 0.5 ÷ number of divisions × 100; A1 1.6 % and 0.3 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which student's method gives the better estimate of the mean length of a Spirogyra cell.
parts.answer: Student Y – the reading covers more divisions so the percentage uncertainty is smaller, and measuring 5 cells averages out variation between cells.
parts.working: B1 Y with reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Calculate the actual size of each structure. Give each answer in the most suitable unit.
(i) a structure 1.0 mm in diameter on a micrograph at × 40 000
(ii) a structure 18 mm long on a micrograph at × 12 000
parts.working: B1 each with suitable unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the identity of each structure, giving a reason.
parts.answer: (i) ribosome – about 20–30 nm in diameter; (ii) mitochondrion – about 1–2 µm long (0.5–1 µm wide); prokaryotic cell also accepted with reason.
parts.working: B1 each with size reasoning.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why structure (i) cannot be seen with a light microscope, however high the magnification.
parts.answer: Its size (25 nm) is less than the resolution of the light microscope (about 200 nm), limited by the wavelength of light.

stem: A transverse section of a young stem was viewed with a ×4 objective, where one eyepiece division = 25 µm. The stem was 64 divisions across and the central pith was 30 divisions across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the stem and of the pith in mm.
parts.answer: stem: 1.6 mm; pith: 0.75 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the stem and pith are circular in section, calculate the percentage of the cross-sectional area occupied by pith. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why measurements of the pith diameter should be taken in two directions at right angles and averaged.
parts.answer: The section is not perfectly circular / may be cut at an angle, so one diameter may not be typical.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student calibrated an eyepiece graticule: one division = 10 µm with the ×10 objective, 2.5 µm with the ×40 objective and 1.0 µm with the ×100 oil-immersion objective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many eyepiece divisions a red blood cell 7.5 µm in diameter would cover with each objective.
parts.working: M1 7.5 ÷ division length; A1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which objective should be used to measure the diameter of red blood cells and calculate the percentage uncertainty if each reading is ± 0.5 division. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: ×100 (oil immersion); 6.7 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student wants to measure the thickness of the cell surface membrane (about 7 nm) of a red blood cell. Explain why no objective on this microscope can be used.
parts.answer: 7 nm is far below the resolution of the light microscope (about 200 nm), so the membrane's two edges cannot be distinguished; an electron microscope is needed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure in an animal cell is made of microtubules arranged as nine triplets in a cylinder?
A centriole
B ribosome
C microvillus
D Golgi body
parts.answer: A centriole
parts.working: Centrioles are short cylinders of nine triplets of microtubules; they lie in pairs in the centrosome. Ribosomes are made of rRNA and protein; microvilli are folds of the cell surface membrane, not built of microtubule triplets; the Golgi body is a stack of membrane-bound cisternae.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement is true of BOTH a ribosome and a centriole?
A It is not surrounded by a membrane.
B It contains RNA.
C It is made of microtubules.
D It is found in prokaryotic cells.
parts.answer: A It is not surrounded by a membrane.
parts.working: Neither ribosomes nor centrioles have a membrane. Only ribosomes contain RNA (rRNA); only centrioles are made of microtubules; prokaryotes have (70S) ribosomes but no centrioles. Distractor D is tempting because ribosomes occur in prokaryotes, but centrioles do not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one difference in appearance between rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) in an electron micrograph.
parts.answer: RER has ribosomes attached to the outer surface of its membranes; SER has no ribosomes (and is often more tubular).
parts.working: 1 mark: ribosomes on RER / none on SER. Accept RER = flattened sacs (cisternae), SER = tubules as an extra detail, but the ribosome point is needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two functions of SER.
parts.answer: Any two: synthesis of lipids (e.g. phospholipids); synthesis of steroids (e.g. steroid hormones); storage of calcium ions (in muscle); detoxification of drugs (in liver)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lipid/phospholipid synthesis; steroid synthesis; Ca²⁺ storage; detoxification. Do not accept 'protein synthesis'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Proteins made on RER are transported to the Golgi body. State how they are carried between these two organelles.
parts.answer: In (transport) vesicles that bud off the RER and fuse with the Golgi body
parts.working: 1 mark: vesicles (pinched off from RER, fusing with Golgi).

stem: Cells in the root cap of a maize seedling secrete a slimy layer of polysaccharide that coats the root tip. In electron micrographs, these cells have very large Golgi bodies with many vesicles near the cell surface membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the Golgi body in the production of this slime.
parts.answer: Golgi body makes/modifies the polysaccharide (and adds it to proteins); packages it into vesicles; vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing slime by exocytosis
parts.working: 1 mark each: Golgi synthesises/modifies polysaccharide (or makes glycoproteins); packages into (secretory) vesicles; vesicles fuse with cell surface membrane / exocytosis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Electron micrographs show that root cap cells also contain many mitochondria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to make ATP; ATP is needed for synthesis of the slime and for movement of vesicles/exocytosis
parts.working: 1 mark: aerobic respiration releases energy as ATP. 1 mark: ATP used for polysaccharide synthesis / vesicle transport / exocytosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Root cap cells are worn away and replaced as the root grows through soil. Suggest one advantage to the plant of the slime layer.
parts.answer: Lubricates the root tip so it pushes through soil more easily / reduces damage to cells by friction
parts.working: 1 mark: lubrication / less friction / protects growing tip.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A liver cell has a volume of 4800 µm³. Mitochondria make up 21 % of this volume and the mean volume of one mitochondrion is 0.56 µm³. Calculate the number of mitochondria in the cell.
parts.answer: 1800 mitochondria

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cardiac muscle cell has a volume of 15 000 µm³, of which 35 % is mitochondria. Calculate how many times greater the total mitochondrial volume is in the cardiac muscle cell than in the liver cell. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.21 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why cardiac muscle cells have such a large volume of mitochondria.
parts.answer: Cardiac muscle contracts continuously throughout life, so needs large amounts of ATP; ATP is made by aerobic respiration in mitochondria
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration / ATP production. 1 mark: continuous contraction needs much ATP / energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is 0.25 mm expressed in nanometres?
A 2.5 × 10³ nm
B 2.5 × 10⁴ nm
C 2.5 × 10⁵ nm
D 2.5 × 10⁶ nm
parts.answer: C 2.5 × 10⁵ nm
parts.working: 1 mm = 1000 µm and 1 µm = 1000 nm, so 1 mm = 10⁶ nm. 0.25 × 10⁶ = 2.5 × 10⁵ nm. B results from multiplying by only 10⁵.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
With a ×100 total magnification, the diameter of the field of view of a light microscope is 1.8 mm. The student then switches to ×400 total magnification. A cheek cell stretches across 0.3 of the diameter of the new field of view. What is the approximate width of the cheek cell?
A 13.5 µm
B 54 µm
C 135 µm
D 540 µm
parts.answer: C 135 µm
parts.working: Field diameter is inversely proportional to magnification: 1.8 mm × 100/400 = 0.45 mm. 0.3 × 0.45 mm = 0.135 mm = 135 µm. D (540 µm) uses the ×100 field diameter without scaling.

stem: Use the formula: magnification = image size ÷ actual size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the image length of a cell of actual length 12 µm viewed at a magnification of ×1500. Give your answer in mm.
parts.answer: 18 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: An image of a chloroplast is 45 mm long at a magnification of ×15 000. Calculate the actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 3 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: A virus particle with an actual diameter of 250 nm has an image diameter of 20 mm on a micrograph. Calculate the magnification.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student would calibrate an eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer.
parts.answer: Place stage micrometer on stage and focus; rotate eyepiece so graticule scale lies alongside/overlaps the micrometer scale; line up the zero marks / find a point where two lines coincide; count eyepiece units equal to a known number of micrometer divisions; calculate the length of one eyepiece unit (= micrometer length ÷ number of eyepiece units)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: micrometer on stage, focused; scales lined up/superimposed; count graticule divisions matching a known micrometer length; divide to find µm per eyepiece unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The stage micrometer scale is 1 mm long and is divided into 100 equal divisions. State the length of one division in µm.
parts.answer: 10 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a stage micrometer cannot simply be used to measure cells directly in the same view.
parts.answer: The cells and the micrometer cannot be on the stage/in focus at the same time (the micrometer is a separate slide)
parts.working: 1 mark: specimen slide and micrometer slide cannot be viewed together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of an electron microscope compared with a light microscope.
parts.answer: Higher resolution (about 0.5 nm compared with about 200 nm); can produce higher useful magnification; shows ultrastructure such as ribosomes, membranes and cristae
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: higher resolution; higher (useful) magnification; organelles/ultrastructure visible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of a light microscope compared with an electron microscope.
parts.answer: Any two: living cells can be viewed; natural colour / coloured stains can be seen; cheaper / portable; simpler and quicker specimen preparation; no vacuum needed
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why specimens for transmission electron microscopy must be very thin.
parts.answer: Electrons must pass through the specimen; thick specimens would absorb/scatter all the electrons so no image forms
parts.working: 1 mark: electrons have low penetrating power / must be transmitted through specimen.

stem: A student in Multan examines a stained blood smear with a light microscope. With the ×40 objective lens, one eyepiece graticule unit has been calibrated as 2.5 µm. The diameters of six red blood cells, in eyepiece units, are: 3.0, 2.8, 3.2, 3.0, 2.9, 3.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the red blood cells in µm.
parts.answer: 7.5 µm
parts.working: M1: mean = 18.0 ÷ 6 = 3.0 eyepiece units. A1: 3.0 × 2.5 = 7.5 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student draws one red blood cell with a diameter of 45 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing, using the mean diameter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A white blood cell on the same slide is 5.0 eyepiece units across. Calculate its actual diameter in µm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student measured six red blood cells rather than one.
parts.answer: Red blood cells vary in size, so a mean of several cells gives a more representative (reliable) value
parts.working: 1 mark: variation between cells / one cell may be unusual; mean is more representative.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student draws a group of guard cells seen with a light microscope. The drawing has a magnification of ×800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length, in mm, that the student should draw a 25 µm scale bar on this drawing.
parts.answer: 20 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A guard cell on the drawing is 36 mm long. Calculate its actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 45 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student enlarges the drawing so that the magnification becomes ×3200. Explain why no further detail can be seen in the enlarged drawing.
parts.answer: Resolution is limited by the light microscope (about 200 nm); enlarging the drawing increases magnification but not resolution, so details closer together than the resolution limit still cannot be distinguished
parts.working: 1 mark: resolution / resolving power does not change. 1 mark: points closer than about 200 nm still appear as one / no new detail.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of the term resolution.
parts.answer: The ability to distinguish between two points that are close together as separate points (the smallest distance between two points that can be seen as separate)
parts.working: 1 mark: two close points distinguished as separate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A light microscope has a resolution of 200 nm. State which of these structures could be seen as separate objects with this microscope: nucleus (diameter 6 µm); chloroplast (length 5 µm); ribosome (diameter 25 nm); thickness of cell surface membrane (7.5 nm).
parts.answer: Nucleus and chloroplast only
parts.working: 1 mark for nucleus and chloroplast. 1 mark for correctly excluding both ribosome and membrane thickness (both smaller than 200 nm).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The resolution of a light microscope is about half the wavelength of the light used. Calculate the resolution when blue light of wavelength 450 nm is used and explain why blue light gives a better image of fine detail than red light of wavelength 700 nm.
parts.answer: 225 nm; shorter wavelength gives smaller resolution distance (red gives 350 nm), so finer detail can be distinguished
parts.working: B1: 225 nm. B1: shorter wavelength → better resolution (smaller distance between distinguishable points).

stem: A transmission electron micrograph of the nucleus of a pancreatic cell has a magnification of ×80 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On the micrograph, one nuclear pore has an image diameter of 9.6 mm. Calculate the actual diameter of the pore in nm.
parts.answer: 120 nm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The whole nuclear envelope (both membranes and the space between them) is 2.4 mm wide on the same micrograph. Calculate its actual width in nm.
parts.answer: 30 nm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answer to (a), explain why nuclear pores cannot be seen with a light microscope.
parts.answer: 120 nm is smaller than the resolution of a light microscope (about 200 nm), so the pore cannot be distinguished
parts.working: 1 mark: pore smaller than ~200 nm resolution limit (magnification is not the problem).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A scanning electron micrograph of a yeast cell from a bakery culture in Lahore has a magnification of ×6000. The image of the cell is circular with a diameter of 36 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the yeast cell in µm.
parts.answer: 6 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating the cell as a sphere, calculate its volume in µm³. Use V = 4/3 πr³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 113 µm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using surface area = 4πr², calculate the surface area : volume ratio of the cell.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A second yeast cell in the same micrograph has an image diameter of 72 mm. Without further measurement, state its surface area : volume ratio and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 0.5 : 1; the diameter (radius) is doubled and SA:V of a sphere = 3/r, so the ratio halves
parts.working: B1: 0.5. B1: SA increases ×4 but volume ×8 / ratio = 3/r, so doubling r halves ratio.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An electron micrograph labelled ×5000 is enlarged to 150 % of its original size on a photocopier. The label is not changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the enlarged copy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mitochondrion is 30 mm long on the enlarged copy. Calculate its actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 4 µm
parts.working: M1: uses ×7500 (not ×5000). A1: 30 000 µm ÷ 7500 = 4 µm. (Using ×5000 gives 6 µm — no credit.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a scale bar printed on the original micrograph would still give correct measurements on the enlarged copy, but the printed magnification would not.
parts.answer: The scale bar is enlarged by the same factor as the image, so its length still represents the same actual length; the printed magnification number stays the same even though the image has become larger, so it is now wrong
parts.working: 1 mark: scale bar scales with image. 1 mark: written magnification value is not changed by enlarging.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The human eye can just distinguish two points 0.1 mm apart. Calculate the minimum magnification needed so that two points 200 nm apart appear 0.1 mm apart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A light microscope can magnify up to ×1500. Explain why magnifying a specimen more than about ×1500 with a light microscope does not help to see more detail.
parts.answer: Resolution is limited to about 200 nm by the wavelength of light; any further magnification just makes the blurred image larger ('empty magnification') without separating more points
parts.working: 1 mark: resolution limited by wavelength of light. 1 mark: extra magnification enlarges blur / no extra detail.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A transmission electron microscope has a resolution of 0.5 nm. Calculate the useful magnification needed for two points 0.5 nm apart to appear 0.1 mm apart.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in many bacteria but not in an animal cell?
A plasmid
B 80S ribosome
C mitochondrion
D Golgi body
parts.answer: A plasmid
parts.working: Plasmids (small circles of DNA) occur in many bacteria but not in animal cells. 80S ribosomes, mitochondria and Golgi bodies are eukaryotic features; bacteria have 70S ribosomes and no membrane-bound organelles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly compares a bacterial cell with a plant cell?
(ribosomes in bacterium | main component of bacterial cell wall | DNA in bacterium)
A 70S | peptidoglycan | circular, not in a nucleus
B 70S | cellulose | circular, not in a nucleus
C 80S | peptidoglycan | linear, in a nucleus
D 80S | cellulose | circular, in a nucleus
parts.answer: A 70S | peptidoglycan | circular, not in a nucleus
parts.working: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes, cell walls of peptidoglycan (murein) and circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm. B is wrong because cellulose is the main component of plant, not bacterial, cell walls.

stem: Salmonella bacteria from a contaminated food sample were examined with an electron microscope. Four structures were described.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name structures P, Q, R and S.
P: a rigid outer layer made of peptidoglycan
Q: one large loop of DNA lying in the cytoplasm
R: small extra loops of DNA, often carrying genes for antibiotic resistance
S: small particles in the cytoplasm, about 20 nm across, where polypeptides are made
parts.answer: P cell wall; Q circular DNA / bacterial chromosome; R plasmids; S 70S ribosomes
parts.working: 1 mark each. For Q accept 'nucleoid'. For S, '70S' not required for the mark but 'ribosome' is.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the typical diameter range of a prokaryotic cell.
parts.answer: About 1–5 µm (accept 0.5–5 µm)
parts.working: 1 mark; units required.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: An E. coli cell is 2 µm long. A human liver cell is 25 µm across. Calculate how many times longer the liver cell is than the bacterium.
parts.answer: 12.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: In ideal conditions an E. coli cell divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Calculate the number of cells produced from one cell after 2 hours, and state one assumption you have made.
parts.answer: 64 cells; assumption: every cell divides every 20 minutes / no cells die / nutrients are not limiting
parts.working: B1: 2 h = 6 generations; 2⁶ = 64. B1: any valid assumption (all cells divide at the same rate, none die, nutrients/space not limiting).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one structure found in E. coli but not in the liver cell.
parts.answer: Any one: cell wall (peptidoglycan); plasmid; 70S ribosomes in the cytoplasm; flagellum (some strains)
parts.working: 1 mark. Do not accept 'ribosomes' without '70S'.

stem: Dengue fever is caused by an enveloped virus that is carried by Aedes mosquitoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the structure of a dengue virus particle differs from the structure of a bacterium such as E. coli.
parts.answer: Any three: virus has RNA (not DNA) as genetic material; virus has a protein capsid, not a peptidoglycan cell wall; virus has no cytoplasm or ribosomes; virus envelope comes from the host cell membrane (bacterium has its own cell surface membrane); virus is much smaller (about 50 nm, not 1–5 µm); no plasmids
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid comparative differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Doctors in Rawalpindi do not prescribe antibiotics to treat dengue fever. Explain why antibiotics would not cure dengue.
parts.answer: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures/processes (e.g. peptidoglycan cell wall or 70S ribosomes); viruses lack these / are not cells and use the host cell's ribosomes and enzymes
parts.working: 1 mark: antibiotics target bacterial features. 1 mark: viruses have no cell wall/ribosomes/metabolism of their own.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: For a sphere, surface area = πd² and volume = πd³/6, so the surface area : volume ratio = 6/d. Calculate the surface area : volume ratio for a spherical bacterium of diameter 1 µm and for a spherical eukaryotic cell of diameter 20 µm.
parts.answer: Bacterium 6.0 µm⁻¹ (6 : 1); eukaryotic cell 0.3 µm⁻¹ (0.3 : 1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the ratio is for the bacterium.
parts.answer: 20 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why bacteria do not need specialised transport systems.
parts.answer: Large SA:V means a large surface for exchange relative to the volume needing supplies; diffusion distances are very short, so diffusion across the cell surface is fast enough
parts.working: 1 mark: large SA relative to volume. 1 mark: short diffusion distance / diffusion alone is enough.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between the DNA of a prokaryotic cell and the DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell.
parts.answer: Prokaryotic DNA is circular, eukaryotic is linear; prokaryotic is free in the cytoplasm, eukaryotic is in a nucleus (enclosed by an envelope); prokaryotic is not associated with histones ('naked'), eukaryotic is wound round histones to form chromatin/chromosomes; prokaryotes often have plasmids too
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three paired differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Bacteria have no mitochondria but many species respire aerobically. Suggest where the enzymes for the later stages of aerobic respiration are found in these bacteria.
parts.answer: On / in the cell surface membrane (and the cytoplasm)
parts.working: 1 mark: cell surface membrane (accept infoldings of membrane).

stem: Poliovirus particles have a diameter of about 30 nm. HIV particles have a diameter of about 120 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the diameter of HIV is than the diameter of poliovirus.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both viruses are roughly spherical. Calculate how many times greater the volume of HIV is.
parts.answer: 64 times
parts.working: M1: volume ∝ d³. A1: 4³ = 64.

parts.label: c
parts.text: HIV has an envelope but poliovirus does not. State the origin of the envelope of HIV.
parts.answer: The cell surface membrane of the host cell it left (taken as the virus buds out)
parts.working: 1 mark: host cell (surface) membrane.

author: HomiLabs

stem: During hot summers, the water of a lake in Punjab turns green because of a bloom of cyanobacteria (photosynthetic bacteria).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cyanobacteria are classified as prokaryotes even though they photosynthesise.
parts.answer: They have no chloroplasts / photosynthetic membranes lie free in the cytoplasm; they have no nucleus or other double-membrane-bound organelles (circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall)
parts.working: 1 mark: no chloroplasts (membrane-bound organelle). 1 mark: any other prokaryotic feature (no nucleus, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of lake water contained 3.6 × 10⁶ cyanobacteria per cm³. Calculate the number in 2.5 dm³ of lake water. Give your answer in standard form.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria. After one phage infects a bacterium, the cell bursts 25 minutes later, releasing 150 new phages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: One phage infects one bacterium. Assuming every new phage infects a fresh bacterium and all bacteria burst at the same time, calculate the number of phages present 50 minutes after the first infection.
parts.working: M1: two cycles in 50 min. A1: 150 × 150 = 22 500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of phages after 75 minutes. Give your answer in standard form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the phage cannot reproduce in a nutrient broth that contains no bacteria.
parts.answer: Viruses have no ribosomes/enzymes/metabolism of their own; they must use the host cell's ribosomes, ATP and nucleotides/amino acids to make new viral nucleic acid and proteins
parts.working: 1 mark: no cellular machinery (ribosomes/enzymes). 1 mark: needs host cell to replicate nucleic acid and make capsid protein.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four features of mitochondria and chloroplasts that support the idea that they were once free-living prokaryotes.
parts.answer: Contain their own circular DNA; have 70S ribosomes; are about the size of bacteria (1–5 µm); surrounded by two membranes (the inner one like a prokaryotic cell membrane); divide by a process like binary fission
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some antibiotics that target 70S ribosomes can cause side effects in human cells. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Mitochondria contain 70S ribosomes; the antibiotic may stop protein synthesis in mitochondria, reducing aerobic respiration/ATP production in human cells
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S. 1 mark: mitochondrial protein synthesis / ATP supply affected.

stem: A student views a rod-shaped bacterium using an oil-immersion objective. One eyepiece unit = 0.25 µm. The bacterium is 10 eyepiece units long and 3.2 eyepiece units wide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length and width of the bacterium in µm.
parts.answer: Length 2.5 µm; width 0.8 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating the bacterium as a cylinder (V = πr²h), calculate its volume in µm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.26 µm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: A yeast cell has a diameter of 5 µm. Treating it as a sphere (V = 4/3 πr³), calculate how many times greater its volume is than that of the bacterium. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 52.1 times

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hand sanitiser containing ethanol rapidly inactivates coronaviruses but is much less effective against norovirus. Using your knowledge of virus structure, suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: Coronavirus has a phospholipid envelope; ethanol (and soap) dissolves/disrupts lipid, destroying the envelope and its attachment proteins, so the virus cannot enter host cells; norovirus has no envelope, only a protein capsid, which is less affected
parts.working: 1 mark: coronavirus is enveloped (phospholipid). 1 mark: ethanol/soap disrupts lipid envelope → attachment glycoproteins lost/cannot infect. 1 mark: norovirus has only a capsid (no lipid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Norovirus has RNA as its genetic material. State two ways in which the RNA of norovirus differs from the DNA of a bacterium.
parts.answer: Any two: RNA is single-stranded, bacterial DNA is double-stranded; RNA contains ribose, DNA deoxyribose; RNA contains uracil, DNA thymine; norovirus RNA is linear, bacterial DNA is circular
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two paired differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is NOT needed for translation?
A RNA polymerase
B ATP
C tRNA
D amino acids
parts.answer: A RNA polymerase
parts.working: RNA polymerase catalyses transcription (making mRNA from DNA), not translation. Translation needs mRNA, ribosomes, tRNA, amino acids and ATP (e.g. to attach amino acids to tRNA). B is wrong because energy from ATP is used during translation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which event takes place during translation but NOT during transcription?
A Hydrogen bonds form between complementary bases.
B Peptide bonds form.
C A nucleic acid strand is used as a template.
D Energy from nucleoside triphosphates (such as ATP) is used.
parts.answer: B Peptide bonds form.
parts.working: Peptide bonds join amino acids only in translation. A happens in both (DNA–mRNA pairing in transcription; codon–anticodon pairing in translation); C happens in both (DNA template; mRNA read); D happens in both (activated nucleotides in transcription; ATP to load amino acids onto tRNA).

stem: A mature mRNA molecule in a human cell is 1650 nucleotides long. It has 120 untranslated nucleotides before the start codon and 210 untranslated nucleotides after the stop codon. The coding region begins with the start codon and ends with one stop codon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
parts.working: M1: coding region = 1650 − 120 − 210 = 1320 nucleotides = 440 codons. A1: 440 − 1 stop codon = 439 amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mean mass of an amino acid residue in the polypeptide is 110 Da. Estimate the mass of the polypeptide in kDa. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 48.3 kDa

parts.label: c
parts.text: One ribosome adds 6 amino acids per second. Calculate the time for one ribosome to make the polypeptide. Give your answer to the nearest second.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the 120 nucleotides before the start codon are not translated, and suggest how the ribosome finds the correct place to begin translation.
parts.answer: Translation begins only at the start codon (AUG), so bases before it are not read as codons; the ribosome binds near the 5′ end of the mRNA and moves along it until it reaches the start codon, where the tRNA carrying methionine (anticodon UAC) pairs with it
parts.working: 1 mark: translation starts at start codon AUG. 1 mark: ribosome attaches/scans along mRNA to the start codon (tRNA-Met anticodon UAC pairs).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of bond holds the two polynucleotide strands of a DNA molecule together?
A phosphodiester bonds
B hydrogen bonds
C glycosidic bonds
D peptide bonds
parts.answer: B hydrogen bonds
parts.working: Complementary bases (A–T and C–G) are joined by hydrogen bonds between the strands. Phosphodiester bonds (A) join nucleotides WITHIN one strand, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecules contain ribose?
1 ATP
2 mRNA
3 tRNA
4 DNA
A 1, 2 and 3 only
B 2 and 3 only
C 1, 2, 3 and 4
D 2, 3 and 4 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 3 only
parts.working: ATP is adenine + ribose + three phosphates; all RNA (mRNA, tRNA) contains ribose. DNA contains deoxyribose, so 4 is excluded. B forgets that ATP contains ribose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two pyrimidine bases found in DNA.
parts.answer: Cytosine and thymine
parts.working: 1 mark for both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the pyrimidine base that is found in RNA but not in DNA.
parts.answer: Uracil
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one structural difference between a purine and a pyrimidine.
parts.answer: Purines have two (fused) rings; pyrimidines have one ring
parts.working: 1 mark: double ring vs single ring. Accept purines are larger.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why, in DNA, a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine.
parts.answer: A purine–pyrimidine pair has three rings in total, so every base pair is the same width; this keeps the distance between the two sugar–phosphate backbones constant (so the double helix has a uniform width)
parts.working: 1 mark: each pair same size (two rings + one ring). 1 mark: constant distance between backbones / uniform helix width. (Two purines would be too wide, two pyrimidines too narrow.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the reaction that joins two nucleotides together.
parts.answer: Condensation
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how two nucleotides are joined in a polynucleotide.
parts.answer: The phosphate group of one nucleotide bonds to the pentose sugar (3′ carbon) of the next nucleotide; forming a phosphodiester bond; water is released
parts.working: 1 mark: phosphate of one nucleotide joined to sugar of the next. 1 mark: phosphodiester bond (with release of water).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A molecule of ATP is similar to one of the nucleotides found in RNA. State two ways in which ATP differs from an RNA nucleotide containing adenine.
parts.answer: ATP has three phosphate groups, the RNA nucleotide has one; ATP is a free molecule / is not joined into a polynucleotide chain
parts.working: 1 mark: three phosphates vs one. 1 mark: ATP not part of a polynucleotide / free in cytoplasm. (Both contain adenine and ribose — do not accept differences in sugar or base.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The molar mass of ATP is 507 g/mol. A resting adult turns over (makes and hydrolyses) about 50 kg of ATP per day. Calculate the number of moles of ATP hydrolysed per day. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 98.6 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrolysis of 1 mol of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases 30.5 kJ. Calculate the energy released per day from this ATP. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The body contains only about 50 g of ATP at any time. Explain how the cell can hydrolyse so much ATP each day.
parts.answer: ATP is constantly regenerated: ADP and phosphate are recombined by condensation using energy from respiration (catalysed by ATP synthase); each ATP molecule is recycled about 1000 times per day
parts.working: 1 mark: ADP + Pi → ATP / recycled. 1 mark: energy from respiration / ATP synthase. Accept calculation 50 000 ÷ 50 = 1000 recycles.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why ATP, rather than glucose, is used as the immediate energy source in cells.
parts.answer: ATP releases energy in small, manageable amounts in a single-step hydrolysis (glucose would release too much energy at once / needs many steps)
parts.working: 1 mark: small amount of energy released per molecule / one-step reaction / quickly.

stem:
The table shows the percentage of each base in nucleic acid samples.
Sample | A | T | G | C | U
Wheat | 27.3 | 27.1 | 22.7 | 22.9 | 0
Bacterium X | 15.2 | 15.0 | 34.9 | 34.9 | 0
Virus Y | 24.0 | 31.0 | 18.0 | 27.0 | 0
Sample Z | 23.0 | 0 | 27.0 | 24.0 | 26.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (A + G) ÷ (T + C) for wheat DNA. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the sample that is single-stranded DNA. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Virus Y; amounts of A and T are not equal and amounts of G and C are not equal, so the bases are not complementary-paired
parts.working: B1: Virus Y. B1: A ≠ T and G ≠ C (no base pairing rule).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what sample Z is. Give a reason.
parts.answer: RNA, because it contains uracil instead of thymine
parts.working: 1 mark: RNA with uracil reason.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Of the double-stranded DNA samples, suggest which would need the highest temperature to separate its two strands. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Bacterium X; it has the highest proportion of G–C pairs (69.8 %), which are joined by three hydrogen bonds rather than two
parts.working: B1: bacterium X. B1: more G–C pairs, each with three hydrogen bonds (A–T has two).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Human chromosome 1 is one double-stranded DNA molecule containing about 249 million base pairs. Adjacent base pairs are 0.34 nm apart along the length of the double helix.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of this DNA molecule in cm. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The double helix makes one complete turn every 10 base pairs. Calculate the number of complete turns in the molecule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The nucleus containing this chromosome has a diameter of about 6 µm. Suggest how such a long molecule fits inside the nucleus.
parts.answer: DNA is wound around histone proteins / coiled and supercoiled (forming chromatin); this packs the molecule into a much shorter, compact structure
parts.working: 1 mark: histones / DNA–protein (chromatin). 1 mark: coiling/folding at several levels.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A linear double-stranded DNA fragment cut from a plasmid contains 5800 nucleotides in total. 1218 of these nucleotides contain guanine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of each base (A, T, G and C) in the molecule.
parts.working: M1: C = G = 1218 (complementary). A1: (5800 − 2436) ÷ 2 = 1682 each for A and T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mean mass of one nucleotide in this DNA is 330 Da. Calculate the mass of the fragment in kDa. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of phosphodiester bonds in the molecule.
parts.working: M1: each strand has 2900 nucleotides, so 2899 phosphodiester bonds. A1: 2 × 2899 = 5798.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During which stage of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
A prophase
B S phase of interphase
C G2 phase of interphase
D anaphase
parts.answer: B S phase of interphase
parts.working: DNA replication takes place in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, so each chromosome has two identical chromatids by the start of mitosis. In G2 (C) the cell checks the replicated DNA and prepares for division; replication is already complete.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Part of a template strand of DNA has the sequence 3′-TACGGA-5′. Which new strand is made against this template?
A 5′-ATGCCT-3′
B 3′-ATGCCT-5′
C 5′-AUGCCU-3′
D 5′-TACGGA-3′
parts.answer: A 5′-ATGCCT-3′
parts.working: Bases pair A–T and C–G, and the new strand is antiparallel to the template, so it runs 5′→3′ opposite the 3′→5′ template: 5′-ATGCCT-3′. B has the correct bases but the wrong orientation; C contains uracil, which is in RNA, not DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why DNA replication is described as semi-conservative.
parts.answer: Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly made strand
parts.working: 1 mark: one old strand kept. 1 mark: one new strand made in each daughter molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how complementary base pairing makes sure that the new DNA molecules are identical to the original.
parts.answer: Each exposed base on the template can pair with only one type of free nucleotide (A with T, C with G); so the sequence of the new strand is determined by the template and both molecules have the same base sequence as the original
parts.working: 1 mark: A–T, C–G only. 1 mark: base sequence copied exactly / new strand complementary to template, matching the other old strand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that DNA is copied exactly before a cell divides by mitosis.
parts.answer: So that both daughter cells receive identical genetic information (all the genes needed)
parts.working: 1 mark: genetically identical daughter cells / no mutations passed on.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage by giving the word for each gap (1)–(6).
'The enzyme DNA helicase breaks the (1) bonds between the bases, so the double helix unwinds and the two strands separate. Each strand acts as a (2). Free (3) in the nucleus pair with the exposed bases by (4) base pairing. The enzyme DNA (5) joins adjacent nucleotides, forming (6) bonds in the new strand.'
parts.answer: (1) hydrogen; (2) template; (3) (activated) nucleotides; (4) complementary; (5) polymerase; (6) phosphodiester
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct gap.

stem: In a section of a human chromosome, the lagging strand is 60 000 nucleotides long. It is made in fragments with a mean length of 150 nucleotides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lagging strand is made as short fragments.
parts.answer: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3′ end of a growing strand (so works only in the 5′→3′ direction); on the lagging strand this direction is away from the replication fork, so the enzyme must keep restarting as more DNA is unwound
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA polymerase adds only to 3′ end / synthesises 5′→3′. 1 mark: strands antiparallel, so lagging strand made away from fork in short pieces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of fragments made on the lagging strand of this section.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assuming the section begins and ends with complete fragments, calculate the number of joins that DNA ligase must make within the section, and name the bond it forms.
parts.answer: 399 joins; phosphodiester bond
parts.working: B1: 400 − 1 = 399. B1: phosphodiester.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A temperature-sensitive mutant of E. coli makes a DNA polymerase that works normally at 30 °C but is inactive at 42 °C. All its other enzymes work at both temperatures. At 30 °C the population doubles every 40 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A culture at 30 °C starts with 2.0 × 10⁶ cells. Calculate the number of cells after 2 hours. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 1.6 × 10⁷ cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the mutant DNA polymerase is inactive at 42 °C although the normal enzyme still works at this temperature.
parts.answer: The mutation changed an amino acid, so some bonds holding the tertiary structure are weaker; at 42 °C these bonds break, the active site changes shape and nucleotides can no longer bind (enzyme denatured)
parts.working: 1 mark: changed primary structure / weaker bonds (hydrogen/ionic) in the mutant protein. 1 mark: broken at 42 °C → active site shape changed / denatured.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The culture is moved to 42 °C. Explain why the cells soon stop dividing.
parts.answer: New DNA strands cannot be made because DNA polymerase cannot join nucleotides (no phosphodiester bonds); so DNA is not replicated and each daughter cell could not receive a complete copy, so division stops
parts.working: 1 mark: no joining of nucleotides / no new strand synthesis. 1 mark: DNA not replicated → no complete copy for each daughter cell, so cell cannot divide.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A eukaryotic chromosome contains 150 million base pairs. Replication proceeds in both directions from each origin of replication (two forks per origin). Each fork copies 50 base pairs per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time, in days, needed to replicate this chromosome if it had only ONE origin of replication. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 17.4 days
parts.working: M1: each fork copies 75 × 10⁶ bp; 75 × 10⁶ ÷ 50 = 1.5 × 10⁶ s. A1: ÷ 86 400 = 17.4 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: S phase in these cells lasts 8 hours. Calculate the minimum number of origins of replication needed to copy the chromosome in this time, assuming all origins start together.
parts.working: M1: one origin copies 2 × 50 × 28 800 = 2.88 × 10⁶ bp in 8 h. A1: 150 × 10⁶ ÷ 2.88 × 10⁶ = 52.1 → 53 (must round up).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why bacteria can replicate their DNA using a single origin, while eukaryotic cells need many.
parts.answer: Bacterial DNA is much shorter (a few million bp), so two forks can copy it in a short time; eukaryotic chromosomes are much longer and replication forks move more slowly
parts.working: 1 mark: eukaryotic DNA far longer (and/or slower forks).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Without correction, DNA polymerase inserts about 1 wrong nucleotide in every 10⁵. Proofreading by DNA polymerase removes 99 % of these errors (reducing them 100-fold). A separate mismatch repair system reduces the remaining errors by a further 1000-fold. A diploid human cell contains 6.4 × 10⁹ nucleotide pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of errors made per replication of the genome before proofreading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of errors remaining after proofreading and after mismatch repair.
parts.answer: 640 after proofreading; 0.64 after mismatch repair

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an error that remains after replication is described as a gene mutation if it lies within a gene, and explain why it is passed on to all the cells descended from the cell in which it occurred.
parts.answer: It is a change in the base sequence of DNA (of a gene); when this DNA is replicated, the changed sequence acts as a template and is copied exactly, so it is passed on to all cells descended from it
parts.working: 1 mark: change in base sequence = mutation. 1 mark: replicated / copied semi-conservatively into later cells.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Onion root tips were placed for 20 minutes in a solution containing radioactive thymidine (a nucleoside of thymine). The tips were then washed, squashed and the cells examined. 48 of 150 cells in the zone of cell division had radioactive nuclei.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why thymidine, rather than uridine, was used to label replicating DNA.
parts.answer: Thymine is found only in DNA (not RNA), so radioactivity shows DNA synthesis only; uridine (uracil) would be built into RNA made in transcription, which happens in all phases
parts.working: 1 mark: thymine only in DNA. 1 mark: uracil/uridine would label RNA / transcription, not replication.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cells that were labelled.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what this percentage shows about the cell cycle of these cells.
parts.answer: About a third (32 %) of the cells were in S phase during the 20 minutes, so S phase takes roughly a third of the cell cycle (assuming cells are dividing non-synchronously)
parts.working: 1 mark: proportion of cells in S phase ≈ proportion of cycle time in S phase.

parts.label: d
parts.text: No radioactivity was found in the chromosomes of cells that were in metaphase at the end of the 20 minutes. Explain this result.
parts.answer: Cells in metaphase had already finished replicating their DNA (in S phase) before the thymidine was added; there was not enough time (20 min) for labelled cells to pass through G2 into mitosis
parts.working: 1 mark: replication completed before label added / no replication during mitosis. 1 mark: 20 min too short for labelled cells to reach metaphase (G2 too long).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change in a gene is most likely to have NO effect on the polypeptide it codes for?
A insertion of one base near the start of the gene
B deletion of one base near the middle of the gene
C substitution of the third base of a codon in the coding sequence
D substitution that changes a codon for an amino acid into a stop codon
parts.answer: C substitution of the third base of a codon in the coding sequence
parts.working: Because the genetic code is degenerate, many codons differing only in the third base code for the same amino acid, so a third-base substitution is often silent. A and B cause frame shifts; D gives a shortened polypeptide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two mutagens.
parts.answer: Any two: ultraviolet light; X-rays / gamma rays (ionising radiation); chemical mutagens such as benzene, mustard gas or carcinogens in tobacco smoke
parts.working: 1 mark each; 'radiation' alone not enough — must name type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a gene mutation can result in an enzyme that does not work.
parts.answer: Change in base sequence of DNA changes the mRNA codon(s) / sequence of triplets; so the amino acid sequence (primary structure) changes; so the protein folds differently (different tertiary structure), changing the shape of the active site so the substrate no longer fits
parts.working: 1 mark each: changed triplet/codon; changed primary structure; changed tertiary structure/active site shape → no enzyme–substrate complexes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a gene and an allele.
parts.answer: A gene is a length of DNA that codes for a polypeptide (and has a fixed locus); an allele is one of the different versions (base sequences) of the same gene
parts.working: 1 mark: gene definition. 1 mark: allele = alternative form of a gene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a new allele arises.
parts.answer: By a gene mutation: a change in the base sequence of the gene (substitution, insertion or deletion)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The allele for a darker coat colour in a population of desert mice arose by a single base substitution. State why a substitution may change only one amino acid in the polypeptide.
parts.answer: It changes only one triplet/codon (no frame shift), so the rest of the triplets are read normally
parts.working: 1 mark: only one codon affected / reading frame unchanged.

stem: The coding sequence of a gene for an enzyme is 1500 nucleotides long, including the stop codon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of amino acids in the normal polypeptide.
parts.working: 1500 ÷ 3 = 500 codons; minus 1 stop codon = 499.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one family, a substitution changes codon 132 into a stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the mutant polypeptide and express it as a percentage of the normal length. Give the percentage to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 131 amino acids; 26.3 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this mutation is likely to have a more serious effect than a substitution in codon 132 that replaces one amino acid with another of similar properties.
parts.answer: The stop codon ends translation early, so most of the polypeptide (including e.g. regions needed for the active site / correct folding) is missing and the protein is non-functional; a similar amino acid would probably not change the tertiary structure much
parts.working: 1 mark: truncated polypeptide lacks most of its sequence / cannot fold correctly. 1 mark: conservative substitution has little effect on shape/function.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mutation X inserts one extra base after the 30th base of the coding sequence of a gene. Mutation Y inserts three extra bases at the same place. Explain why mutation X is likely to have a much greater effect on the polypeptide than mutation Y.
parts.answer: X causes a frame shift: every codon after the insertion is read in a different frame, so all following amino acids change (and a premature stop codon is likely); Y adds one extra codon (one extra amino acid) without changing the reading frame, so the rest of the sequence is normal
parts.working: 1 mark: frame shift in X. 1 mark: all downstream codons/amino acids altered (or early stop). 1 mark: Y adds one amino acid / reading frame kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a single base insertion very near the END of the coding sequence may have little effect.
parts.answer: Only the last few codons/amino acids are changed, so most of the polypeptide is normal
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: In the gene for the β-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin, the sixth triplet of the template strand is CTC. In people with sickle cell anaemia this triplet is CAC.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the mRNA codon transcribed from the normal triplet and from the mutated triplet.
parts.answer: Normal GAG; mutated GUG
parts.working: 1 mark each (complementary to template; U replaces T).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of mutation.
parts.answer: Substitution (base substitution)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The normal codon codes for glutamic acid and the mutated codon codes for valine. Glutamic acid has a charged R group; valine has a non-polar (hydrophobic) R group. Explain how this change leads to sickle-shaped red blood cells when oxygen concentration is low.
parts.answer: Valine on the surface of the β-globin chain is hydrophobic; at low oxygen, haemoglobin molecules stick together via these hydrophobic regions; forming long fibres/chains that distort the red blood cell into a sickle shape
parts.working: 1 mark each: hydrophobic amino acid at surface; haemoglobin molecules bind/aggregate (less soluble); fibres distort cell shape.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Huntington's disease is caused by an allele in which a run of repeated CAG triplets near the start of a gene is longer than normal. People with 40 or more repeats develop the disease.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The codon CAG codes for glutamine. In one person's allele, the repeated region is 135 nucleotides long. Calculate the number of CAG repeats in this allele.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A normal allele has 20 repeats. Calculate how many extra glutamine residues the polypeptide from the person's allele contains.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of gene mutation that has increased the number of repeats.
parts.answer: Insertion (of bases / of whole triplets)
parts.working: 1 mark: insertion (accept duplication/expansion of triplets).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this change adds amino acids but does not alter the amino acids coded for after the repeat region.
parts.answer: The extra bases are added in multiples of three (whole codons), so the reading frame is not shifted; so codons after the repeat are read normally
parts.working: 1 mark: multiples of three / whole codons. 1 mark: no frame shift → downstream sequence unchanged.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The start of an mRNA reads:
AUG CCA GUU ACG GAU AAA UGG UAA
Codons: AUG = Met; CCA = Pro; GUU = Val; ACG = Thr; GAU = Asp; AAA = Lys; UGG = Trp; UAA = stop; CAG = Gln; UUA = Leu; CGG = Arg; AUA = Ile; AAU = Asn; GGU = Gly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the amino acid sequence of the normal polypeptide.
parts.answer: Met–Pro–Val–Thr–Asp–Lys–Trp
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mutation 1 deletes the fifth base (C). Give the first seven amino acids coded for by the mutant mRNA.
parts.answer: Met–Gln–Leu–Arg–Ile–Asn–Gly
parts.working: M1: reading frame shifted: AUG CAG UUA CGG AUA AAU GGU. A1: correct amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second mutation in the same gene inserts a G immediately after the 12th base of the mutant mRNA (straight after the CGG codon). Give the amino acid sequence now coded for.
parts.answer: Met–Gln–Leu–Arg–Asp–Lys–Trp (then stop)
parts.working: M1: new mRNA AUG CAG UUA CGG GAU AAA UGG UAA. A1: sequence.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Compare the polypeptide in (c) with the normal polypeptide and explain why its function may be restored.
parts.answer: Only amino acids 2–4 differ (Gln–Leu–Arg instead of Pro–Val–Thr); the insertion restores the reading frame, so the rest of the polypeptide is normal and if the changed amino acids are not in a critical region (e.g. active site) the protein may still fold and function
parts.working: 1 mark: only three amino acids changed / same length. 1 mark: reading frame restored so remaining sequence normal (function may be kept if changes not critical).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mutation occurs in the DNA of a skin cell on a farmer's arm after years of exposure to sunlight. Explain why this mutation cannot be passed on to the farmer's children.
parts.answer: Skin cells are body (somatic) cells that do not produce gametes; only mutations in cells that give rise to gametes (in the testes/ovaries) are inherited
parts.working: 1 mark: somatic cell. 1 mark: only germ-line/gamete mutations inherited.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two different substitutions each change one amino acid in an enzyme. One has no detectable effect on enzyme activity; the other stops the enzyme working completely. Suggest explanations for this difference.
parts.answer: First: amino acid replaced by one with similar R group / change is on the surface away from the active site, so tertiary structure and active site unchanged; second: change in or near the active site or at a position that forms important bonds (e.g. ionic/disulfide/hydrogen bonds), altering folding/tertiary structure so the active site changes shape and substrate no longer binds
parts.working: 1 mark: similar R group / position not important. 1 mark: second in active site or affects bonds holding tertiary structure. 1 mark: active site shape altered → substrate cannot bind.

stem:
Yeast cells were exposed to different doses of ultraviolet (UV) light and then spread on agar to grow. Mutant colonies (unable to make a particular amino acid) were counted.
UV dose / J m⁻² | surviving cells / 10⁶ | mutant colonies
0 | 50 | 20
10 | 32 | 410
20 | 18 | 650
40 | 5 | 380

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mutation frequency (mutant colonies per 10⁶ surviving cells) for 20 J m⁻². Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 36.1 per 10⁶ survivors

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of UV dose on the mutation frequency and on the number of surviving cells.
parts.answer: As UV dose increases, mutation frequency increases (from 0.4 to 76 per 10⁶ survivors, a 190-fold rise); the number of survivors decreases (from 50 to 5 × 10⁶)
parts.working: 1 mark: frequency increases with data. 1 mark: survival decreases with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of mutant colonies is lower at 40 J m⁻² than at 20 J m⁻², although the mutation frequency is higher.
parts.answer: Many more cells are killed at 40 J m⁻² (only 5 × 10⁶ survive), so even though a higher proportion of survivors are mutants, the total number of mutant cells is smaller
parts.working: 1 mark: far fewer survivors. 1 mark: frequency is a proportion of survivors, so total can fall.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why UV light kills cells as well as causing mutations.
parts.answer: UV damages DNA in many places, so essential genes may be damaged / DNA cannot be replicated or transcribed
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of tissue forms most of the lining of the alveoli?
A ciliated epithelium
B squamous epithelium
C columnar epithelium with goblet cells
D smooth muscle
parts.answer: B squamous epithelium
parts.working: Alveoli are lined by very thin, flattened squamous epithelial cells, giving a short diffusion distance. Ciliated epithelium (A) lines the trachea, bronchi and larger bronchioles but not the alveoli.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly matches a tissue of the gas exchange system with its function?
A goblet cells — move mucus towards the throat
B cartilage — contracts to narrow the airways
C mucous glands — secrete mucus that traps dust and bacteria
D elastic fibres — prevent the trachea collapsing during inspiration
parts.answer: C mucous glands — secrete mucus that traps dust and bacteria
parts.working: Mucous glands (below the epithelium of the trachea and bronchi) secrete mucus that traps particles and pathogens. Goblet cells secrete mucus but cilia move it (A); smooth muscle, not cartilage, contracts (B); cartilage, not elastic fibres, keeps the trachea open (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A child inhales a small bead that completely blocks the right main bronchus. Suggest and explain the effect on gas exchange in the alveoli of the right lung.
parts.answer: Alveoli of the right lung are no longer ventilated; oxygen in them is used up / carbon dioxide builds up, so the concentration gradients disappear and little or no gas exchange occurs there (the left lung still works)
parts.working: 1 mark: no fresh air reaches right-lung alveoli / no ventilation. 1 mark: gradients for O₂ and CO₂ fall → gas exchange stops/greatly reduced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During exercise, the smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchioles relaxes. Describe and explain the effect on air flow to the alveoli.
parts.answer: Bronchioles widen (lumen diameter increases); less resistance so more air reaches the alveoli per minute
parts.working: 1 mark: airways dilate/widen. 1 mark: lower resistance → increased air flow/ventilation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tissue that allows the alveoli to return to their original size during expiration.
parts.answer: Elastic fibres
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the human lungs, each airway divides into two smaller airways. The trachea is generation 0, the two main bronchi are generation 1, and so on. Calculate the number of airways in generation 16.
parts.working: M1: number = 2ⁿ. A1: 2¹⁶ = 65 536.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each generation-16 airway has a diameter of 0.50 mm; the trachea has a diameter of 18 mm. Calculate how many times greater the total cross-sectional area of all generation-16 airways is than the cross-sectional area of the trachea. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 50.6 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how this affects the speed at which air moves in the smallest airways.
parts.answer: Air moves much more slowly (the same volume flows through a much larger total cross-section), so near the alveoli gases move mainly by diffusion
parts.working: 1 mark: much slower air flow in small airways.

stem: A student viewed a stained section of mammal lung through a light microscope with a grid of 100 points in the eyepiece. In one field of view, 68 points fell on air spaces, 26 on alveolar walls and 6 on blood vessels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of points that fell on tissue (alveolar walls and blood vessels together).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of air space to tissue. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student repeated the count in four more randomly chosen fields of view. The percentages of air space were 68, 71, 64, 70 and 67. Calculate the mean and state why using several fields gives a better estimate.
parts.answer: Mean 68 %; one field may not be representative of the whole section (reduces effect of variation)
parts.working: B1: (68 + 71 + 64 + 70 + 67) ÷ 5 = 68 %. B1: more representative / reduces effect of an unusual field.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to decide which tissue a point falls on when it lies on the edge of an alveolar wall, and how the student could deal with this.
parts.answer: Alveolar walls are very thin so boundaries are unclear; set a rule before counting (e.g. count edge points as half, or count only points clearly inside)
parts.working: 1 mark: thin walls / boundary unclear. 1 mark: consistent rule decided in advance.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Descriptions of four airways from a human lung:
W: diameter 8 mm; irregular plates of cartilage; ciliated epithelium with goblet cells; mucous glands
X: diameter 0.4 mm; no cartilage; smooth muscle; no goblet cells; epithelium cells cuboidal with few or no cilia
Y: diameter 18 mm; C-shaped rings of cartilage; ciliated epithelium with goblet cells; mucous glands
Z: diameter 0.9 mm; no cartilage; thick smooth muscle layer; ciliated epithelium with a few goblet cells

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify each airway W, X, Y and Z as trachea, bronchus, larger bronchiole or terminal (smallest) bronchiole.
parts.answer: W bronchus; X terminal bronchiole; Y trachea; Z larger bronchiole
