parts.text: Describe how the student could use iodine solution to compare the activity of amylase at each concentration.
parts.answer: Mix equal volumes of starch and each amylase solution at the same temperature and start a timer; at regular intervals (e.g. every 20 s) put one drop of the mixture into a drop of iodine solution on a spotting tile; record the time when the iodine stays orange-brown (no blue-black); rate = 1 ÷ time; repeat each concentration and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: equal volumes / concentration of starch; same temperature / water bath; sample at regular stated intervals onto iodine; end point = no blue-black / stays orange-brown; rate = 1 ÷ time; repeats and mean.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control.
parts.answer: Replace amylase with the same volume of distilled water (or boiled amylase); the iodine should stay blue-black throughout.
parts.working: B1 water / boiled enzyme instead of amylase, same volume.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to compare catalase activity in potato, carrot and apple. She plans to make an extract of each tissue and add it to hydrogen peroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should prepare the extracts so that they can be compared fairly.
parts.answer: Use the same mass of each tissue (e.g. 10 g, weighed on a balance), cut into small pieces; blend each with the same volume of distilled water (or buffer) for the same time; filter and make each extract up to the same final volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: same mass of tissue; same volume of water / buffer; same blending time; filter / same final volume; use fresh tissue / same age / storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could measure the activity of catalase in each extract.
parts.answer: Add a fixed volume (e.g. 5 cm³) of extract to a fixed volume of the same concentration of hydrogen peroxide in a conical flask at the same temperature; collect the oxygen in an upturned measuring cylinder full of water or a gas syringe; record the volume after a fixed time (e.g. 2 minutes); repeat three times.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: same volume of extract and of H₂O₂ of same concentration; collect O₂ in gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder; volume in a fixed time; same temperature; repeats.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the student should not compare whole pieces of tissue instead of extracts.
parts.answer: Pieces differ in surface area (and shape), so the amount of enzyme exposed to hydrogen peroxide would differ.
parts.working: B1 surface area not equal / enzyme inside cells not all exposed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Polyphenol oxidase (PPO) in apples causes cut surfaces to turn brown. PPO oxidises colourless catechol to a brown product. A student plans to investigate the effect of pH on PPO activity using apple extract, catechol solution, buffer solutions and a colorimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could use a colorimeter to measure the rate of reaction at each pH.
parts.answer: Prepare apple extract in the same way each time (same mass blended with same volume of water, filtered, kept on ice). For each pH (e.g. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) mix a fixed volume of buffer and catechol solution in a cuvette at a constant temperature; zero the colorimeter with a blank (buffer + catechol, no enzyme); add a fixed volume of extract, mix and start the timer; record absorbance every 15 s for 3 minutes using a blue filter (the product is brown); plot absorbance against time and find the initial rate from the gradient at the start; repeat three times at each pH.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: range of ≥5 pH values with buffers; same volume / concentration of catechol and enzyme; extract prepared consistently / kept cold; constant temperature (water bath); blank to zero the colorimeter; suitable filter (complementary colour, e.g. blue); readings at regular intervals over a fixed time; initial rate from gradient / absorbance change in first minute; repeats ×3 and mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Catechol is harmful. State two precautions the student should take.
parts.answer: Wear gloves and eye protection; avoid inhaling it / use in a well-ventilated area; wash hands; use small volumes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible precautions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the initial rate of starch hydrolysis by fungal amylase. Iodine solution forms a blue-black colour with starch; the more starch present, the higher the absorbance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method that uses a colorimeter to find the initial rate of starch hydrolysis at each temperature.
parts.answer: Prepare a calibration curve of absorbance against known starch concentrations with iodine. Place starch and amylase in separate tubes in water baths at each temperature (e.g. 10–60 °C at 10 °C intervals) and equilibrate for 5 minutes. Mix and start timing; at fixed intervals (e.g. every 30 s) remove a fixed volume of mixture into a fixed volume of iodine solution (which stops the reaction and stains the remaining starch); read the absorbance with a red filter after zeroing with water + iodine; convert to starch concentration using the calibration curve; plot starch concentration against time and use the gradient of a tangent at time 0 as the initial rate; repeat three times.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: calibration curve with known starch concentrations; ≥5 temperatures, stated range; water bath and pre-incubation; same volumes / concentrations; samples at regular intervals into iodine (stops reaction); suitable filter (red/orange) and blank; convert absorbance to concentration; initial rate from tangent / early gradient; repeats and means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the samples are added to iodine solution rather than left in the reaction tube until the colorimeter is free.
parts.answer: Adding to iodine stops (or effectively freezes) the reaction at that moment, so each reading represents the starch present at the exact sampling time.
parts.working: B1 reaction would continue / readings must match sampling time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A protease digests casein, the protein that makes milk cloudy; as casein is digested the mixture becomes clearer. A student plans to investigate how casein concentration affects the rate of reaction. She has a 4 % milk suspension, a protease solution, buffer at pH 8, distilled water and a colorimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to make 25 cm³ of each of five different concentrations of milk suspension from the 4 % stock, with the highest concentration being 4 %.
parts.answer: For 4 %, 3.2 %, 2.4 %, 1.6 % and 0.8 %: use 25, 20, 15, 10 and 5 cm³ of stock, made up to 25 cm³ with 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 cm³ of distilled water.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = (concentration ÷ 4) × 25 shown for one. A1 a full set of five concentrations with correct volumes (other evenly spaced sets accepted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could use the colorimeter to measure the rate of reaction at each milk concentration.
parts.answer: Equilibrate milk and protease separately at a constant temperature (e.g. 35 °C water bath); use a buffer of the same pH; zero the colorimeter with distilled water; mix a fixed volume of protease with a fixed volume of milk in a cuvette and start the timer; record absorbance (or % transmission) every 10 s for 2 minutes; the fall in absorbance as casein is digested is used to calculate the initial rate (change in absorbance in the first 30 s); repeat three times at each concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: same volume / concentration of protease; constant temperature and pH (buffer); pre-incubation; colorimeter zeroed / same filter; readings at regular intervals; initial rate from early change / gradient; repeats and mean.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has a catalase extract, hydrogen peroxide of various concentrations, lead nitrate solution, buffer and a gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could find out whether lead ions are a competitive or a non-competitive inhibitor of catalase.
parts.answer: Measure the initial rate of oxygen production at a range of hydrogen peroxide concentrations (e.g. 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6 %, made by dilution from a stock) with no lead nitrate and with one fixed concentration of lead nitrate. Use the same volume and concentration of catalase extract, the same temperature (water bath) and pH (buffer); pre-incubate the enzyme with lead nitrate (or water) for the same time; collect oxygen in a gas syringe and record volume every 10 s, using the first 30 s to calculate initial rate; repeat three times. Plot rate against substrate concentration for both sets. If the inhibited rate approaches the uninhibited rate at high substrate concentrations (same Vmax), inhibition is competitive; if the maximum rate stays lower at all high concentrations (Vmax reduced, Km similar), it is non-competitive.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: range of ≥5 substrate concentrations; dilution from stock described; one fixed inhibitor concentration vs none (control); same enzyme volume / concentration; temperature controlled; pH buffered; pre-incubation of enzyme with inhibitor; gas syringe / initial rate; repeats; compare curves at high [S]: same Vmax = competitive; lower Vmax = non-competitive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the substrate concentrations must include some well above the Km of catalase.
parts.answer: Only at high (near-saturating) substrate concentrations can you see whether the inhibited rate reaches the same Vmax.
parts.working: B1 needed to show whether Vmax is reached / effect overcome.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An enzyme used in a food factory near Karachi has an optimum temperature somewhere between 30 °C and 50 °C. The factory manager wants to know the optimum to the nearest 1 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline a method to find the optimum temperature of this enzyme to the nearest 1 °C.
parts.answer: First do a trial over a wide range (e.g. 20–70 °C at 10 °C intervals) to find the approximate optimum; then repeat at 1 °C intervals around the highest rate (e.g. 36–44 °C) using thermostatically controlled water baths; check temperature with a thermometer reading to 0.1 °C or 0.5 °C; pre-incubate substrate and enzyme separately; keep volumes, concentrations and pH (buffer) the same; measure initial rate (e.g. product formed in the first minute by colorimeter or gas volume); repeat at least three times and use the mean; identify the temperature with the highest mean rate (and check differences are greater than the spread of repeats).
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: preliminary wide-range trial; narrower range at 1 °C steps; precise temperature control (thermostatic bath / digital thermometer); pre-incubation; constant volumes / concentrations / pH buffer; initial rate measured; repeats and mean; compare means with variability (SD / error bars) before stating optimum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using a short reaction time is important when measuring activity at temperatures above the optimum.
parts.answer: Above the optimum the enzyme denatures over time, so a long reaction time would underestimate the rate; a short time (initial rate) measures activity before much denaturation happens.
parts.working: B1 denaturation increases with time at high temperature. B1 initial rate reflects activity before denaturation / long time underestimates.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of pH on salivary amylase. She has buffer solutions of pH 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, 1 % starch, 0.5 % amylase solution, iodine solution and a spotting tile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should make the reaction mixtures for each pH.
parts.answer: For each pH, put the same volume (e.g. 2 cm³) of the buffer solution into a tube with the same volume and concentration of starch; add the same volume of amylase; keep all tubes at the same temperature in a water bath.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: buffer of each pH (≥5 values); same volume / concentration of starch; same volume / concentration of amylase; same temperature (water bath).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student would know when all the starch had been hydrolysed and how a rate could be calculated.
parts.answer: Test one drop every 30 s with iodine on a spotting tile; when it no longer turns blue-black (stays orange-brown) all the starch has gone; rate = 1 ÷ time taken.
parts.working: B1 sampling with iodine, end point = no blue-black. B1 rate = 1 ÷ time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student should stop timing any tube still blue-black after 10 minutes.
parts.answer: At pH values far from the optimum the enzyme may be denatured, so the end point may never be reached; a cut-off time avoids waiting indefinitely (record as 'more than 600 s').
parts.working: B1 reaction may never finish / enzyme denatured; record as > 600 s.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Some sources state that chloride ions (Cl⁻) increase the activity of salivary amylase. A student has sodium chloride, sodium nitrate, starch solution, amylase solution, buffer solutions and laboratory apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to test whether chloride ion concentration affects the activity of amylase. Include a suitable range of concentrations.
parts.answer: Make sodium chloride solutions of e.g. 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08 and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ by dilution of a stock; dialyse or prepare amylase in chloride-free water; add the same volume of each NaCl solution to the same volume of amylase and starch; control pH with a chloride-free buffer (e.g. phosphate); keep temperature constant in a water bath (e.g. 35 °C) with pre-incubation; measure rate by sampling into iodine at fixed intervals (time to end point) or with a colorimeter; repeat three times; include 0 mol dm⁻³ as the control.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: ≥5 Cl⁻ concentrations in sensible range; dilution method; chloride-free enzyme / water; control with no Cl⁻; same volumes / concentrations of starch and amylase; pH buffer without Cl⁻; constant temperature + pre-incubation; valid measurement of rate; repeats.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should use sodium nitrate solutions in a second set of tubes.
parts.answer: To show that any effect is due to chloride ions and not to sodium ions (or to the change in ionic concentration).
parts.working: B1 separates the effect of Cl⁻ from Na⁺ / ionic strength.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pineapple, papaya and kiwi fruit all contain proteases. A student plans to compare the protease activity in extracts of the three fruits. Milk agar is cloudy because it contains the protein casein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could compare the protease activity of the three fruit extracts using milk agar plates.
parts.answer: Prepare each extract the same way: same mass of fresh fruit, blended with the same volume of buffer, filtered (or centrifuged). Use plates of the same thickness of milk agar from the same batch. Cut wells of equal diameter with a sterile cork borer (e.g. 5 mm). Put the same volume of extract (e.g. 0.1 cm³ by micropipette) into each well; include a control well of boiled extract and one of buffer. Incubate all plates at the same temperature (e.g. 30 °C) for the same time (e.g. 24 h). Measure the diameter of the clear zone in two directions at right angles with a ruler, subtract the well diameter (or calculate area of clear zone = πr²). Use at least three plates per fruit and calculate the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: equal mass of fruit / volume of buffer; filtered extract; same agar / depth; equal wells (cork borer); same volume by (micro)pipette; boiled extract control; same incubation temperature and time; diameter measured twice at right angles / area calculated; replicates and mean; aseptic precautions / lids taped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a clear zone forms around a well containing active protease.
parts.answer: Protease diffuses into the agar and hydrolyses casein, which makes the agar cloudy, so the area becomes clear.
parts.working: B1 casein (cloudy protein) hydrolysed by diffusing enzyme.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to find out whether immobilising lactase in calcium alginate beads changes how it responds to temperature. He has lactase solution, sodium alginate solution, calcium chloride solution, milk (containing lactose), glucose test strips or a glucose meter, syringes and water baths.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could make the immobilised lactase beads.
parts.answer: Mix lactase solution with sodium alginate solution; draw the mixture into a syringe and add it drop by drop into calcium chloride solution; leave the beads to harden for a few minutes; strain and rinse with distilled water.
parts.working: B1 lactase mixed with sodium alginate. B1 dropped into calcium chloride (forms calcium alginate beads). B1 left to harden, then rinsed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could compare the effect of temperature on free and immobilised lactase.
parts.answer: Use the same mass of lactase in both: e.g. beads made from 5 cm³ of enzyme solution versus 5 cm³ of free enzyme mixed with alginate-free water. At each temperature (e.g. 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 °C, water bath, pre-incubated) add the same volume and concentration of milk/lactose solution; after a fixed time (e.g. 5 minutes) measure glucose concentration with glucose test strips or a glucose meter (beads removed first); use a control of beads with no enzyme; repeat three times at each temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: equal quantity of enzyme in each form; ≥5 temperatures, water bath, pre-incubation; same volume / concentration of lactose; fixed time / initial rate; glucose measured (test strips / meter / Benedict's with colour standards); control beads without enzyme; repeats.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the control of beads without enzyme is needed.
parts.answer: To show that alginate beads alone do not produce glucose or affect the glucose reading.
parts.working: B1 shows the beads themselves do not cause the result.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction was measured at different substrate concentrations.
Substrate concentration / mmol dm⁻³: 0.5, 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48
Initial rate / units: 7.1, 12.5, 25.0, 33.3, 40.0, 44.4, 47.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by Vmax.
parts.answer: The maximum initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, reached when all the active sites are occupied (enzyme saturated with substrate).
parts.working: B1 maximum rate when enzyme saturated / all active sites occupied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Vmax for this enzyme is 50 units. Use the table to find the Michaelis–Menten constant, Km. Include units.
parts.answer: 3 mmol dm⁻³
parts.working: M1 ½Vmax = 25 units. A1 rate is 25 at 3 mmol dm⁻³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate at 48 mmol dm⁻³ is still slightly below Vmax.
parts.answer: Even at high concentration a few active sites are free at any moment (between one substrate leaving and the next binding), so the enzyme approaches but does not quite reach saturation.
parts.working: B1 not all active sites occupied at every instant / Vmax only approached.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what a low value of Km indicates about an enzyme.
parts.answer: The enzyme has a high affinity for its substrate.
parts.working: B1 high affinity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To immobilise an enzyme, a student mixed enzyme solution with sodium alginate and added the mixture drop by drop to calcium chloride solution. The drops formed jelly-like beads of calcium alginate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the enzyme stays trapped inside the beads while substrate and product molecules can move in and out.
parts.answer: Enzyme molecules are large proteins that become tangled in / cannot pass through the alginate network, but substrate and product molecules are small enough to diffuse through the pores of the gel.
parts.working: B1 enzyme molecules too large to leave the alginate gel. B1 small substrate / product molecules diffuse through pores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the beads are rinsed with distilled water before use.
parts.answer: To remove calcium chloride and any enzyme on the surface of the beads that has not been trapped, so it does not contaminate the product.
parts.working: B1 remove excess CaCl₂ / untrapped enzyme.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two advantages to a food company of using the enzyme in beads rather than dissolved in the reaction mixture.
parts.answer: Any two of: enzyme can be reused; product is not contaminated with enzyme (no separation needed); enzyme is often more stable to temperature/pH; suits a continuous process in a column.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company makes a sweet syrup for soft drinks by passing glucose syrup continuously through a column packed with immobilised glucose isomerase, which converts glucose into fructose. The column is kept at 60 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the company uses immobilised glucose isomerase rather than adding the enzyme to each batch of syrup.
parts.answer: The immobilised enzyme stays in the column and can be reused for months, reducing cost; the syrup leaving the column contains no enzyme, so no purification step is needed; syrup can flow through continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2: reused / cheaper; product free of enzyme; continuous process.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the company converts glucose into fructose.
parts.answer: Fructose tastes sweeter than glucose, so less syrup is needed to sweeten foods.
parts.working: B1 fructose is sweeter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one factor, other than temperature, that the company must control in the column, and why.
parts.answer: pH (with a buffer), because a change in pH would alter the charges in the active site and reduce activity / denature the enzyme; or flow rate, because it controls contact time.
parts.working: B1 pH or flow rate + reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hexokinase and glucokinase both phosphorylate glucose. Hexokinase is found in most cells; glucokinase is found in liver cells.
Hexokinase: Km = 0.1 mmol dm⁻³
Glucokinase: Km = 8 mmol dm⁻³
The rate of each enzyme can be found from: rate ÷ Vmax = [S] ÷ (Km + [S]).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which enzyme has the higher affinity for glucose. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Hexokinase, because its Km (0.1 mmol dm⁻³) is much lower: it reaches half its maximum rate at a much lower glucose concentration.
parts.working: B1 hexokinase. B1 lower Km → ½Vmax at lower concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the equation to calculate the rate of each enzyme, as a percentage of its Vmax, at a blood glucose concentration of 5 mmol dm⁻³. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Hexokinase: 98.0 %; glucokinase: 38.5 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: After a meal, blood glucose in the liver can reach 10 mmol dm⁻³. Explain why it is an advantage that liver cells use glucokinase to take up and store excess glucose.
parts.answer: Glucokinase activity rises considerably between 5 and 10 mmol dm⁻³ (38.5 % to 55.6 % of Vmax), so the liver takes up more glucose only when blood glucose is high; hexokinase is already almost saturated (98–99 %) and could not respond to the rise.
parts.working: B1 glucokinase rate increases with glucose in this range / responds to high glucose. B1 hexokinase already saturated, so cannot respond (or would remove glucose even when low).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
For an enzyme with Vmax = 80 µmol min⁻¹ and Km = 4 mmol dm⁻³, the initial rate is given by:
rate = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S])

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate when the substrate concentration is 4 mmol dm⁻³ and when it is 12 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 4 mmol dm⁻³: 40 µmol min⁻¹; 12 mmol dm⁻³: 60 µmol min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why your answer at 4 mmol dm⁻³ is exactly half of Vmax.
parts.answer: Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax, and 4 mmol dm⁻³ is the Km.
parts.working: B1 [S] = Km gives ½Vmax.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the substrate concentration needed for the rate to reach 75 % of Vmax.
parts.answer: 12 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Tripling the substrate concentration from 4 to 12 mmol dm⁻³ does not triple the rate. Explain why.
parts.answer: At these concentrations many active sites are already occupied, so the rate depends less and less on substrate concentration; adding substrate mostly fills the remaining free sites and the rate approaches Vmax, where enzyme concentration limits.
parts.working: B1 many active sites already occupied / approaching saturation. B1 enzyme becomes limiting / rate approaches Vmax.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction was measured at pH 7 and at pH 5. Vmax is 90 units at both pH values.
Substrate concentration / mmol dm⁻³: 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 32, 64
Rate at pH 7 / units: 18.0, 30.0, 45.0, 60.0, 67.5, 72.0, 80.0, 84.7
Rate at pH 5 / units: 6.9, 12.9, 22.5, 36.0, 45.0, 51.4, 65.5, 75.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to find Km at pH 7 and at pH 5. Include units.
parts.answer: pH 7: Km = 4 mmol dm⁻³; pH 5: Km = 12 mmol dm⁻³
parts.working: B1 ½Vmax = 45 units, reached at 4 mmol dm⁻³ at pH 7. B1 reached at 12 mmol dm⁻³ at pH 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the change in Km shows about the enzyme at pH 5.
parts.answer: The enzyme has a lower affinity for its substrate at pH 5 (a higher substrate concentration is needed to reach half Vmax).
parts.working: B1 lower affinity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the lower pH causes this change.
parts.answer: The higher H⁺ concentration changes the charges (ionisation) of R groups in the active site, so fewer / weaker temporary bonds (e.g. ionic, hydrogen) form with the substrate; the substrate binds less readily and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form at a given substrate concentration.
parts.working: B1 H⁺ alters charges on R groups in / near the active site. B1 substrate binds less well / fewer E–S complexes (shape or charge of active site changed).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the rate at pH 5 as a percentage of the rate at pH 7 at 1 mmol dm⁻³ and at 64 mmol dm⁻³ substrate. Give your answers to 3 significant figures, and state what they show.
parts.answer: 1 mmol dm⁻³: 38.3 %; 64 mmol dm⁻³: 89.5 %. The effect of pH 5 is large at low substrate concentration but small at high substrate concentration, where the rate at both pH values approaches the same Vmax.
parts.working: B1 6.9 ÷ 18.0 × 100 = 38.3 % and 75.8 ÷ 84.7 × 100 = 89.5 %. B1 lower pH matters most at low [S]; at high [S] both approach the same Vmax.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Milk containing 48 g dm⁻³ of lactose is passed through a column of immobilised lactase at different flow rates.
Flow rate / cm³ min⁻¹: 5, 10, 20, 40
Lactose hydrolysed / %: 96, 88, 70, 45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of lactose hydrolysed per hour at a flow rate of 10 cm³ min⁻¹ and at 40 cm³ min⁻¹. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 10 cm³ min⁻¹: 25.3 g h⁻¹; 40 cm³ min⁻¹: 51.8 g h⁻¹
parts.working: M1 volume per hour: 10 × 60 = 600 cm³ = 0.6 dm³ (2.4 dm³ at 40). M1 × 48 g dm⁻³ × fraction hydrolysed. A1 0.6 × 48 × 0.88 = 25.3 g; 2.4 × 48 × 0.45 = 51.8 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two changes to the column, other than reducing the flow rate, that would increase the percentage of lactose hydrolysed at 40 cm³ min⁻¹. Explain one of them.
parts.answer: Any two of: use a longer column / more beads (more enzyme); use smaller beads (larger surface area to volume ratio, shorter diffusion distance); load more lactase into each bead; keep the column at the optimum temperature and pH of lactase. Explanation, e.g.: a longer column means each lactose molecule passes more active sites / spends longer in contact with enzyme, so more E–S complexes form before the milk leaves.
parts.working: B1 two valid changes. B1 explanation linked to more contact with active sites / more E–S complexes per unit volume of milk.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The dairy wants to sell 'lactose-free' milk, which must have at least 90 % of the lactose hydrolysed. Evaluate which flow rate the dairy should use.
parts.answer: Only 5 cm³ min⁻¹ gives ≥ 90 % (96 %); 10 cm³ min⁻¹ gives 88 %, just below the limit, even though it processes more lactose per hour. Faster rates hydrolyse more lactose per hour but the product would not meet the standard, so use 5 cm³ min⁻¹ (or between 5 and 10 if tested), or add a longer / second column to allow faster flow.
parts.working: B1 5 cm³ min⁻¹ meets 90 % (data). B1 trade-off: faster flow gives more mass per hour but fails the standard / suggest longer column or test 6–9 cm³ min⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An enzyme was tested free in solution and immobilised in alginate beads.
Free enzyme: Vmax = 100 units, Km = 1.5 mmol dm⁻³
Immobilised enzyme: Vmax = 90 units, Km = 4.5 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the equation rate = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]) to calculate the rate of each form at 1.5 mmol dm⁻³ substrate. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Free: 50.0 units; immobilised: 22.5 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why Km is higher for the immobilised enzyme.
parts.answer: Substrate has to diffuse through the alginate to reach the enzyme, so the concentration around the active sites is lower than in the solution; a higher substrate concentration in the solution is needed to reach half Vmax. Some active sites may also be partly blocked or distorted by the matrix.
parts.working: B1 diffusion barrier / lower [S] near enzyme. B1 more substrate needed for ½Vmax / active sites less accessible.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why Vmax is lower for the immobilised enzyme.
parts.answer: Some enzyme molecules are damaged (denatured) during immobilisation or their active sites are blocked, so fewer active sites are available.
parts.working: B1 fewer functional active sites.

parts.label: d
parts.text: At 30 mmol dm⁻³ substrate the immobilised enzyme gives 78.3 units and the free enzyme 95.2 units. Using this and your answers to (a), suggest why immobilisation is less of a disadvantage when the substrate concentration is high.
parts.answer: At high substrate concentration the immobilised form gives 82 % of the free rate, compared with 45 % at 1.5 mmol dm⁻³, because diffusion no longer limits supply to active sites.
parts.working: B1 relative difference much smaller at high [S] (with figures), substrate supply no longer limiting.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A company wants to use an immobilised enzyme in a column at 60 °C, with a substrate concentration of 100 mmol dm⁻³. It has two possible enzymes.
Enzyme P: Km = 2 mmol dm⁻³; Vmax = 150 units; optimum temperature 45 °C; time for activity to halve at 60 °C = 10 minutes
Enzyme R: Km = 12 mmol dm⁻³; Vmax = 220 units; optimum temperature 70 °C; time for activity to halve at 60 °C = 6 hours
rate = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S])

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate of each enzyme at 100 mmol dm⁻³ substrate. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: P: 147 units; R: 196 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate which enzyme the company should immobilise for its process.
parts.answer: Choose R. At 100 mmol dm⁻³ substrate both enzymes are close to Vmax, so P's lower Km (higher affinity) gives little advantage; R is faster (196 v 147 units). R's optimum (70 °C) is above 60 °C and its activity half-life at 60 °C is 6 h compared with 10 min for P, so P would be denatured quickly at 60 °C and need frequent replacement. P would only be better at low substrate concentrations or lower temperatures. Data on cost, pH and how each behaves when immobilised are not given.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: R chosen; at high [S] both near Vmax so Km matters little; R faster (figures); R stable at 60 °C (half-life 6 h v 10 min); P denatures / would need frequent replacement; limitation: no data on cost / pH / immobilised behaviour.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A small factory in Lahore uses immobilised enzyme beads to make a food ingredient in batches. With fresh beads, one batch produces 40 kg of product. The beads are reused for ten batches; their activity in each batch, as a percentage of the first batch, is:
100, 98, 95, 93, 90, 88, 85, 83, 80, 78

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of product made by the immobilised beads over the ten batches.
parts.answer: 356 kg
parts.working: M1 sum of percentages = 890 (%). A1 40 × 890 ÷ 100 = 356 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same mass of free enzyme can be used for only one batch. Calculate how many times more product the immobilised enzyme gives.
parts.answer: 8.9 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the activity of the beads falls a little with each batch.
parts.answer: Any two of: some enzyme leaks out of the beads; some enzyme is denatured over time (temperature/pH); beads break up / are lost when separated; active sites become blocked by product or impurities.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Beads of three diameters were made with the same total volume of an alginate–enzyme mixture and placed in the same volume of substrate solution.
Bead diameter / mm: 2, 4, 6
Rate of product formation / µmol min⁻¹: 12.0, 6.3, 4.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of beads of each diameter, using SA:V = 6 ÷ d for a sphere of diameter d.
parts.answer: 2 mm: 3.0 mm⁻¹; 4 mm: 1.5 mm⁻¹; 6 mm: 1.0 mm⁻¹
parts.working: B2 all three correct (B1 for two).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the smallest beads give the highest rate of product formation.
parts.answer: Smaller beads have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so substrate diffuses a shorter distance to reach enzyme inside the beads and more enzyme is close to the surface; more enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time.
parts.working: B1 larger SA:V / shorter diffusion distance. B1 more active sites reached / more E–S complexes per unit time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of using very small beads in an industrial column.
parts.answer: They pack tightly and slow the flow of liquid (or they are harder to make / retain and may be washed out of the column).
parts.working: B1 slow flow / clog column / lost from column.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Glucose biosensors contain an immobilised enzyme that reacts with glucose; the electrical signal is proportional to the rate of the reaction. A designer must choose between two enzymes that react with glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the rate at 20 mmol dm⁻³ glucose to the rate at 2 mmol dm⁻³ glucose for an enzyme with Km = 50 mmol dm⁻³ and for one with Km = 2 mmol dm⁻³. Use rate ∝ [S] ÷ (Km + [S]). Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain which enzyme would make a better sensor for blood glucose over the range 2 to 20 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: The enzyme with Km = 50 mmol dm⁻³: a 10-fold rise in glucose gives a 7.4-fold rise in rate, so the signal is nearly proportional to concentration and readings can be distinguished; the Km = 2 enzyme is close to saturation above a few mmol dm⁻³ (only 1.8-fold), so high glucose values would all give similar readings.
parts.working: B1 high-Km enzyme chosen with ratio nearly proportional. B1 low-Km enzyme saturates, cannot distinguish high concentrations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sensor gives a reading for glucose but not for other sugars in the blood.
parts.answer: The enzyme is specific: only glucose is complementary to its active site.
parts.working: B1 enzyme specific to glucose / active site shape.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student filled thin glass tubes with egg white and boiled them so the egg white set. The tubes were cut into 20 mm lengths and placed in pepsin solutions buffered at pH 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. After 24 hours, the length of egg white digested at each end was measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: pH (of the pepsin solution). Dependent: length of egg white digested (in 24 hours).
parts.working: B1 IV pH. B1 DV length of egg white digested / cleared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why all the tubes must have the same internal diameter.
parts.answer: The surface area of egg white exposed to pepsin at each end must be the same; a wider tube exposes more protein, so more would be digested.
parts.working: B1 same surface area of egg white exposed to enzyme.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could keep the temperature constant for 24 hours.
parts.answer: Put all the tubes in a thermostatically controlled incubator or water bath at e.g. 35 °C.
parts.working: B1 incubator / thermostatic water bath at stated temperature.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two other variables that must be standardised.
parts.answer: Any two of: concentration of pepsin; volume of pepsin solution; length of egg-white tube; time (24 h); how the egg white was cooked.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student is investigating the effect of temperature on the activity of amylase. She will measure the time taken for starch to disappear at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the starch and amylase must be kept in separate tubes in the water bath for 5 minutes before they are mixed.
parts.answer: So that both solutions reach the temperature of the water bath before the reaction starts; otherwise the reaction would begin at room temperature and the temperature during the reaction would not be the intended value.
parts.working: B1 solutions reach the required temperature. B1 reaction occurs at the intended temperature from the start / not room temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student plans to use a beaker of water heated with a Bunsen burner for each temperature. Suggest a better way to control temperature and explain why it is better.
parts.answer: Use a thermostatically controlled water bath (and check with a thermometer); it keeps the temperature constant throughout, whereas a beaker over a Bunsen burner fluctuates.
parts.working: B1 thermostatic water bath. B1 temperature stays constant / does not fluctuate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that would change if the student used a different amylase solution for each temperature.
parts.answer: The concentration / activity of the enzyme.
parts.working: B1 enzyme concentration / activity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To investigate the effect of sucrose concentration on invertase, a student added 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 cm³ of 10 % sucrose solution to five tubes. He then added 1 cm³ of invertase to each tube and measured the glucose produced in 5 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the problem with this method.
parts.answer: The total volume differs between tubes (2 to 10 cm³), so the concentration of invertase differs and sucrose concentration is not the only variable being changed.
parts.working: B1 total volume not kept the same. B1 so enzyme concentration also changes / two variables changing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should change the method.
parts.answer: Make up each tube to the same total volume (e.g. 10 cm³) with distilled water before adding the same volume of invertase: e.g. 2 cm³ sucrose + 8 cm³ water, 4 + 6, and so on.
parts.working: B1 add distilled water to make the same total volume. B1 example volumes / same enzyme volume.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigated the effect of temperature on catalase in yeast. Because the practical took three days, he made a fresh yeast suspension each day by stirring some dried yeast into water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this could make the results invalid.
parts.answer: The concentration of yeast cells (and so the amount of catalase) may differ between the suspensions made on different days, so differences in oxygen produced could be due to enzyme concentration rather than temperature.
parts.working: B1 amount of catalase / yeast concentration varies. B1 another variable affects DV / not a fair comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could avoid this problem.
parts.answer: Make one large batch of yeast suspension for all temperatures (stirred before each sample), or make each suspension with the same mass of yeast in the same volume of water and leave it the same time; do all the temperatures on the same day.
parts.working: B1 single batch / same mass per volume. B1 stir before sampling / same day / same activation time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students measured the volume of oxygen released when a potato extract was added to hydrogen peroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a control using boiled enzyme is better than a control using the same volume of distilled water.
parts.answer: Boiled enzyme contains everything in the extract (other substances, ions, the denatured protein) except active enzyme; any change in the control must therefore be caused by something other than enzyme activity, so the effect is shown to be due to the enzyme. Water does not contain these other substances.
parts.working: B1 boiled extract identical except enzyme denatured. B1 shows that the result is due to enzyme activity, not other substances in the extract.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one experiment the boiled-enzyme control produced a small amount of gas. Suggest two explanations.
parts.answer: Any two of: the extract was not boiled long enough, so some enzyme was still active; hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly on its own; dissolved gas or air bubbles were displaced; temperature rise expanded the gas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student added pieces of potato to hydrogen peroxide of different concentrations and counted bubbles. Her notes say: 'Cut potato into pieces with a knife – some bigger than others. Poured some hydrogen peroxide into each tube. Some tubes were by the window in the sun.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three variables in this method that were not standardised and explain how each could affect the results.
parts.answer: 1. Size / surface area of the potato pieces – more surface area exposes more catalase. 2. Temperature – tubes near the window warmed in sunlight, increasing kinetic energy and rate. 3. Volume of hydrogen peroxide (measured by eye) – different volumes / amounts of substrate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three (variable + effect): piece size / SA; temperature; volume of H₂O₂; potato variety / part of potato; timing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each variable you identified in (a), describe how it could be standardised.
parts.answer: Use a cork borer and ruler to cut cylinders of the same diameter and length (same mass); put all tubes in a water bath at the same temperature; measure hydrogen peroxide with a syringe or measuring cylinder.
parts.working: 1 mark for each matching control method.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student is investigating the effect of pH on the activity of a lipase. The reaction releases fatty acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using buffer solutions is better than adding hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide to set the pH.
parts.answer: Buffers keep the pH constant during the reaction even if acidic or alkaline products are formed; with acid or alkali alone the pH could drift, so the pH would not be the stated value throughout.
parts.working: B1 buffer resists change in pH. B1 pH stays at the intended value during the reaction / products would change pH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the same buffer system (e.g. the same type of salt) should be used for all pH values where possible.
parts.answer: Different buffer salts contain different ions, which might themselves activate or inhibit the enzyme.
parts.working: B1 ions in different buffers could affect enzyme activity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the student could check that each buffer had the intended pH.
parts.answer: Use a calibrated pH meter (or narrow-range indicator paper).
parts.working: B1 pH meter.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compared catalase activity in leaves of two varieties of spinach by blending 5 g of leaves of each variety in 50 cm³ of water and measuring oxygen release.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why measuring catalase activity per gram of leaf may not show whether the enzyme molecules themselves differ between the varieties.
parts.answer: The varieties could contain different amounts (concentrations) of catalase per gram, so a higher activity could be due to more enzyme rather than a more active enzyme; the water content / protein content of leaves may also differ.
parts.working: B1 differences in quantity of enzyme. B1 water / protein content differs, so mass is not equivalent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the extracts could be standardised so that differences in enzyme activity are compared fairly.
parts.answer: Measure total protein (or catalase protein) concentration of each extract and dilute so each has the same protein concentration, or express activity per mg of protein; use leaves of the same age, collected at the same time.
parts.working: B1 standardise by protein concentration / activity per mg protein. B1 same age leaves / same time / same extraction procedure.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student plans to investigate the effect of catalase concentration on the initial rate of oxygen production. In a preliminary experiment, using the highest catalase concentration, she measured:
Hydrogen peroxide concentration / %: 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Initial rate / cm³ s⁻¹: 0.12, 0.23, 0.40, 0.48, 0.48, 0.49

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the substrate must be in excess at every enzyme concentration in this investigation.
parts.answer: If substrate became limiting, the rate would be limited by substrate rather than enzyme concentration, so adding more enzyme would not increase the rate; the results would not show the true effect of enzyme concentration.
parts.working: B1 substrate must not limit rate. B1 otherwise rate does not rise with enzyme concentration / plateau not due to enzyme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the preliminary results to suggest a suitable hydrogen peroxide concentration. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: About 4 % (or higher): with the highest enzyme concentration the rate rises with peroxide up to 3 % and is constant from 3 % to 5 %, so at 4 % the substrate is in excess (not limiting).
parts.working: B1 ≥ 3 % / about 4 %. B1 reasoning: rate stopped increasing above 3 %, so substrate not limiting.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigates whether copper sulfate inhibits amylase, using a colorimeter to measure the absorbance of starch–iodine colour in samples taken from the reaction mixture. Copper sulfate solution is pale blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the purpose of two control tubes the student should include.
parts.answer: 1. Enzyme + starch + water instead of copper sulfate (no inhibitor): gives the uninhibited rate to compare with. 2. Starch + copper sulfate + iodine with no enzyme (or boiled enzyme): shows whether copper sulfate itself changes the colour / absorbance or reacts with iodine or starch.
parts.working: B1 + B1 no-inhibitor control and its purpose. B1 + B1 inhibitor-without-enzyme (or boiled enzyme) control and its purpose (blue copper sulfate affects absorbance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the copper sulfate solution used must have the same final concentration in each tube where it is present.
parts.answer: The amount of inhibition depends on inhibitor concentration, so it must be the same if only the substrate concentration is being varied.
parts.working: B1 inhibition depends on inhibitor concentration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the colorimeter must be zeroed with a blank containing copper sulfate rather than with water.
parts.answer: Copper sulfate is blue and absorbs light, so it would add to the absorbance reading and must be subtracted.
parts.working: B1 copper sulfate absorbs light / coloured.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to compare catalase activity in leaves of neem trees growing beside a busy road and 500 m away from it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three variables, other than distance from the road, that could affect the results, and explain how each could be controlled.
parts.answer: Any three of: plant species / variety – use the same species; leaf age / position – take leaves of the same age (e.g. 4th leaf from tip); time of day of collection – collect all at the same time; storage temperature and time before testing – keep on ice and test within the same time; soil water / shade – choose plants in similar conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variable + control method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this investigation cannot be fully controlled, and how the student should take this into account when drawing conclusions.
parts.answer: In the field, variables such as soil, light and water cannot be kept the same, so differences may be caused by these rather than pollution; the student should collect large random samples, measure these variables, and state that a correlation does not prove that pollution caused the difference.
parts.working: B1 field variables cannot be controlled / confounding variables. B1 large samples / measure other variables / conclusion limited to association, not cause.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student uses a colorimeter to follow the formation of a coloured product in an enzyme-catalysed reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the blank and what it should contain.
parts.answer: The blank sets the colorimeter to zero absorbance; it should contain everything in the reaction mixture except the coloured substance being measured (e.g. buffer + substrate, no enzyme) in the same type of cuvette.
parts.working: B1 zero / calibrate the colorimeter. B1 contains everything except the coloured product (same solvent / cuvette).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables connected with using the colorimeter that must be kept the same for all readings.
parts.answer: Any two of: same filter / wavelength; same cuvette (or matched cuvettes) placed the same way round; same volume in cuvette; cuvettes clean, no fingerprints on clear faces; same time after mixing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has ten tubes containing an enzyme and its substrate at different temperatures. She wants to measure the amount of product after exactly 5 minutes in each tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student cannot simply read all ten tubes one after another at the end of the experiment.
parts.answer: The reaction continues in each tube until it is tested, so tubes read later would have reacted for longer; the reaction time would not be the same for every tube.
parts.working: B1 reaction continues while waiting. B1 reaction times differ / time not standardised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways in which the reaction could be stopped at exactly 5 minutes in every tube.
parts.answer: Any two of: add a fixed volume of strong acid or alkali (changes pH far from optimum); put tubes into a boiling water bath to denature the enzyme; add a stopping reagent such as iodine for starch tests; place tubes in ice (slows reaction greatly).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid methods.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why starting the tubes at 30-second intervals helps the student.
parts.answer: Each tube can be stopped and measured at exactly the same reaction time, one after another, without rushing.
parts.working: B1 allows each tube to be timed / stopped accurately at 5 min.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A juice factory near Multan tested pectinase from a fungus on mango pulp at different pH values. The rate of juice release was measured in arbitrary units.
pH: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Rate / arbitrary units: 22, 55, 80, 61, 30, 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of pH on the rate of juice release.
parts.answer: Rate increases from pH 3 (22) to a maximum at pH 5 (80), then decreases to 9 at pH 8.
parts.working: B1 increase to peak at pH 5. B1 decrease above pH 5, with data quoted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate at pH 7 as a percentage of the rate at pH 5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student concludes that the optimum pH of pectinase is exactly 5. Explain why this conclusion is not fully justified.
parts.answer: pH was tested only at whole-number intervals, so the true optimum could lie anywhere between pH 4 and 6; because the rate at pH 6 (61) is higher than at pH 4 (55), it is probably slightly above 5. Smaller intervals around pH 5 and repeats are needed.
parts.working: B1 intervals too large / optimum could be between 4 and 6. B1 need smaller pH intervals near 5 (and repeats).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The activities of two amylases, A and B, were measured at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90
Rate with A / arbitrary units: 15, 34, 58, 40, 8, 0, 0, 0
Rate with B / arbitrary units: 5, 9, 15, 26, 42, 63, 80, 31

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature of each amylase from these data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One amylase came from human saliva and one from a bacterium living in hot springs. Identify which is which, using the data.
parts.answer: A is from human saliva (optimum 40 °C, near body temperature); B is from the hot-spring bacterium (optimum 80 °C, still active at 90 °C).
parts.working: B1 A human, B bacterium with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of B at 60 °C as a percentage of its rate at 80 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why amylase A has no activity at 70 °C and above.
parts.answer: It is denatured: the bonds holding its tertiary structure break, so the active site loses its shape.
parts.working: B1 denatured / active site shape lost.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measured the rate of oxygen production by a catalase extract with hydrogen peroxide of different concentrations.
Concentration / %: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0
Rate / cm³ s⁻¹: 0.20, 0.41, 0.79, 1.20, 1.58

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the data show.
parts.answer: The rate increases steadily (in proportion) as hydrogen peroxide concentration increases from 0.5 to 4 % (0.20 to 1.58 cm³ s⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 rate increases (proportionally) over the whole range with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concludes: 'The rate will always increase as the concentration of hydrogen peroxide increases.' Explain why this conclusion is not valid.
parts.answer: The data only cover 0.5–4 %, so they cannot show what happens at higher concentrations; at high substrate concentration the active sites become saturated and the rate levels off (Vmax), so the rate will not keep increasing.
parts.working: B1 cannot extrapolate beyond the range tested. B1 enzyme becomes saturated / rate levels off at Vmax.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An enzyme's rate of reaction was measured once at each temperature.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
Rate / arbitrary units: 2.3, 4.1, 6.2, 6.0, 1.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student states: 'The optimum temperature of this enzyme is 40 °C.' Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The highest rate measured was at 40 °C (6.2), but the rate at 50 °C (6.0) is almost the same, so the true optimum probably lies between 40 and 50 °C (around 45 °C); with 10 °C intervals the optimum cannot be found precisely; the difference between 6.2 and 6.0 may be within experimental variation, and there are no repeats to show this.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: highest at 40 °C supports partly; 50 °C almost as high so optimum likely between 40 and 50; intervals too wide; difference small / no repeats or measure of spread.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest further work that would give a better estimate of the optimum temperature.
parts.answer: Repeat at 2 °C (or 1 °C) intervals between 40 and 50 °C, with at least three repeats at each temperature, and use the means (with SD or error bars).
parts.working: B1 smaller intervals between 40 and 50 °C. B1 repeats / means / error bars.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Catalase activity (volume of oxygen in 60 s) was measured in leaf extracts from five plants of each of two wheat varieties.
Variety X: mean 24.6 cm³, standard deviation 3.1 cm³
Variety Y: mean 22.9 cm³, standard deviation 2.8 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two means.
parts.answer: 1.7 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concludes that variety X has more active catalase than variety Y. Discuss whether the data support this conclusion.
parts.answer: Mean of X is higher by 1.7 cm³, which partly supports the conclusion; however, the standard deviations (3.1 and 2.8) are larger than the difference, so the ranges of mean ± SD overlap widely (21.5–27.7 and 20.1–25.7) and the difference may be due to chance; only five samples; a statistical test (t-test) is needed. Also the result may reflect more catalase rather than more active catalase.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: mean X higher supports; SDs larger than difference / overlap; small sample (n = 5); need t-test; activity could reflect amount not activity of enzyme.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction was measured with different concentrations of compound Q. Substrate concentration was the same in every tube.
Concentration of Q / mmol dm⁻³: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8
Rate / µmol min⁻¹: 50, 40, 33, 25, 17

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage inhibition at each concentration of compound Q.
parts.working: M1 (50 − rate) ÷ 50 × 100. A1 all four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concludes: 'The percentage inhibition is directly proportional to the concentration of compound Q.' Use your answers to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Not supported: inhibition increases with concentration, but doubling concentration does not double inhibition (1 → 2 mmol dm⁻³ gives 20 → 34 %; 4 → 8 gives 50 → 66 %); the increase gets smaller as concentration rises.
parts.working: B1 inhibition does increase with concentration. B1 not proportional, with calculated figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the effect of compound Q levels off at high concentrations.
parts.answer: Most of the binding sites on the enzyme molecules are already occupied by Q, so extra Q has less additional effect.
parts.working: B1 binding sites on enzyme (nearly) all occupied.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mangoes were stored at room temperature after picking. Catalase activity was measured in extracts of the flesh every two days.
Days of storage: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Catalase activity / units: 12.0, 10.4, 8.1, 6.3, 4.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean decrease in catalase activity per day over the 8 days.
parts.answer: 1.0 units per day

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concludes: 'Storing mangoes causes their catalase to be broken down.' Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: There is a clear negative correlation (activity falls from 12.0 to 4.0 as storage time increases), which supports a link; but the data do not show the mechanism – activity could fall because less catalase is made as the fruit ripens, or because of inhibitors or changes in pH, not breakdown; other variables (temperature, ripeness at picking) were not stated; only one batch / no repeats.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: negative correlation supports; correlation does not show cause / mechanism; alternative explanation (less synthesis, ripening, inhibitors, pH); no repeats / uncontrolled variables.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one additional measurement that would help to show whether the amount of catalase protein falls during storage.
parts.answer: Measure the concentration of catalase protein (e.g. total protein or a specific antibody test) in extracts at each storage time.
parts.working: B1 measure enzyme/protein quantity (not just activity).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The same amount of substrate was incubated with 1 unit and with 2 units of an enzyme.
Time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15
Product with 1 unit / µmol: 0, 4, 8, 12, 19, 32, 38
Product with 2 units / µmol: 0, 8, 15, 22, 31, 39, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate (in the first 2 minutes) for each enzyme concentration.
parts.answer: 1 unit: 4.0 µmol min⁻¹; 2 units: 7.5 µmol min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes: 'Doubling the enzyme concentration doubles the amount of product formed.' Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Partly true for the rate: the initial rate almost doubles (4.0 to 7.5; in the first minute 4 to 8). But the total amount of product is not doubled: both reach about 40 µmol (38 and 40 at 15 min), because the amount of substrate is the same and limits the final yield. The enzyme speeds up reaching the end point but does not change how much product forms.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: initial rate (nearly) doubles, with data; final amount the same, about 40 µmol; final amount limited by substrate; enzyme changes rate not yield.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate with 2 units of enzyme falls between 5 and 15 minutes.
parts.answer: As substrate is used up its concentration falls, so there are fewer collisions with active sites and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time; by 15 minutes almost all substrate has been converted.
parts.working: B1 substrate concentration decreasing / being used up. B1 fewer collisions / E–S complexes per unit time.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measured the initial rate of reaction at different enzyme concentrations with a fixed substrate concentration.
Enzyme concentration / %: 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0
Initial rate / cm³ min⁻¹: 0.9, 1.8, 2.6, 3.5, 3.9, 4.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate per 1 % of enzyme (rate ÷ enzyme concentration) at 1.0 % and at 3.0 % enzyme. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concludes that 'the rate of reaction is directly proportional to enzyme concentration'. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Supported from 0.5 to 2.0 %: the rate per % stays about constant (1.80, 1.80, 1.73, 1.75). Not supported above 2.0 %: the rate per % falls (1.56 at 2.5 %, 1.33 at 3.0 %) and the rate levels off at about 4.0. The conclusion only holds over the lower range; above 2 % another factor, probably substrate concentration, limits the rate.
parts.working: B1 proportional up to 2.0 % with evidence. B1 not proportional above 2.0 % / levels off with evidence. B1 another factor limits (substrate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could test whether the levelling off is caused by substrate.
parts.answer: Repeat at the higher enzyme concentrations with a higher substrate concentration; if the rate keeps rising, substrate was limiting.
parts.working: B1 increase substrate concentration and compare.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The activity of an enzyme, free and immobilised in alginate beads, was measured at different pH values. Activity is shown as a percentage of the maximum activity of the same form.
pH: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
Free enzyme / %: 20, 55, 90, 100, 62, 25
Immobilised enzyme / %: 45, 70, 92, 100, 85, 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum pH of each form of the enzyme.
parts.answer: Both pH 7
parts.working: B1 both pH 7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A scientist concludes that 'immobilisation makes the enzyme active over a wider range of pH'. Discuss the extent to which the data support this conclusion.
parts.answer: Support: at pH values away from the optimum the immobilised form keeps a higher percentage of its activity (e.g. pH 4: 45 % v 20 %; pH 9: 60 % v 25 %); at pH 6 and 7 they are similar. Limitations: activities are percentages of each form's own maximum, so the immobilised enzyme may still be less active in absolute terms; only one set of results / no repeats or error bars; only one enzyme and one bead type tested; pH inside the beads may differ from the solution (the bead may buffer the enzyme), so the enzyme itself may not be changed.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: higher % at extremes with data; similar near optimum; relative not absolute values; no repeats / variability; only one enzyme / bead type; microenvironment explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the higher activity of the immobilised enzyme at pH 4.
parts.answer: The alginate gel reduces the effect of H⁺ ions on the enzyme (slower diffusion / buffering / support of its structure), so less change happens to the active site.
parts.working: B1 bead protects / buffers / stabilises tertiary structure.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four fungi (A–D) isolated from soil were grown in broth. Equal volumes of each broth were placed in wells in starch agar. After 24 hours the plates were flooded with iodine solution.
Isolate: A, B, C, D, boiled broth of C
Mean diameter of clear zone / mm: 11, 7, 18, 13, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the isolate that produced the most amylase activity. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Isolate C, because it has the largest mean clear zone (18 mm).
parts.working: B1 C + largest clear zone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result for the control well.
parts.answer: Boiled extract contains denatured amylase, so no starch is hydrolysed and the iodine stains the agar blue-black right up to the well.
parts.working: B1 enzyme denatured, starch not broken down.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the diameter of the clear zone may not be a direct measure of the amount of amylase each isolate produces.
parts.answer: The clear zone also depends on how far the enzyme diffuses (molecule size) and how active each amylase is at the incubation temperature/pH, not only on the amount produced.
parts.working: B1 diffusion / differences in activity per molecule / enzyme type.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measured the rate of a reaction catalysed by trypsin once at each of three temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35
Rate / arbitrary units: 6.0, 10.2, 15.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
parts.answer: Rate increases with temperature from 15 to 35 °C (6.0 to 15.5 units).
parts.working: B1 rate rises with temperature over this range, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student cannot be confident in this conclusion.
parts.answer: Only one reading was taken at each temperature, so anomalies cannot be detected and the variability is unknown; only three temperatures were tested, so the pattern between them is uncertain.
parts.working: B1 single readings / no repeats / no measure of variation. B1 only three temperatures / few data points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two changes that would make the conclusion more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat at each temperature at least three times and calculate a mean (with SD or range); include more temperatures (e.g. 5 or more at 5 °C intervals).
parts.working: 1 mark each: repeats + mean / SD; more temperatures.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Tannery effluent containing chromium flows along a channel near Kasur. Soil samples were taken at different distances from the channel and urease activity was measured.
Distance / m: 0, 50, 100, 200, 400
Chromium / mg kg⁻¹: 850, 420, 160, 60, 25
Urease activity / units: 12, 25, 41, 50, 52

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between chromium concentration and urease activity.
parts.answer: As chromium concentration increases, urease activity decreases (negative correlation): from 52 units at 25 mg kg⁻¹ to 12 units at 850 mg kg⁻¹; the activity changes little below about 60 mg kg⁻¹ (50–52).
parts.working: B1 negative correlation. B1 data quoted / little change at low concentrations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that chromium in the effluent inhibits soil urease. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The data are consistent with inhibition (strong negative correlation), but correlation does not show cause. Other factors change with distance from the channel and could explain the result: soil pH, moisture, organic matter or salt from the effluent, or fewer soil microorganisms (which produce urease) rather than inhibition of the enzyme itself. Only one sample per site and no statistical test. A laboratory test adding chromium to urease (or to clean soil) at controlled pH and temperature would be needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: consistent with / supports; correlation not causation; named confounding variable (pH, moisture, salts, organic matter); fewer microbes producing enzyme, not inhibition; one sample per site / no statistics; suggested controlled lab test.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An extract of germinating barley was diluted to three concentrations. The time for each to hydrolyse all the starch in 5 cm³ of 1 % starch solution was recorded.
Extract concentration / %: 0.5, 1.0, 1.5
Time / s: 125, 80, 64

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction, as 1 ÷ time, for each concentration. Give your answers in s⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 1 ÷ time can be used as a measure of rate.
parts.answer: The same amount of starch is broken down in each tube, so a shorter time means a faster reaction; rate is inversely proportional to time.
parts.working: B1 same end point / amount of reaction, so rate ∝ 1 ÷ time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Catalase activity in guava fruit was 36.4 units when picked and 27.3 units after 10 days in a cold store.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in catalase activity after storage. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: −25.0 % (a decrease of 25.0 %)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second student calculated the change as 33.3 %. Explain the mistake the second student made.
parts.answer: They divided by the stored value (27.3) instead of the original value (36.4): (36.4 − 27.3) ÷ 27.3 × 100 = 33.3 %.
parts.working: B1 used the final value as the base / divided by 27.3.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student makes a serial dilution of a 2.0 % trypsin solution. She transfers 1 cm³ of the stock into 9 cm³ of distilled water and mixes it. She then transfers 1 cm³ of this solution into another 9 cm³ of water, and repeats this once more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of trypsin in each of the three diluted solutions.
parts.working: M1 each step divides by 10. A1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more dilute the third solution is than the stock solution.
parts.answer: 1000 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a clean pipette (or a rinsed one) should be used for each transfer.
parts.answer: So that solution from a more concentrated tube is not carried over, which would make the next solution more concentrated than intended.
parts.working: B1 avoids carry-over / contamination changing concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A spinach-leaf extract was added to hydrogen peroxide. In 90 s, 36 cm³ of oxygen were collected in a gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of oxygen collected. (1 mole of gas occupies 24.0 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the equation 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ to calculate the number of moles of hydrogen peroxide broken down.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of hydrogen peroxide breakdown in mol s⁻¹. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.33 × 10⁻⁵ mol s⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student used starch–iodine standards to make a calibration curve. Over the range tested it was a straight line through the origin:
absorbance = 0.25 × starch concentration (g dm⁻³), valid for absorbance 0 to 1.0
During an amylase reaction, samples gave these absorbances: 0.80 at 0 s and 0.53 at 60 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the starch concentration at 0 s and at 60 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of starch hydrolysis over the first 60 s in g dm⁻³ min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 1.08 g dm⁻³ min⁻¹
parts.working: B1 3.20 − 2.12 = 1.08 g dm⁻³ in 1 minute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the calibration equation can only be used for absorbance readings up to 1.0.
parts.answer: The calibration was only made with standards up to that absorbance; above it the relationship may not be linear, so the equation cannot be extrapolated.
parts.working: B1 outside calibration range / not linear at high absorbance.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student plotted volume of oxygen released by catalase against time and drew two tangents.
Tangent at 10 s passes through (2 s, 1.1 cm³) and (22 s, 4.3 cm³).
Tangent at 60 s passes through (30 s, 7.0 cm³) and (90 s, 9.4 cm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction at 10 s from the first tangent.
parts.answer: 0.16 cm³ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate at 60 s from the second tangent.
parts.answer: 0.04 cm³ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster the reaction was at 10 s than at 60 s, and explain the difference.
parts.answer: 4 times faster; by 60 s much of the substrate has been used, so there are fewer collisions and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes per unit time.
parts.working: B1 0.16 ÷ 0.04 = 4. B1 substrate concentration lower later → fewer E–S complexes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A crude extract containing 2.5 mg of protein produced 180 µmol of product in 4 minutes. After purification, a preparation containing 0.8 mg of protein produced 96 µmol of product in 3 minutes under the same conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the specific activity (µmol of product per minute per mg of protein) of the crude extract and of the purified preparation.
parts.answer: Crude: 18 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹; purified: 40 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times the purification increased the specific activity. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.22 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the specific activity increases when an enzyme is purified.
parts.answer: Other proteins that are not the enzyme are removed, so a greater proportion of each mg of protein is the active enzyme.
parts.working: B1 other (inactive) proteins removed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student is preparing sucrose solutions for an investigation of invertase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sucrose needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.20 mol dm⁻³ solution. (Mr of sucrose = 342)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express this concentration as a percentage (mass per volume, g per 100 cm³). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of the 0.20 mol dm⁻³ solution and of distilled water needed to make 40 cm³ of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: 10 cm³ of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ sucrose + 30 cm³ water

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The temperature coefficient of a reaction over a 10 °C interval = rate at (T + 10) °C ÷ rate at T °C.
The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction was measured at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50
Rate / arbitrary units: 0.84, 1.62, 2.95, 1.10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature coefficient for each 10 °C interval: 20–30 °C, 30–40 °C and 40–50 °C. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the values you calculated for 20–40 °C and for 40–50 °C.
parts.answer: Between 20 and 40 °C the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise (about 1.8–1.9), because molecules gain kinetic energy, collide more often and more collisions exceed the activation energy. Between 40 and 50 °C the value is below 1 (0.37) because the enzyme is being denatured, so the rate falls despite the higher kinetic energy.
parts.working: B1 ~2: more kinetic energy / collisions / E–S complexes. B1 more molecules exceed activation energy. B1 < 1 at 40–50 °C because of denaturation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has a 25 mmol dm⁻³ stock solution of a substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of 25 mmol dm⁻³ substrate and distilled water needed to make 20 cm³ of each of 2.5, 5.0, 7.5 and 10.0 mmol dm⁻³ substrate.
parts.working: M1 volume = concentration ÷ 25 × 20. A1 all four correct with water volumes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of substrate, in µmol, in 5 cm³ of the 10.0 mmol dm⁻³ solution.
parts.answer: 50 µmol
parts.working: B1 10.0 mmol dm⁻³ = 10.0 µmol cm⁻³; × 5 = 50 µmol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After 10 minutes, 60 % of this substrate had been converted to product. Calculate the mean rate of product formation in µmol min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 3.0 µmol min⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this mean rate is lower than the initial rate.
parts.answer: Substrate concentration falls during the reaction, so the rate decreases with time; the mean over 10 minutes includes these slower later rates.
parts.working: B1 substrate used up → rate falls over time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student timed how long a lipase took to change the colour of an indicator in four trials at 35 °C: 42 s, 39 s, 45 s, 40 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of the results.
parts.answer: 39 to 45 s (a range of 6 s)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why calculating a mean from four trials is better than using one trial.
parts.answer: It reduces the effect of random errors and allows anomalous results to be identified.
parts.working: B1 reduces effect of random error / anomalies can be spotted.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Papain from raw papaya digests gelatin. Two gelatin cubes were left in solutions at 35 °C for 2 hours and then blotted and weighed.
Cube in papain: 2.40 g before, 1.62 g after
Cube in boiled papain: 2.36 g before, 1.95 g after

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage loss in mass for each cube. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Cube in papain: 32.5 %; cube in boiled papain: 17.4 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why percentage change in mass is used instead of the change in mass.
parts.answer: The cubes had different starting masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison.
parts.working: B1 different initial masses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cube in boiled papain also lost mass.
parts.answer: Gelatin dissolves / melts slightly in the warm solution even without enzyme (or water loss), so not all mass loss is due to enzyme activity.
parts.working: B1 gelatin dissolves / non-enzyme loss.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A column of immobilised glucose isomerase converts 42 % of the glucose entering it into fructose. Glucose syrup containing 400 g dm⁻³ of glucose flows through the column at 2.5 dm³ min⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of fructose, in kg, produced by the column in one day (24 hours).

parts.label: b
