stem: Glucose released by an enzyme was measured with a reagent that forms a coloured product. Known glucose standards gave a straight calibration line: absorbance = 0.04 + 0.045 × glucose concentration (mmol dm⁻³). Two unknown samples, U1 and U2, gave absorbances of 0.36 and 0.58.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the glucose concentration in U1 and U2. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: U1: 7.1 mmol dm⁻³; U2: 12 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should record both the calibration data and the unknown samples.
parts.answer: Two tables (or two sections): calibration table with columns glucose concentration / mmol dm⁻³ | absorbance (repeats and mean); unknowns table with columns sample | absorbance | glucose concentration from calibration / mmol dm⁻³.
parts.working: B1 calibration table with concentration and absorbance. B1 unknowns table including derived concentration with unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The highest standard used was 10 mmol dm⁻³. Comment on the reliability of the value for U2.
parts.answer: U2 lies outside the range of the standards (extrapolated beyond 10 mmol dm⁻³), so it is less reliable; it should be diluted and re-measured.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will investigate how the concentration of sucrose affects the initial rate of hydrolysis of sucrose by invertase, using sucrose concentrations from 0.5 % to 10 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As sucrose concentration increases, the initial rate of hydrolysis increases, until the rate levels off at high concentrations.
parts.working: B1 directional relationship between the two named variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give a biological reason for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: More substrate molecules give more frequent collisions with active sites and more enzyme–substrate complexes per second; at high concentration all active sites are occupied (saturated), so the rate cannot increase further.
parts.working: B1 collisions / E–S complexes. B1 saturation of active sites explains levelling off.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has two tubes, each containing 5 cm³ of 1 % starch at 35 °C. She adds 1 cm³ of 0.5 % amylase to tube A and 1 cm³ of 1.0 % amylase to tube B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the initial rate of maltose production in tube B will compare with tube A. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: About double, because there are twice as many enzyme molecules / active sites, so twice as many enzyme–substrate complexes form per second (substrate is in excess at the start).
parts.working: B1 about twice as fast. B1 twice as many active sites / E–S complexes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how the total mass of maltose produced when the reactions are complete will compare. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The same in both tubes, because both contain the same mass of starch and enzymes are not used up; the extra enzyme only speeds up the reaction.
parts.working: B1 same. B1 same amount of substrate / enzyme does not change the amount of product.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dihydrofolate reductase is needed by dividing cells to make nucleotides. The anti-cancer drug methotrexate has a shape similar to dihydrofolate, the substrate of the enzyme, and binds reversibly to its active site. A student will measure the rate of the enzyme reaction at low and at high dihydrofolate concentration, each with and without methotrexate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of methotrexate at low and at high dihydrofolate concentration.
parts.answer: At low dihydrofolate concentration methotrexate will greatly reduce the rate; at high dihydrofolate concentration it will have much less effect on the rate.
parts.working: B1 large reduction at low substrate concentration. B1 little effect at high concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Methotrexate is a competitive inhibitor: it binds to the active site and competes with dihydrofolate; at high dihydrofolate concentration substrate molecules greatly outnumber methotrexate, so they occupy most active sites.
parts.working: B1 competes for active site. B1 outnumbered at high substrate concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Statements made by a student planning an investigation into catalase:
1 'Catalase activity is higher in actively growing tissues because they produce more hydrogen peroxide.'
2 'If this is correct, extract from the root tip will release more oxygen in 1 minute than extract from the mature root.'
3 'I will use 5 g of each tissue.'
4 'There will be no significant difference between the mean volumes of oxygen from root tip and mature root extracts.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which statement is: (i) a hypothesis, (ii) a prediction, (iii) a null hypothesis.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a hypothesis and a prediction.
parts.answer: A hypothesis is a testable explanation of how or why something happens; a prediction is the specific result expected in the experiment if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Tyrosinase is an enzyme needed to make the pigment melanin. In a mammal, the allele for normal tyrosinase (T) is dominant to the allele for non-functional tyrosinase (t), which causes albinism. A student will test-cross heterozygous animals (Tt) with albino animals (tt) and use a chi-squared test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the expected ratio of offspring, with a reason.
parts.answer: 1 pigmented : 1 albino, because the Tt parent produces T and t gametes in equal numbers and the tt parent produces only t gametes, giving Tt and tt offspring in equal numbers.
parts.working: B1 1 : 1. B1 reason from gametes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for the chi-squared test.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the observed numbers and the numbers expected from a 1 : 1 ratio (any difference is due to chance).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will measure the activity of pepsin on egg white at pH 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 at 37 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the shape of a graph of activity against pH. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Activity will be highest at about pH 2 (the optimum) and lower at pH 1 and above pH 2, falling to (almost) zero by about pH 6–7; pepsin works in the acidic stomach; away from the optimum the H⁺ concentration changes the ionisation of R groups, altering ionic/hydrogen bonds, so the active site shape changes and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 peak at about pH 2. B1 decrease on both sides, near zero at neutral pH. B1 explanation (R-group charges / bonds / active site shape).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it would be wrong to predict that the graph is symmetrical about the optimum.
parts.answer: Effects of pH on the bonds are not the same on each side of the optimum, and above a certain pH the enzyme may be irreversibly denatured, so the fall need not be symmetrical.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to compare catalase activity in young, expanding leaves and old, fully grown leaves of a guava tree.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation, including a biological reason.
parts.answer: Young leaves have higher catalase activity than old leaves, because their cells are more metabolically active (respiring and growing fast), so they produce more hydrogen peroxide that must be broken down / they synthesise more enzyme.
parts.working: B1 directional comparison. B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what results would support your hypothesis and how you would decide whether any difference is significant.
parts.answer: The mean volume of oxygen per gram of young leaf would be higher than for old leaves; use a t-test on repeated measurements (e.g. 10 leaves of each) and compare the calculated t with the critical value at p = 0.05.
parts.working: B1 expected result expressed per unit mass. B1 t-test with repeats and decision rule.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three tubes of amylase solution are treated as follows before being added to starch at 35 °C:
Tube 1: kept at 35 °C throughout
Tube 2: kept at 5 °C for 20 minutes, then warmed to 35 °C
Tube 3: boiled for 10 minutes, then cooled to 35 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the rate of starch hydrolysis in tubes 2 and 3 compared with tube 1.
parts.answer: Tube 2: about the same as tube 1. Tube 3: no (or almost no) hydrolysis.
parts.working: B1 tube 2 same. B1 tube 3 none.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: At 5 °C the enzyme was only inactive (low kinetic energy) — its structure was not changed, so it works normally when warmed. Boiling broke bonds in the tertiary structure and permanently changed the active site shape (denaturation), so cooling does not restore activity.
parts.working: B1 low temperature reversible / not denatured. B1 boiling denatures irreversibly.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the activity of soil phosphatase at 10 sites along a line running away from a cattle shed, and calculates Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between distance and enzyme activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between distance from the cattle shed and phosphatase activity.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the student would use the value of rs to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: Compare the calculated rs (ignoring the sign) with the critical value for n = 10 at p = 0.05; if it is greater than (or equal to) the critical value, reject the null hypothesis: the correlation is significant.
parts.working: B1 compare with critical value for n = 10, p = 0.05. B1 reject if greater.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why 10 sites is better than 5 sites for this test.
parts.answer: With 5 sites the critical value is very high (only a perfect correlation is significant), so a real correlation might not be detected; more sites give more reliable results.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two enzymes, P and Q, catalyse the same reaction. Enzyme P has Km = 0.5 mmol dm⁻³ and Enzyme Q has Km = 5 mmol dm⁻³. Both have the same Vmax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict which enzyme will give the higher rate at a substrate concentration of 0.2 mmol dm⁻³. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Enzyme P: a lower Km means a higher affinity for the substrate, so P's active sites become occupied at much lower substrate concentrations and P reaches a higher fraction of Vmax.
parts.working: B1 P. B1 low Km = high affinity / half Vmax at lower concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use rate = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]) to calculate each enzyme's rate as a percentage of Vmax at 0.2 mmol dm⁻³. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An enzyme has Vmax = 40 units and Km = 5 mmol dm⁻³. Initial rate = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]). A student has a new inhibitor and two hypotheses:
H1: it is a non-competitive inhibitor that halves Vmax and does not change Km.
H2: it is a competitive inhibitor that raises the apparent Km to 15 mmol dm⁻³ and does not change Vmax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the predicted initial rates at [S] = 1, 5, 20 and 40 mmol dm⁻³ under each hypothesis. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 H1 using Vmax 20 and Km 5. A1 H1 values. A1 H2 values (Vmax 40, Km 15).

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the inhibitor, the measured rates were 3, 10, 22 and 30. State which hypothesis is supported and explain how the results at high substrate concentration distinguish between the two.
parts.answer: H2 (competitive). At high substrate concentration the rate approaches the uninhibited value (30 at 40 mmol dm⁻³, close to the H2 prediction of 29.1 and above the H1 prediction of 17.8), whereas a non-competitive inhibitor would keep the rate at or below 20 however much substrate is added; at low concentrations the two predictions are similar and cannot distinguish them.
parts.working: B1 H2. B1 reasoning based on high-[S] values / maximum rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The rate of a reaction catalysed by a yeast enzyme at 25 °C is 12 units. A student hypothesises that between 25 °C and 40 °C the rate doubles for every 10 °C rise (temperature coefficient Q₁₀ = 2). Rate at T₂ = rate at T₁ × Q₁₀^((T₂ − T₁) ÷ 10).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the predicted rates at 35 °C and at 40 °C. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 35 °C: 24 units; 40 °C: 34 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: The measured rates were 23 units at 35 °C and 26 units at 40 °C. Evaluate the hypothesis using these data.
parts.answer: Supported at 35 °C (23 is close to 24) but not at 40 °C (26 is well below 34); above about 35 °C the rate rises less than predicted, probably because some enzyme molecules are starting to denature, so Q₁₀ = 2 only holds at lower temperatures.
parts.working: B1 35 °C fits, 40 °C does not, with data. B1 explanation: denaturation begins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a prediction for the rate at 60 °C, with a reason.
parts.answer: Much lower than at 40 °C (close to zero), because most of the enzyme molecules will be denatured.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student hypothesised: 'Adding calcium ions increases the activity of a bacterial amylase.' She measured activity (mean ± 2SE, n = 5) at four calcium chloride concentrations:
0 mmol dm⁻³: 20.0 ± 1.6
1 mmol dm⁻³: 24.5 ± 1.8
5 mmol dm⁻³: 25.8 ± 2.0
20 mmol dm⁻³: 21.0 ± 1.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the extent to which the data support the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Partly supported: activity at 1 and 5 mmol dm⁻³ is higher than with no calcium and the intervals do not overlap with 0 mmol dm⁻³ (18.4–21.6 vs 22.7–26.3 and 23.8–27.8), so this increase is significant; but 1 and 5 mmol dm⁻³ overlap, so more calcium beyond 1 mmol dm⁻³ gives no significant further increase; at 20 mmol dm⁻³ activity is not significantly different from 0 (19.3–22.7 overlaps 18.4–21.6), so high concentrations do not increase activity.
parts.working: B1 significant increase at 1 and 5 compared with 0, using intervals. B1 no significant difference between 1 and 5. B1 20 mmol dm⁻³ not different from 0 / hypothesis needs to be limited to low concentrations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a revised hypothesis that fits these data.
parts.answer: Low concentrations of calcium ions (about 1–5 mmol dm⁻³) increase amylase activity, but higher concentrations do not.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: An enzyme has Vmax = 60 µmol min⁻¹ and Km = 4 mmol dm⁻³. Initial rate = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the initial rate at [S] = 2, 4, 12 and 36 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 20, 30, 45, 54 µmol min⁻¹
parts.working: M1 substitution. A1 all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why increasing [S] from 12 to 36 mmol dm⁻³ has less effect on the rate than increasing it from 2 to 4 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: Doubling from 2 to 4 raises the rate by 10 (50 %), but tripling from 12 to 36 raises it by only 9 (20 %); at high [S] most active sites are already occupied, so the rate approaches Vmax and enzyme concentration becomes limiting.
parts.working: B1 comparison using calculated values. B1 active sites near saturation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the effect on Vmax and on Km of doubling the enzyme concentration.
parts.answer: Vmax doubles (120 µmol min⁻¹) because there are twice as many active sites; Km stays the same (4 mmol dm⁻³) because the affinity of each enzyme molecule for the substrate does not change.
parts.working: B1 Vmax doubles. B1 Km unchanged with reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a risk assessment, students must distinguish between a hazard and a risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a hazard and a risk.
parts.answer: A hazard is something that has the potential to cause harm (e.g. a corrosive chemical, hot water); a risk is the likelihood (chance) that harm will actually happen, and how serious it would be, in the way the hazard is used.
parts.working: B1 hazard = potential to cause harm. B1 risk = likelihood/chance of harm (and severity).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student uses 1 % trypsin solution. Give one hazard of trypsin and explain how the risk can be reduced without removing the hazard.
parts.answer: Trypsin is a protein that can cause allergic reactions / is an irritant to skin and eyes (sensitiser); wear gloves and eye protection and avoid splashing or making aerosols, so contact is less likely.
parts.working: B1 hazard. B1 precaution reducing likelihood of exposure.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To prepare potato pieces for a catalase investigation, a student uses a cork borer to cut cylinders from a potato and a scalpel to cut them into discs of equal thickness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard and describe two precautions.
parts.answer: Sharp blades (scalpel and cork borer) can cut the skin. Precautions: cut on a white tile (on a firm surface), cutting away from the body and fingers; push the cork borer down onto the tile rather than towards the hand; carry and store the scalpel with the blade covered/pointing down; never try to catch a falling blade.
parts.working: B1 hazard (cuts from sharp blades). 1 mark each for any two precautions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student tests samples for starch with iodine solution and for reducing sugars by heating samples with Benedict's solution in a water bath at about 90 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one hazard of each reagent and one hazard of the heating, and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Iodine solution: stains and is an irritant to eyes/skin — wear eye protection, wipe up spills. Benedict's solution: contains copper sulfate (harmful/irritant) — wear eye protection/gloves, wash hands. Water bath at 90 °C: scalds / spitting of boiling tubes — use a test-tube holder, point tubes away from people, use an electric water bath rather than a flame.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution, max 3.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A class plans to investigate the effect of pH on salivary amylase, using each student's own saliva collected by spitting into a beaker.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard of using saliva and give two precautions.
parts.answer: Saliva may contain pathogens (risk of spreading infection). Precautions: each student uses only their own saliva; label beakers so they are not mixed up; wash hands; disinfect (e.g. with 1 % Virkon) and dispose of saliva and rinse glassware after use; do not share equipment.
parts.working: B1 hazard. 1 mark each for any two precautions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an alternative to saliva that would remove this hazard.
parts.answer: A commercial amylase solution (fungal or bacterial amylase).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A technician makes up a 1 % amylase solution from powdered enzyme. Enzyme powders are respiratory sensitisers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why enzyme powders are a greater hazard than the dilute enzyme solution.
parts.answer: Fine powder can form dust that is breathed in, which can cause asthma/allergy; the solution cannot be inhaled as dust (unless sprayed).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two precautions the technician should take.
parts.answer: Weigh and dissolve the powder in a fume cupboard or with a dust mask; avoid raising dust (add powder gently to water, do not shake the container); wear gloves and eye protection; clean up spilled powder with a damp cloth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Fungi from soil samples are grown on starch agar plates to find which produce amylase. After incubation, the plates will be flooded with iodine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why soil microorganisms present a hazard.
parts.answer: Soil may contain pathogenic microorganisms (and spores can be released), and culturing increases their numbers.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three precautions that should be taken when growing and handling the cultures.
parts.answer: Use aseptic technique (flame loop, work near a Bunsen flame, sterilised equipment); tape the lid on with two or four short strips (do not seal completely); incubate at 25 °C, not 37 °C, to avoid growing human pathogens; do not open plates after incubation except to add iodine under supervision / in a safety cabinet; autoclave plates before disposal; wash hands.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to measure the rate of oxygen release from 20 vol (6 %) hydrogen peroxide by blended liver, collecting the gas in a 50 cm³ gas syringe connected to a sealed flask.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards specific to this set-up and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hydrogen peroxide at 6 % is an irritant/harmful to eyes and skin — use the lowest concentration that works (e.g. 3 %) and wear eye protection. A fast reaction in a sealed flask may build up pressure, forcing the plunger out of the syringe or the bung out of the flask — use a small volume of extract/peroxide so that the gas produced is less than 50 cm³, and check the syringe moves freely. Raw liver may carry pathogens — wear gloves, wash hands, disinfect surfaces.
parts.working: B1 each hazard (any two). B1 each matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using a lower concentration of hydrogen peroxide reduces the risk but may affect the investigation.
parts.answer: Lower concentration is less irritant and gives less gas; but the rate will be lower, so readings may be smaller and need longer timing.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigates inhibition of urease by copper(II) sulfate and lead(II) nitrate solutions at concentrations up to 0.1 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazards of the inhibitor solutions and describe precautions for using them and for disposing of them.
parts.answer: Lead nitrate is toxic (and may harm an unborn child) and an oxidising agent; copper sulfate is harmful if swallowed and an irritant, and harmful to aquatic life. Use: wear gloves and eye protection, use the lowest concentrations needed, do not pipette by mouth, wash hands, clean spills at once. Disposal: collect waste in a labelled container for heavy-metal waste — do not pour down the sink.
parts.working: B1 lead toxic. B1 copper sulfate harmful/environmental. B1 handling precautions. B1 disposal via waste container, not the drain.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To show denaturation, a student heats amylase solution in a boiling tube in a beaker of boiling water on a hot plate for 10 minutes, and then cools the tube. An electric water bath at 40 °C is on the same bench, near the sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this procedure and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Boiling water / hot glass can scald or burn — use tongs or a test-tube holder, let it cool, stand while working. Tube contents can 'bump' and spit when heated — point the tube away from people, do not fill more than one-third, use anti-bumping granules. Electrical equipment near water — keep the hot plate and water bath away from the sink, dry hands, check cables. Hot plate surface stays hot after use — label it / do not touch.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hazards with matching precautions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to use pectinase to extract juice from mangoes. She will peel and chop the fruit with a kitchen knife, blend it in a food blender, add pectinase solution and leave it at 40 °C. She plans to taste the juice at the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a risk assessment by describing three hazards, the risk from each and a precaution.
parts.answer: Sharp knife and blender blades: cuts — use a chopping board, cut away from fingers, unplug blender before removing blades. Pectinase solution: irritant/allergen — gloves and eye protection. Electrical blender near liquids: shock — keep dry, do not overfill. Warm fruit pulp left for a long time: microbial growth.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with risk and matching precaution, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student must not taste the juice.
parts.answer: Food must never be eaten in a laboratory: the juice and equipment may be contaminated with laboratory chemicals or microorganisms, and the enzyme preparation is not food grade.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student wrote this risk assessment for an experiment on the effect of temperature (20–70 °C) on catalase from celery, using 3 % hydrogen peroxide:
1 'Hydrogen peroxide is dangerous — be careful.'
2 'Celery is a hazard — wear gloves.'
3 'Water baths are hot — risk of burns.'
4 'Overall risk: high, so the experiment should be done by the teacher.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate each statement and suggest a better version.
parts.answer: 1 Too vague: name the hazard (3 % hydrogen peroxide is an irritant to eyes/skin) and the precaution (wear eye protection; rinse with water if splashed). 2 Celery is not a significant hazard (unless allergic); gloves are not needed for celery — they would be sensible for hydrogen peroxide. 3 Identifies hazard but no precaution: use tongs/test-tube holders, keep water at 70 °C or below, do not touch the bath walls. 4 Overestimated: low concentrations and small volumes, with simple precautions, make the overall risk low; students can do it.
parts.working: B1 for each statement evaluated with an improved version.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lipase activity can be followed using milk, sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator. Phenolphthalein is supplied dissolved in ethanol. The tubes are warmed in a water bath at up to 50 °C. A student suggests speeding up warming by holding the tubes over a Bunsen flame.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why heating over a Bunsen flame is unsuitable here.
parts.answer: The phenolphthalein solution contains ethanol, which is highly flammable — the vapour could ignite near a flame; heating directly also gives uneven, uncontrolled temperature (and contents may spit).
parts.working: B1 ethanol flammable. B1 uncontrolled temperature / spitting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two other hazards in this experiment and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Sodium carbonate solution: irritant to eyes — wear eye protection. Lipase solution: allergen/irritant — avoid skin contact, gloves. Phenolphthalein: harmful (possible carcinogen in large amounts) — use only a few drops, avoid contact, wash hands. Hot water bath — tongs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two hazards with precautions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a safer way to warm the tubes.
parts.answer: Use a thermostatically controlled electric water bath (no naked flames), allowing time for tubes to reach the temperature.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Protease activity is measured by the biuret test: biuret reagent contains sodium hydroxide and copper(II) sulfate. The student also uses a centrifuge to remove undigested solid protein before testing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazards of biuret reagent and give precautions, including first aid if it splashes into the eye.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive/irritant to eyes and skin (alkali can cause serious eye damage); copper sulfate is harmful/irritant. Precautions: wear eye protection (goggles), gloves, use small volumes, add reagent carefully. First aid: rinse the eye with plenty of clean running water for at least 10 minutes and get medical help.
parts.working: B1 NaOH corrosive / eye damage. B1 goggles + gloves / small volumes. B1 first aid: flood eye with water for ≥ 10 min, seek help.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two precautions when using the centrifuge.
parts.answer: Balance the tubes (equal masses opposite each other); close the lid before starting and do not open it until the rotor has stopped; use tubes that are not cracked and are capped.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to compare catalase activity in leaves of trees growing beside a busy highway near Islamabad and in a park 1 km away. She will collect the leaves herself, then grind them with sand and test the extracts with 3 % hydrogen peroxide in the school laboratory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify hazards in the fieldwork part of the investigation and give suitable precautions.
parts.answer: Traffic: risk of being hit by vehicles — work away from the road edge, wear a high-visibility vest, go with a partner. Plants (thorns, sap, insects/stinging insects, allergies) — gloves, long sleeves. Air pollution / exhaust fumes — limit time spent near the road. Permission/lone working — tell someone where you are going, get permission from the landowner/park authority.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one hazard in the laboratory part and give a precaution.
parts.answer: Sand and pestle grinding can splash extract/sand into eyes — eye protection; or hydrogen peroxide irritant — goggles; or dust/pollutants on leaves — wash leaves and hands.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a risk assessment should consider people other than the student.
parts.answer: Others nearby (classmates, the public, drivers) could be harmed by the activity, e.g. spills on the floor, broken glass, or a student stepping into traffic, so precautions must protect them too.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the internal structure of a chloroplast is adapted for the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Many thylakoid membranes stacked into grana give a large surface area; they hold the photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase; the small thylakoid space lets a proton gradient build up quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: large surface area of thylakoid membranes / grana; photosystems (chlorophyll) held in membranes; electron transport chain in membrane; ATP synthase in membrane; small volume of thylakoid space for steep H⁺ gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the stroma is adapted for the light-independent stage.
parts.answer: It contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, e.g. rubisco, and surrounds the thylakoids so ATP and reduced NADP diffuse only a short distance to it.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes of Calvin cycle / rubisco in stroma. 1 mark: close to thylakoids, short diffusion distance for ATP and reduced NADP (or contains RuBP / CO₂ dissolved).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why chloroplasts in leaf palisade cells store carbohydrate as starch rather than as glucose.
parts.answer: Starch is insoluble so it does not lower the water potential of the cell / affect osmosis; it is compact and does not leave the chloroplast.
parts.working: 1 mark insoluble / osmotically inactive; 1 mark compact / large store in small space / cannot diffuse out.

stem: Pigments from fenugreek (methi) leaves were separated by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moved 9.5 cm from the origin. A yellow-green spot moved 6.4 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of the yellow-green spot. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front = 6.4 ÷ 9.5 (M1) = 0.67 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carotene has an Rf value of 0.94 in this solvent. Calculate how far carotene moved from the origin. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 8.9 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour of the spots formed by carotene and by chlorophyll a.
parts.answer: Carotene: orange (yellow-orange); chlorophyll a: blue-green.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorophyll a is called the primary pigment. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll a is found in the reaction centre of each photosystem; it is the pigment that is photoactivated and emits electrons, so it converts light energy into chemical energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: in reaction centre (P680/P700). 1 mark: emits (excited) electrons / directly involved in the light reactions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two accessory pigments and state their role.
parts.answer: Any two of chlorophyll b, carotene, xanthophyll; they absorb light of other wavelengths (that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly) and pass the energy to chlorophyll a in the reaction centre.
parts.working: 2 marks for two named accessory pigments; 1 mark for absorbing a wider range of wavelengths and passing energy to the reaction centre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the two regions of the visible spectrum that chlorophyll a absorbs most strongly.
parts.answer: Blue-violet (about 430 nm) and red (about 660 nm).
parts.working: Both needed for 1 mark.

stem: Leaf pigments were spotted at one corner of a square sheet of chromatography paper. Solvent 1 was run up the paper until its front was 10.0 cm from the origin. One spot, X, had moved 6.0 cm and looked brownish-green. The paper was dried, turned through 90° and run in solvent 2, whose front moved 8.0 cm. Spot X split into two spots that had moved 2.4 cm and 5.6 cm in the second direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of spot X in solvent 1 and the Rf values of the two new spots in solvent 2.
parts.answer: Solvent 1: 0.60. Solvent 2: 0.30 and 0.70.
parts.working: M1 for distance ÷ solvent front; A1 for all three values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why spot X contained two pigments but they only separated in solvent 2.
parts.answer: The two pigments had the same (very similar) solubility in solvent 1 and the same attraction to the paper, so they moved together; in solvent 2 their solubilities differ, so they move at different speeds and separate.
parts.working: 1 mark: separation depends on solubility in solvent / adsorption to paper; 1 mark: similar in solvent 1 so same Rf; 1 mark: different in solvent 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the pigment spots must be identified by Rf value rather than by the distance moved.
parts.answer: Distance moved depends on how far the solvent travels, which differs between runs; Rf is a ratio that stays constant for a pigment in a given solvent.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The chlorophyll content of leaves from the sunny top and the shaded base of a large mango tree was measured (mg per g of leaf).
Sun leaves: chlorophyll a 2.4, chlorophyll b 0.8
Shade leaves: chlorophyll a 2.1, chlorophyll b 1.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of chlorophyll a to chlorophyll b for each type of leaf. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Sun leaves 3.0; shade leaves 2.1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorophyll b is found mainly in the light-harvesting (antenna) complexes of the photosystems. Suggest how the lower ratio in shade leaves is an advantage to the tree.
parts.answer: Shade leaves have relatively more light-harvesting pigment around each reaction centre; so they absorb more of the dim light (including wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly); more energy is funnelled to the reaction centres, so the rate of photosynthesis in low light is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: larger antenna / more light harvesting per reaction centre; absorbs wider range / more of the scarce light; more energy passed to chlorophyll a / more photoactivation, so more ATP and reduced NADP in low light.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Chinar (plane) tree leaves in the hills turn orange in autumn. Pigment content (µg per cm² of leaf) was measured every two weeks.
Week: 0, 2, 4, 6
Chlorophyll: 42, 30, 14, 4
Carotenoids: 9.0, 8.4, 7.6, 6.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in chlorophyll and in carotenoids between week 0 and week 6. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll 90.5 %; carotenoids 24.4 %
parts.working: 1 mark each; percentage decrease = (start − end) ÷ start × 100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain why the leaves change colour from green to orange.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll is broken down much faster than carotenoids; green chlorophyll no longer masks the yellow-orange carotenoids, which now absorb blue light and reflect yellow/orange.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorophyll falls faster / carotenoids mostly remain. 1 mark: carotenoids no longer masked so orange colour seen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the rate of photosynthesis of these leaves changes over the six weeks. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: It decreases, because there is much less chlorophyll a (and fewer photosystems) so less light energy is absorbed and fewer electrons are emitted from reaction centres.
parts.working: 1 mark: decreases; 1 mark: less chlorophyll a / reaction-centre pigment so less light absorbed / less ATP and reduced NADP.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three structural features that chloroplasts and mitochondria have in common.
parts.answer: Double membrane (envelope); their own circular DNA; 70S ribosomes; ATP synthase in an internal membrane; an internal fluid with enzymes (stroma / matrix).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two structural differences between a chloroplast and a mitochondrion.
parts.answer: Chloroplast has separate internal thylakoid membranes stacked into grana, while the mitochondrial inner membrane is folded into cristae; chloroplast contains photosynthetic pigments (chlorophyll) and starch grains, mitochondria do not; chloroplasts are usually larger.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid comparative differences (both organelles must be referred to).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ATP synthase in the chloroplast faces the stroma.
parts.answer: Protons are pumped into (and accumulate in) the thylakoid space and flow back through ATP synthase into the stroma; ATP is made on the stroma side, where it is used in the Calvin cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark: H⁺ diffuse from thylakoid space to stroma through ATP synthase; 1 mark: ATP released into stroma where Calvin cycle needs it.

stem: A mutant of a barley plant cannot make chlorophyll b. In bright sunlight it grows almost as fast as normal plants, but in dim light it grows much more slowly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mutant grows more slowly in dim light.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment in the light-harvesting system; it absorbs wavelengths (e.g. about 450–480 nm and 640 nm) that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly; without it less light energy is absorbed and passed to the reaction centres; in dim light, light intensity is the limiting factor, so less photoactivation, less ATP and reduced NADP, a slower Calvin cycle and less growth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: chlorophyll b = accessory pigment / in antenna complex; absorbs other wavelengths; passes energy to chlorophyll a in reaction centre; light is limiting in dim light so rate falls (fewer electrons, less ATP / reduced NADP).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the mutant grows almost normally in bright sunlight.
parts.answer: In bright light there is plenty of light energy even with fewer pigments, so light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature limits the rate in both plants.
parts.working: 1 mark: light not limiting / enough absorbed by chlorophyll a and carotenoids; 1 mark: rate limited by CO₂ / temperature in both.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A filament of a green alga was placed on a microscope slide with aerobic bacteria that move towards oxygen. Light was passed through a prism so that each part of the filament received a different band of wavelengths. After 10 minutes the bacteria next to each part were counted.
400–450 nm: 38 bacteria
450–500 nm: 30 bacteria
500–550 nm: 6 bacteria
550–600 nm: 8 bacteria
600–650 nm: 20 bacteria
650–700 nm: 42 bacteria
700–750 nm: 3 bacteria

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the number of bacteria can be used to compare the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths.
parts.answer: Photosynthesis releases oxygen from photolysis of water; the aerobic bacteria move towards (gather where) oxygen is released, so more bacteria where the rate of photosynthesis is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen made in light-dependent stage / photolysis; 1 mark: bacteria attracted to / cluster at highest O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain why the bacteria were most numerous at 400–450 nm and 650–700 nm and few at 500–550 nm.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll a and b absorb strongly in blue-violet and red light, so most photoactivation and photolysis there; green light (500–550 nm) is absorbed least (mostly reflected/transmitted), only a little by carotenoids, so little oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: blue and red absorbed by chlorophylls; 1 mark: more light absorbed → more electrons/photolysis → more O₂; 1 mark: green poorly absorbed / reflected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The data form a type of spectrum. Name this spectrum and suggest one limitation of the method.
parts.answer: Action spectrum. Limitation: bacteria counts are an indirect measure (bacteria may also respond to light, temperature or nutrients / move slowly / O₂ diffuses between regions, the light bands may differ in intensity).
parts.working: 1 mark: action spectrum; 1 mark: any valid limitation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seedlings were grown on a herbicide that stops the synthesis of carotenoids but not of chlorophyll. In bright light the new leaves were white. In very dim light the new leaves were pale green.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carotenoids protect chlorophyll from damage by excess light energy. Use this information to explain the results.
parts.answer: Without carotenoids, excess absorbed light energy is not dissipated safely; chlorophyll is damaged/destroyed (photo-oxidised) in bright light so the leaves are white; in dim light little excess energy is absorbed, so chlorophyll survives and the leaves are green.
parts.working: 1 mark each: carotenoids normally absorb / remove excess energy (or harmful reactive oxygen); bright light destroys chlorophyll so white; dim light less damage so chlorophyll stays.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effect of the herbicide on the rate of photosynthesis of the pale green leaves, even in dim light.
parts.answer: Rate is lower: carotenoids are accessory pigments that absorb blue-green light (about 450–500 nm) and pass energy to chlorophyll a, so fewer wavelengths are absorbed and less light energy reaches reaction centres.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower rate; 1 mark: carotenoids absorb other wavelengths / pass energy to reaction centre.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A wheat field near Lahore was studied on a clear winter day. The rate of photosynthesis was very low at 07:00 and rose steadily until about 11:00.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three environmental factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Light intensity; carbon dioxide concentration; temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'water' or 'chlorophyll' alone as these are not the three syllabus limiting factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which factor limited the rate at 07:00. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Light intensity; the sun is low in the early morning so little light is absorbed, little ATP and reduced NADP are made, and the rate rises as light increases during the morning.
parts.working: 1 mark: light intensity; 1 mark: low light → little photoactivation / rate rises as light increases.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a sugar beet leaf was measured at 0.04 % CO₂ and two temperatures.
Light intensity / arbitrary units: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Rate at 15 °C: 0, 2.8, 4.6, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0
Rate at 25 °C: 0, 2.8, 5.3, 7.4, 8.1, 8.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the factor limiting the rate at a light intensity of 2 units. Give a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Light intensity; the rate is the same (2.8) at both temperatures, so temperature is not limiting, and the rate rises as light increases.
parts.working: 1 mark light intensity; 1 mark same rate at both temperatures / rate increases with light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the factor limiting the rate at 15 °C and a light intensity of 10 units. Give a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Temperature; the rate has levelled off at 5.0, so more light has no effect, but it is higher (8.1) at 25 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark temperature; 1 mark plateau and higher rate at 25 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the factor limiting the rate at 25 °C and a light intensity of 10 units.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark (accept amount of rubisco / chlorophyll as alternative).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Many vegetable farmers in southern Punjab grow tomatoes in polythene tunnels during winter. Some burn natural gas in heaters inside the tunnels at night and in the early morning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which burning gas inside the tunnel can increase the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: It raises the temperature, so the enzymes of the Calvin cycle (e.g. rubisco) work faster; combustion releases CO₂, which raises the CO₂ concentration for fixation by rubisco.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher temperature / more kinetic energy for enzymes; more CO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On hot afternoons the farmers roll up the sides of the tunnels. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To stop the temperature rising above the optimum (enzymes denature / stomata close); and to let fresh air in so the CO₂ concentration, used up by photosynthesis, does not limit the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: prevents overheating / temperature above optimum; 1 mark: replaces CO₂ used up.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a citrus leaf in bright light was measured at different CO₂ concentrations at 20 °C and 30 °C.
CO₂ / %: 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.09
Rate at 20 °C: 1.5, 4.0, 5.6, 6.0, 6.0
Rate at 30 °C: 1.6, 4.4, 7.1, 9.0, 9.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate when the temperature is raised from 20 °C to 30 °C at 0.07 % CO₂. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why raising the temperature has almost no effect on the rate at 0.01 % CO₂.
parts.answer: At 0.01 % CO₂ the CO₂ concentration is the limiting factor; rubisco can only fix as much CO₂ as is available, so speeding up the enzymes by raising temperature does not increase the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ is limiting; 1 mark: rate depends on CO₂ supply to rubisco, not on enzyme speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate at 20 °C levels off above 0.07 % CO₂.
parts.answer: CO₂ is no longer limiting; temperature now limits, as the Calvin cycle enzymes (rubisco) are working at their maximum rate at 20 °C (enzyme molecules have limited kinetic energy).
parts.working: 1 mark: another factor (temperature) limiting; 1 mark: enzyme rate limited by kinetic energy at 20 °C.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A lettuce grower in Murree covers a greenhouse with shade netting. One layer of netting lets through 60 % of the light falling on it. The rate of photosynthesis of the lettuce leaves (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹) was measured at different light intensities (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹) at 22 °C and normal CO₂:
Light: 0, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200
Rate: −1.0, 6.0, 11.0, 14.0, 15.0, 15.0, 15.0
At midday the light outside the greenhouse is 1800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the light intensity reaching the leaves at midday under one layer of netting and under two layers of netting.
parts.answer: One layer: 1080; two layers: 648 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain why one layer of netting does not reduce the rate of photosynthesis at midday, but two layers do.
parts.answer: With one layer (1080) the light is still above about 800, where the rate has levelled off at 15.0, so light is not the limiting factor (CO₂ or temperature limits); with two layers (648) the light is below 800, on the rising part of the curve (rate about 14), so light becomes the limiting factor and the rate falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate levels off (15.0) from about 800 so light not limiting above this; 1 mark: 1080 is above this so rate unchanged / another factor (CO₂, temperature) limits; 1 mark: 648 is below it so light limits and rate is lower (about 14).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one benefit to the grower of using one layer of netting in summer.
parts.answer: It lowers leaf temperature and water loss (less wilting / stomatal closure, less heat damage) without reducing the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Measurements were made on cotton leaves in a field near Faisalabad on a hot June day.
Time: 06:00, 09:00, 12:00, 15:00, 18:00
Light / µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹: 150, 1200, 2000, 1700, 300
Leaf temperature / °C: 28, 34, 42, 41, 33
Rate of CO₂ uptake / µmol m⁻² s⁻¹: 8, 30, 22, 20, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the factor limiting the rate at 06:00. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Light intensity; it is very low (150) and the rate rises as light increases during the morning.
parts.working: 1 mark factor; 1 mark data-based reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rate at 12:00 is lower than at 09:00 even though the light is brighter. Suggest two explanations.
parts.answer: Leaf temperature (42 °C) is above the optimum, so Calvin cycle enzymes such as rubisco start to denature / lose activity; the leaves lose water in the heat, so stomata partly close, less CO₂ diffuses into the leaf and CO₂ becomes limiting; (also more respiration at high temperature reduces net uptake).
parts.working: 2 marks per explanation: cause (high temperature / stomatal closure / respiration) + effect on photosynthesis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why raising the temperature from 15 °C to 25 °C has little effect on the rate of photosynthesis in dim light but a large effect in bright light.
parts.answer: In dim light, light intensity is limiting: the light-dependent stage makes little ATP and reduced NADP, and the photochemical reactions are hardly affected by temperature, so warming has little effect. In bright light, ATP and reduced NADP are plentiful and the rate is limited by the enzyme-controlled Calvin cycle; higher temperature gives rubisco and other enzymes more kinetic energy, more enzyme–substrate complexes, so the rate rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: dim light – light limiting; 1 mark: light absorption / photoactivation not temperature dependent / ATP & reduced NADP supply limits; 1 mark: bright light – Calvin cycle (enzyme) limiting; 1 mark: more kinetic energy → more successful collisions / ESCs.

stem:
Oxygen released by a piece of Elodea was collected for 10 minutes under five conditions.
A: low light, 0.01 % CO₂, 20 °C – 0.40 cm³
B: high light, 0.01 % CO₂, 20 °C – 0.42 cm³
C: high light, 0.05 % CO₂, 20 °C – 1.10 cm³
D: high light, 0.05 % CO₂, 30 °C – 1.65 cm³
E: low light, 0.05 % CO₂, 30 °C – 0.44 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen release in condition C in mm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 110 mm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use conditions A, B and C to identify the factor limiting the rate in condition A. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: CO₂ concentration. Raising light (A → B) hardly changes the rate (0.40 → 0.42 cm³), so light is not limiting; raising CO₂ in high light (B → C) greatly increases it, so CO₂ was limiting in B and, since A and B are almost the same, in A as well.
parts.working: 1 mark CO₂; 1 mark A vs B comparison; 1 mark B vs C comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use conditions C, D and E to identify the factors limiting the rate in conditions C and E.
parts.answer: C: temperature (raising temperature from 20 °C to 30 °C in D increases the rate from 1.10 to 1.65 cm³). E: light intensity (E has the same CO₂ and temperature as D but much lower rate).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An indoor vertical farm in Islamabad grows lettuce under LED lights. The rate of photosynthesis (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹) was measured at 22 °C.
Light 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, CO₂ 400 ppm: 8.2
Light 400, CO₂ 400 ppm: 11.0
Light 400, CO₂ 1000 ppm: 14.6
Light 200, CO₂ 1000 ppm: 9.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate (i) when light is doubled at 400 ppm CO₂, (ii) when CO₂ is raised to 1000 ppm at light 400, and (iii) when CO₂ is raised to 1000 ppm at light 200. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why raising the CO₂ concentration has a much smaller effect at light 200 than at light 400.
parts.answer: At light 200, light intensity is the main limiting factor; the light-dependent stage supplies only a little ATP and reduced NADP; so GP cannot be reduced and RuBP regenerated faster, and extra CO₂ cannot be fixed much faster. At light 400 more ATP and reduced NADP are available, so CO₂ becomes limiting and extra CO₂ raises the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: light limiting at 200; 1 mark: ATP / reduced NADP supply restricts Calvin cycle (RuBP regeneration); 1 mark: at 400 CO₂ limiting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The farm currently runs at light 200 and 400 ppm. Suggest which single change the manager should make first, giving a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Increase the light intensity: it gives a 34.1 % increase compared with only 9.8 % for adding CO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark for choice with comparison of data (also accept discussion of electricity cost against yield).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A plant was kept at a very low CO₂ concentration (0.005 %) and 25 °C. The light intensity was increased in steps, but the rate of photosynthesis did not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the light-independent stage, why increasing the light intensity did not increase the rate.
parts.answer: CO₂ is the limiting factor; rubisco can only fix a little CO₂ with RuBP, so little GP is formed; only a little ATP and reduced NADP are therefore used to reduce GP to triose phosphate; ADP and NADP are not regenerated fast enough, so extra light cannot increase the light-dependent stage either; RuBP accumulates because it is regenerated but not used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: CO₂ limiting; little CO₂ fixed by rubisco / little GP; little ATP and reduced NADP used; NADP / ADP not regenerated so light-dependent stage cannot go faster; RuBP builds up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of raising the CO₂ concentration to 0.04 % at the highest light intensity used.
parts.answer: The rate would increase (because CO₂ is no longer limiting at that light intensity).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Microalgae are grown for biofuel in shallow outdoor ponds. In a dense culture the light intensity (arbitrary units) fell with depth:
Surface: 1800; 5 cm: 450; 10 cm: 110; 15 cm: 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the light intensity at 10 cm as a percentage of the surface value. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis per cell is much lower at 15 cm than near the surface.
parts.answer: Light intensity is very low at 15 cm because cells above absorb (shade) the light; light is the limiting factor, so less photoactivation, less ATP and reduced NADP, and a slower Calvin cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-shading / light absorbed by cells above; 1 mark: light limiting → less ATP / reduced NADP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The ponds are kept shallow (about 25 cm) and the water is kept moving by paddle wheels. Suggest two reasons why the paddles increase the total yield.
parts.answer: Cells are moved between the dark depths and the bright surface, so all cells get some light; mixing spreads dissolved CO₂ (and nutrients) so CO₂ does not become limiting near the surface; it stops cells settling or overheating at the surface.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Five statements describe events in non-cyclic photophosphorylation, in the wrong order.
P: light energy is absorbed by photosystem II
Q: excited electrons pass to an electron acceptor and then along a chain of electron carriers
R: energy released by the electrons is used to pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space
S: the electrons are excited again at photosystem I
T: the electrons combine with NADP and H⁺ to form reduced NADP

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the letters in the correct order.
parts.answer: P, Q, R, S, T
parts.working: 1 mark for the full correct sequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the source of the electrons that replace those lost from photosystem II.
parts.answer: Water, split by photolysis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the enzyme that uses the H⁺ gradient produced in R, and state its product.
parts.answer: ATP synthase; ATP (from ADP and inorganic phosphate).
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'ATPase'.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the precise location of the light-dependent stage in a chloroplast.
parts.answer: The thylakoid membranes (of the grana and intergranal lamellae).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three products of non-cyclic photophosphorylation and state what happens to each.
parts.answer: ATP – used in the Calvin cycle (to reduce GP and regenerate RuBP); reduced NADP – used to reduce GP to triose phosphate; oxygen – diffuses out of the leaf (or is used in respiration).
parts.working: 1 mark for each product with its fate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the light-dependent stage stops if the supply of NADP runs out.
parts.answer: NADP is the final electron acceptor; without it electrons cannot leave photosystem I, so the carriers stay reduced and electron flow (and photolysis) stops.
parts.working: 1 mark final electron acceptor; 1 mark electron flow stops / no more electrons accepted from PSII / no photolysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.answer: Only photosystem I is involved; light excites electrons in the reaction centre chlorophyll of PSI; they pass to an electron acceptor and along electron carriers; they return to PSI (not to NADP); energy released pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space and ATP is made by ATP synthase (chemiosmosis).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the listed points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one product of non-cyclic photophosphorylation that is not made by cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.answer: Reduced NADP (or oxygen).
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem:
Two cultures of a green alga were given water and carbon dioxide containing different isotopes of oxygen. ¹⁸O is a heavy, non-radioactive isotope.
Culture 1: water labelled with ¹⁸O, normal CO₂ – the oxygen gas released contained ¹⁸O
Culture 2: normal water, CO₂ labelled with ¹⁸O – the oxygen gas released contained almost no ¹⁸O

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what these results show about the source of the oxygen released in photosynthesis.
parts.answer: It comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process that releases this oxygen and state where it happens.
parts.answer: Photolysis of water; at photosystem II, on the thylakoid-space (lumen) side of the thylakoid membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest where the ¹⁸O from the labelled CO₂ in culture 2 would be found after an hour of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: In organic compounds made in the Calvin cycle, e.g. GP, triose phosphate, sugars / starch (and some in water).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The herbicide DCMU binds to a protein in photosystem II and stops electrons passing from photosystem II to the electron transport chain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of DCMU on the release of oxygen by a leaf in light.
parts.answer: Oxygen release stops; photosystem II cannot pass on its electrons, so it cannot accept new electrons from water and photolysis stops.
parts.working: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why DCMU stops the production of reduced NADP.
parts.answer: Electrons reaching NADP come from photosystem II via photosystem I in non-cyclic flow; with no electrons flowing from PSII, PSI has no replacement electrons for NADP.
parts.working: 1 mark: electrons for NADP come from PSII/water; 1 mark: none reach PSI to replace those given to NADP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a little ATP can still be made in DCMU-treated chloroplasts in light, but the plant still dies.
parts.answer: Cyclic photophosphorylation around photosystem I still works, making ATP; but there is no reduced NADP, so GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate – no sugars are made and the plant starves.
parts.working: 1 mark cyclic photophosphorylation continues; 1 mark no reduced NADP → Calvin cycle stops / no carbohydrate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Paraquat is a herbicide that takes electrons from photosystem I before they can reach NADP. It then passes them to oxygen, making reactive substances that damage membranes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of paraquat on the production of reduced NADP. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Reduced NADP production falls / stops, because the electrons are diverted to paraquat instead of to NADP (via NADP reductase).
parts.working: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why oxygen release by photolysis may continue for a time after paraquat is applied.
parts.answer: Electrons still flow from PSII to PSI and on to paraquat, so PSII keeps losing electrons and water keeps being split to replace them.
parts.working: 1 mark electron flow continues (paraquat is an electron acceptor); 1 mark PSII electrons replaced by photolysis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why paraquat kills leaves faster in bright light than in dim light.
parts.answer: More light means more electron flow, so more electrons reach paraquat and more damaging reactive substances are made.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In non-cyclic photophosphorylation, assume that each electron moving from water to NADP needs one photon absorbed at photosystem II and one photon absorbed at photosystem I. Two electrons are needed to reduce one molecule of NADP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation for photolysis is 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. Calculate the number of photons needed to release one molecule of oxygen.
parts.answer: 8 photons
parts.working: 4 electrons per O₂ (M1); 4 × 2 photons = 8 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Making one molecule of glucose in the Calvin cycle uses 12 molecules of reduced NADP. Calculate the minimum number of photons absorbed by non-cyclic photophosphorylation to supply this reduced NADP.
parts.answer: 48 photons
parts.working: 12 × 2 = 24 electrons (M1); 24 × 2 = 48 photons (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the true number of photons absorbed per glucose is higher than your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Extra ATP is needed (the Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP per 2 reduced NADP), so some cyclic photophosphorylation also absorbs photons; some absorbed energy is lost as heat / fluorescence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: extra ATP via cyclic; energy losses (heat/fluorescence); some light absorbed by pigments not transferred to reaction centres.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three ways in which the light-dependent stage makes the H⁺ concentration in the thylakoid space higher than in the stroma.
parts.answer: Photolysis of water releases H⁺ inside the thylakoid space; energy from electrons moving along the electron transport chain is used to pump H⁺ from the stroma into the thylakoid space; H⁺ are removed from the stroma when NADP is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this H⁺ gradient is used to make ATP.
parts.answer: H⁺ diffuse down their concentration (electrochemical) gradient from the thylakoid space into the stroma through ATP synthase; this flow drives the enzyme to join ADP and Pi (chemiosmosis).
parts.working: 1 mark facilitated diffusion through ATP synthase; 1 mark ADP + Pi → ATP / chemiosmosis.

stem:
Rates of oxygen release by a suspension of green algal cells were measured under three light treatments of equal total intensity.
Light of 680 nm only: 6.0 units
Light of 710 nm only: 2.0 units
680 nm and 710 nm together: 11.2 units
Photosystem II absorbs strongly up to about 680 nm; photosystem I also absorbs at longer wavelengths up to about 710 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the rate with both wavelengths together to the sum of the rates with each wavelength alone. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate with 710 nm light alone is so low.
parts.answer: 710 nm light excites mainly photosystem I; photosystem II is hardly activated, so there is little photolysis and little non-cyclic electron flow (mainly cyclic, which releases no oxygen).
parts.working: 1 mark PSI only activated; 1 mark little PSII activity / photolysis so little O₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate with both wavelengths together is greater than the sum of the separate rates.
parts.answer: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation needs both photosystems working together in series; with both wavelengths, PSII and PSI are both excited, so electrons flow from water through both photosystems to NADP at a much faster rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: two photosystems work in series; 1 mark: both activated together → full non-cyclic flow / more photolysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A suspension of isolated thylakoids (total volume 2.0 cm³, containing 0.05 mg chlorophyll) was placed in an oxygen electrode with potassium ferricyanide, an artificial electron acceptor. No NADP was present. The light was switched on at 1 minute.
Time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Oxygen / µmol dm⁻³: 250, 250, 268, 286, 304

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen release in µmol dm⁻³ per minute after the light was switched on.
parts.answer: 18 µmol dm⁻³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen release in µmol per mg chlorophyll per hour. (1 cm³ = 0.001 dm³)
parts.answer: 43.2 µmol per mg chlorophyll per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why oxygen was released even though there was no NADP, and predict what would happen without ferricyanide.
parts.answer: Ferricyanide accepts electrons in place of NADP (it is reduced), so electrons keep flowing from PSII and water keeps being split, releasing oxygen. Without it, the electron carriers would quickly all become reduced, electron flow and photolysis would stop, and oxygen release would stop almost at once.
parts.working: 1 mark ferricyanide = electron acceptor; 1 mark electron flow / photolysis continues; 1 mark prediction with reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare chemiosmosis in the thylakoid membrane of a chloroplast with chemiosmosis in the inner membrane of a mitochondrion. Give one similarity and three differences.
parts.answer: Similarity: in both, electrons passing along an electron transport chain release energy to pump H⁺ across a membrane, and H⁺ flow back through ATP synthase to make ATP. Differences: source of energy – light (photoactivated chlorophyll) in chloroplasts, oxidation of reduced NAD/FAD in mitochondria; H⁺ are pumped into the thylakoid space in chloroplasts but into the intermembrane space in mitochondria; final electron acceptor – NADP in chloroplasts, oxygen in mitochondria; ATP is made in the stroma vs in the matrix; water is split in chloroplasts but formed in mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid similarity; 1 mark each for any three comparative differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP made in the chloroplast is not the main source of ATP for active transport in a root hair cell.
parts.answer: Root hair cells have no chloroplasts (no light underground); chloroplast ATP is used in the Calvin cycle in the stroma, and ATP for the rest of the cell comes from respiration in mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A suspension of algal cells in bright light was given carbon dioxide containing radioactive carbon (¹⁴CO₂). Samples were killed in hot ethanol after different times and the radioactive compounds were identified.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After 2 seconds almost all of the radioactivity was in one compound. Name this compound and explain why it is labelled first.
parts.answer: Glycerate 3-phosphate (GP); CO₂ combines with RuBP (catalysed by rubisco) and the 6C product immediately splits into two molecules of GP.
parts.working: 1 mark GP; 1 mark explanation (carbon fixation by rubisco).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the samples were killed in hot ethanol.
parts.answer: To denature the enzymes immediately, so the reactions stop at that exact time.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one compound that would become radioactive later than the compound in (a).
parts.answer: Triose phosphate (then hexose / sucrose / starch / RuBP / amino acids).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two stages of the Calvin cycle that use ATP.
parts.answer: Reduction of GP to triose phosphate; regeneration of RuBP from triose phosphate.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the stage that uses reduced NADP and the role of reduced NADP in it.
parts.answer: Reduction of GP to triose phosphate; it provides hydrogen (electrons) to reduce GP.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the NADP and ADP made in the Calvin cycle.
parts.answer: They return (diffuse) to the thylakoids to be reduced / phosphorylated again in the light-dependent stage.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: This question is about six turns of the Calvin cycle, in which six molecules of CO₂ are fixed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many molecules of RuBP combine with CO₂.
parts.working: One RuBP per CO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many molecules of GP and of triose phosphate are formed.
parts.answer: GP 12; triose phosphate 12
parts.working: Each 6C intermediate gives 2 GP; each GP is reduced to one triose phosphate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ten of the triose phosphate molecules are used to regenerate RuBP. Show by counting carbon atoms that this is enough to regenerate all the RuBP used.
parts.answer: 10 × 3 = 30 carbon atoms; 6 RuBP × 5 = 30 carbon atoms, so the numbers match.
parts.working: 1 mark each calculation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what the other two triose phosphate molecules can be used to make.
parts.answer: One molecule of a hexose (e.g. glucose), which can be made into sucrose, starch or cellulose.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the following word equation for carbon fixation: ribulose bisphosphate + carbon dioxide → ……
parts.answer: Two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) (via an unstable 6C intermediate).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the chloroplast carbon fixation takes place.
parts.answer: The stroma.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Calvin cycle is called the light-independent stage even though it stops within a minute of darkness.
parts.answer: Its reactions do not use light directly; but they need ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage, which stop being made in the dark, so the cycle soon stops.
parts.working: 1 mark no direct use of light; 1 mark depends on ATP / reduced NADP from light-dependent stage.

stem: A spinach leaf of mass 2.4 g contains 18 mg of soluble protein per gram of leaf. Rubisco makes up 25 % of this soluble protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of rubisco in the whole leaf. Give your answer in mg to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rubisco catalyses only a few reactions per second, which is very slow for an enzyme. Suggest why leaves contain such a large amount of rubisco.
parts.answer: Each molecule fixes CO₂ slowly, so a very large number of rubisco molecules is needed to fix CO₂ fast enough to keep up with the ATP and reduced NADP made in bright light (and to make enough sugar for growth).
parts.working: 1 mark: low turnover so many molecules needed; 1 mark: to achieve a high overall rate of CO₂ fixation / match the light-dependent stage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why plants that are short of nitrate fix less carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and so proteins such as rubisco; less rubisco means less CO₂ fixation.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A potato tuber stores 120 g of starch. Treat the starch as glucose units (C₆H₁₀O₅, Mr 162). Fixing one molecule of CO₂ and regenerating RuBP uses 3 ATP and 2 reduced NADP. Ignore any ATP used to join the glucose units together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of glucose units in the stored starch. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ fixed, ATP used and reduced NADP used in the Calvin cycle to make this starch. Give each answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: CO₂ 4.44 mol; ATP 13.3 mol; reduced NADP 8.89 mol
parts.working: 6 CO₂ per glucose unit: 0.7407 × 6 = 4.44 (1 mark); × 3 = 13.3 ATP (1 mark); × 2 = 8.89 reduced NADP (1 mark). Allow follow-through from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The starch is made in the tuber from sucrose that was carried from the leaves. Suggest why triose phosphate is converted to sucrose rather than to glucose for transport.
parts.answer: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so it is less reactive and is not used up (respired) on the way; it is soluble so it can be carried in phloem sap without being used by the cells it passes.
parts.working: 1 mark non-reducing / less reactive / not metabolised in transit; 1 mark soluble / transported in phloem.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Leaves in bright light were treated with a substance that inhibits the enzyme that converts GP to triose phosphate. Light and CO₂ supply were not changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the changes in the concentrations of GP, triose phosphate and RuBP in the next few minutes.
parts.answer: GP rises, because it is still made from RuBP and CO₂ but cannot be converted; triose phosphate falls, because it is no longer made but is still used (to regenerate RuBP, make sugars); RuBP falls, because it is still used to fix CO₂ but cannot be regenerated without triose phosphate.
parts.working: 1 mark for all three predictions; 1 mark each for explanations of GP, triose phosphate and RuBP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the concentration of reduced NADP in the stroma. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: It rises, because reduced NADP is used only in the reduction of GP, which has stopped, while the light-dependent stage keeps making it (until NADP runs out).
parts.working: 1 mark rise; 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Triose phosphate made in the Calvin cycle can be used to make many organic compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two carbohydrates made from triose phosphate and state the use of each in a plant.
parts.answer: Any two of: sucrose – transport in phloem; starch – energy store; cellulose – cell walls; glucose – respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each named carbohydrate with a correct use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Triose phosphate can be used to make amino acids and lipids. State one other substance (or element) the plant needs to make amino acids, and name the two parts of a triglyceride that triose phosphate can form.
parts.answer: Nitrogen as nitrate (or ammonium) ions (also sulfur for some amino acids); glycerol and fatty acids.
parts.working: 1 mark nitrate / nitrogen; 1 mark each for glycerol and fatty acids.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Making one mole of glucose in the Calvin cycle uses 18 moles of ATP and 12 moles of reduced NADP. Hydrolysis of one mole of ATP releases 30.5 kJ. Oxidation of one mole of reduced NADP releases 220 kJ. Complete oxidation of one mole of glucose releases 2870 kJ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy supplied by ATP and reduced NADP to make one mole of glucose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency with which this energy is stored in glucose. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The overall efficiency of photosynthesis, from light energy reaching a leaf to energy in glucose, is much lower than your answer to (b). Suggest three reasons.
parts.answer: Some light is reflected, transmitted or hits non-photosynthetic parts; only certain wavelengths are absorbed (green poorly); energy is lost as heat in electron transport and ATP synthesis; some glucose is used in respiration; other factors (CO₂, temperature) limit the rate so not all light is used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Algal cells in light were given ¹⁴CO₂ for 2 seconds and then transferred to normal CO₂ (a pulse–chase experiment). The percentage of the total radioactivity in four groups of compounds was measured.
Time after start / s: 2, 5, 10, 30, 60
GP: 85, 60, 40, 20, 12
Triose phosphate: 10, 25, 30, 25, 18
RuBP: 0, 5, 12, 20, 20
Hexose phosphates and sucrose: 5, 10, 18, 35, 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the radioactivity that was not in GP at 10 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the data show the order in which these compounds are made.
parts.answer: GP has most label first (85 % at 2 s), so it is the first product of fixation; triose phosphate rises next (peak about 10 s) as GP is reduced; label in sugars rises steadily later (to 50 %) and RuBP becomes labelled only after triose phosphate, so both are made from triose phosphate.
parts.working: 1 mark GP first; 1 mark TP second / intermediate; 1 mark sugars and RuBP last, made from TP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the percentage in GP falls after 2 seconds even though fixation continues.
parts.answer: No more ¹⁴CO₂ is supplied (chase with unlabelled CO₂), so new GP is unlabelled; labelled GP is converted to triose phosphate and then to other compounds.
parts.working: 1 mark: new GP is unlabelled; 1 mark: labelled GP is used up / converted.

author: HomiLabs

stem: During a drought, the stomata of a wheat crop close for much of the day while the leaves are still brightly lit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why stomatal closure reduces the rate of the Calvin cycle.
parts.answer: Less CO₂ diffuses into the leaf, so the CO₂ concentration in the air spaces and stroma falls; rubisco fixes less CO₂ with RuBP, so less GP and triose phosphate are formed.
parts.working: 1 mark less CO₂ enters; 1 mark less fixation by rubisco / less GP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a slower Calvin cycle affects non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
