parts.answer: Use an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid; use a thermometer reading to 0.1 °C or a digital temperature probe; read at eye level; stir before reading.
parts.working: 1 mark each, matched to errors in (a).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student forgot to set the colorimeter to zero with a blank before measuring absorbances of starch–iodine standards and samples. All readings were 0.08 too high. State whether this is a random or a systematic error and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Systematic error; because it shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction (rather than varying unpredictably).
parts.working: B1 systematic; B1 same amount/direction for every reading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether this error would affect the starch concentrations of the samples read from her calibration curve.
parts.answer: No (or very little): the standards and the samples were all shifted by the same 0.08, so the calibration curve is shifted by the same amount and the samples are read against it correctly; it would matter if the standards and samples were measured at different times with different zero errors.
parts.working: B1 no effect / cancels; B1 because standards and samples shifted equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the emulsion test, a student measured the cloudiness of each tube with a colorimeter. She found that the absorbance of the same tube fell from 0.62 to 0.48 over 10 minutes. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Small lipid droplets join together (coalesce) into larger droplets and rise to the surface, so the emulsion becomes less cloudy in the light path over time.
parts.working: B1 droplets coalesce/separate; B1 rise to surface → less turbidity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this would affect the comparison of different samples, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: If samples are read at different times after mixing, readings are not comparable (later readings lower); read every tube at the same fixed time (e.g. exactly 1 minute) after mixing, mixing in the same way.
parts.working: B1 effect; B1 fixed reading time improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student heated water and recorded a start temperature of 21.0 °C and a final temperature of 25.0 °C with a thermometer that has an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C for each reading. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise.
parts.working: temperature rise = 4.0 °C; total uncertainty = 2 × 0.5 = ±1.0 °C (M1); 1.0/4.0 × 100 = 25 % (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to reduce this percentage uncertainty.
parts.answer: Use a thermometer/temperature probe with a smaller uncertainty (e.g. ±0.1 °C); heat for longer (or use a smaller mass) so the temperature rise is larger.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Students compared how long gelatin took to set in a fridge after adding different fruit extracts. Each student tilted their tube 'every so often' and decided when it had set. Identify two sources of error in this method.
parts.answer: End-point is subjective (different students judge 'set' differently); checking interval not fixed, so set time not known precisely; opening the fridge changes temperature; tubes in different positions in the fridge at different temperatures.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the end-point could be made more objective.
parts.answer: Define setting as when the gelatin does not move when the tube is tilted to 45° (or tipped horizontal) for 5 seconds, checking every minute; or measure time for a small ball bearing to sink through it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wanted to compare the starch content of two potatoes. She cut one small cube from the skin end of potato A and one from the centre of potato B, crushed each in water and tested with iodine using a colorimeter. Explain two reasons why her comparison may not be valid.
parts.answer: Starch is not evenly distributed in a potato (the centre may contain more/less than the outer region), so different parts are not comparable; only one sample from each potato, so not representative; cubes may not be equal mass.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Starch grains settle to the bottom of a suspension. Explain how this could cause error and how to prevent it.
parts.answer: Samples taken from the top of a settled suspension contain less starch than those from the bottom; stir/shake the suspension immediately before taking each sample (or boil to dissolve starch).
parts.working: B1 error; B1 improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two methods were used to measure the lipid content (%) of the same batch of sesame seed flour, five times each:
method 1: 12.1, 12.6, 11.8, 12.4, 12.2
method 2: 10.9, 13.6, 11.2, 14.0, 12.4
Calculate the mean and the standard deviation (using n − 1) for each method. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: method 1: mean 12.22, SD 0.30; method 2: mean 12.42, SD 1.39
parts.working: means (B1); SD formula s = √[Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)] used (M1); SDs 0.30 and 1.39 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to compare the reliability (precision) of the two methods.
parts.answer: The means are almost the same (12.22 and 12.42), but method 2 has a much larger SD (1.39 vs 0.30), so its readings are more spread out; method 1 is more precise/repeatable.
parts.working: B1 similar means; B1 method 1 smaller SD → more precise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student needs to dilute a juice 1 in 100. Method X: add 0.10 cm³ of juice (pipette uncertainty ±0.01 cm³) to 9.90 cm³ of water. Method Y: two 1 in 10 dilutions, each made by adding 1.00 cm³ (uncertainty ±0.01 cm³) to 9.00 cm³ of water. Ignoring the uncertainty in the water volumes, calculate the percentage uncertainty of each method.
parts.answer: Method X: 10 %; method Y: 2 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which method is better and suggest one further way to reduce error in method Y.
parts.answer: Method Y, because larger volumes are measured so the percentage error is smaller; mix thoroughly at each step before transferring, and use a clean pipette for each transfer (or use calibrated volumetric glassware).
parts.working: B1 Y with reason; B1 improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student used the biuret test and a colorimeter to compare the protein content of grape juice, apple juice and beetroot juice. The grape and beetroot juices are strongly coloured. Explain why this could give inaccurate results.
parts.answer: The natural pigments absorb light themselves, so absorbance is higher than that due to the biuret colour alone; this overestimates protein in the coloured juices.
parts.working: B1 pigments absorb light; B1 overestimates protein.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many plant pigments change colour when the pH changes. Suggest why this makes the error harder to correct, and describe a suitable blank for each juice.
parts.answer: Biuret reagent is alkaline, so the pigment's colour (and absorbance) in the test tube differs from its colour in the juice alone; a blank for each juice should contain the same volume of that juice plus the same volume of sodium hydroxide solution (same pH) but no copper sulfate (made up with water); zero the colorimeter with this blank before reading that juice.
parts.working: B1 alkaline reagent changes pigment colour; B1 blank contains juice + NaOH (no CuSO₄); B1 zero with that juice's own blank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigated whether storing potatoes in a fridge makes them sweeter. She bought one potato on Monday and stored it in the fridge, bought a different potato on Friday, and on Friday cut a slice from each, crushed it and compared the colours of the Benedict's test by eye. Identify three significant sources of error in her procedure and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: 1 Potatoes may differ in variety/age/initial sugar content → use potatoes of the same variety from the same batch, and test some at the start (day 0) as a baseline. 2 Only one potato per treatment → use at least five potatoes per treatment and calculate means. 3 Fridge temperature unknown and room-storage control not stated → measure fridge temperature with a thermometer and store a control group at room temperature for the same time. 4 Slices not standardised (mass, part of potato) → use the same mass from the same region, crushed in the same volume of water. 5 Colour judged by eye → use a colorimeter or glucose colour standards.
parts.working: For each of three errors: 1 mark for the error, 1 mark for a matching improvement (max 6).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The starch content of potatoes fell from 18.5 g per 100 g to 14.2 g per 100 g during three weeks of cold storage. Calculate the percentage decrease. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what happened to the starch.
parts.answer: It was hydrolysed into sugars (e.g. reducing sugars such as glucose).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.5 % (mass per volume) glucose solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose (Mr 180) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ glucose solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has a 2.0 % sucrose solution. Calculate the volumes of this solution and of distilled water needed to make 20 cm³ of 0.3 % sucrose solution.
parts.answer: 3.0 cm³ of 2.0 % sucrose + 17.0 cm³ water

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the apparatus that should be used to measure these volumes accurately.
parts.answer: A graduated pipette or syringe (or burette) for each volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The time for a glucose solution to show the first colour change in the Benedict's test was measured five times: 48 s, 52 s, 50 s, 55 s, 49 s. Calculate the mean time and the range.
parts.answer: mean 50.8 s; range 7 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction as 1/mean time, in s⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When amylase was added to starch, the reducing sugar concentration rose from 0.9 mg cm⁻³ to 3.6 mg cm⁻³ in 15 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of reducing sugar production, in mg cm⁻³ min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 0.18 mg cm⁻³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this mean rate is likely to be lower than the initial rate.
parts.answer: The rate falls as starch (substrate) is used up, so the mean over 15 minutes includes slower later rates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A short chain of 5 α-glucose molecules is formed during starch digestion. Calculate its Mr. (Mr glucose 180, water 18.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water, in g, needed to hydrolyse 0.20 mol of this chain completely into glucose.
parts.working: 4 water per chain → 0.20 × 4 = 0.80 mol water (M1); × 18 = 14.4 g (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert a 0.25 mol dm⁻³ glucose solution (Mr 180) into a concentration in g dm⁻³ and in % (g per 100 cm³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, of a 1.5 % sucrose solution (Mr 342). Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.044 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.5 g of powdered masoor daal was shaken with water and made up to 25 cm³ of extract. The extract was diluted 1 in 4, and the diluted extract was found from a biuret calibration curve to contain 1.2 mg cm⁻³ of protein. Calculate the mass of protein, in mg, in the 25 cm³ of extract.
parts.answer: 120 mg
parts.working: 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 mg cm⁻³ in extract (M1); × 25 = 120 mg (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of protein in the daal powder, assuming all the protein was extracted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the true percentage is likely to be higher than the value calculated.
parts.answer: Not all the protein dissolves/is extracted from the powder (some remains in the residue).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 60 g samosa contains 18% fat. Each gram of fat releases 37 kJ when respired. Calculate the energy, in kJ, available from the fat in the samosa.
parts.answer: 400 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this as a percentage of a daily energy requirement of 9000 kJ. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 50 g portion of uncooked rice is 78% starch, and 22% of this starch is amylose; the rest is amylopectin. Calculate the masses of amylose and amylopectin in the portion. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: amylose 8.58 g; amylopectin 30.42 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express the ratio of amylose to amylopectin in the form 1 : n. Give n to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Rice varieties with more amylopectin are stickier when cooked. Suggest which feature of amylopectin's structure might cause this.
parts.answer: Its many branches (1,6 glycosidic bonds) make it less tightly packed than the amylose helix, so it absorbs water and the many short chains/–OH groups bind to neighbouring grains (forming hydrogen bonds).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A single polypeptide has an Mr of 23400. When amino acids are joined in a polypeptide, each amino acid residue (amino acid minus water) has a mean Mr of 110, and one extra water molecule (Mr 18) belongs to the two ends of the chain. Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide, to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of peptide bonds in this polypeptide.
parts.working: One fewer than the number of amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the calculated number of amino acids is only an estimate.
parts.answer: The R groups differ, so the Mr of residues varies; 110 is only a mean, and the actual composition is not known.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 150 g of sunflower oil was heated by a 24 W heater for 150 s. Its temperature rose by 11.5 °C. Calculate the energy supplied, in J, and the specific heat capacity of the oil in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Give the specific heat capacity to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The data-book value for sunflower oil is 2.0 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Calculate the percentage difference between the experimental value and the data-book value. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 4.3 % higher

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why heat loss to the surroundings makes the experimental value higher than the true value, and suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: Some of the energy supplied is lost to the air/container instead of heating the oil, so the measured temperature rise is smaller than it should be; dividing by a smaller ΔT gives a larger value of c; improvement: insulate the container (polystyrene cup, lid) / stir / use a container of low heat capacity.
parts.working: B1 smaller ΔT → larger calculated c; B1 improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graph shows reducing sugar concentration (mg cm⁻³) against time (min) when sucrose was hydrolysed by the enzyme invertase. A tangent drawn to the curve at time 0 passes through (0, 0) and (4, 2.6). A tangent drawn at 10 minutes passes through (6, 4.1) and (16, 6.1). Calculate the rate of reaction at 0 minutes and at 10 minutes.
parts.answer: 0.65 mg cm⁻³ min⁻¹ at 0 min; 0.20 mg cm⁻³ min⁻¹ at 10 min

parts.label: b

parts.answer: 3.25 times

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Sucrose (substrate) is used up, so its concentration falls; fewer successful collisions/enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time.
parts.working: B1 substrate concentration falls; B1 fewer ES complexes/collisions.

parts.label: a

Name the most suitable statistical test for each investigation and give a reason for each choice.
(i) Comparing the mean starch content of two potato varieties (10 potatoes each).
(ii) Finding whether there is a correlation between the number of days a banana has been stored and its reducing sugar content.
(iii) Finding whether the numbers of starchy and sweet kernels on a maize cob fit an expected 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.answer: (i) t-test – comparing two means of continuous data; (ii) Spearman's rank correlation (or Pearson's if both variables are normally distributed and the relationship is linear) – testing for a correlation between two variables; (iii) chi-squared test – comparing observed with expected numbers in categories.
parts.working: 1 mark each test with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compared the lipid content of groundnuts grown with and without a fertiliser, using six seeds from each group. State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean lipid content of groundnuts grown with and without the fertiliser.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She calculated t = 3.12. There were 10 degrees of freedom, and the critical value at p = 0.05 is 2.23. State what she can conclude and explain your answer.
parts.answer: t (3.12) is greater than the critical value (2.23); so the null hypothesis is rejected: there is a significant difference in mean lipid content (probability that the difference is due to chance is less than 5%).
parts.working: B1 comparison; B1 reject null / significant difference.

parts.label: b

parts.working: B1 comparison; B1 not significant/fits ratio.

The starch content (g per 100 g) of six potatoes of each of two varieties was:

variety Cardinal: 15.9, 16.6, 16.1, 17.0, 15.7, 16.4
Calculate the mean and standard deviation (n − 1) for each variety. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Diamant mean 17.65, SD 0.60; Cardinal mean 16.28, SD 0.48
parts.working: means (B1); SDs 0.60 (B1) and 0.48 (B1).

parts.label: b

parts.label: a
parts.text: A maize cob from a cross between two plants heterozygous for a gene affecting starch production had 412 starchy (smooth) kernels and 124 sweet (wrinkled) kernels. Calculate the expected numbers for a 3 : 1 ratio and the value of χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give χ² to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: expected 402 and 134; χ² = 1.00

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of χ² for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 1.00 < 3.84, so there is no significant difference between observed and expected numbers; the results fit a 3 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sweet kernels contain more sucrose and less starch than starchy kernels. Suggest why they are wrinkled when dry.
parts.answer: More sucrose (soluble) lowers the water potential, so developing kernels take up more water by osmosis; when they dry out they lose more water and the coat wrinkles/shrinks.
parts.working: B1 sucrose lowers water potential/more water taken up; B1 more water lost on drying → wrinkled.

Calculate the mean, standard deviation (n − 1) and standard error (SE = s/√n) for each brand. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b

State the number of degrees of freedom and use the critical values below to reach a conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dihybrid cross between pea plants heterozygous for seed shape (round/wrinkled) and seed colour (yellow/green) gave: round yellow 296; round green 104; wrinkled yellow 112; wrinkled green 32. Calculate χ² for an expected 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: 1.46 < 7.82, so the difference is not significant; the results fit a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Wrinkled seeds lack a working starch-branching enzyme, which makes the 1,6 glycosidic bonds of amylopectin. Suggest how the starch in wrinkled seeds differs from that in round seeds.
parts.answer: Wrinkled seeds contain less amylopectin (fewer branched molecules) and a higher proportion of amylose; they also have less starch overall and more sucrose (unconverted sugar).
parts.working: B1 less amylopectin/more amylose (less branching); B1 less starch/more sugar.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The reducing sugar content (%) of ten honey samples bought in different markets was: 72.1, 73.4, 71.8, 72.9, 73.0, 72.5, 61.2, 72.7, 73.1, 72.2. Identify the value that is very different from the others and suggest a biological or commercial explanation for it.
parts.answer: 61.2 %; the honey may have been adulterated with sucrose syrup (a non-reducing sugar) or water, lowering its reducing sugar content (or bees fed on sugar syrup).
parts.working: B1 61.2; B1 plausible reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Excluding this value, calculate the mean, the standard error (SE = s/√n, s using n − 1) and the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 SE). Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether a line graph or a bar chart should be used to present each set of results and give a reason.
(i) Protein content of five different kinds of daal.
(ii) Turbidity of albumin solution after heating at 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80 °C.
(iii) Mean lipid content of three nut species with error bars.
parts.answer: (i) bar chart – independent variable is categoric (types of daal); (ii) line graph – independent variable (temperature) is continuous; (iii) bar chart – nut species is categoric (bars with error bars).
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measured the absorbance of a starch–iodine mixture at starch concentrations of 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 g dm⁻³. State which variable should go on each axis and write suitable axis labels.
parts.answer: x-axis: starch concentration / g dm⁻³; y-axis: absorbance (no units / arbitrary units).
parts.working: B1 correct axes; B1 labels with units in the correct format.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the points should be plotted and the line drawn.
parts.answer: Plot points accurately as small crosses or encircled dots; draw a ruled straight line of best fit (as a calibration line), or join points with ruled straight lines, not extrapolating beyond the data.
parts.working: B1 plotting; B1 line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On a calibration graph, the points (0.4 g dm⁻³, absorbance 0.31) and (0.6 g dm⁻³, absorbance 0.45) are joined by a straight line. A sample gives an absorbance of 0.4. Calculate the starch concentration of the sample. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.53 g dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student would show this reading on the graph.
parts.answer: Draw a horizontal line from absorbance 0.4 to the calibration line, then a vertical line down to the x-axis and read the concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to present the mean lipid content of seeds of five species (sunflower, mustard, sesame, maize, wheat) as a bar chart.
parts.answer: Species on the x-axis and mean lipid content / % on the y-axis with a linear scale starting at zero; bars of equal width, separated by gaps (data are discrete categories); each bar labelled with the species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: axes correct with label/units; scale from zero; equal-width bars; gaps between bars; bars labelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Equal masses of water and of cooking oil were heated with identical heaters:
time / s: 0, 60, 120, 180, 240
water temperature / °C: 20.0, 22.4, 24.9, 27.3, 29.8
oil temperature / °C: 20.0, 25.1, 30.0, 35.2, 40.1
Describe the results shown by these data.
parts.answer: Both temperatures rise steadily (linearly) with time; oil rises faster than water; after 240 s the oil has risen by 20.1 °C and the water by 9.8 °C, about twice as much.
parts.working: B1 both increase steadily; B1 oil faster; B1 data quoted with units.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Biuret calibration data:
protein / mg cm⁻³: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
absorbance: 0.00, 0.11, 0.24, 0.35, 0.47, 0.60
Explain why the student should draw a straight line of best fit through the origin rather than joining the points.
parts.answer: The points lie close to a straight line, so random errors make individual points scatter; a line of best fit averages out these errors, and the origin is a real data point (no protein = zero absorbance after zeroing).
parts.working: B1 points scatter due to random error / best fit averages; B1 origin justified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gradient of the best-fit line through the origin is 0.0593 absorbance units per mg cm⁻³. A sample of soy milk has an absorbance of 0.3. Calculate its protein concentration. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.1 mg cm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bar chart shows the mean reducing sugar content of guava, apple and mango juice, with error bars of ±2 standard errors. State what these error bars represent.
parts.answer: The 95 % confidence interval – the range within which we can be 95 % confident the true (population) mean lies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The error bars for guava and apple overlap, but those for apple and mango do not. Explain what can be concluded.
parts.answer: Guava and apple: the difference between their means may be due to chance (not significant); apple and mango: the difference is likely to be significant (real).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graph of water temperature against heating time is a straight line passing through (60 s, 24.0 °C) and (240 s, 33.0 °C). Calculate the gradient, giving the units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The heater supplied 50 J s⁻¹ to 250 g of water. Use the gradient to calculate the specific heat capacity of water, c = power ÷ (mass × gradient).
parts.answer: 4.0 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is better to use the gradient of the line than a single pair of readings.
parts.answer: The gradient uses all the data/the best-fit line, reducing the effect of random error in individual readings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The protein content of 40 individual chickpea seeds was measured, and the results were grouped into classes: 18.0–18.9, 19.0–19.9, 20.0–20.9, 21.0–21.9 and 22.0–22.9 % protein. The frequencies were 4, 9, 15, 8 and 4. State the type of chart that should be drawn and explain why the bars should touch.
parts.answer: A histogram; protein content is a continuous variable, so there are no gaps between the classes.
parts.working: B1 histogram; B1 continuous data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the modal class and describe the shape of the distribution.
parts.answer: Modal class 20.0–20.9 % (15 seeds); the distribution is roughly symmetrical/normal, with most seeds near the middle and few at the extremes (4 in each end class).
parts.working: B1 modal class; B1 shape.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Glucose standards gave the following colorimeter readings after Benedict's test:
glucose / %: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8
reading: 0.00, 0.16, 0.33, 0.47, 0.55
A fruit juice gave a reading of 0.62. Explain why the student cannot use the graph to find the glucose concentration of the juice.
parts.answer: 0.62 is higher than the highest standard (0.55), so the concentration would have to be found by extrapolation; the curve is already levelling off (0.47 → 0.55), so its shape beyond 0.8 % is unknown.
parts.working: B1 outside range/extrapolation; B1 line not linear/levelling off so unreliable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in reading per 0.2 % glucose between 0.0 and 0.4 % and between 0.6 and 0.8 %, and suggest why it is smaller at higher concentrations.
parts.answer: 0.165 per 0.2 % (0–0.4 %); 0.08 per 0.2 % (0.6–0.8 %); Benedict's reagent (Cu²⁺) is becoming used up/limiting at high glucose concentrations.
parts.working: B1 both values; B1 reagent limiting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Starch and sugar content (g per 100 g) of bananas during ripening:
day: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
starch: 20, 16, 10, 5, 2
sugar: 1, 5, 11, 15, 18
The student plotted both sets of data on one graph. Describe how she should arrange the axes and distinguish the two lines.
parts.answer: Day on the x-axis; one y-axis for both if same units and range (g per 100 g, 0–20), or a second y-axis on the right labelled clearly; different symbols (e.g. × and ⊙) and a key; points joined by ruled lines.
parts.working: B1 axes; B1 key/different symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming straight lines between the plotted points, calculate the day on which the starch and sugar contents were equal, and the value at that time. Give both answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: between days 2 and 4 starch falls 3 g per day from 16 and sugar rises 3 g per day from 5 (M1); 16 − 3t = 5 + 3t → t = 1.833 days after day 2 (M1); day 3.83, value 10.50 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the total of starch + sugar is not constant during ripening.
parts.answer: Some sugar is used in respiration (and water content changes), so carbohydrate is lost/total mass changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Absorbance of starch–iodine mixtures:
starch / g dm⁻³: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
absorbance: 0.00, 0.21, 0.40, 0.57, 0.68, 0.73, 0.75
Describe the shape of the graph of absorbance against starch concentration and state the range of concentrations that is suitable for a calibration curve.
parts.answer: Approximately linear (straight) from 0 to about 2–3 g dm⁻³, then the gradient decreases and the curve levels off towards 0.75; only the linear part, about 0–3 g dm⁻³, is suitable.
parts.working: B1 shape; B1 suitable range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the curve levels off at high starch concentrations.
parts.answer: Iodine becomes limiting (all used up), so no more complex forms; the solution is so dark that almost no light passes through, so the colorimeter cannot detect further increases.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in absorbance per g dm⁻³ between 0 and 2 g dm⁻³, and between 4 and 6 g dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 0.20 and 0.035 per g dm⁻³
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student plotted a graph of the time taken for albumin to turn opaque against temperature. Her graph had these features:
• the x-axis was labelled 'temp' and the y-axis 'time'
• the y-axis scale went 0, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 s with equal spacing
• points were plotted as large dots
• a smooth curve was drawn from the origin through the points and continued past the last point
• the plotted points used only about one quarter of the grid.
Identify five faults and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: 1 Axis labels lack units → temperature / °C and time / s. 2 Non-linear y-axis scale → use a uniform linear scale. 3 Large dots hide the exact position → use small crosses or encircled dots. 4 Line drawn through the origin and extrapolated beyond the data → draw only between first and last points (no data at 0 °C). 5 Small use of grid → choose scales so data occupy more than half of the grid in each direction.
parts.working: 1 mark per fault with its correction (max 5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mean reducing sugar (g per 100 g) of potatoes stored for 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12 days was 0.12, 0.25, 0.31, 0.44, 0.52. Each mean is from 4 potatoes; the standard deviations were 0.02, 0.018, 0.03, 0.024, 0.028. Calculate the value of 2 × SE (SE = s/√n) for day 3 and day 6, and state whether the error bars for these two days overlap.
parts.answer: day 3: ±0.018; day 6: ±0.030; bars 0.268 (top of day 3) and 0.280 (bottom of day 6) – they do not overlap
parts.working: SE = s/2 (M1); 2SE = 0.018 and 0.030 (A1); compares 0.268 with 0.280 → no overlap (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should join the points with ruled straight lines rather than draw a line of best fit through the origin, and suggest what the non-overlapping error bars indicate.
parts.answer: There is no reason to assume a straight-line/proportional relationship and day 0 is not zero sugar (0.12), so the line should not pass through the origin; points joined point-to-point show the actual data; non-overlapping 95 % CIs suggest the increase between days 3 and 6 is significant.
parts.working: B1 justification of joining points/not through origin; B1 significance of non-overlap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iodine solution turned blue-black on a cut potato but stayed orange-brown on a cut ripe grape. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Potato cells store carbohydrate as starch, which forms a blue-black complex with iodine; ripe grapes store carbohydrate as sugars (glucose/fructose), which do not react with iodine.
parts.working: B1 potato contains starch; B1 grape contains sugars not starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two equal cubes of fresh beetroot of the same size were placed in test-tubes of water, one at 5 °C and one at 60 °C. Red pigment left the beetroot much faster in the hot water. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Heat increases the kinetic energy of the water and pigment molecules, so the pigment diffuses out faster; heat also damages the cell surface and vacuole membranes (denaturing membrane proteins and making the phospholipid bilayer leaky), so the red pigment escapes from the vacuole more quickly.
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy → faster diffusion/movement of pigment; B1 heat denatures membrane proteins/damages membranes; B1 membranes become more permeable, so pigment leaves the vacuole and cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Raw egg white is a clear liquid, but when an egg is fried, the white becomes solid and opaque. Explain this change.
parts.answer: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions in the albumin; the proteins lose their tertiary structure/unfold (denature); the unfolded chains tangle and bond together, forming an insoluble solid that scatters light.
parts.working: B1 bonds broken; B1 denaturation/loss of 3D shape; B1 aggregation/insoluble.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A boy in Gilgit feels much colder when he comes out of a swimming pool on a windy day than when he is dry. Explain why.
parts.answer: Water on his skin evaporates (faster in wind); water has a high latent heat of vaporisation, so evaporation removes a lot of heat energy from his skin (to break hydrogen bonds).
parts.working: B1 evaporation; B1 high latent heat removes much heat from skin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A salad dressing of oil and lemon juice separates into two layers when left to stand. Explain why.
parts.answer: Oil (triglycerides) is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; water molecules are more attracted to each other, so the oil forms a separate layer (on top, as it is less dense).
parts.working: B1 oil non-polar/no H bonds with water; B1 water molecules attract each other, oil separates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When egg yolk, which contains phospholipids, is added and shaken, the dressing stays mixed. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails; they surround tiny oil droplets with tails in the oil and heads facing the water, so the droplets stay dispersed (emulsion).
parts.working: B1 hydrophilic/hydrophobic parts; B1 orientation around droplets keeps them apart.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When ethanol was added to a clear solution of a globular protein, the protein formed a white precipitate. Explain this result.
parts.answer: In water, hydrophobic R groups are folded inside and hydrophilic R groups are on the outside, which keeps the protein soluble; ethanol is less polar than water and disrupts hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds; the protein unfolds/denatures and the exposed hydrophobic regions stick together, so it comes out of solution.
parts.working: B1 normal arrangement of R groups/solubility; B1 ethanol disrupts hydrophobic interactions/H bonds; B1 denatures/aggregates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When lemon juice is added to warm milk, the milk protein casein forms solid curds (as in paneer making). Explain this result.
parts.answer: Lemon juice contains acid (H⁺ ions) that lowers the pH; the H⁺ ions neutralise the negative charges on casein molecules; without charges to repel each other, the molecules come together/bond and precipitate as curds (the change in charge also breaks ionic bonds and changes shape).
parts.working: B1 H⁺/lower pH; B1 charges on R groups changed/neutralised; B1 molecules no longer repel → aggregate/precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potato discs were placed in either 5 % glucose solution or a 5 % starch suspension for 1 hour. The discs in glucose lost 8 % of their mass; the discs in starch gained 3 % of their mass, the same as discs in distilled water. Explain these results.
parts.answer: 5 % glucose solution has many dissolved solute molecules, so its water potential is lower than that of the potato cells; water left the cells by osmosis (mass decrease); starch is insoluble/has very few, very large molecules, so the suspension has almost the same water potential as pure water, which is higher than the cells, so water entered (mass increase like water).
parts.working: B1 glucose lowers water potential; B1 osmosis out of cells; B1 starch insoluble/few molecules → behaves like water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two trays, one of water and one of dry soil, each 2 cm deep, were left in the sun for 2 hours. The temperature of the water rose by 6 °C and that of the soil by 15 °C. Explain this result and suggest why it is important for aquatic organisms.
parts.answer: Water has a high specific heat capacity, because much of the energy absorbed is used to break hydrogen bonds between water molecules rather than increasing their kinetic energy; so the water warms less than soil for the same energy; aquatic organisms live in a stable temperature, so enzymes stay near their optimum/no denaturation.
parts.working: B1 high SHC; B1 linked to hydrogen bonds; B1 importance for organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student chewed a small piece of bread for 2 minutes. Before chewing, an extract of the bread stayed blue with Benedict's solution; after chewing it turned orange. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Saliva contains amylase; amylase hydrolyses glycosidic bonds in starch; producing maltose, which is a reducing sugar and gives a positive Benedict's test.
parts.working: B1 salivary amylase; B1 hydrolysis of starch; B1 maltose is reducing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Collagen in tendons does not dissolve in water. However, when collagen is boiled for a long time it forms gelatin, which dissolves in hot water and forms a gel (jelly) when cooled. Explain these observations.
parts.answer: In collagen, three polypeptides form a triple helix held by many hydrogen bonds, and molecules are joined by covalent cross-links into fibrils/fibres, so it is insoluble; long boiling breaks the hydrogen bonds (and some cross-links), so the chains separate into single polypeptides (gelatin) that dissolve in hot water; on cooling, hydrogen bonds re-form between parts of the chains, forming a network that traps water molecules – a gel.
parts.working: 1 mark each: structure of collagen explains insolubility; heat breaks H bonds/cross-links → separate chains; gelatin chains soluble/interact with water; on cooling H bonds re-form a network trapping water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Samples of dried seeds were burnt in a calorimeter. Energy released per gram: sunflower 25 kJ; groundnut 24 kJ; wheat 15 kJ; rice 14 kJ. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Sunflower and groundnut seeds store mainly lipid (triglycerides), while wheat and rice store mainly starch; lipids contain more C–H bonds and less oxygen per gram than carbohydrates; so more energy is released per gram when they are oxidised.
parts.working: B1 oil seeds vs starch seeds; B1 more C–H bonds/H and less O in lipids; B1 more energy per gram.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The accepted value for pure triglyceride is about 39 kJ g⁻¹. Suggest two reasons why the values for sunflower and groundnut seeds are lower.
parts.answer: The seeds are not pure lipid (they also contain protein, carbohydrate, fibre and water); heat is lost to the surroundings in the calorimeter/incomplete combustion.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Blood from a person with sickle cell anaemia was placed in a sealed slide and the oxygen was removed. After 30 minutes, many red blood cells had become sickle-shaped. When oxygen was supplied again, most cells returned to a normal shape. Explain these results.
parts.answer: In HbS, a glutamic acid (charged) is replaced by valine (non-polar) on the surface of the β-chains; when deoxygenated, the shape of HbS exposes a hydrophobic region that binds to the valine of another molecule; HbS molecules polymerise into long insoluble fibres that distort the cell into a sickle shape; when oxygen binds again, the haemoglobin changes shape, the fibres dissolve and the cell returns to normal.
parts.working: 1 mark each: amino acid change and R group property; deoxygenated HbS sticks together (hydrophobic interaction); fibres/polymers distort cell; reoxygenation reverses it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A length of dialysis (Visking) tubing was filled with a mixture of starch and glucose solutions and placed in a beaker of distilled water. After 30 minutes, the water outside gave a positive Benedict's test but a negative iodine test. In a second experiment, amylase was also placed inside the tubing with starch only; after 30 minutes, the water outside gave a positive Benedict's test. Explain these results.
parts.answer: The tubing is partially permeable, with pores that let small molecules through but not large ones; glucose molecules are small and diffused out down a concentration gradient, so the water outside contained reducing sugar; starch molecules are too large to pass through, so no starch was outside (negative iodine); in the second experiment amylase hydrolysed starch into maltose, which is small enough to diffuse out and is a reducing sugar.
parts.working: 1 mark each: partially permeable/pore size; glucose small → diffuses out; starch too large; amylase converts starch to maltose that diffuses out.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
As hydrogencarbonate ions diffuse out of a red blood cell into the plasma, which ion moves into the cell to keep the charges balanced?
A chloride ions
B hydrogen ions
C potassium ions
D sodium ions
parts.answer: A chloride ions
parts.working: The chloride shift: Cl⁻ diffuses in as HCO₃⁻ diffuses out, so the cell stays electrically neutral. B is wrong: H⁺ ions are formed inside the cell and stay there, where haemoglobin buffers them; they do not enter from the plasma.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin have an S (sigmoid) shape?
A Each haem group has a different, fixed affinity for oxygen.
B After the first oxygen molecule binds, the haemoglobin molecule changes shape so that further oxygen molecules bind more easily.
C Oxygen binds to the globin polypeptide chains first and to the haem groups later.
D Carbon dioxide leaves haemoglobin as oxygen binds, so its affinity for oxygen falls.
parts.answer: B After the first oxygen molecule binds, the haemoglobin molecule changes shape so that further oxygen molecules bind more easily.
parts.working: Cooperative binding: binding of the first O₂ changes the quaternary shape, raising the affinity of the other haem groups, so the curve rises steeply in the middle. D is wrong: losing CO₂ would raise, not lower, the affinity, and it does not explain the shape.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the level of protein structure shown by a haemoglobin molecule and the number of polypeptide chains it contains.
parts.answer: Quaternary structure; four polypeptide chains (two α-globin and two β-globin).
parts.working: B1 quaternary; B1 four chains (accept 2 α + 2 β).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of the iron ion in each haem group.
parts.answer: The Fe²⁺ ion binds (reversibly) to one oxygen molecule.
parts.working: B1 Fe²⁺ combines with one O₂ / forms oxyhaemoglobin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: One red blood cell contains about 2.8 × 10⁸ haemoglobin molecules. Calculate the maximum number of oxygen molecules this red blood cell can carry.
parts.answer: 1.12 × 10⁹ oxygen molecules
parts.working: M1 4 O₂ per haemoglobin (one per haem); A1 4 × 2.8 × 10⁸ = 1.12 × 10⁹.

stem:
P₅₀ is the partial pressure of oxygen at which haemoglobin is 50 % saturated. Values from one laboratory study (rounded):
human 3.6 kPa
llama (lives in the Andes at about 4,000 m) 2.9 kPa
house mouse 5.3 kPa

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the lower P₅₀ value of the llama shows about its haemoglobin compared with human haemoglobin.
parts.answer: Llama haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen; its dissociation curve lies to the left of the human curve.
parts.working: B1 higher affinity; B1 curve to the left / 50 % saturated at a lower pO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this is an advantage to a llama living at 4,000 m.
parts.answer: The partial pressure of oxygen in the air and alveoli is low at altitude; llama haemoglobin can still load oxygen and become (almost) fully saturated in the lungs.
parts.working: B1 low pO₂ in alveoli at altitude; B1 haemoglobin still loads / is highly saturated, so enough O₂ is carried.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the haemoglobin of a mouse has a higher P₅₀ than human haemoglobin.
parts.answer: The mouse is small with a large surface area to volume ratio, so it loses heat quickly and has a high metabolic rate; it needs a high rate of aerobic respiration; haemoglobin with a lower affinity unloads oxygen more readily in the tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: large SA:V / loses heat fast; high rate of respiration / metabolic rate; lower affinity so O₂ released more easily to tissues (at higher pO₂).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A woman in Lahore has iron-deficiency anaemia. Her blood contains 87 g of haemoglobin per dm³. A healthy woman of the same age has 145 g dm⁻³. When fully saturated, 1 g of haemoglobin combines with 1.34 cm³ of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum volume of oxygen that 1 dm³ of blood can carry for the healthy woman and for the patient. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Healthy woman 194 cm³; patient 117 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the patient's haemoglobin concentration compared with the healthy woman.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The patient becomes tired and breathless when climbing stairs. Explain why.
parts.answer: Less haemoglobin, so less oxygen carried to muscles; less aerobic respiration / less ATP; more anaerobic respiration so lactate builds up; breathing rate rises to try to obtain more oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: less O₂ carried / delivered; less aerobic respiration / ATP; anaerobic respiration / lactate / oxygen debt; increased breathing / heart rate to compensate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Myoglobin is a red pigment found in muscle cells. Percentage saturation with oxygen:
pO₂ 1 kPa: myoglobin 70 %, haemoglobin 10 %
pO₂ 2 kPa: myoglobin 85 %, haemoglobin 25 %
pO₂ 4 kPa: myoglobin 94 %, haemoglobin 60 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Myoglobin is a single polypeptide with one haem group. Explain why its oxygen dissociation curve is not S-shaped.
parts.answer: With only one haem group there is no cooperative binding: binding of oxygen cannot change the affinity of other haem groups, so the curve is hyperbolic.
parts.working: B1 only one haem / binds one O₂; B1 no cooperative binding / no change in shape that raises affinity of further sites.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain how myoglobin helps to supply oxygen to respiring muscle cells.
parts.answer: Myoglobin has a much higher affinity than haemoglobin (70 % vs 10 % saturated at 1 kPa); it takes oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin in muscle capillaries; it keeps a store of oxygen that it releases only when pO₂ in the muscle falls very low, e.g. during intense exercise.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher affinity (data quoted); loads O₂ from haemoglobin at low pO₂; acts as a store, releasing O₂ only at very low pO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The muscles of Weddell seals contain much more myoglobin than human muscle. Suggest the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Seals hold their breath during long dives; the large myoglobin store supplies oxygen for aerobic respiration in the muscles while no air is breathed.
parts.working: B1 long dives / breath-holding; B1 O₂ store for aerobic respiration (delays anaerobic respiration / lactate).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Acetazolamide is a drug that inhibits carbonic anhydrase. Some trekkers take it on the route to K2 base camp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of acetazolamide on the rate of formation of hydrogencarbonate ions in red blood cells passing through respiring tissues. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The rate falls; carbonic anhydrase normally catalyses CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃, so without it far less carbonic acid forms to dissociate into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻.
parts.working: B1 slower / less HCO₃⁻; B1 carbonic anhydrase catalyses formation of carbonic acid, which dissociates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how acetazolamide could affect the release of oxygen to respiring tissues.
parts.answer: Fewer H⁺ ions are produced inside the red blood cell; fewer H⁺ combine with haemoglobin to form haemoglobinic acid; the Bohr shift is smaller, so less oxygen is unloaded at a given pO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fewer H⁺; less haemoglobinic acid / less change in haemoglobin shape; smaller Bohr effect so less O₂ released.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why carbon dioxide is still removed from the tissues even when carbonic anhydrase is fully inhibited.
parts.answer: Some CO₂ dissolves in the plasma; some combines with haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin; the uncatalysed reaction with water still happens slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: dissolved in plasma; carbaminohaemoglobin; slow uncatalysed formation of carbonic acid.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences in appearance between a neutrophil and a lymphocyte in a stained blood smear.
parts.answer: Neutrophil has a lobed nucleus, lymphocyte a large round nucleus; neutrophil has much granular cytoplasm, lymphocyte only a thin rim of cytoplasm.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: lobed vs round nucleus; much vs little cytoplasm; granular cytoplasm in neutrophil; neutrophil usually larger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one function of each type of cell.
parts.answer: Neutrophil: phagocytosis of bacteria. Lymphocyte: specific immune response, e.g. B-lymphocytes secrete antibodies / T-lymphocytes destroy infected cells.
parts.working: B1 phagocytosis; B1 antibody production or other correct lymphocyte role.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A patient in Multan with a bacterial infection has 11.2 × 10⁹ neutrophils per dm³ of blood. The normal value is 4.5 × 10⁹ per dm³. Calculate how many times greater the patient's count is, to 2 significant figures, and suggest a reason for the increase.
parts.answer: 2.5 times; more neutrophils are produced to engulf the bacteria.
parts.working: A1 11.2 ÷ 4.5 = 2.5; B1 more phagocytes to destroy bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Purkyne tissue carries the wave of excitation down the septum to the apex of the ventricles before it spreads up the ventricle walls. Why is this an advantage?
A The atria and ventricles contract at the same time.
B The ventricles contract from the base upwards, pushing blood back into the atria.
C The ventricles contract from the apex upwards, pushing blood towards the arteries.
D The semilunar valves open before the ventricles contract.
parts.answer: C The ventricles contract from the apex upwards, pushing blood towards the arteries.
parts.working: Contraction starting at the apex squeezes blood upwards towards the aorta and pulmonary artery, emptying the ventricles fully. A is wrong: the AVN delay ensures the atria contract first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cardiac muscle is described as myogenic. State what this means.
parts.answer: It contracts without needing impulses from nerves; the heartbeat starts within the muscle itself (at the SAN).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by systole and by diastole.
parts.answer: Systole: contraction of the heart muscle (of atria or ventricles). Diastole: relaxation of the heart muscle, when the chambers fill.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During atrial systole, state which valves are open and which are closed.
parts.answer: Atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves open; semilunar valves closed.
parts.working: B1 AV open; B1 semilunar closed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A red blood cell enters the right atrium from the vena cava. List, in order, the chambers, valves and blood vessels it passes through until it leaves the heart in the aorta.
parts.answer: Right atrium → tricuspid (right atrioventricular) valve → right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral, left atrioventricular) valve → left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta.
parts.working: B1 right side chambers + tricuspid in order; B1 pulmonary valve and pulmonary artery; B1 lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium; B1 bicuspid, left ventricle, aortic valve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood into the heart.
parts.answer: Pulmonary vein

stem: The maximum pressure measured in the left ventricle of a healthy adult was 16.0 kPa. The maximum pressure in the right ventricle was 3.5 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the maximum pressure in the left ventricle is than in the right ventricle. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the right ventricle produces a much lower pressure than the left ventricle.
parts.answer: The right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs, which are close to the heart; a lower pressure avoids damage to the thin-walled lung capillaries and avoids forming too much tissue fluid in the lungs; the left ventricle must pump blood through the whole body against much greater resistance.
parts.working: 1 mark each: right pumps to lungs only / short distance; high pressure would damage lung capillaries / cause fluid in alveoli; left pumps to whole body / more resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both ventricles must pump the same volume of blood in each beat.
parts.answer: The two sides are in series in a double circulation; all blood from the lungs returns to the left side, so if volumes differed blood would build up in one circuit.
parts.working: B1 same blood passes through both circuits in turn; B1 otherwise blood accumulates in lungs or body.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A cricketer's heart rate rises from 72 beats per minute at rest to 160 beats per minute while bowling.
At rest: atrial systole lasts 0.10 s and ventricular systole 0.30 s.
At 160 beats per minute: atrial systole lasts 0.07 s and ventricular systole 0.22 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of diastole (the time when both atria and ventricles are relaxed) at rest and during exercise. Give your answers in seconds to 3 decimal places.
parts.answer: At rest 0.433 s; during exercise 0.085 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the length of diastole.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why stroke volume may fall if the heart rate becomes very high, and why the heart muscle itself may then receive less oxygen.
parts.answer: Ventricles fill during diastole, so a very short diastole means less time to fill and a smaller volume pumped per beat; the coronary arteries supplying the ventricle muscle are squeezed during systole, so most coronary flow happens in diastole and shorter diastole reduces it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less filling time; smaller end-diastolic volume so lower stroke volume; coronary flow mostly during diastole / vessels compressed in systole.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An ultrasound scan of a patient in Islamabad measured the volume of blood in the left ventricle. At the end of diastole it was 128 cm³ and at the end of systole it was 52 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the stroke volume.
parts.answer: 76 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ejection fraction is the percentage of the end-diastolic volume that is pumped out in one beat. Calculate the ejection fraction to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The heart rate is 70 beats per minute. Calculate the cardiac output in dm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 5.32 dm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the position of the bicuspid valve and of the aortic semilunar valve while the ventricle volume falls from 128 cm³ to 52 cm³, and explain why.
parts.answer: Bicuspid valve closed because ventricular pressure is higher than atrial pressure; aortic valve open because ventricular pressure is higher than aortic pressure.
parts.working: B1 bicuspid closed + reason; B1 aortic open + reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a patient with complete heart block, the atrioventricular node (AVN) no longer conducts. The atria contract 75 times per minute but the ventricles contract only 35 times per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the atria and the ventricles beat at different rates.
parts.answer: The SAN still sets the rate of the atria; the wave of excitation cannot pass through the AVN and Purkyne tissue to the ventricles, so the ventricles contract with their own slower myogenic rhythm.
parts.working: B1 SAN still excites atria; B1 excitation not passed via AVN, ventricles beat at own (slower) myogenic rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the effect on the patient's cardiac output and one symptom this could cause.
parts.answer: Cardiac output falls (fewer ventricular beats per minute); less oxygen reaches the brain and muscles, causing dizziness, fainting or tiredness.
parts.working: B1 lower cardiac output; B1 suitable symptom linked to less O₂ supply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An artificial pacemaker is fitted. Its electrode stimulates the ventricle wall near the apex 70 times per minute. Suggest why the electrode is placed near the apex.
parts.answer: Excitation then spreads up from the apex, as it would from Purkyne tissue, so the ventricles contract from the bottom upwards and push blood up into the arteries.
parts.working: B1 imitates Purkyne tissue / spread from apex; B1 ventricles contract upwards, emptying into arteries.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In mitral valve disease, the bicuspid (left atrioventricular) valve no longer closes completely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State when the bicuspid valve should be closed during the cardiac cycle and explain why.
parts.answer: During ventricular systole; pressure in the left ventricle is higher than in the left atrium, and the closed valve stops blood flowing back into the atrium.
parts.working: B1 ventricular systole; B1 prevents backflow into atrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effects of the leaking valve on the pressure in the left atrium and on the volume of blood entering the aorta in each beat.
parts.answer: Some blood is forced back into the left atrium during ventricular systole, so left atrial pressure rises; less of the ventricle's blood leaves through the aortic valve, so the volume entering the aorta per beat falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each: backflow into atrium in ventricular systole; atrial pressure higher; less blood into aorta / lower stroke volume to body.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Patients with this condition often become breathless. Suggest why.
parts.answer: High pressure in the left atrium is passed back to the pulmonary veins and lung capillaries; more tissue fluid forms in the lungs, which increases the diffusion distance for gas exchange.
parts.working: B1 raised pressure in pulmonary veins / lung capillaries; B1 fluid in lungs / less efficient gas exchange.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The chambers of the heart are full of blood. Explain why the heart muscle still needs its own blood supply from the coronary arteries.
parts.answer: The walls (especially the ventricle wall) are too thick for oxygen to diffuse in from the blood in the chambers fast enough; cardiac muscle contracts continuously and needs a constant supply of oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 wall too thick / diffusion distance too long; B1 high demand for O₂ / glucose for respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the heart muscle if a branch of a coronary artery becomes completely blocked.
parts.answer: The muscle supplied by that branch gets no oxygen, cannot respire aerobically, stops contracting and may die (a heart attack).
parts.working: B1 no O₂ to that part; B1 cells die / cannot contract.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?
A aorta
B pulmonary artery
C pulmonary vein
D vena cava
parts.answer: B pulmonary artery
parts.working: The pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. D is wrong: the vena cava carries deoxygenated blood towards the heart.

stem:
Descriptions of three blood vessels seen in a section of tissue:
W – wall one cell thick, made of endothelium only; diameter about 8 µm.
X – narrow lumen; wall mostly smooth muscle with a few elastic fibres; diameter about 0.1 mm.
Y – thin wall with little muscle; wide lumen; valves present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify vessels W, X and Y.
parts.answer: W capillary; X arteriole; Y vein
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the smooth muscle in the wall of vessel X.
parts.answer: When it contracts the lumen narrows (vasoconstriction), reducing blood flow to the capillaries it supplies; when it relaxes the lumen widens and flow increases.
parts.working: B1 contracts → narrows lumen; B1 controls/reduces flow to capillary bed (or reverse for relaxation).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: All blood vessels are lined with endothelium. Describe this tissue and suggest why its smooth surface is important.
parts.answer: A single layer of thin, flat (squamous) cells; a smooth lining reduces friction / resistance to blood flow.
parts.working: B1 description; B1 reduces friction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of each of these vessels: aorta, pulmonary vein, vena cava.
parts.answer: Aorta: carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body. Pulmonary vein: carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Vena cava: carries deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
parts.working: B1 each.

stem:
Mean blood pressure along the systemic circulation:
aorta 12.5 kPa; large arteries 12.0 kPa; small arteries 10.5 kPa; start of arterioles 9.5 kPa; start of capillaries 4.0 kPa; end of capillaries 2.0 kPa; venules 1.5 kPa; vena cava 0.4 kPa

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in mean blood pressure as blood passes through the arterioles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the greatest fall in pressure occurs in the arterioles.
parts.answer: Arterioles have narrow lumens and muscular walls, giving high resistance (friction) to blood flow; their smooth muscle can constrict them further.
parts.working: B1 narrow lumen / high resistance; B1 friction with walls / constriction by smooth muscle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the aorta the pressure rises and falls between 10.7 kPa and 16.0 kPa with every heartbeat, but in the capillaries it is steady. Explain why.
parts.answer: Pressure in the aorta rises when the left ventricle contracts and falls in diastole; elastic fibres in artery walls stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing the flow; by the time blood reaches the capillaries, friction and the elastic recoil have evened out the pulses.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rise and fall linked to ventricular systole/diastole; elastic stretch and recoil smooths pressure; pulses damped / lost by friction in many small vessels.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The cardiac output of a resting woman is 5.4 dm³ min⁻¹. The cross-sectional area of her aorta is 4.5 cm². The total cross-sectional area of all her capillaries is 3000 cm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the flow rate of blood leaving the heart is 90 cm³ s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 5.4 dm³ min⁻¹ = 5400 cm³ ÷ 60 s = 90 cm³ s⁻¹
parts.working: B1 correct conversion shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mean velocity = flow rate ÷ total cross-sectional area. Calculate the mean velocity of blood in the aorta and in the capillaries. Give both answers in mm s⁻¹.
parts.answer: Aorta 200 mm s⁻¹; capillaries 0.30 mm s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: A capillary is 0.6 mm long. Calculate the time a red blood cell takes to pass through it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the slow flow in capillaries is an advantage.
parts.answer: More time for exchange of oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide by diffusion between blood and tissue fluid, so exchange is more complete.
parts.working: B1 more time; B1 for diffusion / exchange of named substances.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how blood returns to the heart from the legs when a person walks.
parts.answer: Pressure in veins is low; contracting leg (skeletal) muscles squeeze the veins and push blood along; valves in the veins close to prevent backflow, so blood can only move towards the heart.
parts.working: 1 mark each: low pressure in veins; skeletal muscle squeezes veins; valves prevent backflow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During a long flag ceremony at the Wagah border, a guard standing very still faints. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Without leg muscle contraction blood pools in the leg veins; less blood returns to the heart, so cardiac output falls and the brain receives too little blood / oxygen.
parts.working: B1 blood pools / less venous return; B1 less blood / O₂ to brain.

stem: With age, the walls of the aorta and large arteries gain collagen and lose elastic fibres, so they become stiffer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the effect on systolic (maximum) blood pressure in the aorta. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Systolic pressure rises, because the stiff wall cannot stretch to absorb the surge of blood from the left ventricle.
parts.working: B1 higher; B1 less stretching of the wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the effect on diastolic (minimum) blood pressure. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Diastolic pressure falls, because less elastic recoil occurs between beats to keep pushing blood forward and maintain pressure.
parts.working: B1 lower; B1 less recoil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the left ventricle wall of such a person may become thicker over many years.
parts.answer: The ventricle has to contract more strongly to pump blood into the stiff, high-pressure arteries; the extra work makes the muscle enlarge.
parts.working: B1 works harder against higher pressure / resistance; B1 muscle grows.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a photomicrograph at a magnification of ×1200, the lumen of a capillary measures 9.0 mm across. Calculate the actual diameter of the lumen in µm.
parts.answer: 7.5 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Red blood cells have a diameter of about 7 µm. Suggest two consequences of this for gas exchange in the capillary.
parts.answer: Red blood cells pass in single file and touch / are close to the capillary wall, so the diffusion distance is short; they move slowly, giving more time for exchange.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: single file; close to wall / short diffusion path; slow flow / more time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why capillary walls have no smooth muscle or elastic fibres.
parts.answer: Blood pressure in capillaries is low and steady, so no need to withstand or smooth pressure; a wall of endothelium only keeps the diffusion distance short.
parts.working: B1 low / steady pressure; B1 thin wall for exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A giraffe's head can be 2 m above its heart. Suggest why the left ventricle of a giraffe produces a much higher pressure than a human left ventricle.
parts.answer: Blood must be pushed up about 2 m against gravity to reach the brain; a higher pressure is needed to maintain flow to the brain.
parts.working: B1 against gravity / height to brain; B1 to keep enough blood flow to the brain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The arteries in a giraffe's lower legs have very thick muscular walls and narrow lumens. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Gravity adds to the pressure in the legs, so the arteries there carry blood at very high pressure; thick walls resist bursting and narrow lumens reduce the flow and pressure reaching the leg capillaries.
parts.working: B1 very high pressure in legs; B1 thick wall withstands it / narrow lumen limits flow to capillaries.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The skin on a giraffe's legs is thick and tight. Suggest how this helps to prevent fluid building up in the leg tissues.
parts.answer: Tight skin raises the pressure of the tissue fluid, which opposes the high hydrostatic pressure forcing fluid out of the capillaries, so less tissue fluid forms.
parts.working: B1 raises tissue fluid pressure; B1 reduces net outward filtration.

stem: A fish has a single circulation: the heart pumps blood to the gills, and from the gills blood flows straight on to the rest of the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a single circulation and a double circulation.
parts.answer: In a single circulation blood passes through the heart once in each complete circuit of the body; in a double circulation it passes through the heart twice, once for the lungs (pulmonary) and once for the body (systemic).
parts.working: B1 once per circuit; B1 twice – pulmonary and systemic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why blood reaches the body capillaries of a fish at low pressure.
parts.answer: Blood is pumped first through the gill capillaries; much pressure is lost by friction in these narrow vessels before it flows on to the body without returning to the heart.
parts.working: B1 passes through gill capillaries first; B1 pressure lost there / not re-pumped.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage to a mammal of the blood returning to the heart after passing through the lungs.
parts.answer: The heart can raise the pressure again, so oxygenated blood reaches the tissues quickly at high pressure; this supports the high metabolic rate of an endotherm.
parts.working: B1 pressure raised again / faster delivery; B1 linked to high metabolic rate / maintaining body temperature.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two components of blood that are absent, or almost absent, from tissue fluid.
parts.answer: Large plasma proteins (e.g. albumin, fibrinogen); (red blood cells and platelets are also absent from tissue fluid).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: plasma proteins / albumin; fibrinogen / clotting proteins; red cells; platelets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these components stay in the blood.
parts.answer: They are too large to pass through the small gaps between the endothelial cells of the capillary wall; so they are not forced out with water and small solutes.
parts.working: B1 too large; B1 gaps / pores in capillary wall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by tissue fluid.
parts.answer: The fluid that surrounds and bathes the cells of a tissue, formed from plasma that has left the capillaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of tissue fluid in supplying glucose to a muscle cell.
parts.answer: Glucose leaves the blood in the fluid forced out of the capillary; it then diffuses (or moves by facilitated diffusion) from the tissue fluid into the muscle cell down a concentration gradient.
parts.working: B1 glucose carried out of capillary into tissue fluid; B1 then enters cell from tissue fluid by (facilitated) diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Not all tissue fluid returns to the capillaries. Name the fluid formed when the excess enters the lymphatic vessels, and state where it eventually goes.
parts.answer: Lymph; it is returned to the blood in veins near the heart (the subclavian veins in the chest).
parts.working: B1 lymph; B1 returns to blood / veins.

stem: In one capillary, 0.8 mm long, the hydrostatic pressure of the blood falls steadily from 4.2 kPa at the arterial end to 1.5 kPa at the venous end. The plasma proteins draw water into the capillary with an effect equal to 3.3 kPa along the whole length. Ignore the pressures of the tissue fluid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net pressure at the arterial end and at the venous end of the capillary, and state the direction in which fluid moves at each end.
parts.answer: Arterial end 0.9 kPa outwards (fluid leaves the capillary); venous end 1.8 kPa inwards (fluid returns to the capillary).
parts.working: B1 0.9 kPa out; B1 1.8 kPa in.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the arterial end at which there is no net movement of fluid. Give your answer in mm to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 hydrostatic pressure must fall by 4.2 − 3.3 = 0.9 kPa out of a total fall of 2.7 kPa; A1 0.9 ÷ 2.7 × 0.8 = 0.27 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the plasma proteins cause water to move into the capillary.
parts.answer: Plasma proteins stay in the capillary and lower the water potential of the plasma below that of the tissue fluid; water moves into the capillary by osmosis down the water potential gradient.
parts.working: B1 proteins lower water potential of plasma; B1 osmosis into capillary.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shopkeeper in Saddar stands behind his counter for ten hours. By evening his ankles are swollen. Explain why.
parts.answer: Gravity and pooling of blood raise the hydrostatic pressure in the leg veins and capillaries; more fluid is forced out at the arterial end and less returns at the venous end; tissue fluid builds up faster than the lymph vessels can remove it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher hydrostatic pressure in leg capillaries; more filtration / less reabsorption; lymph cannot drain it all.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why walking about at intervals reduces the swelling.
parts.answer: Contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins (and lymph vessels) and, with their valves, push blood and lymph towards the heart; this lowers venous and capillary pressure so less tissue fluid forms and more is drained.
parts.working: B1 muscle pump / valves move blood and lymph; B1 lower capillary pressure / more drainage.

stem: Albumin is the main plasma protein and is made in the liver. A patient with severe liver disease has a plasma albumin concentration of 24 g dm⁻³; the normal value is 42 g dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the patient's plasma albumin concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the low albumin concentration leads to fluid building up in the tissues.
parts.answer: Less protein in the plasma means its water potential is less negative / higher; the water potential gradient from tissue fluid into the capillary at the venous end is smaller; less water returns by osmosis, so tissue fluid accumulates (oedema).
parts.working: 1 mark each: plasma water potential higher; smaller gradient / less osmosis back into capillary; tissue fluid accumulates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A doctor gives an infusion of albumin into a vein. Suggest why this can reduce the swelling for a short time.
parts.answer: The plasma water potential falls again, so more water is drawn back from the tissue fluid into the capillaries by osmosis; it is temporary because the liver still cannot make enough albumin.
parts.working: B1 lowers plasma water potential so more water returns; B1 temporary because cause (liver damage) remains / albumin is broken down.

author: HomiLabs

stem: When a wasp stings a child in Swat, cells in the skin release histamine. Histamine makes the arterioles in the area dilate and makes the walls of the capillaries more permeable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the release of histamine leads to swelling of the skin around the sting.
parts.answer: Capillary walls become more permeable, so plasma proteins leak out into the tissue fluid; the water potential of the tissue fluid falls / the difference in water potential between plasma and tissue fluid is reduced; less water returns to the capillaries by osmosis at the venous end; also dilated arterioles raise capillary hydrostatic pressure so more fluid is forced out; tissue fluid accumulates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: more permeable capillaries; proteins enter tissue fluid; water potential gradient reduced; less reabsorption by osmosis; higher hydrostatic pressure from dilation; fluid accumulates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why holding a cold pack on the sting reduces the swelling.
parts.answer: Cold causes the arterioles supplying the area to constrict; less blood flows into the capillaries, so their hydrostatic pressure falls and less fluid is forced out.
parts.working: B1 vasoconstriction / less blood flow; B1 lower hydrostatic pressure, less tissue fluid formed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: When the right ventricle is weak, blood builds up in the venae cavae and the pressure in the systemic veins rises. Explain why tissue fluid then builds up in the legs.
parts.answer: Raised venous pressure is passed back to the venous ends of the capillaries; the hydrostatic pressure there is higher than normal, so it is no longer much lower than the inward (osmotic) effect of the plasma proteins; less tissue fluid returns to the blood, so it accumulates.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher pressure at venous end of capillaries; less net inward movement / less reabsorption by osmosis; fluid accumulates (oedema).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why weakness of the left ventricle instead causes fluid to collect in the lungs.
parts.answer: Blood backs up in the left atrium and pulmonary veins, raising pressure in the lung capillaries; more fluid is forced out into the lung tissue and alveoli.
parts.working: B1 pressure rises in pulmonary veins / lung capillaries; B1 more tissue fluid in lungs.

stem: In an adult, about 20 dm³ of fluid leaves the blood capillaries each day and about 17 dm³ of it is reabsorbed into the capillaries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the fluid leaving the capillaries that is returned to the blood by the lymphatic system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of lymph flow in cm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 125 cm³ per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lymphatic filariasis is a disease, spread by mosquitoes, in which parasitic worms block lymph vessels. Explain why an affected leg can swell enormously.
parts.answer: The excess tissue fluid that should drain into the lymph vessels cannot leave the tissue; it accumulates every day, so the leg swells (lymphoedema).
parts.working: B1 lymph cannot drain / excess fluid not removed; B1 accumulates continuously.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why lymph vessels contain valves.
parts.answer: Lymph is at very low pressure, so valves stop it flowing backwards and keep it moving towards the heart.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how carbon dioxide produced by a respiring liver cell reaches the blood.
parts.answer: CO₂ diffuses out of the liver cell into the tissue fluid; it then diffuses through the thin capillary wall into the plasma; both steps are down a concentration gradient, kept steep because the blood flow carries CO₂ away.
parts.working: 1 mark each: diffuses from cell into tissue fluid; diffuses through capillary wall into blood; down a concentration gradient maintained by blood flow.

parts.label: b
