parts.text: State one other waste substance that leaves a liver cell in the same way.
parts.answer: Urea
parts.working: B1 urea (do not accept water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Red blood cells are not found in tissue fluid, but some white blood cells are. Explain why.
parts.answer: Red blood cells cannot pass through the capillary wall and stay in the blood; some white cells (e.g. neutrophils) can change shape and squeeze out between the endothelial cells.
parts.working: B1 red cells too large / cannot leave; B1 white cells squeeze between endothelial cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage for white blood cells to be able to enter tissue fluid.
parts.answer: They can reach pathogens that have entered the tissues, e.g. through a cut, and destroy them by phagocytosis.
parts.working: B1 reach site of infection in tissues; B1 phagocytosis / destroy pathogens.

stem: After a road accident in Faisalabad, a man loses about 1 dm³ of blood and his arterial blood pressure falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the effect of the blood loss on the hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries, and how this helps to restore the blood volume.
parts.answer: Blood pressure falls, so capillary hydrostatic pressure is lower; less fluid is forced out at the arterial end; the inward osmotic movement due to plasma proteins is now greater, so more tissue fluid moves into the capillaries and adds to blood volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lower capillary hydrostatic pressure; less filtration out; more water moves in by osmosis, increasing blood volume.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the concentration of plasma proteins in the patient's blood falls over the next few hours.
parts.answer: Water drawn in from the tissue fluid contains almost no protein, so it dilutes the plasma proteins that remain; the lost proteins take time to be replaced.
parts.working: B1 protein-free fluid dilutes plasma; B1 lost proteins not yet replaced.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: During exercise, the volume of tissue fluid in working muscles increases. Explain why.
parts.answer: Arterioles to the muscle dilate, so more blood enters the capillaries at higher hydrostatic pressure, forcing out more fluid; respiration produces solutes (e.g. lactate, ions) that lower the water potential of the tissue fluid; so less water returns to the capillaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each: arteriole dilation; higher hydrostatic pressure → more filtration; solutes from respiration lower water potential of tissue fluid / less reabsorption.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how increased lymph flow during exercise helps the muscle.
parts.answer: It removes the extra tissue fluid (and any leaked protein), so the fluid does not accumulate and the diffusion distance between capillaries and muscle cells stays short.
parts.working: B1 removes excess fluid; B1 keeps diffusion distance short / prevents swelling.

stem: In the brain, the endothelial cells of capillaries are joined by tight junctions, with no gaps between them. In the liver, the capillaries (sinusoids) have large gaps between the endothelial cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how the tissue fluid around liver cells differs in composition from the tissue fluid around brain cells.
parts.answer: Tissue fluid in the liver contains much more plasma protein (and other large molecules) because they pass through the large gaps; tissue fluid in the brain contains very little protein.
parts.working: B1 more protein / large molecules in liver tissue fluid; B1 linked to gaps vs tight junctions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of each type of capillary for the organ it supplies.
parts.answer: Liver: liver cells can take up and release large molecules such as plasma proteins (e.g. albumin they make) and absorbed food molecules quickly. Brain: harmful substances, toxins and many pathogens in the blood are kept away from the neurones.
parts.working: B1 liver advantage; B1 brain advantage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a drug made of large protein molecules may be very effective against a liver infection but have little effect on an infection in the brain.
parts.answer: The drug can pass through the gaps in liver capillaries into the tissue fluid, but it cannot cross the tight junctions of brain capillaries, so it does not reach the infected brain tissue.
parts.working: B1 reaches liver tissue; B1 cannot leave brain capillaries.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student at a college in Hyderabad has been told that ethanol slows the heart. She plans to test this using Daphnia (water fleas), whose heart can be seen beating through the transparent body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method the student could use to investigate the effect of ethanol concentration on the heart rate of Daphnia. Your method should allow valid, reliable results to be collected.
parts.answer: Use at least five ethanol concentrations (e.g. 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 %) made by diluting a stock with pond water; place one Daphnia in a cavity slide with a set volume of solution; leave for a set time (e.g. 5 min) to acclimatise; count heartbeats under the microscope for a set time (e.g. 20 s) and convert to beats per minute; keep temperature constant (water bath / room at 20 °C, slide not heated by lamp); use Daphnia of similar size; use a fresh Daphnia for each trial; repeat at least 3 times per concentration and calculate a mean; 0 % (pond water only) acts as the control.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: suitable range of ≥5 concentrations; how made (dilution of stock with pond water); method of measuring heart rate (count in set time under microscope, convert to bpm); acclimatisation time standardised; temperature controlled with method; similar size/age Daphnia / same volume; repeats ≥3 with mean; control of 0 % ethanol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the student can reduce harm to the Daphnia.
parts.answer: Keep the time each Daphnia spends in ethanol and under the lamp as short as possible; return surviving Daphnia to pond water / their habitat; use the smallest number of animals needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible points.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student in Gujranwala wants to plan an investigation using classmates as volunteers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could find out whether body position (lying down, sitting, standing) affects resting pulse rate.
parts.answer: Use the same volunteers for all three positions; take pulse at the wrist (or with a pulse monitor) after the person has been in the position for a set time, e.g. 3 min; count for 60 s (or 30 s × 2); keep other factors the same: no exercise or caffeine beforehand, same time of day, same room temperature; repeat each position at least three times / use at least 10 volunteers and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: three positions as IV; pulse counted in set time / bpm; set time in position before reading; standardised variables (≥2); repeats / several volunteers + mean; order of positions varied or rest between.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each person should stay still in the position for a few minutes before the pulse is taken.
parts.answer: So the pulse rate settles at a steady value after the change of position (any short-term change has passed).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A butcher in Rawalpindi supplies a student with a fresh piece of goat aorta and a piece of vena cava.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to compare the elastic recoil of rings cut from an artery and from a vein of the same animal.
parts.answer: Cut rings of the same width (e.g. 5 mm) from the artery and the vein using a ruler and scalpel; hang each ring on a hook / clamp and measure its length; hang a known mass (e.g. 20 g) on it for a set time (e.g. 1 min) and measure the stretched length; remove the mass and measure the length again after a set time; calculate the percentage recoil = (stretched − final) ÷ (stretched − original) × 100; use several masses or repeat with at least 3 rings of each vessel and find means; keep the tissue moist / same temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: rings same width; length measured with ruler / against scale; known mass added; set time loaded; length after removing mass; calculation of recoil (or percentage); repeats / several rings + mean; tissue kept moist / same temperature / from same animal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The artery rings and vein rings had different starting lengths. Explain how the student should process the results so that they can be compared fairly.
parts.answer: Calculate percentage change (e.g. percentage extension and percentage recoil) rather than actual change in length; because a longer ring will stretch further for the same mass.
parts.working: B1 percentage / proportional change; B1 reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety precaution.
parts.answer: Cut away from fingers on a tile with a sharp scalpel; wear gloves and wash hands after handling raw tissue.
parts.working: B1 any sensible precaution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of step height on the time taken for heart rate to return to its resting value after a step test.
parts.answer: Measure resting heart rate (e.g. with a pulse monitor) after 5 min sitting; use at least four step heights, e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50 cm; step up and down for a set time (e.g. 3 min) at a set rate controlled by a metronome; measure heart rate every 30 s after stopping; record the time taken to return to within ±2 bpm of the resting rate; same volunteers for each height with full recovery between tests (e.g. different days / 20 min rest); repeat or use many volunteers and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: resting rate measured first; range of ≥4 heights; set duration; set stepping rate (metronome); how recovery measured / definition of recovery; rest between tests / same person; repeats + mean; other standardised variable (e.g. same footwear, no food or caffeine).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two precautions to keep volunteers safe.
parts.answer: Volunteers should be healthy with no heart or breathing problems (health questionnaire / consent); stop immediately if they feel faint or unwell; use a stable step with a non-slip surface.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the effect of breath-hold time on blood oxygen saturation could be investigated using a pulse oximeter clipped to a finger.
parts.answer: Volunteer sits and breathes normally until the SpO₂ reading is steady and records it; volunteer holds breath for set times, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 s (timed with a stopwatch); record the lowest SpO₂ reading during / just after each hold; rest until SpO₂ returns to normal between holds; keep the same finger, hand still and warm; repeat each time three times and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: baseline reading; range of hold times; how SpO₂ recorded (lowest / at end); recovery between trials; standardised variables (finger, posture, no movement); repeats + mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the volunteer should not take deep breaths just before holding the breath.
parts.answer: Deep breathing (hyperventilation) changes blood CO₂ and oxygen levels before the hold; this would change the starting conditions so readings would not be comparable / it can be unsafe.
parts.working: B1 alters CO₂ / O₂ at start; B1 so not standardised (or safety).

stem: Capillary refill time is the time taken for colour to return to the skin after it has been pressed until pale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of water temperature on capillary refill time in the fingers.
parts.answer: Use water baths at ≥5 temperatures, e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 °C, checked with a thermometer; hand placed in water for a set time (e.g. 2 min) then dried; press a fingertip / nail with the same pressure for a set time, e.g. 5 s; release and time how long the pale area takes to turn pink again (stopwatch or video); same finger, same hand height (level with heart), same lighting; repeat three times per temperature with rest in between and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: range of temperatures + how controlled; immersion time standardised; press with set pressure/time; timing of refill; standardised variables; repeats + mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to standardise the pressure applied to the fingertip and how this could be improved.
parts.answer: Pressure applied by a thumb varies between trials; use the same mass / a spring-loaded device or press on a balance to a set reading.
parts.working: B1 problem; B1 improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student in Karachi notices that her father's blood pressure seems higher after he drinks strong coffee.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should plan an investigation into the effect of caffeine on the systolic blood pressure of adult volunteers.
parts.answer: Volunteers avoid caffeine for at least 12 h beforehand and are healthy adults who consent; measure resting systolic pressure with a digital monitor after 5 min seated, arm at heart level; give drinks containing different known masses of caffeine (e.g. 0, 50, 100, 150 mg) in the same volume of decaffeinated coffee; measure blood pressure again after a set time (e.g. 45 min) under the same conditions; double-blind: neither volunteer nor tester knows the dose; same time of day, no exercise or food; calculate change in systolic pressure; repeat / use ≥10 volunteers per dose and find mean change.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: no caffeine beforehand; baseline reading; how BP measured & standardised posture; range of doses / known mass; same volume / decaf vehicle; set time before second reading; double-blind or placebo; repeats / sample size + mean change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one group should be given decaffeinated coffee with no added caffeine.
parts.answer: It is a placebo / control: it shows the effect of drinking warm coffee and of expecting a change, so any extra change in the other groups can be put down to caffeine.
parts.working: B1 control / placebo; B1 allows effect of caffeine alone to be identified.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one ethical point the student must consider.
parts.answer: Obtain informed consent and allow volunteers to withdraw; exclude people with heart problems, pregnancy or caffeine sensitivity; keep results anonymous.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to find out whether the tempo of music affects heart rate in teenagers.
parts.answer: Use the same piece of music played at different tempos (e.g. 60, 90, 120, 150 beats per minute) at the same volume through headphones; volunteer seated and resting for 5 min; measure resting heart rate with a pulse monitor; play each tempo for a set time (e.g. 3 min) and record heart rate at the end; rest with silence between tempos until heart rate returns to resting; same time of day, no caffeine; repeat with many volunteers and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: range of tempos (same music); same volume; resting baseline; set listening time; heart rate measurement method; rest between; repeats / many volunteers + mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the order in which the tempos are played should be changed for different volunteers.
parts.answer: So that any effect of time / getting bored or relaxed during the session does not always affect the same tempo.

stem: A student needs 20 cm³ of each of five ethanol solutions (0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 %) to study Daphnia heart rate. She has a 10 % ethanol stock solution and pond water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a dilution table: for each concentration (0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 %), state the volume of 10 % stock and the volume of pond water needed.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = (required % ÷ 10) × 20; A2 all five correct (A1 for three or four correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the apparatus you would use to measure the volumes accurately.
parts.answer: A graduated pipette or syringe (e.g. 10 cm³ or 20 cm³), not a beaker.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why pond water, not distilled water, is used to dilute the stock.
parts.answer: Daphnia live in pond water; distilled water would change the ion concentration / water potential and could itself affect the heart rate or harm the animals.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student at a university in Peshawar wants to find out whether there is a relationship between the number of hours of exercise people do each week and their resting heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could select the people for the study so that the results are valid and representative.
parts.answer: Use a large sample, e.g. at least 30 people; select randomly (e.g. random numbers from a class list) rather than choosing friends; include a wide range of exercise hours; match / record age and sex, or use only one age group and sex; exclude smokers and people on heart medication.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: large sample size; random selection; wide range of exercise hours; control/record age, sex; exclude smokers / medication / illness.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the data should be collected and how the relationship should be tested.
parts.answer: Record exercise hours using a diary or fitness tracker over the same week; measure resting heart rate in the same way for everyone (seated 5 min, morning, pulse monitor for 60 s, three readings and mean); plot a scatter graph; use Spearman's rank correlation to test whether there is a significant correlation.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: reliable measure of exercise; standardised measurement of resting rate; repeated readings + mean; scatter graph; Spearman's rank (or correlation test) with null hypothesis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of light intensity on the heart rate of Daphnia.
parts.answer: Change light intensity by placing a lamp at different distances (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cm) or using a dimmer, measured with a light meter; place a heat filter / tank of water between lamp and Daphnia, or use an LED, and check temperature with a thermometer; acclimatise each Daphnia for a set time; count heartbeats for a set time with a microscope (low light from the microscope kept constant) or film it; use Daphnia of similar size; repeat with at least 3 animals per intensity and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: way of varying intensity; measure intensity (light meter); heat filter / LED / monitor temperature; acclimatisation time; method of measuring heart rate; similar Daphnia / same volume; repeats + mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why controlling the temperature is particularly important in this investigation.
parts.answer: A lamp gives out heat as well as light, so a closer lamp would also warm the water; temperature itself affects heart rate (rate of enzyme-controlled reactions), so it would be a confounding variable.
parts.working: B1 lamp heats water; B1 temperature affects heart rate, so results invalid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate how the duration of moderate exercise affects systolic blood pressure.
parts.answer: Use exercise durations of e.g. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 min on an exercise bicycle at a fixed resistance and pedalling rate; measure resting systolic pressure first, seated for 5 min, cuff on the upper arm at heart level; measure immediately (within 30 s) after each period of exercise; full rest between trials until pressure is back to resting; same volunteer, same arm, same cuff; repeat each duration three times / several volunteers and calculate mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: range of durations; fixed intensity (resistance / rate); baseline; standardised measurement; timing of measurement after exercise; rest between; repeats + mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a digital monitor that takes 40 s to give a reading could lead to inaccurate results.
parts.answer: Blood pressure begins to fall as soon as exercise stops; a reading taken over 40 s will be lower than the true value at the end of exercise.
parts.working: B1 pressure falls quickly after exercise; B1 reading underestimates.

stem: Students from Karachi (sea level) go on a field trip to Naltar (about 2,900 m). They want to measure blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) with a pulse oximeter at both places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the students should plan the comparison so that any difference in SpO₂ can be linked to altitude.
parts.answer: Measure the same group of students at both sites (or matched groups); use the same pulse oximeter, same finger, after sitting at rest for a set time, e.g. 10 min; take readings at the same time of day; measure at a set time after arrival at altitude (e.g. after 24 h); take three readings each and use means; exclude smokers / anyone ill; use a large sample.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: same individuals / matched sample; same instrument & method; rest before reading; same time of day / time after arrival; repeats and mean; exclusions; sample size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two variables that are difficult to control in this field study.
parts.answer: Physical activity during the trip / climbing before the reading; air temperature (cold fingers affect readings); sleep, illness, hydration, how quickly each person adjusts to altitude.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the statistical test that could be used and the type of data it needs.
parts.answer: A t-test, comparing two means of continuous data that are approximately normally distributed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student skips with a rope for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 minutes and measures her heart rate immediately after each period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: duration of skipping. Dependent: heart rate immediately after skipping.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that should be standardised.
parts.answer: Skipping rate (skips per minute); same person / fitness; rest time before each test; time between stopping and measuring.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student hangs different masses on rings cut from a sheep's aorta and measures how much each ring stretches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: mass hung on the ring. Dependent: length (or extension) of the ring.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and explain why one of them must be standardised.
parts.answer: Width of each ring; time the mass is left on before measuring; temperature / moisture of the tissue; same artery and part of the artery. E.g. a wider ring contains more tissue, so the same mass gives a different extension; the rings must be the same width to compare them fairly.
parts.working: B2 three variables (B1 for two); B1 explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Theophylline is a stimulant found in tea. A student adds solutions of theophylline to Daphnia on a cavity slide and counts the heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this investigation.
parts.answer: Daphnia placed in pond water with no theophylline, under the same conditions (same volume, temperature, time).
parts.working: B1 no theophylline / pond water only; B1 all other conditions the same.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the control.
parts.answer: To show that any change in heart rate is due to theophylline and not to handling, light or time on the slide.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four variables that should be standardised when measuring a person's blood pressure with a digital monitor, and how each is standardised.
parts.answer: Posture: seated, back supported, feet flat; arm position: upper arm supported at the level of the heart; rest time: sit quietly for 5 min first; same arm and correct cuff size; no talking, caffeine, smoking or exercise in the previous 30 min.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four variable + method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the arm must be at the level of the heart.
parts.answer: If the arm is below the heart, the weight of the column of blood adds to the pressure and the reading is too high (above the heart, too low).
parts.working: B1 gravity / height of blood column affects pressure; B1 direction of error.

stem: Researchers compare the resting blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) of 30 trekkers in the Hunza valley (about 2,500 m) with that of 30 office workers in Islamabad (about 500 m), all measured on the same day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables, other than altitude, that might affect SpO₂ and cannot be controlled in this field study.
parts.answer: Age; smoking; fitness; time since arriving at altitude; recent exercise; lung or heart disease; temperature of fingers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the researchers could reduce the effect of these variables on their conclusion.
parts.answer: Match the two groups for age, sex and smoking, or exclude smokers and people who are ill; record these variables and use a large random sample so they average out.
parts.working: B1 matching / exclusion; B1 large random sample / recording for analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a laboratory, samples of sheep blood are exposed to gas mixtures with different partial pressures of oxygen, and the percentage saturation of haemoglobin is measured with a spectrophotometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the temperature must be controlled at 37 °C.
parts.answer: Temperature affects the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen (higher temperature shifts the curve to the right); 37 °C is body temperature, so results are valid for the body.
parts.working: B1 temperature changes affinity / curve position; B1 37 °C = body temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the partial pressure of carbon dioxide must also be kept constant.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide lowers the pH (more H⁺) and reduces the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen (Bohr effect); a changing pCO₂ would change saturation independently of pO₂.
parts.working: B1 Bohr effect / CO₂ lowers affinity; B1 so it would be a confounding variable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: partial pressure of oxygen. Dependent: percentage saturation of haemoglobin.
parts.working: B1 both.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students compare the recovery time after exercise of members of a hockey team and non-members.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The students define recovery time as 'the time taken for heart rate to return to resting'. Explain why this definition needs to be made more precise.
parts.answer: Heart rate fluctuates and may never return exactly to the resting value; a precise rule such as 'first time heart rate is within ±3 bpm of the resting rate for 1 minute' makes the measurement repeatable.
parts.working: B1 heart rate fluctuates / exact value may not be reached; B1 precise criterion stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant during the exercise itself.
parts.answer: Exercise intensity (speed / resistance / stepping rate); duration of exercise; type of exercise.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compares the resting heart rates of 20 male and 20 female students in her school in Quetta.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and explain why it is a categoric variable.
parts.answer: Sex (male or female); it has categories, not numerical values.
parts.working: B1 sex; B1 categories / not measured on a scale.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised.
parts.answer: Age; fitness / amount of exercise; time of day; rest before measurement; no caffeine; same method of measuring pulse.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem: When the face is put into cold water, heart rate falls (the diving reflex). A student investigates the effect of water temperature (5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 °C) on this response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature of the water. Dependent: heart rate during the face immersion.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and suggest how.
parts.answer: Duration of immersion (e.g. 20 s timed with stopwatch); breath held throughout, same depth of breath; posture (seated, leaning forward); area of face immersed; rest between trials until heart rate returns to resting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three with method.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student collects published values of body mass and resting heart rate for 15 species of mammal, from shrews to elephants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: body mass of the mammal species. Dependent: resting heart rate.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this cannot be treated as a controlled experiment.
parts.answer: Body mass cannot be changed by the investigator; the species differ in many other ways (e.g. diet, activity, habitat, temperature), which cannot be controlled.
parts.working: B1 IV not manipulated; B1 other variables differ / uncontrolled.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three variables that must be standardised when measuring capillary refill time.
parts.answer: Pressure applied; time the nail is pressed; which finger is used; height of hand relative to heart; lighting when judging the colour; room temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the end point (return of colour) could be judged more objectively.
parts.answer: Record the fingertip on video and compare frames with a colour chart, or use the same observer each time; judge against a reference finger not pressed.
parts.working: B1 method; B1 explanation of why more objective.

stem: A nurse wants to find out whether the width of the blood pressure cuff affects the reading. She measures the blood pressure of each volunteer with a narrow, a standard and a wide cuff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and suggest why it is a problem if the readings are always taken in the same order (narrow, then standard, then wide cuff).
parts.answer: Independent: width of the cuff. Blood pressure may change during the session (e.g. falls as the person relaxes, or the arm is repeatedly compressed); this would always affect the later cuffs, so the effect of cuff size could not be separated from the effect of order.
parts.working: B1 cuff width; B1 pressure changes over time / repeated compression; B1 order confounds results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other ways to make the comparison valid.
parts.answer: Use a random order for each volunteer; leave a set rest time (e.g. 2 min) between readings; same arm and posture; several volunteers with different arm circumferences.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Volunteers spend 2 hours either sitting with their legs down or lying with their legs raised. The circumference of one ankle is measured before and after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: posture (sitting with legs down vs lying with legs raised). Dependent: change in ankle circumference.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that should be standardised and one way to make the measurement of the dependent variable reliable.
parts.answer: Duration (2 h); same tape measure; same activity (no walking); same room temperature; mark the measuring point on the ankle with a pen so it is measured at the same place each time / repeat three times.
parts.working: B2 two standardised variables; B1 reliability method.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃. A student mixes CO₂-saturated water with a buffer containing an indicator and different dilutions of a red blood cell extract, and times how long the indicator takes to change colour as the pH falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable, the dependent variable and how the dependent variable could be converted into a rate.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of carbonic anhydrase (blood extract). Dependent: time taken for the indicator to change colour. Rate = 1 ÷ time (s⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 IV; B1 DV; B1 rate = 1/t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the carbon dioxide solution must be freshly prepared and kept on ice, and the reaction mixture kept at a constant temperature.
parts.answer: CO₂ escapes from solution over time and more slowly from cold water, so the substrate concentration would vary; temperature affects the rate of the enzyme-catalysed reaction (and the uncatalysed one), so it must be constant; otherwise differences in time would not be due only to enzyme concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each: CO₂ lost so substrate concentration changes; cold keeps more CO₂ dissolved; temperature affects enzyme activity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student counts the heartbeats of a Daphnia under a microscope for 15 s and multiplies by 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the student's counts may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: The heart beats very fast (about 3–4 times per second), so beats are missed or counted twice; the Daphnia moves, so the heart goes out of view or focus.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: beats too fast to count; Daphnia moves / out of focus; losing count / human error; slide warms up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements.
parts.answer: Film the heart through the microscope with a phone and count beats in slow motion; restrict movement with a small amount of cotton wool / petroleum jelly or a smaller drop of water; tap a pencil on paper for each beat and count the dots.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two practical improvements.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures a person's pulse at the neck for 10 s and multiplies the count by 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: If the count could be wrong by one beat, state the uncertainty in the heart rate in beats per minute.
parts.answer: ±6 beats per minute
parts.working: ±1 beat in 10 s × 6 = ±6 bpm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty for a heart rate of 72 beats per minute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student instead counts for a full 60 s. Calculate the new percentage uncertainty for the same heart rate and explain why this is an improvement.
parts.answer: 1.4 %; an error of one beat is now a much smaller fraction of the total count, so the result is more accurate (precise).
parts.working: A1 1 ÷ 72 × 100 = 1.4 %; B1 explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the length of rings of artery before and after hanging masses on them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each length is read with a ruler to ±0.5 mm. The extension of a ring is found by subtracting two readings. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in an extension of 16 mm. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 uncertainty in a difference = 0.5 + 0.5 = ±1 mm; A1 1 ÷ 16 × 100 = 6.25 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to reduce the uncertainty in measuring the length of the ring.
parts.answer: Use a ruler / scale with smaller divisions or digital callipers; fix the scale directly behind the ring and read at eye level to avoid parallax; use larger masses so the extension is larger; photograph the ring next to a scale and measure the image.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Heart rate of Daphnia in 0.5 % caffeine solution, four trials (beats per minute): 248, 252, 196, 250

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result.
parts.answer: 196 beats per minute (trial 3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean heart rate, ignoring the anomalous result.
parts.answer: 250.0 beats per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the anomalous result and what the student should do about it.
parts.answer: The Daphnia might have been damaged, smaller / older, or not given enough time to acclimatise; the count may have been interrupted. Repeat that trial with a new Daphnia and leave out the anomaly from the mean.
parts.working: B1 plausible reason; B1 repeat / exclude from mean.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school nurse in Abbottabad measures a student's blood pressure three times, one minute apart. Systolic readings: 132, 121, 119 mmHg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the first reading is often higher than the later readings.
parts.answer: The person is anxious or not yet relaxed (e.g. the 'white-coat' effect) when first measured; the cuff squeezing the arm for the first time can also raise pressure; after a few minutes they relax and pressure falls.
parts.working: B1 anxiety / not relaxed; B1 settles with time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement to the method so that the result is a better estimate of resting blood pressure.
parts.answer: Rest seated for 5 min before measuring; take three readings 1–2 min apart, discard the first and use the mean of the other two.
parts.working: B1 rest first; B1 repeat and mean (discarding first).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the effect of caffeine on Daphnia heart rate with a microscope lit by a filament lamp. Each Daphnia is under the lamp for about 5 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the microscope lamp could cause a systematic error in this investigation.
parts.answer: The lamp heats the small volume of water on the slide, so its temperature rises during each count; heart rate rises with temperature, so all readings are too high (and increase the longer the slide is under the lamp).
parts.working: B1 lamp warms water; B1 raises heart rate / readings biased in one direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to reduce this error.
parts.answer: Use a cold LED light source or place a heat filter / beaker of water between lamp and slide; switch the lamp on only while counting; measure the temperature of the water after each count; put the slide on a cooled stage / limit time under the lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a step test, each volunteer steps on and off a bench for 3 minutes at whatever speed they choose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the stepping rate should be standardised and how this could be done.
parts.answer: A faster rate means more work per minute and a larger rise in heart rate; use a metronome set to a fixed number of steps per minute.
parts.working: B1 reason; B1 metronome / fixed beat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other source of error in a step test and an improvement.
parts.answer: Different step heights / leg lengths – use the same step and volunteers of similar height; delay in measuring heart rate after stopping – use a chest-strap heart rate monitor that records continuously.
parts.working: B1 error; B1 matching improvement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three reasons why a pulse oximeter reading may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: Cold fingers with poor blood flow; movement of the hand or finger; nail polish or artificial nails; bright light falling on the sensor; probe not fitting properly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the reliability of the readings could be improved.
parts.answer: Keep the hand still and warm and take several readings after the value has been steady for 30 s, then calculate a mean.

stem: A digital blood pressure monitor is found to read 0.5 kPa higher than a calibrated reference instrument every time it is used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether this is a random error or a systematic error, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Systematic error; it shifts every reading in the same direction by the same amount.
parts.working: B1 systematic; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student repeats each measurement five times and the readings are very close together. Explain why the mean is still not accurate.
parts.answer: Repeats reduce the effect of random error and show the readings are precise / repeatable; but every reading is 0.5 kPa too high, so the mean is also 0.5 kPa too high – precision is not the same as accuracy.
parts.working: B1 repeats only reduce random error / readings precise; B1 bias remains, so mean is inaccurate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the error could be corrected.
parts.answer: Calibrate the monitor against a reference (e.g. a standard sphygmomanometer) and subtract 0.5 kPa from every reading.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Heart rate of Daphnia (beats per minute), three trials at each ethanol concentration:
0 %: 182, 186, 184
1 %: 160, 171, 149
2 %: 140, 138, 143

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range of the readings for each concentration.
parts.answer: 0 %: 4; 1 %: 22; 2 %: 5 beats per minute
parts.working: A2 all three correct (A1 two correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean heart rate at 1 % ethanol.
parts.answer: 160.0 beats per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the least reliable result and suggest what should be done.
parts.answer: 1 % ethanol, because the readings have the largest range / spread; carry out more repeats at 1 % (and check for anomalies) before calculating the mean.
parts.working: B1 1 % with reason; B1 more repeats.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To find out the mean resting heart rate of adults in Lahore, a student measures 12 volunteers at one gym.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student's sample may not allow a valid conclusion about the population of a city.
parts.answer: All 12 people are from one gym, so they are probably fitter than average / not representative (sampling bias); the sample is small, so a few unusual individuals affect the mean; volunteers chose themselves, so not random.
parts.working: 1 mark each: not representative / bias; small sample; not random / self-selected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the sampling could be improved.
parts.answer: Select a larger sample (e.g. 50+) at random from several places (e.g. different areas, workplaces, ages), recording age and sex.
parts.working: B1 larger; B1 random / several sites.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an investigation of elastic recoil, a student left masses on artery rings for between 30 s and 3 min before measuring the length, depending on how busy she was.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why this introduces an error into the results.
parts.answer: Artery tissue keeps stretching slowly while the mass is on (creep); a ring left longer has a larger extension, so differences are partly due to time, not the mass or vessel.
parts.working: B1 continued stretching over time; B1 so extension depends on time loaded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement and explain why it would make the results more valid.
parts.answer: Leave each mass on for exactly the same time (e.g. 60 s, timed with a stopwatch) before reading; then only the mass / type of vessel varies.
parts.working: B1 fixed timed loading; B1 only IV varies.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Haemoglobin concentration is estimated by diluting a blood sample, placing it in a cuvette and measuring its absorbance of green light with a colorimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three sources of error in this method.
parts.answer: Red blood cells settle in the cuvette, so absorbance changes with time; the cuvette is not wiped / has fingerprints; colorimeter not zeroed with a blank each time; diluted blood clots; inaccurate dilution with a measuring cylinder; air bubbles in the cuvette.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest improvements for two of the errors you gave.
parts.answer: Lyse the cells / mix by inverting just before reading, and read at a fixed time; zero with a blank of the diluting solution before each sample; handle cuvettes by the ridged sides; use a micropipette for dilution; add anticoagulant.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two matching improvements.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student's reaction time when starting and stopping a stopwatch adds an uncertainty of about ±0.2 s. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a capillary refill time of 2.5 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the timing could be made more accurate.
parts.answer: Film the fingertip with a phone and use the time stamps / frame count to find when the colour returns; use the same person to judge the end point each time against a colour reference.
parts.working: B1 video / frames; B1 standardised end point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why repeating the measurement and calculating a mean improves reliability.
parts.answer: Random errors in judging the end point and in reaction time tend to cancel out, and anomalies can be identified.

stem:
Heart rate of one athlete running on a treadmill at different speeds:
Speed / km h⁻¹: 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14
Heart rate / beats per minute: 70, 92, 110, 131, 150, 168, 176

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between treadmill speed and heart rate.
parts.answer: Heart rate increases as speed increases; the increase is roughly steady (about 18–21 bpm per 2 km h⁻¹) from 4 to 12 km h⁻¹; it then levels off, rising only 8 bpm between 12 and 14 km h⁻¹ (approaching the maximum heart rate).
parts.working: 1 mark each: positive relationship; quoted data; levels off at high speed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why heart rate levels off at the highest speeds.
parts.answer: The heart is approaching its maximum rate for this person.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Resting heart rates of two groups of men aged 30–40:
Smokers (n = 12): mean 78 bpm, standard deviation 9 bpm
Non-smokers (n = 12): mean 74 bpm, standard deviation 10 bpm

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concludes that smoking increases resting heart rate. Use the data to discuss whether this conclusion is justified.
parts.answer: Smokers have a higher mean (78 vs 74 bpm); but the difference (4 bpm) is small compared with the standard deviations (9 and 10), so the spread of data overlaps greatly; the samples are small (12); no statistical test was done, so the difference may be due to chance; other variables (fitness, age, caffeine) were not controlled, and a correlation does not show cause.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: mean higher (data); small difference vs SD / overlap; small sample; no statistical test / may be chance; uncontrolled variables / correlation not causation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test that should be used.
parts.answer: t-test

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean heart rate of Daphnia at different concentrations of theophylline:
Concentration / mmol dm⁻³: 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6
Heart rate / beats per minute: 180, 196, 214, 236, 228, 190

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of theophylline concentration on heart rate.
parts.answer: Heart rate rises with concentration from 180 to a peak of 236 bpm at 0.4 mmol dm⁻³; it then falls at higher concentrations, to 190 bpm at 1.6 mmol dm⁻³ (still above the control).
parts.working: 1 mark each: increases to a maximum; peak at 0.4 (236); decreases above 0.4 with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student's hypothesis was 'the higher the concentration of theophylline, the higher the heart rate'. State whether the data support this hypothesis. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Only partly / no: the hypothesis is supported up to 0.4 mmol dm⁻³, but at higher concentrations heart rate decreases.
parts.working: B1 partly / not fully; B1 reason referring to fall above 0.4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what further work would show the concentration giving the maximum heart rate more precisely.
parts.answer: Test more concentrations between 0.2 and 0.8 mmol dm⁻³ (e.g. 0.3, 0.5, 0.6).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Passengers on a 7-hour flight from Islamabad to Manchester had their ankle circumference measured before and after the flight.
Group A (15 passengers, stayed seated): mean increase 1.2 cm
Group B (15 passengers, walked in the aisle every hour): mean increase 0.4 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in mean increase in ankle circumference between the two groups.
parts.answer: 0.8 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion from these results.
parts.answer: Walking in the aisle every hour reduces the increase in ankle circumference (swelling) during a long flight.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the conclusion should be treated with caution.
parts.answer: Only 15 per group / no statistical test / passengers not randomly assigned / other factors such as age, weight or socks not controlled.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂):
Residents of Karachi measured in Karachi: 98 %
Residents of Skardu (2,200 m) measured in Skardu: 95 %
Visitors from Karachi measured in Skardu one day after arrival: 91 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the SpO₂ of the three groups.
parts.answer: Visitors at altitude have the lowest mean SpO₂ (91 %), 7 percentage points below Karachi residents (98 %); Skardu residents are in between (95 %), only 3 below Karachi.
parts.working: B1 order of groups; B1 data quoted with comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that people who live at altitude gradually become adapted. Discuss whether the data support this conclusion.
parts.answer: Supports: residents have higher SpO₂ than visitors breathing the same air; but the data do not show a gradual change because no one was measured over time; residents may differ genetically or in fitness; samples/SDs not given, so significance unknown.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: supports via residents > visitors; no data over time; other differences between groups; no statistics / sample size.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student calculated Spearman's rank correlation coefficient for body mass and resting heart rate of 10 species of mammal. rs = −0.82. The critical value for 10 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.65.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the student can conclude from the value of rs.
parts.answer: There is a significant negative correlation between body mass and resting heart rate (|rs| = 0.82 > 0.65); so the null hypothesis of no correlation is rejected at p = 0.05.
parts.working: B1 significant; B1 negative correlation / larger mammals have lower heart rates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student writes: 'A large body mass causes a low heart rate.' Explain why this conclusion is not justified by the data.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show causation; another factor linked to body size, such as a lower metabolic rate per gram or smaller surface area to volume ratio, may be the cause.
parts.working: B1 correlation ≠ cause; B1 named other factor (e.g. SA:V / metabolic rate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a biological explanation for the correlation.
parts.answer: Small mammals have a larger SA:V ratio and lose heat faster, so they need a higher metabolic rate per gram; more oxygen must be delivered per gram of tissue, so the heart beats faster.
parts.working: B1 SA:V / heat loss; B1 higher metabolic rate needs faster O₂ delivery.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rings from a goat's aorta and vena cava were stretched with a 50 g mass and released. Mean percentage recoil:
Aorta rings (n = 5): 96 %
Vena cava rings (n = 5): 71 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
parts.answer: Artery rings recoil more than vein rings, so the artery wall is more elastic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in terms of the structure of the walls.
parts.answer: Arteries have a thick layer containing many elastic fibres in their walls; veins have few elastic fibres and a thin wall.
parts.working: B1 artery many elastic fibres; B1 vein few.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is not valid to conclude that all arteries are more elastic than all veins.
parts.answer: Only one artery and one vein from one animal were tested / arteries differ (e.g. aorta vs muscular arteries).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean systolic blood pressure of 2,000 adults in a health survey in Punjab:
Age / years: 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69
Systolic pressure / mmHg: 117, 120, 125, 131, 138

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean systolic pressure from the youngest to the oldest group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend and state whether the rate of increase changes with age.
parts.answer: Systolic pressure increases with age; the increase per decade gets larger (3, 5, 6, 7 mmHg), so it rises faster in older groups.
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 rate increases with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: These data came from measuring different people of each age at one time. Explain why they do not prove that each person's blood pressure rises with age.
parts.answer: Different individuals in each group, so the change in any one person was not followed over time (cross-sectional, not longitudinal); older groups may differ in diet, lifestyle or medical history from younger people today.
parts.working: B1 not same individuals followed over time; B1 other differences between generations / groups.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Percentage saturation of haemoglobin at two partial pressures of CO₂:
pO₂ / kPa: 2, 4, 6, 12
Low pCO₂ / %: 35, 75, 88, 97
High pCO₂ / %: 22, 58, 78, 96

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in percentage saturation between low and high CO₂ at 2 kPa and at 4 kPa.
parts.answer: 2 kPa: 13 percentage points; 4 kPa: 17 percentage points

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion from the data.
parts.answer: At the same pO₂, a higher partial pressure of CO₂ lowers the percentage saturation of haemoglobin (the curve shifts right); the effect is negligible at high pO₂ (97 vs 96 % at 12 kPa).
parts.working: B1 higher CO₂ → lower saturation; B1 little effect at high pO₂ (data).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Twenty adults with slightly high blood pressure drank either beetroot juice or a placebo drink every day for 2 weeks (10 per group).
Mean fall in systolic pressure: beetroot juice 4.2 mmHg, placebo 1.1 mmHg.
A t-test gave t = 1.62. The critical value at p = 0.05 with 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what can be concluded from the t-test.
parts.answer: t = 1.62 is less than the critical value 2.10, so the difference is not significant at p = 0.05; accept the null hypothesis – the difference in fall in pressure is probably due to chance.
parts.working: B1 comparison with critical value; B1 not significant / accept null.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The juice company advertises: 'Beetroot juice lowers blood pressure – proven by science.' Evaluate this claim using the data.
parts.answer: The mean fall was larger with juice (4.2 vs 1.1 mmHg), which seems to support it; but the difference was not significant; samples were small (10 per group) and the trial only lasted 2 weeks; so the claim is not justified.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: larger mean fall quoted; not significant; small sample / short trial; claim not justified.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Numbers of Daphnia carrying eggs in samples of 300 Daphnia from each of three ponds were compared with a chi-squared test. χ² = 9.4. Degrees of freedom = 2. Critical value at p = 0.05 = 5.99.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the result of the chi-squared test shows.
parts.answer: χ² = 9.4 is greater than 5.99, so there is a significant difference (p < 0.05) between the observed and expected numbers; the proportion of Daphnia carrying eggs differs between the ponds.
parts.working: B1 9.4 > 5.99; B1 significant difference / reject null hypothesis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that the pond with the most egg-carrying Daphnia has the most food. Explain why the data do not support this conclusion.
parts.answer: The test only shows that the proportions differ, not why; food supply was not measured – other factors (water temperature, predators, age of the population, time of year) could be responsible.
parts.working: B1 test shows difference only, not cause; B1 other possible causes / diet not measured.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean capillary refill time of three volunteers after warming or cooling the hand:
Hand temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 35
Capillary refill time / s: 3.8, 2.6, 1.9, 1.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in capillary refill time between 10 °C and 35 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown.
parts.answer: Capillary refill time decreases as hand temperature increases; the decrease is greatest at low temperatures and becomes small between 30 and 35 °C (1.9 to 1.8 s).
parts.working: B1 negative relationship; B1 levels off at higher temperatures with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why only a tentative conclusion can be made.
parts.answer: Only three people were tested / no repeats or statistics / few temperatures.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Body mass and heart mass of four mammals:
Mouse: body 0.025 kg, heart 0.00013 kg
Human: body 70 kg, heart 0.33 kg
Horse: body 500 kg, heart 3.6 kg
Elephant: body 4000 kg, heart 20 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart mass as a percentage of body mass for each mammal, to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Mouse 0.52 %; human 0.47 %; horse 0.72 %; elephant 0.50 %
parts.working: A2 all four correct (A1 two or three).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes: 'Heart mass is about the same proportion of body mass in all mammals.' Discuss this conclusion.
parts.answer: Supported for three of the four (about 0.5 %) across a huge range of body masses; the horse is an exception (0.72 %), perhaps because it is bred for running; only one individual of four species, so cannot generalise to all mammals.
parts.working: 1 mark each: supported for most (data); horse exception with suggestion; small sample / one individual per species.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mean resting stroke volume: 12 marathon runners 95 cm³; 12 non-athletes of the same age 70 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the mean stroke volume of the athletes is greater than that of the non-athletes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that endurance training increases stroke volume. Explain why these data alone cannot show this.
parts.answer: The two groups are different people measured at one time; athletes may have had larger hearts before training (people with large stroke volumes may choose endurance sport); stroke volume was not measured before and after training in the same people.
parts.working: B1 not before/after in same people; B1 alternative explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Daphnia P: 58 beats counted in 15 s. Daphnia Q: 47 beats counted in 12 s. Calculate the heart rate of each in beats per minute.
parts.answer: P 232 beats per minute; Q 235 beats per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the counts must be converted to beats per minute before they are compared.
parts.answer: The counts were made over different times, so the raw numbers are not comparable; a rate per minute is.

stem: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At rest, a woman's cardiac output is 6.3 dm³ min⁻¹ and her heart rate is 84 beats per minute. Calculate her stroke volume in cm³.
parts.answer: 75 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: During exercise her cardiac output is 18.0 dm³ min⁻¹ and her stroke volume is 120 cm³. Calculate her heart rate.
parts.answer: 150 beats per minute

author: HomiLabs

stem: A man in Sialkot reduced the salt in his diet for 8 weeks. His blood pressure fell from 142/92 mmHg to 131/86 mmHg (systolic/diastolic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in systolic and in diastolic pressure. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Systolic 7.7 %; diastolic 6.5 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a percentage change is useful when comparing the effect on different people.
parts.answer: People start with different blood pressures, so percentage change allows a fair comparison of the size of the effect.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student makes a ten-fold serial dilution of an adrenaline solution of concentration 1.0 mg cm⁻³ to test on Daphnia. Each tube contains 10 cm³ in total; tube 1 is ten times more dilute than the stock, tube 2 ten times more dilute than tube 1, and so on.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how tube 1 is made from the stock solution.
parts.answer: Add 1 cm³ of stock solution to 9 cm³ of distilled water / Ringer's solution and mix.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of adrenaline in tube 4, in µg cm⁻³.
parts.answer: 0.1 µg cm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which tube contains 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mg cm⁻³.
parts.answer: Tube 5

author: HomiLabs

stem: Recovery time after a 3-minute step test, five trials for one volunteer (s): 145, 152, 149, 210, 148

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean recovery time without it.
parts.answer: 210 s is anomalous; mean = 148.5 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean if the anomalous result is included, and state how much it changes the mean.
parts.answer: 160.8 s; 12.3 s larger

author: HomiLabs

stem: At the end of a 400 m run, a student's heart rate was 150 beats per minute. 3 minutes later it was 96 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of fall in heart rate during the first 3 minutes of recovery, in beats per minute per minute.
parts.answer: 18 beats per minute per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Heart rate reached the resting value of 66 beats per minute 4 minutes later. Calculate the mean rate of fall over the whole 7-minute recovery period.
parts.answer: 12.0 beats per minute per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the difference between the two answers shows.
parts.answer: Heart rate falls fastest at the start of recovery and more slowly later.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Blood flows through a leg muscle at 0.8 dm³ min⁻¹. Arterial blood entering the muscle contains 19.5 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³; venous blood leaving it contains 12.0 cm³ per 100 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen taken up by the muscle each minute.
parts.answer: 60 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the oxygen arriving in the arterial blood that is removed by the muscle.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A blood sample is diluted 1 in 200 and placed on a haemocytometer. Each small square is 0.05 mm × 0.05 mm and the depth of the chamber is 0.1 mm. A total of 480 red blood cells are counted in 80 small squares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of diluted blood over the 80 small squares, in mm³.
parts.answer: 0.02 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of red blood cells per mm³ of undiluted blood. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 4.8 × 10⁶ per mm³
parts.working: M1 480 ÷ 0.02 = 24 000 per mm³ of diluted blood; A1 × 200 = 4.8 × 10⁶.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why cells touching two of the four sides of a square are counted, but those touching the other two sides are not.
parts.answer: So that cells on the boundary lines are not counted twice (in two neighbouring squares).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Lengths of two rings (mm):
Artery ring: original 20, with mass attached 32, after removing mass 21
Vein ring: original 20, with mass attached 38, after removing mass 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Percentage recoil = (stretched length − final length) ÷ (stretched length − original length) × 100. Calculate the percentage recoil of each ring.
parts.answer: Artery 91.7 %; vein 44.4 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage extension of each ring while the mass was attached.
parts.answer: Artery 60 %; vein 90 %

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mouse: body mass 0.025 kg, cardiac output 0.020 dm³ min⁻¹.
Human: body mass 70 kg, cardiac output 5.0 dm³ min⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cardiac output per kg of body mass for each species, in dm³ min⁻¹ kg⁻¹. Give the human value to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Mouse 0.80; human 0.071 dm³ min⁻¹ kg⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mouse value is than the human value.
parts.answer: 11.2 times
parts.working: 0.800 ÷ 0.07143 = 11.2 (use the unrounded human value).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the mouse needs a much higher cardiac output per kg.
parts.answer: Large surface area to volume ratio, so it loses heat rapidly; higher metabolic rate / respiration per gram needs more oxygen delivered per gram each minute.
parts.working: B1 SA:V / heat loss; B1 higher metabolic rate needs more O₂.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A heart beats 72 times per minute with a stroke volume of 70 cm³. Calculate the volume of blood pumped by the left ventricle in 24 hours, in dm³, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7260 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The body contains about 5 dm³ of blood. Calculate how many times the whole blood volume passes through the left ventricle in a day, to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 1452 times

stem: A photomicrograph of a blood smear has a scale bar 20 mm long labelled 10 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the image.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A red blood cell in the image is 14 mm across. Calculate its actual diameter in µm.
parts.answer: 7.0 µm

author: HomiLabs

stem: A patient's systolic pressure is 16.0 kPa and diastolic pressure is 10.7 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic pressure + (systolic pressure − diastolic pressure) ÷ 3. Calculate the mean arterial pressure in kPa to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 12.5 kPa

parts.label: b
parts.text: 1 kPa = 7.5 mmHg. Convert the systolic and diastolic pressures to mmHg, to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 120 / 80 mmHg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mean arterial pressure is closer to the diastolic pressure than to the systolic pressure.
parts.answer: In each cardiac cycle the artery spends longer at pressures near diastolic (diastole lasts longer than systole).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Daphnia is filmed at 25 frames per second. Ten heartbeats take 62 frames.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute, to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 242 beats per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: The start and end of the 10 beats can each only be judged to the nearest frame, so the count could be 61 or 63 frames. Calculate the heart rate for each of these and hence the uncertainty in the result.
parts.answer: 61 frames: 246; 63 frames: 238 beats per minute; uncertainty about ±4 beats per minute
parts.working: M1 both values calculated; A1 ±4 bpm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the uncertainty could be reduced.
parts.answer: Count more beats (e.g. 30) so one frame is a smaller fraction of the total, or use a higher frame rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student records heart rate every 30 s for 5 minutes after a sprint.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph the student should draw and which variable goes on each axis.
parts.answer: A line graph; time after exercise (min) on the x-axis, heart rate (beats per minute) on the y-axis.
parts.working: B1 line graph; B1 axes correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of the axes that the student must include.
parts.answer: Axis labels with units (e.g. 'Time after exercise / min'); linear, even scales using at least half the grid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the points should be joined with straight lines or a smooth curve rather than shown as a bar chart.
parts.answer: Both variables are continuous, so readings between the measured times are meaningful.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the resting heart rates of 60 students and groups them into classes: 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, 80–89, 90–99 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of chart that should be drawn and explain your choice.
parts.answer: A histogram, because the data are continuous and grouped into class intervals (the bars touch).
parts.working: B1 histogram; B1 continuous grouped data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a bar chart with gaps would be used instead to show the mean heart rate of each of four sports teams.
parts.answer: Sports team is a categoric (discontinuous) variable, so bars are separate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Heart rate after exercise:
Time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Heart rate / beats per minute: 162, 138, 118, 104, 95, 90

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of fall of heart rate between 0 and 1 min and between 4 and 5 min.
parts.answer: 24 and 5 beats per minute per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster heart rate falls in the first minute than in the fifth minute.
parts.answer: 4.8 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the curve you would expect if these data were plotted.
parts.answer: A curve falling steeply at first, then becoming less steep and levelling off towards the resting rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Volume of blood in the left ventricle of a dog during one cardiac cycle:
Time / s: 0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.35, 0.45, 0.60
Volume / cm³: 118, 126, 130, 104, 72, 60, 82, 112

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate at which blood leaves the ventricle between 0.10 s and 0.35 s, in cm³ s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 280 cm³ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: On a graph of ventricle volume against time, state how the rate of ejection at a single instant could be found.
parts.answer: Draw a tangent to the curve at that time; calculate its gradient (change in volume ÷ change in time).
parts.working: B1 tangent; B1 gradient calculation.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean resting heart rate of two groups of students, shown on a bar chart with error bars of ±2 standard errors (approximately 95 % confidence intervals):
Trained: mean 68 bpm, standard error 1.5
Untrained: mean 74 bpm, standard error 2.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the values at the bottom and top of the error bar for each group.
parts.answer: Trained: 65 to 71; untrained: 70 to 78 beats per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: The error bars overlap. State what this suggests about the difference between the means.
parts.answer: The difference may not be significant / could be due to chance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the error bars would be drawn on a bar chart.
parts.answer: A vertical line through the top of each bar from mean − 2SE to mean + 2SE, with short horizontal caps.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Heart rates to be plotted range from 58 to 186 beats per minute. The y-axis of the graph paper has 8 large squares, each divided into 10 small squares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a suitable scale for the y-axis and explain your choice.
parts.answer: Start at 40 and use 20 beats per minute per large square, giving 40–200; this covers 58–186 and uses most of the grid.
parts.working: B1 suitable scale covering range; B1 uses more than half of grid / easy to read.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the y-axis need not start at zero.
parts.answer: No values are near zero; starting at 0 would squash the data into a small part of the grid.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plots the resting heart rate against hours of exercise per week for 25 adults.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be drawn.
parts.answer: A scatter graph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the points should not be joined dot to dot.
parts.answer: Each point is a different person / independent measurement, not a series over time; the aim is to show a trend, so a line of best fit (if any) is drawn instead.
parts.working: B1 independent individuals; B1 trend / line of best fit.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student wants to plot resting heart rate against body mass for these mammals:
shrew 0.003 kg, mouse 0.025 kg, cat 4 kg, human 70 kg, elephant 4000 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why plotting body mass on a linear scale would not be useful.
parts.answer: The masses range over more than a million-fold; on a linear scale the shrew, mouse and cat would all be crowded at zero and differences between them could not be seen.
parts.working: B1 huge range; B1 small values bunched together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate log₁₀ of each body mass, to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Shrew −2.52; mouse −1.60; cat 0.60; human 1.85; elephant 3.60
parts.working: A2 all five correct (A1 three or four).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has data for the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin at pH 7.4 and at pH 7.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how both sets of data should be presented on one graph.
parts.answer: Plot both curves on the same axes (pO₂ on x-axis, % saturation on y-axis), using different symbols or line styles, and include a key.
parts.working: B1 same axes; B1 different symbols + key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 3 kPa, saturation is 57 % at pH 7.4 and 45 % at pH 7.2. Fully saturated blood carries 20 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³. Calculate the extra volume of oxygen released by 100 cm³ of blood at pH 7.2.
parts.answer: 2.4 cm³

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plotted the mean heart rate of Daphnia against caffeine concentration. Her graph had heart rate on the x-axis and concentration on the y-axis; the axis labels were 'heart rate' and 'caffeine'; the concentration scale was marked 0, 0.5, 2, 5; points were drawn as large dots and joined with a ruler, and the line was continued to the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four mistakes in the student's graph.
parts.answer: Axes the wrong way round (independent variable, concentration, should be on the x-axis); no units on the axes; uneven scale (0, 0.5, 2, 5); points joined with a ruler dot-to-dot / extended through the origin without data; plotting with large blobs instead of small crosses.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student extends the straight line to predict the heart rate at 8 mg cm⁻³ of caffeine. Explain why this prediction is unreliable.
parts.answer: It is extrapolation beyond the range of the data (0–2 mg cm⁻³); the relationship may not stay linear – at high concentrations the heart rate may level off or fall because caffeine becomes toxic.
parts.working: B1 extrapolation outside range; B1 relationship may change / toxic effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find the heart rate at 8 mg cm⁻³.
parts.answer: Carry out the experiment at 8 mg cm⁻³ (and other concentrations between 2 and 8) and measure it.

author: HomiLabs
stem: A student plotted the mean heart rate of Daphnia against caffeine concentration for 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mg cm⁻³ and drew a straight line of best fit through the points.
Pressure in the aorta of a resting student was recorded every 0.05 s. Maximum pressure was 16.2 kPa and minimum pressure was 10.6 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the pulse pressure (maximum − minimum pressure).
parts.answer: 5.6 kPa

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pressure peaks at 0.20 s and again at 0.95 s. Calculate the heart rate.
parts.answer: 80 beats per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph of aortic pressure against time between the peaks.
parts.answer: A rapid rise to the peak followed by a slower fall, with a small notch / brief rise when the semilunar valve closes.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Standard haemoglobin solutions were used to draw a calibration line:
Haemoglobin / g dm⁻³: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200
Absorbance: 0.00, 0.21, 0.42, 0.63, 0.84

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the calibration line.
parts.answer: 0.0042 dm³ g⁻¹ (absorbance per g dm⁻³)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient's diluted blood has an absorbance of 0.55. Use the gradient to calculate the haemoglobin concentration, to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 131 g dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using the graph is more reliable than comparing the patient's sample with just one standard.
parts.answer: The line uses several standards, so random errors in one standard have less effect and it confirms the relationship is linear.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A graph of blood flow rate into the aorta against time is a triangle: flow rises from 0 to a peak of 450 cm³ s⁻¹ and falls back to 0, all within 0.32 s. For the rest of the cycle the flow rate is zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The volume pumped in one beat equals the area under the graph of flow rate against time. Calculate the stroke volume.
parts.answer: 72 cm³
parts.working: M1 area of triangle = ½ × 0.32 × 450; A1 = 72 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The heart rate is 75 beats per minute. Calculate the cardiac output in dm³ min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 5.4 dm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the flow rate is zero for the rest of the cycle.
parts.answer: The aortic semilunar valve is closed during diastole, so no blood leaves the ventricle.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to measure heart rate after running on the spot for 30, 60, 90, 120 and 150 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: The longer the time spent running on the spot, the higher the heart rate immediately afterwards.
parts.working: B1 must link IV and DV with a direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the shape of a graph of heart rate against running time and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Heart rate rises with running time and then levels off; muscles need more oxygen and produce more CO₂, but the heart rate cannot rise above its maximum.
parts.working: B1 rise then plateau; B1 explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A doctor in Bahawalpur compares the systolic blood pressure of 25 smokers and 25 non-smokers using a t-test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this comparison.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean systolic blood pressure of smokers and non-smokers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the alternative hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is a significant difference between the mean systolic blood pressure of smokers and non-smokers.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the heart rate of Daphnia will change if the temperature of the water is raised from 15 °C to 25 °C.
parts.answer: Heart rate will increase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Daphnia is an ectotherm, so its body temperature follows the water temperature; molecules have more kinetic energy, so enzyme-controlled reactions (respiration, muscle contraction) are faster.
parts.working: B1 ectotherm / body temp = water temp; B1 more kinetic energy / faster enzyme reactions.

parts.label: c
