parts.text: Predict what would happen above about 35 °C and explain.
parts.answer: Heart rate would fall (and the Daphnia may die), because enzymes and other proteins begin to denature.
parts.working: B1 fall; B1 denaturation.

stem: A student collects data on body mass and resting stroke volume for 12 adults.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is a positive correlation between body mass and resting stroke volume in adults.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the null hypothesis for Spearman's rank correlation test.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between body mass and resting stroke volume.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a biological reason for the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Larger people have larger hearts with bigger ventricles, so each beat ejects more blood (larger stroke volume).
parts.working: B1 larger heart / ventricle; B1 more blood pumped per beat.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A geneticist suspects that blood group O is more common in one of three cities. She records how many people in a sample from each city have blood group O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis for a chi-squared test on these data.
parts.answer: There is no difference in the proportion of people with blood group O between the three cities / any difference is due to chance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the null hypothesis is used rather than the researcher's own hypothesis.
parts.answer: Statistical tests calculate the probability that the observed differences arose by chance if there were no real difference; the null hypothesis can then be rejected or accepted at p = 0.05.
parts.working: B1 test measures probability of chance result; B1 reject / accept at 0.05.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how increasing the partial pressure of carbon dioxide will affect the percentage saturation of haemoglobin at pO₂ 3 kPa.
parts.answer: Percentage saturation will decrease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: CO₂ enters red blood cells and forms carbonic acid (catalysed by carbonic anhydrase), which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; H⁺ binds to haemoglobin, forming haemoglobinic acid, which lowers its affinity for oxygen; so more oxygen is released (Bohr shift).
parts.working: 1 mark each: carbonic acid → H⁺; H⁺ binds haemoglobin; lower affinity / curve shifts right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why 'exercise is good for your heart' is not a testable hypothesis.
parts.answer: It does not name measurable variables / 'good' cannot be measured.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite it as a testable hypothesis.
parts.answer: People who do more hours of aerobic exercise per week have a lower resting heart rate (or a larger stroke volume).
parts.working: B1 measurable IV; B1 measurable DV with direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothesis 1: 'Caffeine changes the heart rate of Daphnia.' Hypothesis 2: 'Caffeine increases the heart rate of Daphnia.' Explain the difference between them.
parts.answer: Hypothesis 1 is non-directional – it predicts a change in either direction; hypothesis 2 is directional – it predicts the direction of the change.
parts.working: B1 non-directional; B1 directional.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a scientist might choose hypothesis 2, and what evidence would be needed to support it.
parts.answer: Previous knowledge (caffeine is a stimulant) suggests an increase; the heart rate at higher caffeine concentrations must be significantly higher than in the control.
parts.working: B1 based on prior knowledge; B1 significant increase compared with control.

stem: A team of climbers from Lahore spends 4 weeks at a base camp at 5,000 m in the Karakoram. Their red blood cell counts are measured every week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the red blood cell count of the climbers will change over the 4 weeks.
parts.answer: It will gradually increase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Lower partial pressure of oxygen at altitude means haemoglobin is less saturated in the lungs, so less oxygen reaches tissues; the kidneys release a hormone that stimulates bone marrow to produce more red blood cells; more haemoglobin increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood; this takes days to weeks.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: low pO₂ / less saturation; stimulus to bone marrow (hormone from kidney); more haemoglobin / O₂ capacity; takes time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what will happen to the count after the climbers return to sea level for several weeks.
parts.answer: It will gradually fall back towards the sea-level value.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to test whether compression socks reduce ankle swelling on long bus journeys from Karachi to Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Wearing compression socks reduces the increase in ankle circumference during long periods of sitting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological basis for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Sitting still raises hydrostatic pressure in the leg capillaries and veins, so more tissue fluid forms; compression socks increase the pressure in the tissue fluid outside the capillaries; so less fluid is forced out and more returns / lymph and venous return are helped.
parts.working: 1 mark each: high hydrostatic pressure when sitting; socks raise external / tissue fluid pressure; less net filtration / more drainage.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis linking hand temperature and capillary refill time.
parts.answer: As hand temperature increases, capillary refill time decreases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give a biological reason for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: In warm conditions arterioles in the skin dilate, so more blood flows into the skin capillaries and they refill faster; cold causes vasoconstriction.
parts.working: B1 vasodilation in warm / vasoconstriction in cold; B1 faster refill with more blood flow.

stem:
Hypothesis: 'Faster music increases heart rate.' Results (10 volunteers):
Tempo / beats per minute: 60, 90, 120, 150
Mean heart rate / bpm: 72, 72, 75, 77
Standard deviation: 6, 7, 6, 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the results support the hypothesis. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Partly: the means show heart rate higher at 120 and 150 bpm than at 60 bpm, which supports it; but 90 bpm gives the same mean as 60 bpm and the standard deviations (about 6–7) are larger than most differences, so the differences may not be significant; a statistical test is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: overall trend supports; 60 = 90 not supported; SDs overlap / need statistical test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be improved to give stronger evidence.
parts.answer: Use more volunteers; randomise the order of tempos; rest between tempos; carry out a statistical test (e.g. t-test between 60 and 150).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the myoglobin concentration in the swimming muscles of a sperm whale compares with that in the leg muscles of a cow. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Higher in the whale; it dives for long periods without breathing; myoglobin stores oxygen in muscles and releases it at very low pO₂, allowing aerobic respiration to continue during the dive.
parts.working: B1 higher; B1 long dives; B1 oxygen store released at low pO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a prediction about the colour of the whale's muscle compared with the cow's, giving a reason.
parts.answer: Darker (almost black-red), because myoglobin is a red pigment and there is much more of it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis, including the biological mechanism, that the student could test.
parts.answer: Increasing the concentration of caffeine increases the heart rate of Daphnia because caffeine stimulates the pacemaker (SAN-like region) to send waves of excitation more often.
parts.working: B1 IV and DV with direction; B1 mechanism.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the result for the control (pond water only) and explain why it is needed.
parts.answer: Heart rate should stay about the same over time; this shows that any increase is due to caffeine, not to handling, light or temperature.
parts.working: B1 no change; B1 reason.

author: HomiLabs
stem: A student investigates the effect of caffeine on the heart rate of Daphnia by adding caffeine solution to Daphnia on a cavity slide and counting heartbeats.
During a football match in Lyari, a player's heart rate rises from 70 to 170 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why heart rate increases during exercise.
parts.answer: Muscles respire faster, so they need more oxygen and glucose and produce more carbon dioxide; a higher heart rate increases cardiac output; so blood delivers oxygen and removes CO₂ faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more respiration / more O₂ needed; more CO₂ / heat produced; higher cardiac output / faster delivery.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student's heart rate was still 110 beats per minute four minutes after a 200 m sprint.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why heart rate and breathing rate remain high for several minutes after exercise has stopped.
parts.answer: During intense exercise some anaerobic respiration produced lactate; extra oxygen is needed after exercise (oxygen debt) to oxidise lactate / convert it back to glucose in the liver; blood must also continue to remove CO₂ and heat, and restore oxygen stores in myoglobin.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: anaerobic respiration / lactate; oxygen debt; lactate removed using O₂; CO₂ / heat removal; restore myoglobin / ATP stores.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean heart rate of Daphnia at different temperatures:
Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35
Heart rate / bpm: 110, 160, 215, 280, 300, 210

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in heart rate between 10 °C and 25 °C.
parts.answer: Daphnia is an ectotherm, so the temperature of its tissues rises; enzymes and molecules have more kinetic energy, so respiration and muscle contraction are faster, and the pacemaker fires more often.
parts.working: B1 kinetic energy / more collisions; B1 faster enzyme-controlled reactions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the fall in heart rate at 35 °C.
parts.answer: Above the optimum, enzymes (and other proteins such as membrane channels) start to denature as hydrogen bonds break; fewer active sites function, so reactions slow.
parts.working: B1 denaturation; B1 change in active site / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rings of artery and vein were stretched with the same mass. When the mass was removed, the artery ring recoiled by 94 % but the vein ring by only 52 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lower elastic recoil of vein walls does not stop blood returning to the heart.
parts.answer: Veins carry blood at low pressure, so their walls do not need to recoil; valves stop blood flowing backwards; contracting skeletal muscles squeeze the veins and push blood towards the heart.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: low pressure, so no need for recoil; valves prevent backflow; skeletal muscle squeezes veins (muscle pump).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this property is important to the artery in the body.
parts.answer: The artery wall stretches when blood is pumped in during systole and recoils in diastole; this smooths the flow and maintains pressure between beats.
parts.working: B1 stretch in systole; B1 recoil maintains pressure / smooth flow.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Climbers resting at Fairy Meadows camp (about 3,300 m) and at 4,500 m on the way to Nanga Parbat had a mean SpO₂ of 90 % and 84 %. At sea level their SpO₂ was 98 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the climbers' blood oxygen saturation is lower at 4,500 m than at sea level.
parts.answer: Atmospheric pressure is lower, so the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is lower; haemoglobin loads less oxygen in the lungs.
parts.working: B1 lower pO₂; B1 less loading of haemoglobin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why their heart rate at rest is higher at altitude.
parts.answer: Each dm³ of blood carries less oxygen, so to deliver the same amount of oxygen to tissues per minute the cardiac output must rise.
parts.working: B1 less O₂ per volume of blood; B1 more blood pumped per minute.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A national hockey player has a resting heart rate of 48 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 110 cm³. An untrained student has a resting heart rate of 75 and a stroke volume of 70 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cardiac output of each person in dm³ min⁻¹ and state what this shows.
parts.answer: Hockey player 5.28 dm³ min⁻¹; student 5.25 dm³ min⁻¹. Their resting cardiac outputs are almost the same, so the larger stroke volume of the athlete is balanced by a lower heart rate.
parts.working: B1 110 × 48 = 5280 cm³ min⁻¹ = 5.28 dm³ min⁻¹ and 70 × 75 = 5250 cm³ min⁻¹ = 5.25 dm³ min⁻¹; B1 similar output reached with fewer beats per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how training increases stroke volume.
parts.answer: The ventricle wall muscle becomes thicker / stronger and the ventricle larger, so it fills with and ejects more blood in each beat.
parts.working: B1 stronger / thicker muscle; B1 larger chamber / more complete emptying.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a standing adult, mean arterial pressure was about 24 kPa in the feet and about 8 kPa in the head.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the blood pressure in the arteries of the feet is higher than in the arteries of the head when a person is standing.
parts.answer: The weight of the column of blood above the feet adds to the pressure produced by the heart (gravity); the head is above the heart, so blood must be pushed up against gravity and pressure is lower.
parts.working: B1 gravity / weight of blood column adds in feet; B1 against gravity to head.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the person lies down, the pressures in the head and feet become almost equal. Explain why.
parts.answer: The head, heart and feet are at the same level, so gravity no longer adds or subtracts pressure.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Blood leaving a resting forearm muscle was 70 % saturated with oxygen. Blood leaving the same muscle during hand-grip exercise, at a similar pO₂, was 55 % saturated. The blood from the exercising muscle had a higher carbon dioxide concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the percentage saturation of the blood leaving the active muscle was lower than that leaving the resting muscle, although the pO₂ of the two muscles was similar.
parts.answer: Active muscle produces more CO₂ (and heat); CO₂ forms carbonic acid in red blood cells, which releases H⁺; H⁺ binds to haemoglobin and lowers its affinity for oxygen (Bohr effect), so more oxygen is unloaded.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more CO₂ in active muscle; H⁺ from carbonic acid binds haemoglobin; lower affinity / Bohr shift, more O₂ released.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A patient with severe anaemia (haemoglobin 70 g dm⁻³) has a resting heart rate of 98 beats per minute. After three months of iron treatment her haemoglobin is 130 g dm⁻³ and her resting heart rate is 74 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the resting heart rate of the anaemic patient is higher than normal.
parts.answer: Less haemoglobin, so each dm³ of blood carries less oxygen; to supply the tissues with enough oxygen, more blood must be delivered per minute; cardiac output is raised by increasing the heart rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less haemoglobin / less O₂ per dm³; tissues need same O₂ supply; higher heart rate increases cardiac output.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: On Earth, gravity keeps more blood and tissue fluid in the legs. Suggest why astronauts' faces become puffy in space while their legs become thinner.
parts.answer: Without gravity, blood and fluid are no longer pulled down into the legs, so more is redistributed to the upper body and head; hydrostatic pressure in the head and face capillaries rises; more tissue fluid forms there, while less forms in the legs.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no gravitational pooling in legs; fluid shifts to head / upper body; higher capillary hydrostatic pressure in face → more tissue fluid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why astronauts may feel faint when they first stand up after returning to Earth.
parts.answer: Blood volume / leg vessel tone has adapted to weightlessness; on standing, blood pools in the legs, venous return and cardiac output fall, so less blood reaches the brain.
parts.working: B1 pooling in legs / less venous return; B1 less blood to brain.

stem: Pakistani middle-distance runners trained for 3 weeks at a high-altitude camp. Their mean haemoglobin concentration rose from 148 to 157 g dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in haemoglobin concentration over the 3 weeks.
parts.answer: At altitude the low pO₂ means less oxygen reaches the tissues; the kidneys detect low oxygen and release a hormone that stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow; more red blood cells means more haemoglobin per dm³; this takes days to weeks because new cells must be made and mature.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: low pO₂ / less O₂ to tissues; hormone from kidney; stimulates bone marrow; more red cells; time needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the increase helps the athletes when they return to compete at sea level.
parts.answer: Blood can carry more oxygen per dm³, so more oxygen is delivered to muscles; more aerobic respiration and less lactate, improving endurance.
parts.working: B1 higher O₂ carrying capacity; B1 more aerobic respiration / endurance.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Blood of 20 heavy smokers and 20 non-smokers in Lahore was tested.
Mean carboxyhaemoglobin: smokers 7 %, non-smokers 1 %.
Mean red blood cell count: smokers 5.4 × 10⁶ mm⁻³, non-smokers 5.0 × 10⁶ mm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the smokers have a higher percentage of carboxyhaemoglobin.
parts.answer: Tobacco smoke contains carbon monoxide; CO binds to haem much more strongly than oxygen (and almost irreversibly), so it stays attached.
parts.working: B1 CO in smoke; B1 high affinity / binds strongly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the smokers also have a higher red blood cell count.
parts.answer: With some haemoglobin blocked by CO, less oxygen reaches the tissues; this stimulates the production of more red blood cells to compensate.
parts.working: B1 less O₂ delivered; B1 more red cells made in compensation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: When seals dive, their heart rate falls from about 100 to 10 beats per minute and the arterioles supplying their limbs and gut constrict.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how slowing the heart and constricting the arterioles to the limbs helps a diving mammal to survive a long dive.
parts.answer: A slower heart uses less ATP / oxygen; constricting arterioles to limbs and gut reduces their blood flow, so oxygenated blood is kept for the brain and heart; the oxygen store lasts longer; limb muscles use myoglobin oxygen / anaerobic respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: less O₂ used by heart; blood diverted to brain / heart; O₂ lasts longer; limbs rely on myoglobin / anaerobic respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When a person puts their face in cold water while holding their breath, heart rate falls by about 10–25 %. Suggest why the fall is greater in cold water than in warm water.
parts.answer: Cold receptors in the face trigger the reflex more strongly (the reflex is a response to cold water on the face).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A volunteer's capillary refill time was 1.8 s after her hand had been in water at 35 °C and 3.9 s after it had been in water at 10 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the capillary refill time is longer when the hand is cold.
parts.answer: Cold causes the smooth muscle in the walls of the skin arterioles to contract (vasoconstriction); the lumen narrows so less blood flows into the skin capillaries; so the capillaries take longer to fill again after being pressed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: arterioles constrict; less blood flow to capillaries; slower refill.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: Systolic blood pressure (mmHg) of six nurses at a hospital in Hyderabad: 118, 124, 121, 130, 115, 126

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean systolic pressure, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 122.3 mmHg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation, to 2 decimal places, using s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
parts.answer: 5.47 mmHg
parts.working: M1 deviations from mean squared; M1 Σ = 149.33, ÷ 5 = 29.87; A1 √29.87 = 5.47.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: Resting heart rate (bpm) of nine students: 64, 70, 68, 75, 72, 66, 71, 69, 74

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation, each to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Mean 69.89 bpm; s = 3.59 bpm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean (SE = s ÷ √n), to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) and state what it means.
parts.answer: 67.50 to 72.28 bpm; we can be 95 % confident that the true mean resting heart rate of the population lies in this range.
parts.working: B1 limits; B1 meaning.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: Capillary refill time (s) of two groups of eight volunteers. Group C put one hand in water at 10 °C; group W put one hand in water at 30 °C: / Group C (10 °C): 3.6, 4.1, 3.8, 4.4, 3.2, 4.0, 3.9, 3.5 / Group W (30 °C): 2.1, 2.5, 1.9, 2.8, 2.2, 2.6, 2.0, 2.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation of each group, to 2 decimal places, using s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
parts.answer: Group C 0.38 s; group W 0.31 s.
parts.working: B1 means 3.81 s and 2.31 s used; B1 s = 0.38 and 0.31 (Σ(x − x̄)² = 0.99 and 0.69).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t, to 2 decimal places, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t for 14 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 2.14. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: 8.67 > 2.14, so reject the null hypothesis: capillary refill time is significantly longer at 10 °C than at 30 °C.
parts.working: B1 comparison with 2.14; B1 significant difference with direction.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: Altitude and mean red blood cell count of residents of nine villages in northern Pakistan: / Altitude / m: 300, 900, 1500, 1900, 2300, 2700, 3100, 3500, 4000 / Red blood cell count / million per mm³: 4.8, 5.1, 4.9, 5.4, 5.3, 5.7, 5.6, 6.0, 5.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rank both variables (lowest = 1) and calculate Σd².
parts.answer: Altitude ranks 1 to 9; red blood cell count ranks 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6, 9, 8; Σd² = 8.
parts.working: M1 correct ranks; A1 Σd² = 8 (each d = ±1 for eight of the nine pairs and 0 for one).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 9 at p = 0.05 is 0.70. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.70, so there is a significant positive correlation: higher altitude is associated with a higher red blood cell count.
parts.working: B1 comparison with 0.70; B1 significant positive correlation.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
100 children were tested for anaemia in each of three districts:
District P: 38 anaemic, 62 not anaemic
District Q: 25 anaemic, 75 not anaemic
District R: 22 anaemic, 78 not anaemic

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of anaemic and non-anaemic children in each district, if there were no difference between districts.
parts.answer: Anaemic 28.33; non-anaemic 71.67 in each district

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 sum of six terms (3.298 + 1.304 + 0.392 + 0.155 + 1.416 + 0.560); A1 7.12 (rounding each term first gives 7.13).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom and, using the critical value 5.99 at p = 0.05, a conclusion.
parts.answer: df = (3 − 1)(2 − 1) = 2; 7.12 > 5.99, so the difference between districts is significant – anaemia is not equally common in the three districts.
parts.working: B1 df = 2; B1 conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the statistical test for each investigation:
(i) comparing mean haemoglobin concentration of 20 men and 20 women
(ii) testing for a relationship between age and systolic blood pressure in 15 people
(iii) comparing the numbers of people with blood groups A, B, AB and O in a sample with expected numbers.
parts.answer: (i) t-test; (ii) Spearman's rank correlation; (iii) chi-squared test
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one condition that data must meet for a t-test to be suitable.
parts.answer: Continuous data that are approximately normally distributed (with similar variance); two independent groups.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: A t-test compares the resting heart rates of 9 swimmers and 11 non-swimmers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of t for 18 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 2.10. The calculated value is 2.45. State what this shows.
parts.answer: 2.45 > 2.10, so the probability that the difference is due to chance is less than 5 %; reject the null hypothesis – the difference between the means is significant.
parts.working: B1 comparison; B1 significant / reject null.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: The heart rates of 16 students after a 1 km walk have a standard deviation of 8.4 bpm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.answer: 2.1 bpm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sample size is increased to 64 and s stays the same. Calculate the new standard error and explain what this shows.
parts.answer: 1.05 bpm; a larger sample gives a smaller SE, so the sample mean is a more reliable estimate of the population mean.
parts.working: B1 1.05; B1 larger n → more reliable mean.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Heart rate after climbing five floors of stairs:
Group A (office workers, n = 25): mean 82 bpm, s = 6
Group B (security guards, n = 25): mean 76 bpm, s = 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2SE, where SE = s ÷ √n) for each group.
parts.answer: Group A: 79.6 to 84.4 bpm; group B: 74.0 to 78.0 bpm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what can be concluded from the two intervals.
parts.answer: They do not overlap, so the difference between the means is likely to be significant.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Resting heart rates (bpm) of two groups of five students:
Group X: 70, 72, 71, 69, 73
Group Y: 60, 82, 71, 65, 77

parts.label: a
parts.text: Both groups have a mean of 71 bpm. Calculate the standard deviation of each group to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the standard deviations show about the two groups.
parts.answer: Group Y's heart rates are much more spread out about the mean than group X's; so the mean represents group X much better / group X is more uniform.
parts.working: B1 Y more variable; B1 mean less representative for Y.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: For 12 students, a student calculated Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between hours of sleep per night and resting heart rate: rs = −0.54. The critical value for n = 12 at p = 0.05 is 0.59.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion from this result.
parts.answer: 0.54 < 0.59, so the correlation is not significant at p = 0.05; accept the null hypothesis of no correlation between hours of sleep and resting heart rate.
parts.working: B1 comparison; B1 not significant / accept null.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why Spearman's rank correlation was used rather than Pearson's correlation coefficient.
parts.answer: Spearman's does not require the data to be normally distributed or the relationship to be linear; it tests for a monotonic relationship using ranks, and the sample is small.
parts.working: B1 no assumption of normal distribution; B1 linear not needed / ranks / monotonic.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
100 men aged 50 were surveyed:
Smokers (50): 30 with high blood pressure, 20 normal
Non-smokers (50): 18 with high blood pressure, 32 normal

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers for each of the four cells if smoking has no effect on blood pressure.
parts.answer: Smokers: 24 high, 26 normal; non-smokers: 24 high, 26 normal
parts.working: M1 expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total (50 × 48 ÷ 100); A1 all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ², to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 5.77 > 3.84, so there is a significant association between smoking and high blood pressure.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Systolic blood pressure (mmHg) of people eating a high-salt and a low-salt diet:
High salt (n = 14): mean 132.4, s = 11.2
Low salt (n = 12): mean 124.1, s = 9.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate t, to 2 decimal places, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the degrees of freedom. The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for this number of degrees of freedom is 2.06. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: df = 24; 2.03 < 2.06, so the difference is not significant at p = 0.05 – accept the null hypothesis.
parts.working: B1 df 24; B1 conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the researcher should not conclude that salt has no effect on blood pressure.
parts.answer: t is very close to the critical value; with larger samples the difference might prove significant (a non-significant result does not prove no effect).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
For eight students, exercise intensity score and heart rate after exercise (bpm) were recorded:
Intensity score: 3.1, 4.5, 2.2, 5.8, 3.9, 6.4, 1.7, 5.0
Heart rate / bpm: 71, 78, 66, 85, 80, 82, 64, 76

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the ranking (lowest = 1) and calculate Σd².
parts.answer: Exercise ranks: 3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 8, 1, 6; Heart-rate ranks: 3, 5, 2, 8, 6, 7, 1, 4; Σd² = 10

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)) to 2 decimal places, and state a conclusion given that the critical value for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.74.
parts.answer: rs = 0.88; 0.88 > 0.74, so there is a significant positive correlation between exercise intensity and heart rate after exercise.
parts.working: B1 0.88; B1 conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four events in aerobic respiration are listed.
P: glucose is phosphorylated using ATP
Q: acetyl coenzyme A is formed
R: oxaloacetate is regenerated
S: triose phosphate is oxidised by removal of hydrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each event P, Q, R and S, name the stage of aerobic respiration in which it occurs.
parts.answer: P glycolysis; Q link reaction; R Krebs cycle; S glycolysis
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the precise location in a eukaryotic cell of the stage in which event Q occurs.
parts.answer: Mitochondrial matrix
parts.working: B1 matrix of the mitochondrion (not just 'mitochondrion').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why two ATP molecules are used at the start of glycolysis even though the aim of respiration is to make ATP.
parts.answer: Phosphorylation makes glucose more reactive / lowers the activation energy for splitting it into two triose phosphates; more ATP (4) is made later, so there is a net gain of 2 ATP.
parts.working: B1 phosphorylated glucose (hexose bisphosphate) is more reactive / less stable so it can be split; B1 4 ATP are produced later giving a net gain of 2.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of carbon atoms in each of these molecules: glucose, pyruvate, the acetyl group of acetyl coenzyme A, citrate and oxaloacetate.
parts.answer: glucose 6; pyruvate 3; acetyl group 2; citrate 6; oxaloacetate 4
parts.working: 2 marks all five correct; 1 mark for three or four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of molecules of carbon dioxide released in the link reaction and in the Krebs cycle from one molecule of glucose, and state the total.
parts.answer: link reaction 2; Krebs cycle 4; total 6
parts.working: M1 2 pyruvate × 1 CO₂ = 2 in the link reaction; 2 turns × 2 CO₂ = 4 in Krebs; A1 total 6 (all six carbons of glucose leave as CO₂).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the process in which carbon dioxide is removed from a respiratory intermediate.
parts.answer: Decarboxylation
parts.working: B1 decarboxylation.

stem: Coenzymes play an important part in the reactions of glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the role of NAD in these stages.
parts.answer: NAD accepts hydrogen (is reduced) when dehydrogenase enzymes remove hydrogen from intermediates; it carries the hydrogen to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen acceptor / becomes reduced NAD in dehydrogenation; B1 carries hydrogen (protons and electrons) to the electron transport chain / cristae.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of coenzyme A.
parts.answer: It carries the acetyl (2C) group from the link reaction into the Krebs cycle.
parts.working: B1 combines with the acetyl group and transfers it to oxaloacetate / into the Krebs cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other hydrogen carrier, apart from NAD, that is reduced in the Krebs cycle.
parts.answer: FAD
parts.working: B1 FAD.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is needed to make a coenzyme used by the enzyme complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A. People whose diet is mainly polished white rice can develop thiamine deficiency (beriberi).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how thiamine deficiency affects the concentration of pyruvate in cells. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Pyruvate concentration rises, because the link reaction is slowed so pyruvate made in glycolysis is not converted to acetyl coenzyme A.
parts.working: B1 pyruvate increases; B1 because the enzyme (pyruvate dehydrogenase) of the link reaction works more slowly / pyruvate is not decarboxylated and dehydrogenated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Patients with thiamine deficiency often have high concentrations of lactate in the blood. Explain why.
parts.answer: Excess pyruvate is reduced to lactate by reduced NAD (lactate dehydrogenase), which regenerates NAD so that glycolysis can continue to supply ATP.
parts.working: B1 pyruvate converted to lactate; B1 this regenerates NAD / allows glycolysis to continue when the link reaction is limited.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why nerve cells and heart muscle are among the first tissues affected by thiamine deficiency.
parts.answer: They have a high demand for ATP and rely heavily on aerobic respiration of glucose / pyruvate; less acetyl CoA enters the Krebs cycle so less reduced NAD and ATP are produced.
parts.working: B1 high ATP demand (impulses, active transport, continuous contraction); B1 depend on aerobic respiration via the link reaction / Krebs cycle so ATP supply falls.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A liver cell completely oxidises 3.0 × 10⁶ molecules of glucose per second by aerobic respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of molecules of reduced NAD produced per second in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle together.
parts.answer: 3.0e+07 molecules per second (3.0 × 10⁷)
parts.working: M1 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 reduced NAD per glucose; A1 10 × 3.0 × 10⁶ = 3.0 × 10⁷ s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of molecules of carbon dioxide released per second.
parts.answer: 1.8e+07 (1.8 × 10⁷) per second

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of this carbon dioxide that is released in the Krebs cycle. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why no carbon dioxide is released in glycolysis.
parts.answer: Glycolysis involves no decarboxylation: the 6C glucose is split into two 3C molecules, so all carbon atoms remain in pyruvate.
parts.working: B1 no decarboxylation / glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (2 × 3C), no carbon lost.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Isolated mitochondria were suspended in a buffer containing pyruvate, coenzyme A, NAD and a very small concentration of oxaloacetate. The rate of oxygen uptake was low. When extra oxaloacetate was added, the rate of oxygen uptake increased sharply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why only a small amount of oxaloacetate is needed in a cell for the Krebs cycle to continue for long periods.
parts.answer: Oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end of each turn of the cycle, so each molecule is used again and again (it is not used up).
parts.working: B1 oxaloacetate combines with acetyl CoA to form citrate; B1 it is regenerated at the end of each turn / reused.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why adding extra oxaloacetate increased the rate of oxygen uptake by the mitochondria.
parts.answer: More acetyl CoA can combine with oxaloacetate to form citrate, so more turns of the Krebs cycle per unit time; more reduced NAD and reduced FAD are produced; more electrons pass along the electron transport chain to oxygen, the final acceptor.
parts.working: B1 more citrate formed / more turns of Krebs cycle; B1 more dehydrogenation / more reduced NAD and FAD; B1 more electrons passed to oxygen via the electron transport chain so more O₂ used.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A cell was broken up and centrifuged to separate a mitochondria fraction from the cytoplasm (cytosol) fraction. Samples were placed in four tubes with an oxygen electrode. Oxygen uptake after 10 minutes:
tube 1: mitochondria + glucose — no oxygen uptake
tube 2: mitochondria + pyruvate — high oxygen uptake
tube 3: cytosol + glucose — no oxygen uptake
tube 4: mitochondria + cytosol + glucose — high oxygen uptake
All tubes contained NAD, ADP and phosphate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result for tube 1.
parts.answer: Glycolysis enzymes are in the cytoplasm, not in mitochondria, so glucose cannot be converted to pyruvate; mitochondria cannot use glucose directly (no carrier for glucose in the mitochondrial membranes).
parts.working: B1 enzymes of glycolysis are in the cytosol / not in mitochondria; B1 glucose not converted to pyruvate so no substrate for the link reaction / Krebs cycle, so no reduced NAD for the electron transport chain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result for tube 3.
parts.answer: Glycolysis can take place, producing pyruvate and reduced NAD, but there is no electron transport chain (it is on the inner mitochondrial membrane) so oxygen is not used.
parts.working: B1 glycolysis occurs / pyruvate is made; B1 no electron transport chain / cristae, so no oxygen used as final electron acceptor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use all four results to explain what tube 4 shows about the link between glycolysis and the mitochondria.
parts.answer: The cytosol converts glucose to pyruvate in glycolysis; the pyruvate is then taken into the mitochondria for the link reaction and Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation uses oxygen.
parts.working: B1 glucose → pyruvate in cytosol; B1 pyruvate enters mitochondria where link reaction / Krebs / electron transport (O₂ use) occur; both fractions needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In this question, assume that each reduced NAD produces 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD produces 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. Per molecule of glucose: glycolysis produces 2 reduced NAD and a net 2 ATP; the link reaction produces 2 reduced NAD; the Krebs cycle (two turns) produces 6 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD and 2 ATP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of ATP molecules that can be credited to each stage (glycolysis, link reaction, Krebs cycle), including ATP later made from the reduced coenzymes formed in that stage.
parts.answer: glycolysis 7; link reaction 5; Krebs cycle 20

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total ATP yield that can be credited to the Krebs cycle. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Most ATP credited to the Krebs cycle is not made in the Krebs cycle itself. Explain this statement.
parts.answer: Only 2 ATP are made directly by substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle; the rest are made by oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis via ATP synthase) on the inner membrane using the hydrogen carried by reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
parts.working: B1 only 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation in the matrix; B1 the rest by oxidative phosphorylation / electron transport chain / ATP synthase using reduced NAD and FAD.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a rare inherited condition, the Krebs cycle enzyme that converts the 4C compound fumarate to malate is almost inactive. Fumarate accumulates in the cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effect of this condition on the number of turns of the Krebs cycle per minute.
parts.answer: The number of turns falls, because malate and then oxaloacetate are not regenerated, so less acetyl CoA can combine with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
parts.working: B1 fewer turns / cycle slows; B1 oxaloacetate not regenerated so acetyl CoA cannot enter / less citrate formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cells produce less ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
parts.answer: Fewer dehydrogenation reactions so less reduced NAD (and reduced FAD) is produced; fewer electrons pass along the electron transport chain, fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made by ATP synthase.
parts.working: B1 less reduced NAD / FAD produced; B1 less electron transport / smaller proton gradient so less chemiosmosis / ATP synthase activity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cells of affected people rely more on glycolysis and produce more lactate.
parts.answer: Glycolysis still produces some ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation; pyruvate that cannot be oxidised in the mitochondria is reduced to lactate, regenerating NAD so glycolysis can continue.
parts.working: B1 glycolysis provides ATP independent of the Krebs cycle; B1 pyruvate → lactate regenerates NAD.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Five events in oxidative phosphorylation are listed in random order.
1 Protons diffuse back into the matrix through ATP synthase.
2 Reduced NAD releases hydrogen at the inner mitochondrial membrane.
3 Hydrogen atoms split into protons and electrons.
4 Electrons pass along a series of carriers.
5 Energy from electrons is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the numbers 1 to 5 in the correct order.
parts.answer: 2, 3, 4, 5, 1 (events 4 and 5 happen together as electrons move down the chain, so 2, 3, 5, 4, 1 is also accepted)
parts.working: 2 marks for the correct order; 1 mark if only one event is out of place. Event 1 must come last, because the proton gradient has to be built by events 4 and 5 before protons flow back through ATP synthase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process in which ATP is made as protons move down their concentration gradient.
parts.answer: Chemiosmosis
parts.working: B1 chemiosmosis (accept oxidative phosphorylation).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why oxygen is described as the final electron acceptor.
parts.answer: It accepts electrons from the last carrier of the electron transport chain (and combines with protons to form water), allowing the chain to keep working.
parts.working: B1 receives electrons at the end of the chain / removes electrons from last carrier.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the part of the mitochondrion where each of the following is found: the electron transport chain; ATP synthase; the enzymes of the Krebs cycle; the highest concentration of protons.
parts.answer: electron transport chain: inner membrane / cristae; ATP synthase: inner membrane / cristae; Krebs enzymes: matrix; highest proton concentration: intermembrane space
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the inner mitochondrial membrane must be impermeable to protons except through ATP synthase.
parts.answer: So that the proton gradient (high in intermembrane space, low in matrix) can be maintained; protons can only flow back through ATP synthase, so the energy of the gradient is used to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
parts.working: B1 maintains the proton (electrochemical) gradient; B1 protons only return through ATP synthase so ATP is made.

stem: Measurements from electron micrographs of a liver mitochondrion gave an outer membrane area of 12 µm² and an inner membrane area of 58 µm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of inner membrane area to outer membrane area. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the folding of the inner membrane into cristae increases the rate of ATP production.
parts.answer: Folding gives a larger surface area for more electron transport chains and ATP synthase molecules, so more oxidative phosphorylation can occur at once.
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more electron carriers / ATP synthase so more ATP made per unit time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one feature, other than cristae, that you would expect to see in a liver cell that has a high rate of aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: Many mitochondria per cell (accept large matrix containing many enzymes).
parts.working: B1 many mitochondria / large mitochondria.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In actively respiring mitochondria, the pH of the intermembrane space was measured as 7.0 and the pH of the matrix as 7.8. pH = −log₁₀[H⁺].

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the proton concentration is in the intermembrane space than in the matrix. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 6.3 times
parts.working: M1 difference of 0.8 pH units so ratio = 10⁰·⁸; A1 6.3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this difference in proton concentration is produced.
parts.answer: Energy released as electrons pass along the electron transport chain is used by carrier proteins to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space (active transport).
parts.working: B1 energy from electron transfer along carriers; B1 protons pumped from matrix to intermembrane space.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the pH of the matrix if ATP synthase were blocked while electron transport briefly continued. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The matrix pH would rise slightly (become more alkaline) as protons continue to be pumped out but cannot return through ATP synthase.
parts.working: B1 pH rises / matrix more alkaline; B1 protons removed but no return route.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rotenone is a pesticide that stops electrons passing from reduced NAD to the first carrier of the electron transport chain. Reduced FAD passes its electrons to a different carrier further along the chain. Isolated mitochondria were given either malate (whose oxidation produces reduced NAD) or succinate (whose oxidation produces reduced FAD), with and without rotenone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of rotenone on oxygen uptake by mitochondria given malate. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake falls to (almost) zero, because electrons from reduced NAD cannot enter the chain so no electrons reach oxygen.
parts.working: B1 oxygen uptake stops / falls greatly; B1 electrons from reduced NAD cannot enter / pass along the chain to oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why mitochondria given succinate still take up oxygen in the presence of rotenone.
parts.answer: Reduced FAD donates electrons to a carrier after the point blocked by rotenone, so electrons still pass along the rest of the chain to oxygen.
parts.working: B1 FAD enters the chain at a later carrier / bypasses the blocked step; B1 electrons still reach oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why less ATP is made per molecule of succinate oxidised than per molecule of malate oxidised.
parts.answer: Electrons from reduced FAD pass through fewer proton pumps, so fewer protons are pumped into the intermembrane space; less ATP is made by ATP synthase (about 1.5 instead of 2.5).
parts.working: B1 fewer proton pumps / fewer protons pumped; B1 so fewer ATP produced by chemiosmosis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mitochondria were placed in a buffer containing pyruvate, oxygen and phosphate. The rate of oxygen uptake was 12 nmol min⁻¹. When ADP was added, the rate rose to 58 nmol min⁻¹. When all the ADP had been converted to ATP, the rate fell back to 12 nmol min⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster oxygen was taken up after ADP was added. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oxygen uptake was low when no ADP was present.
parts.answer: Without ADP, ATP synthase cannot make ATP, so protons do not flow back into the matrix; the proton gradient builds up until pumping is very difficult; electron transport slows, so less oxygen is used.
parts.working: B1 ATP synthase needs ADP (and Pi) / no ATP synthesis; B1 protons do not return to the matrix so the gradient becomes very steep; B1 electron transport / proton pumping slows so less O₂ reduced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this effect is useful in a living muscle cell.
parts.answer: The rate of respiration automatically matches the demand for ATP: when ATP is used and ADP rises, respiration speeds up; when resting, substrate is not wasted.
parts.working: B1 respiration rate matches ATP demand / substrate is conserved at rest.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume that 10 protons are pumped into the intermembrane space for each reduced NAD oxidised, 6 protons for each reduced FAD, and that 4 protons must flow back into the matrix (including transport of ADP and phosphate) for each ATP made. Calculate the number of ATP made per reduced NAD and per reduced FAD.
parts.answer: reduced NAD 2.5 ATP; reduced FAD 1.5 ATP

parts.label: b
parts.text: One glucose molecule gives 10 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD and 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. Use your answers to (a) to calculate the total ATP yield per glucose.
parts.answer: 32 ATP

parts.label: c
parts.text: In some cells about 15 % of the protons pumped leak back across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase. Calculate the new total ATP yield per glucose, assuming substrate-level phosphorylation is unchanged.
parts.answer: 27.8 ATP
parts.working: M1 oxidative phosphorylation yield 28 × 0.85 = 23.8; A1 23.8 + 4 = 27.8 ATP.

stem: Oligomycin is an antibiotic that blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. A suspension of respiring mitochondria with plenty of substrate, ADP and phosphate was set up in an oxygen electrode. Oligomycin was added at 4 minutes. At 8 minutes the uncoupler DNP, which makes the inner membrane freely permeable to protons, was added.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the change in the rate of oxygen uptake after oligomycin was added.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake falls to near zero; protons can no longer flow back through ATP synthase, so the proton gradient builds up; the gradient slows and then stops proton pumping, so electron transport stops and oxygen is no longer reduced.
parts.working: B1 rate falls (to near zero); B1 protons cannot return through ATP synthase / gradient builds up; B1 electron transport chain slows / stops so O₂ not used as final acceptor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the change in the rate of oxygen uptake and in ATP production after DNP was added.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake increases again (rapidly) because protons leak back through the membrane, removing the gradient so electron transport and proton pumping restart; ATP production stays near zero because ATP synthase is still blocked and the proton gradient is dissipated; energy is released as heat.
parts.working: B1 oxygen uptake rises; B1 gradient dissipated so electron transport resumes; B1 no ATP made (ATP synthase blocked / gradient lost) / energy lost as heat.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A teenager had muscle weakness and tired very quickly. After a short walk, her blood lactate concentration was 6.5 mmol dm⁻³ (normal after the same walk: 1.5 mmol dm⁻³). A muscle biopsy showed mitochondria with very few, short cristae.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how having few cristae reduces the ATP available for muscle contraction.
parts.answer: Smaller surface area of inner membrane; fewer electron transport chains and ATP synthase molecules; less oxidative phosphorylation, so far less ATP per glucose (most ATP normally comes from oxidative phosphorylation).
parts.working: B1 smaller area of inner membrane; B1 fewer electron carriers / ATP synthase; B1 less oxidative phosphorylation / chemiosmosis so less ATP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the high blood lactate concentration after mild exercise.
parts.answer: Reduced NAD cannot be reoxidised quickly by the electron transport chain; pyruvate accumulates and is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD; glycolysis continues to provide some ATP; lactate diffuses into the blood.
parts.working: B1 reduced NAD not reoxidised by ETC / Krebs and link slowed; B1 pyruvate converted to lactate, regenerating NAD; B1 allows glycolysis / ATP production to continue, lactate passes into blood.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mitochondria were isolated from locust flight muscle and from rat liver. Measurements:
flight muscle: oxygen uptake 460 nmol O₂ min⁻¹ per mg mitochondrial protein; cristae membrane area 7.2 m² per g of mitochondria
liver: oxygen uptake 95 nmol O₂ min⁻¹ per mg mitochondrial protein; cristae membrane area 2.4 m² per g of mitochondria

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the oxygen uptake per mg protein and the cristae area per gram are in flight muscle mitochondria than in liver mitochondria. Give each answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: oxygen uptake 4.8 times; cristae area 3.0 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concluded that the difference in oxygen uptake is caused only by the difference in cristae area. Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The difference in oxygen uptake (4.8×) is larger than the difference in cristae area (3.0×), so cristae area alone cannot explain it; flight muscle may have a greater density of electron transport chains per unit area or more Krebs enzymes in the matrix / faster supply of substrate; correlation does not prove cause and only one sample of each.
parts.working: B1 ratios differ (4.8 vs 3.0) so other factors involved; B1 suggestion: more carriers / ATP synthase per µm², more matrix enzymes, more ADP available; B1 correlation not causation / data from one tissue sample each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why locust flight muscle needs mitochondria with such a high rate of oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Flight muscle contracts very rapidly and continuously, needing a very high rate of ATP production by aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 very high and sustained ATP demand for rapid contraction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In yeast cells without oxygen, pyruvate is converted to ethanol in two steps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the 2-carbon intermediate formed in the first step and the other product of this step.
parts.answer: Ethanal; carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 ethanal; B1 carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the second step, naming the enzyme involved.
parts.answer: Ethanal is reduced to ethanol by reduced NAD (which is oxidised to NAD), catalysed by alcohol dehydrogenase.
parts.working: B1 ethanal reduced to ethanol using reduced NAD; B1 alcohol dehydrogenase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the net number of ATP molecules produced per glucose molecule by this pathway.
parts.working: B1 2 (from glycolysis).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why anaerobic respiration releases much less energy (ATP) per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: Only glycolysis takes place (2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation); without oxygen as final electron acceptor the electron transport chain stops, so no oxidative phosphorylation; the link reaction and Krebs cycle cannot run; much of the energy remains in lactate or ethanol.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: only glycolysis / 2 ATP; no oxygen to accept electrons so no oxidative phosphorylation; no link reaction / Krebs cycle; energy remains in lactate / ethanol (not fully oxidised).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in a cell anaerobic respiration takes place.
parts.answer: Cytoplasm (cytosol)
parts.working: B1 cytoplasm.

stem: Naan and bread dough is made with flour, water, sugar and yeast and left in a warm place for an hour before baking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the dough rises.
parts.answer: Yeast respires the sugar (anaerobically once oxygen in the dough is used up), producing carbon dioxide gas that is trapped as bubbles in the dough.
parts.working: B1 yeast respires sugar / glucose; B1 carbon dioxide released and trapped in dough.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dough is left in a warm place rather than in a refrigerator.
parts.answer: Respiration is enzyme-controlled; at warm temperatures enzymes have more kinetic energy and more frequent enzyme–substrate collisions, so CO₂ is produced faster; in a refrigerator enzymes work very slowly.
parts.working: B1 enzymes of respiration; B1 faster rate at warmer temperature / more collisions (not denatured at room warmth).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the ethanol produced by the yeast when the dough is baked.
parts.answer: It evaporates (is driven off by the heat of the oven).
parts.working: B1 evaporates.

author: HomiLabs

stem: After a cricketer bowls a fast over, she continues to breathe deeply for several minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the oxygen debt.
parts.answer: The extra oxygen taken in after exercise, above the resting amount, that is needed to remove the lactate produced (and restore oxygen stores / ATP).
parts.working: B1 extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down / convert lactate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to lactate after exercise.
parts.answer: Lactate is carried in the blood to the liver; it is oxidised back to pyruvate (regenerating reduced NAD); some pyruvate is oxidised in the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation to CO₂ and water; most is converted to glucose (and then glycogen) in the liver.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: carried in blood to liver; converted to pyruvate; some oxidised by aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle) to CO₂ and water; rest converted to glucose / glycogen.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Yeast was grown in a sealed industrial fermenter containing sugar-cane molasses diluted with water, at a distillery making fuel ethanol. Readings:
time / h: 0, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72
dissolved oxygen / % of starting value: 100, 40, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0
ethanol / g dm⁻³: 0, 0.2, 1.5, 6.0, 22, 60, 64

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the changes in dissolved oxygen and ethanol concentration in the first 12 hours.
parts.answer: Oxygen falls rapidly to zero because yeast respires aerobically, using oxygen; little ethanol is produced while oxygen is present; once oxygen is used up (8–12 h) yeast respires anaerobically, so ethanol concentration starts to rise.
parts.working: B1 oxygen falls to 0 by 12 h as used in aerobic respiration; B1 ethanol low while O₂ present; B1 rises as O₂ runs out / anaerobic respiration (fermentation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the ethanol concentration levels off between 48 and 72 hours.
parts.answer: Sugar is used up / becomes limiting; ethanol concentration becomes toxic and kills or inhibits the yeast (denatures enzymes / damages membranes).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: substrate (sugar) running out; ethanol toxic to yeast.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fermenter is sealed after the start.
parts.answer: To keep oxygen out so the yeast respires anaerobically and produces ethanol (also prevents contamination).
parts.working: B1 keep anaerobic so ethanol produced.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In this question use these data. Complete aerobic oxidation of 1 mol of glucose releases 2870 kJ. Conversion of 1 mol of glucose to 2 mol of lactate releases 197 kJ. Hydrolysis of 1 mol of ATP releases 30.5 kJ; 2 mol of ATP are made per mol of glucose converted to lactate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy in glucose that is released when glucose is converted to lactate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy released in lactate formation that is trapped in ATP. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to explain why lactate is not a waste of energy for the body.
parts.answer: Over 90 % of the energy of the glucose is still in the lactate; lactate is later converted to pyruvate / glucose in the liver and can be respired aerobically, so this energy is recovered.
parts.working: B1 most energy (about 93 %) remains in lactate; B1 lactate reconverted to pyruvate / glucose and used.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dahi (yoghurt) is made by adding a little old yoghurt, which contains Lactobacillus bacteria, to warm milk and leaving it at about 40 °C for several hours. The milk sugar lactose is broken down to glucose and galactose, which the bacteria respire anaerobically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product of anaerobic respiration in Lactobacillus and explain why the pH of the milk falls.
parts.answer: Lactate (lactic acid); lactic acid releases hydrogen ions, lowering the pH.
parts.working: B1 lactate / lactic acid; B1 acid / H⁺ ions accumulate so pH falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why fermentation slows down and stops after some hours even though sugar is still present.
parts.answer: The low pH changes the ionic and hydrogen bonds in the bacteria's enzymes, changing the active site shape (denaturing them), so respiration and growth slow and stop.
parts.working: B1 pH becomes too low / acidic; B1 enzymes denatured / active site shape altered.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the milk is kept at about 40 °C rather than at 20 °C.
parts.answer: 40 °C is close to the optimum temperature of the bacteria's enzymes, so fermentation is faster.
parts.working: B1 near optimum temperature for bacterial enzymes / faster respiration.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Wheat fields in parts of Sindh sometimes become waterlogged after heavy rain or poor drainage. Wheat roots are not adapted to waterlogging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why waterlogging causes the roots to respire anaerobically.
parts.answer: Water fills the air spaces between soil particles; oxygen diffuses very slowly through water so the roots receive too little oxygen for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 air spaces filled with water; B1 little oxygen reaches roots (slow diffusion in water).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves of the wheat plants turn yellow when the soil stays waterlogged for several days.
parts.answer: Anaerobic respiration produces little ATP; root cells take up mineral ions such as nitrate and magnesium by active transport, which needs ATP; less uptake, so less chlorophyll (and protein) can be made, leaves turn yellow.
parts.working: B1 less ATP from anaerobic respiration; B1 less active transport / uptake of mineral ions; B1 nitrate / magnesium needed for chlorophyll so less chlorophyll.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why root cells may die after long waterlogging.
parts.answer: Ethanol accumulates to toxic concentrations (or not enough ATP to maintain the cells).
parts.working: B1 ethanol toxicity / ATP shortage.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crucian carp can survive for months in ponds covered by ice where there is almost no oxygen. Their muscles carry out lactate fermentation, but then convert the lactate to ethanol, which diffuses out of the fish across the gills into the water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the fish must regenerate NAD to survive without oxygen.
parts.answer: Glycolysis needs NAD to accept hydrogen when triose phosphate is oxidised; without regenerated NAD glycolysis would stop and no ATP would be made.
parts.working: B1 NAD needed as hydrogen acceptor in glycolysis; B1 otherwise glycolysis / ATP production stops.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the advantage to the fish of converting lactate to ethanol rather than keeping the lactate.
parts.answer: Lactate would build up in the tissues and blood, lowering pH and denaturing enzymes; ethanol is a small (uncharged) molecule that can diffuse out across the gills into the large volume of water, so no toxic build-up occurs and long periods of anaerobic respiration are possible.
parts.working: B1 lactate accumulation lowers pH / is harmful; B1 ethanol diffuses out of the body through gills; B1 so anaerobic respiration can continue for months.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of this adaptation.
parts.answer: The energy remaining in ethanol is lost from the body (it cannot be later reconverted to glucose), so more glucose (glycogen store) is used.
parts.working: B1 energy in ethanol is lost / glycogen stores used up faster.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare lactate fermentation in mammals with ethanol fermentation in yeast, giving two similarities and two differences.
parts.answer: Similarities: both start with glycolysis producing 2 ATP; both regenerate NAD by reducing a product using reduced NAD; both occur in the cytoplasm. Differences: ethanol pathway releases CO₂, lactate pathway does not; ethanol pathway has two steps (via ethanal), lactate pathway one step; enzymes differ (pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase vs lactate dehydrogenase); lactate pathway is reversible, ethanol pathway is not.
parts.working: Max 2 similarities, max 2 differences, 1 mark each from the list.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why lactate can be converted back to pyruvate but ethanol cannot be converted back to pyruvate.
parts.answer: In lactate formation no carbon is lost: lactate (3C) is simply reduced pyruvate and lactate dehydrogenase catalyses a reversible reaction; in ethanol formation CO₂ is removed (decarboxylation), so ethanol has only 2C and the reaction is irreversible.
parts.working: B1 lactate still has 3 carbons / reversible reduction; B1 ethanol pathway loses CO₂ so cannot be reversed.

stem:
Samples were taken from two muscles of a sheep. Results:
muscle X: mitochondria 2 % of cell volume; lactate dehydrogenase activity high; myoglobin content low
muscle Y: mitochondria 9 % of cell volume; lactate dehydrogenase activity low; myoglobin content high

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest which muscle is better suited to short bursts of very rapid contraction. Explain your answer using the data.
parts.answer: Muscle X: high lactate dehydrogenase activity so pyruvate rapidly converted to lactate, regenerating NAD and allowing fast glycolysis / ATP production without waiting for oxygen; few mitochondria and little myoglobin show it does not rely on aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 muscle X; B1 high LDH allows rapid anaerobic respiration / NAD regeneration; B1 few mitochondria / low myoglobin so not dependent on oxygen supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why muscle Y can contract for long periods without fatigue.
parts.answer: Many mitochondria give a high rate of aerobic respiration (link reaction, Krebs, oxidative phosphorylation) producing much more ATP per glucose; myoglobin stores oxygen; little lactate produced so pH does not fall.
parts.working: B1 many mitochondria / aerobic respiration; B1 more ATP per glucose (about 32 vs 2); B1 myoglobin stores oxygen / little lactate accumulation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: During a 10-second sprint, a muscle broke down glucose anaerobically at 0.60 µmol per gram per second. During a long run, the same muscle broke down glucose aerobically at 0.050 µmol per gram per second. Assume 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically and 32 ATP per glucose aerobically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of ATP production, in µmol per gram per second, in each case.
parts.answer: anaerobic 1.2 µmol g⁻¹ s⁻¹; aerobic 1.6 µmol g⁻¹ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster glucose is used during the sprint than during the long run.
parts.answer: 12 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why anaerobic respiration can be used for only short periods even though it supplies ATP rapidly.
parts.answer: It uses glucose / glycogen 12 times faster for a similar ATP rate, so stores are quickly depleted; lactate accumulates and lowers pH, inhibiting enzymes and causing fatigue; an oxygen debt builds up.
parts.working: B1 glucose / glycogen used very quickly (wasteful); B1 lactate accumulation / low pH / fatigue; B1 oxygen debt must be repaid.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In 30 minutes, germinating gram (chickpea) seeds took in 50 cm³ of oxygen and gave out 45 cm³ of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ) of the seeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the main respiratory substrate being used. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Protein, because an RQ of about 0.9 is typical of protein (carbohydrate 1.0, lipid 0.7).
parts.working: B1 protein; B1 RQ 0.9 matches protein / between lipid 0.7 and carbohydrate 1.0.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oleic acid is a fatty acid found in olive oil and mustard (sarson) oil. Its complete oxidation is:
C₁₈H₃₄O₂ + 25.5O₂ → 18CO₂ + 17H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ for the respiration of oleic acid. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the RQ of lipids is lower than the RQ of carbohydrates.
parts.answer: Lipids contain far fewer oxygen atoms relative to carbon and hydrogen than carbohydrates, so more oxygen must be taken in to oxidise the hydrogen to water and carbon to CO₂; oxygen uptake is greater than CO₂ output.
parts.working: B1 lipids contain relatively little oxygen / more H per C; B1 more O₂ needed relative to CO₂ released.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A simple respirometer consists of a boiling tube containing germinating seeds on a wire gauze above soda lime. The tube is connected by a three-way tap to a syringe and to a U-shaped capillary tube containing coloured liquid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of each of the following: the soda lime; the coloured liquid in the capillary; the syringe.
parts.answer: soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide; coloured liquid shows the change in gas volume (moves towards the seeds as oxygen is used); syringe resets the liquid to its starting position and measures the volume of oxygen used
parts.working: B1 each: absorbs CO₂; shows volume change / movement measured; resets liquid / measures volume.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the liquid moves towards the seeds.
parts.answer: The seeds take in oxygen; the carbon dioxide they release is absorbed by soda lime; so the volume (pressure) of gas in the tube decreases and the liquid is drawn towards the seeds.
parts.working: B1 oxygen used and CO₂ absorbed; B1 gas volume / pressure in tube decreases.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Yeast in a sealed flask of glucose solution produced 30 cm³ of carbon dioxide while taking in 12 cm³ of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the RQ is greater than 1.
parts.answer: Some of the yeast are respiring anaerobically, producing CO₂ (by decarboxylation of pyruvate to ethanal) without taking in any oxygen; so CO₂ output exceeds O₂ uptake.
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration / fermentation occurring; B1 CO₂ released without O₂ uptake.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
When the amino acid alanine is respired in the body, its nitrogen is removed as urea. The overall equation is:
2C₃H₇O₂N + 6O₂ → 5CO₂ + 5H₂O + CO(NH₂)₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ for alanine. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why proteins are not normally the main respiratory substrate in a well-fed person.
parts.answer: Amino acids are mainly used to make proteins (enzymes, structural proteins); they are only respired when carbohydrate and lipid stores are low; their nitrogen must first be removed (deamination), producing urea.
parts.working: B1 needed for protein synthesis / growth; B1 only respired when carbohydrate and fat are scarce / must be deaminated first.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the RQ for alanine is closer to 1 than the RQ for a fatty acid.
parts.answer: Alanine contains more oxygen relative to its carbon and hydrogen than a fatty acid does.
parts.working: B1 higher proportion of oxygen in the molecule.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A respirometer contained 3.0 g of germinating maize grains and potassium hydroxide solution at 25 °C. After 15 minutes the liquid in the capillary was returned to its starting position using the syringe. The syringe reading changed from 0.80 cm³ to 0.44 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in cm³ per gram per hour.
parts.answer: 0.48 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the syringe reading decreased.
parts.answer: Oxygen was absorbed by the grains and CO₂ absorbed by the KOH, so gas volume fell; air from the syringe was pushed in to replace the lost volume, returning the liquid to its starting point.
parts.working: B1 volume of gas in tube reduced by oxygen uptake; B1 syringe plunger pushed in to restore level / volume pushed in equals O₂ used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the results are expressed per gram of grains.
parts.answer: So that results from samples with different masses can be compared.
parts.working: B1 allows comparison between different masses / standardises.

author: HomiLabs

stem: During the month of Ramadan, a healthy adult who fasts from dawn to sunset had her RQ measured at different times. Just after the pre-dawn meal (sehri), it was 0.97. Late in the afternoon it was 0.74.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in RQ during the day.
parts.answer: After the meal the main substrate is carbohydrate (RQ close to 1.0); as the day goes on, blood glucose and liver glycogen are used up; the body switches to respiring more lipid (fat stores), so RQ falls towards 0.7.
parts.working: B1 RQ ≈ 1 shows carbohydrate; B1 carbohydrate / glycogen stores depleted during fast; B1 increasing use of lipid gives RQ near 0.7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how her RQ would change in the hour after she breaks the fast with dates and a meal rich in rice. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: RQ rises back towards 1.0, because carbohydrate from dates (sugars) and rice (starch) is digested and becomes the main respiratory substrate.
parts.working: B1 RQ increases towards 1; B1 carbohydrate becomes main substrate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Germinating seeds were sealed in a 500 cm³ flask of air for two hours. A gas analyser gave these percentages by volume:
start: oxygen 21.0 %, carbon dioxide 0.04 %
after 2 hours: oxygen 17.2 %, carbon dioxide 3.9 %
Assume the total gas volume stayed at 500 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used and the volume of carbon dioxide produced.
parts.answer: oxygen 19.0 cm³; carbon dioxide 19.3 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the RQ to 2 decimal places and suggest the respiratory substrate.
parts.answer: RQ = 1.02; carbohydrate
parts.working: M1 19.3 ÷ 19.0 = 1.02; A1 carbohydrate (RQ ≈ 1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the RQ might be slightly above 1.0 in this experiment.
parts.answer: Some anaerobic respiration in the centre of the seeds / as oxygen falls (or measurement error of the gas analyser).
parts.working: B1 some anaerobic respiration releasing CO₂ without O₂ uptake (accept measurement uncertainty).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Assume carbohydrate has an RQ of 1.0 and lipid an RQ of 0.70. When a mixture of substrates is respired, the overall RQ is the weighted mean of the RQs, weighted by the proportion of the oxygen used for each substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tissue uses 60 % of its oxygen to respire carbohydrate and 40 % to respire lipid. Calculate the overall RQ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A migrating bird has an RQ of 0.79. Calculate the percentage of its oxygen used for carbohydrate respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an RQ of 0.88 does not prove that a tissue is respiring protein.
parts.answer: The same value can be produced by a mixture of carbohydrate and lipid; RQ shows the overall ratio of CO₂ to O₂, not which molecules are respired.
parts.working: B1 mixture of carbohydrate and lipid gives same RQ; B1 RQ is an average / cannot identify substrates on its own.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seeds of mustard (sarson) were studied as they ripened on the plant. Ripening seeds convert sugars from the leaves into stored oil (lipid). Their measured RQ was 1.3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the RQ of ripening oil seeds is greater than 1.
parts.answer: Carbohydrate contains much more oxygen relative to carbon and hydrogen than lipid; converting carbohydrate to lipid releases the extra oxygen within the molecules, and some carbon is lost as CO₂ (from decarboxylation, e.g. pyruvate → acetyl CoA) without oxygen being taken in; so CO₂ output is greater than O₂ uptake.
parts.working: B1 carbohydrate is oxygen-rich, lipid oxygen-poor; B1 conversion releases CO₂ (decarboxylation) without using O₂; B1 so CO₂ released > O₂ taken in.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the same seeds germinate, the RQ is about 0.7 for the first few days. Explain why.
parts.answer: The stored oil (lipid) is the main respiratory substrate during early germination; lipids have an RQ of about 0.7.
parts.working: B1 lipid stores being respired; B1 lipid RQ ≈ 0.7.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A respirometer containing 2.5 g of germinating peas and soda lime was set up beside a thermobarometer (identical tube containing glass beads). The capillary tubes have an internal radius of 0.5 mm.
