In 15 minutes the liquid in the respirometer moved 18 mm towards the peas, while the liquid in the thermobarometer moved 3 mm away from the beads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the liquid in the thermobarometer moved.
parts.answer: The temperature in the room rose / the atmospheric pressure fell, so the gas in the tube expanded and pushed the liquid away from the beads.
parts.working: B1 change in temperature or atmospheric pressure; B1 gas expanded so liquid pushed away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per gram per hour. Use V = πr²l and give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 26.4 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹
parts.working: M1 corrected distance 18 + 3 = 21 mm (the same expansion also acted against the respirometer reading); M1 V = π × 0.5² × 21 = 16.5 mm³; A1 16.5 ÷ 2.5 × 4 = 26.4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the respirometer and thermobarometer should be placed in the same water bath.
parts.answer: So that both experience the same temperature (and pressure) changes, making the correction valid.
parts.working: B1 same conditions so correction is valid.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two respirometers with soda lime and capillary tubes of internal diameter 1.0 mm were kept at 25 °C. In 20 minutes, the liquid moved 30 mm with 4.0 g of earthworms and 42 mm with 1.5 g of blowfly larvae (maggots).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake of each animal in mm³ per gram per hour. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: earthworms 17.7 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹; maggots 66.0 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹
parts.working: M1 radius = 0.5 mm, V = πr²l: 23.6 mm³ and 33.0 mm³; M1 ÷ mass × 3 (per hour); A1 17.7 and 66.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the rate per gram is for maggots than for earthworms. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.7 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one biological reason for the difference.
parts.answer: Maggots are actively feeding and growing rapidly so have a high metabolic rate (or earthworms have a lower activity / body contains more water and non-respiring tissue per gram).
parts.working: B1 any sensible: higher activity / growth rate of maggots; earthworm mass includes gut contents / water.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why all living organisms need a continuous supply of energy.
parts.answer: To carry out work such as active transport, movement and synthesis of large molecules (anabolic reactions), and to maintain body temperature in some animals; cells are constantly using energy so it must be continuously released from respiration.
parts.working: B1 energy needed for named work (any two of active transport, anabolic reactions / synthesis, movement / muscle contraction, nerve impulses, cell division); B1 used continuously so constant supply needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name four processes in a cell that use ATP.
parts.answer: Any four of: active transport (e.g. sodium–potassium pump); muscle contraction; protein synthesis (or DNA replication / synthesis of polysaccharides); cell division; movement of vesicles (endocytosis / exocytosis); phosphorylating glucose in glycolysis; nerve impulse transmission (restoring resting potential).
parts.working: 2 marks for four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a word equation for the hydrolysis of ATP and name the enzyme that catalyses it.
parts.answer: ATP + water → ADP + phosphate (Pi) + energy; ATP hydrolase (ATPase)
parts.working: B1 equation with water and both products; B1 ATP hydrolase / ATPase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrolysis of one ATP releases a small quantity of energy (30.5 kJ mol⁻¹). Explain why this is an advantage to a cell.
parts.answer: Energy is released in small, manageable amounts that match the needs of individual reactions, so little is wasted as heat; and it is released in a single quick step.
parts.working: B1 small amounts suited to cellular reactions / less wasted as heat; B1 released quickly in one step (one reaction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: ATP is a phosphorylated nucleotide. Name the three components of an ATP molecule.
parts.answer: Adenine (a base), ribose (a pentose sugar) and three phosphate groups.
parts.working: 2 marks all three; 1 mark for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which ATP is similar to an adenine nucleotide in RNA and one way in which it differs.
parts.answer: Similar: both contain adenine; both contain ribose (and phosphate). Different: ATP has three phosphate groups, the RNA nucleotide has one (ATP is not part of a polynucleotide chain).
parts.working: B1 adenine; B1 ribose; B1 three phosphates vs one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation.
parts.answer: Substrate-level: a phosphate group is transferred directly from a phosphorylated intermediate to ADP, catalysed by an enzyme. Oxidative: ATP is made by ATP synthase using energy from a proton gradient set up by the electron transport chain (chemiosmosis).
parts.working: B1 direct transfer of phosphate from substrate molecule to ADP; B1 ATP synthase / proton gradient / chemiosmosis / electron transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each type, state one stage of respiration where it occurs.
parts.answer: Substrate-level: glycolysis or Krebs cycle. Oxidative: electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae).
parts.working: B1 glycolysis / Krebs; B1 inner membrane / ETC.

stem: Energy values: carbohydrate 15.8 kJ g⁻¹, protein 17.0 kJ g⁻¹, lipid 39.4 kJ g⁻¹. A student in Karachi ate 300 g of carbohydrate, 60 g of protein and 70 g of lipid in one day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy in the food eaten.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of this energy that came from lipid. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The energy values above are for complete respiration in the body. Suggest two reasons why the energy the body actually gains from this food is less than the value calculated in (a).
parts.answer: Not all the food is digested and absorbed, so some energy is lost in faeces; nitrogen from protein is excreted as urea, which still contains unoxidised energy; some energy is lost as heat during digestion and metabolism.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: incomplete digestion/absorption (energy lost in faeces); energy still in urea from protein; energy lost as heat.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose is the main respiratory substrate but ATP, not glucose, is the immediate source of energy for cell processes. Give three reasons why ATP is better suited to this role.
parts.answer: ATP is hydrolysed in a single step, releasing energy immediately (glucose needs many steps); energy released in small, useful quantities (glucose would release too much at once, wasting heat); ATP is small and soluble so moves easily within the cell to where energy is needed; ATP is used in all cells / reactions (universal) and is quickly regenerated from ADP.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: one-step hydrolysis / immediate; small quantities; soluble / easily moved; universal / easily regenerated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP is described as an immediate energy source rather than an energy store.
parts.answer: ATP is not stored in large amounts; it is made and used continuously (rapid turnover); it is unstable (readily hydrolysed) so cannot hold energy for long.
parts.working: B1 small quantities in cells / rapidly used and remade; B1 unstable / readily hydrolysed so not suitable for storage.

stem:
Food factories test the cleanliness of surfaces using an ATP swab. The swab is mixed with the enzyme luciferase and its substrate luciferin; light is produced in proportion to the ATP present. Readings (relative light units, RLU) from a dairy plant in Lahore:
milk tank after cleaning: 46 RLU
milk tank before cleaning: 3600 RLU
conveyor belt after cleaning: 820 RLU
The plant's pass limit is 150 RLU.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the amount of ATP on a surface indicates how much living material or food residue is present.
parts.answer: All living cells (bacteria, yeast, and cells in food) contain ATP because it is the universal energy currency; more cells / residue means more ATP.
parts.working: B1 all cells contain ATP / universal energy currency; B1 more ATP = more cells / organic residue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in RLU achieved by cleaning the milk tank. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, what the factory should do about the conveyor belt.
parts.answer: Clean it again (and retest), because 820 RLU is above the 150 RLU limit.
parts.working: B1 reclean because above limit.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Stearic acid (C₁₈H₃₆O₂, Mr 284) is a fatty acid and glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, Mr 180) is a carbohydrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of hydrogen atoms per unit of relative molecular mass (H atoms ÷ Mr) for each molecule, and how many times greater this is for stearic acid. Give the final answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: stearic acid 0.127; glucose 0.067; 1.9 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why respiring 1 g of lipid releases more energy than respiring 1 g of carbohydrate.
parts.answer: Most energy from respiration comes from oxidising hydrogen; more hydrogen atoms per gram means more reduced NAD / FAD formed; more electrons pass along the electron transport chain and more protons are pumped, so more ATP is made by chemiosmosis (and more water formed).
parts.working: B1 more hydrogen per gram; B1 more reduced NAD / reduced FAD; B1 more proton pumping / more ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A kidney tubule cell pumps 1.5 × 10⁸ sodium ions per second out of the cell using sodium–potassium pumps. Each pump hydrolyses one ATP to move 3 sodium ions out (and 2 potassium ions in). Assume 32 ATP per glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of ATP molecules hydrolysed per second by the pumps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of glucose molecules the cell must respire aerobically each second to supply this ATP. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the ATP is used to move sodium ions against their concentration gradient.
parts.answer: ATP binds to the carrier protein and is hydrolysed; the phosphate attaches to the protein (phosphorylation), changing its shape; the shape change moves the bound sodium ions to the other side of the membrane and releases them.
parts.working: B1 ATP hydrolysed at the carrier / ATPase site; B1 phosphate binds to carrier changing its shape (conformational change); B1 ions carried across / released on other side.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why kidney tubule cells contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: To produce large amounts of ATP by aerobic respiration for active transport.
parts.working: B1 large ATP supply for active transport.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Complete aerobic oxidation of one molecule of glucose (Mr 180) yields 32 ATP. Complete oxidation of one molecule of the fatty acid palmitic acid (Mr 256) yields 106 ATP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of ATP produced per gram of each substrate, to 3 significant figures, and how many times greater the yield per gram is for palmitic acid (to 3 significant figures).
parts.answer: glucose 0.178 mol g⁻¹; palmitic acid 0.414 mol g⁻¹; 2.33 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Despite this, mammals store some carbohydrate as glycogen in muscles and liver. Suggest two advantages of glycogen over lipid as an energy store.
parts.answer: Glycogen can be hydrolysed to glucose very quickly when energy is suddenly needed; glucose can be respired anaerobically, but fatty acids cannot (they need oxygen / Krebs cycle); glucose is the main fuel for the brain.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: rapid mobilisation; can supply anaerobic respiration / glycolysis; glucose needed by brain / red blood cells.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Isolated frog muscle fibres were placed in three dishes and observed for 2 minutes:
dish 1: Ringer's salt solution only — no contraction
dish 2: Ringer's solution + 1 % glucose — no contraction
dish 3: Ringer's solution + 0.25 % ATP — fibres contracted within seconds

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the fibres in dish 3 contracted.
parts.answer: ATP was hydrolysed by ATPase in the muscle fibres, releasing energy (and phosphate) directly used for contraction (cross-bridge cycling).
parts.working: B1 ATP is the immediate energy source for contraction; B1 hydrolysed by ATPase releasing energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why glucose did not cause contraction in dish 2.
parts.answer: Glucose is not used directly for contraction; it must first be respired (glycolysis, Krebs, oxidative phosphorylation) to make ATP, which takes time; isolated fibres may have little glucose uptake / the stimulus to contract was absent.
parts.working: B1 glucose must be respired to make ATP first; B1 multi-step / slow, or no stimulus / limited uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dish 1 was included.
parts.answer: As a control to show that the salt solution alone does not cause contraction, so the effect in dish 3 is due to ATP.
parts.working: B1 control: shows contraction is due to ATP not the solution.

author: HomiLabs

stem: When protein is burned completely in a calorimeter, it releases about 23.6 kJ g⁻¹. When it is respired in the human body, the useful energy is only about 17.0 kJ g⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy in protein that is not released in the body. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the energy released from protein in the body is less than in a calorimeter.
parts.answer: In the body amino acids are deaminated; the amino groups are converted to urea, which is excreted; urea still contains carbon and hydrogen that have not been oxidised, so its chemical energy is lost; in the calorimeter the protein is completely oxidised (including nitrogen).
parts.working: B1 deamination; B1 nitrogen excreted as urea; B1 urea contains unoxidised C / H / energy that is lost, whereas calorimeter oxidises completely.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of carbon dioxide production by yeast in glucose solution, collecting the gas in a gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the apparatus the student needs, apart from yeast and glucose solution.
parts.answer: Conical flask / boiling tube with bung and delivery tube; gas syringe; thermostatically controlled water baths (or water bath and thermometer); stopwatch; measuring cylinder or syringe for volumes; balance.
parts.working: 2 marks for five suitable items; 1 mark for three or four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should make sure that the yeast suspension is at the required temperature when timing starts.
parts.answer: Place the yeast suspension and glucose solution separately in the water bath for about 10 minutes before mixing (equilibration); check the temperature with a thermometer inside the tube before starting.
parts.working: B1 pre-incubate both solutions in water bath / equilibrate for stated time (e.g. 5–10 min); B1 check with thermometer in the mixture.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has 100 cm³ of 10 % glucose solution and distilled water. She needs 20 cm³ of each of these concentrations: 10 %, 8 %, 6 %, 4 % and 2 % glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the volumes of 10 % glucose solution and distilled water needed to make each concentration.
parts.answer: 10 %: 20 cm³ + 0 cm³; 8 %: 16 + 4; 6 %: 12 + 8; 4 %: 8 + 12; 2 %: 4 + 16 (volumes of glucose solution + water)
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = required concentration ÷ 10 × 20; A2 all five correct (A1 for three or four).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a suitable piece of apparatus for measuring these volumes accurately.
parts.answer: Graduated pipette or syringe (or burette)
parts.working: B1 pipette / syringe / burette (not beaker).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compares carbon dioxide production by yeast in two sugar solutions by counting the bubbles that leave the end of a delivery tube placed under water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a better way of measuring the carbon dioxide produced.
parts.answer: Collect the gas in a gas syringe or in an inverted measuring cylinder filled with water (displacement), and read the volume at regular time intervals.
parts.working: B1 gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder over water; B1 record volume at fixed intervals / over fixed time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why your method gives more accurate results than counting bubbles.
parts.answer: Bubbles can be different sizes, so the number of bubbles does not represent volume; bubbles may be missed when produced quickly; the volume is a quantitative measurement in cm³.
parts.working: B1 bubbles vary in size; B1 volume measured directly in cm³ / bubbles hard to count at high rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will use respirometers containing soda lime (or potassium hydroxide solution) and live blowfly larvae (maggots) to compare respiration rates at 15 °C, 20 °C and 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this investigation and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Soda lime / KOH is corrosive (alkali): wear eye protection and gloves, do not touch, wrap soda lime in gauze. Maggots may carry microorganisms: wash hands after handling / wear gloves. Glass capillary may break: handle carefully. Hot water bath: avoid scalding.
parts.working: For each of two hazards: B1 hazard identified; B1 matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to make sure the investigation is ethical.
parts.answer: Keep the temperature range within what the larvae survive naturally (not above about 30 °C), keep them separated from the soda lime by gauze, use the fewest larvae possible and return them to suitable conditions afterwards.
parts.working: B1 any one sensible welfare point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: DCPIP is a blue dye that becomes colourless when it is reduced by hydrogen released by dehydrogenase enzymes in respiring yeast. A student wants to investigate the effect of pH on the rate of respiration in yeast using DCPIP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method the student could use. Your method should allow the student to collect valid and reliable results.
parts.answer: Use buffer solutions at pH 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 (at least five values); in each tube put the same volume (e.g. 5 cm³) of yeast suspension of the same concentration, the same volume of buffer and the same volume and concentration of glucose; equilibrate at 30 °C in a water bath; add the same volume of DCPIP (e.g. 1 cm³), mix, start timing; record time for blue colour to disappear (compare with a colour standard of yeast without DCPIP); control tube with boiled yeast at each pH; repeat three times at each pH and calculate means; rate = 1/time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: at least five pH values using buffers; same volume and concentration of yeast (and glucose); constant temperature with water bath (stated value); same volume of DCPIP added and timing started; end point judged against a colour standard / time to colourless; boiled yeast control or no-yeast control; three repeats and mean; rate = 1/t. Max 6.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to compare the rate of oxygen uptake of germinating wheat grains with that of dry (dormant) wheat grains using a respirometer with a syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should carry out this comparison so that the results are valid.
parts.answer: Use the same mass of grains in each respirometer (e.g. 5 g, weighed on a balance); place soda lime (CO₂ absorbent) in each, separated by gauze; keep both at the same temperature in a water bath and leave to equilibrate with tap open; close tap, start timing, measure distance moved / reset with syringe after a fixed time (e.g. 10 min); set up a control with glass beads or boiled grains of the same mass/volume; repeat three times and calculate a mean rate per gram per hour.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: same mass of grains; CO₂ absorbent; constant temperature / water bath; equilibration time before closing tap; measurement of volume over fixed time (syringe / capillary); control with beads or boiled grains; replicates and mean; rate per g per h. Max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student should not use grains that have been soaked in water for very different times.
parts.answer: The stage of germination affects the respiration rate, so it would be an uncontrolled variable.
parts.working: B1 stage of germination / water content would differ and affect respiration rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has a carbon dioxide sensor connected to a data logger. She wants to investigate the effect of glucose concentration on the rate of respiration of yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how she could use the sensor to obtain a rate of respiration for each glucose concentration.
parts.answer: Place a fixed volume of yeast suspension and glucose solution in a sealed chamber containing the CO₂ sensor; record CO₂ concentration at intervals (e.g. every 10 s) for a fixed time (e.g. 10 minutes); plot CO₂ concentration against time; the rate is the gradient of the linear part of the graph (change in CO₂ ÷ time); flush the chamber with air and rinse between trials.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: sealed chamber with sensor; same volume of yeast and glucose solution; record at regular intervals for fixed time; rate from gradient / change ÷ time; reset / flush chamber between runs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable range and interval of glucose concentrations.
parts.answer: e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 % (at least five concentrations including 0 %).
parts.working: B1 at least five concentrations, evenly spaced, sensible range.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student thinks that ripening mangoes respire faster than unripe mangoes. Mangoes of three ripeness stages (green, turning, fully ripe) are available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could test this idea.
parts.answer: Place one whole mango of known mass in a sealed container of known volume with a CO₂ (or O₂) sensor / data logger; keep at constant temperature in the dark; record CO₂ concentration at start and after a fixed time (e.g. 30 minutes); calculate rate as change in CO₂ per kg per hour; use at least three mangoes of each stage (same variety, similar size); use an empty container as a control.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: sealed container and CO₂/O₂ sensor (or limewater/hydrogencarbonate indicator with colour standards); constant temperature; dark (to avoid photosynthesis in green skin); fixed time; rate per unit mass; replicates of each stage, same variety; control. Max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mangoes should be kept in the dark during the measurements.
parts.answer: Green skin may photosynthesise in light, taking up CO₂ and giving out O₂, which would affect the measurements.
parts.working: B1 avoid photosynthesis altering gas concentrations.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of oxygen uptake by woodlice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a suitable range of temperatures and explain your choice.
parts.answer: e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C; at least five values within the range woodlice meet naturally, so they are not harmed (ethical) and enzymes are not denatured.
parts.working: B1 five or more temperatures in a sensible range (about 5–30 °C); B1 reason: ethical / natural range / avoid harm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student would make sure that differences in oxygen uptake were due to temperature only.
parts.answer: Use the same mass (or number and size) of woodlice for each trial; same volume of soda lime and same respirometer / capillary size; allow the same acclimatisation time at each temperature; same time of day / woodlice not recently fed; measure for the same length of time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three standardised variables with how they are kept constant.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Baker's yeast and a yeast strain used in sugar-cane ethanol distilleries are thought to differ in their tolerance to ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the effect of ethanol concentration on the rate of respiration of the two yeast strains. Include a hypothesis and how you would analyse the results.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: the distillery strain respires faster than baker's yeast at high ethanol concentrations (or: rate falls less with increasing ethanol). Prepare ethanol solutions 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 % by dilution of stock; equal cell density of each strain (same mass of yeast per volume or matched turbidity with colorimeter); same volume and concentration of glucose; constant temperature 30 °C with water bath; equilibrate; measure CO₂ volume with gas syringe (or DCPIP time / CO₂ sensor) over fixed time; three or more replicates; control with no yeast / boiled yeast; calculate mean rate and SD; plot rate against ethanol concentration for both strains on one graph; use a t-test at each concentration (or compare concentrations giving 50 % reduction in rate); risk: ethanol is flammable — no naked flames.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 8: testable hypothesis; independent variable with at least five concentrations and how made; both strains with matched cell density; dependent variable measured (method + units); temperature controlled with stated value; glucose controlled; replicates (≥3); control; graph of mean rate vs concentration for each strain; statistical test (t-test) and why; safety (flammable ethanol).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to find the respiratory quotient (RQ) of germinating sunflower seeds at 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could use respirometers to obtain the measurements needed, and how the RQ is then calculated.
parts.answer: Set up two identical respirometers with the same mass of seeds in a water bath at 25 °C; one contains KOH / soda lime to absorb CO₂, the other contains the same volume of water instead; equilibrate with taps open, then close and measure the distance moved by the liquid after the same time; the movement in the KOH tube gives oxygen uptake (x); the movement in the water tube gives the difference between O₂ taken in and CO₂ given out (y, towards seeds if O₂ > CO₂); CO₂ produced = x − y; RQ = (x − y) ÷ x; repeat and use means; use a thermobarometer for each.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: two respirometers same mass of seeds; one with KOH / soda lime, one with water; constant temperature / equilibration; KOH reading = O₂ uptake; water reading = O₂ − CO₂; RQ = CO₂ ÷ O₂ with formula; repeats / thermobarometer.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Caffeine is found in tea, which is drunk widely in Pakistan. A student wonders whether caffeine affects the rate of respiration of yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the rate of respiration of yeast with caffeine and without caffeine (or: caffeine concentration has no effect on the rate).
parts.working: B1 null hypothesis correctly expressed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plan an investigation to test this hypothesis. Include the statistical test you would use.
parts.answer: Prepare caffeine solutions (e.g. 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 g dm⁻³) by dilution; same volume of yeast suspension of same concentration and same glucose concentration in each tube; constant temperature (water bath 30 °C), equilibrate; measure rate using DCPIP decolourisation time or CO₂ volume in gas syringe over fixed time; at least 5 replicates per concentration; control with 0 caffeine (distilled water); compare 0 and each caffeine concentration with a t-test (or use Spearman's rank / correlation for concentration vs rate); 5 % significance level.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: range of caffeine concentrations; matched yeast and glucose; temperature controlled; rate measurement method; replicates; control; named appropriate statistical test with comparison / p = 0.05.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mung bean seeds were soaked and left to germinate. A student wants to find out how the rate of respiration changes over the first 10 days of germination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could obtain reliable results for the rate of respiration on each day.
parts.answer: Germinate a large batch of seeds of the same variety at the same time under the same conditions (temperature, water, dark/light); each day take a random sample of seedlings; measure oxygen uptake in a respirometer with soda lime at a constant temperature for a fixed time; repeat with three samples each day; calculate rate per gram.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: same batch / variety, same start; same germination conditions; random sample each day; respirometer / sensor at constant temperature; fixed time; replicates; rate per unit mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate should be expressed per gram of dry mass rather than per gram of fresh mass, and state one disadvantage of using dry mass.
parts.answer: Fresh mass changes greatly as seedlings take up water, which does not respire, so fresh mass would not reflect the amount of tissue; but dry mass is found by drying (killing) the seedlings, so a separate sample must be used.
parts.working: B1 water content varies / water uptake increases fresh mass; B1 drying kills the seedlings so measurements need a different sample.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ten seeds of maize had a total dry mass of 2.40 g before germination. After six days of germination in the dark, ten seedlings had a total dry mass of 2.04 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the decrease in dry mass.
parts.answer: Stored starch (and lipid) is respired to release energy for growth; carbon is lost as carbon dioxide; seedlings in the dark cannot photosynthesise to replace it.
parts.working: B1 food stores respired; B1 carbon lost as CO₂ / no photosynthesis in dark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Four replicate tubes of yeast in sucrose solution produced these volumes of CO₂ in 5 minutes: 4.2 cm³, 4.5 cm³, 6.9 cm³ and 4.3 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result.
parts.answer: 6.9 cm³
parts.working: B1 6.9 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume, excluding the anomalous result, to 2 decimal places, and the mean rate of CO₂ production in cm³ min⁻¹ to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: mean 4.33 cm³; rate 0.87 cm³ min⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem: A respirometer containing germinating peas showed an oxygen uptake of 0.45 cm³ in 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert this volume to mm³.
parts.answer: 450 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 1800 mm³ h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: The peas had a mass of 6.0 g. Calculate the rate in mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 300 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Time taken for DCPIP to become colourless in tubes of yeast with different glucose concentrations:
0.5 %: 85 s
1.0 %: 64 s
2.0 %: 52 s
4.0 %: 47 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of decolourisation (1/t) for each concentration in s⁻¹. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct to 3 s.f.; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 1/t can be used as a measure of the rate of respiration.
parts.answer: Rate is inversely proportional to the time taken to reach the same end point (same amount of DCPIP reduced), so a shorter time means a faster rate.
parts.working: B1 same amount of DCPIP reduced each time so rate ∝ 1/time.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Total volume of CO₂ in a gas syringe attached to a flask of yeast and glucose solution:
0 min: 0.0 cm³; 2 min: 3.5 cm³; 4 min: 7.8 cm³; 6 min: 12.0 cm³; 8 min: 15.2 cm³; 10 min: 17.4 cm³; 12 min: 18.6 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of CO₂ production in cm³ min⁻¹ for each 2-minute interval.
parts.working: M1 difference ÷ 2; A2 all six correct (A1 four or five).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease from the highest interval rate to the rate in the final interval. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the fall in rate.
parts.answer: Glucose is being used up (substrate concentration falls) or ethanol accumulates.
parts.working: B1 substrate depletion / ethanol build-up.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The temperature coefficient Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ rate at T. The rate of oxygen uptake by germinating barley was 0.62 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 20 °C and 1.18 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Q₁₀ for this temperature range. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming Q₁₀ stays the same, predict the rate at 40 °C. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.25 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹
parts.working: B1 1.18 × 1.903 (unrounded Q₁₀) = 2.25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the actual rate measured at 40 °C was lower than your prediction.
parts.answer: At high temperatures respiratory enzymes begin to denature (hydrogen bonds break, active sites change shape), so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form; Q₁₀ does not stay constant.
parts.working: B1 enzyme denaturation; B1 active site changes / fewer E–S complexes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A graph shows the volume of oxygen absorbed by blowfly larvae against time. A student drew a tangent to the curve at 5 minutes. The tangent passes through the points (2 min, 1.0 cm³) and (8 min, 7.6 cm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake at 5 minutes, with units.
parts.answer: 1.1 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student chose two points far apart on the tangent.
parts.answer: Reading points far apart reduces the percentage error in reading the coordinates, giving a more accurate gradient.
parts.working: B1 smaller percentage error in readings.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Yeast respiring anaerobically produced 480 cm³ of CO₂ at room temperature. One mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at room temperature. The equation for ethanol fermentation is C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Mr of glucose = 180.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose that was fermented.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the mass of glucose that would be needed to produce the same volume of CO₂ by aerobic respiration, and explain why it is different.
parts.answer: 0.60 g; in aerobic respiration each glucose produces 6 CO₂ instead of 2.
parts.working: B1 0.60 g (0.020 ÷ 6 × 180); B1 6 CO₂ per glucose aerobically.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) of two groups of germinating seeds, three replicates each:
seeds at 20 °C: 12.1, 12.9, 12.2
seeds at 30 °C: 16.5, 17.2, 16.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean for each group to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean oxygen uptake from 20 °C to 30 °C, to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the range of each group and comment on what the ranges suggest about the reliability of the data.
parts.answer: 20 °C range 0.8; 30 °C range 0.7; replicates are close together and the ranges do not overlap, suggesting the results are repeatable and the difference is likely to be real.
parts.working: B1 both ranges; B1 small ranges / no overlap so reliable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: At rest, a 25 g mouse uses 2.0 cm³ of oxygen per minute, and a 70 kg human uses 250 cm³ of oxygen per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the oxygen uptake of each, in cm³ per kg per hour. Give the human value to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: mouse 4800 cm³ kg⁻¹ h⁻¹; human 214 cm³ kg⁻¹ h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mouse's rate per kg is. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 22.4 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a biological explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: The mouse has a much larger surface area to volume ratio, so it loses heat faster; it must respire faster per kg to generate heat and keep body temperature constant.
parts.working: B1 larger SA:V ratio / faster heat loss; B1 more respiration to replace heat / maintain body temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a respirometer experiment the liquid moved 12 mm in 300 s. The ruler reads to the nearest 1 mm, so the uncertainty is ±0.5 mm. The stopwatch uncertainty is ±1 s. The capillary radius is 0.50 ± 0.01 mm. Volume V = πr²l.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the distance, in the time and in r². Give each to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: distance 4.2 %; time 0.33 %; r² 4.0 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the total percentage uncertainty in the rate of oxygen uptake (V ÷ t) by adding the percentage uncertainties. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one change that would most reduce the total percentage uncertainty.
parts.answer: Measure for longer so that the liquid moves a greater distance (reducing the percentage uncertainty in distance), or use a capillary with a more precisely known radius.
parts.working: B1 longer time / larger distance (or more precise capillary bore).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Five replicate measurements of the rate of CO₂ production by yeast at 35 °C (mm³ min⁻¹): 14.2, 15.8, 13.5, 16.1, 15.4.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation. Give the standard deviation to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: mean 15.0 mm³ min⁻¹; s = 1.11 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 25 °C the mean rate was 9.6 mm³ min⁻¹ with s = 0.95. Explain what the standard deviations suggest about whether the difference between 25 °C and 35 °C is likely to be real.
parts.answer: The difference between means (5.4) is much larger than either standard deviation, and mean ± 2s ranges do not overlap, so the difference is probably real / significant (a t-test would confirm).
parts.working: B1 difference in means much greater than SDs / no overlap of mean ± s (or 2s); B1 likely significant, confirm with t-test.

author: HomiLabs

stem: When carbohydrate is respired, about 20.1 kJ of energy is released for every 1 dm³ of oxygen used. A resting student uses 0.30 dm³ of oxygen per minute. During a 45-minute brisk walk his oxygen uptake is 1.2 dm³ per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in 24 hours at rest, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra energy released during the 45-minute walk compared with resting for the same time, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 814 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the figure of 20.1 kJ per dm³ would be inaccurate if the student were respiring mainly lipid.
parts.answer: The energy released per dm³ of oxygen depends on the substrate; lipid needs more oxygen per unit of CO₂ (RQ 0.7), so the energy per dm³ O₂ is different (slightly lower).
parts.working: B1 different substrate gives a different energy per dm³ O₂ (RQ differs).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student collected the CO₂ produced by yeast in an inverted measuring cylinder full of water held in a trough of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the volume of gas collected may be less than the volume of CO₂ produced.
parts.answer: Some CO₂ dissolves in the water in the cylinder / trough (CO₂ is quite soluble), and some may dissolve in the yeast solution before leaving.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ dissolves in water; B1 so not all is collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement to the method.
parts.answer: Use a gas syringe instead (or saturate the water with CO₂ first / collect over oil).
parts.working: B1 gas syringe / pre-saturate water / layer of oil.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured the time for methylene blue to decolourise in a single tube of yeast suspension at each of five temperatures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student should repeat the experiment at each temperature.
parts.answer: To check that the results are repeatable / reliable, to identify anomalous results and to allow a mean to be calculated, which reduces the effect of random errors.
parts.working: B1 identify anomalies; B1 calculate a mean / reduce effect of random error / check repeatability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the student would decide whether a result is anomalous.
parts.answer: It does not fit the pattern / is very different from the other replicates at that temperature (or does not lie close to the line of best fit).
parts.working: B1 differs greatly from other replicates / pattern.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an experiment with DCPIP and yeast, the student judged by eye when the blue colour had disappeared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a source of error.
parts.answer: Judging the end point is subjective; it is difficult to decide exactly when the blue colour has gone, especially as the yeast suspension is cloudy / cream coloured, so the times may be inaccurate.
parts.working: B1 subjective end point; B1 gradual colour change / cloudy yeast makes it hard to see.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to reduce this error.
parts.answer: Compare each tube with a colour standard (yeast + water without DCPIP) against a white background; use a colorimeter to measure absorbance at fixed times; same person judges every tube.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigated the effect of temperature on yeast respiration by placing tubes in beakers of water that had been heated to the required temperature with a Bunsen burner and then left on the bench.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this method could give unreliable results.
parts.answer: The water would cool towards room temperature during the experiment, so the temperature of the yeast would not stay constant; the actual temperature would differ from the stated one.
parts.working: B1 temperature falls / fluctuates; B1 so the independent variable is not controlled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Use a thermostatically controlled water bath and check the temperature with a thermometer in the tube during the experiment.
parts.working: B1 thermostatic water bath (with thermometer check).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student used respirometers to compare respiration rates of maggots at two temperatures. He used 10 maggots in each respirometer, picked at random from a container.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using 10 maggots in each tube may make the comparison unfair.
parts.answer: Maggots vary in size / mass, so the total mass of respiring tissue in each tube may be different; rate depends on mass.
parts.working: B1 maggots differ in mass / size / age; B1 more tissue gives more oxygen uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Use the same total mass of maggots (weighed) in each tube and express the rate per gram.
parts.working: B1 same mass / rate per gram.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student set up a respirometer with germinating seeds and soda lime. After 20 minutes the coloured liquid had hardly moved, although the seeds were known to be respiring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two possible reasons for this result.
parts.answer: The apparatus was not airtight (air leaked in through a loose bung or joint); the soda lime was exhausted / no longer absorbing CO₂; the tap was left open.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could test whether the apparatus is airtight.
parts.answer: With the tap closed, push the syringe plunger in a little: if the apparatus is airtight the liquid moves and stays in its new position; if it gradually returns, there is a leak. Seal joints with petroleum jelly.
parts.working: B1 move syringe / apply pressure and observe whether liquid stays displaced; B1 seal with petroleum jelly / check bungs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student pipetted yeast suspension from a stock bottle into six tubes, one after the other, over 15 minutes. The tubes filled last showed the fastest rates of respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for this result.
parts.answer: Yeast cells settle at the bottom of the stock bottle over time, so later samples taken from lower down (or from a more concentrated suspension) contain more yeast cells.
parts.working: B1 yeast settles / sediments; B1 later samples had more cells (uneven concentration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how to improve the method.
parts.answer: Stir or swirl the stock suspension immediately before taking each sample; prepare all tubes quickly; randomise the order in which treatments are filled.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student took a respirometer containing seeds from a cool store room at 15 °C, placed it in a water bath at 30 °C, closed the tap immediately and started timing. The liquid first moved away from the seeds, then towards them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the liquid first moved away from the seeds.
parts.answer: The air inside the tube was warming up and expanding, increasing the volume / pressure and pushing the liquid away; this was greater than the volume of oxygen taken in.
parts.working: B1 gas warmed and expanded; B1 outweighed oxygen uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student should change the method.
parts.answer: Leave the respirometer in the water bath with the tap open for 10–15 minutes to equilibrate before closing the tap; use a thermobarometer to correct for any remaining changes.
parts.working: B1 equilibrate with tap open for stated time; B1 thermobarometer.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three students each measured the rate of oxygen uptake by germinating mung beans at 25 °C using the same method. Results (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹):
student A: 34, 36, 35
student B: 22, 41, 30
student C: 35, 34, 52

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the reliability of the results of the three students.
parts.answer: A's results are close together so they are repeatable / reliable; B's results are widely spread (range 19) so not reliable; C has two close results and one anomalous result (52), which should be excluded or repeated.
parts.working: B1 A reliable / small range; B1 B unreliable / large range; B1 C has an anomaly (52).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why student B's results might vary so much.
parts.answer: Different masses / stages of germination of beans in each run; leaks in the apparatus; temperature not equilibrated; inaccurate reading of the meniscus; timing errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible reasons.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student tested whether peas or maize grains produce more CO₂ by passing the air from containers of each through limewater and noting which limewater went cloudy first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this method gives only limited information.
parts.answer: Limewater gives a qualitative result (cloudy or not) or only a time; the degree of cloudiness is difficult to judge and does not measure the volume of CO₂; different masses of seeds may have been used.
parts.working: B1 qualitative / subjective judgement of cloudiness; B1 no quantitative volume / rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a method that would give quantitative results.
parts.answer: Use a CO₂ sensor and data logger in sealed containers with equal masses of seeds, or use hydrogencarbonate indicator and a colorimeter calibrated with known CO₂ concentrations, and measure over a fixed time.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ sensor / colorimeter with indicator / respirometer; B1 equal masses and fixed time.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a respirometer investigation, the student made these errors:
1 the capillary tube was labelled as having a radius of 0.50 mm but it was actually 0.45 mm
2 the room temperature varied by up to 2 °C during the experiment
3 the student read the meniscus from different angles

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each error, state whether it is a systematic error or a random error, and explain your choice.
parts.answer: 1 systematic: every volume would be calculated too large by the same proportion. 2 random: changes in temperature affect readings unpredictably up or down. 3 random: parallax error varies from reading to reading in either direction.
parts.working: B1 each correct classification with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which of these errors would not affect a comparison of rates at two temperatures if the same capillary tube was used for both.
parts.answer: Error 1: the radius error multiplies every volume by the same factor, so the relative difference / ratio between temperatures is unchanged (only the absolute values are wrong).
parts.working: B1 error 1 (systematic radius error); B1 same proportional error in both, so comparison / ratio still valid.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigated the effect of temperature on yeast respiration. He used one tube at each of 20 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C, measuring CO₂ volume after 10 minutes. Results: 20 °C: 3 cm³; 40 °C: 11 cm³; 60 °C: 2 cm³. He concluded that the optimum temperature for yeast respiration is 40 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the reliability of the method and the validity of the conclusion.
parts.answer: Only one tube at each temperature so no repeats / no way to identify anomalies or calculate means; only three temperatures with large 20 °C intervals, so the optimum could be anywhere between about 30 °C and 50 °C; a single 10-minute reading does not give the initial rate; no evidence that other variables (yeast and glucose concentration, equilibration) were controlled; conclusion that the optimum is exactly 40 °C is not justified — only that it is between 20 °C and 60 °C, most likely near 40 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: no replicates; too few temperatures / intervals too large; optimum could be anywhere between 20/30 and 50/60 °C; single end-point reading not a rate; control variables not stated; conclusion only tentative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation should be improved to locate the optimum more precisely.
parts.answer: Repeat with smaller intervals around 40 °C (e.g. 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 °C) with at least three replicates each, and measure volume at several times to find initial rates.
parts.working: B1 smaller intervals around 40 °C; B1 replicates / initial rate from several readings.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A dissolved-oxygen probe was used to follow oxygen uptake by a yeast suspension. Before the experiment, the probe gave a reading of 9.6 mg dm⁻³ in air-saturated water at 25 °C, whose true value is 8.3 mg dm⁻³. At the end of the experiment, the probe gave a reading of 10.1 mg dm⁻³ in the same water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage error in the probe reading at the start, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the problems shown by these readings and suggest how to deal with them.
parts.answer: The probe was not calibrated (systematic error — readings too high); the reading drifted during the experiment, so the error changed over time; calibrate the probe against air-saturated water and oxygen-free water (zero) before use, re-check calibration during the experiment and correct readings for drift.
parts.working: B1 probe not calibrated / systematic error; B1 drift during experiment; B1 calibrate before (two-point) and check / correct during or after.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured oxygen uptake of germinating seeds over 48 hours in a sealed respirometer at 25 °C. The rate increased steadily throughout. When the seeds were examined at the end, there was white fungal growth on them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the fungal growth could have affected the results.
parts.answer: Fungi (microorganisms) also respire and take up oxygen, so the measured oxygen uptake includes their respiration and is greater than that of the seeds alone; the increase over time may be partly due to fungal growth.
parts.working: B1 fungi respire / use oxygen; B1 overestimate of seed respiration / rising rate partly due to fungi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the method could be improved to deal with this.
parts.answer: Surface-sterilise the seeds (e.g. with dilute sodium hypochlorite, then rinse) before use; use sterile apparatus; set up a control with boiled (dead) seeds that are not sterilised to measure microbial respiration; use a shorter experiment time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigated whether yeast respires glucose, fructose and galactose at different rates, by measuring the volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: type of sugar (respiratory substrate). Dependent: volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes (rate of CO₂ production).
parts.working: B1 IV type of sugar; B1 DV volume of CO₂ in 10 min / rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised.
parts.answer: Any three: temperature; concentration of sugar; volume of sugar solution; mass / concentration of yeast; pH; time yeast was activated / age of yeast suspension; type of yeast.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two respirometers were set up in a water bath. Tube A contained 10 g of germinating seeds and soda lime. Tube B contained 10 cm³ of glass beads and soda lime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of tube B.
parts.answer: It is a control (thermobarometer) that shows changes in volume due to temperature or atmospheric pressure only, not respiration, so tube A's readings can be corrected.
parts.working: B1 control / thermobarometer; B1 detects volume changes caused by temperature / pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tube B contains glass beads of the same volume as the seeds rather than being empty.
parts.answer: So that the volume of air in both tubes is the same, so a given temperature or pressure change causes the same volume change.
parts.working: B1 same air volume in both tubes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an investigation of CO₂ production by yeast in glucose solution, a student set up an extra tube containing yeast that had been boiled and cooled, with glucose solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this tube was set up.
parts.answer: As a control to show that CO₂ production is due to respiration by living yeast (enzymes), and not to any other reaction or factor; boiling denatures the enzymes.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 boiled yeast enzymes denatured / shows CO₂ comes from living yeast respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other suitable control tube.
parts.answer: Living yeast with distilled water instead of glucose (or glucose solution without yeast).
parts.working: B1 yeast without glucose / glucose without yeast.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measured how the rate of oxygen uptake by woodlice changed with the temperature of the respirometer. The following were listed:
mass of woodlice; temperature; volume of oxygen taken up per minute; time of day; volume of soda lime

parts.label: a
parts.text: From the list, identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and three variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: volume of oxygen taken up per minute. Controlled: mass of woodlice, time of day, volume of soda lime.
parts.working: B1 IV; B1 DV; B1 all three controlled variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why time of day should be controlled.
parts.answer: Woodlice may be more active at certain times (e.g. at night), changing their respiration rate.
parts.working: B1 activity / metabolic rate varies with time of day.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how each of these variables can be kept constant in an investigation of yeast respiration: temperature; pH; volume of glucose solution.
parts.answer: Temperature: thermostatically controlled water bath (check with thermometer). pH: add the same volume of a buffer solution of fixed pH. Volume: measure with a graduated pipette or syringe.
parts.working: B1 each correct method.

stem: A student will investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration in yeast using DCPIP. She must make sure every tube contains the same concentration of yeast cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which she could standardise the concentration of yeast.
parts.answer: Weigh the same mass of dried yeast and dissolve in the same volume of water; or use a colorimeter to adjust the suspension to the same absorbance (turbidity); or count cells with a haemocytometer and dilute to the same density.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two methods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why yeast suspensions should be activated in glucose solution for the same length of time before each trial.
parts.answer: The respiration rate of yeast increases as it becomes active after rehydration (and cell number may increase with time); different activation times would add an uncontrolled variable affecting rate.
parts.working: B1 rate / activity of yeast changes with time after rehydration; B1 would affect dependent variable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Volunteers had their RQ measured after eating a meal, to find out how the type of meal affects the respiratory substrate used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables, other than the meal, that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any three: time since meal; activity / exercise level (measure at rest); time since last meal before the test (overnight fast); mass of food / energy content of meal; age, sex or fitness of volunteers; room temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same volunteers should be tested with each type of meal.
parts.answer: Individuals differ in metabolic rate and RQ; using the same people removes the effect of these differences so changes can be attributed to the meal.
parts.working: B1 individuals vary in metabolism; B1 same people controls this / fair comparison.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compared the respiration rates of germinating seeds of chickpea, wheat and sunflower using a respirometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the comparison may not be valid if the student used 20 seeds of each species.
parts.answer: The seeds differ greatly in size / mass, so the mass of respiring tissue would differ; rate should be compared per unit mass.
parts.working: B1 seeds differ in size / mass; B1 use the same mass / rate per gram.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other variables that would be difficult to control between species and explain why each matters.
parts.answer: Stage of germination (species germinate at different rates); water content of seeds; type of stored food (lipid vs starch) changing oxygen uptake relative to CO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two variables with reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student made 2 % (20 g dm⁻³) solutions of glucose (Mr 180) and sucrose (Mr 342) to compare respiration by yeast with each sugar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of each solution in mol dm⁻³, to 3 significant figures, and how many times more molecules of glucose there are per dm³. Give the ratio to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: glucose 0.111 mol dm⁻³; sucrose 0.0585 mol dm⁻³; ratio 1.9

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why using equal molar concentrations might be a better way to control the substrate concentration in this investigation.
parts.answer: Each sucrose molecule is hydrolysed into one glucose and one fructose, so equal percentage solutions do not provide equal numbers of hexose units / molecules; equal molarity (or equal hexose content) makes the comparison of sugars fair.
parts.working: B1 equal % gives different numbers of molecules; B1 fairer comparison of substrate available / sucrose gives two hexoses.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student used a respirometer to measure the rate of respiration of leaves from a mint plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the respirometer must be kept in the dark.
parts.answer: In light the leaves photosynthesise, taking in CO₂ and releasing oxygen; this would counteract / mask oxygen uptake by respiration, so the measured volume change would not show respiration only.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis in light; B1 releases O₂ / alters gas volume so respiration not measured accurately.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could check that no light was reaching the leaves.
parts.answer: Wrap the tube in aluminium foil / black paper and use a light meter / check no oxygen output in a tube without soda lime (or work in a darkened room).
parts.working: B1 any sensible check / method of exclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A drug that may block the electron transport chain is only soluble in ethanol. Researchers will test its effect on oxygen uptake by isolated mitochondria by adding 0.1 cm³ of the drug dissolved in ethanol to 5 cm³ of mitochondrial suspension.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the control experiments that should be carried out and explain the purpose of each.
parts.answer: Add 0.1 cm³ of ethanol alone (solvent control) to show that any effect is due to the drug, not the ethanol; mitochondria with no additions (to measure normal oxygen uptake); suspension buffer without mitochondria plus drug (to show the drug does not react with oxygen itself / affect the electrode); a known inhibitor (e.g. cyanide) as a positive control to show the method detects inhibition.
parts.working: B1 solvent (ethanol) control; B1 explanation; B1 any other control (no mitochondria / no addition / positive control); B1 its purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant when adding the drug to the suspension.
parts.answer: Concentration / volume of mitochondria (protein content); temperature; concentration of respiratory substrate; concentration of ADP and phosphate; pH (buffer); oxygen concentration at the start.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compared the rate of respiration of soil microorganisms in soil samples from a wheat field, a mango orchard and a roadside verge near Multan. She sealed 100 g of each soil in a jar with a CO₂ sensor for 1 hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables that would be difficult to control in this study and explain how she could deal with each.
parts.answer: Soil moisture: measure and adjust to same water content (or record); soil temperature at collection: equilibrate all samples at the same temperature before measurement; organic matter / plant roots / invertebrates: sieve soil to remove roots and animals; time since collection / depth of sampling: collect at the same depth on the same day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables with a sensible way of dealing with them (control, standardise or record).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why she should take several samples from different places in each site.
parts.answer: Soil is very variable within a site; several random samples give a representative mean and allow variability to be assessed (e.g. with standard deviation / statistical test).
parts.working: B1 variation within site; B1 representative mean / allows statistical comparison.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to investigate whether sodium chloride concentration affects the rate of respiration of yeast. He realises that adding salt also lowers the water potential of the solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how he could design a control to find out whether any effect is caused by the low water potential rather than by sodium chloride itself.
parts.answer: Set up a second series using a solute that is not toxic and not respired by yeast (e.g. mannitol / sorbitol) at concentrations giving the same water potentials as each NaCl solution; if the rate falls equally with mannitol, the effect is due to water potential; if NaCl reduces the rate more, the ions themselves have an effect.
parts.working: B1 another solute not used as a substrate (mannitol / sorbitol / PEG); B1 matched water potential (osmotic concentration); B1 compare the two series to separate the effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable and two standardised variables in the main experiment.
parts.answer: IV: NaCl concentration. Standardised: any two of glucose concentration, temperature, yeast concentration, volume, pH.
parts.working: B1 IV; B1 two standardised variables.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A study tested whether a caffeine drink increases resting metabolic rate (measured by oxygen uptake) in adults. Volunteers drank either the caffeine drink or an identical-tasting drink without caffeine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the drink without caffeine was used and why it was made to taste the same.
parts.answer: It is a placebo control showing the effect of drinking (fluid, volume, sugar) without caffeine; identical taste means volunteers do not know which they received, so expectations / behaviour do not affect the results.
parts.working: B1 placebo / control for drink itself; B1 volunteers unaware so no psychological bias.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the study should be double-blind.
parts.answer: So the researchers measuring oxygen uptake also do not know which drink each volunteer had, preventing unconscious bias in measurement or recording.
parts.working: B1 researchers unaware, avoiding bias.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two variables relating to the volunteers that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Habitual caffeine intake (tea/coffee drinking); time since last meal (fasting); activity before the test (rest period); time of day; age / body mass; smoking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Volume of CO₂ produced by yeast in glucose solution in 10 minutes at different temperatures:
10 °C: 0.8 cm³; 20 °C: 2.1 cm³; 30 °C: 4.6 cm³; 40 °C: 6.3 cm³; 50 °C: 2.4 cm³; 60 °C: 0.2 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results between 10 °C and 40 °C.
parts.answer: As temperature rises, the enzymes and substrate molecules of respiration have more kinetic energy; more frequent successful collisions, more enzyme–substrate complexes, so faster respiration and more CO₂.
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy / more collisions; B1 more enzyme–substrate complexes so faster respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results between 40 °C and 60 °C.
parts.answer: Respiratory enzymes are denatured: hydrogen bonds break, the active site changes shape so substrates no longer fit; fewer enzyme–substrate complexes; at 60 °C nearly all enzymes denatured / yeast killed.
parts.working: B1 denaturation / bonds broken; B1 active site shape changed so fewer E–S complexes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Oxygen uptake of dry wheat grains was 0.02 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹. Wheat grains soaked in water for 2 days took up 145 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference in oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Water activates the enzymes in the grains (and hydrolyses stored starch to sugars); respiration increases greatly to provide ATP for growth (cell division, protein synthesis) of the embryo; dry grains are dormant with very little metabolic activity.
parts.working: B1 water needed to activate enzymes / metabolism; B1 starch hydrolysed to glucose for respiration; B1 ATP needed for growth / dry grains dormant.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Yeast was placed in tubes containing 5 % solutions of different sugars. After 30 minutes, CO₂ had been produced with glucose, fructose and sucrose, but not with lactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why no CO₂ was produced with lactose.
parts.answer: The yeast has no lactase enzyme (and no lactose carrier), so it cannot hydrolyse lactose into glucose and galactose; lactose cannot enter glycolysis.
parts.working: B1 yeast lacks lactase / cannot hydrolyse lactose; B1 so no respiratory substrate enters glycolysis / no uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why CO₂ was produced with sucrose.
parts.answer: Yeast produces sucrase (invertase), which hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose that can be respired.
parts.working: B1 sucrase / invertase hydrolyses sucrose to monosaccharides.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Tube 1 contained living yeast, glucose and DCPIP. Tube 2 contained boiled yeast, glucose and DCPIP. After 10 minutes, tube 1 was colourless and tube 2 was still blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results.
parts.answer: In tube 1 dehydrogenase enzymes removed hydrogen from respiratory intermediates (e.g. in glycolysis); the hydrogen reduced the DCPIP, which became colourless; in tube 2 boiling had denatured the dehydrogenase enzymes, so no hydrogen was released and DCPIP stayed blue.
parts.working: B1 dehydrogenases remove hydrogen in respiration; B1 DCPIP reduced / accepts hydrogen → colourless; B1 enzymes in boiled yeast denatured.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Blood lactate concentration of a footballer running on a treadmill at increasing speeds:
8 km h⁻¹: 1.2 mmol dm⁻³; 10 km h⁻¹: 1.4; 12 km h⁻¹: 1.9; 14 km h⁻¹: 3.8; 16 km h⁻¹: 7.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why lactate rises only slightly up to 12 km h⁻¹ but sharply above this speed.
parts.answer: At low speeds oxygen supply to muscles is enough for most ATP to come from aerobic respiration; above about 12 km h⁻¹ the demand for ATP exceeds what aerobic respiration can supply because oxygen delivery is limited; muscles respire anaerobically, pyruvate is reduced to lactate (to regenerate NAD) and lactate builds up in the blood.
parts.working: B1 low speed: aerobic respiration meets ATP demand; B1 high speed: oxygen supply insufficient / ATP demand exceeds aerobic supply; B1 anaerobic respiration / pyruvate → lactate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rate of CO₂ production by yeast at different glucose concentrations (cm³ min⁻¹):
0 %: 0.0; 0.5 %: 0.8; 1 %: 1.5; 2 %: 2.4; 4 %: 2.9; 8 %: 3.0; 16 %: 3.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in rate between 0 % and 2 % glucose.
parts.answer: Glucose is the limiting factor; more glucose molecules means more glucose taken into cells and more frequent collisions with glycolytic enzymes, so more enzyme–substrate complexes and faster respiration.
parts.working: B1 glucose limiting; B1 more E–S complexes / more substrate for glycolysis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate levels off above 4 % glucose.
parts.answer: Another factor is now limiting: all the active sites of the enzymes (or glucose carrier proteins in the membrane) are occupied / saturated; extra glucose cannot increase the rate; rate limited by enzyme / carrier number or temperature.
parts.working: B1 enzymes / carriers saturated; B1 another factor limiting (e.g. enzyme concentration, temperature).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Time for methylene blue to decolourise in yeast suspensions buffered at different pH values:
pH 3: 410 s; pH 4: 190 s; pH 5: 120 s; pH 6: 135 s; pH 7: 260 s; pH 8: 600 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the pH at which the rate of respiration was fastest.
parts.answer: pH 5
parts.working: B1 pH 5 (shortest time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate is lower at pH 8 than at pH 5.
parts.answer: At pH 8 the concentration of hydrogen ions is far from the optimum; ionic and hydrogen bonds in the enzymes (dehydrogenases) are disrupted; the shape of the active site changes so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form and less hydrogen is released to reduce methylene blue.
parts.working: B1 pH away from optimum; B1 ionic / hydrogen bonds affected, active site shape changed; B1 fewer E–S complexes so slower dehydrogenation / methylene blue reduction.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mitochondria isolated from beef heart were given different substrates and their oxygen uptake measured (nmol O₂ min⁻¹ mg⁻¹ protein):
no substrate: 2; glucose: 2; pyruvate: 85; succinate: 110

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why glucose did not increase oxygen uptake but pyruvate did.
parts.answer: Glycolysis enzymes are in the cytoplasm, not in mitochondria, so glucose cannot be converted to pyruvate; pyruvate is actively transported into the matrix where the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and FAD; these pass electrons along the electron transport chain to oxygen.
parts.working: B1 glycolysis does not occur in mitochondria; B1 pyruvate enters matrix / link reaction / Krebs; B1 reduced NAD / FAD donate electrons to ETC, oxygen used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why there was a small oxygen uptake with no substrate added.
parts.answer: Some respiratory substrates / intermediates remained inside the mitochondria from the cells.
parts.working: B1 endogenous substrate left in mitochondria.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Apples harvested in Kalam (Swat) are stored in cold stores at 2 °C with 2 % oxygen and 3 % carbon dioxide. They stay fresh for months. If the oxygen concentration falls below 1 %, the apples develop an alcoholic taste.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the storage conditions slow the deterioration of the apples.
parts.answer: Low temperature reduces kinetic energy so enzymes of respiration (and ripening) work slowly; low oxygen limits aerobic respiration (less oxygen as final electron acceptor); high CO₂ also slows respiration; less substrate (sugar) is used, so fruit stays firm and sweet for longer.
parts.working: B1 low temperature slows enzyme activity; B1 low oxygen reduces aerobic respiration; B1 less sugar / stored food used up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the alcoholic taste when oxygen falls below 1 %.
parts.answer: Too little oxygen for the electron transport chain; the apple cells respire anaerobically, converting pyruvate to ethanol (to regenerate NAD), which accumulates in the fruit.
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration; B1 ethanol produced / accumulates.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student squeezed a clothes peg as many times as possible with one hand. Number of squeezes in each 30-second interval: 0–30 s: 62; 30–60 s: 51; 60–90 s: 40; 90–120 s: 31.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the number of squeezes fell.
parts.answer: Muscles needed ATP faster than aerobic respiration could supply because oxygen delivery was limited; anaerobic respiration produced lactate, lowering pH, which inhibits enzymes (and contraction); fewer ATP available, muscle fatigue.
parts.working: B1 oxygen supply insufficient / anaerobic respiration; B1 lactate accumulates / pH falls; B1 less ATP / enzymes inhibited so fatigue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student's other hand, used after a 5-minute rest, performed at the starting rate again.
parts.answer: The rested muscles had normal ATP and oxygen supplies and no lactate accumulation.
parts.working: B1 no lactate / oxygen debt / full ATP and creatine phosphate / glycogen stores.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Yeast was placed in a sealed flask of glucose solution with an air space above it. Readings at intervals:
time / min: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80
O₂ uptake per 20 min / cm³: —, 4.0, 3.1, 0.9, 0.1
CO₂ output per 20 min / cm³: —, 4.0, 4.6, 6.2, 6.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ for each 20-minute interval to 2 significant figures where possible.
parts.working: M1 CO₂ ÷ O₂ for each; A1 1.0, 1.5, 6.9 and 68 (all four).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes in RQ.
parts.answer: At first all respiration is aerobic using glucose (carbohydrate RQ 1.0); as oxygen in the flask is used up, an increasing proportion of glucose is respired anaerobically to ethanol; this releases CO₂ (decarboxylation of pyruvate) without oxygen uptake, so RQ rises far above 1.
parts.working: B1 RQ 1 = aerobic respiration of carbohydrate; B1 oxygen depleted so more anaerobic respiration; B1 CO₂ produced without O₂ uptake, RQ rises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the total CO₂ output per interval increased even though less oxygen was used.
parts.answer: Anaerobic respiration yields only 2 ATP per glucose, so the yeast must break down glucose much faster to meet its ATP needs; each glucose fermented releases 2 CO₂, so total CO₂ rises.
parts.working: B1 less ATP per glucose anaerobically so faster glycolysis; B1 more glucose fermented releasing CO₂.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oxygen uptake by isolated rat liver mitochondria at different ADP concentrations (all other substrates in excess):
ADP / µmol dm⁻³: 0, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400
O₂ uptake / nmol min⁻¹: 10, 28, 45, 58, 64, 65

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why oxygen uptake increases as ADP concentration increases from 0 to 100 µmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: ADP is a substrate for ATP synthase; more ADP means more ATP synthesis, so more protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase; the proton gradient is reduced, so electron transport and proton pumping can proceed faster; more electrons reach oxygen per minute.
parts.working: B1 ADP substrate for ATP synthase; B1 more protons flow back / gradient used; B1 electron transport faster so more O₂ reduced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why oxygen uptake levels off above 200 µmol dm⁻³ ADP.
parts.answer: ATP synthase molecules are working at their maximum rate (saturated with ADP) or the electron transport chain is working at its maximum rate; another factor such as number of carriers / ATP synthase is limiting.
parts.working: B1 ATP synthase / ETC saturated / at maximum rate; B1 another factor limiting.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Blood lactate concentration at a running speed of 14 km h⁻¹:
untrained students (mean of 12): 6.1 mmol dm⁻³
students after 10 weeks of endurance training (same 12 students): 2.7 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest explanations for the lower lactate concentration after training.
parts.answer: Training increases the number of mitochondria (and cristae) in muscle fibres, so more aerobic respiration; more capillaries in muscles and larger stroke volume increase oxygen delivery; more myoglobin stores oxygen; so less anaerobic respiration and less lactate formed; faster removal of lactate by the liver / heart.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: more mitochondria; more capillaries / better blood supply; increased cardiac output / stroke volume; more myoglobin; higher proportion of ATP from aerobic respiration; faster lactate removal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same students were tested before and after training.
parts.answer: To remove the effect of differences between individuals (genetic, fitness), so any change is due to training.
parts.working: B1 controls for individual variation.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Pea seeds were germinated in the light. Every two days, 20 seedlings were dried and weighed, and the oxygen uptake of another 20 was measured.
day: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12
