dry mass of 20 seedlings / g: 4.0, 3.9, 3.6, 3.3, 3.2, 3.5, 4.1
oxygen uptake / mm³ h⁻¹: 2, 60, 210, 380, 420, 410, 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the changes in dry mass between day 0 and day 8.
parts.answer: Dry mass falls because stored starch is respired to provide ATP for growth; carbon is lost as CO₂; the seedlings cannot yet photosynthesise (no / few green leaves) to replace it.
parts.working: B1 stored food respired, carbon lost as CO₂; B1 little or no photosynthesis yet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes in dry mass after day 8, even though oxygen uptake remained high.
parts.answer: Leaves have opened and photosynthesis begins; the rate of photosynthesis exceeds the rate of respiration, so there is a net gain in organic material / dry mass.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis begins in green leaves; B1 photosynthesis > respiration so net gain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why oxygen uptake rose so sharply between day 0 and day 6.
parts.answer: Water uptake activates enzymes and hydrolysis of stores provides substrate; rapid cell division and growth need large amounts of ATP, and the mass of respiring tissue increases.
parts.working: B1 enzymes activated / substrate made available; B1 ATP for growth / more cells respiring.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two investigations were carried out with yeast:
Investigation 1: volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes with five different sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose, maltose, lactose).
Investigation 2: volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph or chart that should be used to present the results of each investigation. Explain your choices.
parts.answer: Investigation 1: bar chart, because the independent variable (type of sugar) is categorical / discontinuous, with bars separated. Investigation 2: line graph, because temperature is a continuous variable, with points joined by straight lines or a smooth curve.
parts.working: B1 bar chart; B1 sugar type is categorical / discontinuous; B1 line graph; B1 temperature is continuous.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student is plotting a graph of oxygen uptake by germinating seeds (cm³) against time (min).

parts.label: a
parts.text: List four features of a well-drawn graph of these results.
parts.answer: Independent variable (time) on the x-axis and dependent variable (oxygen uptake) on the y-axis; both axes labelled with quantity and unit (e.g. time / min); linear scales chosen so the points fill more than half the grid; points plotted accurately as small crosses or circled dots; a smooth line of best fit or straight lines joining points, not extended beyond the data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Total volume of CO₂ produced by yeast: 4 min: 7.8 cm³; 6 min: 12.0 cm³. The points are joined by a straight line on a graph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the straight line between these points to estimate the volume at 5 min.
parts.answer: 9.9 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name for estimating a value between plotted points and explain why it is more reliable than estimating a value beyond the last point.
parts.answer: Interpolation; values between measured points are supported by data on both sides, whereas extrapolation assumes the trend continues beyond the data, which may not be true (e.g. glucose may run out).
parts.working: B1 interpolation; B1 extrapolation assumes trend continues / no data beyond range.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student must plot volumes of CO₂ from 0 to 18.6 cm³ on the y-axis of a grid that has 10 large squares vertically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a suitable scale for the y-axis and explain your choice.
parts.answer: 2 cm³ per large square (0 to 20 cm³): it uses over half the grid (18.6 of 20) and is easy to read; awkward scales such as 1.86 per square or 3 per square should be avoided.
parts.working: B1 2 cm³ per large square (0–20); B1 data fill most of the grid and scale is easy to read / in simple multiples.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the line of best fit should not be extended past the last data point.
parts.answer: There is no evidence of what happens beyond the measured range.
parts.working: B1 no data / trend may change.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bar chart shows the mean rate of respiration of yeast with glucose and with maltose. Each bar has an error bar showing ± 2 standard errors. The error bars for glucose and maltose overlap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the error bars show.
parts.answer: The variability / spread of the replicate results about the mean (an estimate of the range within which the true mean probably lies — about 95 % confidence).
parts.working: B1 spread of data / reliability of mean / 95 % confidence interval.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what can be concluded from the overlapping error bars.
parts.answer: The difference between the means is probably not significant; it could be due to chance / random variation, so we cannot conclude that yeast respires glucose and maltose at different rates.
parts.working: B1 difference not significant / could be due to chance; B1 no valid conclusion about a real difference.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A line graph of oxygen uptake by germinating wheat against temperature was drawn. Two points on the straight part of the line are (10 °C, 4.2 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) and (30 °C, 15.6 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of this part of the line, with units.
parts.answer: 0.57 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ °C⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the gradient represents.
parts.answer: The increase in the rate of oxygen uptake for each 1 °C rise in temperature.
parts.working: B1 change in rate per °C.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean rate of CO₂ production by yeast (cm³ min⁻¹) and standard deviation (SD), 5 replicates each:
20 °C: mean 0.42, SD 0.05
30 °C: mean 0.95, SD 0.07
40 °C: mean 1.38, SD 0.21
50 °C: mean 0.61, SD 0.18

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to show the variability of the data on a line graph of mean rate against temperature.
parts.answer: Plot each mean, then draw a vertical error bar through each point extending one SD above and below the mean (e.g. 40 °C from 1.17 to 1.59), with short horizontal caps.
parts.working: B1 error bars at each mean; B1 extending ± 1 SD (correct example values).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the SD values are larger at 40 °C and 50 °C than at 20 °C.
parts.answer: At higher temperatures enzymes in different samples are partly denatured to different extents / small differences in temperature have larger effects; more random variation in rate between replicates.
parts.working: B1 denaturation begins / rate very sensitive to small temperature differences; B1 more variable results between replicates.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A graph of oxygen uptake by maggots was plotted at 10, 15, 20 and 25 °C. A student used the line to predict the uptake at 45 °C and at 17 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain which of the two predictions is more reliable.
parts.answer: 17 °C is within the measured range (interpolation), so it is supported by data on either side; 45 °C is far outside the range (extrapolation) and enzymes may be denatured / maggots may die, so the trend is unlikely to continue.
parts.working: B1 17 °C more reliable – interpolation; B1 45 °C extrapolation beyond range / denaturation changes the trend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an additional range of temperatures that would allow the student to find the temperature at which the rate is highest.
parts.answer: e.g. 30, 35, 40 °C (ethical limits permitting) — extend the range above 25 °C with small intervals.
parts.working: B1 extend range above 25 °C with suitable intervals.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student recorded the following total volumes of oxygen absorbed by germinating peas: 0 min 0.0 cm³; 2 min 0.9; 4 min 1.9; 6 min 2.7; 8 min 3.8; 10 min 4.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether the student should join the points dot to dot or draw a line of best fit.
parts.answer: A straight line of best fit, because the points follow a linear trend and the small irregularities are due to experimental error; the line shows the overall rate and averages out random errors.
parts.working: B1 line of best fit (straight); B1 data scattered about a linear trend / averages out random error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the rate of oxygen uptake from the overall trend in cm³ min⁻¹, using the first and last values.
parts.answer: 0.46 cm³ min⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rate of oxygen uptake of blowfly larvae (mm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹): 10 °C: 0.9; 15 °C: 1.3; 20 °C: 1.9; 25 °C: 2.8; 30 °C: 3.9; 35 °C: 3.5; 40 °C: 1.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results shown, using figures from the data.
parts.answer: The rate increases as temperature increases from 10 °C (0.9) to a maximum at 30 °C (3.9); the increase gets steeper with temperature (0.4 per 5 °C at first, 1.1 between 25 and 30 °C); above 30 °C the rate falls, sharply to 1.2 at 40 °C.
parts.working: B1 increase to maximum at 30 °C with figures; B1 increase becomes steeper (accelerates); B1 decrease above 30 °C with figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of the curve you would draw through these points.
parts.answer: A smooth curve rising more and more steeply to a peak near 30 °C, then falling steeply.
parts.working: B1 smooth curve with peak near 30 °C and steep fall.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a respirometer study, both the oxygen uptake and the CO₂ output of germinating castor-oil seeds (cm³ per day per 10 seeds) were measured over 10 days. Oxygen uptake ranged from 2 to 48, and CO₂ output from 1.4 to 47.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how both sets of data could be shown on one graph, and why this is useful.
parts.answer: Plot both against time on the same axes with one y-axis (same units, same scale) and a key distinguishing the two lines; it shows directly how the ratio CO₂ : O₂ (RQ) changes over time.
parts.working: B1 same axes / key (same units so one y-axis); B1 allows comparison / RQ changes visible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a second graph that would show the change in respiratory substrate more clearly, and describe what it might show.
parts.answer: A graph of RQ (CO₂ ÷ O₂) against time: RQ near 0.7 early (lipid stores used) rising towards 1.0 as seedlings begin to use carbohydrate (e.g. after photosynthesis begins).
parts.working: B1 RQ against time; B1 shows change from about 0.7 (lipid) towards 1.0 (carbohydrate).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The body mass of five mammals ranges from a 0.02 kg mouse to a 600 kg horse (rat 0.25 kg, rabbit 3.0 kg, human 60 kg). A student wants to plot mass-specific oxygen uptake against body mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate log₁₀ of each body mass, to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: mouse −1.70; rat −0.60; rabbit 0.48; human 1.78; horse 2.78
parts.working: 2 marks all five correct; 1 mark three or four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plotting log₁₀(body mass) on the x-axis is better than plotting body mass itself.
parts.answer: The masses range over more than four orders of magnitude; on a linear scale the four small animals would be crowded together near zero; a log scale spreads the points evenly so the trend can be seen.
parts.working: B1 very wide range (several orders of magnitude); B1 small values crowded on linear scale / log scale spreads them out.

check: round(math.log10(0.02), 2) == -1.7 and round(math.log10(0.25), 2) == -0.6 and round(math.log10(3.0), 2) == 0.48 and round(math.log10(60), 2) == 1.78 and round(math.log10(600), 2) == 2.78
author: HomiLabs

stem:
Total volume of CO₂ from yeast at two glucose concentrations:
time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
2 % glucose / cm³: 0, 1.6, 3.0, 4.1, 4.9, 5.4
8 % glucose / cm³: 0, 2.0, 3.9, 5.7, 7.4, 9.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mean rate over 5 minutes is not a good measure for comparing the two concentrations, and state what should be used instead.
parts.answer: For 2 % glucose the rate decreases over time (curve flattens as glucose is used), so the mean rate over 5 minutes underestimates the true rate at the start; the initial rate (gradient of a tangent at t = 0, or over the first minute) should be compared.
parts.working: B1 rate not constant / curve flattens for 2 %; B1 use initial rate / tangent at time 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the first minute of data, calculate the ratio of the initial rates (8 % : 2 %).
parts.answer: 1.25 (8 % rate 2.0 cm³ min⁻¹, 2 % rate 1.6 cm³ min⁻¹)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a frequency table using the classes 10.0–11.9, 12.0–13.9, 14.0–15.9 and 16.0–17.9.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of chart that should be drawn from this table and describe how it differs from a bar chart.
parts.answer: A histogram: the variable on the x-axis is continuous, so the bars touch (no gaps) and the area / height represents frequency; a bar chart is used for categorical data with gaps between bars.
parts.working: B1 histogram; B1 bars touch because data are continuous (bar chart has gaps / categories).

stem: A student will measure the rate of oxygen uptake of maggots at 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As temperature increases from 10 °C to 30 °C, the rate of oxygen uptake by maggots increases.
parts.working: B1 clear relationship between IV and DV that can be tested.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological basis for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Maggots are ectotherms, so their body temperature follows the surroundings; higher temperature gives respiratory enzymes more kinetic energy, more enzyme–substrate collisions, faster respiration and more oxygen used.
parts.working: B1 body temperature follows environment / ectotherm; B1 enzyme activity increases with temperature (below optimum).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will compare the rate of CO₂ production by baker's yeast and brewer's yeast in the same glucose solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the rates of CO₂ production by baker's yeast and brewer's yeast.
parts.working: B1 'no (significant) difference' between the two strains.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a statistical test the student could use to test the null hypothesis, and state what the student must collect to use it.
parts.answer: t-test; several replicate measurements (e.g. at least 5) of rate for each strain, so means and standard deviations can be calculated.
parts.working: B1 t-test; B1 replicate data for each strain / means and SD.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two respirometers each contain 5 g of germinating wheat grains, which respire only carbohydrate. Respirometer A contains soda lime; respirometer B contains water instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the movement of the liquid in each respirometer. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: A: liquid moves towards the grains because oxygen is taken in and the CO₂ given out is absorbed. B: liquid does not move (or hardly moves) because with carbohydrate the RQ is 1, so the volume of CO₂ released equals the volume of oxygen taken in.
parts.working: B1 A moves towards grains; B1 O₂ used, CO₂ absorbed; B1 B no movement; B1 RQ = 1 / equal volumes of O₂ and CO₂.

author: HomiLabs

stem: With 1 cm³ of yeast suspension, methylene blue took 240 s to decolourise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the time taken with 2 cm³ of the same yeast suspension (all other conditions the same). Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: About 120 s (about half the time), because there are twice as many yeast cells / dehydrogenase enzymes, so methylene blue is reduced twice as fast.
parts.working: B1 about half / ~120 s; B1 more enzymes / cells so faster reduction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the actual time might not be exactly half.
parts.answer: Other factors such as glucose concentration or oxygen concentration may become limiting, or the end point is judged inaccurately.
parts.working: B1 another limiting factor / measurement error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cyanide stops the electron transport chain. A suspension of yeast in glucose solution was given a small dose of cyanide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the oxygen uptake and the CO₂ production of the yeast. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake stops (falls to almost zero) because electrons can no longer be passed to oxygen; CO₂ production continues (at a lower or similar rate) because yeast can respire anaerobically, converting pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂.
parts.working: B1 oxygen uptake stops; B1 electron transport chain blocked / oxygen not final acceptor; B1 CO₂ production continues; B1 anaerobic respiration / ethanol fermentation releases CO₂.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Germinating sunflower seeds store mainly lipid; germinating wheat grains store mainly starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis about the RQs of these seeds during early germination.
parts.answer: Germinating sunflower seeds have a lower RQ (about 0.7) than germinating wheat grains (about 1.0).
parts.working: B1 sunflower RQ lower than wheat (with or without values).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Sunflower seeds respire lipid, which contains relatively little oxygen, so more O₂ is needed per CO₂ released (RQ 0.7); wheat respires carbohydrate from starch (RQ 1.0).
parts.working: B1 lipid RQ 0.7 because less oxygen in molecule; B1 starch / carbohydrate RQ 1.0.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A respirometer containing soda lime and germinating sunflower seeds (RQ 0.70) showed 40 mm of liquid movement in 30 minutes. An identical respirometer contained water instead of soda lime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the distance and direction the liquid would move in the respirometer with water in 30 minutes.
parts.answer: 12 mm towards the seeds
parts.working: M1 CO₂ produced = 0.70 × 40 = 28 mm equivalent; A1 net movement 40 − 28 = 12 mm towards the seeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the direction of movement.
parts.answer: More oxygen is taken in than CO₂ released, so the gas volume in the tube falls.
parts.working: B1 O₂ uptake > CO₂ output so volume decreases.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher plans to grow yeast in glucose solutions containing 0, 4, 8, 12 and 16 % ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the rate of CO₂ production will change as the ethanol concentration increases. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The rate will decrease as ethanol concentration increases, possibly falling to almost zero at 12–16 %; ethanol is toxic: it damages cell membranes (dissolves in the phospholipid bilayer) and denatures enzymes, so respiration slows.
parts.working: B1 rate decreases with increasing ethanol; B1 ethanol damages membranes; B1 denatures / inhibits enzymes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a small concentration of ethanol (4 %) may have little effect.
parts.answer: Yeast is tolerant of low ethanol concentrations because it produces ethanol naturally in fermentation.
parts.working: B1 yeast tolerates low ethanol / adapted to its own product.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at higher CO₂ concentrations and purple at lower CO₂ concentrations. Three sealed tubes each contain indicator and a gauze platform:
tube 1: germinating mung beans
tube 2: mung beans boiled and cooled
tube 3: glass beads

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube after 2 hours. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: Tube 1 yellow: the beans respire and release CO₂; tube 2 red: boiled beans are dead, enzymes denatured, no respiration; tube 3 red: glass beads do not respire.
parts.working: B1 tube 1 yellow with reason; B1 tube 2 red with reason; B1 tube 3 red with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the tubes should be kept in the dark if green seedlings are used.
parts.answer: Green seedlings would photosynthesise in light, removing CO₂ (indicator may stay red or turn purple).
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis removes CO₂.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A biologist thinks that smaller mammals have higher respiration rates per gram of body mass than larger mammals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write this idea as a testable hypothesis and predict the shape of a graph of oxygen uptake per kg against body mass.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: as body mass increases, the rate of oxygen uptake per kg of body mass decreases. Graph: a curve falling steeply at low masses and levelling off at high masses (negative correlation).
parts.working: B1 testable hypothesis with direction; B1 decreasing curve / negative correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological reason for this prediction.
parts.answer: Smaller mammals have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so they lose heat faster; they respire faster per gram to produce heat and maintain a constant body temperature.
parts.working: B1 larger SA:V / greater heat loss; B1 more respiration to replace heat.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Muscle from the breast of pigeons (which fly long distances) and from the breast of domestic chickens (which fly only in short bursts) are to be compared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Formulate a hypothesis relating the number of mitochondria in a muscle to the type of activity it performs, and make three predictions that would follow if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: muscles used for long periods of sustained activity contain more mitochondria per unit volume than muscles used for short bursts. Predictions: pigeon breast muscle has a greater volume of mitochondria per cell; pigeon muscle takes up more oxygen per gram at rest / when stimulated; chicken breast muscle has higher lactate dehydrogenase activity / produces more lactate; pigeon muscle has more myoglobin / capillaries (darker colour).
parts.working: B1 hypothesis linking mitochondria number to sustained activity; 1 mark each for up to three valid predictions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a correlation between mitochondria number and sustained activity would not prove the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Other differences between species (e.g. capillary density, myoglobin, enzyme concentrations) may also explain endurance; correlation does not show cause.
parts.working: B1 other variables / correlation is not causation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A trained runner takes part in a 3-hour marathon, drinking only water. Her RQ was 0.95 at the start of the race.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how her RQ changes over the 3 hours. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: RQ falls gradually from about 0.95 towards about 0.75–0.8; at first carbohydrate (muscle and liver glycogen, blood glucose) is the main substrate; as glycogen stores become depleted, an increasing proportion of energy comes from lipid (fatty acids from adipose tissue), which has an RQ of 0.7.
parts.working: B1 RQ falls (towards 0.7–0.8); B1 glycogen / carbohydrate used first and depleted; B1 more lipid respired, RQ 0.7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect on her RQ of drinking a glucose drink at 2 hours, and explain.
parts.answer: RQ would rise towards 1.0 because the glucose is absorbed and respired, providing more carbohydrate as substrate.
parts.working: B1 RQ increases; B1 more carbohydrate respired.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Succinate dehydrogenase from mitochondria reduces the blue dye DCPIP as it oxidises succinate. Malonate is a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme. A student plans to measure the rate of DCPIP reduction at different succinate concentrations, with and without a fixed concentration of malonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the curves of rate against succinate concentration with and without malonate will compare. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Both curves rise and level off; the curve with malonate is lower at low succinate concentrations; at high succinate concentrations the two curves approach the same maximum rate. Malonate competes with succinate for the active site; at high succinate concentrations succinate molecules outcompete malonate, so most active sites bind succinate.
parts.working: B1 rate lower with malonate at low succinate; B1 same maximum rate reached at high succinate; B1 malonate competes for active site (similar shape); B1 high succinate outcompetes inhibitor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a null hypothesis that could be tested at one succinate concentration.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the rate of DCPIP reduction with and without malonate (at this succinate concentration).
parts.working: B1 correct null hypothesis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The oxygen uptake of a lizard (an ectotherm) and a mouse (an endotherm) of similar mass will be measured at environmental temperatures of 10 °C and 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the oxygen uptake of each animal will change from 10 °C to 30 °C. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Lizard: uptake increases at 30 °C because its body temperature rises with the environment, increasing enzyme activity / metabolic rate. Mouse: uptake decreases at 30 °C because it needs to generate less heat by respiration to maintain its body temperature (more heat needed at 10 °C).
parts.working: B1 lizard increases; B1 body temperature follows environment / enzymes faster; B1 mouse decreases (higher at 10 °C); B1 respiration produces heat to keep constant body temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict which animal will have the higher oxygen uptake at 10 °C.
parts.answer: The mouse (much higher).
parts.working: B1 mouse.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean volume of CO₂ produced by yeast in 15 minutes (cm³), three replicates each:
glucose 8.4; fructose 8.1; sucrose 6.2; maltose 3.5; starch 0.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conclusions that can be drawn from these results.
parts.answer: Yeast respires glucose and fructose fastest (at similar rates); disaccharides sucrose and maltose are respired more slowly than monosaccharides; starch is hardly respired at all.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid conclusions supported by the figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why starch produced almost no CO₂.
parts.answer: Yeast does not secrete amylase (cannot hydrolyse starch), and starch molecules are too large to enter the cells.
parts.working: B1 no amylase / starch not hydrolysed / too large to be absorbed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rate of oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) of seeds soaked for 2 days at 25 °C:
maize 95; chickpea 140; mustard 210

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that mustard seeds respire faster than maize seeds because mustard seeds are smaller. Explain whether the data support this conclusion.
parts.answer: The data show mustard has the highest rate per gram (210 vs 95), but no data on seed size were collected, so the reason cannot be concluded from these results; other differences (e.g. stored food type, germination stage) could explain it.
parts.working: B1 data show mustard faster per gram; B1 no data on size / cause not tested.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what further information would be needed to judge whether the differences are significant.
parts.answer: Replicate results with a measure of spread (standard deviation / error bars) or a statistical test.
parts.working: B1 replicates / SD / statistical test.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The RQ of germinating seeds of a plant was measured: day 1: 0.72; day 3: 0.71; day 5: 0.78; day 7: 0.90; day 9: 0.99.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what conclusion can be drawn about the main respiratory substrate during the 9 days.
parts.answer: On days 1–3 the main substrate is lipid (RQ about 0.7); from day 5 onwards there is a change to a mixture and then to carbohydrate by day 9 (RQ about 1.0).
parts.working: B1 lipid early (RQ ≈ 0.7); B1 changes to carbohydrate by day 9 (RQ ≈ 1.0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a reason for the change.
parts.answer: Lipid stores are used up and/or the seedlings begin to photosynthesise, producing carbohydrate.
parts.working: B1 lipid stores depleted / photosynthesis provides carbohydrate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two cricketers ran the same 400 m shuttle test. Blood lactate (mmol dm⁻³) immediately after: player A 4.2; player B 9.6. Both had 1.1 at rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion about the two players' respiration during the test.
parts.answer: Player B relied more on anaerobic respiration (produced more lactate) than player A.
parts.working: B1 B more anaerobic respiration / A more aerobic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the difference and explain why it cannot be confirmed from these data alone.
parts.answer: Player A may be fitter / have more mitochondria or better oxygen supply to muscles; but only one test was done on each player, and speed / effort may have differed, so the cause is not shown by the data.
parts.working: B1 reason (fitness, more mitochondria, capillaries); B1 single measurement / effort not controlled / other variables.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) of seeds kept at 25 °C:
dry seeds: 0.1, 0.1, 0.2
seeds soaked for 24 h: 48, 52, 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion and use the data to support it.
parts.answer: Soaked (germinating) seeds respire much faster than dry seeds: mean about 50 compared with about 0.13 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ (several hundred times faster).
parts.working: B1 conclusion; B1 supporting figures / comparison of means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the conclusion is valid only for this type of seed at 25 °C.
parts.answer: Only one species and one temperature were tested, so the results cannot be generalised to other species or conditions.
parts.working: B1 only one species / one temperature tested.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compared the rate of CO₂ production by yeast at 30 °C in 0.5 mol dm⁻³ glucose and 0.5 mol dm⁻³ maltose (5 replicates each). A t-test gave t = 3.42. The critical value at p = 0.05 with 8 degrees of freedom is 2.31.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what conclusion can be drawn from the t-test.
parts.answer: t (3.42) is greater than the critical value (2.31), so the null hypothesis is rejected; there is a significant difference between the rates with glucose and with maltose (the probability that the difference is due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 3.42 > 2.31 so reject null hypothesis; B1 significant difference / less than 5 % probability due to chance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the degrees of freedom were calculated.
parts.answer: Total number of replicates minus 2: (5 + 5) − 2 = 8.
parts.working: B1 n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 8.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Data from five rat tissues:
tissue: mitochondria per cell; oxygen uptake / µl g⁻¹ h⁻¹
skin: 60; 210
liver: 1700; 1150
kidney: 1300; 1700
heart muscle: 3000; 2400
brain: 900; 1800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between number of mitochondria and oxygen uptake, using data, and identify any tissue that does not fit the pattern.
parts.answer: Only a weak, broadly positive trend: skin (60 mitochondria, uptake 210) has the fewest mitochondria and the lowest uptake, and heart (3000, 2400) has the most mitochondria and a high uptake. But brain (900 mitochondria) has a higher uptake (1800) than liver (1700 mitochondria, 1150), and kidney (1300) has a higher uptake than liver despite fewer mitochondria. Brain and liver do not fit the pattern.
parts.working: B1 weak / broadly positive trend stated, with data quoted; B1 brain and/or liver (or kidney) identified as not fitting; B1 the data do not show a clear positive correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these data do not prove that the number of mitochondria determines the rate of oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show causation; other factors differ between tissues (size of mitochondria, cristae density, ATP demand, enzyme activity); only one sample from each tissue / no replicates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two yeast strains were grown in glucose solution with different ethanol concentrations. Rate of CO₂ production as a percentage of the rate with 0 % ethanol:
ethanol / %: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16
strain P: 100, 92, 70, 31, 5
strain Q: 100, 75, 38, 9, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion about the ethanol tolerance of the two strains. Support it with data.
parts.answer: Strain P is more tolerant of ethanol than strain Q: at 8 % P still respires at 70 % of its maximum rate while Q is at 38 %; at 12 % P 31 % vs Q 9 %.
parts.working: B1 P more tolerant; B1 comparative figures at the same concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which strain is better for producing a fuel ethanol solution of about 12 %. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: Strain P, because it continues to respire / ferment at 12 % ethanol (31 % of maximum), whereas Q almost stops.
parts.working: B1 P with reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean rate of oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) ± standard deviation, 6 replicates each, for woodlice kept in dry and damp soil:
dry: 52 ± 9
damp: 58 ± 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that woodlice in damp soil respire faster than those in dry soil. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The mean is higher in damp soil (58 vs 52); but the difference (6) is smaller than either standard deviation and the ranges mean ± SD overlap widely (43–61 and 48–68), so the difference is probably not significant / may be due to chance; a t-test is needed; conclusion not supported.
parts.working: B1 mean higher in damp; B1 SDs overlap / difference smaller than SD; B1 not likely to be significant / needs statistical test so conclusion not valid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be changed to give a more certain conclusion.
parts.answer: Increase the number of replicates (larger sample) and use a t-test (also standardise mass / temperature).
parts.working: B1 more replicates / statistical test.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rate of oxygen uptake of aphids feeding on cotton plants in Faisalabad was measured before and 2 hours after spraying a new insecticide (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹):
before: 3.1
after: 5.8
unsprayed control aphids, same times: 3.0 and 3.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of the sprayed aphids, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What conclusion can be drawn about the effect of the insecticide? Use the control data in your answer.
parts.answer: The insecticide increases the respiration rate of the aphids, since the control rate hardly changed (3.0 to 3.2), so the increase is not due to time of day or handling.
parts.working: B1 insecticide increases rate; B1 control unchanged so effect due to insecticide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way the insecticide might cause this effect.
parts.answer: It may act as an uncoupler, allowing protons to leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane so more oxygen is used without making ATP (or it increases activity / stress).
parts.working: B1 sensible suggestion, e.g. uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For eight mammal species, a student ranked body mass and resting oxygen uptake per kg. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was rₛ = −0.89. The critical value at p = 0.05 for n = 8 is 0.738.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the conclusion that can be drawn.
parts.answer: The magnitude 0.89 is greater than 0.738, so there is a significant negative correlation: as body mass increases, oxygen uptake per kg decreases (less than 5 % probability the correlation is due to chance).
parts.working: B1 0.89 > 0.738 so significant; B1 negative correlation described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this result does not show that body mass itself causes the lower oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show causation; another factor linked to mass, such as surface area to volume ratio / heat loss, or activity level, may be the cause.
parts.working: B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 named alternative factor (SA:V, activity, diet).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oxygen concentration in a chamber containing isolated mitochondria was recorded. Additions and rates of oxygen uptake (nmol min⁻¹):
0–2 min: mitochondria + pyruvate: 8
2–5 min: ADP added: 45
5–8 min: compound X added: 1
8–11 min: DNP (an uncoupler that makes the inner membrane permeable to protons) added: 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in rate when ADP was added.
parts.answer: ADP allows ATP synthase to work; protons flow back through ATP synthase, reducing the gradient, so electron transport and proton pumping speed up and more oxygen is used.
parts.working: B1 ADP substrate for ATP synthase / protons flow through ATP synthase; B1 electron transport faster / more O₂ reduced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce whether compound X acts on the electron transport chain or on ATP synthase. Explain how the data support your conclusion.
parts.answer: X acts on the electron transport chain. If X blocked only ATP synthase, adding DNP would let protons leak back, the gradient would be removed and electron transport (oxygen uptake) would restart; but oxygen uptake stayed at 1 after DNP, so electrons cannot reach oxygen — the chain itself is blocked.
parts.working: B1 ETC; B1 DNP would restore O₂ uptake if only ATP synthase blocked; B1 no restoration so electron flow to O₂ blocked.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A company claims that a slimming supplement 'burns fat by speeding up metabolism'. In a trial, 10 mice given the supplement for 4 weeks were compared with 10 control mice:
oxygen uptake: +28 % compared with controls
ATP concentration in muscle: −15 %
body temperature: +0.9 °C
body mass change: −6 % (controls +1 %)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a conclusion about how the supplement acts, using all four results.
parts.answer: The supplement probably uncouples oxidative phosphorylation: oxygen uptake (electron transport) increases but less ATP is made, so the energy from the proton gradient is released as heat (higher body temperature); more substrate including fat is respired to meet ATP needs, causing mass loss.
parts.working: B1 uncoupling / protons leak across inner membrane; B1 more O₂ used but less ATP, energy lost as heat; B1 more fat respired to compensate so mass falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the trial supports the company's claim for use in humans.
parts.answer: Supports increased respiration and mass loss in mice; but small sample (10 per group), no statistical test given; mice not humans; 4 weeks only — long-term safety unknown; raised temperature and reduced ATP suggest possible danger (like DNP); mass loss not shown to be fat (could be water / muscle).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid evaluation points (max 1 for support).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Soil respiration (CO₂ release, g m⁻² day⁻¹) was measured monthly in a field in Punjab, together with soil temperature and soil moisture:
Jan: 1.2 (12 °C, 22 %)
Apr: 3.6 (28 °C, 15 %)
Jun: 2.1 (38 °C, 5 %)
Aug: 6.4 (32 °C, 30 %)
Oct: 3.0 (25 °C, 18 %)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that soil respiration increases with temperature. Evaluate this conclusion using the data.
parts.answer: Partly supported: January (12 °C) has the lowest rate and April/August have higher rates; but June has the highest temperature (38 °C) and only a low rate (2.1), while August (32 °C) has the highest rate; moisture also varies — June was very dry (5 %) and August wettest (30 %); so moisture is a confounding variable and temperature alone does not explain the pattern; only one reading per month, no replicates.
parts.working: B1 some support with data; B1 June anomaly / not a consistent increase; B1 moisture confounding / no replicates or statistics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a biological explanation for the low rate in June.
parts.answer: Very dry soil: microorganisms and roots lack water for enzyme activity / metabolism, so they become dormant or die; very high temperature may also denature enzymes.
parts.working: B1 lack of water limits microbial / root metabolism; B1 high temperature may denature enzymes / kill organisms.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A recording electrode inside an axon gave these readings of membrane potential during one action potential:
0 ms: −70 mV; 0.5 ms: −55 mV; 1.0 ms: +35 mV; 1.5 ms: −20 mV; 2.0 ms: −80 mV; 3.5 ms: −70 mV

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the resting potential of this axon.
parts.answer: −70 mV
parts.working: B1 −70 mV (reading at 0 ms and again at 3.5 ms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the time interval during which the axon is depolarising most rapidly, and name the ion moving at this time and its direction.
parts.answer: Between 0.5 ms and 1.0 ms; sodium ions (Na⁺) diffuse into the axon.
parts.working: B1 0.5–1.0 ms (−55 to +35 mV). B1 Na⁺ moving in, through voltage-gated sodium channels.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the change in potential between 1.0 ms and 1.5 ms.
parts.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuses out, so the inside becomes less positive (repolarisation).
parts.working: 1 mark each: Na⁺ channels close / K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuses out down its electrochemical gradient, removing positive charge.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the potential at 2.0 ms is lower than the resting potential.
parts.answer: Hyperpolarisation: K⁺ channels are slow to close, so too many K⁺ ions leave.
parts.working: B1 K⁺ channels stay open briefly after resting potential is reached, so extra K⁺ diffuses out (hyperpolarisation).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A dentist in Lahore injects a local anaesthetic, lidocaine, near a nerve in the lower jaw before filling a tooth. Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in neurone membranes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated in a myelinated neurone.
parts.answer: At the nodes of Ranvier.
parts.working: B1 nodes of Ranvier (gaps between Schwann cells).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the patient feels no pain while the tooth is drilled.
parts.answer: Na⁺ cannot enter the sensory neurone, so the membrane cannot depolarise to threshold; no action potentials are generated or conducted; no impulses reach the brain (sensory area), so pain is not perceived.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no Na⁺ influx / no depolarisation; threshold not reached so no action potential; impulses do not reach the brain so no sensation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The patient's lip also feels numb and may droop slightly. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Lidocaine also blocks sodium channels in other sensory and motor neurones in the area (e.g. to the lip skin and lip muscles).
parts.working: B1 nearby sensory neurones (numbness) and/or motor neurones (drooping) are also blocked, because all neurones use the same type of channel.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between the structure of a motor neurone and a sensory neurone.
parts.answer: Motor: cell body at one end, inside the CNS, with many dendrites; long axon. Sensory: cell body part-way along, in a ganglion outside the CNS; long dendron and short axon.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: position of cell body (end vs part-way along/side branch); cell body in CNS vs in a ganglion just outside the CNS; motor has many dendrites on cell body, sensory has a long dendron/dendrite carrying impulses to the cell body; motor has long axon, sensory has short axon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of a relay neurone.
parts.answer: Carries impulses from sensory neurones to motor neurones (within the CNS).
parts.working: B1 links/transmits impulses between sensory and motor neurones inside the brain or spinal cord.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the cells that wrap around the axon of a peripheral motor neurone and state one function of the layer they form.
parts.answer: Schwann cells; the myelin sheath insulates the axon so the impulse jumps between nodes (saltatory conduction), making conduction faster.
parts.working: B1 Schwann cells. B1 myelin insulates / prevents ion movement except at nodes / speeds up conduction.

stem:
Concentrations of two ions inside and outside a resting giant axon (mmol dm⁻³):
K⁺: inside 400, outside 20
Na⁺: inside 50, outside 440

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated K⁺ is inside the axon than outside, and how many times more concentrated Na⁺ is outside than inside.
parts.answer: K⁺: 20 times; Na⁺: 8.8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these concentration differences are set up and how they lead to a resting potential with the inside negative.
parts.answer: Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (K⁺ leak channels) so K⁺ diffuses out faster than Na⁺ diffuses in; more positive charge leaves than enters, so the inside is negative.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: active transport by Na⁺/K⁺ pump, ATP; 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in; more K⁺ channels open/membrane more permeable to K⁺; K⁺ diffuses out down its gradient; net loss of positive charge.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A respiratory inhibitor is added. Suggest what will happen to the resting potential over the next hour and explain why it does not disappear immediately.
parts.answer: The resting potential gradually falls towards zero; no ATP so the pump stops, but the existing ion gradients take time to run down by diffusion.
parts.working: B1 resting potential gradually lost / becomes less negative. B1 pump stops (no ATP) but gradients already present only slowly dissipate by leakage.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A basketball player in Karachi is 1.95 m tall. The sensory neurone from a touch receptor in the skin of his big toe to his spinal cord is 1.05 m long and conducts impulses at 60 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for an impulse to travel the length of this neurone. Give your answer in ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how local currents cause an action potential to move along an unmyelinated axon.
parts.answer: Na⁺ entering at the depolarised region diffuses sideways inside the axon to the next region; this depolarises the next region to threshold; voltage-gated Na⁺ channels there open, creating a new action potential further along.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Na⁺ ions diffuse along the inside (local circuit) to the adjacent resting region; this region is depolarised to threshold; voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open there, so the action potential is regenerated next to the previous one.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the action potential cannot move back towards the receptor.
parts.answer: The region just behind is in its refractory period (Na⁺ channels cannot reopen yet).
parts.working: B1 the membrane just behind is refractory / Na⁺ channels inactivated.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The speed of conduction along a sciatic nerve fibre from a frog was measured at different temperatures:
Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25
Speed / m s⁻¹: 12, 16, 21, 27

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in conduction speed between 10 °C and 25 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why conduction speed increases with temperature.
parts.answer: Ions have more kinetic energy so diffuse faster; channel and pump proteins change shape (open/close) faster / Na⁺/K⁺ pump (an enzyme) works faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: faster diffusion of Na⁺/K⁺ (more kinetic energy); voltage-gated channels open and close more quickly; faster active transport by Na⁺/K⁺ pump / more ATP from faster respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why conduction would stop at very high temperatures, such as 50 °C.
parts.answer: Channel proteins and pump proteins are denatured.
parts.working: B1 proteins (channels/pumps) denature, so ion movement cannot be controlled.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why conduction along a myelinated neurone uses less ATP per impulse than conduction along an unmyelinated neurone of the same length.
parts.answer: Ion movement occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, so far fewer Na⁺ and K⁺ ions cross the membrane per impulse; fewer ions must then be pumped back by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump; less ATP is used.
parts.working: 1 mark each: depolarisation only at nodes (saltatory conduction); fewer ions move in total; less active transport/pumping to restore gradients so less ATP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a high speed of conduction is an advantage in a motor neurone to the leg muscles of a cheetah.
parts.answer: Impulses reach the muscles quickly, so the muscles contract and respond rapidly; allows fast coordinated movement to catch prey.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rapid response/short delay; fast coordinated muscle contraction for chasing prey.

stem:
Two toxins were applied separately to isolated axons.
Tetrodotoxin (TTX), from pufferfish, blocks voltage-gated sodium channels.
Tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated potassium channels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of TTX on the response of the axon to a stimulus.
parts.answer: No action potential; Na⁺ cannot enter, so no depolarisation beyond a tiny local change and threshold is never reached.
parts.working: B1 no action potential. B1 no Na⁺ influx so no depolarisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of TEA on the shape of an action potential.
parts.answer: Depolarisation still occurs normally, but repolarisation is much slower so the action potential is prolonged/broader; K⁺ can only leave through leak channels; little or no hyperpolarisation.
parts.working: B1 depolarisation unaffected (Na⁺ channels work). B1 repolarisation slowed/action potential lasts longer. B1 K⁺ cannot leave through voltage-gated channels (only slow leakage); no hyperpolarisation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why TEA would reduce the maximum frequency of impulses the axon can carry.
parts.answer: Each action potential and refractory period lasts longer, so fewer can occur per second.
parts.working: B1 longer action potential/refractory period means a longer minimum gap between impulses.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hyperkalaemia is a condition in which the concentration of K⁺ ions in the tissue fluid is higher than normal. It may occur in patients with kidney failure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the resting potential of neurones becomes less negative in hyperkalaemia.
parts.answer: The K⁺ concentration gradient across the membrane is reduced; so fewer K⁺ ions diffuse out through K⁺ leak channels; less net loss of positive charge, so the inside is less negative.
parts.working: 1 mark each: smaller K⁺ gradient (outside concentration higher); less K⁺ diffusion out; less positive charge lost, inside less negative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how mild hyperkalaemia would affect the size of stimulus needed to produce an action potential. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: A smaller stimulus is needed; the resting potential is already closer to the threshold (about −55 mV).
parts.working: B1 smaller stimulus. B1 less depolarisation needed to reach threshold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Severe hyperkalaemia keeps membranes partly depolarised for a long time. Suggest why this can stop neurones firing altogether.
parts.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels become inactivated when the membrane stays depolarised; they cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises, so no action potentials (like a permanent refractory period).
parts.working: 1 mark each: sodium channels inactivated/stay closed; membrane cannot repolarise to reset channels so no new action potentials.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A nerve was stimulated at one point. Two recording electrodes were placed on the same nerve fibre, 45 mm and 105 mm from the stimulating electrode. The action potential reached the first electrode 0.9 ms after the stimulus and the second electrode 2.1 ms after the stimulus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of conduction between the two recording electrodes in m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 50 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the speed is calculated from the two recording electrodes rather than from the stimulating electrode to the first recording electrode.
parts.answer: There is a delay at the stimulating electrode before an action potential is set up; using the difference between two recordings removes this delay, so only conduction time is measured.
parts.working: 1 mark each: delay/latency in starting the action potential at the stimulus site; difference cancels it out / measures only propagation time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, whether this fibre is myelinated.
parts.answer: Myelinated; 50 m s⁻¹ is much faster than unmyelinated mammalian/amphibian fibres (about 0.5–10 m s⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 myelinated, because the speed is high (saltatory conduction).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of the ultrastructure of a striated (skeletal) muscle fibre.
parts.answer: Multinucleate; contains many myofibrils made of repeating sarcomeres; sarcolemma with T-tubules; extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum; many mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: many nuclei (syncytium); myofibrils with sarcomeres/light and dark bands; sarcolemma/cell membrane with T-tubules; sarcoplasmic reticulum around myofibrils; many mitochondria; sarcoplasm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why muscle fibres contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Aerobic respiration produces a lot of ATP; ATP is needed for myosin heads to detach and recock, and for active transport of Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mitochondria are site of aerobic respiration/ATP production; ATP used for myosin head movement/detachment or Ca²⁺ pumping.

stem:
The events below occur when a skeletal muscle contracts. They are not in the correct order.
P Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges.
Q Ca²⁺ ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
R Acetylcholine binds to receptors on the sarcolemma.
S Ca²⁺ binds to troponin and tropomyosin moves away from the binding sites on actin.
T Depolarisation spreads along T-tubules.
U Myosin heads tilt, pulling actin towards the centre of the sarcomere (power stroke).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the letters in the correct order.
parts.answer: R, T, Q, S, P, U
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 if one pair is reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of ATP in the cycle of cross-bridge formation after the power stroke.
parts.answer: ATP binds to the myosin head, causing it to detach from actin; ATP is hydrolysed, re-cocking the head ready to bind again.
parts.working: 1 mark each: detachment of myosin head; hydrolysis of ATP returns head to its original position.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name each structure described.
(i) the cell surface membrane of a muscle fibre
(ii) the membrane-bound store of calcium ions in a muscle fibre
(iii) the line at each end of a sarcomere to which the thin filaments are attached
(iv) the region in the centre of a sarcomere that contains only thick filaments
parts.answer: (i) sarcolemma (ii) sarcoplasmic reticulum (iii) Z line (Z disc) (iv) H zone (H band)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which band of a sarcomere stays the same length during contraction.
parts.answer: The A band.
parts.working: B1 A band (the length of the thick myosin filaments).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two similarities and two differences between a neuromuscular junction and a cholinergic synapse between two neurones.
parts.answer: Similarities: both release acetylcholine by exocytosis after Ca²⁺ influx; both have ACh receptors (ligand-gated Na⁺ channels) on the postsynaptic membrane and acetylcholinesterase. Differences: NMJ postsynaptic membrane is the sarcolemma (muscle) not a neurone; NMJ is always excitatory and one impulse always triggers an action potential (no summation needed); NMJ postsynaptic membrane is folded with more receptors; NMJ is the end of the pathway (no further neurone).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two similarities (ACh; Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle exocytosis; receptors on postsynaptic membrane; AChE; one-way transmission) and two differences (muscle vs neurone postsynaptic cell; always excitatory; one impulse enough/no summation; folded postsynaptic membrane with many receptors).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that a single impulse at a neuromuscular junction is always enough to produce an action potential in the muscle fibre.
parts.answer: Ensures muscle responds reliably every time the motor neurone fires, giving precise control of movement.
parts.working: B1 reliable/precise response, no failure of contraction.

stem: A rare mutation changes the troponin protein in some muscle fibres so that it can no longer bind calcium ions. All other proteins are normal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the roles of troponin and tropomyosin in a normal resting muscle fibre.
parts.answer: Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin; troponin holds tropomyosin in this blocking position.
parts.working: 1 mark each: tropomyosin blocks binding sites on actin; troponin attached to tropomyosin/holds it in place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of the mutation on the ability of affected fibres to contract.
parts.answer: Affected fibres cannot contract; Ca²⁺ is released normally but cannot bind troponin; tropomyosin is not moved, binding sites stay covered, so no cross-bridges form.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no contraction; troponin cannot change shape/move tropomyosin; actin binding sites blocked so myosin heads cannot bind.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease. Antibodies bind to acetylcholine receptors on the sarcolemma at neuromuscular junctions and cause many receptors to be destroyed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why people with myasthenia gravis have weak muscles that tire easily.
parts.answer: Fewer ACh receptors, so fewer Na⁺ channels open when ACh is released; depolarisation of the sarcolemma is smaller and may not reach threshold; fewer fibres produce action potentials/contract.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fewer receptors for ACh to bind; less Na⁺ entry/smaller depolarisation; threshold not reached in some fibres so fewer fibres contract.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The drug pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Suggest how this drug improves muscle strength in these patients.
parts.answer: ACh is not broken down as quickly so it stays in the cleft longer and at a higher concentration; it binds repeatedly to the remaining receptors, giving greater depolarisation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ACh remains in cleft longer/more ACh; more binding to remaining receptors so threshold reached.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A myofibril in a relaxed biceps muscle is 10 mm long and is made of sarcomeres that are each 2.5 µm long. During a strong contraction each sarcomere shortens by 0.4 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of sarcomeres along the length of this myofibril.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much the whole myofibril shortens, in mm, and the percentage shortening.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the myofibril can only shorten by a limited amount.
parts.answer: Shortening stops when the thin filaments meet/overlap in the centre and the thick filaments reach the Z lines; filaments cannot shorten themselves, they only slide.
parts.working: 1 mark each: filaments do not change length, they slide; limited by thick filaments hitting Z lines/actin filaments meeting.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a type of skeletal muscle, each thick (myosin) filament is 1.6 µm long and each thin (actin) filament extends 1.1 µm from the Z line. A sarcomere in a resting muscle is 2.8 µm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of the I band and the length of the H zone in this resting sarcomere.
parts.answer: I band 1.2 µm; H zone 0.6 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sarcomere length at which the H zone just disappears.
parts.answer: 2.2 µm
parts.working: B1 2 × 1.1 = 2.2 µm (thin filaments meet in the centre).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the sarcomere length beyond which the thick and thin filaments would no longer overlap at all, and explain why the muscle could produce no force at this length.
parts.answer: 3.8 µm; no myosin heads can reach actin, so no cross-bridges can form.
parts.working: B1 1.6 + 2 × 1.1 = 3.8 µm. B1 no overlap of actin and myosin. B1 no cross-bridges/power strokes so no tension.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The common krait, a snake found in Pakistan, produces a venom containing α-bungarotoxin. This toxin binds almost irreversibly to acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions, but does not open them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a bite from this snake can cause paralysis of skeletal muscles.
parts.answer: Toxin blocks ACh receptors so ACh cannot bind; ligand-gated Na⁺ channels do not open; no depolarisation/action potential in the sarcolemma, so no Ca²⁺ release and no contraction (flaccid paralysis).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: toxin occupies receptor binding sites; ACh cannot bind; no Na⁺ entry/no depolarisation of sarcolemma; no Ca²⁺ release from SR so no cross-bridges.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a drug that inhibits acetylcholinesterase is less effective against this venom than against a reversible receptor blocker.
parts.answer: Raising ACh concentration lets ACh compete with a reversible blocker, but the toxin is bound almost irreversibly, so extra ACh cannot displace it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: AChE inhibitor increases ACh in the cleft (competes); irreversible binding not displaced by ACh.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why victims may die even though the heart continues to beat.
parts.answer: Breathing muscles (diaphragm and intercostal muscles) are skeletal muscles and are paralysed, so ventilation stops.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm/intercostals paralysed → respiratory failure (cardiac muscle is myogenic).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Muscle fibres were treated with glycerol so that their membranes became fully permeable to small molecules and ions. Their lengths were measured before and after placing them in different solutions.
Solution 1: ATP only → no change in length
Solution 2: Ca²⁺ only → no change in length
Solution 3: ATP and Ca²⁺ → fibres shortened by 22 %
Solution 4: ATP, Ca²⁺ and an inhibitor of myosin ATPase → no change in length

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for solutions 1 and 2.
parts.answer: Solution 1: without Ca²⁺, tropomyosin still covers the binding sites, so cross-bridges cannot form. Solution 2: Ca²⁺ exposes binding sites but there is no ATP to energise the myosin heads/allow cycling.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for solutions 3 and 4.
parts.answer: 3: Ca²⁺ uncovers binding sites and ATP allows repeated cross-bridge cycling, so filaments slide. 4: ATP cannot be hydrolysed by the myosin head, so no recocking/power strokes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the glycerol treatment was needed for this experiment.
parts.answer: To let ATP and Ca²⁺ reach the myofibrils directly, bypassing the need for nerve stimulation and the sarcolemma.
parts.working: B1 substances can cross the membrane to reach the filaments.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Venus fly trap closes its two lobes in about 0.3 s after an insect touches the trigger hairs. If the insect keeps moving, the lobes seal tightly and glands on the inner surface secrete digestive enzymes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this closure cannot be caused by cell growth.
parts.answer: Growth (cell division/elongation) takes hours or days; closure takes a fraction of a second.
parts.working: B1 growth is far too slow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the advantage of secreting enzymes only after the trapped insect has continued to stimulate the hairs.
parts.answer: Avoids wasting energy/enzymes on non-food objects (e.g. raindrops, debris); only secretes when live prey is definitely inside.
parts.working: 1 mark each: saves enzymes/ATP/resources; only when prey present (not false alarm).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of enzyme needed to digest the insect's muscle proteins and suggest how the plant uses the products.
parts.answer: Proteases (peptidases); amino acids absorbed and used as a source of nitrogen to make proteins/nucleotides.
parts.working: B1 protease. B1 amino acids/nitrogen for protein or nucleic acid synthesis (soil is poor in nitrogen).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where auxin is made in a shoot.
parts.answer: In the shoot tip (apical meristem).
parts.working: B1 tip/apex of shoot, young leaves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of auxin on cells in the zone of elongation just behind the shoot tip.
parts.answer: Auxin stimulates the cells to elongate; cell walls become more stretchable so cells take up water and grow longer.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cell elongation; walls loosened so cells expand by water uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the membrane protein activated by auxin that moves hydrogen ions into the cell wall, and the wall proteins that are then activated by the low pH.
parts.answer: Proton pump (H⁺-ATPase); expansins.
parts.working: B1 proton pump/H⁺ pump. B1 expansins.

stem:
The following events happen when a barley grain germinates. They are not in order.
A Gibberellin diffuses to the aleurone layer.
B Maltose and glucose are used by the embryo for respiration and growth.
C The grain absorbs water.
D Amylase is secreted into the endosperm.
E The embryo releases gibberellin.
F Genes for amylase are transcribed in aleurone cells.
G Starch is hydrolysed to maltose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the letters in the correct order.
parts.answer: C, E, A, F, D, G, B
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the barley grain the starch is stored.
parts.answer: In the endosperm.
parts.working: B1 endosperm.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which plant hormones are transported, and compare this with the transport of animal hormones.
parts.answer: Plant hormones move from cell to cell by diffusion and active transport, and over longer distances in xylem or phloem; animal hormones are carried dissolved in blood plasma.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cell to cell (diffusion/active transport through cells); in xylem or phloem; animal hormones in blood plasma (no specialised gland in plants).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which plant hormones are similar to animal hormones in how they act on cells.
parts.answer: Both bind to specific receptors on/in target cells (and can change gene expression).
parts.working: B1 specific receptors / act at low concentration / change gene expression.

stem: When gibberellin reaches an aleurone cell, it binds to a receptor. In the absence of gibberellin, a DELLA protein prevents a transcription factor from binding to the promoter of the amylase gene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how gibberellin causes amylase to be produced.
parts.answer: Gibberellin–receptor complex causes the DELLA protein to be broken down; the transcription factor is released; it binds to the promoter, RNA polymerase transcribes the amylase gene; mRNA translated to amylase.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: DELLA broken down/degraded (marked for destruction by proteasome); transcription factor freed; binds promoter; transcription of amylase gene by RNA polymerase; translation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this control mechanism is described as 'removing a brake' rather than 'pressing an accelerator'.
parts.answer: Gibberellin does not activate the gene directly; it removes a repressor (DELLA) that normally blocks transcription.
parts.working: B1 removes an inhibitor.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oat coleoptile tips were cut off and placed on agar blocks for 3 hours. Each block was then placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile kept in the dark. After 2 hours the angle of curvature was measured.
Number of tips placed on the block: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8
Mean curvature / °: 0, 5, 10, 18, 21

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the coleoptiles curved away from the side on which the block was placed.
parts.answer: Auxin diffused from the tips into the agar, then into the coleoptile on one side only; cells on that side elongated more; so the coleoptile bent towards the other side.
parts.working: 1 mark each: auxin from tips enters block; auxin moves down one side only; more elongation on that side so curvature away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between number of tips and curvature.
parts.answer: Curvature increases with number of tips, almost proportionally up to 4 tips; then increases less (levels off) from 4 to 8 tips.
parts.working: 1 mark each: positive relationship / roughly doubles 1→2 tips; levels off at high numbers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the block with no tips was included.
parts.answer: Control to show that agar alone does not cause curvature.
parts.working: B1 control.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A gardener in Islamabad pinches off the tips of young chilli plants. The plants then grow many side branches and become bushier.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain this effect.
parts.answer: Auxin is made at the shoot tip and moves down the stem; it inhibits growth of the lateral buds (apical dominance); removing the tip removes this auxin so lateral buds grow into side shoots.
parts.working: 1 mark each: auxin produced at tip; auxin inhibits lateral buds (apical dominance); removal lowers auxin so side buds grow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what would happen if a paste containing auxin were placed on the cut tip, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Side branches would not grow (or grow much less); the auxin replaces that from the tip and still inhibits lateral buds.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lateral bud growth suppressed; supplied auxin acts like the natural tip.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Fusicoccin is a toxin made by a fungus that attacks almond and peach trees. It permanently activates the proton pumps in plant cell membranes. Vanadate is a substance that inhibits these proton pumps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of fusicoccin on the growth of stem segments in the absence of auxin. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Segments elongate rapidly even without auxin; H⁺ pumped into the cell walls lowers the pH; expansins are activated and loosen the bonds between cellulose microfibrils; cells take up water and extend.
parts.working: 1 mark each: elongation increases; H⁺ pumped into wall/low pH; expansins/wall loosening then water uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of vanadate on auxin-induced elongation and explain how this supports the acid-growth hypothesis.
parts.answer: Auxin no longer causes elongation; shows auxin acts through proton pumping (lowering wall pH).
parts.working: 1 mark each: elongation blocked; supports that proton pump activity is needed for auxin's effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fusicoccin makes leaves wilt even when soil water is available.
parts.answer: Proton pumps in guard cells are activated so stomata open widely and stay open, causing excessive transpiration.
parts.working: B1 stomata kept open → water loss faster than uptake.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Half-seeds of barley were placed on starch agar for 48 hours. The agar was then flooded with iodine solution and the diameter of the clear zone around each half-seed was measured.
Half with embryo: 14 mm
Half without embryo: 2 mm
Half without embryo + gibberellin (10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³): 9 mm
Half without embryo + gibberellin (10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³): 13 mm
Half without embryo + gibberellin (10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³) + an inhibitor of transcription: 2 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the clear zones show.
parts.answer: Starch has been hydrolysed by amylase that diffused out of the half-seed.
parts.working: B1 starch broken down by amylase (no blue-black).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using all the data, explain the role of the embryo and of gibberellin.
parts.answer: Without the embryo almost no amylase is made; gibberellin can replace the embryo; so the embryo is the source of gibberellin; more gibberellin gives more amylase.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no embryo → little amylase; GA restores amylase production; effect increases with GA concentration (embryo supplies GA).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the result with the transcription inhibitor shows.
parts.answer: Gibberellin acts by causing transcription of the amylase gene (new synthesis), not by activating amylase already present.
parts.working: 1 mark each: GA effect needs transcription; amylase is newly synthesised (gene expression switched on).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Venus fly traps were touched twice on the trigger hairs with different time intervals between the two touches.
Interval / s: 5, 15, 30, 45, 60
Percentage of traps closing: 100, 95, 60, 10, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of the interval between touches on trap closure.
parts.answer: Up to 15 s almost all traps close; closure falls steeply between 15 and 45 s; none close at 60 s.
parts.working: 1 mark each: high closure at short intervals; decreases to 0 at 60 s (with data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each touch produces an action potential in the trap. Suggest an explanation for the results.
parts.answer: Each action potential raises the level of a signal (e.g. Ca²⁺ concentration) in the cells; one action potential alone is below the threshold for closure; if a second arrives before the signal has fallen back, the threshold is reached; the signal decays with time, so longer intervals fail.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: first action potential alone insufficient; it raises a signal such as Ca²⁺ concentration; second adds to it (summation) to reach threshold; signal decays over ~30 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest an advantage of this 'counting' mechanism.
parts.answer: Prevents closure by single accidental stimuli (raindrops/debris), saving energy.
parts.working: B1 avoids false closures.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two mutant varieties of a cereal plant are studied.
Mutant X: produces a DELLA protein that cannot bind the gibberellin–receptor complex.
Mutant Y: produces no functional DELLA protein at all.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the height of each mutant compared with normal plants, and explain your predictions.
parts.answer: X: dwarf, because DELLA cannot be broken down, so it keeps blocking the transcription factors needed for growth genes. Y: tall (slender), because there is no DELLA to inhibit the transcription factors, so growth genes are always expressed.
parts.working: B1 X dwarf. B1 DELLA not degraded so transcription of growth genes stays blocked. B1 Y tall. B1 no repressor so growth genes transcribed regardless of GA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of spraying each mutant with gibberellin, giving a reason.
parts.answer: No change in either; X cannot respond because DELLA is not broken down; Y is already at maximum growth/has no DELLA to remove.
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each response, state whether it is controlled mainly by the nervous system, the endocrine system, or both. Give a reason in each case.
(i) blinking when dust blows towards the eye
(ii) breast development during puberty
(iii) the heart beating faster when a dog suddenly barks
parts.answer: (i) nervous: very rapid, short-lived, localised reflex. (ii) endocrine: slow, long-lasting changes over months (oestrogen). (iii) both: sympathetic nerves act within a second and adrenaline from the adrenal glands prolongs the effect.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which the nervous and endocrine systems are similar.
parts.answer: Both use chemical signals that bind to specific receptors / both coordinate responses to stimuli.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each hormone of the menstrual cycle (FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone), state the gland or structure that secretes it and give one of its functions.
parts.answer: FSH – anterior pituitary – stimulates follicle development/oestrogen secretion. LH – anterior pituitary – triggers ovulation / formation of corpus luteum. Oestrogen – developing follicles (ovary) – repairs/thickens endometrium; controls FSH/LH. Progesterone – corpus luteum – maintains endometrium; inhibits FSH and LH.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct row (source and function).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two endocrine glands, and one hormone secreted by each.
parts.answer: e.g. pancreas (islets) – insulin/glucagon; adrenal gland – adrenaline; pituitary – ADH/FSH/LH; ovary – oestrogen/progesterone.
parts.working: 1 mark each correct gland + hormone pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how hormones are transported from endocrine glands to their target organs.
parts.answer: Dissolved in blood plasma.
parts.working: B1 in the blood (plasma).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why endocrine glands have a very good blood supply but no ducts.
parts.answer: Hormones are secreted directly into the blood (ductless); many capillaries carry hormones away quickly to the whole body.
parts.working: 1 mark each: secreted into blood not a duct; capillaries/rapid removal and distribution.

stem: Some hormones, such as oestrogen and progesterone, are steroids. Others, such as insulin and ADH, are proteins or peptides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why steroid hormones can bind to receptors inside the cytoplasm or nucleus of target cells, while peptide hormones bind to receptors on the cell surface membrane.
parts.answer: Steroids are lipid-soluble/non-polar, so they diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer; peptide hormones are large and polar/water-soluble, so they cannot cross; they act via receptors on the membrane (and second messengers).
parts.working: 1 mark each: steroid lipid-soluble crosses bilayer; peptides polar/large cannot cross; peptide uses surface receptor + second messenger/signalling cascade.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the concentrations of FSH and LH stay low during the days after ovulation.
parts.answer: After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum; it secretes large amounts of progesterone (and some oestrogen); progesterone inhibits secretion of FSH and LH by the anterior pituitary (negative feedback).
parts.working: 1 mark each: corpus luteum forms; secretes progesterone; negative feedback on anterior pituitary/hypothalamus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why menstruation begins if the egg is not fertilised.
parts.answer: The corpus luteum degenerates, so progesterone falls; the endometrium is no longer maintained and breaks down.
parts.working: 1 mark each.
