stem: A combined contraceptive pill is taken daily for 21 days, followed by 7 days without hormone (or with inactive tablets). A progesterone-only pill is taken every day without a break.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bleeding usually occurs during the 7 days without the combined pill.
parts.answer: Hormone (progesterone/oestrogen) levels fall; the endometrium is no longer maintained, so it breaks down (a withdrawal bleed).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Progesterone-only pills do not always prevent ovulation. Suggest two other ways in which they could prevent pregnancy.
parts.answer: Thicken cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass through; make the endometrium thin/unsuitable for implantation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the progesterone-only pill must be taken at about the same time each day.
parts.answer: Synthetic hormone is broken down quickly, so its concentration must not fall too low between doses (or mucus thins).
parts.working: B1 hormone concentration must be kept above an effective level.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A neurotransmitter and a hormone are both chemical messengers. Give one similarity and three differences between them.
parts.answer: Similarity: both bind to specific receptors (complementary shape) on target cells. Differences: neurotransmitter crosses a tiny synaptic cleft by diffusion, hormone travels in the blood; neurotransmitter acts in milliseconds, hormone in seconds to hours; neurotransmitter affects one cell/very localised, hormone affects many target cells all over the body; neurotransmitter broken down quickly so short effect, hormone effect lasts longer.
parts.working: B1 similarity. 1 mark each for three differences.

stem: A woman in Peshawar records the lengths of her last six menstrual cycles: 28, 30, 27, 29, 31 and 28 days. Ovulation usually happens about 14 days before the next menstruation starts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean cycle length, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 28.8 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the mean to predict on which day of the next cycle ovulation is most likely. Explain your answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Urine test strips detect LH. Explain why a positive LH test helps to predict ovulation more accurately than the calculation.
parts.answer: Ovulation follows the LH surge by about a day; the surge is measured directly in the current cycle, whereas cycle length varies from cycle to cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark each: LH surge triggers ovulation (shortly after); cycle lengths vary so average is approximate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
After a sudden loud noise, a student's heart rate and blood adrenaline concentration were recorded.
Time after noise: 0 s, 2 s, 30 s, 1 min, 3 min, 10 min
Heart rate / beats min⁻¹: 72, 95, 110, 108, 96, 76
Adrenaline / arbitrary units: 1, 1, 6, 9, 5, 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the heart rate rose within 2 s although the adrenaline concentration had not yet changed.
parts.answer: The first increase is caused by the nervous system; impulses in sympathetic neurones to the SAN act within milliseconds; adrenaline takes time to be secreted and carried in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark each: nervous (sympathetic) control is rapid; hormone needs secretion and transport in blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the heart rate remained high for several minutes.
parts.answer: Adrenaline secreted by the adrenal glands circulates in the blood and keeps stimulating the heart until it is broken down (e.g. in the liver).
parts.working: 1 mark each: adrenaline still present in blood; removed/broken down only slowly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the data to suggest why both systems are needed to deal with danger.
parts.answer: Nervous system gives an immediate response; the endocrine system sustains and spreads the response to many organs (e.g. liver glycogenolysis, breathing) over minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rapid initial response; longer-lasting, widespread response.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: For most of the menstrual cycle, oestrogen inhibits secretion of LH. Shortly before ovulation, a high concentration of oestrogen instead stimulates a large release of LH. Explain why this is an example of positive feedback, and why it is useful.
parts.answer: A rise in oestrogen causes a rise in LH, which stimulates the follicle to produce even more oestrogen, so the change is amplified; this gives a sudden large LH surge that causes ovulation at the right time.
parts.working: 1 mark each: change increases further rather than being reversed; LH and oestrogen stimulate each other; produces rapid surge that triggers ovulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this positive feedback stops after ovulation.
parts.answer: The follicle has ruptured and becomes the corpus luteum, which makes mainly progesterone; progesterone inhibits LH (negative feedback).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: In an IVF clinic in Karachi, a woman is given daily injections of FSH for about 10 days. When ultrasound shows several large follicles, she is given a single injection of a hormone that acts like LH. Eggs are collected 36 hours later. After an embryo is placed in the uterus, she is given progesterone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the FSH injections are given.
parts.answer: FSH stimulates several follicles to develop at once (instead of one), so several eggs can be collected.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the LH-like injection is timed so that eggs are collected 36 hours later.
parts.answer: It mimics the LH surge which triggers final maturation of eggs and ovulation; eggs must be collected just before they would be released from the follicles.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why progesterone is given after the embryo is transferred.
parts.answer: To keep the endometrium thick and maintained so the embryo can implant; normal corpus luteum function may be inadequate after the treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline into the blood when it receives impulses from sympathetic neurones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the adrenal medulla is said to link the nervous system and the endocrine system.
parts.answer: It is stimulated by nerve impulses (neurotransmitter from neurones) but its output is a hormone secreted into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Adrenaline cannot enter its target cells. Explain how it can still cause liver cells to release glucose within seconds.
parts.answer: Adrenaline binds to receptors on the cell surface membrane; activates a G protein and adenylyl cyclase, producing cAMP (second messenger); a cascade of enzymes (kinases) is activated, amplifying the signal and activating glycogen phosphorylase to break down glycogen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: surface receptor; G protein / adenylyl cyclase; cAMP second messenger; enzyme cascade/amplification; glycogenolysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the role of each of these in transmission at a cholinergic synapse.
(i) voltage-gated calcium ion channels in the presynaptic membrane
(ii) synaptic vesicles
(iii) receptor proteins in the postsynaptic membrane
(iv) acetylcholinesterase
parts.answer: (i) open when the action potential arrives, letting Ca²⁺ diffuse into the knob, which triggers vesicle fusion. (ii) store acetylcholine and release it by exocytosis. (iii) bind acetylcholine and open, allowing Na⁺ into the postsynaptic neurone. (iv) hydrolyses acetylcholine so the signal stops/receptors are freed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to acetylcholine after it has bound to the receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, including how it is recycled.
parts.answer: ACh leaves the receptor and is hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase into choline and ethanoic acid (acetate); these diffuse back across the cleft; they are taken into the presynaptic knob; ACh is resynthesised (using acetyl coenzyme A and ATP) and packaged into vesicles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of: hydrolysis by AChE; into choline + ethanoate/acetate; diffuse back to presynaptic membrane; reabsorbed (active transport/uptake); ACh resynthesised using ATP; stored in vesicles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of recycling acetylcholine.
parts.answer: Saves energy/materials; ACh supply is quickly restored for further impulses.

stem: A presynaptic action potential produces a depolarisation of 6 mV in the postsynaptic neurone. The resting potential of the postsynaptic neurone is −70 mV and its threshold is −55 mV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depolarisation needed to reach threshold.
parts.answer: 15 mV

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the smallest number of presynaptic neurones that must fire at the same time to produce an action potential in the postsynaptic neurone.
parts.working: B1 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5, so 3 neurones needed (2 give only 12 mV).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name this type of summation, and describe the other type of summation.
parts.answer: Spatial summation; temporal summation is when one presynaptic neurone fires several impulses in rapid succession, so the depolarisations add up.
parts.working: B1 spatial. B1 temporal = repeated impulses from the same neurone close together in time.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student wrote these statements about a cholinergic synapse. Each contains one error.
1 Acetylcholine crosses the synaptic cleft by active transport.
2 The receptors for acetylcholine are found on the presynaptic membrane.
3 Sodium ions entering the presynaptic knob cause the vesicles to fuse with the membrane.
4 Acetylcholinesterase is found inside the synaptic vesicles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rewrite each statement correctly.
parts.answer: 1 ACh crosses the cleft by diffusion. 2 The receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane. 3 Calcium ions entering the knob cause vesicle fusion. 4 AChE is in the synaptic cleft/on the postsynaptic membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a reflex arc, the total path from receptor to effector is 1.20 m and impulses travel at 100 m s⁻¹ along all the neurones. The time from stimulus to the start of depolarisation of the muscle fibre was 14.0 ms. The pathway includes two synapses and one neuromuscular junction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for conduction along the neurones, in ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the rest of the time is due to delays at the junctions, calculate the mean delay at each junction. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there is a delay at each synapse.
parts.answer: Transmission is chemical: Ca²⁺ entry, exocytosis of vesicles, diffusion of ACh across the cleft and binding/opening of receptors all take time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of these steps.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Botulinum toxin, made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, prevents synaptic vesicles from fusing with the presynaptic membrane at cholinergic synapses and neuromuscular junctions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why food poisoning by this toxin causes floppy (flaccid) paralysis.
parts.answer: No exocytosis so no ACh released; no ACh binds to receptors on the sarcolemma, so no depolarisation/action potential in muscle; muscles cannot contract and stay relaxed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Doctors inject tiny amounts of this toxin into individual muscles to treat painful muscle spasms. Suggest why it is effective and why the injection must be repeated every few months.
parts.answer: It stops the overactive motor neurone signalling to that muscle only, so the spasm stops; the neurone eventually grows new terminals/replaces the damaged proteins, so the effect wears off.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In an experiment, the duration and size of postsynaptic depolarisations were measured at a cholinergic synapse, before and after adding drug D.
Without drug D: peak depolarisation 20 mV, lasting 2 ms
With drug D: peak depolarisation 28 mV, lasting 15 ms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how drug D acts. Explain your answer using the data.
parts.answer: Drug D inhibits acetylcholinesterase; ACh is not broken down so it stays in the cleft longer and keeps binding receptors (longer depolarisation); ACh builds up to a higher concentration so more channels are open at once (larger peak).
parts.working: 1 mark each: AChE inhibitor; longer duration explained; larger amplitude explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one effect drug D would have on the muscles of a person exposed to it.
parts.answer: Prolonged contraction/spasms/twitching, then possible paralysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The synaptic cleft at a cholinergic synapse is about 20 nm wide. Explain why it is important that the cleft is so narrow.
parts.answer: Diffusion is fast over a short distance, so transmission is quick; ACh stays concentrated enough to bind many receptors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that acetylcholine is removed from the receptors very quickly.
parts.answer: Otherwise the postsynaptic membrane would stay depolarised/keep firing; removal allows the next impulse to be transmitted separately and stops continuous stimulation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why presynaptic neurones that fire very frequently contain a large amount of rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus in their cell bodies.
parts.answer: To make and package proteins needed at the synapse (e.g. enzymes for ACh synthesis, channel proteins, vesicle membrane proteins) to replace those used.
parts.working: 1 mark each: protein synthesis (RER); packaging/vesicles (Golgi).

stem: At some synapses in the brain, the transmitter released binds to receptors that are chloride ion channels. When these channels open, Cl⁻ ions diffuse into the postsynaptic neurone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect on the membrane potential of the postsynaptic neurone and explain why this makes an action potential less likely.
parts.answer: Inside becomes more negative (hyperpolarised, e.g. −75 mV); further from threshold; more excitatory input/greater depolarisation is needed to reach threshold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A neurone receives input from one excitatory synapse and one of these inhibitory synapses at the same time. Explain why it may not produce an action potential even though the excitatory input alone would.
parts.answer: The hyperpolarisation from the inhibitory synapse cancels some of the depolarisation from the excitatory synapse (summation of opposite effects), so threshold is not reached.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why inhibitory synapses are important in the nervous system.
parts.answer: Allow integration/fine control, e.g. preventing unwanted responses or relaxing an antagonistic muscle.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The peak postsynaptic depolarisation was measured at a synapse bathed in solutions with different calcium ion concentrations.
Ca²⁺ / mmol dm⁻³: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0
Peak depolarisation / mV: 2, 5, 11, 18
When magnesium ions (Mg²⁺), which block calcium channels, were added to the 2.0 mmol dm⁻³ solution, the peak depolarisation fell to 3 mV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of calcium ion concentration on the postsynaptic response.
parts.answer: Higher Ca²⁺ gives larger depolarisation (2 mV to 18 mV); more Ca²⁺ diffuses into the presynaptic knob per impulse; more vesicles fuse and more ACh is released, so more receptor channels open.
parts.working: 1 mark each: trend with data; more Ca²⁺ influx; more ACh released/more Na⁺ channels opened.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of Mg²⁺.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ blocks Ca²⁺ channels so less Ca²⁺ enters; fewer vesicles release ACh so depolarisation is small.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of peak depolarisation at 4.0 mmol dm⁻³ to that at 1.0 mmol dm⁻³, and state whether the response is proportional to the Ca²⁺ concentration.
parts.answer: 3.6 : 1; not proportional (Ca²⁺ increased 4 times but response only 3.6 times).
parts.working: B1 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6. B1 not proportional, with reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lambert–Eaton syndrome is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack the voltage-gated calcium ion channels in presynaptic membranes at neuromuscular junctions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why patients have muscle weakness.
parts.answer: Fewer Ca²⁺ channels so less Ca²⁺ enters the presynaptic knob; fewer vesicles fuse and less ACh is released; depolarisation of the sarcolemma may not reach threshold, so fewer muscle fibres contract.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Strength in these patients often improves briefly during repeated, rapid muscle activity. Suggest why.
parts.answer: With rapid repeated impulses, Ca²⁺ builds up inside the knob before it can be removed; so more ACh is released with each later impulse.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this disease does not affect the heart rate directly.
parts.answer: Heartbeat is myogenic (started by the SAN), not dependent on neuromuscular junctions with skeletal muscle.

author: HomiLabs

stem: At some synapses the transmitter is not broken down by an enzyme in the cleft. Instead, it is taken back into the presynaptic neurone by transporter proteins (reuptake). Some antidepressant drugs block these transporters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how blocking reuptake affects transmission at these synapses.
parts.answer: Transmitter remains in the cleft longer and at a higher concentration; it continues to bind postsynaptic receptors; so the postsynaptic response is larger/longer-lasting (more frequent action potentials).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why such drugs often take several weeks to have their full effect, even though they block transporters within hours.
parts.answer: The nervous system adapts: e.g. the number of receptors or the amount of transmitter made changes slowly (gene expression/protein synthesis takes time).
parts.working: 1 mark each: slow changes in receptor/transmitter levels; protein synthesis/gene expression changes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A doctor taps a patient's leg just below the kneecap. The lower leg kicks forward. This is the knee-jerk reflex. Only one synapse in the spinal cord is involved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of receptor stimulated and the effector.
parts.answer: Stretch receptor (in the thigh muscle/muscle spindle); the quadriceps (thigh) muscle.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which type of neurone is missing from this reflex arc compared with a hand-withdrawal reflex.
parts.answer: Relay neurone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why doctors test this reflex.
parts.answer: To check that the sensory and motor neurones and the spinal cord are working normally.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define each term: (i) receptor (ii) effector (iii) receptor potential
parts.answer: (i) a cell/structure that detects a stimulus (a change in the environment) and converts it to an electrical signal. (ii) a muscle or gland that carries out a response. (iii) a change in membrane potential of a receptor cell caused by a stimulus; its size depends on the stimulus strength.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a receptor potential is described as graded but an action potential is not.
parts.answer: Receptor potential size varies with stimulus strength; action potential is always the same size (all-or-nothing).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each stimulus to the type of receptor that detects it, and give one example of a receptor cell or organ for each.
(i) light (ii) chemicals in food (iii) pressure on the skin (iv) temperature
parts.answer: (i) photoreceptor – rod/cone cells in the retina. (ii) chemoreceptor – taste bud cells/olfactory cells. (iii) mechanoreceptor – Pacinian corpuscle/touch receptor. (iv) thermoreceptor – nerve endings in the skin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: When a person walks from a dim room into bright sunshine, their pupils constrict within a second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the receptors and the effectors in this reflex.
parts.answer: Receptors: photoreceptors (rods/cones) in the retina. Effectors: circular muscles of the iris.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage that this response is a reflex.
parts.answer: It is very fast and automatic; protects the retina from damage by too much light before the brain consciously decides.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A girl in Multan steps on a sharp stone and lifts her foot before she feels the pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the cell bodies of the sensory neurone and the motor neurone are found.
parts.answer: Sensory: in a ganglion (dorsal root ganglion) just outside the spinal cord. Motor: in the grey matter of the spinal cord.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why she feels pain a short time after her foot has moved.
parts.answer: The relay neurone also passes impulses up the spinal cord to the brain; the path is longer and involves more synapses, so awareness comes after the motor response.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A pressure receptor in the skin was stimulated with increasing pressure and its receptor (generator) potential was measured. An action potential is produced in the sensory neurone only when the receptor potential reaches 10 mV.
Pressure / arbitrary units: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8
Receptor potential / mV: 3, 7, 12, 18, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between pressure and receptor potential.
parts.answer: Receptor potential increases with pressure; it rises steeply at low pressure and levels off at high pressure (only +2 mV from 4 to 8).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the lowest pressure in the table that would produce action potentials. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2 units; receptor potential (12 mV) is above threshold (10 mV); at 1 unit it is only 7 mV.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the receptor potential levels off at high pressure.
parts.answer: All the stretch-mediated ion (Na⁺) channels are already open.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A constant stimulus was applied to a receptor for 10 s and the frequency of impulses in its sensory neurone was recorded.
Time / s: 0, 1, 2, 5, 10
Impulses per second: 40, 30, 20, 8, 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in impulse frequency between 0 s and 10 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: This decrease is called adaptation. Suggest the advantage of adaptation to an animal.
parts.answer: Unchanging, unimportant stimuli (e.g. clothes on skin) are ignored; the nervous system is free to respond to new changes/danger.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the brain would detect that the stimulus had become stronger at 10 s.
parts.answer: Impulse frequency would increase (more action potentials per second).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hand-withdrawal reflex, the sensory neurone is 0.80 m long and conducts at 65 m s⁻¹. The motor neurone is 0.80 m long and conducts at 80 m s⁻¹. There are two synapses in the spinal cord and one neuromuscular junction, each with a delay of 0.6 ms. Ignore the conduction time in the very short relay neurone between the two spinal synapses. The muscle starts to shorten 10 ms after it is first depolarised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total time from stimulus to the start of muscle shortening. Give your answer in ms to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A voluntary response to the same stimulus takes about 200 ms. Explain why the reflex is much faster.
parts.answer: Reflex involves few neurones and synapses (spinal cord only); the voluntary response involves the brain, many more synapses and decision-making.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Many people with long-term type 2 diabetes in Pakistan develop damage to sensory neurones in their feet (peripheral neuropathy). They are advised to inspect their feet every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why damage to sensory neurones means a small cut or blister may go unnoticed.
parts.answer: Impulses from pain/touch receptors are not conducted to the brain (or are reduced), so the person does not feel the injury.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why these patients are also more likely to trip or lose balance.
parts.answer: Less sensory information about foot position/pressure from receptors; reflex adjustments of leg muscles are slower or absent.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Amiloride is a drug that blocks the sodium ion channels in the membranes of taste receptor cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of amiloride on a person's ability to taste salt, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Salt taste is reduced; Na⁺ cannot enter the chemoreceptor cells, so they do not depolarise (smaller receptor potential); less Ca²⁺ entry/less transmitter release, so fewer action potentials in the sensory neurone.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some salt taste remains even with a high dose of amiloride. Suggest one explanation.
parts.answer: There are other routes for Na⁺ entry/other receptors not blocked by amiloride, or not all channels are blocked.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why amiloride does not stop the person tasting sweet foods.
parts.answer: Sweet taste uses different receptors (receptor proteins for sugars), not Na⁺ channels.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A man whose spinal cord was completely cut in the neck region after a road accident in Lahore is still able to show the knee-jerk reflex, but he cannot feel the tap on his knee and cannot move his legs voluntarily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the knee-jerk reflex still occurs.
parts.answer: The reflex arc passes only through the lower spinal cord below the injury; sensory and motor neurones and the synapse are undamaged.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why he cannot feel the tap.
parts.answer: Impulses cannot travel up the spinal cord past the injury to the brain (sensory cortex), so there is no conscious sensation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why he cannot move his legs voluntarily even though his leg muscles and motor neurones work.
parts.answer: Impulses from the brain cannot pass down the spinal cord to the motor neurones.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a two-point touch test, two blunt points are pressed on the skin at different separations. The smallest separation at which a person can feel two separate points is recorded.
Fingertip: 2 mm
Palm: 10 mm
Forearm: 38 mm
Back: 42 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the separation threshold is on the back than on the fingertip.
parts.answer: 21 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the differences in the results in terms of touch receptors and sensory neurones.
parts.answer: Fingertips have a much higher density of touch receptors; each sensory neurone serves a small area (small receptive field); so two close points stimulate different neurones; on the back receptors are sparse and each neurone serves a large area, so both points may stimulate the same neurone and feel like one.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: receptor density; size of area served by one neurone; separate neurones needed for two sensations; brain interprets one neurone's signal as one point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage for fingertips to have a low threshold.
parts.answer: Allows fine discrimination of texture/shape for manipulating objects precisely.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Capsaicin is the chemical that makes chillies hot. It binds to a receptor protein in the membranes of sensory nerve endings in the mouth. This receptor is a cation channel that is also opened by temperatures above about 43 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how eating chilli produces impulses that the brain interprets as burning heat.
parts.answer: Capsaicin opens the cation channels so Na⁺ (and Ca²⁺) diffuse in; the nerve ending depolarises (receptor potential) above threshold, producing action potentials; these travel along the same neurones used for heat, so the brain interprets them as heat.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: People in Pakistan who eat spicy food every day often become less sensitive to chilli. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Repeated stimulation desensitises the receptors / fewer receptors / channels inactivated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Capsaicin creams are used to relieve some types of long-term pain. Suggest how they work.
parts.answer: After an initial burning, the sensory nerve endings become desensitised, so fewer pain impulses are sent.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Students drank decaffeinated coffee to which different masses of caffeine had been added. Their reaction time to a light on a screen was measured 30 minutes later.
Caffeine / mg: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200
Mean reaction time / ms: 262, 248, 236, 233, 241

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of caffeine on reaction time.
parts.answer: Reaction time decreases as caffeine increases from 0 to 150 mg (262 to 233 ms), with the decrease getting smaller; at 200 mg reaction time increases again to 241 ms (still faster than with no caffeine).
parts.working: 1 mark each: decrease to 150 mg with data; increase at 200 mg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in reaction time between 0 mg and 150 mg. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student concludes that 'the more caffeine you drink, the faster you react'. Explain why this conclusion is not supported.
parts.answer: At 200 mg the reaction time was slower than at 150 mg (and 100 mg), so it is not true for all doses.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The leaflets of Mimosa pudica (touch-me-not, chhui-mui) fold up when touched and reopen later. The time taken for leaflets to reopen was recorded at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35
Mean time to reopen / min: 32, 24, 17, 13, 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results.
parts.answer: Time to reopen decreases from 32 min at 15 °C to a minimum of 13 min at 30 °C, then increases to 15 min at 35 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each: decrease to 30 °C; slight rise at 35 °C (with data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that the optimum temperature for reopening is exactly 30 °C. Explain why this conclusion cannot be made from these results.
parts.answer: Temperatures were only tested at 5 °C intervals; the true optimum could be anywhere between 25 °C and 35 °C; more temperatures (e.g. 1 °C intervals) are needed around 30 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A plant nursery in Lahore dipped stem cuttings of a rose variety into solutions of a synthetic auxin for 10 seconds before planting them. After three weeks the number of roots on each cutting was counted.
Auxin / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.1, 1, 10, 100
Mean number of roots per cutting: 3, 6, 11, 14, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of auxin concentration on root formation.
parts.answer: Number of roots increases from 0 to 10 mg dm⁻³ (3 to 14 roots); at 100 mg dm⁻³ it falls to 4, only slightly more than with no auxin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the concentration the nursery should use, and suggest why a higher concentration should not be used.
parts.answer: 10 mg dm⁻³ (in this range); 100 mg dm⁻³ inhibits rooting (high auxin concentrations inhibit root growth) and wastes auxin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cuttings without auxin still formed some roots.
parts.answer: Cuttings contain their own natural auxin (from buds/leaves).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oat coleoptiles were lit from one side for 4 hours. Twenty coleoptiles were used in each group.
Group 1: tip covered by a light-proof cap → 2 bent towards the light
Group 2: tip uncovered, lower part wrapped in foil → 18 bent towards the light
Group 3: nothing covered → 19 bent towards the light

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what can be concluded about the region of the coleoptile that detects light. Use the data to explain your answer.
parts.answer: The tip detects light; when only the tip is covered few bend (2/20), but covering the lower part has almost no effect (18/20, similar to 19/20).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The bending happens in the region below the tip. Suggest what this shows about the response.
parts.answer: A signal (auxin) must pass from the tip down to the growing region, where cells elongate.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why two coleoptiles with covered tips still bent.
parts.answer: Cap not fitted tightly/light leaked in, or natural variation.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student studied the effect of caffeine on the heart rate of Daphnia (water fleas) at 20 °C.
Caffeine / %: 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8
Mean heart rate / beats min⁻¹: 220, 236, 251, 268, 270

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student concludes: 'Heart rate increases in proportion to caffeine concentration.' Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Heart rate increases with caffeine, but not in proportion: doubling 0.1 → 0.2 adds 15 beats, 0.2 → 0.4 adds 17, and 0.4 → 0.8 adds only 2, so it levels off; a proportional relationship would also pass through the origin, which it cannot (220 at 0).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: positive trend agreed; not proportional — increases are not doubled; levels off at high concentration; intercept is not zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the results may not apply to humans.
parts.answer: Daphnia is an invertebrate with a different heart and nervous control; doses not comparable.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Eight students recorded the hours they slept the night before and then did a computer reaction test.
Sleep / hours: 4.0, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0
Reaction time / ms: 285, 262, 270, 248, 251, 233, 228, 231

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by these data.
parts.answer: Negative correlation: more sleep is linked with shorter reaction time (levelling off above about 7–8 hours).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that lack of sleep causes slower reactions. Give three reasons why this conclusion is not fully justified.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show causation; only eight students/one night (small sample); other variables not controlled (caffeine, time of day, practice, age, screen use); sleep hours self-reported/inaccurate; one test per student.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Dwarf pea plants were sprayed with gibberellin solution once a week for four weeks. Ten plants were used in each group. Mean increase in height ± standard deviation:
Water only: 18.2 ± 2.1 cm
Gibberellin 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³: 29.5 ± 4.8 cm
Gibberellin 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³: 33.0 ± 5.2 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mean height increase is with 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ gibberellin than with water. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss what can be concluded about the effect of the two gibberellin concentrations. Refer to the standard deviations.
parts.answer: Both concentrations increase growth compared with water; the means ± SD for water (16.1–20.3) do not overlap with either gibberellin group, so this effect is likely to be real; the ranges for the two gibberellin concentrations overlap widely (24.7–34.3 and 27.8–38.2), so there may be no real difference between them; a statistical test (t-test) is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: gibberellin increases height; no overlap with control; overlap between the two GA groups so difference may not be significant; suggestion of t-test/more replicates.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student squeezed a spring-loaded clothes peg between thumb and forefinger as many times as possible, for five consecutive minutes without resting.
Minute: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Number of squeezes: 62, 51, 44, 39, 36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in squeezes from minute 1 to minute 5. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the pattern and suggest a biological explanation.
parts.answer: Number of squeezes falls each minute, but the fall gets smaller; muscle fatigue: oxygen supply cannot meet demand so anaerobic respiration increases; lactate builds up and ATP supply for cross-bridge cycling and Ca²⁺ pumping falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each: pattern with decreasing rate of decline; ATP shortage/anaerobic respiration; lactate/acid build-up reduces contraction.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Aleurone layers from barley grains were incubated in gibberellin solutions. A sample of each incubation liquid was then added to starch solution, and the time for the starch to disappear (no blue-black colour with iodine) was measured.
Gibberellin / mol dm⁻³: 0, 10⁻⁹, 10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁶
Time / min: more than 60, 48, 30, 16, 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of starch breakdown, as 1000 ÷ time, for 10⁻⁸ and 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ gibberellin. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 33.3 min⁻¹ and 83.3 min⁻¹ (arbitrary units)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion from these results.
parts.answer: As gibberellin concentration increases, more amylase is released by the aleurone layer (faster starch breakdown), with the effect smaller between 10⁻⁷ and 10⁻⁶.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the result for 0 mol dm⁻³ cannot be used to calculate a rate.
parts.answer: The exact time is unknown (end point not reached within 60 min).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Nerve conduction speed in the legs was measured in adults with type 2 diabetes in a hospital in Faisalabad. Patients were grouped by years since diagnosis.
Years since diagnosis: 0–2, 3–5, 6–10, more than 10
Number of patients: 34, 28, 22, 12
Mean conduction speed / m s⁻¹: 52, 49, 45, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor claims that 'diabetes causes nerve damage that gets worse every year'. Discuss the extent to which these data support this claim.
parts.answer: Support: conduction speed falls as time since diagnosis increases (52 → 40 m s⁻¹), consistent with progressive damage. Limitations: no comparison group without diabetes; patients diagnosed longer ago are probably older and age itself slows conduction; grouped data so cannot show change every year; no measure of spread/statistical test; different and small group sizes (only 12 in last group); different individuals in each group (not followed over time); other factors such as blood glucose control not taken into account.
parts.working: B1 trend described with data. 1 mark each for up to three limitations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how a better study could test the claim.
parts.answer: Measure the same patients every year over many years (longitudinal), and compare with age-matched people without diabetes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The lowest concentration of sodium chloride solution that could be tasted (taste threshold) was found for 40 non-smokers and 40 smokers of the same age range.
Non-smokers: mean 0.012 mol dm⁻³, 95 % confidence interval 0.010–0.014 mol dm⁻³
Smokers: mean 0.019 mol dm⁻³, 95 % confidence interval 0.015–0.023 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the confidence intervals allow you to conclude.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference between the means is likely to be significant (not due to chance); smokers have a higher taste threshold (are less sensitive to salt).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the confidence interval for smokers is wider than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: Smokers' results are more variable (larger standard deviation), since sample sizes are equal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the study does not prove that smoking damages salt receptors.
parts.answer: It is a correlation; smokers may differ in other ways (diet, salt intake, alcohol); no measurement of receptors themselves; habitual salty food could raise threshold.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two points.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A study compared 21 students who play action video games for more than 10 hours a week with 21 who never play. Mean reaction times were 182 ms and 214 ms. A t-test gave t = 3.9; the critical value at p = 0.05 for 40 degrees of freedom is 2.02.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the t-test result shows.
parts.answer: t (3.9) is greater than 2.02, so the null hypothesis is rejected; there is a significant difference in mean reaction time (probability of the difference being due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A news website reports that 'playing video games makes your reactions faster'. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: There is a significant difference, but the study is comparative/correlational, so cause cannot be established; people with naturally fast reactions may choose to play games; groups may differ in age, sex, sleep, or practice with screens/keyboards; a controlled study training non-players would be needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of these points.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The time for Venus fly traps to close after two touches of the trigger hairs was measured at four temperatures. Five traps were tested at each temperature.
Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40
Mean closure time / s: 0.80, 0.42, 0.25, 0.31
Range / s: 0.71–0.92, 0.36–0.47, 0.21–0.30, 0.24–0.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of temperature on closure time between 10 °C and 30 °C.
parts.answer: Closure time decreases (0.80 to 0.25 s) as temperature rises; more kinetic energy so ions/water move faster across membranes; proton pumps/enzymes and ion channels work faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the results show that closure is slower at 40 °C than at 30 °C.
parts.answer: Mean is higher at 40 °C (0.31 vs 0.25 s), but the ranges overlap (0.24–0.40 and 0.21–0.30), so the difference may not be real; only 5 traps; a statistical test is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Reaction times of eight students to a sound were measured with a computer program:
245, 262, 238, 251, 270, 244, 259, 255 ms
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1))

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean reaction time.
parts.answer: 253 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation tells you about these data.
parts.answer: How spread out the reaction times are around the mean.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
In 16 healthy adults, the simple reaction time (time to press a key after a light flashes) was measured. Mean = 312 ms; standard deviation = 24 ms.
Standard error SM = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = mean ± 2 × SM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.answer: 6.0 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval.
parts.answer: 300 to 324 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the 95 % confidence interval means.
parts.answer: It is a range that is likely to contain the true population mean: a 95 % confidence level means that about 95 % of intervals calculated this way from repeated samples would contain the true mean.
parts.working: B1 a range that estimates/likely contains the true population mean. B1 95 % confidence refers to repeated sampling (about 95 % of such intervals contain the true mean), not a 95 % probability for this one interval.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the most suitable statistical test for each investigation and give a reason.
(i) Is there a significant difference between mean reaction times of 15 left-handed and 15 right-handed students?
(ii) Is there a correlation between auxin concentration (8 concentrations) and mean root length?
(iii) Do the numbers of tall and dwarf plants in an F2 generation fit a 3 : 1 ratio?
parts.answer: (i) t-test: comparing two means of continuous, normally distributed data. (ii) Spearman's rank correlation: testing for a correlation between two variables (data need not be normally distributed). (iii) chi-squared test: comparing observed counts in categories with expected numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, test with reason.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: Two groups of 12 students measured their reaction times. Both groups had a mean of 230 ms. Group A had a standard deviation of 8 ms and group B had a standard deviation of 31 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which group's results are more variable and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Group B; larger standard deviation means values are more spread out from the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for group A, using SM = s ÷ √n and mean ± 2 × SM. Give the limits to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 225 to 235 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why group B's results may be so variable.
parts.answer: Wider range of ages/sleep/caffeine/practice, or inconsistent method (e.g. different equipment, distractions).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Reaction times (ms) of eight sprinters from a Lahore athletics club and eight students who do no regular sport:
Sprinters: 198, 205, 189, 210, 201, 195, 207, 192
Non-athletes: 221, 214, 230, 209, 226, 218, 235, 212
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)
Sprinters: s = 7.44 ms. Non-athletes: s = 9.13 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean for each group.
parts.answer: Sprinters 199.6 ms; non-athletes 220.6 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 14 degrees of freedom is 2.14. State the null hypothesis and what you can conclude.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: there is no significant difference between the mean reaction times of sprinters and non-athletes. t = 5.04 > 2.14, so reject the null hypothesis: the difference is significant (sprinters react faster).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Eight students recorded how many hours they slept, then attempted a hand–eye coordination task and counted their errors.
Sleep / hours: 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0
Errors: 14, 11, 12, 9, 10, 6, 7, 4
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1))

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value for 8 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.738. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: |rs| = 0.929 > 0.738, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant negative correlation between hours of sleep and number of errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Tall pea plants (Le Le) were crossed with dwarf plants (le le). The F1 plants were self-pollinated. The F2 generation contained 312 tall plants and 88 dwarf plants.
χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers of tall and dwarf plants for a 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.answer: 300 tall, 100 dwarf

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ².

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of χ² for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: 1.92 < 3.84, so accept the null hypothesis; the difference between observed and expected is not significant/due to chance; the results fit a 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Dwarf bean plants were treated with gibberellin or water. Mean final heights and standard errors:
Water: mean 18.2 cm, SM = 0.6 cm
Gibberellin: mean 41.5 cm, SM = 1.4 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2SM) for each group.
parts.answer: Water 17.0–19.4 cm; gibberellin 38.7–44.3 cm
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to state whether the difference between the means is likely to be significant. Explain.
parts.answer: Yes; the 95 % confidence intervals do not overlap, so the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: Nerve conduction speed in the median nerve was measured in 16 adult volunteers. Mean = 52.4 m s⁻¹, standard deviation = 4.8 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.answer: 1.2 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2SM).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A patient's conduction speed is 47.0 m s⁻¹. A student says that because this is outside the confidence interval the patient must have a nerve disorder. Explain why this reasoning is wrong.
parts.answer: The confidence interval describes where the population mean lies, not the range of normal individuals; individual values vary much more (SD 4.8, so about 43–62 m s⁻¹ covers most healthy people), and 47.0 is within normal variation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The time taken for Mimosa leaflets to reopen after being touched was measured for ten plants at 20 °C and ten plants at 30 °C.
20 °C / min: 18, 22, 20, 25, 19, 23, 21, 24, 17, 22
30 °C / min: 14, 16, 13, 18, 15, 12, 17, 15, 16, 14

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation for each temperature. Give the standard deviations to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 20 °C: mean 21.1 min, s = 2.60 min. 30 °C: mean 15.0 min, s = 1.83 min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10, and at p = 0.001 it is 3.92. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: t = 6.07 > 3.92, so the difference is significant even at p = 0.001; reject the null hypothesis; leaflets reopen significantly faster at 30 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Closure time of Venus fly traps was measured at eight temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36
Closure time / s: 0.62, 0.55, 0.50, 0.41, 0.43, 0.33, 0.30, 0.31

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for a Spearman's rank test on these data.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between temperature and closure time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs, using rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks of closure time (smallest = 1): 8, 7, 6, 4, 5, 3, 1, 2. M1 Σd² = 164. A1 1 − 984 ÷ 504 = −0.952.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.738. Explain why a significant correlation does not show that temperature affects closure time at all temperatures.
parts.answer: The correlation only applies within 15–36 °C; at higher temperatures proteins denature so the trend would reverse; there is also a slight rise from 33 to 36 °C, so the trend may already be levelling off.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Ninety students were each tested with a visual, a sound and a touch stimulus. For each student the stimulus with the fastest reaction time was recorded.
Visual: 18 students; Sound: 31 students; Touch: 41 students

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis and calculate the expected number for each stimulus.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: there is no difference in the number of students reacting fastest to each type of stimulus; expected = 30 each.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom. The critical values are 5.99 (p = 0.05) and 9.21 (p = 0.01). State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 2 degrees of freedom; 8.87 > 5.99 so reject the null hypothesis at p = 0.05 (but not at p = 0.01); the type of stimulus significantly affects which gives the fastest reaction.
parts.working: B1 df = 2. B1 conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The diameters of the clear zones (mm) produced on starch agar by six barley half-seeds without embryos, soaked in gibberellin, were:
15.2, 16.8, 14.9, 17.5, 16.1, 15.8
For six half-seeds with embryos, the mean was 13.6 mm and the 95 % confidence interval was 12.9–14.3 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean, standard deviation and standard error of the gibberellin group. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval and compare it with the half-seeds with embryos.
parts.answer: 15.25–16.85 mm (15.3–16.8 mm); it does not overlap 12.9–14.3, so the gibberellin group produced significantly larger clear zones.
parts.working: B1 16.05 ± 0.80. B1 no overlap → significant difference.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The two-point touch threshold on the fingertip was measured for eight guitar players and eight people who play no instrument.
Guitar players / mm: 2.1, 1.8, 2.4, 1.9, 2.2, 2.0, 1.7, 2.3
Non-players / mm: 2.4, 2.2, 2.6, 2.0, 2.5, 2.3, 2.7, 2.1
Both groups have a standard deviation of 0.245 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 14 degrees of freedom is 2.14. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 2.45 > 2.14, so the difference is significant; guitar players have a lower threshold (more sensitive fingertips).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the result might be different if the investigation were repeated with another sample of 8 + 8 people.
parts.answer: t is only just above the critical value; with small samples, chance variation between individuals could easily give t below 2.14; larger samples are needed to be confident.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to find out whether background noise affects reaction time. She has a computer program that shows a green square at random intervals and records the time taken to click the mouse, a sound-level meter and a speaker playing recorded traffic noise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method she could use. Include how she will vary the noise, what she will measure and how she will make the results reliable.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: IV = noise level, e.g. 0 (quiet), 50, 60, 70, 80 dB, set with volume and checked with sound-level meter at the ear; DV = reaction time from program (ms); same volunteer(s) for all levels or several volunteers; same hand/mouse/chair/screen distance; practice trials before recording; at least 5 (e.g. 10) trials at each level and calculate a mean; random order of noise levels to avoid practice/fatigue effects; rest between sets; same time of day/no caffeine; quiet room with no other distractions; random interval between stimuli so clicks cannot be anticipated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the noise should not exceed about 85 dB.
parts.answer: Louder sounds could damage hearing (risk) / be uncomfortable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mung bean (moong) seeds are germinated on damp paper. A student wants to investigate the effect of auxin (IAA) concentration on root growth of the seedlings. She has a solution of IAA at 1 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she should prepare a suitable range of IAA concentrations.
parts.answer: Serial dilution by factor of 10: e.g. 1 cm³ of stock + 9 cm³ distilled water to give 10⁻⁴, repeat to 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁸; plus distilled water as a control.
parts.working: 1 mark each: tenfold serial dilution with volumes; at least five concentrations including a water control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how she should carry out the investigation and collect results.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: seedlings with roots of similar starting length (e.g. 5 mm) selected; measure initial root length with ruler; place e.g. 10 seedlings in a Petri dish on filter paper soaked with a fixed volume (e.g. 5 cm³) of each solution; same temperature (incubator 25 °C)/dark; same time (48 h); measure final root length and calculate mean change in length; repeat each concentration (three dishes); lids on to prevent evaporation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Leaflets of Mimosa pudica fold when touched and later reopen. A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the time taken for leaflets to reopen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for this investigation.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: use plants of same age/size, same variety; place in temperature-controlled room/incubator/water bath around pot at e.g. 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C; allow time to acclimatise (e.g. 30 min) and check with thermometer; touch a leaf in a standard way (e.g. same glass rod, same force, same position, once); start stopwatch when touched; record time until leaflets fully reopen (define end point); same light intensity (lamp at fixed distance) and humidity; test several leaves/plants at each temperature (at least 5) and find a mean; leave time between tests on the same leaf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same leaf should not be tested twice in quick succession.
parts.answer: It may not have fully recovered; repeated touching can reduce its response (it may become less responsive/ not close fully).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A teacher wants students to investigate the effect of gibberellin concentration on the percentage germination of wheat seeds after 5 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the method the students should use.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: range of GA concentrations (e.g. 0, 10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³) by serial dilution; same number of seeds (e.g. 50) from the same batch per dish; soak or place on filter paper with same volume of solution; dishes covered and kept at same temperature in the dark; define germination (radicle visible/≥ 2 mm); count germinated seeds daily or after 5 days and calculate percentage; three replicate dishes per concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the seeds should come from the same batch.
parts.answer: Seeds from different batches may differ in age, storage, viability, genetics, so this controls a variable affecting germination.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Grip strength can be measured with a hand dynamometer (reading in kg). A student wants to investigate how the time spent repeatedly squeezing a hand gripper affects the maximum grip strength of the muscles of the forearm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for this investigation, including how to make the results valid and reliable.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for seven of: measure maximum grip with dynamometer before exercise (mean of 3 with rest between); IV: duration of gripper exercise e.g. 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 s; squeeze at a fixed rate (e.g. metronome, one per second); measure maximum grip immediately after each period; full rest (e.g. 10 min) between durations so muscles recover, or different days; same hand, same arm position (e.g. elbow at 90°, seated); several volunteers of similar age/sex/fitness; same gripper; repeat and calculate mean; express as percentage of starting strength; no warm-up differences; stop if pain (risk).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to compare the taste threshold for salt (the lowest NaCl concentration that can be tasted) of students who add extra salt to their food with that of students who do not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she could prepare the solutions and find each person's taste threshold.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: serial dilution of food-grade NaCl in bottled/distilled water (e.g. 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125, 0.006 mol dm⁻³ or finer steps); fresh clean cups/sterile cotton buds for each person; present solutions in random/coded order including plain water (blind) or start from lowest; volunteer rinses mouth with water between samples; same volume and temperature of solution; record lowest concentration correctly identified as salty; repeat to confirm; no eating/smoking for 1 h before.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each volunteer should not be told which cup contains which solution.
parts.answer: To prevent bias/guessing affecting the response (blind test).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify one safety or hygiene precaution.
parts.answer: Use food-grade salt and clean, single-use cups; do not use laboratory glassware; volunteers with high blood pressure/illness excluded; samples spat out.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The diameter of the pupil changes with light intensity. A student wants to investigate this using a lamp, a light meter and a camera that can photograph the eye next to a millimetre scale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of light intensity on pupil diameter.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: darkened room; volunteer sits with head on chin rest at fixed distance from lamp; vary light intensity (dimmer or distance) and measure with light meter at eye level, at least 5 intensities; allow time to adapt (e.g. 1 min) at each intensity; photograph eye with mm scale beside it at same distance; measure pupil diameter from photo using scale; repeat (3 photos each) and calculate mean; same eye; several volunteers; random order or allow recovery.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the lamp should never be very bright or shone directly into the eye for a long time.
parts.answer: Could damage the retina.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Water fleas (Daphnia) are transparent, so their heart can be seen under a microscope. A student wants to investigate the effect of caffeine concentration on Daphnia heart rate. He has a 1 % caffeine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how he should carry out the investigation.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: dilute stock to give e.g. 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 % using pond water; place one Daphnia in a small volume of solution on a cavity slide with cotton fibres to restrict movement; leave for a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) to equilibrate; count heartbeats for 15 s using a tally counter, multiply by 4; same temperature (e.g. cold light source/not too long under microscope lamp); use a fresh Daphnia of similar size for each concentration (or rinse and rest); at least 5 Daphnia per concentration; mean heart rate calculated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one ethical point about this investigation and how it could be addressed.
parts.answer: Animals may be harmed — use the minimum number, short exposure, return them to pond water afterwards / use an invertebrate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Segments of wheat coleoptiles, 10 mm long, elongate when floated in IAA (auxin) solution. A student wants to find out whether auxin acts by lowering the pH of the cell walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to test whether acidic conditions alone cause the same elongation as auxin.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: cut segments of equal length (10 mm) from below the tip with a sharp blade; remove tip so no natural auxin; float in buffer solutions of different pH (e.g. 3.5, 4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5) without auxin; plus a set in auxin solution at pH 6.5 (neutral buffer) and a buffer-only control at pH 6.5; same number of segments (e.g. 10) per dish; same volume of solution; same temperature in the dark; same time (e.g. 18 h); measure final length with ruler/graph paper or eyepiece graticule; calculate mean percentage increase; compare acid-only elongation with auxin elongation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the segments are kept in the dark.
parts.answer: Light can affect auxin distribution and growth, so it is a confounding variable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher wants to find out whether there is a correlation between age and the two-point touch threshold on the palm of the hand, using people aged 10 to 80 years from a town in Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the investigation should be carried out, including how participants are chosen and how the threshold is measured.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: random or stratified sample across ages, e.g. at least 5 people in each decade (large sample); exclude people with diabetes/nerve disease or calloused hands; informed consent (and parental consent for children); use dividers/two-point tool; apply points at same pressure to same area of palm; participant's eyes closed; randomly alternate one and two points to check for guessing; start with large separation and decrease in 1 mm steps; threshold = smallest separation correctly felt as two in e.g. 3 out of 3 trials; same tester and room temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the statistical test that should be used and why.
parts.answer: Spearman's rank correlation (or Pearson's if both normally distributed); to test whether there is a significant correlation between two variables.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A botanical garden in Islamabad has 30 Venus fly trap plants. A student wants to investigate the effect of temperature on the time traps take to close after being stimulated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to obtain valid and reliable results.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for seven of: plants placed in growth chamber/ incubator at e.g. 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C with time to acclimatise (e.g. 1 h); same light intensity and humidity; select traps of similar size/age that have not closed recently; stimulate two trigger hairs in a standard way with a fine brush/hair, within e.g. 5 s; record with a high-speed video camera (or slow-motion phone) with a timer; measure time from second touch to complete closure (defined end point) frame by frame; one trap per plant per temperature or allow full reopening (e.g. 24 h) before reuse; use different traps for each temperature in random order; at least 5 traps per temperature; calculate mean and SD.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each trap should not be tested many times.
parts.answer: Each closure uses energy and traps can only close a limited number of times before dying; repeated closure may change response time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dwarf pea plants respond to gibberellin. A student plans to test the hypothesis that the increase in height caused by gibberellin depends on its concentration. She has 60 dwarf pea seedlings, a gibberellin solution of 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ and a spray bottle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the method, including the experimental design and the measurements.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: concentrations 0 (with same solvent/wetting agent), 10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴ by serial dilution; 10 seedlings per treatment, randomly assigned; seedlings same age/initial height (measure initial height); same volume sprayed (e.g. same number of sprays) at same time weekly; shield other plants when spraying; same soil, pot size, watering, light, temperature (randomise positions in greenhouse); measure height from soil to tip weekly for 4 weeks; calculate mean increase in height.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how she would decide whether the difference between two of the treatments is significant.
parts.answer: Use a t-test on the height increases of the two groups (calculate SD of each); compare t with the critical value at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom; if t is greater, the difference is significant.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student believes that reaction time improves with practice. He has a computer reaction-time program.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to test this, including how he will control for fatigue and how the results will be processed.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: volunteers who have not used the program before; each volunteer does e.g. 10 blocks of 10 trials; record mean reaction time of each block; short fixed rest between blocks to reduce fatigue; same time of day, same hand, same screen distance; random stimulus intervals; several (e.g. 15) volunteers; plot mean reaction time against block number; use Spearman's rank to test correlation; compare first and last blocks with a t-test; second session another day to separate learning from fatigue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why reaction time might stop improving after many blocks.
parts.answer: There is a physiological limit (conduction time, synaptic delays), or fatigue/boredom balances learning.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to investigate how the intensity of light from one side affects the curvature of oat coleoptiles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method she could use.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: coleoptiles grown in the dark until a set length (e.g. 20 mm); same number (e.g. 10) per treatment; lamp placed at one side, different distances or a dimmer to vary intensity, measured with light meter; all other light excluded (box with a slit/dark room); same time of exposure (e.g. 3 h); same temperature (heat shield/water filter to stop the lamp heating); measure angle of curvature with a protractor from a photograph; calculate mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the coleoptiles must be grown in the dark before the experiment.
parts.answer: So they are straight/have not already bent towards light, and auxin is evenly distributed at the start.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a nerve conduction study, an impulse travelled 360 mm along a nerve in 6.0 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of conduction in m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 60 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how long, in ms, the impulse would take to travel 0.15 m at the same speed.
parts.answer: 2.5 ms

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student's mean reaction time was 0.284 s before a session of brisk exercise and 0.247 s immediately after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in reaction time. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 13.0 % decrease

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert both reaction times to ms.
parts.answer: 284 ms and 247 ms

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student makes a stock solution of IAA (auxin), Mr = 175.2, at 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of IAA needed to make 250 cm³ of stock solution, in mg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She makes a series of tenfold dilutions. State how many dilutions are needed to reach 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, and how to make 10 cm³ of each dilution.
parts.answer: Four dilutions; 1 cm³ of the previous solution + 9 cm³ of distilled water.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Lengths of the roots of eight seedlings grown in 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³ auxin for 3 days:
23, 25, 22, 8, 24, 26, 21, 25 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean root length without it. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 8 mm is anomalous; mean = 23.7 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the range of the remaining results.
parts.answer: 5 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the anomalous result.
parts.answer: Damaged seed/root, seed not viable or germinated late.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A microelectrode in a sensory neurone from a stretch receptor recorded 37 action potentials in 2.5 s when a muscle was stretched slightly, and 92 action potentials in 2.5 s when it was stretched more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of impulses in each case, in Hz (impulses per second).
parts.answer: 14.8 Hz and 36.8 Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the frequency is with the larger stretch. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.5 times

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The length of a coleoptile was measured every 2 hours after a block containing auxin was placed on its cut tip.
Time / h: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Length / mm: 12.0, 13.4, 15.1, 16.9, 18.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of growth over the 8 hours, in mm h⁻¹. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.78 mm h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the 2-hour interval with the fastest growth and calculate the rate in that interval.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in length over 8 hours. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student counted the heartbeats of a Daphnia for 15 s before and after adding a caffeine solution.
Before: 55 beats in 15 s
After: 67 beats in 15 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart rate before and after in beats min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 220 and 268 beats min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why counting for 15 s and multiplying by 4 gives a less accurate result than counting for a full minute.
parts.answer: Any miscount (e.g. one beat) is multiplied by 4; partial beats at start/end make a larger percentage error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: On an electron micrograph of a skeletal muscle fibre, one sarcomere measures 18 mm from Z line to Z line. The actual length of the sarcomere is 2.4 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The H zone on the same micrograph measures 3.0 mm. Calculate its actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 0.4 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The micrograph shows the A band as 12 mm long. Calculate the actual length of the A band and the total actual length of the I band in this sarcomere.
parts.answer: A band 1.6 µm; I band 0.8 µm

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student has a 2.0 % caffeine stock solution and distilled water. She needs 20 cm³ of each of the following: 0.1 %, 0.2 %, 0.4 %, 0.8 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of stock solution and water needed for each concentration.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = 20 × (C ÷ 2.0). A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of stock solution needed.
parts.answer: 15 cm³

author: HomiLabs

stem: Extracts from barley aleurone layers were added to starch solution. The time for the starch to be completely broken down was 40 min for the extract from layers incubated in water and 10 min for the extract from layers incubated in gibberellin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of starch breakdown (1000 ÷ time, in arbitrary units) for each extract.
parts.answer: 25 and 100 arbitrary units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate caused by gibberellin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 1000 ÷ time can be used as a measure of rate.
parts.answer: Rate is inversely proportional to the time taken for the same amount of starch to be broken down.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The mean time for Mimosa leaflets to reopen was 21.1 min at 20 °C and 15.0 min at 30 °C.
The temperature coefficient Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10) °C ÷ rate at T °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reopening (1 ÷ time) at each temperature, in min⁻¹. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0474 min⁻¹ and 0.0667 min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Q₁₀ for reopening between 20 °C and 30 °C. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Many enzyme-controlled processes have a Q₁₀ of about 2. Suggest why the Q₁₀ for reopening is lower.
parts.answer: Reopening depends partly on physical processes such as diffusion/osmotic water movement, which are less affected by temperature than enzyme reactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coleoptile segments, each 10.0 mm long, were floated in either buffer alone or buffer with auxin for 18 hours. Mean final lengths: buffer alone 11.2 mm; buffer with auxin 14.8 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in length for each treatment.
parts.answer: Buffer 12 %; auxin 48 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in length caused by auxin alone, and express it as a ratio of the increase with auxin to the increase without auxin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of auxin-induced growth in µm h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 200 µm h⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Barley grains were germinated in three dishes of 50 grains for each treatment.
Gibberellin: 46, 44, 47 germinated
Water: 31, 28, 34 germinated

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean percentage germination for each treatment. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Gibberellin 91.3 %; water 62.0 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more grains failed to germinate in water than in gibberellin. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.4 times
parts.working: M1 failures: water 150 − 93 = 57; gibberellin 150 − 137 = 13. A1 57 ÷ 13 = 4.4.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a clinical test of the median nerve, the nerve was stimulated at the wrist and then at the elbow, and the time to the start of the response in a thumb muscle (latency) was recorded.
Stimulus at wrist: 3.4 ms
Stimulus at elbow: 7.8 ms
Distance between the two stimulation points: 24.0 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the conduction speed between the elbow and wrist. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the speed cannot be calculated simply as the distance from the wrist to the muscle divided by 3.4 ms.
parts.answer: The 3.4 ms includes the delay at the neuromuscular junction and the time for the muscle fibres to depolarise, not just conduction; subtracting two latencies cancels these delays.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
