parts.text: Predict the latency if the nerve were stimulated 12.0 cm above the elbow. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 10 ms

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the time taken for Venus fly traps to close after their trigger hairs are touched twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: time taken for the trap to close.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and describe how one of them could be controlled.
parts.answer: e.g. size/age of trap, light intensity, humidity, way hairs are touched, time between the two touches, time since the trap last closed/fed; e.g. touch with the same fine brush, two touches 5 s apart timed with a stopwatch.
parts.working: B2 three variables (B1 for two). B1 one method of control.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Barley grains were soaked in gibberellin solutions of different concentrations, and the percentage that germinated in 4 days was recorded. One dish of grains was soaked in distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the dish soaked in distilled water.
parts.answer: It is a control; shows how many grains germinate without added gibberellin, so any increase can be attributed to the gibberellin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables, other than those mentioned, that must be kept the same for all dishes.
parts.answer: e.g. number of grains, variety/batch of grains, temperature, volume of solution, light/dark, soaking time.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Volunteers did a computer reaction test, then drank 250 cm³ of an energy drink containing caffeine and repeated the test 30 minutes later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three variables that should be controlled for each volunteer.
parts.answer: e.g. no other caffeine that day; same hand and mouse; same distance from screen; same time of day; same room/no distractions; same number of practice trials; same sleep/no exercise before.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a second group should drink a drink that looks and tastes the same but contains no caffeine.
parts.answer: Acts as a placebo/control; shows whether improvement is due to practice, the sugar/drink itself or expectation, rather than caffeine.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student counts how many leaflets on a Mimosa leaf fold when the leaf tip is touched with different numbers of light taps (1 to 5 taps).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: IV: number of taps. DV: number of leaflets that fold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two variables that should be controlled and why each could affect the results.
parts.answer: Force of each tap — stronger taps may cause more folding; time since the leaf was last touched — a recently touched leaf may not have recovered; also temperature/light/age of leaf.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Moong seedlings were grown on filter paper soaked in different auxin concentrations at 25 °C for 2 days, and root length was measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of variable that temperature is in this investigation, and explain why it must be kept at 25 °C.
parts.answer: A standardised (controlled) variable; temperature affects rate of growth (enzymes/respiration), so changes would affect root length independently of auxin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could keep the volume of solution available to each seedling the same throughout the 2 days.
parts.answer: Use the same volume per dish and cover the dishes (lids/cling film) to prevent evaporation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Daphnia heart rate is counted under a microscope after placing the animal in a caffeine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of the water around the Daphnia must be controlled, and describe how it could be done.
parts.answer: Daphnia is ectothermic so heart rate rises with temperature; microscope lamp heats the slide; use a cold light source/LED or a heat filter, limit time under the lamp, monitor temperature with a thermometer/keep in water bath before counting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: reason (rate depends on temperature); lamp heating; method of control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each Daphnia should be left in the solution for the same time before counting.
parts.answer: Caffeine takes time to enter the body/reach the heart; effect may change with time of exposure, so time must be standardised.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students measured the two-point touch threshold on the back of the hand of 20 volunteers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables that must be standardised when applying the points, and explain why one of them matters.
parts.answer: Pressure applied; both points touching at exactly the same time; same area of skin; volunteer's eyes closed; skin temperature; e.g. greater pressure stimulates more receptors over a wider area, so two points may be felt at smaller separations.
parts.working: B3 three variables. B1 explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the tester should sometimes apply only one point.
parts.answer: To check whether the volunteer is guessing/to detect false reports of 'two'.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compares the grip strength of the dominant and non-dominant hand of 15 classmates using a hand dynamometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Same dynamometer; same body position (standing, arm by side, elbow angle); same number of attempts and rest between attempts; time of day; no exercise beforehand; same encouragement.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the order in which the hands are tested should be varied between volunteers.
parts.answer: Testing one hand first every time could introduce fatigue or practice effects that bias the comparison; alternating/randomising order cancels this.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coleoptile segments were floated in solutions to investigate the role of pH in auxin-induced elongation. The tip of each coleoptile was removed before the segments were cut.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the tips were removed.
parts.answer: Tips produce natural auxin, which would add to/confound the effect of the treatments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each solution was made with a buffer.
parts.answer: To keep the pH constant throughout the experiment; cells pump H⁺ which would otherwise change the pH of the solution.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a suitable control for the experiment testing whether auxin works at neutral pH.
parts.answer: Segments in the same neutral buffer without auxin.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seedlings are placed in a box with a single opening facing a lamp, to study bending towards the light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lamp's heat must be controlled and suggest how.
parts.answer: Heat could cause uneven growth/drying on one side, making temperature a second variable; place a water filter/heat shield between lamp and box, or use an LED lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the box must exclude light from all other directions.
parts.answer: So that only the direction of the lamp's light affects bending.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher wants to test whether caffeine tablets improve reaction time. 40 volunteers are available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher should use a placebo and a double-blind design, and why each is needed.
parts.answer: Half (randomly allocated) receive an identical-looking tablet without caffeine (placebo); this controls for the expectation effect/psychological effect of taking a tablet; double-blind: neither volunteers nor the person testing know who received which tablet (coded); prevents bias in how the test is run or results recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark each: placebo described; reason; double-blind described; reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why volunteers should be randomly allocated to the two groups.
parts.answer: To avoid systematic differences between groups (e.g. age, habitual caffeine use), so other variables are spread evenly.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a field study in Sindh, the reaction times of 200 people aged 15–75 were recorded at community health camps to look for a correlation with age.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is not possible to control variables in the same way as in a laboratory experiment.
parts.answer: Age cannot be assigned by the researcher; participants differ in many other ways (health, sleep, eyesight, caffeine, education/computer use) that cannot be fixed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three ways the researcher could reduce the effect of these other variables.
parts.answer: Large sample size; record and exclude people with conditions such as diabetes or poor eyesight; same equipment, instructions and time of day; equal numbers of men and women in each age group/matching; ask about caffeine/sleep and analyse separately.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student uses Venus fly traps from several plants. Some traps are newly opened and some have closed and reopened several times. Some have recently digested an insect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why these differences are a problem for an investigation into the effect of light intensity on closure speed.
parts.answer: Trap age and recent activity/feeding may affect closure speed (energy reserves, cell turgor, ion gradients), so they are uncontrolled variables that could mask or mimic an effect of light.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could design the investigation so these variables do not bias the results.
parts.answer: Use only traps of similar age that have not closed or fed recently, or randomly allocate traps to light intensities so differences are spread evenly; record trap history; use large numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Half-seeds of barley without embryos were placed on starch agar with gibberellin. A student found clear zones even on a control plate with boiled half-seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the boiled half-seeds were included as a control.
parts.answer: To show that any starch breakdown needs living aleurone cells (amylase made by the seed), not other factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why clear zones appeared around the boiled half-seeds, and how each problem could be prevented.
parts.answer: Bacteria or fungi on the seed surface secrete amylase onto the starch: surface-sterilise the seeds (e.g. brief dilute bleach, then rinse) and use sterile agar. Boiling was too brief, so some amylase was not denatured: boil for longer (e.g. 10 minutes) before use.
parts.working: 1 mark for each cause (max 2): microbes on the seed secreting amylase; incomplete denaturation of the enzyme by short boiling. 1 mark for each matching prevention (max 2): sterilise seeds and agar; boil for longer.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to investigate how temperature affects the time taken for Mimosa leaflets to reopen after being touched.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a suitable hypothesis.
parts.answer: As temperature increases (up to an optimum), the time taken for leaflets to reopen decreases.
parts.working: B1 states a testable relationship between IV and DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give a biological explanation for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Reopening depends on movement of ions and water into cells/active transport; higher temperature gives more kinetic energy and faster enzyme/pump activity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to compare the mean reaction times of students who play a musical instrument and students who do not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis suitable for a t-test.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean reaction times of students who play an instrument and those who do not.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the alternative hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is a significant difference between the mean reaction times of the two groups.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Auxin stimulates elongation of shoot cells at low concentrations, but high concentrations inhibit root growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how root length of seedlings will change as auxin concentration increases from 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: Root length decreases as auxin concentration increases: at the lowest concentrations the roots are only slightly shorter than the control, and at 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ they are much shorter. Roots are more sensitive to auxin than shoots, so they are inhibited at concentrations that promote shoot elongation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: root length falls as concentration rises (negative trend); inhibition at high concentrations, and roots already shorter at low concentrations because they are more sensitive than shoots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment should include a control with no auxin.
parts.answer: To compare each concentration with normal growth and see whether it stimulates or inhibits.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to add caffeine to the water around Daphnia and count the heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As caffeine concentration increases, the heart rate of Daphnia increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a prediction for the shape of a graph of heart rate against caffeine concentration, with a reason.
parts.answer: Heart rate rises then levels off (plateau); at high concentrations all receptors/targets are affected so no further increase (or toxic decrease).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Taste buds are replaced regularly, but the number of taste buds falls in older people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis about the relationship between age and the taste threshold for salt.
parts.answer: The taste threshold for salt increases with age (older people need saltier solutions to detect salt).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological reasoning behind your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Fewer taste buds/chemoreceptor cells means fewer receptor cells are stimulated at low concentrations; a higher concentration is needed to produce enough receptor potentials/impulses to be detected.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coleoptiles were lit from one side. In group P, a thin mica plate (impermeable to auxin) was inserted vertically into the tip on the shaded side, cutting off the shaded half of the tip from the region below. In group Q, the mica plate was inserted on the lit side in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict whether each group will bend towards the light. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: P: little or no bending; auxin moves towards the shaded side but cannot pass down that side, so the shaded side does not elongate more. Q: bends towards the light (like normal); auxin that moved to the shaded side can pass down; shaded side elongates more.
parts.working: B1 P prediction. B1 P reason. B1 Q prediction. B1 Q reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the hypothesis that this experiment tests.
parts.answer: Bending towards light is caused by auxin moving down the shaded side of the coleoptile.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to compare reaction times to a touch on the shoulder and to a touch on the ankle, using a computer key press.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict which stimulus will give the longer reaction time and explain why.
parts.answer: Ankle; the sensory pathway from the ankle to the brain is longer, so conduction takes more time.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The difference in path length is about 1.2 m and conduction speed is about 60 m s⁻¹. Calculate the predicted difference in reaction time.
parts.answer: 20 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the measured difference may be hard to detect.
parts.answer: 20 ms is small compared with the variation between trials (often ±20–30 ms) so many repeats are needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Plants heterozygous for a recessive allele that makes them unable to respond to gibberellin are crossed. A student counts the tall and dwarf offspring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the expected ratio and the null hypothesis for a chi-squared test.
parts.answer: 3 tall : 1 dwarf; there is no significant difference between the observed and expected (3 : 1) numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Of 240 offspring, predict the expected number of dwarf plants.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to measure nerve conduction speed in a volunteer's forearm before and after the arm has been cooled in cold water for 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis and give a biological reason for it.
parts.answer: Cooling the arm will decrease conduction speed; at lower temperature ions diffuse more slowly; voltage-gated channels open and close more slowly (and Na⁺/K⁺ pump slower).
parts.working: B1 hypothesis. 1 mark each for two reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how the speed will change in the 20 minutes after the arm is removed from the water.
parts.answer: It will gradually increase back to the original value as the arm warms.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The pupil of the eye changes size depending on the brightness of the light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis about the effect of light intensity on pupil diameter.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases, pupil diameter decreases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the shape of a graph of pupil diameter against light intensity and explain the shape.
parts.answer: Diameter falls steeply at low intensities then levels off at high intensity, because the pupil has a minimum size (circular muscles fully contracted).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two hypotheses are proposed to explain how auxin causes stem cells to elongate quickly.
Hypothesis 1: auxin lowers the pH of the cell wall.
Hypothesis 2: auxin increases synthesis of new cell wall material.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe an experiment that could distinguish between these hypotheses, and state the results predicted by each hypothesis.
parts.answer: Float segments in auxin solution in a strong neutral buffer (pH 7) versus auxin in unbuffered solution, and acid buffer (pH 4.5) without auxin. Hypothesis 1 predicts: no rapid elongation with auxin in neutral buffer, and elongation in acid buffer without auxin. Hypothesis 2 predicts: elongation with auxin even in neutral buffer, and no elongation in acid without auxin. (Alternatively inhibit cellulose synthesis.)
parts.working: B1 suitable experiment (buffer/acid/inhibitor). B1 control. B1 prediction for hypothesis 1. B1 prediction for hypothesis 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is possible for both hypotheses to be partly correct.
parts.answer: Rapid early elongation may be due to acidification while longer-term growth needs new wall synthesis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A nerve contains many axons with different thresholds. A single stimulus of increasing voltage was applied and the total electrical response of the whole nerve was recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the size of the total response will change as stimulus voltage increases from zero. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: No response at very low voltage (below all thresholds); then the response increases as voltage increases, as more axons reach threshold; each axon gives an all-or-nothing action potential, so total depends on the number of axons firing; it reaches a maximum when all axons fire and does not increase further.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this does not contradict the all-or-nothing principle.
parts.answer: All-or-nothing applies to each individual axon; the nerve's graded response comes from different numbers of axons firing.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student writes: 'Exercise is good for your reactions.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is not a testable hypothesis, and rewrite it as one.
parts.answer: It does not name measurable variables or a direction/quantity; e.g. 'Mean reaction time to a visual stimulus is shorter after 10 minutes of moderate cycling than before it.'
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the results you would expect if your hypothesis is correct and if it is wrong.
parts.answer: Correct: significantly lower mean reaction time after exercise (t-test, p < 0.05). Wrong: no significant difference (or longer times).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A barley variety has a mutation in the DELLA protein so that it is not broken down when gibberellin binds to its receptor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the results of placing embryo-free half-seeds of this variety on starch agar containing gibberellin, compared with normal barley. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Little or no clear zone with the mutant, but a large clear zone with normal barley; DELLA remains and keeps inhibiting the transcription factor; amylase gene not transcribed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of adding extra gibberellin to the mutant half-seeds.
parts.answer: No (or very little) increase; extra gibberellin cannot cause breakdown of the mutant DELLA.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured reaction time with a computer program that flashes a red circle and records the time to press the space bar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this method.
parts.answer: Anticipation if the circle appears at regular intervals; distractions/noise; changes in attention or fatigue; keyboard delay; finger not resting on key in same position.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement for each source of error you identified.
parts.answer: Random time intervals; quiet room/headphones; rest between sets; finger kept resting on the key; same keyboard.
parts.working: 1 mark each, matched.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The time for Mimosa leaflets to reopen was measured with a stopwatch by watching the leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the end point is difficult to judge.
parts.answer: Leaflets reopen gradually, so deciding when they are 'fully open' is subjective.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to make the timing more accurate.
parts.answer: Define the end point (e.g. leaflets at 90 % of original angle); time-lapse video with a timer; same observer; compare with photo of the leaf before touching.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seedling roots were measured with a 30 cm ruler marked in mm. Some roots were curved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the curved roots may give inaccurate measurements and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: A straight ruler underestimates a curved length; lay a piece of thread along the root then measure the thread / straighten gently on graph paper.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the uncertainty in each reading and explain why it is significant for roots that are only 5 mm long.
parts.answer: ±0.5 mm (half the smallest division); 0.5 ÷ 5 = 10 % error, which is large.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student found it hard to count the heart rate of Daphnia because the heart beats more than 200 times a minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways to improve the accuracy of the counts.
parts.answer: Video the heart through the microscope and replay in slow motion; use a tally counter; count dots on paper with a pencil; count for longer (e.g. 30–60 s).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why repeating the count three times for each Daphnia improves reliability.
parts.answer: Allows anomalous counts to be identified and a mean calculated, reducing the effect of random counting errors.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between random errors and systematic errors, with one example of each in a ruler-drop reaction test.
parts.answer: Random errors vary unpredictably between readings (e.g. reading the ruler at slightly different points, varying attention); systematic errors shift all readings in the same direction (e.g. always reading from the bottom of the thumb instead of the top, or the ruler's zero not at the fingers).
parts.working: 1 mark each: random definition; example; systematic definition; example.

stem: The curvature of coleoptiles was measured by placing a protractor against each coleoptile while it was still growing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two problems with this method.
parts.answer: Difficult to align protractor with curved tip/parallax; coleoptile may be touched or damaged; the coleoptile continues to bend during measuring; different readers judge the angle differently.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improved method.
parts.answer: Photograph (or trace a shadowgraph of) each coleoptile at the same time and measure the angle on the image with a protractor/software, using a standard reference line.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ten volunteers each squeezed a hand dynamometer three times with their dominant hand. The readings for one volunteer were 38, 37 and 26 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous reading and suggest a cause.
parts.answer: 26 kg; volunteer not gripping fully/fatigue/poor grip position/hand slipped.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to improve the reliability of the results for all volunteers.
parts.answer: Practice attempt; standard posture; rest of e.g. 1 min between attempts; more attempts and use mean (excluding anomalies); standard encouragement; same time of day.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Clear zones around barley half-seeds on starch agar were measured with a ruler. Some zones were oval and had fuzzy edges.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how the size of each clear zone should be measured to improve accuracy.
parts.answer: Measure two diameters at right angles and take the mean (or calculate area); use a ruler against a white background/through a hand lens; consistent judgement of edge (e.g. where blue-black colour starts).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why zones may be oval.
parts.answer: The half-seed is not round/enzyme diffuses unevenly; agar not level so uneven thickness.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a test of the taste threshold for salt, volunteers tasted solutions starting from the most concentrated and working down to the weakest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this order could cause an error.
parts.answer: Receptors adapt to/salt remains from the strong solutions, so weak solutions may not be detected; the threshold would be overestimated.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements.
parts.answer: Start with weakest solution and work upwards; rinse the mouth with distilled water between samples; wait a set time between samples; random order including water blanks.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A lamp was placed 10 cm from Mimosa plants in an investigation of light intensity. The temperature near the leaves rose from 24 °C to 31 °C during the experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this temperature rise affects the validity of the investigation.
parts.answer: Temperature is not controlled, so it becomes a second variable; changes in response could be due to temperature rather than light intensity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be improved.
parts.answer: Use an LED (cool) lamp or a heat filter (water bath/glass tank) between lamp and plant; monitor temperature with a thermometer; carry out in a temperature-controlled room.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A thermometer used to set water baths for a temperature investigation on coleoptile growth always reads 2 °C higher than the true temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of error and explain how it affects the results and conclusions.
parts.answer: Systematic error; every actual temperature is 2 °C lower than recorded; the pattern/trend is unchanged, but values such as the optimum temperature would be recorded 2 °C too high.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the accuracy and the precision of the measurements in this case.
parts.answer: Readings may be precise (consistent, close together) but not accurate (not close to the true value).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean at 15 °C without it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, comment on the reliability of the results at 25 °C and 35 °C.
parts.answer: Results are quite variable (ranges 0.29–0.48 and 0.22–0.40) and the ranges overlap, so the difference between 25 °C and 35 °C may not be real; only five traps.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to the investigation.
parts.answer: More traps per temperature; video recording to time closure; traps of similar size/age; more temperatures; calculate SD/95 % CI or t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: The time for starch to disappear (iodine test on drops taken every 30 s) was used to measure amylase activity. Times ranged from 12 min to 48 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a time of 12 min and in a time of 48 min, if each time has an uncertainty of ±0.5 min. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the colour end point is a further source of error, and how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Judging when the blue-black colour has completely gone is subjective; use a colour standard/ colour chart or a colorimeter to measure absorbance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two-point thresholds were measured with dividers against a ruler marked in mm. Mean thresholds were 1.5 mm on the fingertip and 30 mm on the forearm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in each measurement, if each has an uncertainty of ±0.5 mm. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the fingertip measurements could be made more precise.
parts.answer: Use a two-point device/calipers with finer graduations (e.g. 0.1 mm or 0.5 mm steps); smaller steps between separations tested.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the term assimilates.
parts.answer: Substances made by the plant (e.g. sucrose, amino acids) that are transported in the phloem.
parts.working: B1 substances made by the plant / products of photosynthesis and metabolism, e.g. sucrose or amino acids, moved in phloem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In summer a potato tuber is a sink, but when it sprouts in spring it acts as a source. Explain this change.
parts.answer: Summer: sucrose arrives from leaves and is unloaded and converted to starch for storage, so the tuber is a sink. Spring: starch is hydrolysed to sugars, loaded into phloem as sucrose and transported to the growing shoots (sinks), so the tuber is a source.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: summer – sucrose unloaded from phloem and stored as starch; spring – starch hydrolysed / converted to sucrose; sucrose loaded into phloem and moved to growing shoot/buds, which have no leaves yet / cannot photosynthesise enough.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why phloem is said to transport in both directions in a stem, even though sap in a single sieve tube flows one way at a time.
parts.answer: Different sieve tubes in the same stem can carry sap upwards (to young leaves, flowers, fruits) and downwards (to roots, storage organs) at the same time, depending on where the sources and sinks are.
parts.working: B1 different sieve tubes can flow in opposite directions at the same time; B1 because sinks are both above (shoot tip, fruits) and below (roots) the source leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a leaf, sucrose is first moved into a companion cell. How does sucrose then move from the companion cell into the sieve tube element?
A by active transport through carrier proteins in the sieve tube element membrane
B by diffusion through plasmodesmata
C by osmosis through aquaporins
D by co-transport with hydrogen ions leaving the sieve tube element
parts.answer: B by diffusion through plasmodesmata
parts.working: Sucrose is at a higher concentration in the companion cell than in the sieve tube element, so it diffuses through the many plasmodesmata linking the two cells; no carrier protein or ATP is needed for this step. The main distractor A is wrong for that reason. Distractor D is wrong because H⁺ are not pumped out of sieve tube elements; co-transport with H⁺ moves sucrose into companion cells from the leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of the process by which phloem sap moves along a sieve tube.
parts.answer: Mass flow.
parts.working: B1 mass flow (accept pressure flow).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water enters the sieve tubes near a source and leaves them near a sink.
parts.answer: At the source sucrose is loaded, lowering the water potential of the sieve tube sap, so water enters by osmosis from the xylem/surrounding cells. At the sink sucrose is removed (used or stored), so the water potential of the sap rises and water leaves by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 loading sucrose at source lowers water potential (more negative); B1 water enters by osmosis (from xylem); B1 unloading at sink raises water potential so water moves out by osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two differences between transport in the phloem and the transpiration stream in the xylem.
parts.answer: Phloem: living cells, needs energy (ATP) for loading, can move up or down, carries sucrose/amino acids. Xylem: dead vessels, passive, only upwards, carries water and mineral ions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two contrasts: living v dead cells; active loading/needs ATP v passive; two directions v upwards only; sucrose/amino acids v water/mineral ions; driven by hydrostatic pressure gradient (positive pressure) v tension (negative pressure).

stem: A mango fruit on a tree in Multan gained 36 g of dry mass over 30 days. The total cross-sectional area of phloem in the fruit stalk was 0.12 cm². Assume all the dry mass arrived through the phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate at which dry mass entered the fruit, in g h⁻¹ per cm² of phloem. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.417 g h⁻¹ cm⁻²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the true rate of translocation into the fruit is higher than the value you calculated.
parts.answer: Some of the sucrose arriving is used in respiration by the fruit cells (releasing CO₂), so it does not appear as dry mass gain; some water/assimilates may also move out or be used for other processes.
parts.working: B1 some sucrose respired by the growing fruit; B1 so mass lost as CO₂ / not counted in dry mass gain. Accept: some assimilate used for synthesis of compounds lost, e.g. volatile scent.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fruit is described as a sink.
parts.answer: It receives and uses or stores assimilates (sucrose) delivered by the phloem.
parts.working: B1 site where assimilates are unloaded and used/stored.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Discs cut from bean leaves were floated on a sucrose solution at pH 5.5 and the uptake of sucrose into the companion cells was measured.
Treatment – relative sucrose uptake
control, pH 5.5 – 24
cyanide added, pH 5.5 – 3
no cyanide, pH 8.0 – 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result with cyanide, which stops aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: Without respiration, no ATP is made, so proton pumps in companion cell membranes stop; no H⁺ gradient forms, so sucrose co-transport into companion cells almost stops.
parts.working: B1 no / little ATP produced; B1 proton pumps (H⁺–ATPase) cannot pump H⁺ out, so no H⁺ gradient for co-transport of sucrose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why raising the pH of the bathing solution to 8.0 also reduced sucrose uptake.
parts.answer: pH 8 means a low H⁺ concentration outside the cells, so the H⁺ concentration gradient into the companion cells is small; fewer H⁺ move in through the co-transporter, so less sucrose is carried in with them.
parts.working: B1 fewer H⁺ outside / smaller H⁺ (proton) gradient; B1 less H⁺ diffusion through co-transporter proteins so less sucrose moved with them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why some sucrose uptake still occurred with cyanide.
parts.answer: Some sucrose diffused in / some ATP still made by anaerobic respiration or remaining H⁺ gradient for a short time.
parts.working: B1 any one reasonable suggestion: diffusion; a little ATP from anaerobic respiration/glycolysis; existing H⁺ gradient not yet run down.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sap was collected from aphid stylets inserted into the stem of a sunflower plant at three distances below the mature leaves.
distance below leaves / cm – sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³
10 – 0.82
40 – 0.64
70 – 0.47

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: Sucrose concentration in the sieve tube sap falls with distance from the source leaves (0.82 → 0.64 → 0.47 mol dm⁻³).
parts.working: B1 concentration decreases the further down / away from the leaves, with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this concentration gradient produces mass flow of sap down the stem.
parts.answer: High sucrose concentration near the leaves gives a low water potential, so water enters by osmosis and hydrostatic pressure is high; lower sucrose near the roots means less water enters/water leaves, so pressure is lower; sap flows down the hydrostatic pressure gradient.
parts.working: B1 high solute concentration at top → lower water potential → water enters by osmosis; B1 high hydrostatic (turgor) pressure near source; B1 sap moves by mass flow from high to low pressure (towards the sink).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the sucrose concentration is still well above zero at the base of the stem.
parts.answer: Sucrose is still being carried on to sinks in the roots; it is only unloaded where it is used or stored.
parts.working: B1 sucrose not yet unloaded / still in transit to the root sinks.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sugar beet root cells store sucrose at a concentration higher than that in the phloem sap. Explain why unloading sucrose into these cells needs energy.
parts.answer: Sucrose must move against its concentration gradient, so it is moved by active transport (using ATP / a proton gradient made with ATP).
parts.working: B1 against the concentration gradient; B1 active transport / co-transport needing ATP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a potato tuber, sucrose is unloaded down a concentration gradient. Explain how the tuber keeps this gradient.
parts.answer: Sucrose entering the tuber cells is converted to starch (via glucose/fructose), keeping the sucrose concentration in the cells low, so sucrose keeps diffusing in.
parts.working: B1 sucrose converted into starch (insoluble); B1 so sucrose concentration in sink cells stays lower than in sieve tubes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other way in which sucrose is used at a sink such as a root tip.
parts.answer: Respiration to release energy / to make cellulose for new cell walls.
parts.working: B1 respiration or synthesis of cellulose / other molecules for growth.

stem: A bean plant had eight leaves, numbered 1 (oldest, at the base) to 8 (youngest, at the top). Leaves 1–6 were fully expanded; leaves 7 and 8 were still growing. Leaf 5 was supplied with ¹⁴CO₂ for 30 minutes. After 4 hours, radioactivity was found in leaves 7 and 8, the shoot tip and the roots, but almost none in leaves 3 and 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why radioactivity was found both above and below leaf 5.
parts.answer: Leaf 5 is a mature source; sinks are present both above (shoot apex, young expanding leaves 7–8, which use sucrose for growth) and below (roots); sucrose moves by mass flow in different sieve tubes towards each sink.
parts.working: B1 leaf 5 is a source (photosynthesising, exporting sucrose); B1 young leaves/apex above and roots below are sinks; B1 transport in different sieve tubes / both directions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why almost no radioactivity was found in leaves 3 and 4.
parts.answer: These are mature leaves, which are sources themselves: they make more sucrose than they use and export it, so they do not import assimilates; their sucrose concentration/pressure is high so sap does not flow into them.
parts.working: B1 mature leaves are sources/photosynthesise for themselves; B1 high sucrose concentration / hydrostatic pressure, so no mass flow into them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict how the distribution of radioactivity would differ if the plant had been flowering, with pods developing. Give a reason.
parts.answer: More radioactivity in the developing pods/seeds (and less in roots and young leaves), because developing seeds are strong sinks storing large amounts of assimilate.
parts.working: B1 more ¹⁴C in pods/seeds; B1 seeds/fruits are strong sinks (store starch, protein, oil), taking priority over roots/young leaves.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a sieve tube of a squash plant, sap moved at 0.6 m h⁻¹. The sieve tube had a circular cross-section of internal radius 12 µm. The sap contained 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. Area of a circle = πr².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of sap passing through the sieve tube in one hour, in m³. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sucrose carried through the sieve tube in one hour, in µg. (1 m³ = 1000 dm³; Mr of sucrose = 342.) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two features of the sieve tube element that allow such fast flow.
parts.answer: No nucleus and very few organelles (no vacuole) leave the lumen open; sieve plates with large pores let sap pass from one element to the next; elements joined end to end form a continuous tube.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two features linked to low resistance: few organelles/no nucleus; sieve plate pores; continuous tube of elements end to end.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Water potentials were estimated at a source (P) and a sink (Q) of a cotton plant.
location – xylem water potential / MPa – sieve tube sap water potential / MPa
P (source leaf) – −0.5 – −1.6
Q (developing boll) – −0.7 – −0.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of water potential, why water moves from the xylem into the sieve tube at P.
parts.answer: At P the sieve tube sap (−1.6 MPa) has a lower (more negative) water potential than the xylem (−0.5 MPa), so water moves into the sieve tube by osmosis down the water potential gradient.
parts.working: B1 sieve tube water potential lower than xylem (quote figures); B1 osmosis down water potential gradient (through partially permeable membrane).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water leaves the sieve tube at Q.
parts.answer: Sucrose is unloaded at Q, so the sieve tube water potential rises to −0.4 MPa, above the xylem (−0.7 MPa); water moves out by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 sucrose removed raises water potential of sap; B1 now higher than xylem so water leaves by osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During a drought the xylem water potential near P fell to −2.0 MPa. Suggest and explain the effect on translocation.
parts.answer: The xylem water potential is now lower than the sieve tube sap, so water does not enter (or leaves) the sieve tube at P; hydrostatic pressure at the source falls, so the pressure gradient and mass flow decrease.
parts.working: B1 water no longer enters / moves out of sieve tube; B1 lower hydrostatic pressure at source so slower mass flow/translocation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water enters a root hair cell from the soil.
parts.answer: The soil water has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm/vacuole of the root hair cell (which contains dissolved ions and sugars), so water moves in by osmosis through the partially permeable cell surface membrane.
parts.working: B1 soil water has higher (less negative) water potential than the cell; B1 osmosis across partially permeable membrane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how root hairs increase the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: They greatly increase the surface area of the root in contact with soil water.
parts.working: B1 large surface area (for osmosis).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fields in parts of Punjab have become salty after years of irrigation. Explain why crops on these fields may wilt even when the soil is wet.
parts.answer: Dissolved salts lower the water potential of the soil water; the gradient into the root is reduced or reversed, so less water (or none) enters by osmosis and water may even leave the root cells.
parts.working: B1 salts lower soil water potential; B1 smaller/reversed water potential gradient so less water uptake by osmosis (water may be lost).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property of water molecules is mainly responsible for the continuous column of water in a xylem vessel being pulled upwards as a whole?
A adhesion of water molecules to lignin in the vessel walls
B cohesion between water molecules caused by hydrogen bonding
C root pressure produced by active transport of ions
D the high specific heat capacity of water
parts.answer: B cohesion between water molecules caused by hydrogen bonding
parts.working: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules (cohesion) let the tension created by transpiration pull the whole column up. Adhesion (A) helps the water stick to the walls and resist gravity but does not by itself transmit the pull along the column; root pressure (C) only pushes water a short distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transpiration.
parts.answer: Loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves.
parts.working: B1 loss of water vapour from leaves/stems (mainly via stomata).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the route by which water leaves a leaf, starting in a xylem vessel in a vein.
parts.answer: Water leaves the xylem and moves to mesophyll cells by osmosis or through cell walls (apoplast); it evaporates from the wet surfaces of mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces; water vapour diffuses through the air spaces; then out through the open stomata down a water vapour potential gradient into the air.
parts.working: 1 mark each: from xylem to mesophyll cells (apoplast/symplast/osmosis); evaporation from mesophyll cell wall surfaces; into air spaces; water vapour diffuses out through stomata (down a water potential / concentration gradient).

stem: On a cool, still morning in a lawn in Islamabad, small droplets of liquid were seen at the tips of the grass blades. The air was saturated with water vapour. The droplets had disappeared by midday.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how root pressure is produced.
parts.answer: Cells of the endodermis/root actively transport mineral ions into the xylem, lowering the water potential of the xylem sap; water then enters the xylem by osmosis, creating a positive pressure that pushes water up.
parts.working: B1 active transport of ions into xylem (using ATP); B1 lowers water potential so water follows by osmosis, giving a pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why droplets were seen in the early morning but not at midday.
parts.answer: At night stomata are closed and humidity is high, so transpiration is very low; the xylem is not under tension and root pressure pushes water out through the leaf tips. At midday transpiration is fast, the xylem is under tension and water is pulled up, so it is not forced out.
parts.working: B1 night: little/no transpiration (stomata closed, humid, cool); B1 root pressure forces water out at leaf tips/hydathodes; B1 midday: high transpiration creates tension in xylem / cohesion-tension dominates, so no excess water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why root pressure alone cannot supply water to the top of a 20 m tree.
parts.answer: Root pressure is far too small to push a water column that high.
parts.working: B1 pressure produced is too low (only supports a column of a few metres).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The transpiration rate of a wheat crop near Faisalabad was measured on a clear summer day.
time – transpiration rate / mm h⁻¹
02:00 – 0.05
06:00 – 0.12
10:00 – 0.68
14:00 – 0.92
18:00 – 0.35
22:00 – 0.05

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how transpiration rate changed over the 24 hours.
parts.answer: Very low (0.05) at night from 22:00 to 04:00; rose from 06:00 to a peak of 0.92 at 14:00; then fell to 0.35 at 18:00 and back to 0.05 by 22:00.
parts.working: B1 low at night and peak in the afternoon (14:00); B1 data quoted with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes between 06:00 and 14:00.
parts.answer: Light causes stomata to open, so the stomatal aperture increases; temperature rises, increasing evaporation from mesophyll cell walls and the kinetic energy of water molecules; humidity falls, steepening the water potential gradient between leaf air spaces and air.
parts.working: B1 stomata open in light (aperture increases); B1 rising temperature increases evaporation/diffusion; B1 lower humidity gives steeper water potential/diffusion gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate at 18:00 is still much higher than at 04:00 even though the stomata are only slightly open.
parts.answer: The air is still warm and dry at 18:00, so the diffusion gradient is steep; at 04:00 it is cool and humid.
parts.working: B1 temperature high / humidity low at 18:00 compared with night.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student used a bubble potometer with a capillary tube of internal diameter 0.8 mm. At 20 °C the bubble moved 36 mm in 4 minutes. The room heater was then switched on; at 35 °C the bubble moved 63 mm in 3 minutes. Volume = πr² × distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake at each temperature in mm³ min⁻¹. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 20 °C: 4.52 mm³ min⁻¹; 35 °C: 10.6 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate from 20 °C to 35 °C.
parts.working: B1 (21 − 9) ÷ 9 × 100 = 133 % (same with volumes).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, so more water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out faster; warm air can also hold more water vapour, lowering relative humidity and steepening the gradient; faster transpiration pulls water up the xylem faster.
parts.working: B1 more evaporation / faster diffusion (more kinetic energy); B1 steeper water vapour gradient OR more transpiration pull so more uptake.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why transpiration is described as an inevitable consequence of gas exchange in leaves.
parts.answer: Stomata must open to let CO₂ diffuse in for photosynthesis; the mesophyll cell surfaces must be moist for gases to dissolve and diffuse; so water evaporates from these surfaces and water vapour diffuses out through the same open stomata.
parts.working: B1 stomata open for CO₂ uptake; B1 moist cell surfaces / large surface area of mesophyll exposed to air spaces; B1 water vapour diffuses out of the open stomata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which transpiration is useful to a plant.
parts.answer: It moves mineral ions up from the roots in the transpiration stream; evaporation cools the leaves; it supplies water to leaf cells for photosynthesis and turgor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: transport of mineral ions; cooling by evaporation; supply of water to leaves (photosynthesis/turgor).

stem:
Water potentials were measured along the pathway in a 25 m tall eucalyptus tree on a sunny afternoon.
soil −0.3 MPa; root xylem −0.6 MPa; leaf xylem −1.2 MPa; leaf mesophyll cells −1.5 MPa; air −95 MPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the formula pressure = ρgh, where ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.81 m s⁻², to calculate the pressure difference in MPa needed just to hold a column of water 25 m high (1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The measured difference in water potential between the root xylem and the leaf xylem was 0.6 MPa. Suggest why this is larger than your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Extra tension is needed to overcome the resistance/friction to water flow through the narrow xylem vessels, pits and cell walls, as well as to support the column against gravity.
parts.working: B1 resistance to flow / friction against vessel walls; B1 extra pressure gradient needed to move water at a rate, not just hold it still.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the low water potential of the air causes water to move up the xylem of the tree.
parts.answer: Air has a very low (very negative) water potential, so water vapour diffuses out of the leaf and water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls; water moves from the xylem into the leaf cells to replace it, creating tension in the xylem; cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonds) pulls the whole column up; adhesion to vessel walls helps.
parts.working: B1 water lost by evaporation/transpiration down the gradient to air; B1 creates tension/negative pressure in leaf xylem; B1 cohesion (H-bonds) means the column is pulled up as a whole (accept adhesion as extra point).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an air bubble (embolism) stops water moving up that vessel.
parts.answer: The air bubble breaks the continuous column of water; cohesion can no longer transmit the tension from the leaves, so water below the bubble is not pulled up.
parts.working: B1 water column broken / not continuous; B1 cohesion-tension cannot act across the gap (no pull transmitted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how pits in xylem vessel walls allow water transport to continue after an embolism.
parts.answer: Water can move sideways through pits into neighbouring vessels and pass around the blocked vessel, then back into the column above it.
parts.working: B1 lateral movement through pits to adjacent vessels; B1 bypasses the air-filled vessel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Embolisms are more likely when the tension in the xylem is very high. Suggest why they are common in plants during a drought in the Thar Desert.
parts.answer: Dry, hot air and dry soil make the water potential gradient very steep, so tension in the xylem becomes very high; dissolved gas comes out of solution / the column breaks, forming bubbles.
parts.working: B1 low soil water and high transpiration give very high tension (very negative pressure); B1 column breaks / air drawn in / cavitation.

stem:
Detached leaves of two species, X and Y, were kept in the same conditions for one hour.
leaf – leaf area / cm² – water lost / g h⁻¹ – stomatal density / mm⁻²
X – 45 – 0.81 – 220
Y – 120 – 1.56 – 310

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water loss of each leaf in mg h⁻¹ cm⁻².
parts.answer: X: 18.0 mg h⁻¹ cm⁻²; Y: 13.0 mg h⁻¹ cm⁻²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss per stoma for each species, in µg h⁻¹. (1 mm² = 0.01 cm²) Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: X: 0.818 µg h⁻¹; Y: 0.419 µg h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Species Y has more stomata per mm² but loses less water per cm². Suggest two features of leaf Y that could explain this.
parts.answer: Stomata sunken in pits or covered by hairs, which trap humid air and reduce the water vapour gradient; thicker cuticle; stomata partly closed / smaller pores.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: sunken stomata / hairs (humid layer, thicker boundary layer); smaller stomatal pores or partly closed stomata; thicker waxy cuticle; stomata only on lower surface / in grooves.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about a mature phloem sieve tube element is correct?
A It has thick lignified walls with pits.
B It has no nucleus and is linked to a companion cell by plasmodesmata.
C It has no cytoplasm and no cell surface membrane.
D It has no end walls, so it forms a completely open tube.
parts.answer: B It has no nucleus and is linked to a companion cell by plasmodesmata.
parts.working: A mature sieve tube element loses its nucleus and most organelles but keeps a cell surface membrane and a thin layer of cytoplasm; plasmodesmata link it to its companion cell. D is wrong because the end walls remain as sieve plates with pores; open tubes with no end walls describe xylem vessels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf, a vascular bundle is seen in the midrib. State whether the xylem is nearer the upper or the lower epidermis.
parts.answer: Nearer the upper epidermis (phloem is below it, nearer the lower epidermis).
parts.working: B1 upper (adaxial) side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two functions of the xylem in a leaf.
parts.answer: Brings water to the leaf for photosynthesis and to replace water lost by transpiration; brings mineral ions (e.g. nitrate, magnesium); lignified tissue helps support the leaf blade.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: supplies water (photosynthesis / turgor / transpiration); supplies mineral ions; support.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the veins branch so that no mesophyll cell is far from a vein.
parts.answer: Water, ions and sucrose move between veins and mesophyll cells by diffusion/osmosis and through cell walls, which is slow over long distances; short distances keep supply and removal fast.
parts.working: B1 movement into/out of mesophyll by diffusion/osmosis (slow); B1 short diffusion distance so fast supply of water and removal of sucrose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each feature of a xylem vessel element, explain how it helps the vessel carry water: (i) no end walls; (ii) no cytoplasm or organelles; (iii) lignified walls; (iv) pits.
parts.answer: (i) forms a continuous, unbroken tube / column of water; (ii) less resistance, nothing blocks flow; (iii) strengthens wall so vessel does not collapse under tension, and makes it waterproof; (iv) water can move sideways into neighbouring vessels or cells.
parts.working: 1 mark per feature correctly explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one function of xylem other than transporting water.
parts.answer: Transport of mineral ions / support of the plant.
parts.working: B1 mineral ions or mechanical support.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the position of the xylem in a young dicotyledonous root compared with a young stem.
parts.answer: Root: xylem in the centre, often in a star/X shape, with phloem between its arms. Stem: xylem in a ring of separate vascular bundles near the outside, on the inner side of each bundle with phloem outside it.
parts.working: B1 root: central / star shape with phloem between arms; B1 stem: in vascular bundles arranged in a ring towards the outside, xylem on the inside of each bundle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how each arrangement suits the forces acting on the organ.
parts.answer: A central core of strong lignified tissue in the root resists pulling forces as the shoot sways and the root anchors the plant; a ring of lignified tissue near the outside of the stem resists bending in the wind.
parts.working: B1 root – central strengthening resists pulling / tension; B1 stem – peripheral ring resists bending.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the layer of cells immediately surrounding the vascular tissue in a root.
parts.answer: Pericycle (with the endodermis outside it).
parts.working: B1 pericycle (accept endodermis).

stem: An electron micrograph of phloem is described. A long cell with no nucleus has a cross wall at each end perforated by large pores (P); the inside of this long cell (Q) is mostly empty apart from a thin lining of cytoplasm against the wall. Beside it lies a narrow cell (R) with a large nucleus, dense cytoplasm, many ribosomes and many mitochondria. Fine channels (S) through the shared wall connect R with Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify structures P, Q, R and S.
parts.answer: P sieve plate; Q sieve tube element (lumen with thin layer of cytoplasm); R companion cell; S plasmodesmata.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cell R has many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration; ATP is needed by the proton pumps that set up the H⁺ gradient used to load sucrose by co-transport.
parts.working: B1 ATP from (aerobic) respiration; B1 for active loading of sucrose / proton pumping.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Phloroglucinol in hydrochloric acid stains lignin red. Cellulose cell walls are not stained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which tissues in a transverse section of a sunflower stem would be stained red by this stain.
parts.answer: Xylem (vessel elements) and any sclerenchyma fibres (e.g. a cap of fibres outside the phloem).
parts.working: B1 xylem; B1 sclerenchyma / fibres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the phloem would not be stained red.
parts.answer: Sieve tube elements and companion cells have cellulose walls that are not lignified.
parts.working: B1 phloem walls not lignified (cellulose only).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why lignin is important for the function of xylem vessels when transpiration is fast.
parts.answer: Fast transpiration puts the water in the xylem under great tension (negative pressure); the rigid lignified walls stop the vessels collapsing inwards, so the water column stays continuous.
parts.working: B1 water under tension/negative pressure; B1 lignin prevents the vessel from collapsing.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete the comparison of a sieve tube element and a companion cell for: nucleus; ribosomes; cell surface membrane; cytoplasm (amount and density).
parts.answer: Sieve tube element: no nucleus; no ribosomes; cell surface membrane present; only a thin layer of cytoplasm. Companion cell: nucleus present; many ribosomes; cell surface membrane present; dense cytoplasm.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct row (4 rows), with both cell types given in each row.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the companion cell keeps the sieve tube element alive.
parts.answer: Through the plasmodesmata it supplies proteins (made on its ribosomes), ATP and other substances that the sieve tube element cannot make because it has no nucleus or ribosomes.
parts.working: B1 supplies proteins / ATP / metabolites; B1 via plasmodesmata, because sieve tube element lacks nucleus and ribosomes.

stem: For water moving through a tube, the volume flowing per second is proportional to r⁴, where r is the tube's radius (other conditions the same).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many vessels of diameter 20 µm are needed to carry the same volume of water per second as one vessel of diameter 80 µm.
parts.answer: 256 vessels
parts.working: M1 rate ∝ r⁴ so ratio = (40 ÷ 10)⁴ (or (80 ÷ 20)⁴); A1 = 256.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plants in cold or dry places often have narrow vessels. Suggest why, despite your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Narrow vessels are less likely to form air bubbles (embolisms) under high tension or when ice forms, and an embolism blocks only a small part of the total flow; many vessels give back-up routes.
parts.working: B1 narrow vessels resist embolism/cavitation (or freeze-thaw bubbles); B1 one blocked vessel removes only a small fraction of flow capacity / safer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why wide vessels in a tall tree need thick lignified walls.
parts.answer: The water inside is under high tension, so the wide wall must resist collapse.
parts.working: B1 resist collapse under tension (wider tubes collapse more easily).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why xylem vessel elements can work as dead, empty cells, whereas sieve tube elements must be living.
parts.answer: Water moves up the xylem passively by cohesion-tension, driven by evaporation; no membranes or energy are needed in the vessels, and empty tubes give least resistance. Translocation depends on loading sucrose, which needs living cells; a partially permeable cell surface membrane is needed so water enters by osmosis and hydrostatic pressure builds up for mass flow.
parts.working: B1 xylem flow passive / driven by transpiration (no ATP in vessels); B1 empty lumen = least resistance; B1 phloem needs a partially permeable membrane to let water in by osmosis / build hydrostatic pressure; B1 sucrose loading/unloading is active (living companion cells/sieve tubes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the sieve tube element keeps a thin layer of cytoplasm and a cell surface membrane, but loses its nucleus and vacuole.
parts.answer: The membrane is needed for osmosis and to keep sucrose in; losing nucleus and vacuole leaves more space so sap flows with less resistance.
parts.working: B1 membrane retains solutes / allows pressure; B1 loss of large organelles reduces resistance to mass flow.

stem: A sieve plate is a disc of diameter 20 µm at the end of a sieve tube element. It has 20 circular pores, each of diameter 1.0 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the sieve plate area that is open pore. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why sap can still move quickly through a sieve plate that is only about 5 % open.
parts.answer: The hydrostatic pressure gradient along the tube is large, so sap is pushed through the pores; the pores are wide enough and numerous enough that the sieve plate adds resistance but does not stop flow.
parts.working: 1 mark: large hydrostatic pressure gradient pushes sap through; 1 mark: pores are wide enough and many enough, so resistance stays low (sieve plates still add some resistance).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wrote: 'Phloem sieve tubes are just like xylem vessels: both are tubes of cells joined end to end with their end walls removed, so both carry sap by the same mechanism.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Partly correct: both are long tubes formed from cells joined end to end. But sieve tubes keep perforated end walls (sieve plates), xylem vessels have no end walls; sieve tube elements are living with a membrane and thin cytoplasm, vessels are dead and empty; vessel walls are lignified, sieve tube walls are cellulose. Mechanisms differ: xylem by cohesion-tension (negative pressure, passive), phloem by mass flow under positive hydrostatic pressure set up by active loading; xylem moves water upwards only, phloem moves assimilates in either direction.
parts.working: B1 correct similarity (cells end to end forming tubes); then 1 mark each, max 4: sieve plates v no end walls; living with membrane v dead/empty; cellulose v lignified walls; tension (negative pressure) v positive hydrostatic pressure; passive v active loading; one direction v both directions.

stem: A student is given a slide of a transverse section of a young sunflower stem and is asked to make a plan diagram.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three things the student should do, and two things the student should not do, when drawing a low-power plan diagram of this section.
parts.answer: Do: use a sharp pencil with clear, continuous lines; draw only the outlines of the tissue regions; keep the correct proportions of the tissues; make the drawing large (fill most of the space). Do not: draw individual cells; use shading; use sketchy or overlapping lines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three 'do' points (sharp pencil / clear continuous lines; tissue outlines only; correct proportions; large size) and any two 'do not' points (no cells; no shading; no sketchy lines; no arrowheads on label lines).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name four tissues the student should label on the plan of this stem.
parts.answer: Any four of: epidermis, cortex, vascular bundle, xylem, phloem, pith (accept sclerenchyma / fibres).
parts.working: 2 marks for four correct; 1 mark for two or three.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student's plan diagram of a transverse section of a buttercup root has these features: the stele is shaded in with pencil; some cortex cells are drawn individually; label lines have arrowheads and two of them cross; the word 'xylem' is written inside the drawing; the outer edge is made of several short, overlapping strokes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four errors in this drawing and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: Shading – remove; individual cells drawn – show only tissue outlines; arrowheads on label lines – use plain lines that touch the tissue; label lines crossing – arrange lines so they do not cross; labels written on the drawing – write labels outside the drawing (with ruled lines); sketchy double lines – use single clear lines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four errors with correction.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features that should be visible in a high-power drawing of three xylem vessel elements seen in longitudinal section.
parts.answer: The vessel elements joined end to end with no (or remnants of) end walls; the pattern of lignin thickening (e.g. spiral or rings) on the walls; pits in the walls; the empty lumen (no contents).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: elements end to end / continuous tube; lignin thickening pattern drawn accurately; pits; no cell contents; correct relative widths.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a high-power drawing should show only a few cells.
parts.answer: So that detail of each cell can be shown accurately and large enough.
parts.working: B1 detail / accuracy of individual cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order from the upper surface, the tissue layers that should be outlined in a plan diagram of a transverse section through the blade of a dicotyledonous leaf.
parts.answer: Upper epidermis (with cuticle); palisade mesophyll; spongy mesophyll (with vascular bundle / vein); lower epidermis.
parts.working: B1 upper epidermis then palisade; B1 spongy mesophyll; B1 lower epidermis (accept vascular bundle within mesophyll).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should not draw the chloroplasts in this plan diagram.
parts.answer: A plan shows only the outlines of tissues, not cells or organelles.
parts.working: B1 plan diagrams show tissue regions only.

stem: Using an eyepiece graticule, a student measured a transverse section of a root. The whole root was 120 eyepiece units across and the stele (vascular cylinder) was 30 eyepiece units across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student draws the outline of the whole root as a circle 90 mm in diameter. Calculate the diameter she should draw for the stele.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why measuring with the eyepiece graticule before drawing improves the plan.
parts.answer: It keeps the proportions of the tissues correct.
parts.working: B1 correct proportions/relative sizes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature of the endodermis that could be shown in a plan diagram and one that could only be shown in a high-power drawing.
parts.answer: Plan: the position of the endodermis as a thin ring around the stele. High-power: individual endodermal cells / thickened (Casparian strip) walls.
parts.working: B1 plan: outline/ring position; B1 high-power: individual cells or wall details.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: List what the student should include in a high-power drawing of one stoma and the cells immediately around it, from an epidermal peel of a leaf.
parts.answer: Two kidney-shaped guard cells drawn to the correct shape and proportion; the pore between them; chloroplasts in the guard cells (and none, or very few, in ordinary epidermal cells); the nucleus of each guard cell if visible; the thicker inner walls of the guard cells; the outlines of neighbouring epidermal cells, in correct proportion.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: two guard cells correct shape; pore; chloroplasts in guard cells; nuclei; uneven wall thickness; adjacent epidermal cells in proportion; clear continuous lines, no shading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two labels the student should add.
parts.answer: Guard cell; stomatal pore; chloroplast; epidermal cell; cell wall; nucleus.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

stem: A student is drawing a longitudinal section of phloem at high power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should show the difference in width between the sieve tube element and its companion cell.
parts.answer: Draw the companion cell much narrower than the sieve tube element, with widths in the same ratio as in the specimen (measured with a graticule).
parts.working: B1 companion cell narrower, in correct proportion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three other features that should be shown in a high-power drawing of a sieve tube element and its companion cell in longitudinal section.
parts.answer: Sieve plate(s) at the ends of the sieve tube element; the companion cell running alongside with its nucleus; dense contents of companion cell compared with the almost empty sieve tube element; walls drawn as clear lines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: sieve plate; nucleus in companion cell; companion cell contents dense; sieve tube lumen almost empty; cell walls clear; correct length relationship.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student drew one vascular bundle from a stem section. The drawing is 75 mm wide. The actual width of the vascular bundle, measured with a calibrated eyepiece graticule, was 0.5 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student adds a scale bar representing 100 µm. Calculate how long the scale bar should be on the drawing.
parts.answer: 15 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a scale bar is more useful than writing the magnification if the drawing will be enlarged on a photocopier.
parts.answer: The scale bar is enlarged by the same factor as the drawing, so it stays correct; a written magnification would become wrong.
parts.working: B1 scale bar changes size with the drawing.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four features of a good high-power drawing of three adjacent endodermal cells and the pericycle cells next to them.
parts.answer: Only the few cells asked for; large drawing; clear, continuous lines with no shading; correct shapes and relative sizes of the cells; cell walls shown with their thickness where visible (e.g. thickened endodermal walls); only structures actually seen drawn.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should draw what is seen on the slide rather than a textbook diagram.
parts.answer: Drawings are a record of the actual specimen; textbook diagrams may differ from it.
parts.working: B1 records actual observations / specimen may differ.

stem:
Two students drew plan diagrams of the same buttercup root section, in which the stele is about one quarter of the root diameter.
Drawing A: large; cortex shown as many small circles (cells); stele drawn about half the root diameter; stele shaded; one label line ends in an arrow.
Drawing B: occupies about one third of the space given; cortex, endodermis and stele shown only as outlines; stele about one quarter of the root diameter; ruled label lines touching each tissue; no shading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the rules for plan diagrams, decide which drawing is better. Give three reasons from the descriptions.
parts.answer: Drawing B is better (B1): it shows only tissue outlines with no cells; the stele is in correct proportion (about a quarter of the diameter); it has ruled label lines that stop at the tissue; it has no shading. Drawing A shows cells, is shaded, has the stele too large and a label line with an arrow.
parts.working: B1 B is better; then 1 mark each for three valid reasons comparing A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Drawing B has one fault. Identify it and explain why it matters.
parts.answer: It is drawn very small (one third of the space), so detail and proportions are hard to show/check.
parts.working: B1 too small – drawings should fill most of the space so detail is clear.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a vascular bundle, the actual width of the bundle was 0.40 mm and the width of the xylem region was 0.16 mm. A student drew the bundle 60 mm wide and drew the xylem 36 mm wide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of xylem width to bundle width in the specimen and in the drawing.
parts.answer: Specimen 0.40; drawing 0.60

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage error in the proportion of xylem in the drawing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the width the student should have drawn for the xylem.
parts.answer: 24 mm

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the student could avoid this error in future drawings.
parts.answer: Measure the tissues with the eyepiece graticule (or ruler on the image) first and scale each measurement by the same factor.
parts.working: B1 measure first and scale / use graticule readings.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The stem section is large and has twenty similar vascular bundles in a ring. The student is told to draw a plan of one sector containing three vascular bundles. Explain why this is acceptable and describe how the edges of the sector should be shown.
parts.answer: The section is symmetrical/repetitive, so a sector shows all the tissues and their arrangement; it allows a larger drawing with correct proportions; the cut edges of the sector should be shown as straight (ruled) lines from the centre, clearly not tissue boundaries.
parts.working: B1 sector is representative / shows all tissues because bundles are repeated; B1 allows drawing large enough to show proportions; B1 sector edges drawn as straight lines (e.g. from centre outwards) / not as tissue boundaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two tissues that must be included in the sector so that the plan represents the whole stem.
parts.answer: Epidermis and cortex at the outside, and pith at the centre (plus vascular bundles with xylem and phloem).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: epidermis; cortex; pith; vascular bundle with xylem and phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write three annotations (short notes, not just labels) for a drawing of xylem vessel elements in longitudinal section, each linking a visible structure to its function.
