parts.text: A student compared the number of stomata per mm² on leaves from plants grown in sun and in shade. State three variables she should standardise when choosing leaves.
parts.answer: Species/variety; leaf age or position on the plant (e.g. 4th leaf from tip); part of the leaf sampled (e.g. halfway between midrib and edge); surface of leaf (lower); time of collection.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an investigation, the phloem of some branches of a lemon tree was removed by ringing. Describe a suitable control.
parts.answer: Similar branches on the same tree (same size, number of leaves and fruits, same side) left un-ringed, or with bark cut and replaced, and treated otherwise the same.
parts.working: B1 un-ringed similar branches; B1 same tree/conditions/same handling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of this control.
parts.answer: To show that any change (e.g. in fruit size) is caused by removing the phloem and not by other factors.
parts.working: B1 show effect is due to the ring/IV only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student changes humidity around a shoot by enclosing it in a plastic bag with different amounts of wet cotton wool. Explain why temperature might change with humidity and how this could affect the results.
parts.answer: Evaporation of water from the wet cotton cools the air in the bag (and a sealed bag may warm up in light); temperature affects rate of transpiration, so the change in rate could be due to temperature, not humidity.
parts.working: B1 evaporation causes cooling / bag warms; B1 temperature also affects transpiration rate – confounding variable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could monitor and control temperature.
parts.answer: Place a thermometer/temperature probe inside the bag; place the apparatus in a constant-temperature room or water-jacketed chamber / use a heat filter between lamp and bag; record temperature at every reading.
parts.working: B1 measure inside bag; B1 method of keeping constant.

stem: To investigate the effect of light intensity on transpiration, a student placed a 100 W filament lamp at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm from a shoot in a potometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the problem with this design.
parts.answer: Moving the lamp closer also raises the temperature of the shoot, so both light intensity and temperature change; it is not possible to tell which caused the increase.
parts.working: B1 lamp heats shoot / temperature changes; B1 so two variables change together (not valid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to solve this problem.
parts.answer: Place a glass tank of water / heat filter between the lamp and the shoot; use an LED lamp (little heat); keep the lamp at a fixed distance and change intensity with neutral-density filters or a dimmer, checking with a light meter; monitor temperature at the leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A scientist tests whether an inhibitor dissolved in ethanol reduces sucrose uptake by leaf discs floated on a buffered sucrose solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for the inhibitor treatment.
parts.answer: Leaf discs from the same leaves in the same buffer and sucrose solution with the same volume of the solvent used for the inhibitor, but no inhibitor; same time and temperature.
parts.working: B1 same discs/solution without inhibitor; B1 includes solvent (vehicle) control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why leaf discs for all treatments should be cut from the same leaves and mixed at random.
parts.answer: Leaves differ in age and sucrose-loading ability; random allocation of discs from all leaves spreads this variation evenly across treatments so it does not bias one group.
parts.working: B1 variation between leaves; B1 random allocation avoids bias.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compared transpiration rates of rose bushes in two gardens, one in Murree and one in Karachi, on the same day. Explain why this is not a fair test of the effect of altitude.
parts.answer: Many variables differ between the gardens (temperature, humidity, wind, light, soil water, variety and age of bushes), not just altitude.
parts.working: B1 many uncontrolled variables; B1 named examples.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the comparison more valid.
parts.answer: Use the same rose variety of the same age; measure and record temperature, humidity, light and wind at each site; take measurements at the same time of day on several days; many plants per site.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each investigation, state whether the independent variable is continuous or categorical, and the type of graph to plot: (i) rate of transpiration of five different plant species; (ii) rate of transpiration at five temperatures.
parts.answer: (i) categorical – bar chart; (ii) continuous – line graph (plotted points joined with straight lines or a line of best fit).
parts.working: B1 each correct pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why points on a graph of rate against temperature should not be joined to zero if no reading was taken at 0 °C.
parts.answer: There is no evidence of the value at 0 °C, so it would be an extrapolation not supported by data.
parts.working: B1 no data there / extrapolation.

stem: A scientist plans to measure the rate of sap exudation from aphid stylets on willow stems kept at different temperatures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two variables, other than temperature, that would be difficult to control in this investigation and explain how each could affect the results.
parts.answer: Aphid stylet blocking – flow may stop for reasons other than temperature; distance of stylet from source/sink – sap pressure and composition differ along the stem; age and health of plants/source leaf photosynthesis rate; time of day/light affecting sucrose loading; humidity affecting xylem water potential.
parts.working: 2 marks per variable: B1 variable; B1 how it affects rate of exudation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the effect of one of these variables could be reduced.
parts.answer: Insert stylets at the same distance from the source leaf / use plants of same age / keep same light conditions / discard samples where flow stops early.
parts.working: B1 valid method.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cotton plants of cultivars P and Q were grown side by side in a field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to compare the rate of water loss from leaf discs of two cultivars of cotton. Explain why cutting discs with a cork borer is better than using whole leaves.
parts.answer: Discs all have the same surface area, so water loss can be compared directly; avoids variation in leaf size/shape and midrib.
parts.working: B1 standard area; B1 removes leaf size variation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discs cut from the same leaf are more similar than discs from different leaves. Explain how the student could use this to design the experiment, and what statistical test would match this design.
parts.answer: Use a paired design: from each of several plants take a leaf of the same position/age from each cultivar (or compare discs from the same leaf position), so each pair shares conditions; repeat for many pairs; analyse the differences within pairs (a paired t-test) – in an unpaired design use a t-test on independent samples.
parts.working: B1 pair/match samples (same age/position/conditions); B1 many replicates; B1 suitable statistical test (t-test, paired if matched).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A scientist will compare mean xylem vessel diameter in wheat grown with irrigation and wheat grown without irrigation (rain only). State four variables she must standardise and explain why one of them is important.
parts.answer: Variety/cultivar; growth stage/age of plants; position on plant sampled (e.g. same internode or leaf); soil type/fertiliser; time of sampling; method of sectioning and measuring. Explanation e.g. vessel diameter varies along a stem (often wider towards the base), so sampling different positions would give differences unrelated to water supply.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four variables (max 4); B1 one explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student set up a second potometer with no shoot, its tubing sealed with a stopper, alongside the potometer with the shoot. Explain why this is a useful control.
parts.answer: It shows whether the bubble moves for reasons other than water uptake by the shoot, e.g. leaks, evaporation, or expansion/contraction of the water as temperature changes.
parts.working: B1 checks for movement not caused by the shoot; B1 named cause (leak / temperature expansion / evaporation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: During the experiment the bubble in the control potometer moved 4 mm in the opposite direction to the one in which uptake moves it, as the room warmed. Explain this and say how the student should correct the readings from the potometer with a shoot.
parts.answer: Water expands as it warms, pushing the bubble back (away from the shoot); the same expansion would occur in the potometer with the shoot, making its readings too small; add 4 mm (adjusted for the same time and capillary) to the distance moved by the bubble in the potometer with the shoot.
parts.working: B1 thermal expansion of water; B1 underestimates uptake in the test potometer; B1 add the control movement to the test reading (correction).

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Rates of water loss from six potted coriander plants (g h⁻¹): 4.2, 3.8, 4.6, 4.0, 4.4, 3.6.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate.
parts.answer: 4.1 g h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation tells you about the data.
parts.answer: How spread out the values are around the mean (variation between plants).
parts.working: B1 spread / variability about the mean.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Twelve measurements of stomatal pore length had a mean of 9.6 µm and a standard deviation of 0.84 µm.
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between standard deviation and standard error.
parts.answer: SD measures the spread of the individual measurements around the mean; SE measures how precisely the sample mean estimates the true (population) mean, and it gets smaller as the sample size increases.
parts.working: B1 SD = spread of data; B1 SE = reliability/precision of the mean (depends on n).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Sixteen readings of water uptake by a shoot gave a mean of 18.6 mm³ min⁻¹ and a standard deviation of 2.4 mm³ min⁻¹.
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for the mean.
parts.answer: 17.4 to 19.8 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another plant had a 95 % confidence interval of 20.5 to 22.9 mm³ min⁻¹. What does this suggest about the difference between the two plants?
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference between the means is likely to be significant (not due to chance).
parts.working: B1 no overlap; B1 difference likely real / significant.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: A t-test was used to compare the mean stomatal density of two varieties of rice, with 10 leaves of each variety. The calculated value of t was 3.46.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean stomatal densities of the two varieties.
parts.working: B1 no (significant) difference between means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for this number of degrees of freedom is 2.10. State and explain the conclusion.
parts.answer: t = 3.46 is greater than 2.10, so reject the null hypothesis: the difference in mean stomatal density is significant (probability that it is due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 3.46 > 2.10 so reject null hypothesis; B1 difference significant / not due to chance (p < 0.05).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Choose the most suitable statistical test for each investigation, from: t-test; Spearman's rank correlation; chi-squared test. (i) Is there a correlation between leaf area and the number of stomata per leaf in 12 plants? (ii) Is the mean xylem vessel diameter different in plants from two habitats? (iii) Do the numbers of aphids on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves differ from an expected 1 : 1 ratio?
parts.answer: (i) Spearman's rank correlation; (ii) t-test; (iii) chi-squared test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Mean xylem vessel diameter (µm) in stems of seven well-watered and seven drought-treated sunflower plants.
watered: 12.4, 13.1, 11.8, 12.9, 13.5, 12.2, 12.7
drought: 10.9, 11.6, 10.4, 11.2, 11.8, 10.7, 11.3
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂); degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation for each group. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Watered: mean 12.66, s = 0.57; drought: mean 11.13, s = 0.50
parts.working: B1 both means; B1 s watered 0.57; B1 s drought 0.50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 12 degrees of freedom is 2.18. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 5.33 > 2.18, so the difference is significant: drought-treated plants have significantly smaller vessel diameters (reject the null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 compare with critical value and conclude correctly.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Height and mean xylem vessel diameter of nine young trees of one species.
height / cm: 45, 62, 38, 80, 55, 71, 90, 50, 66
vessel diameter / µm: 28, 35, 31, 44, 30, 41, 52, 33, 36
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between plant height and mean xylem vessel diameter.
parts.working: B1 no correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of rs for n = 9 at p = 0.05 is 0.700. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.92 > 0.700, so reject the null hypothesis: there is a significant positive correlation between height and vessel diameter.
parts.working: B1 correct conclusion with comparison.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: 100 aphids were placed on a bean plant. After 2 hours, 68 were on young, growing leaves and 32 were on old, mature leaves (equal leaf areas of each). χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the expected numbers if aphids show no preference.
parts.answer: 50 and 50

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ².

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of χ² for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State and explain a conclusion.
parts.answer: 12.96 > 3.84, so the difference from 1 : 1 is significant; aphids prefer the young leaves (perhaps because young leaves are sinks with sieve tubes rich in incoming sucrose and amino acids, or have thinner tissues).
parts.working: B1 significant / reject null; B1 aphids prefer young leaves (any sensible reason).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Transpiration rate of 10 irrigated and 10 unirrigated sorghum plants.
irrigated: mean 24.5, standard deviation 2.8 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹
unirrigated: mean 19.2, standard deviation 3.4 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for each group. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Irrigated: 22.7 to 26.3; unirrigated: 17.0 to 21.4 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: What can you conclude?
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the irrigated plants have a significantly higher mean transpiration rate.
parts.working: B1 no overlap → significant difference.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
The distance travelled by dye in 20 minutes in eight stems of a plant in a sunny position (cm): 22, 31, 18, 27, 35, 24, 29, 20.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation. Give the standard deviation to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same measurement on a shaded plant gave a mean of 14.2 cm and s = 1.9 cm. Compare the variability of the two sets of data.
parts.answer: The sunny plant's data are much more variable (s = 5.80 v 1.9; also larger relative to the mean).
parts.working: B1 comparison using s.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Stomatal density (per mm²) of leaves from a shrub species on an exposed hilltop and in a sheltered valley.
hilltop (n = 6): 38, 45, 41, 50, 36, 44
valley (n = 8): 33, 40, 29, 37, 35, 31, 38, 34
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂); degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the degrees of freedom and use the critical values to state a conclusion. Critical values at p = 0.05: 10 df 2.23; 12 df 2.18; 14 df 2.14.
parts.answer: 12 df; 3.15 > 2.18, so the difference is significant – the hilltop plants have a significantly higher stomatal density (reject the null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 df = 6 + 8 − 2 = 12; B1 correct conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the result does not show that the difference is caused by exposure to wind.
parts.answer: Other factors differ between the sites (light, temperature, soil water, genetics), so cause cannot be shown from a field comparison.
parts.working: B1 other uncontrolled factors / correlation not cause.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Light intensity (klx) and transpiration rate (g h⁻¹) were recorded for a potted plant on ten occasions.
light: 12, 18, 18, 25, 30, 34, 34, 41, 47, 52
rate: 0.9, 1.4, 1.1, 1.8, 1.6, 2.4, 2.2, 2.0, 2.9, 2.7
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate rs, using the mean of the tied ranks where values are equal. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of rs for n = 10 at p = 0.05 is 0.648. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.648: significant positive correlation between light intensity and transpiration rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rank was used rather than a t-test.
parts.answer: The aim is to test for a correlation between two variables measured on the same plants, not a difference between two means.
parts.working: B1 correlation, not difference between groups.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem: Ninety seedlings of a desert shrub were planted in each of three soil types (loam, sandy loam, sand) and left without watering. After 8 weeks, 85 seedlings had survived in total: loam 38, sandy loam 30, sand 17. χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number surviving in each soil if soil type has no effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of χ² at p = 0.05 is 5.99 for 2 degrees of freedom. Explain why there are 2 degrees of freedom and state the conclusion.
parts.answer: Three categories − 1 = 2 df; 7.93 > 5.99 so soil type has a significant effect on survival (reject null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 df = number of categories − 1; B1 conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
stem:
Rates of water uptake (mm³ min⁻¹), five readings each.
shoot X: mean 15.4, standard deviation 3.2
shoot Y: mean 12.1, standard deviation 3.0
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean for each shoot. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Shoot X: 1.43 mm³ min⁻¹; shoot Y: 1.34 mm³ min⁻¹
parts.working: M1 SE = s ÷ √n: 3.2 ÷ √5 = 1.43 (X) and 3.0 ÷ √5 = 1.34 (Y); A1 both correct with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student drew error bars of ± 1 standard deviation and said 'the bars overlap, so the difference is not significant'. Another drew ± 2 SE bars. Explain which error bars are more useful and what the overlap shows.
parts.answer: ± 2 SE (95 % CI) bars show how reliable each mean is, so they are appropriate for judging whether means differ; SD bars show the spread of the data, not the reliability of the mean. Here the 95 % CIs are about 12.5 to 18.3 (X) and 9.4 to 14.8 (Y), which overlap (12.5 to 14.8), so the difference between the means may not be significant – a t-test or more replicates are needed.
parts.working: B1 2SE/CI bars show reliability of means; B1 SD shows variability, not suited to comparing means; B1 CIs overlap so no evidence of significant difference / need more data or a t-test.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student used a potometer with a leafy shoot in still air at 20 °C. The student then placed a fan so that air blew across the leaves and repeated the measurement at 20 °C. Distance moved by the air bubble in 10 minutes: still air 14 mm; with fan 37 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble in the experiment with the fan, in mm min⁻¹.
parts.working: B1 37 mm ÷ 10 min = 3.7 mm min⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bubble moved further when the fan was blowing over the leaves.
parts.answer: Moving air carries away water vapour from around the leaf surface, so the water vapour concentration gradient between the leaf air spaces and the air outside stays steep. Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata faster, so transpiration increases and more water is drawn up the xylem, moving the bubble further.
parts.working: 1 mark: moving air removes water vapour from the leaf surface; 1 mark: steeper/maintained concentration gradient so faster diffusion out of stomata; 1 mark: more water lost by transpiration so more drawn up the xylem (transpiration pull).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Potato cylinders of equal size were weighed, placed in sucrose solutions for 1 hour, and weighed again. Percentage change in mass: 0.0 mol dm⁻³ +12.0 %; 0.2 mol dm⁻³ +4.0 %; 0.4 mol dm⁻³ −3.0 %; 0.6 mol dm⁻³ −9.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate, by linear interpolation between the two nearest results, the sucrose concentration at which there was no change in mass. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.31 mol dm⁻³ (approximately)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mass of the cylinders increased in 0.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: Pure water has a higher water potential than the potato cells, so water enters the cells by osmosis across the partially permeable membranes. The cells become turgid and the cylinders gain mass.
parts.working: B1 water potential of the cells is lower than that of pure water; B1 water enters by osmosis so cells swell (turgid).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cylinders lost mass in 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: The sucrose solution has a lower (more negative) water potential than the cells, so water leaves the cells by osmosis. The cells lose turgor and the cylinders lose mass.
parts.working: B1 solution water potential lower than the cell contents; B1 water leaves by osmosis, cells become flaccid.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The sap in a sieve tube of a sunflower contains 0.30 mol dm⁻³ sucrose at 25 °C. Use ψₛ = −iCRT, where i = 1, R = 0.00831 MPa dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T = 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the solute potential of the sap, in MPa, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pressure potential in the sieve tube is +0.20 MPa. Calculate the water potential of the sap, and state the direction in which water moves between the xylem (−0.45 MPa) and the sieve tube.
parts.answer: Water potential = −0.74 + 0.20 = −0.54 MPa; water moves from the xylem into the sieve tube by osmosis, because the xylem has the higher water potential.
parts.working: M1 ψ = ψₛ + ψₚ = −0.74 + 0.20 = −0.54 MPa; A1 water moves from xylem (−0.45) to sieve tube (−0.54), down the water potential gradient.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Leaves of two plants were detached and weighed, then left on the laboratory bench for 6 hours. Leaves of a tropical rainforest plant lost 42 % of their fresh mass. Leaves of a desert succulent lost 6 % of their fresh mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the percentage mass loss was for the rainforest leaves than for the succulent leaves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the succulent leaves lost much less mass.
parts.answer: Any three of: a thick waxy cuticle reduces evaporation through the epidermis; few stomata, or stomata sunken in pits, reduce the area through which vapour can escape; stomata closed in the day so little vapour escapes at the hottest time; a small surface area to volume ratio; water-storing tissue keeps the cells turgid and reduces the water potential gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: thick waxy cuticle; few or sunken stomata; stomata closed in the day; small surface area to volume ratio; water-storage tissue.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured the rate of water uptake by a shoot at five temperatures in a potometer. Results (mm³ min⁻¹): 10 °C 2; 20 °C 5; 30 °C 9; 40 °C 12; 45 °C 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rate of water uptake changes between 10 °C and 40 °C.
parts.answer: It increases steadily, from 2 to 12 mm³ min⁻¹, as the temperature rises.
parts.working: B1 rate increases with temperature (2 → 5 → 9 → 12 mm³ min⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate fell between 40 °C and 45 °C.
parts.answer: At 45 °C the enzymes and proteins in the roots and guard cells are denatured, and the cell membranes are damaged, so active processes such as ion uptake are impaired. The stomata may also close, which reduces the pull of transpiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: enzymes/proteins denatured in roots or guard cells; membranes damaged and less selectively permeable; less active uptake of ions so less water taken up; stomata close, reducing transpiration pull.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the rate from 40 °C to 45 °C.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three bean plants were stood with their cut bases in eosin dye for 2 hours. Plant W (normal): dye reached 18 cm up the stem. Plant X: a complete ring of bark (phloem and cambium) was removed 5 cm above the base; dye reached 18 cm. Plant Y: a ring of xylem was cut out 5 cm above the base, with the bark and phloem left intact; dye reached only 5 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for plant X.
parts.answer: Water and dissolved dye move up the stem in the xylem, not the phloem. Removing the bark and phloem does not block the xylem, so the dye still rises to 18 cm.
parts.working: B1 transport of water/dye is in the xylem; B1 phloem removal does not interrupt the xylem, so dye still reaches 18 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for plant Y.
parts.answer: The xylem vessels are the route for the dye, so the cut-out ring of xylem blocks its movement; the dye cannot cross the gap and stops at 5 cm. Phloem does not carry water upwards.
parts.working: B1 xylem is the pathway and the gap breaks it so dye stops at the gap (5 cm); B1 phloem does not carry water/dye up the stem.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion the student can draw from the three plants.
parts.answer: Water (and dissolved dye) moves up the stem in the xylem, not in the phloem.
parts.working: B1 xylem conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students measured the rate of water loss from a leaf (mg cm⁻² h⁻¹) in moving air: 0 m s⁻¹ 2.1; 1 m s⁻¹ 3.4; 2 m s⁻¹ 4.0; 3 m s⁻¹ 4.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water loss from 0 to 3 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate levelled off between 2 and 3 m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: The layer of still air (boundary layer) next to the leaf is already as thin as it can become, so faster air cannot reduce it further. The water vapour gradient is close to its maximum, and the stomatal aperture now limits the rate of diffusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: boundary layer already at its minimum thickness so faster wind has little effect; 1 mark: water vapour gradient near maximum or stomata are the limiting factor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that must be kept the same in this investigation.
parts.answer: Temperature (or humidity, light intensity, leaf area, type of leaf).
parts.working: B1 any one control variable that would affect transpiration.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student claims that a potometer measures the rate of transpiration. In one test the shoot took up 4.8 cm³ of water in 2 hours, while the shoot's mass fell by 4.1 g over the same period (equivalent to 4.1 cm³ of water lost).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water taken up that was not lost by transpiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water uptake can be greater than the water lost by transpiration.
parts.answer: Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis as a reactant, and some is retained in the tissues to maintain turgor and for growth. Only the water lost as vapour is measured by the mass change.
parts.working: B1 water used in photosynthesis (a reactant); B1 water retained in cells for turgor / growth so not lost as vapour.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A leaf of a plant was supplied with ¹⁴CO₂ in light. After 2 hours, radioactive sugar was detected in the phloem sap below the leaf and in the roots, but not in the xylem sap above the leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the label was found in the phloem below the leaf but not in the xylem above it.
parts.answer: Sucrose made in photosynthesis is loaded into the sieve tubes and moved in the phloem. The xylem carries water and minerals upwards from the roots, so no labelled sugar enters it.
parts.working: B1 labelled sucrose is made and loaded into phloem sieve tubes; B1 xylem carries water/minerals from roots, not sugars from the leaf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the labelled sugar reached the roots.
parts.answer: The roots are a sink, and sucrose moves from the source (the leaf) to sinks through the phloem by mass flow.
parts.working: B1 roots are a sink; phloem transports sucrose from source to sink.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the label in the roots if a ring of phloem below the leaf were removed.
parts.answer: Less labelled sugar would reach the roots, and the label would build up in the phloem above the ring.
parts.working: B1 phloem route blocked so less label reaches roots; label accumulates above the ring.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two leaves were weighed for water loss in one hour in the same room. Leaf P had an area of 60 cm² and lost 0.42 g of water. Leaf Q had an area of 45 cm² and lost 0.33 g of water. Leaf P has stomata only on its lower surface; leaf Q has stomata on both surfaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water loss per cm² per hour for each leaf, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why leaf Q may lose more water per cm² than leaf P, even though the total difference is small.
parts.answer: Leaf Q has stomata on both surfaces, so there are more stomata per cm² of leaf and more pores for water vapour to escape through; leaf Q may also have a thinner cuticle.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: stomata on both surfaces / more stomata per cm²; thinner cuticle; more open stomata because of the shaded environment.

author: HomiLabs

stem: On a calm, humid night a student cut a sunflower stem 5 cm above the soil and joined the cut end to a vertical glass tube. Over 10 hours overnight, sap rose 8 cm up the tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate at which the sap rose, in mm h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 8 mm h⁻¹
parts.working: B1 80 mm ÷ 10 h = 8 mm h⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the rise would be different if the stem had been cut in dry air rather than under water.
parts.answer: Air would be drawn into the xylem vessels when the stem was cut, breaking the continuous water column (cohesion), so the sap would not rise as far, if at all.
parts.working: 1 mark: air enters the xylem vessels; 1 mark: the continuous water column is broken so pressure cannot push sap up.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Potato cells were placed in a 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution at 25 °C. The water potential of the potato cells was −0.9 MPa. Use ψ = −iCRT, where i = 1 for sucrose, R = 0.00831 MPa dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T = 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water potential of the sucrose solution, in MPa, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which way water moves between the cells and the solution, and explain why.
parts.answer: Water moves out of the cells into the solution by osmosis, because the solution has a lower (more negative) water potential (−1.24 MPa) than the cells (−0.9 MPa). Water moves from higher to lower water potential.
parts.working: B1 water moves out of the cells; B1 solution has a lower water potential than the cells, so water moves down the water potential gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cells lose turgor when water leaves them.
parts.answer: As water leaves, the cell contents shrink and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall, so the pressure potential falls and the cell becomes flaccid (plasmolysis).
parts.working: B1 pressure potential falls as the protoplast shrinks away from the wall / cell becomes flaccid.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bean leaves were examined through the day. Stomata were closed at night, opened after dawn as light increased, and closed again when the soil dried out during the afternoon of a hot day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the movement of potassium ions causes the stomata to open in the morning.
parts.answer: Potassium ions are pumped into the guard cells by active transport, using ATP. The water potential of the guard cells falls, so water enters by osmosis and the guard cells become turgid. The uneven thickening of the walls causes the guard cells to bend apart, opening the pore.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: K⁺ actively transported into guard cells (ATP / proton pump); water potential falls; water enters by osmosis and guard cells swell/turgid; uneven wall thickening makes them bend apart, opening the stoma.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a shortage of water in the leaves closes the stomata, with reference to abscisic acid (ABA).
parts.answer: ABA is produced when the plant is short of water. It causes potassium ions to leave the guard cells, so their water potential rises, water leaves by osmosis, the guard cells lose turgor and the stomata close.
parts.working: 1 mark: ABA produced in drought and causes K⁺ to leave guard cells; 1 mark: water leaves by osmosis, guard cells lose turgor and stomata close.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student set up two potometers using leafy shoots cut from the same plant. Shoot 1 was cut under water and the bubble moved 22 mm in 10 minutes. Shoot 2 was cut in air. Within 30 seconds the cut was exposed to air, and the bubble moved only 1 mm in the next 10 minutes, although the shoot looked healthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble in shoot 1, and the percentage reduction in the rate for shoot 2 compared with shoot 1.
parts.working: B1 shoot 1 rate = 2.2 mm min⁻¹; B1 percentage reduction = (22 − 1)/22 × 100 = 95.5 % (shoot 2 rate 0.1 mm min⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why shoot 2 transpired so much less than shoot 1.
parts.answer: When shoot 2 was cut in air, air entered the xylem vessels. Air bubbles (an embolism) break the continuous water column, so cohesion is lost and the transpiration pull cannot be transmitted up the xylem, so little water is moved.
parts.working: 1 mark: air enters the xylem vessels when cut in air; 1 mark: continuous water column broken / cohesion lost; 1 mark: transpiration pull cannot be transmitted so little water is drawn up.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to investigate the effect of relative humidity on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot using a potometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a suitable hypothesis for an investigation into the effect of relative humidity on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot.
parts.answer: As relative humidity increases, the rate of transpiration decreases, because the water potential (water vapour concentration) gradient between the leaf and the air is smaller, so less water vapour diffuses out through the stomata.
parts.working: B1 correct relationship (higher humidity → lower transpiration); B1 biological reason: smaller concentration gradient so slower diffusion of vapour through stomata.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what will happen to the rate of transpiration if the plant is moved from a dim cupboard into bright sunlight, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The rate of transpiration will increase, because light makes the stomata open for photosynthesis, so more water vapour diffuses out of the leaf.
parts.working: B1 rate increases; B1 stomata open in light, allowing more water vapour to diffuse out.

stem: A student predicts that the rate of water uptake will double when the temperature rises from 10 °C to 20 °C. Results: 10 °C 3.0 mm³ min⁻¹; 20 °C 5.5 mm³ min⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water uptake from 10 °C to 20 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Is the prediction supported? Give a reason.
parts.answer: No. The rate increased by 83 %, not 100 %, so it did not double.
parts.working: B1 prediction not supported: increase is less than 100 % (rate less than doubled).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable null hypothesis for an investigation into the effect of sucrose concentration on the mass of potato cylinders.
parts.answer: There is no effect of sucrose concentration on the percentage change in mass of potato cylinders (no correlation between them).
parts.working: B1 states no relationship/effect between sucrose concentration and percentage change in mass.

stem: A plant has been kept in bright light for a week, with its leaves making sucrose by photosynthesis. It is then moved into darkness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what happens to sucrose loading into the phloem at the leaves, and to the rate of mass flow in the phloem, over the next few hours. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Loading of sucrose into the phloem falls and the rate of mass flow falls.
parts.working: B1 less sucrose is made by photosynthesis, so less is loaded into sieve tubes; B1 the sieve tube water potential rises, less water enters by osmosis, hydrostatic pressure falls and mass flow slows.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student's hypothesis: 'Increasing the temperature increases the rate of transpiration.' Results: 15 °C 0.8 g h⁻¹; 25 °C 1.4 g h⁻¹; 35 °C 2.3 g h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in the rate of transpiration for each 10 °C rise between 15 °C and 35 °C.
parts.working: M1 (2.3 − 0.8) = 1.5 g h⁻¹ over two 10 °C steps; A1 1.5 ÷ 2 = 0.75 g h⁻¹ per 10 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the data support the hypothesis.
parts.answer: The data support the hypothesis: the rate rises at each step (0.8 → 1.4 → 2.3 g h⁻¹). However, only three temperatures were tested with no repeats, so the pattern is not yet reliable and more temperatures and repeats are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: data show a rise in rate with temperature, so supports the hypothesis; 1 mark: limitation - only three temperatures and no repeats, so cannot be sure of the pattern.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A tree with many leaves is compared with the same tree after all its leaves have been removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of removing all the leaves from the tree on the rate of water uptake by its roots, and explain your prediction using the cohesion–tension theory.
parts.answer: The rate of water uptake will fall. With no leaves there is little transpiration, so less tension (pull) is created in the xylem; the water column is pulled up less and less water is taken up by the roots.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate of water uptake falls; 1 mark: fewer leaves so less transpiration and less tension in the xylem; 1 mark: less water pulled up the column so less absorbed by roots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable in this comparison.
parts.answer: The number (or area) of leaves on the tree.
parts.working: B1 number/area of leaves (leaf removal).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Leaf discs were treated with cyanide, which blocks respiration and so reduces ATP production. Sucrose loading into the phloem was measured in µmol. Control discs loaded 10.4 µmol; cyanide-treated discs loaded 2.1 µmol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a prediction for this experiment, based on the hypothesis that sucrose loading into the phloem requires ATP.
parts.answer: Leaf discs treated with cyanide will load less sucrose than untreated (control) discs.
parts.working: B1 cyanide inhibits respiration/ATP so loading is reduced compared with control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in sucrose loading in the cyanide-treated discs compared with the control.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the data support the hypothesis, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Yes. Loading fell by about 80 % when respiration (ATP production) was blocked, which supports the idea that loading uses energy from ATP. A control with a different inhibitor would be needed to check cyanide acts only through ATP.
parts.working: 1 mark: data support hypothesis - loading fell sharply when ATP production blocked; 1 mark: an extra control or other inhibitor needed to confirm cyanide's effect is through ATP.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Plant A has many small stomata; plant B has few large stomata. The leaves of both plants have the same total stomatal pore area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a hypothesis comparing the transpiration rate of plant A and plant B.
parts.answer: Plant A, with many small stomata, will have a higher rate of transpiration than plant B, with few large stomata of the same total pore area, because diffusion through many small pores is faster per unit area (the diffusion gradients overlap less).
parts.working: 1 mark: plant A higher rate (testable comparison); 1 mark: many small pores diffuse faster per unit area than one large pore of the same total area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one variable that must be kept the same in this comparison.
parts.answer: Total stomatal pore area (or leaf area, temperature, humidity, light intensity).
parts.working: B1 any one controlled variable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to use a potometer to investigate the effect of wind speed on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables in a potometer investigation of wind speed.
parts.answer: Independent variable: wind speed (m s⁻¹) from a fan. Dependent variable: distance moved by the bubble in a fixed time (rate of transpiration).
parts.working: B1 IV wind speed; B1 DV distance moved by bubble per time (rate of transpiration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a prediction for this investigation, with a reason.
parts.answer: As wind speed increases, the rate of transpiration increases (up to a limit), because moving air removes water vapour from the leaf surface, keeping the diffusion gradient steep.
parts.working: B1 prediction: rate increases with wind speed, with biological reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student predicts that the rate of transpiration will fall in a straight line as relative humidity rises. Results (arbitrary units): 40 % humidity – 5.0; 60 % – 3.8; 80 % – 2.0; 90 % – 1.8; 100 % – 1.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's prediction using the data.
parts.answer: The prediction is partly supported: the rate falls as humidity rises. But the fall is not linear: it is steepest between 60 % and 80 % (−1.8 units) and levels off at 90–100 % (−0.1 units between 90 % and 100 %). Near 100 % the water vapour gradient is almost zero, so transpiration cannot fall much further, and a small loss continues through the cuticle.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate falls as humidity rises (partly supported); 1 mark: not linear – the fall slows to a small change near 90–100 %; 1 mark: the gradient is near zero, so the rate approaches a minimum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the rate from 80 % to 100 % humidity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student's hypothesis: 'The rate of xylem flow in a stem is proportional to the cross-sectional area of its xylem.' Stem A: xylem area 2.0 mm², flow 3.6 mm³ h⁻¹. Stem B: xylem area 3.5 mm²; observed flow 5.9 mm³ h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the flow predicted for stem B by the hypothesis, using stem A.
parts.working: B1 flow per mm² = 1.8; 1.8 × 3.5 = 6.3 mm³ h⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between the predicted and observed flows for stem B, as a percentage of the predicted flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the hypothesis is supported, and suggest one reason for the difference.
parts.answer: Broadly supported, since the observed flow is within about 6 % of the prediction. The difference could be due to differences in the diameter or number of xylem vessels per unit area, or to measurement error.
parts.working: 1 mark: hypothesis broadly supported (within 6 %); 1 mark: a valid reason, e.g. vessel diameter/number differs, or measurement error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student writes: 'Plants transpire because they have stomata.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the flaw in the statement and rewrite it as a testable hypothesis.
parts.answer: The statement is an explanation of a fact rather than a testable relationship between two variables. Testable hypothesis: as the stomatal density on a leaf increases, the rate of transpiration increases, because more pores allow more diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf.
parts.working: 1 mark: not testable / no measurable variables named; 1 mark: a hypothesis with an IV, DV and a biological reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis for your testable hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between stomatal density and the rate of transpiration.
parts.working: B1 null hypothesis: no relationship/correlation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In summer, a complete ring of bark (including the phloem and cambium, but not the xylem) is removed from around a tree trunk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of the ring on the thickness of the bark above the ring after 2 months, and explain.
parts.answer: The bark above the ring will swell and thicken, because sucrose and other phloem products moving down from the leaves cannot pass the ring and accumulate above it. Tissue below the ring receives less sugar and may shrink or die.
parts.working: 1 mark: swelling/thickening above ring; 1 mark: phloem sap (sucrose) cannot pass the ring so accumulates above; 1 mark: tissue below ring receives less sugar (shrinks or dies).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what happens to the xylem flow above the ring, and explain.
parts.answer: The xylem flow above the ring continues, because the ring removes only the bark and phloem and leaves the xylem intact; water still moves up by the transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem flow continues; 1 mark: ring removes only the phloem/bark, xylem intact so transpiration pull still moves water up.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of error that could make the bubble move too slowly in a potometer.
parts.answer: Any two of: an air leak at a joint of the apparatus; air bubbles already in the xylem of the shoot; a bubble that sticks in the capillary tube; a capillary tube with uneven bore (so the volume per mm is not constant).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid sources of error (leaks, air in xylem, bubble sticking, uneven bore).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student should wait about 10 minutes after setting up the potometer before taking the first reading.
parts.answer: Cutting and handling the shoot disturbs it; the shoot needs time to reach a steady rate of water uptake, so early readings may be too fast or too slow and are not representative.
parts.working: 1 mark: disturbance from setting up or cutting affects uptake; 1 mark: time is needed to reach a steady (equilibrated) rate before readings are valid.

stem: A student repeated the measurement of the distance moved by the bubble in 5 minutes three times with the same shoot. Readings: 4.2 mm, 4.6 mm and 4.4 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range of the three readings as a percentage of their mean, and state whether the readings are reliable.
parts.answer: Range = 0.4 mm; 0.4 ÷ 4.4 × 100 = 9.1 %. The readings are close together, so the measurement is repeatable (reliable).
parts.working: B1 range 0.4 mm and 0.4 ÷ 4.4 × 100 = 9.1 %; B1 small spread, so the readings are reproducible (reliable).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one thing that these three readings cannot show about the measurement.
parts.answer: Whether the measurement is accurate, i.e. whether the mean is close to the true value (a systematic error would shift all three readings equally).
parts.working: B1 repeats show precision (reliability) only, not accuracy or systematic error.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest an improvement that would make the measurement of the bubble movement more reliable.
parts.answer: Measure over a longer time (for example 10 minutes), so the distance moved is larger and the percentage uncertainty in reading the ruler is smaller. Mark the start and end positions of the bubble carefully, reading the ruler at eye level.
parts.working: 1 mark: longer timing interval gives a larger distance and a smaller percentage error; 1 mark: precise marking and reading at eye level (avoiding parallax).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could check that the potometer is airtight.
parts.answer: Seal all the joints with petroleum jelly and fill the apparatus with water. Check that no air bubbles appear and that the bubble does not move when the apparatus is set up, showing that there are no leaks.
parts.working: 1 mark: sealing joints and filling with water, with a test method; 1 mark: result to look for - no bubbles appear or the bubble does not move when no leaves are transpiring (no leaks).

stem: Four mass-loss readings for potato cylinders in the same solution were: 0.12 g, 0.15 g, 0.14 g and 0.42 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest a likely cause.
parts.answer: The anomalous result is 0.42 g. A likely cause is that the cylinder was not blotted dry, or was damaged, or was weighed incorrectly, so its mass was not due to the sucrose treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.42 g identified as anomalous; 1 mark: valid cause, e.g. not blotted dry, cylinder damaged, or weighing error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean mass loss using only the concordant results, to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student estimated the rate of water uptake from one reading: the bubble moved 6 mm in 5 minutes, giving a rate of 1.2 mm min⁻¹. The ruler has marks at 1 mm intervals and the start and end positions were judged by eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the distance, if the uncertainty of reading the ruler is ±0.5 mm and the distance is 6 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one reading is not reliable, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: A single reading cannot show whether the result can be repeated, and any random error in that one reading is not averaged out. Repeat the measurement at least three times and calculate the mean and range.
parts.working: 1 mark: one reading cannot show reproducibility / random error not averaged out; 1 mark: repeat at least three times and calculate a mean (and range).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two students recorded the time for the bubble to move 10 mm in the same potometer. Student 1 measured 4.0 min; student 2 measured 4.6 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between the two students' times, as a percentage of student 1's time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the type of error most likely to cause the difference between the two readings.
parts.answer: Random error: each student judged the start and stop of the bubble differently and had a different reaction time with the stopwatch. Repeating and averaging the readings would reduce this error.
parts.working: 1 mark: random error; 1 mark: different judgement / reaction time when starting and stopping the timer, reduced by repeats and a mean.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cobalt chloride paper turns from blue to pink when it contacts water. A student uses it to compare the transpiration rates of two leaves by placing a dry paper on each leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one limitation of using cobalt chloride paper to compare the rates of transpiration of two leaves.
parts.answer: It only shows whether water vapour is present (a qualitative result); it does not measure how much water is lost. Judging the end of the colour change is also subjective.
parts.working: B1 qualitative only / no measurement of volume or mass lost / subjective end point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement that would give a quantitative measure of transpiration.
parts.answer: Weigh the plant or leaf at the start and end of the test (or at regular intervals) to measure the mass of water lost, or use a potometer to measure the distance the bubble moves.
parts.working: 1 mark: a quantitative method (mass loss balance or potometer); 1 mark: measured at set intervals so rate can be calculated.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between random error and systematic error.
parts.answer: Random error causes readings to vary unpredictably above and below the true value; systematic error shifts all readings consistently in one direction.
parts.working: B1 random: unpredictable variation about true value; systematic: consistent bias in one direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of random error and one example of systematic error in a transpiration experiment.
parts.answer: Random: judging the bubble's position differently each time. Systematic: a ruler with a zero error, or a potometer joint that always leaks, so every reading is too small.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid random error example (judging bubble position, reaction time); 1 mark: valid systematic example (zero error, consistent leak, faulty timer).

stem: A student measured the rate of water uptake in a potometer in a room with a window open, causing draughts across the apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the draught could affect the readings.
parts.answer: Moving air removes water vapour from the leaf surface, so transpiration increases and the bubble moves faster. Draughts vary from one run to another, so the readings are inconsistent.
parts.working: 1 mark: moving air increases transpiration so readings are higher; 1 mark: draught varies between runs so readings are inconsistent (random error).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements and explain why each would improve reliability.
parts.answer: Any two, each with a reason: shield the apparatus from the window or move it into a draught-free room, so air movement is the same in every run; keep the temperature and humidity constant (for example in a growth chamber), so the transpiration rate is controlled and readings can be repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid improvements and 1 mark each for a reason that links it to reliability (controls a variable / reduces random variation).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student concluded that wind speed increases transpiration, using one potometer reading at 0 m s⁻¹ (distance 6 mm) and one at 3 m s⁻¹ (distance 15 mm) in 5 minutes. The two readings were taken on different days, from different plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's conclusion.
parts.answer: The conclusion is not reliable. Each wind speed has only one reading, and the two readings came from different plants on different days, so plant size, leaf area, temperature and humidity may have varied. The difference could be due to these uncontrolled variables, not to the wind.
parts.working: 1 mark: only one reading each, so no mean or range; 1 mark: different plants/days, so uncontrolled variables (leaf area, temperature, humidity) may explain the difference; 1 mark: conclusion not valid until variables controlled and repeats made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the variables could be controlled and how many repeats should be made.
parts.answer: Use the same plant and leaf area, with the same conditions on the same day. Repeat at least three times at each wind speed and calculate the mean rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: same plant / leaf area / conditions (controlled); 1 mark: at least three repeats at each wind speed, with a mean.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The bubble moved 25 mm (±1 mm) in 10 minutes (±0.5 min).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble and the percentage uncertainty in the rate, as the sum of the percentage uncertainties in the distance and the time.
parts.answer: Rate = 2.5 mm min⁻¹ (25 ÷ 10). Percentage uncertainty in distance = 1 ÷ 25 × 100 = 4 %; in time = 0.5 ÷ 10 × 100 = 5 %; total = 9 %.
parts.working: B1 rate = 2.5 mm min⁻¹; B1 distance uncertainty 4 %; B1 total 4 % + 5 % = 9 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which measurement gives the largest percentage uncertainty, and suggest how to reduce it.
parts.answer: Timing gives the largest percentage uncertainty (5 %). Timing over a longer period (for example 20 minutes) means the same reaction-time error is a smaller percentage of the total time.
parts.working: 1 mark: time (5 %) is the largest; 1 mark: longer timing interval reduces the percentage error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Potometer P has a capillary tube of internal diameter 0.5 mm. Potometer Q has a capillary tube of internal diameter 1.0 mm. A bubble moves 10 mm in each tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water (mm³) represented by a movement of 10 mm in each tube. Use V = πr²h, where r is half the internal diameter. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Potometer P: 1.96 mm³ (π × 0.25² × 10); potometer Q: 7.85 mm³ (π × 0.5² × 10).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which potometer gives the more sensitive measurement, and state one disadvantage of that tube.
parts.answer: Potometer P, with the narrower tube, is more sensitive: a given volume of water taken up moves the bubble further. A disadvantage is that the bubble is more likely to stick or be hard to move, so readings may be less reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: P is more sensitive (same volume gives larger distance); 1 mark: disadvantage - bubble may stick or be slower to move / more affected by small errors.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance crosses the phospholipid bilayer of a cell surface membrane most rapidly by simple diffusion?
A glucose
B carbon dioxide
C potassium ions
D amino acids
parts.answer: B carbon dioxide
parts.working: CO₂ is small and non-polar, so it passes between the hydrophobic fatty acid tails. Glucose and amino acids are polar and K⁺ is charged, so they need channel or carrier proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each of these components of a cell surface membrane:
(i) channel protein
(ii) carrier protein
(iii) cholesterol
(iv) glycolipid
parts.answer: (i) forms a water-filled pore that lets specific ions/polar molecules through by facilitated diffusion; (ii) binds a specific molecule and changes shape to move it across (facilitated diffusion or active transport); (iii) regulates fluidity/stability of the membrane, reduces permeability to water and ions; (iv) cell recognition / acts as antigen / receptor, helps cells attach to each other.
parts.working: 1 mark each: (i) hydrophilic pore for ions/polar molecules; (ii) binds specific solute, changes shape; (iii) controls fluidity / mechanical stability / reduces leakage of polar substances; (iv) recognition / antigen / cell adhesion / receptor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Membranes are found inside eukaryotic cells as well as around them. State three roles of membranes inside cells, giving an example of an organelle for each.
parts.answer: Compartmentalisation – keeps enzymes/reactions separate, e.g. lysosome keeps hydrolytic enzymes away from cytoplasm; site of attachment of enzymes / electron carriers, e.g. inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae) or thylakoid membranes in chloroplasts; transport/packaging of proteins in vesicles, e.g. rough ER and Golgi body; control of entry/exit of substances, e.g. nuclear envelope with pores.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three roles each with a correct example: separating reactions (lysosome/nucleus); holding enzymes or electron carriers (cristae/thylakoids); forming vesicles for transport (ER/Golgi); controlling what enters an organelle (nuclear envelope).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Wheat plants that survive cold winters in the north of Pakistan increase the proportion of cholesterol-like sterols and unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes in autumn. What is the main effect of this change at low temperatures?
A The membrane becomes more rigid, so fewer ions leak out.
B The membrane stays fluid enough for membrane proteins to work.
C Glycoproteins are replaced by glycolipids.
D The phospholipids form a single layer instead of a bilayer.
parts.answer: B The membrane stays fluid enough for membrane proteins to work.
parts.working: Kinks in unsaturated fatty acid tails stop phospholipids packing tightly, and sterols disrupt close packing at low temperature, so the membrane does not become a rigid gel and carriers/channels/enzymes can still move and function. A is the opposite effect; C and D are not caused by this change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the stages of cell signalling in which a signalling molecule released by one cell causes a response in a target cell some distance away.
parts.answer: Signalling cell releases the signal molecule (e.g. by exocytosis); it travels (by diffusion or in the blood) to the target cell; binds to a specific receptor (protein/glycoprotein) on the cell surface membrane with a complementary shape; receptor changes shape and activates a G protein/enzyme inside; a second messenger (e.g. cyclic AMP) is produced; this starts a cascade of enzyme activation that amplifies the signal and produces the response.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: release by signalling cell; transport to target; binding to complementary receptor on cell surface membrane; change in receptor shape / G protein activated; second messenger formed (e.g. cAMP); amplification / enzyme cascade → specific response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a signalling molecule that is a small, lipid-soluble steroid does not need a receptor on the cell surface membrane.
parts.answer: It is non-polar/lipid-soluble so it diffuses through the phospholipid bilayer; it binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus instead.
parts.working: 1: dissolves in / diffuses through bilayer; 1: receptor inside the cell (cytoplasm/nucleus).

stem:
Barley seedlings were grown at 5 °C or at 25 °C. The fatty acids of the root cell membrane phospholipids were analysed.
Growth temperature / °C: 5, 25
Percentage of fatty acids that are unsaturated / %: 78, 54

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain how the composition of the membranes differs between the two groups of plants.
parts.answer: Plants grown at 5 °C have 24 percentage points more unsaturated fatty acids (78 % v 54 %). Unsaturated fatty acid tails have C=C double bonds that make kinks, so the phospholipids cannot pack closely; this keeps the membrane fluid at low temperature.
parts.working: 1: data quote / difference of 24 %; 1: C=C double bonds cause kinks; 1: phospholipids less tightly packed → membrane stays fluid at low temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important for root cells to keep their membranes fluid at low temperatures.
parts.answer: Membrane proteins (carriers, channels, pumps) must be able to change shape/move to take up ions and water; vesicles must be able to fuse with membranes; a rigid membrane may crack/leak.
parts.working: Any two: carrier/channel proteins can work (ion uptake); proteins can move within bilayer; endocytosis/exocytosis possible; avoids rigid membrane breaking.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an electron micrograph of a liver cell, the cell surface membrane appears as two dark lines separated by a pale line. The total width of this 'railway track' on the photograph is 3.5 mm. The magnification is ×500 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual thickness of the membrane in nm.
parts.answer: 7 nm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the membrane appears as two dark lines with a pale line between them.
parts.answer: The dark lines are the hydrophilic phosphate heads (which take up the heavy-metal stain) of the two layers of phospholipids; the pale line is the hydrophobic fatty acid tails in the middle of the bilayer, which do not take up stain.
parts.working: 1: dark = phosphate heads/ hydrophilic regions stained; 1: pale = fatty acid tails / hydrophobic core.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a historical experiment, all the lipids were extracted from 4.0 × 10⁹ red blood cells and spread on the surface of water as a layer one molecule thick. The lipid layer covered 1.10 m². The surface area of one red blood cell was taken to be 140 µm². (1 µm² = 1 × 10⁻¹² m²)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the red blood cells in m².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the area of the lipid layer to the surface area of the cells. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what this result suggests about the structure of the cell surface membrane, and why red blood cells were a good choice for this experiment.
parts.answer: The lipid covers about twice the cell surface area, so the membrane is a lipid bilayer (two molecules thick) with heads facing water on both sides. Mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles, so all the lipid comes from the cell surface membrane.
parts.working: 1: ratio ≈ 2 → two layers / bilayer; 1: hydrophilic heads face the aqueous medium on each side / tails inward; 1: no nucleus/organelles so only the surface membrane contributes lipid.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Liver cells respond to the hormone glucagon by breaking down glycogen. Liver cells were treated with a protease enzyme that digests proteins on the outer surface of the cells only, then washed. They were then exposed to either glucagon or to a lipid-soluble steroid hormone that also produces a response in liver cells.
Treatment: no protease + glucagon → response; protease + glucagon → no response; protease + steroid → response

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results.
parts.answer: Glucagon is water-soluble and cannot cross the bilayer, so it acts through a protein receptor on the outer surface of the membrane; the protease digested/changed the shape of the receptor so glucagon could not bind and no second messenger was made. The steroid crosses the bilayer and binds to a receptor inside the cell, which the protease (acting only outside) did not reach.
parts.working: 1: glucagon binds to a (glyco)protein receptor on the cell surface; 1: protease hydrolyses receptor / binding site lost so no response; 1: steroid diffuses through bilayer to internal receptor, not affected by protease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the cells were washed after protease treatment and before the hormone was added.
parts.answer: To remove the protease so that it could not digest the hormone (glucagon is a peptide) or continue acting during the test.
parts.working: 1: remove protease so it cannot hydrolyse glucagon/peptide hormone (or keep only one variable changed).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a healthy intestinal cell, a signalling molecule binds to a receptor and activates a G protein. The G protein activates an enzyme that makes cyclic AMP (cAMP) from ATP. The G protein normally switches itself off after a few seconds. Cholera toxin changes the G protein so that it cannot switch itself off. cAMP causes chloride ion channels in the cell surface membrane to open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cAMP is described as a second messenger.
parts.answer: The signalling molecule (first messenger) does not enter the cell; cAMP is produced inside the cell when the receptor is activated and carries the signal on to enzymes/channels in the cytoplasm.
parts.working: 1: first messenger stays outside / binds surface receptor; 1: cAMP made inside cell and relays/passes on the signal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the information to suggest why infection with cholera causes large volumes of watery faeces.
parts.answer: The G protein stays active, so cAMP is made continuously; chloride channels stay open and Cl⁻ ions move out of cells into the lumen of the intestine; this lowers the water potential of the lumen, so water leaves the cells by osmosis into the lumen.
parts.working: 1: continuous cAMP production / signal never switched off; 1: Cl⁻ secreted into lumen continuously; 1: lower water potential in lumen → water moves out by osmosis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would NOT increase the rate of diffusion of oxygen from the alveoli into the blood?
A a larger surface area of alveoli
B a steeper concentration gradient of oxygen
C a thicker layer of cells between the air and the blood
D a higher temperature in the lungs
parts.answer: C a thicker layer of cells between the air and the blood
parts.working: Rate of diffusion is greater with larger surface area and steeper gradient, and is faster at higher temperature (more kinetic energy). A thicker barrier increases the diffusion distance, so it lowers the rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define water potential and state its value for pure water at atmospheric pressure.
parts.answer: Water potential is the tendency of water to move out of a solution/system (by osmosis); pure water has a water potential of 0 kPa.
parts.working: 1: tendency of water (molecules) to move from a region; 1: pure water = 0 (kPa) / highest value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define osmosis.
parts.answer: Net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane.
parts.working: 1: net movement of water from higher to lower water potential; 1: through a partially permeable membrane.

stem: Slices of cucumber are firm when placed in tap water but become soft and floppy after 30 minutes in strongly salted water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cucumber slices become soft in salted water.
parts.answer: Salt water has a lower water potential than the cucumber cells; water leaves the cells by osmosis through the partially permeable cell surface membrane; the vacuole and cytoplasm shrink, so the cells lose turgor / become flaccid (and may plasmolyse).
parts.working: 1: solution has lower water potential than cells; 1: water leaves by osmosis across partially permeable membrane; 1: loss of turgor / cells flaccid / plasmolysis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why slices left in tap water do not burst.
parts.answer: The cellulose cell wall is strong/inelastic and resists further expansion, so pressure potential builds up until water stops entering.
parts.working: 1: cell wall resists expansion / pressure potential rises.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A muscle cell is respiring aerobically. Explain why oxygen diffuses into the cell from the tissue fluid.
parts.answer: The cell uses oxygen in respiration, so the oxygen concentration inside is lower than in tissue fluid; oxygen molecules move down this concentration gradient (net movement) through the bilayer, because they are small and non-polar.
parts.working: 1: oxygen used in respiration keeps concentration inside low / gradient maintained; 1: net movement down gradient through phospholipid bilayer (small, non-polar).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why this diffusion does not need ATP.
parts.answer: Diffusion is passive – it uses the kinetic energy of the molecules, not energy from respiration.
parts.working: 1: passive / kinetic energy of molecules.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A plant cell has a solute potential of −800 kPa and a pressure potential of +300 kPa. It is placed in a solution with a water potential of −600 kPa. Which row is correct?
A water potential of cell −1100 kPa; water enters the cell
B water potential of cell −500 kPa; water enters the cell
C water potential of cell −500 kPa; water leaves the cell
D water potential of cell −1100 kPa; water leaves the cell
parts.answer: C water potential of cell −500 kPa; water leaves the cell
parts.working: ψ = ψs + ψp = −800 + 300 = −500 kPa. The solution (−600 kPa) has a lower water potential, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis. A/D add the values wrongly; B gives the wrong direction.

stem:
Three neighbouring cells in a leaf have these values.
Cell X: solute potential −950 kPa, pressure potential +350 kPa
Cell Y: solute potential −700 kPa, pressure potential +200 kPa
Cell Z: solute potential −1200 kPa, pressure potential +500 kPa
X is next to both Y and Z.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water potential of each cell.
parts.answer: X −600 kPa; Y −500 kPa; Z −700 kPa

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of net water movement between the cells and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Y → X → Z. Water moves by osmosis from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential: −500 → −600 → −700 kPa.
parts.working: 1: Y to X and X to Z; 1: from higher to lower water potential by osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why cell Z can have the highest pressure potential even though it has the lowest water potential.
parts.answer: Z has the most negative solute potential (most solutes), so it has taken in water until its wall exerts a large pressure; pressure potential rises but not enough to cancel the very low solute potential.
parts.working: 1: very negative solute potential / high solute concentration draws in water; 1: wall pushes back → high ψp, but ψs + ψp still lowest.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student filled a length of Visking tubing with a mixture of starch solution and glucose solution, tied both ends, rinsed the outside and placed it in a boiling tube of distilled water. After 30 minutes she tested samples of the water outside the tubing.
Iodine test on outside water: stays orange-brown
Benedict's test on outside water: orange precipitate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain these results.
parts.answer: Glucose is a small molecule that passes through the pores of the partially permeable tubing and diffuses down its concentration gradient into the water, so Benedict's is positive; starch molecules are too large to pass through the pores, so no starch outside and iodine stays orange-brown.
parts.working: 1: Visking tubing is partially permeable / has small pores; 1: glucose small, diffuses out down concentration gradient; 1: starch too large, stays inside.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain any change in the mass of the tubing during the 30 minutes.
parts.answer: Mass increases: the contents have a lower water potential (solutes inside) than distilled water, so water enters by osmosis.
parts.working: 1: increase; 1: water enters by osmosis as water potential inside is lower.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Strips of red onion epidermis were placed in sucrose solutions for 20 minutes. 50 cells of each strip were examined with a microscope and the percentage of cells that were plasmolysed was recorded.
Sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³: 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50
Cells plasmolysed / %: 4, 22, 41, 68, 90
Incipient plasmolysis is taken to be the point where 50 % of cells are plasmolysed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use linear interpolation between two readings to find the sucrose concentration that causes incipient plasmolysis. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.42 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student was given the conversion water potential (kPa) = −2500 × sucrose concentration (mol dm⁻³). Use your unrounded answer to (a) to estimate the solute potential of the onion cells. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: −2500 × 0.4167 = −1041.7 → −1040 kPa (accept −1050 kPa from 0.42). At incipient plasmolysis ψp = 0, so ψ of cell = ψs = ψ of solution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the water potential of the cells is equal to their solute potential at incipient plasmolysis.
parts.answer: The protoplast is just pulling away from the wall, so the wall exerts no pressure: pressure potential is zero, so ψ = ψs.
parts.working: 1: pressure potential = 0 (wall no longer pushing on protoplast).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A potato cell has a solute potential of −1100 kPa and a pressure potential of +400 kPa. It is placed in a large volume of solution with a water potential of −900 kPa and left until no further net movement of water occurs. Assume the solute potential of the cell does not change significantly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water potential of the cell at the start and its pressure potential at equilibrium.
parts.answer: start ψ = −700 kPa; at equilibrium ψp = +200 kPa
parts.working: ψ start = −1100 + 400 = −700 kPa (B1). At equilibrium ψ cell = ψ solution = −900 kPa (M1); ψp = −900 − (−1100) = +200 kPa (A1).

parts.label: b
