parts.text: State one other variable the student should have controlled and explain how it could be controlled.
parts.answer: The mass or size of the apple pieces: cut with a cork borer to the same size and weigh each piece before the experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark: named variable (size or mass of pieces). 1 mark: a valid method to control it.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to investigate whether membrane thickness affects the rate at which a dye diffuses through a membrane. She has membranes of two thicknesses, 0.5 mm and 1.5 mm, cut to the same area, and a dye solution at a fixed concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a variable plan by identifying: the independent variable; the dependent variable; two controlled variables; and one control experiment.
parts.answer: Independent: membrane thickness (0.5 mm and 1.5 mm). Dependent: rate of diffusion, for example the absorbance of the receiving water after a fixed time. Controlled: temperature, dye concentration, volume of dye and water, membrane area, stirring and time. Control: the same set-up with water and no dye on either side, to zero the colorimeter.
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable. 1 mark: dependent variable. 1 mark: two named controlled variables. 1 mark: a valid control experiment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why she should use more than one membrane of each thickness.
parts.answer: Repeats show whether the results are reliable and allow a mean and spread to be calculated. A single membrane may have an individual defect or variation in pores, so the result may reflect that one sample.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeats show reliability and allow a mean and spread. 1 mark: a single membrane may have an individual defect or variation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A photomicrograph of a nucleus shows a diameter of 36 mm. The magnification of the photomicrograph is ×1200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the nucleus in µm.
parts.answer: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 36 mm ÷ 1200 = 0.030 mm = 30 µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: 36 ÷ 1200 (0.030 mm). 1 mark: 30 µm (converting mm to µm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the equation that links magnification, image size and actual size.
parts.answer: magnification = image size ÷ actual size
parts.working: 1 mark: correct equation rearranged or stated.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student calibrated an eyepiece graticule against a stage micrometer using a ×100 objective lens. 20 eyepiece divisions lined up exactly with 3 stage micrometer divisions, each 10 µm long. She then measured a bacterial cell as 14 eyepiece divisions long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece division in µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1.5 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the length of the bacterial cell in µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: 21 µm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student changes to a ×40 objective lens. Calculate the length of one eyepiece division at ×40.
parts.answer: Magnification falls from ×100 to ×40, so each division is larger: 1.5 × 100 ÷ 40 = 3.75 µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: method (1.5 × 100 ÷ 40, inverse to magnification). 1 mark: 3.75 µm.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A micrograph includes a scale bar. The scale bar represents 20 µm and measures 3.4 cm long on the printout. A cell on the same printout measures 5.1 cm across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the cell in µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct ratio using the scale bar. 1 mark: 30 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the printout.
parts.answer: 3.4 cm = 34 000 µm; magnification = 34 000 µm ÷ 20 µm = ×1700.
parts.working: 1 mark: converting 3.4 cm to 34 000 µm and dividing by 20 µm. 1 mark: ×1700.

author: HomiLabs

stem: At a total magnification of ×100, the diameter of the field of view under a microscope is 1.8 mm. A student changes to a higher-power objective lens so that the total magnification becomes ×400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the diameter of the field of view at ×400, in µm.
parts.answer: Field of view is inversely proportional to magnification. 1.8 mm = 1800 µm; 1800 × 100 ÷ 400 = 450 µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1800 µm (converting mm to µm). 1 mark: 1800 × 100 ÷ 400 = 450 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cell has a length of 75 µm. Calculate how many such cells could be laid end to end across the field of view at ×400.
parts.working: 1 mark: 450 ÷ 75. 1 mark: 6 cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a field of view at a higher magnification shows fewer cells.
parts.answer: A higher magnification shows a smaller area of the specimen, so fewer cells are in view.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller area seen at higher magnification.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured the length of a plant cell under the microscope before and after treating the tissue with a solution. Before treatment the cell measured 25.0 µm; after treatment it measured 20.5 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in length.
parts.working: 1 mark: (change ÷ original) × 100. 1 mark: −18 % (a decrease of 18 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the cell increased or decreased in length, and explain in terms of water potential.
parts.answer: The cell decreased in length, shrinking because the treatment solution had a lower water potential than the cell contents, so water left the cell by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: decrease in length. 1 mark: solution with lower water potential than the cell, so water leaves by osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student should measure several cells.
parts.answer: Cells vary in size, so several cells give a mean and show the variation between cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: cells vary, so a mean and spread are needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The thickness of a cell surface membrane is about 7.5 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert this thickness into µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.0075 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this thickness into mm.
parts.working: 1 mark: 7.5 × 10⁻⁶ mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an electron microscope is needed to see the membrane.
parts.answer: The membrane is far smaller than the resolution limit of the light microscope (about 200 nm), so it cannot be resolved. An electron microscope has a much higher resolution, down to about 0.5 nm, so it can resolve the membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: the membrane is below the resolution of a light microscope (about 200 nm). 1 mark: the electron microscope resolves much smaller distances.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A photomicrograph of a root cell shows the cell width as 19.8 mm. The printed magnification is ×450.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the real width of the cell in µm.
parts.working: 1 mark: 19.8 ÷ 450 (mm). 1 mark: 44 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the printed magnification may not be the exact magnification of the picture.
parts.answer: The picture has been enlarged or reduced after printing, so the printed magnification is only correct for the original size.
parts.working: 1 mark: picture resized, so printed magnification no longer applies.

author: HomiLabs

stem: At ×40 total magnification, 1 eyepiece division equals 2.5 µm on a calibrated graticule. A student changes to a ×100 objective lens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece division at ×100 and explain your method.
parts.answer: 2.5 × 40 ÷ 100 = 1.0 µm. The magnification has increased 2.5 times (100 ÷ 40), so each division represents 2.5 times less length.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1.0 µm. 1 mark: method, the division length falls in inverse proportion to magnification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mitochondrion is 7.5 µm long. Calculate how many eyepiece divisions it spans at ×100.
parts.answer: 7.5 ÷ 1.0 = 7.5 divisions.
parts.working: 1 mark: 7.5 ÷ 1.0. 1 mark: 7.5 divisions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A stage micrometer has divisions 10 µm long. 22 stage micrometer divisions line up exactly with 35 eyepiece graticule divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece division in µm, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: 220 µm used as the total length. 1 mark: 6.29 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the value in part (a) is an estimate.
parts.answer: The lines never line up perfectly, so reading the alignment is approximate; the value depends on the person reading it, so calibrating over more divisions gives a more accurate value.
parts.working: 1 mark: alignment is read by eye and is approximate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measured the diameter of five red blood cells in the same field of view and recorded these diameters in µm: 9.1, 8.6, 9.4, 8.9, 9.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter in µm, to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark: 9.0 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the range of the results.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.8 µm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student should not use only one measurement as the diameter of a red blood cell.
parts.answer: Cells vary in size, so one cell may not represent the population. Several cells give a mean and show the spread of sizes.
parts.working: 1 mark: biological variation between cells. 1 mark: a mean and spread give a more reliable estimate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A photomicrograph contains a scale bar. The scale bar represents 10 µm and measures 4.6 cm on the printed picture. A nucleus measures 1.8 cm across on the same picture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the nucleus in µm, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct ratio using the scale bar. 1 mark: 3.91 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the picture.
parts.answer: 4.6 cm = 46 000 µm; magnification = 46 000 µm ÷ 10 µm = ×4600.
parts.working: 1 mark: 4.6 cm converted to 46 000 µm. 1 mark: ×4600.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a scale bar is more useful than a printed magnification when a picture is enlarged or reduced.
parts.answer: The scale bar is printed on the picture, so it is resized with the picture and its measurement stays correct. A printed magnification only applies to the original size.
parts.working: 1 mark: the scale bar changes size with the picture. 1 mark: a printed magnification is correct only for the original size.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the diameter of a cell in an image with a ruler marked in 1 mm divisions. The reading is 4.0 mm, and the uncertainty in the reading is ±0.5 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the measurement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the student could reduce the percentage uncertainty.
parts.answer: Measure a larger length, such as the total width of ten cells in a row divided by 10, so the same uncertainty is a smaller fraction of the value. Use a finer scale, such as a graticule or stage micrometer.
parts.working: 1 mark: measure a larger length and average. 1 mark: use a finer scale (graticule or micrometer).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A cylindrical cell is approximated as a cylinder with radius 3.0 µm and length 9.0 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the cell in µm³, using V = πr²h. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct substitution into πr²h. 1 mark: 254 µm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this volume is only an approximation.
parts.answer: Cells are not perfect cylinders, so their shape is irregular. The radius and length are estimates from a single measurement, which is also limited by the resolution of the microscope.
parts.working: 1 mark: real cells are not perfect cylinders. 1 mark: measured dimensions are estimates with limited accuracy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert the volume in part (a) into cm³.
parts.answer: 1 cm = 10 000 µm, so 1 cm³ = 10¹² µm³. 254 µm³ = 2.54 × 10⁻¹⁰ cm³.
parts.working: 1 mark: 2.54 × 10⁻¹⁰ cm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The diameter of the field of view at ×400 is 450 µm. A student models the field of view as a circle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of the field of view in µm², using A = πr². Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark: r = 225 µm and substitution. 1 mark: 1.59 × 10⁵ µm².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert the area in part (a) into mm².
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.159 mm².

parts.label: c
parts.text: A cell has a diameter of 10 µm. Estimate how many such cells would fit in the field of view if they could be packed without gaps, and explain why this is an overestimate.
parts.answer: Cell area = π × 5² = 78.5 µm²; field area ÷ cell area = 159 043 ÷ 78.5 ≈ 2025 cells. This is an overestimate because round cells cannot be packed without gaps between them.
parts.working: 1 mark: cell area π × 5². 1 mark: 2025 cells (about 2000). 1 mark: round cells leave gaps, so the estimate is too high.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to compare the rate at which two solutes of similar size cross an artificial lipid bilayer that has no protein channels. Urea is uncharged, with relative molecular mass 60. Sodium chloride is ionic. Both are at the same concentration on one side of the membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Urea crosses the lipid bilayer faster than sodium chloride, because urea is uncharged and dissolves in the lipid, whereas the charged ions cannot pass through the hydrophobic core.
parts.working: 1 mark: a clear, directional and testable statement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no difference in the rate at which urea and sodium chloride cross the lipid bilayer.
parts.working: 1 mark: no difference between the rates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: the solute (urea or sodium chloride). Dependent: the rate of movement, for example the time taken to reach equal concentration on both sides.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cells from a plant are placed in pure water and in 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution for 30 minutes, then examined under a microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what happens to the cell in each solution and explain your predictions.
parts.answer: In pure water the cell gains water by osmosis, because the water has a higher water potential than the cell contents; the cell becomes turgid and the protoplast is pressed against the cell wall. In 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose the solution has a lower water potential, so water leaves by osmosis; the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis).
parts.working: 1 mark: gain of water in pure water, with turgor. 1 mark: explanation using water potential and osmosis. 1 mark: water loss in sucrose, with a lower water potential outside. 1 mark: plasmolysis, the protoplast pulls away from the wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature of the plant cell that stops it bursting in pure water.
parts.answer: The cell wall is strong and resists the pressure from the vacuole, so the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting.
parts.working: 1 mark: the cell wall resists expansion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student tests whether adding cyanide affects the uptake of glucose by a cell culture. Cyanide stops the production of ATP. Glucose enters the cells by two routes: facilitated diffusion through carrier proteins, and active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis.
parts.answer: Cyanide reduces the rate of glucose uptake by the cells, because active transport needs ATP from aerobic respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: directional and testable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: Cyanide has no effect on the rate of glucose uptake by the cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: no effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the result and explain why the uptake does not fall to zero.
parts.answer: Uptake falls but does not reach zero, because glucose still enters by facilitated diffusion through carrier proteins down its concentration gradient, which needs no ATP.
parts.working: 1 mark: uptake falls but not to zero. 1 mark: facilitated diffusion down the gradient needs no ATP.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Visking tubing is used as a model of a partially permeable membrane. Two tubes are set up: tube 1 contains 1 % glucose solution and tube 2 contains 1 % starch solution. Both are placed in distilled water at 20 °C. After 30 minutes the water outside each tube is tested for glucose with Benedict's reagent and for starch with iodine solution. Glucose has relative molecular mass 180; starch molecules are very large.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the result of each test and explain each prediction.
parts.answer: Tube 1: glucose passes out through the pores, so the Benedict's test on the outside water is positive (a colour change from blue to green, yellow or red). Tube 2: starch molecules are too large to pass through the pores, so the iodine test on the outside water is negative (no blue-black colour).
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose positive outside. 1 mark: small molecules pass through the pores. 1 mark: starch negative outside. 1 mark: starch molecules are too large for the pores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable, and one control for this model.
parts.answer: Independent: the type of solute (glucose or starch), or the molecular size. Control: tubing with distilled water inside, placed in the same conditions, to show that the tubing does not give false positives.
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable. 1 mark: a valid control.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher heats a sample of cells to 60 °C for 5 minutes, then cools them to 37 °C and measures the uptake of glucose by active transport and the diffusion of oxygen directly across the lipid bilayer. The results of the heated cells are compared with unheated cells kept at 37 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how heating will affect (i) the uptake of glucose by active transport and (ii) the diffusion of oxygen across the bilayer. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: (i) Active transport is greatly reduced or stopped: heat denatures the carrier proteins so they cannot change shape, and it also damages the enzymes that make ATP. (ii) Oxygen diffusion is little affected: it is small and non-polar, diffuses directly through the bilayer without carriers, and heating may even increase fluidity slightly.
parts.working: 1 mark: (i) active transport reduced. 1 mark: (i) carriers denatured and ATP production lost. 1 mark: (ii) oxygen diffusion unchanged or slightly increased. 1 mark: (ii) small non-polar molecule diffusing without carriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a control that would show the effect in (i) is due to heat denaturation, not to the time spent away from 37 °C, and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: Cells kept at 37 °C for the same time, but not heated. Any difference from the heated cells is then caused by the heating, not by time or handling.
parts.working: 1 mark: unheated cells kept for the same time. 1 mark: isolates the effect of heat.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A cell has a fixed number of glucose carrier proteins in its membrane. Glucose enters the cell by facilitated diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an if-then prediction for what happens to the rate of uptake at a high glucose concentration if the number of carrier proteins is doubled.
parts.answer: If the number of carrier proteins doubles, the maximum rate of glucose uptake will roughly double, because at high glucose concentration the rate is limited by the number of carriers.
parts.working: 1 mark: the rate increases (roughly doubles). 1 mark: at high concentration the carriers are saturated, so the number of carriers limits the rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what results would show that the number of carriers is the limiting factor at high glucose concentration but not at low concentration.
parts.answer: At low glucose the rate depends on the glucose concentration, not the carrier number, because the carriers are not fully occupied. At high glucose the rate is set by the number of carriers, which are all occupied.
parts.working: 1 mark: at low glucose, the rate depends on concentration, not the number of carriers. 1 mark: at high glucose, the rate depends on the number of carriers.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Membranes contain phospholipids with saturated fatty acid tails (straight) or unsaturated tails (with kinks). A student plans to test how temperature affects membrane fluidity, using artificial membranes made from two lipid mixtures: one with mostly saturated tails and one with mostly unsaturated tails.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the fluidity of each membrane changes as temperature falls, and explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Both membranes become less fluid as temperature falls, because the molecules have less kinetic energy and move less. The saturated membrane becomes rigid at a higher temperature, because its straight tails pack closely together. The unsaturated membrane stays fluid to lower temperatures, because the kinks stop the tails packing closely.
parts.working: 1 mark: both membranes lose fluidity as temperature falls. 1 mark: less kinetic energy, so less movement. 1 mark: saturated tails pack closely and become rigid at a higher temperature. 1 mark: unsaturated kinks keep the membrane fluid at lower temperatures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the dependent variable.
parts.answer: For example, the rate of diffusion of a dye through the membrane, or the measured fluidity.
parts.working: 1 mark: a measurable indicator of fluidity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A drug is found to stop endocytosis in cells but to have no effect on simple diffusion of small molecules. Cells are exposed to fluorescent dextran (a large polysaccharide) and to small glucose molecules, with and without the drug.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the results for the uptake of dextran and of glucose, with and without the drug, and explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Dextran uptake is strongly reduced by the drug, because a large molecule can only enter by endocytosis, which forms vesicles at the membrane. Glucose uptake is not changed by the drug, because glucose enters through carrier proteins by facilitated diffusion and not by endocytosis. Without the drug both are taken up normally.
parts.working: 1 mark: dextran uptake reduced. 1 mark: large molecules need endocytosis. 1 mark: glucose unchanged. 1 mark: glucose uses carriers, not endocytosis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a control that would confirm the drug does not damage the cell membrane.
parts.answer: Treat cells with the drug and a dye that only enters dead or damaged cells (such as trypan blue), and compare with untreated cells; little dye uptake shows the membranes are intact.
parts.working: 1 mark: a damage indicator dye in drug-treated and untreated cells. 1 mark: little uptake shows the membrane is intact.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to test whether the surface area of a cell affects the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis, with a direction.
parts.answer: Cells with a larger surface area to volume ratio take up oxygen faster per unit of volume.
parts.working: 1 mark: directional and testable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no relationship between surface area to volume ratio and the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: no relationship.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict which cell, a small cell or a large cell, will supply oxygen to its centre more efficiently, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: The small cell, because it has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so there is more membrane available per unit of cell volume for oxygen to diffuse across.
parts.working: 1 mark: small cell (larger SA:V). 1 mark: more membrane per unit volume for diffusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A potato cylinder is placed in pure water at 20 °C. Its mass is measured every 10 minutes until the mass stops increasing, after about 2 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the shape of the graph of mass against time, and explain why the curve levels off.
parts.answer: The mass rises quickly at first, then more slowly, and levels off. The water potential gradient is steepest at first and falls as the cells take up water. The cell wall and turgor pressure resist further expansion, so net uptake stops at equilibrium.
parts.working: 1 mark: rapid rise at first. 1 mark: the gradient falls as the cells gain water. 1 mark: turgor pressure and the cell wall stop net uptake at equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the mass if the cylinder were placed in 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose instead, and explain.
parts.answer: The mass would fall, because the sucrose solution has a lower water potential than the cell contents, so water leaves by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: mass falls. 1 mark: lower water potential outside, so water leaves by osmosis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The rate of glucose uptake into a cell increases with glucose concentration but levels off at high concentration. At 4 mmol dm⁻³ the uptake rate is 60 % of the maximum rate, and the maximum rate is 150 nmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of uptake at 4 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 0.60 × 150 = 90 nmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark: 90 nmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the rate of uptake if the glucose concentration is increased to 40 mmol dm⁻³, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The rate would be close to the maximum, about 150 nmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹ and not much higher. At this concentration almost all the carrier proteins are occupied, so a further increase in glucose has little effect; the rate is limited by the number of carriers.
parts.working: 1 mark: close to the maximum (about 150). 1 mark: carriers almost all occupied (saturated). 1 mark: rate limited by carrier number, not glucose concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Light intensity is known to affect the uptake of mineral ions by plant roots. A student plans an investigation of this effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Light intensity has no effect on the rate of mineral ion uptake by plant roots.
parts.working: 1 mark: no effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a prediction for what happens to ion uptake as light intensity increases, and give a reason based on the source of ATP.
parts.answer: Uptake increases as light intensity increases (up to a limit), because photosynthesis in the leaves increases and supplies more sugars to the roots. Respiration in the roots uses these sugars to make more ATP, which powers active transport of the ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: uptake increases with light. 1 mark: more photosynthesis, so more sugars supplied to the roots. 1 mark: more respiration, so more ATP for active transport.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Leaf discs are placed in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution and in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ glucose solution. Glucose can enter the cells by facilitated diffusion, but sucrose cannot cross the cell membrane. The mass of the discs is measured over 2 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the change in mass of the discs in each solution over 2 hours and explain each prediction.
parts.answer: Sucrose: the discs lose mass steadily, because water leaves by osmosis and the sucrose cannot enter the cells to reduce the water potential difference. Glucose: the discs lose mass at first but then regain some mass or lose less, because glucose enters the cells down its gradient, which lowers the water potential inside, so water re-enters.
parts.working: 1 mark: sucrose loss of mass. 1 mark: sucrose cannot enter, so the gradient persists. 1 mark: glucose loss at first, then recovery or smaller loss. 1 mark: glucose enters down its gradient, reducing the water potential difference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one control used in this investigation.
parts.answer: Leaf discs placed in distilled water.
parts.working: 1 mark: discs in distilled water.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Human red blood cells are placed in 0.30 mol dm⁻³ urea solution (urea passes freely through the membrane) and in 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sodium chloride (which does not pass freely through the membrane). The volume of the cells in each solution is observed for 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the change in volume of the cells in each solution during the 10 minutes and explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Sodium chloride: the cells shrink, because the solution has a lower water potential than the cells, so water leaves by osmosis and the sodium chloride does not enter to balance it. Urea: little change at first, because the urea concentration is about isotonic with the cell contents; urea then enters the cells and water follows by osmosis, so the cells slowly swell.
parts.working: 1 mark: sodium chloride cells shrink, water leaves by osmosis. 1 mark: NaCl cannot cross, so shrinkage continues. 1 mark: urea little change at first. 1 mark: urea enters over time and water follows, so swelling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: Cells in 0.15 mol dm⁻³ sodium chloride (about 0.9 %, isotonic with the cells): their volume should not change. This shows that the changes are caused by the solutes and not by handling.
parts.working: 1 mark: cells in isotonic 0.15 mol dm⁻³ NaCl. 1 mark: no change shows the solute effects, not handling, cause the changes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will cut 2 cm cubes of apple with a scalpel on a white tile, then place each cube in a beaker of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution at room temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Scalpel: very sharp and can cut fingers, so cut on the tile, cut away from the body and keep the blade covered when not in use. Glass beakers: can break and cut, so check for cracks, handle with care and clear up breakages at once.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Low risk: the materials are not harmful and the main hazard (the scalpel) can be controlled with simple precautions.
parts.working: 1 mark: low, with a reason based on the hazards and controls.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student heats a water bath with a Bunsen burner to 60 °C for an osmosis experiment. A bottle of ethanol, used to make a dye solution, is kept on the bench close to the burner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Ethanol is highly flammable, and its vapour can catch fire from the flame: keep ethanol away from the flame and keep the bottle closed. Hot water can scald: use a thermostatically controlled electric water bath, or handle the beakers with tongs and wear eye protection.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4). Accept: beaker tipping (stable tripod, heatproof mat); burns from hot apparatus (let it cool).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium risk: a flammable liquid is kept close to an open flame and hot water is used, so the risk is higher unless the precautions are followed.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium, with the reason that flammable liquid and flame are close.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student stains a yeast suspension with methylene blue solution, which is harmful if swallowed and irritates the eyes. She then views the stained cells under a microscope, using a glass coverslip.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this investigation and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Methylene blue is harmful if swallowed and irritates the eyes: wear goggles and gloves, wipe up spills and never pipette by mouth. The glass coverslip and slide can break and cut fingers: handle them by the edges and put broken glass in the glass bin. Accept also: hot microscope lamp (switch off before handling).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to hold cells in a water bath at 60 °C for 30 minutes to denature the membrane proteins. The water bath is an electric model standing on the bench near a sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hot water can scald the skin: use tongs and heatproof gloves, and let the bath cool before emptying it. Electricity and water near the sink: keep the cable and plug away from water, keep the bath on a dry surface and switch off before handling; avoid spills.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium risk: hot water and electrical equipment near water are both hazards, but they can be controlled with simple precautions.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium, with a reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to check the temperature safely and accurately.
parts.answer: Use a thermometer placed in the water bath, and read it through the glass or without touching the hot water.
parts.working: 1 mark: thermometer in the bath, read without contact with hot water.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to collect cheek cells from her own mouth with a cotton bud, place them in a salt solution, add a stain and view them under a microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one biological hazard and one chemical hazard, and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Biological: cells from the mouth may carry microorganisms, so use only her own cells, do not share the cotton bud, and disinfect the bench afterwards. Chemical: the stain (for example methylene blue) is harmful if swallowed and irritates the eyes, so wear goggles and gloves and wipe up spills.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and justify it. Say how the risk would change if the cells came from other people.
parts.answer: Low risk with the student's own cells, dilute solutions and simple precautions. The risk would be higher if cells from other people were used, because of possible infections.
parts.working: 1 mark: low risk, with a justification based on own cells and controls. 1 mark: higher risk if other people's cells are used.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student will prepare 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution to adjust the pH of buffer solutions for an investigation into diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazard in this investigation and state one precaution.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive and can burn skin and eyes. Wear goggles and gloves, add solid to water slowly with stirring, and wash splashes at once with plenty of water.
parts.working: 1 mark: corrosive (burns the skin and eyes). 1 mark: a valid precaution (goggles, gloves, washing spills).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the solution should be as dilute as the experiment allows.
parts.answer: A more dilute solution is less corrosive and less likely to cause severe burns, so the risk is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower concentration gives a lower risk.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student prepares wet mounts of cells on glass slides, covers them with coverslips and views them under a microscope with an electric lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Broken glass slides or coverslips can cut the fingers: handle by the edges and put broken glass in a glass bin. The electric lamp can give an electric shock and gets very hot: check the cable, switch off and let it cool before changing the bulb. Accept also: liquid spilt near the lamp (wipe spills at once and keep liquids away from the lamp).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student views cells stained with a fluorescent dye under an ultraviolet (UV) lamp. She holds the lamp close to the cells and does not wear eye protection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazard and explain why it is a risk.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet light can damage the eyes and skin. The damage may not be felt at the time and can appear later, and it is greater when the lamp is close and the exposure is long.
parts.working: 1 mark: UV damages eyes and skin. 1 mark: damage may be delayed, and risk rises with closeness and time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two precautions.
parts.answer: Wear UV-blocking goggles or safety glasses; keep the lamp at a distance and switch it off when not in use; limit the exposure time; use a shield or box around the lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid precautions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the overall level of risk, before and after the precautions are used.
parts.answer: Medium risk without precautions, because the lamp is held close and no eye protection is worn; low risk once goggles, distance and short exposure are used.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium before precautions. 1 mark: low after precautions, with a reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Students grow a yeast culture at 30 °C in a flask on the bench for an experiment on membrane transport. At the end of the experiment the culture is poured down the sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Yeast cultures can contaminate the bench and hands: wipe the bench with disinfectant and wash hands after handling. Pouring the culture down the sink can contaminate the drains: disinfect the culture first and then pour it away with plenty of water, following the school's disposal rules.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Low risk: yeast is a non-pathogenic microorganism, and hygiene and disinfection control the risk.
parts.working: 1 mark: low, with a reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student heats 100 cm³ of water in a beaker on a tripod over a Bunsen burner to 80 °C, to test the effect of temperature on red blood cell membranes. She then transfers the hot water to test-tubes using a glass pipette.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hot water spilling or scalding: use a heatproof beaker, tongs and a stable tripod or heatproof mat. The glass pipette can break and cut: wrap it in a cloth, or use a plastic pipette. Accept also: a Bunsen flame near loose hair or flammable items (tie back hair, keep items away).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the risk is higher than in an experiment at 30 °C.
parts.answer: Water at 80 °C can cause severe burns, and it can boil and spit, so injuries are more serious if it spills. The precautions must be stricter.
parts.working: 1 mark: more severe burns or spitting at 80 °C. 1 mark: stricter precautions are needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student proposes to dissolve a stain in ethanol, apply it to cells on a slide, and then dry the slide over a Bunsen burner before viewing it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the proposed method. Identify the main hazard, explain why it is a risk, and suggest a safer alternative.
parts.answer: The main hazard is ethanol, which is highly flammable: its vapour can ignite near the open flame and cause a fire. A safer alternative is a water-based stain, with the slide air-dried at room temperature or dried on a heat block with no open flame.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethanol is highly flammable. 1 mark: vapour can ignite near the flame. 1 mark: a water-based stain or air-drying. 1 mark: overall unacceptable as proposed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the level of risk as proposed, and whether the method should go ahead.
parts.answer: High risk as proposed. It should not go ahead with the flame; the safer method should be used and approved by the teacher before work starts.
parts.working: 1 mark: high risk. 1 mark: do not proceed as proposed; use the safer method with teacher approval.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student uses 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid to adjust the pH of a buffer solution for an osmosis experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazard and suggest a precaution.
parts.answer: Sulfuric acid is corrosive and burns the skin and eyes, and damages clothing: wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves, add the acid to water slowly and wash spills with plenty of water.
parts.working: 1 mark: corrosive (burns skin and eyes). 1 mark: a valid precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why 0.5 mol dm⁻³ acid is safer than 2.0 mol dm⁻³ acid.
parts.answer: A lower concentration is less corrosive, so a splash causes less severe injury.
parts.working: 1 mark: less corrosive at lower concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student grows a non-pathogenic bacterial culture on an agar plate at 25 °C for 2 days, and makes a second plate of sterile agar as a control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Bacteria can contaminate hands and benches: wash hands and disinfect the bench before and after work. The plate lid can be opened and let bacteria into the air: keep the lid taped shut and do not open the plates. Accept also: plates must be sterilised before disposal (for example in an autoclave).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk.
parts.answer: Low risk for a non-pathogenic strain used with aseptic technique.
parts.working: 1 mark: low, with the reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans an experiment with four parts: (1) cutting tissue with a scalpel; (2) using 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide; (3) heating water to 60 °C with a Bunsen burner; and (4) using an electric balance on the bench next to the water bath.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rank the hazards from most to least serious, and justify your order.
parts.answer: Most serious: sodium hydroxide, which is corrosive and can cause permanent eye damage. Next: the open flame with hot water, which can cause fire and burns. Then the scalpel, which can be controlled, and the balance, which only becomes a hazard if water is spilt on it.
parts.working: 1 mark: sodium hydroxide ranked as most serious, with a reason. 1 mark: flame and hot water ranked next, with a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each hazard, state one control measure.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide: goggles and gloves, and wash splashes at once. Bunsen flame: tie back hair, keep flammable items away, or use an electric water bath. Scalpel: cut on a tile, away from the body, and keep the blade covered. Electric balance: keep it away from water and wipe spills at once.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sensible control measure (max 4).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the overall risk level before and after the controls, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium before the controls, because of the corrosive chemical and the flame; low after the controls, because each hazard is reduced to an acceptable level.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium before controls, low after. 1 mark: reason based on the controls reducing each hazard.

author: HomiLabs
